Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Saddanītippakaraṇaṃ (padamālā)

The Saddanīti Treatise (The Garland of Words)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Dhīrehi [M 0.0001] magganāyena, yena buddhena desitaṃ;

Sitaṃ dhammamidhaññāya, ñāyate amataṃ padaṃ.

By the wise, by the method of the path, which was taught by the Buddha; having understood the stainless Dhamma here, the deathless state is realized.

Taṃ namitvā mahāvīraṃ, sabbaññuṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Mahākāruṇikaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, visuddhaṃ suddhidāyakaṃ.

Having paid homage to that great hero, the Omniscient One, the Leader of the world, the greatly compassionate, the supreme, the pure, the giver of purity.

Saddhammañcassa pūjetvā, suddhaṃ santamasaṅkhataṃ;

Atakkāvacaraṃ suṭṭhu, vibhattaṃ madhuraṃ sivaṃ.

And having honored his True Dhamma, pure, peaceful, unconditioned; beyond the sphere of reasoning, well-expounded, sweet, and auspicious.

Saṅghassa ca’ñjaliṃ katvā, puññakkhettassa tādino;

Sīlasamādhipaññādi-visuddhaguṇajotino.

And having made añjali to the Sangha, the steadfast field of merit; shining with the pure virtues of morality, concentration, wisdom, and so forth.

Namassanādipuññassa, katassa ratanattaye;

Tejasāhaṃ pahantvāna, antarāye asesato.

Through the merit of homage and other deeds done towards the Triple Gem; by its power, may I completely dispel all obstacles without remainder.

Lokanītiviyattassa, satthu saddhammanītino;

Sāsanatthaṃ pavakkhāmi, saddanītimanākulaṃ.

For the sake of the Teaching, I shall explain the Saddanīti without confusion, following the Teacher, the guide of the True Dhamma, who is skilled in worldly conduct.

Āsavakkhayalābhena, hoti sāsanasampadā;

Āsavakkhayalābho ca, saccādhigamahetuko.

The prosperity of the Dispensation comes through the gain of the destruction of the taints; and the gain of the destruction of the taints has the realization of the truths as its cause.

Saccādhigamanaṃ [M 0.0002] tañca, paṭipattissitaṃ mataṃ;

Paṭipatti ca sā kāmaṃ, pariyattiparāyaṇā.

And that realization of the truths is considered to be dependent on practice; and that practice, indeed, has learning as its supreme goal.

Pariyattābhiyuttānaṃ, viditvā saddalakkhaṇaṃ;

Yasmā na hoti sammoho, akkharesu padesu ca.

For those devoted to learning, having understood the grammatical characteristics; because there is no confusion regarding letters and words.

Yasmā cāmohabhāvena, akkharesu padesu ca;

Pāḷiyatthaṃ vijānanti, viññū sugatasāsane.

And because, through freedom from confusion regarding letters and words, the discerning ones in the Dispensation of the Fortunate One understand the meaning of the Pāli.

Pāḷiyatthāvabodhena, yoniso satthusāsane;

Sappaññā paṭipajjanti, paṭipattimatandikā.

Through the understanding of the meaning of the Pāli, wisely in the Teacher's Dispensation, the wise practice diligently, unwearied in practice.

Yoniso paṭipajjitvā, dhammaṃ lokuttaraṃ varaṃ;

Pāpuṇanti visuddhāya, sīlādipaṭipattiyā.

Having practiced wisely, they attain the supreme, supramundane Dhamma through the pure practice of morality and so forth.

Tasmā tadatthikā suddhaṃ, nayaṃ nissāya viññunaṃ;

Bhaññamānaṃ mayā sadda-nītiṃ gaṇhantu sādhukaṃ.

Therefore, those desirous of that, relying on the pure method of the discerning ones, may they grasp well the Saddanīti being explained by me.

Dhātu dhātūhi nipphanna-rūpāni ca salakkhaṇo;

Sandhināmādibhedo ca, padānaṃ tu vibhatti ca.

Roots, and forms derived from roots along with their characteristics; and the distinctions of sandhi, nominals, and so forth; and the inflections of words.

Pāḷinayādayocceva-mettha nānappakārato;

Sāsanassopakārāya, bhavissati vibhāvanā.

And the methods of Pāli and so forth, in various ways, will be elucidated here for the benefit of the Dispensation.

1. Savikaraṇākhyātavibhāga

1. Division of Verbs with Vikaraṇa Affixes

Tattha dhātūti kenaṭṭhena dhātu? Sakatthampi dhāretīti dhātu, atthātisayayogato paratthampi dhāretīti dhātu, vīsatiyā upasaggesu yena kenaci upasaggena atthavisesakāraṇena paṭibaddhā atthavisesampi dhāretīti dhātu, “ayaṃ imissā attho, ayamito paccayo paro”tiādinā anekappakārena paṇḍitehi dhāriyati esātipi dhātu, vidahanti viduno etāya saddanipphattiṃ ayalohādimayaṃ [M 0.0003] ayalohādidhātūhi viyātipi dhātu. Evaṃ tāva dhātusaddassattho veditabbo.

Here, in what sense is a 'dhātu' (root/element)? A 'dhātu' is so called because it upholds its own meaning; because of its association with an abundance of meanings, it upholds the meanings of others; because, connected with any of the twenty prefixes, due to a specific cause of meaning, it also upholds a specific meaning; and because it is understood by the wise in many ways, such as 'this is its meaning, this is the condition from that,' it is also a 'dhātu'; and also because the discerning ones produce word-formations by means of it, just as iron and other metals are formed from iron and other elements, it is a 'dhātu.' Thus, the meaning of the word 'dhātu' should be understood in this way.

Dhātusaddo jinamate, itthiliṅgattane mato;

Satthe pulliṅgabhāvasmiṃ, kaccāyanamate dvisu.

The word 'dhātu' is considered to be of feminine gender according to the view of the Victor; in this treatise, it is of masculine gender; and according to the view of Kaccāyana, it is in both genders.

Atha vā jinamate “tato gotamidhātūnī”ti ettha dhātusaddo liṅgavipallāse vattati “pabbatāni vanāni cā”ti ettha pabbatasaddo viya, na panettha vattabbaṃ “aṭṭhivācakattā napuṃsakaniddeso”ti aṭṭhivācakattepi “dhātuyo”ti itthiliṅgadassanato. Bhūvādayo saddā dhātavo. Seyyathidaṃ? Bhū i ku ke takka taka taki sukaiccādayo. Gaṇato te aṭṭhavidhā bhūvādigaṇo rudhādigaṇo divādigaṇo svādigaṇo kiyādigaṇo gahādigaṇo tanādigaṇo curādigaṇo cāti. Idāni tesaṃ vikaraṇasaññite paccaye dassessāma. Anekavidhā hi paccayā nānappakāresu nāmanāma kitanāma samāsanāma taddhitanāmākhyātesu pavattanato. Saṅkhepato pana duvidhāva nāmapaccayo ākhyātapaccayo cāti. Tatrāpi ākhyātapaccayā duvidhā vikaraṇapaccayanovikaraṇapaccayavasena. Tattha vikaraṇapaccayo akārādisattarasavidho aggahitaggahaṇena pannarasavidho ca. Novikaraṇapaccayo pana kha cha sādinekavidho. Ye rūpanipphattiyā upakārakā atthavisesassa jotakā vā ajotakā vā lopanīyā vā alopanīyā vā, te saddā paccayā.

Alternatively, according to the view of the Victor, in the phrase 'tato gotamidhātūnī,' the word 'dhātu' functions with a gender alteration, similar to how the word 'pabbata' is used in the neuter plural 'pabbatāni vanāni ca.' One should not, however, argue from this that 'dhātu' is in the neuter gender because it denotes bones, for even when denoting bones, the feminine form 'dhātuyo' is seen. Words like 'bhū' are roots. For example: bhū, i, ku, ke, takka, taka, taki, suka, and so on. By groups, they are of eight kinds: the bhū-group, the rudh-group, the div-group, the svā-group, the kiyā-group, the gahā-group, the tanā-group, and the curā-group. Now we shall show the affixes designated as 'vikaraṇa' for these. Indeed, affixes are of many kinds because they operate in various ways in nominals, verbal nouns, compound nouns, derived nouns, and finite verbs. But in brief, there are only two kinds: nominal affixes and verbal affixes. Among these, verbal affixes are of two kinds: vikaraṇa affixes and novikaraṇa affixes. Of these, vikaraṇa affixes are of seventeen kinds, beginning with 'a', or fifteen kinds by including what is not already included. However, novikaraṇa affixes are of several kinds, such as 'kha,' 'cha,' and 'sā,' and so on. Those sounds that are helpful in the formation of forms, whether they indicate a specific meaning or not, whether they are elided or not elided, are called affixes.

Paṭicca kāraṇaṃ taṃ taṃ, entīti paccayātha vā;

Paṭicca saddanipphatti, ito etīti paccayā.

Dependent on this and that cause, they come; hence they are affixes. Or alternatively, dependent on the formation of words, from this they come; hence they are affixes.

Nāmikappaccayānaṃ [M 0.0004] yo, vibhāgo āvi hessati;

Nāmakappe yato tasmā, na taṃ vitthārayāmase.

Whatever distinction of nominal affixes will become clear; therefore, since it is in the section on nominals, we do not elaborate on it.

Yo novikaraṇānaṃ tu, paccayānaṃ vibhāgato;

So panākhyātakappamhi, vitthārenā’gamissatīti.

As for the classification of the novikaraṇa affixes, that will come in detail in the section on finite verbs.

Iccānekavidhesu paccayesu “vikaraṇapaccayā nāma ime”ti sallakkhetabbā. Kathaṃ? Bhūvādigaṇato apaccayo hoti kattari, rudhādigaṇato akārivaṇṇekārokārapaccayā honti kattari, pubbamajjhaṭṭhāne niggahītāgamo ca, divādigaṇato yapaccayo hoti kattari, svādigaṇato ṇu ṇā uṇāpaccayā honti kattari, kiyādigaṇato nāpaccayo hoti kattari, gahādigaṇato ppa ṇhāpaccayā honti kattari, tanādigaṇato o yirapaccayā honti kattari, curādigaṇato ṇe ṇayapaccayā honti kattari.

Thus, among the various kinds of affixes, these should be noted as 'vikaraṇa affixes.' How? From the bhū-group, the 'a' affix occurs in the agentive sense; from the rudh-group, the 'a', 'i', 'e', and 'o' affixes occur in the agentive sense, and also the insertion of a nasal augment in the initial or middle position; from the div-group, the 'ya' affix occurs in the agentive sense; from the svā-group, the 'ṇu', 'ṇā', and 'uṇā' affixes occur in the agentive sense; from the kiyā-group, the 'nā' affix occurs in the agentive sense; from the gahā-group, the 'ppa' and 'ṇhā' affixes occur in the agentive sense; from the tanā-group, the 'o' and 'yira' affixes occur in the agentive sense; from the curā-group, the 'ṇe' and 'ṇaya' affixes occur in the agentive sense.

Akāro ca ivaṇṇo ca, e okārā ca yo tathā;

Ṇu ṇā uṇā ca nā ppa ṇhā-yirā ṇe ṇayapaccayā.

The affix 'a', and the affix 'i', and likewise 'e' and 'o', and 'ya'; the affixes 'ṇu', 'ṇā', 'uṇā', and 'nā'; also the affixes 'ppa', 'ṇhā', 'yira', 'ṇe', and 'ṇaya'.

Aggahitaggahaṇena, evaṃ pannarase’ritā;

Vikaraṇavhayā ete, paccayāti vibhāvaye.

By including what was not included, thus fifteen are enumerated. One should understand these to be the affixes called vikaraṇa.

Ye evaṃ niddiṭṭhehi vikaraṇapaccayehi tadaññehi ca sappaccayā aṭṭhavidhā dhātugaṇā suttantesu bahūpakārā, tesvāyaṃ bhūvādigaṇo. Bhū sattāyaṃ, bhūdhātu vijjamānatāyaṃ vattati. Sakammikākammikāsu dhātūsu ayaṃ akammikā dhātu, na pana “dhammabhūto”tiādīsu pattiatthavācikā aparā bhūdhātu viya sakammikā. Esā hi pariabhiādīhi upasaggehi yuttāyeva sakammikā bhavati, na upa parā pātuādīhi upasagganipātehi yuttāpi. Ato imissā siddhāni rūpāni dvidhā ñeyyāni akammakapadāni sakammakapadāni cāti.

Among the eight kinds of root groups, which are very useful in the suttas, along with these thus-indicated vikaraṇa affixes and other affixes, this is the bhū-group. The root 'bhū' is in the sense of 'being'; the root 'bhū' functions in the sense of existence. Among transitive and intransitive roots, this is an intransitive root. However, it is not transitive like the other root 'bhū' which denotes the sense of 'attainment' in expressions such as 'dhammabhūto.' Indeed, this one becomes transitive only when combined with prefixes such as 'pari' and 'abhi', but not even when combined with prefixes and particles such as 'upa', 'parā', and 'pātu'. Therefore, its established forms should be understood in two ways: as intransitive words and as transitive words.

Suddhakattukriyāpadaniddesa

Exposition of Purely Active Verbs

Tatra [M 0.0005] bhavati ubbhavati samubbhavati pabhavati parābhavati sambhavati vibhavati, bhoti sambhoti vibhoti pātubhavati pātubbhavati pātubhoti, imāni akammakapadāni. Ettha pātuiti nipāto, so “āvibhavati tirobhavatī”tiādīsu āvi tironipātā viya bhūdhātuto nipphannākhyātasaddassa neva visesakaro, na ca sakammakattasādhako. Uiccādayo upasaggā, te pana visesakarā, na sakammakattasādhakā. Yesamattho kammena sambandhanīyo na hoti, tāni padāni akammakāni. Akammakapadānaṃ yathārahaṃ sakammakākammakavasena attho kathetabbo. Paribhoti paribhavati, abhibhoti abhibhavati, adhibhoti adhibhavati, atibhoti atibhavati, anubhoti anubhavati, samanubhoti samanubhavati, abhisambhoti abhisambhavati, imāni sakammakapadāni. Ettha pariiccādayo upasaggā, te bhūdhātuto nipphannākhyātasaddassa visesakarā ceva sakammakattasādhakā ca. Yesamattho kammena sambandhanīyo, tāni padāni sakammakāni. Sakammakapadānaṃ sakammakavasena attho kathetabbo, kvaci akammakavasenapi. Evaṃ suddhakattukriyāpadāni bhavanti. Uddesoyaṃ.

Herein, 'bhavati', 'ubbhavati', 'samubbhavati', 'pabhavati', 'parābhavati', 'sambhavati', 'vibhavati', 'bhoti', 'sambhoti', 'vibhoti', 'pātubhavati', 'pātubbhavati', 'pātubhoti'—these are intransitive verbs. Here, 'pātu' is a particle; it is neither a modifier of, nor an establisher of intransitivity for, the verb derived from the root 'bhū', just like the particles 'āvi' and 'tiro' in 'āvibhavati', 'tirobhavati', and so forth. Prefixes like 'u' are modifiers, but they do not establish intransitivity. Words whose meaning is not connected with an object are intransitive. The meaning of intransitive words should be explained as appropriate, in terms of transitivity or intransitivity. 'Paribhoti', 'paribhavati', 'abhibhoti', 'abhibhavati', 'adhibhoti', 'adhibhavati', 'atibhoti', 'atibhavati', 'anubhoti', 'anubhavati', 'samanubhoti', 'samanubhavati', 'abhisambhoti', 'abhisambhavati'—these are transitive verbs. Here, prefixes like 'pari' are modifiers of the verb derived from the root 'bhū' and also establish transitivity. Words whose meaning is connected with an object are transitive. The meaning of transitive words should be explained in terms of transitivity, though sometimes also in terms of intransitivity. Thus are pure active verbs. This is the summary.

Tatra bhavatīti hoti vijjati paññāyati sarūpaṃ labhati. Ubbhavatīti uppajjati sarūpaṃ labhati. Samubbhavatīti samuppajjati sarūpaṃ labhati. Pabhavatīti hoti sambhavati. Atha vā pabhavatīti yato kutoci sandati, na vicchijjati, avicchinnaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ visarati. Parābhavatīti parābhavo hoti byasanaṃ āpajjati avuddhiṃ pāpuṇāti. Sambhavatīti suṭṭhu bhavati vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjati. Vibhavatīti ucchijjati vinassati vipajjati, visesato vā bhavati sampajjati. Bhoti sambhoti vibhotīti imāni “bhavati [M 0.0006] sambhavati vibhavatī”ti imehi yathākkamaṃ samānaniddesāni. Pātubhavatīti pakāsati dissati paññāyati pākaṭaṃ hoti. Pātubbhavati pātubhotīti imāni “pātubhavatī”ti iminā samānaniddesāni. Evaṃ akammakapadānaṃ yathārahaṃ sakammakākammakavasena atthakathanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evamuttaratrāpi aññesampi akammakapadānaṃ.

Therein, 'bhavati' means it is, it exists, it is known, it obtains its own form. 'Ubbhavati' means it arises, it obtains its own form. 'Samubbhavati' means it arises together, it obtains its own form. 'Pabhavati' means it is, it comes into being. Or else, 'pabhavati' means it flows from somewhere, it is not cut off, it remains uninterrupted, it spreads to that place. 'Parābhavati' means it declines, it meets with ruin, it reaches non-growth. 'Sambhavati' means it thrives, it attains growth, increase, and abundance. 'Vibhavati' means it perishes, it is destroyed, it comes to ruin, or it especially becomes, it succeeds. 'Bhoti', 'sambhoti', 'vibhoti'—these are synonymous definitions with 'bhavati', 'sambhavati', 'vibhavati', respectively. 'Pātubhavati' means it manifests, it appears, it is known, it becomes evident. 'Pātubbhavati', 'pātubhoti'—these are synonymous definitions with 'pātubhavati'. Thus, the explanation of intransitive words should be seen as appropriate, in terms of transitivity or intransitivity. Similarly, this also applies to other intransitive words hereafter.

Paribhotidukādīsu pana sattasu dukesu yathākkamaṃ dve dve padāni samānatthāni, tasmā dve dve padāniyeva gahetvā niddisissāma. Tatra paribhoti paribhavatīti paraṃ hiṃsati pīḷeti, atha vā hīḷeti avajānāti. Abhibhoti abhibhavatīti paraṃ ajjhottharati maddati. Adhibhoti adhibhavatīti paraṃ abhimadditvā bhavati attano vasaṃ vattāpeti. Atibhoti atibhavatīti paraṃ atikkamitvā bhavati. Anubhoti anubhavatīti sukhadukkhaṃ vedeti paribhuñjati sukhadukkhapaṭisaṃvedī hoti. Samanubhoti samanubhavatīti sukhadukkhaṃ suṭṭhu vedeti suṭṭhu paribhuñjati suṭṭhu sukhadukkhapaṭisaṃvedī hoti. Abhisambhoti abhisambhavatīti paraṃ ajjhottharati maddati. Evaṃ sakammakapadānaṃ sakammakavasena atthakathanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Katthaci pana gacchatīti pavattatīti evaṃ akammakavasenapi. Evamuttaratrāpi aññesaṃ sakammakapadānaṃ.

In the seven pairs beginning with 'paribhoti', two words in each pair have the same meaning; therefore, we will explain them by taking two words at a time. Here, 'paribhoti' and 'paribhavati' mean to harm or oppress another, or else to despise or look down upon. 'Abhibhoti' and 'abhibhavati' mean to overwhelm or crush another. 'Adhibhoti' and 'adhibhavati' mean to overpower another and bring them under one's control. 'Atibhoti' and 'atibhavati' mean to surpass another. 'Anubhoti' and 'anubhavati' mean to experience pleasure and pain, to partake of it, and to be one who feels pleasure and pain. 'Samanubhoti' and 'samanubhavati' mean to thoroughly experience pleasure and pain, to thoroughly partake of it, and to be one who thoroughly feels pleasure and pain. 'Abhisambhoti' and 'abhisambhavati' mean to overwhelm or crush another. Thus, the explanation of transitive words should be seen in terms of transitivity. However, sometimes, as with 'gacchati' meaning 'proceeds', it should be seen in terms of intransitivity as well. Similarly, this applies to other transitive words hereafter.

Apaccayo paro hoti, bhūvādigaṇato sati;

Suddhakattukriyākhyāne, sabbadhātukanissite.

The suffix 'a' is placed after a root from the bhū-group, in the case of pure active verbs which are formed with the sabbadhātuka endings.

Ayaṃ suddhakattukriyāpadānaṃ niddeso.

This is the exposition of pure active verbs.

Hetukattukriyāpadaniddesa

Exposition of Causative Active Verbs

Bhāveti vibhāvetisambhāveti paribhāveti, evaṃ hetukattukriyāpadāni bhavanti. Ekakammakavasenesamattho gahetabbo[M 0.0007]. Pacchimassa pana dvikammakavasenapi. Paribhāvāpeti abhibhāvāpeti anubhāvāpeti, evampi hetukattukriyāpadāni bhavanti. Dvikammakavasenesamattho gahetabbo. Iccevaṃ dvidhā hetukattukriyāpadāni ñeyyāni, aññānipi gahetabbāni.

'Bhāveti', 'vibhāveti', 'sambhāveti', 'paribhāveti'—thus are causative active verbs. Their meaning should be understood in terms of a single object. But for the last one, it can also be in terms of two objects. 'Paribhāvāpeti', 'abhibhāvāpeti', 'anubhāvāpeti'—thus also are causative active verbs. Their meaning should be understood in terms of two objects. Thus, causative active verbs are to be known in two ways, and others should also be included.

Tatra bhāvetīti puggalo bhāvetabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci bhāveti āsevati bahulīkaroti, atha vā bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti. Vibhāvetīti bhāvetabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci vibhāveti visesena bhāveti, vividhena vā ākārena bhāveti bhāvayati vaḍḍheti, atha vā vibhāvetīti abhāveti antaradhāpeti. Sambhāvetīti yassa kassaci guṇaṃ sambhāveti sambhāvayati suṭṭhu pakāseti ukkaṃseti. Paribhāvetīti paribhāvetabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci paribhāveti paribhāvayati samantato vaḍḍheti. Evaṃ ekakammakavasenattho gahetabbo. Atha vā paribhāvetīti vāsetabbaṃ vatthuṃ paribhāveti paribhāvayati vāseti gandhaṃ gāhāpeti. Evaṃ dvikammakavasenāpi attho gahetabbo. Paribhāvāpetīti puggalo puggalena sapattaṃ paribhāvāpeti hiṃsāpeti, atha vā paribhāvāpetīti hīḷāpeti avajānāpeti. Abhibhāvāpetīti puggalo puggalena sapattaṃ abhibhāvāpeti ajjhottharāpeti. Anubhāvāpetīti puggalo puggalena sampattiṃ anubhāvāpeti paribhojeti.

Therein, 'bhāveti' means a person cultivates whatever should be cultivated, practices it repeatedly, or increases it; or, 'bhāveti' means develops. 'Vibhāveti' means one cultivates whatever should be cultivated in a special way, develops it through various methods, develops, cultivates or increases it. Alternatively, 'vibhāveti' means one does not cultivate it or lets it disappear. 'Sambhāveti' means one praises someone’s virtues, extols them, makes them shine, or elevates them. 'Paribhāveti' means one fully develops whatever should be developed, expands it thoroughly. Thus, the meaning should be understood in terms of a single object. Alternatively, 'paribhāveti' means one perfumes an object to be perfumed, makes it fragrant, or impregnates it with scent. Thus, the meaning should also be understood in terms of a double object. 'Paribhāvāpeti' means one makes another person harm an enemy; or, 'paribhāvāpeti' means causes them to despise or look down upon someone. 'Abhibhāvāpeti' means one makes another person overwhelm an enemy, or subdue them. 'Anubhāvāpeti' means one makes another person experience prosperity or partake in it.

Payutto kattunā yoge, ṭhitoyevāppadhāniye;

Kriyaṃ sādheti etassa, dīpakaṃ sāsane padaṃ.

Employed by the agent, standing indeed in a subordinate position, it accomplishes the action; this word in the Dispensation is an illuminator of this.

Karaṇavacanaṃyeva, yebhuyyena padissati;

Ākhyāte kāritaṭṭhānaṃ, sandhāya kathitaṃ idaṃ.

The instrumental expression is mostly seen; this is said with reference to the causative position in the verb.

Na [M 0.0008] nāme kāritaṭṭhānaṃ, “bodhetā” itiādikaṃ;

“Sunakhehipi khādāpenti”, iccādīni padāni ca;

Āharitvāna dīpeyya, payogakusalo budho.

The causative position is not in nouns, such as 'bodhetā', and so forth. And words like 'They make even dogs eat', etc.—having brought them, the wise one skilled in usage should clarify.

Tatridaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ kammatthadīpakaṃ, upayogasāmivacanānipi taddīpakāni yojetabbāni. Kathaṃ? Paribhāvāpetīti puggalo puggalaṃ sapattaṃ paribhāvāpetīti, tathā paribhāvāpetīti puggalo puggalassa sapattaṃ paribhāvāpetīti. Sesāni nayānusārena niddisitabbāni. Evaṃ sabbānetāni karaṇopayogasāmivacanāni kammatthadīpakāniyeva honti, tasmā dvikammakavasenattho gahetabbo.

Here, this instrumental expression clarifies the object, and expressions of usage and possession should also be applied to clarify it. How? 'Paribhāvāpeti' means a person causes another person to despise an enemy. Similarly, 'paribhāvāpeti' means a person causes someone to despise another's enemy. The remaining cases should be explained following the same method. Thus, all these instrumental, applicative, and possessive terms serve to clarify the object. Therefore, the meaning should be understood in terms of a double object.

Ayaṃ hetukattukriyāpadānaṃ niddeso.

This is the exposition of causative active verbs.

Kammakriyāpadaniddesa

Exposition of Passive Verbs

Bhaviyate vibhaviyate paribhaviyate abhibhaviyate anubhaviyate paribhūyate abhibhūyate anubhūyate, evaṃ kammuno kriyāpadāni bhavanti. Aññathā ca bhaviyyate vibhaviyyate paribhaviyyate abhibhaviyyate anubhaviyyate paribhuyyate abhibhuyyate anubhuyyateti. Ettha kammuno kriyāpadāniyeva kammakattuno kriyāpadāni katvā yojetabbāni. Visuñhi kammakattuno kriyāpadāni na labbhanti.

It is produced, it is dissolved, it is despised, it is overcome, it is experienced, it is overwhelmed, it is subdued, it is undergone—thus are the verbal forms of the object. And otherwise, it would be produced, it would be dissolved, it would be despised, it would be overcome, it would be experienced, it would be overwhelmed, it would be subdued, it would be undergone. Here, the verbal forms of the object themselves should be construed as the verbal forms of the agent-object. For verbal forms of the agent-object are not found separately.

Tatra bhaviyateti bhāvetabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci puggalena bhāviyate āseviyate bahulīkariyate, atha vā bhaviyateti vaḍḍhiyate. Vibhaviyateti vibhāvetabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci puggalena vibhaviyate visesena bhaviyate, vividhena [M 0.0009] vā ākārena bhaviyate vaḍḍhiyate, atha vā vibhaviyateti abhaviyate antaradhāpiyate. Paribhaviyateti sapatto puggalena paribhaviyate hiṃsiyate, atha vā paribhaviyateti hīḷiyate avajāniyate. Abhibhaviyateti sapatto puggalena abhibhaviyate ajjhotthariyate abhimaddiyate. Anubhaviyateti sampatti puggalena anubhaviyate paribhuñjiyate. Paribhūyatetiādīni tīṇi “paribhaviyate”tiādīhi tīhi samānaniddesāni. Sesāni pana yathāvuttehi yaṃ kammameva padhānato gahetvā niddisiyati padaṃ, taṃ kammatthadīpakaṃ. Tasmā kattari ekavacanena niddiṭṭhepi yadi kammaṃ bahuvacanavasena vattabbaṃ, bahuvacanantaññeva kammuno kriyāpadaṃ dissati. Yadi panekavacanavasena vattabbaṃ, ekavacanantaññeva. Tathā kattari bahuvacanena niddiṭṭhepi yadi kammaṃ ekavacanavasena vattabbaṃ, ekavacanantaññeva kammuno kriyāpadaṃ dissati. Yadi pana bahuvacanavasena vattabbaṃ, bahuvacanantaññeva. Kathaṃ? Bhikkhunā dhammo bhaviyate, bhikkhunā dhammā bhaviyante, bhikkhūhi dhammo bhaviyate, bhikkhūhi dhammā bhaviyanteti. Iminā nayena sabbattha kammuno kriyāpadesu vohāro kātabbo. Yasmiṃ pana kammuno kriyāpade kammatthadīpake kammabhūtassevatthassa kattubhāvaparikappo hoti, taṃ kammakattutthadīpakaṃ, taṃ kammuno kriyāpadato visuṃ na labbhati. Ayaṃ panettha atthaviññāpane payogaracanā. Sayameva paribhaviyate dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇaṃ bālo tappaccayā aññehi paribhūtopi, sayameva abhibhaviyate pāpakārī niraye nirayapālehi abhibhūtopi tathārūpassa kammassa sayaṃ katattāti. Ettha hi sayameva pīyate pānīyaṃ, sayameva kaṭo kariyatetiādīsu viya [M 0.0010] sukhābhisaṅkharaṇīyatā labbhateva, tato kammakattutā ca.

Therein, 'bhaviyate' means that which should be cultivated—whatever a person cultivates, frequents, or makes much of; or, 'bhaviyate' means it increases. 'Vibhaviyate' means that which should be differentiated—whatever a person differentiates, cultivates in a special way, or cultivates in various ways; or, 'vibhaviyate' means it is not brought into being and disappears. 'Paribhaviyate' means an enemy is treated with contempt by a person—is harmed; or, 'paribhaviyate' means is despised or disrespected. 'Abhibhaviyate' means an enemy is overcome by a person—is overwhelmed or crushed. 'Anubhaviyate' means prosperity is experienced by a person—is enjoyed. The three beginning with 'paribhūyate' have the same explanation as the three beginning with 'paribhaviyate'. Furthermore, a word that is indicated by taking the object itself as primary is an indicator of the object's meaning. Therefore, even when the agent is indicated in the singular, if the object is to be expressed in the plural, the verbal form of the object appears in the plural. If, however, it is to be expressed in the singular, it appears in the singular. Likewise, even when the agent is indicated in the plural, if the object is to be expressed in the singular, the verbal form of the object appears in the singular. If, however, it is to be expressed in the plural, it appears in the plural. How so? 'The Dhamma is cultivated by a monk,' 'the Dhammas are cultivated by a monk,' 'the Dhamma is cultivated by monks,' 'the Dhammas are cultivated by monks.' In this manner, usage should be applied to the verbal forms of the object in all cases. However, when, in a verbal form of the object that indicates the object's meaning, there is a conceptualization of the agent-state for the very thing that is the object, that is an 'indicator of the agent-object meaning,' and it is not found separately from the verbal form of the object. Herein, this is the construction of usage for making the meaning known. A fool, speaking harsh speech, is reviled by his very self, even while being despised by others on account of it; an evildoer is overcome by his very self, even while being overcome in hell by the hell-wardens, because such an action was done by himself. For here, just as in examples such as 'water is drunk by itself,' 'a mat is made by itself,' the state of being easily accomplished is certainly obtained, and from that, the agent-object state as well.

Ayaṃ kammuno kriyāpadānaṃ niddeso.

This is the explanation of the verbal forms of the object.

Bhāvakriyāpadaniddesa

Explanation of Impersonal Verbal Forms

Bhūyate bhaviyate ubbhaviyate, evaṃ bhāvassa kriyāpadāni bhavanti. Aññathā ca bhuyyate bhaviyyate ubbhaviyyateti. Tatra yathā ṭhīyatepadassa ṭhānanti bhāvavasena atthakathanamicchanti, evaṃ bhūyatetiādīnampi bhavanantiādinā bhāvavasena atthakathanamicchitabbaṃ. Yathā ca ṭhānaṃ ṭhiti bhavanantiādīhi bhāvavācakakitantanāmapadehi saddhiṃ sambandhe chaṭṭhiyojanamicchanti, na tathā ṭhīyate bhūyatetiādīhi bhāvavācakākhyātapadehi saddhiṃ sambandhe chaṭṭhiyojanā icchitabbā sambandhe pavattachaṭṭhiyantasaddehi asambandhanīyattā ākhyātikapadānaṃ. Yasmiṃ payoge yaṃ kammuno kriyāpadena samānagatikaṃ katvā vinā kammena niddisiyati kriyāpadaṃ, kattuvācakapadaṃ pana paccattavacanena vā karaṇavacanena vā niddisiyati, taṃ tattha bhāvatthadīpakaṃ. Na hi sabbathā kattāramanissāya bhāvo pavattati. Evaṃ santepi bhāvo nāma kevalo bhavanalavanapacanādiko dhātuatthoyeva. Akkharacintakā pana “ṭhīyate bhūyate”tiādīsu bhāvavisayesu karaṇavacanameva payuñjanti “nanu nāma pabbajitena sunivatthena bhavitabbaṃ supārutena ākappasampannenā”tiādīsu viya, tasmā tesaṃ mate “tena ubbhaviyate”ti karaṇavacanena yojetabbaṃ. Jinamatena pana “so bhūyate”tiādinā paccattavacaneneva. Saccasaṅkhepappakaraṇe hi dhammapālācariyena, niddesapāḷiyaṃ pana dhammasenāpatinā, dhajaggasuttante bhagavatā ca bhāvapadaṃ paccattavacanāpekkhavasenu’ccāritaṃ.

There is being, there is becoming, there is arising—thus are the verbal forms of state. And otherwise, there would be being, there would be becoming, there would be arising. Therein, just as they desire to explain the word 'ṭhīyate' as 'ṭhāna' in the sense of state, so too with 'bhūyate' and so forth, the meaning should be desired to be explained in the sense of state, such as 'bhavana' (being). And just as they desire the use of the genitive case in connection with primary nominal derivatives denoting state, such as 'ṭhāna,' 'ṭhiti,' 'bhavana,' etc., the use of the genitive case should not be desired in connection with finite verbs denoting state, such as 'ṭhīyate,' 'bhūyate,' etc., because finite verbal forms cannot be connected with words ending in the genitive case that express relation. In any usage where a verbal form is indicated without an object, having been made similar in form to a verbal form of the object, while the word indicating the agent is indicated either by the nominative or instrumental case, there it signifies the meaning of state. For the state does not in every case proceed without depending on an agent. Even so, the state is merely the meaning of the root, such as being, cutting, cooking, and so on. Grammarians, however, in contexts pertaining to state, such as in 'ṭhīyate,' 'bhūyate,' etc., employ only the instrumental case—just as in phrases like 'Surely, a renunciant should be well-clothed, well-covered, and composed in demeanor.' Therefore, according to their view, 'tena ubbhaviyate' should be construed with the instrumental case. But according to the view of the Victor, it is with the nominative case, as in 'so bhūyate.' For in the treatise Saccasaṅkhepa by the teacher Dhammapāla, in the Niddesa Pāḷi by the General of the Dhamma, and in the Dhajagga Sutta by the Blessed One, the verbal form of state has been uttered with reference to the nominative case.

Kathito [M 0.0011] saccasaṅkhepe, paccattavacanena ve,

“Bhūyate” iti saddassa, sambandho bhāvadīpano.

In the Saccasaṅkhepa it is stated that the connection of the word 'bhūyate' with the nominative case indeed illuminates the state.

Niddesapāḷiyaṃ “rūpaṃ, vibhoti vibhaviyyati”;

Iti dassanato vāpi, paccattavacanaṃ thiraṃ.

In the Niddesa Pāḷi: 'Form perishes, it is disintegrated.' From this passage also, the nominative case is established.

Tathā dhajaggasuttante, munināhaccabhāsite;

“So pahīyissati” iti, pāḷidassanatopi ca.

Likewise, in the Dhajagga Sutta, spoken emphatically by the Sage, from seeing the Pāḷi text, 'It will be abandoned,' as well.

Pāramitānubhāvena, mahesīnaṃva dehato;

Santi nipphādanā, neva, sakkatādivaco viya.

By the power of the perfections, as from the bodies of the great seers, there are accomplishments; not, indeed, like words such as 'honored' and so forth.

Paccattadassaneneva, purisattayayojanaṃ;

Ekavacanikañcāpi, bahuvacanikampi ca;

Kātabbamiti no khanti, parassapadaādike.

That, merely by seeing the nominative case, the application of the three persons, both singular and plural, should be made in the active voice and so forth—this we do not approve.

Tasmā rūpaṃ vibhaviyyati, rūpāni vibhaviyyanti, tvaṃ vibhaviyyasi, tumhe vibhaviyyatha, ahaṃ vibhaviyyāmi, mayaṃ vibhaviyyāma, rūpaṃ vibhaviyyate, rūpāni vibhaviyyante iccevamādi jinavacanānurūpato yojetabbaṃ. Atrāyaṃ padasodhanā –

Therefore, 'rūpaṃ vibhaviyyati' (form is disintegrated), 'rūpāni vibhaviyyanti' (forms are disintegrated), 'tvaṃ vibhaviyyasi' (you are disintegrated), 'tumhe vibhaviyyatha' (you all are disintegrated), 'ahaṃ vibhaviyyāmi' (I am disintegrated), 'mayaṃ vibhaviyyāma' (we are disintegrated), 'rūpaṃ vibhaviyyate' (form is disintegrated), 'rūpāni vibhaviyyante' (forms are disintegrated)—thus it should be construed in accordance with the Victor's word. Herein is the analysis of the word:

Vibhaviyyatīti idaṃ, kammapadasamānakaṃ;

Na ca kammapadaṃ nāpi, kammakattupadādikaṃ.

'Vibhaviyyati'—this is similar to a verbal form of the object; yet it is neither a verbal form of the object nor a verbal form of the agent-object and so forth.

Yadi kammapadaṃ etaṃ, paccattavacanaṃ pana;

Kammaṃ dīpeyya karaṇa-vacanaṃ kattudīpakaṃ.

If this were a verbal form of the object, then the nominative case would indicate the object, and the instrumental case would indicate the agent.

Yadi kammakattupadaṃ, “pīyate”ti padaṃ viya;

Siyā sakammakaṃ, netaṃ, tathā hotīti dīpaye.

If it were a verbal form of the agent-object, like the word 'pīyate,' it would be transitive; that this is not so, it shows.

Yadi kattupadaṃ etaṃ, vibhavatipadaṃ viya;

Vinā yapaccayaṃ tiṭṭhe, na tathā tiṭṭhate idaṃ.

If this were a verbal form of the agent, like the word 'vibhavati,' it would stand without the 'ya' suffix; but this does not stand so.

Na kattari bhuvādīnaṃ, gaṇe yapaccayo ruto;

Divādīnaṃ gaṇeyeva, kattari samudīrito.

The 'ya' suffix is not taught for the agent-voice in the bhū-group of roots; it is declared for the agent-voice only in the div-group.

Na [M 0.0012] bhūdhātu divādīnaṃ, dhātūnaṃ dissate gaṇe;

Bhūvādikacurādīnaṃ, gaṇesuyeva dissati.

The root 'bhū' is not seen in the div-group of roots; it is seen only in the bhū-group and the cur-group.

“Vibhaviyyati” iccādo, tasmā yapaccayo pana;

Bhāveyevāti viññeyyaṃ, viññunā samayaññunā.

Therefore, in 'vibhaviyyati' and the like, the 'ya' suffix should be understood by the wise one who knows the system as being only in the sense of state.

Ettha hi pākaṭaṃ katvā, bhāvakārakalakkhaṇaṃ;

Dassayissāmahaṃ dāni, sakkaccaṃ me nibodhatha.

For here, having made manifest the characteristic of the state and the case-relations, I will now explain; listen to me with care.

“Tisso gacchati”iccatra, kattāraṃ kattuno padaṃ;

“Dhammo desiyati”ccatra, kammaṃ tu kammuno padaṃ.

In 'Tisso gacchati' (Tissa goes), the word of the agent indicates the agent; in 'Dhammo desiyati' (The Dhamma is taught), the word of the object indicates the object.

Sarūpato pakāseti, tasmā te pākaṭā ubho;

Tathā vibhaviyyatīti-ādibhāvapadaṃ pana.

They reveal their own form, therefore both are evident. So too, the word of state, beginning with 'vibhaviyyati,' however,

Sarūpato na dīpeti, kārakaṃ bhāvanāmakaṃ;

Dabbabhūtaṃ tu kattāraṃ, pakāseti sarūpato.

It does not indicate the factor named 'state' as to its own form; but it reveals the agent, which is a substantial entity, as to its own form.

Kattāraṃ pana dīpentaṃ, kattusannissitampi taṃ;

Bhāvaṃ dīpeti svākāro, paccayena vibhāvito.

Though it indicates the agent, and is dependent on the agent, its own form, made distinct by the suffix, indicates the state.

Yasmā ca kattubhāvena, bhāvo nāma na tiṭṭhati;

Kattāva kattubhāvena, bhāvaṭṭhāne ṭhito tato.

And since the state does not exist with the nature of an agent, therefore the agent itself, with the nature of an agent, stands in the place of the state.

Yajjevaṃ kattuvohāro, bhāvassa tu kathaṃ siyā;

“Sāvakānaṃ sannipāto, ahosi”itiādisu.

If this is so, and there is usage of the agent, how then can there be usage of the state? As in 'Sāvakānaṃ sannipāto ahosi' (There was a gathering of disciples) and similar cases.

Iti ce nissayānaṃ tu, vasā nissitasambhavā;

Kattuṭṭhānepi bhāvassa, kattupaññatti sijjhati.

If it is said thus: 'But due to the power of the supports, there is the arising of the supported,' then even in the place of the agent, the designation of the state as agent is accomplished.

Kārake kattukammavhe, kriyāsannissaye yathā;

Dhārentī āsanathālī, kriyādhāroti kappitā.

Just as in the case of the factors called agent and object, which are dependent on the action, a plate holding a seat is designated as the locus of action.

Tathā bhāvapadaṃ dhīrā, kattāraṃ bhāvanissayaṃ;

Dīpayantampi kappenti, bhāvassa vācakaṃ iti.

So too, the wise designate the word of state as indicating the state, even though it indicates the agent as dependent on the state.

Keci [M 0.0013] adabbabhūtassa, bhāvassekattato bravuṃ;

Bhāvedekavacovādi-purisasseva hotiti.

Some say that because the state is non-substantial, it is singular; and that in the case of the state, there is only the singular number and first person.

Pāḷiṃ patvāna tesaṃ tu, vacanaṃ appamāṇakaṃ;

“Te saṃkilesikā dhammā, pahīyissanti” iti hi.

But their words, upon reaching the Pāḷi, are unauthoritative; for it is said: 'Te saṃkilesikā dhammā pahīyissanti' (Those defiling states will be abandoned).

Pāṭho pāvacane diṭṭho, tasmā evaṃ vademase;

Paccattadassaneneva, purisattayayojanaṃ.

The reading is seen in the teaching, therefore we speak thus: By seeing the nominative case alone, there is the connection with the three persons.

Vacanehi yutaṃ dvīhi, icchitabbanti no ruci;

Bhāve kriyāpadaṃ nāma, pāḷiyaṃ atiduddasaṃ;

Tasmā taggahaṇūpāyo, vutto ettāvatā mayāti.

That it should be connected with the two numbers merely by wishing is not our view. The word for action in the state is indeed exceedingly difficult to see in the Pāḷi; therefore, the method for grasping it has been explained thus far by me.

Ayaṃ bhāvassa kriyāpadānaṃ niddeso.

This is the exposition of the verbs of state.

Evaṃ suddhakattukriyāpadāni hetukattukriyāpadāni kammuno kriyāpadāni, bhāvassa kriyāpadāni cāti catudhā, kammakattukriyāpadehi vā pañcadhā bhūdhātuto nipphannāni kriyāpadāni nānappakārena niddiṭṭhāni, etāni lokiyānaṃ bhāvabhedavasena vohārabhedo hotīti dassanatthaṃ visuṃ visuṃ vuttāni. Atthato pana kammakattubhāvakārakattayavasena tividhāneva. Hetukattā hi suddhakattusaṅkhāte kārake tassaṅgabhāvato saṅgahamupagacchati, tathā kammakattā kammakārake, bhāvo pana kevalo. So hi gamanapacanalavanādivasenānekavidhopi kriyāsabhāvattā bhedarahito kārakantaro. Evaṃ santepi dabbasannissitattā dabbabhedena bhijjati. Tena pāvacane bhāvavācakaṃ padaṃ bahuvacanantampi dissati. Ākhyātikapade bhāvakārakavohāro niruttinayaṃ nissāya gato, atthato pana bhāvassa kārakatā nupapajjati. So hi na [M 0.0014] kiñci janeti, na ca kriyāya nimittaṃ. Kriyānimittabhāvoyeva hi kārakalakkhaṇaṃ. Iti mukhyato vā hetuto vā bhāvassa kārakatā na labbhati. Evaṃ santepi so karaṇamattattā kārakaṃ. Tathā hi karaṇaṃ kāro, kriyā, tadeva kārakanti bhāvassa kārakatā daṭṭhabbā. Yasmā pana kriyānimittabhāvoyeva kārakalakkhaṇaṃ, tasmā nāmikapade kārakalakkhaṇe bhāvakārakanti vohāraṃ pahāya kattukammakaraṇasampadānāpādānādhikaraṇānaṃ channaṃ vatthūnaṃ kattukārakakammakārakantiādi vohāro kariyati veyyākaraṇehi. Evaṃ niruttinayaṃ nissāya vuttaṃ bhāvakārakañca dve ca kammakattukārakānīti kārakattayaṃ bhavati. Taddīpakañcākhyātikapadaṃ tikārakaṃ.

Thus, verbs, derived from the root bhū, are explained in various ways as fourfold: verbs of the pure agent, verbs of the causative agent, verbs of the object, and verbs of the state; or as fivefold with verbs of the object-as-agent. These are stated separately to show that the difference in usage arises from the difference in worldly states. In meaning, however, they are just threefold, according to the three factors: agent, object, and state. For the causative agent is included in the factor called the pure agent, as it is a part of it. Similarly, the object-as-agent is included in the object-factor, while the state is separate. For the state, though of many kinds—such as going, cooking, cutting—is without distinction because it has the nature of action, and is a different kind of factor. Even so, because it is dependent on substance, it is divided according to the division of substance. Therefore, in the scriptures, a word indicating the state is also seen with a plural ending. In a finite verb, the usage 'state-factor' is based on the method of grammar, but in meaning, the factor-hood of the state is not established. For it neither generates anything, nor is it a cause for the action. The characteristic of a factor is precisely being a cause for the action. Thus, primarily or causally, the factor-hood of the state is not obtained. Even so, because it is merely the doing, it is a factor. For 'doing' (karaṇaṃ) is 'making' (kāro), which is action (kriyā), and that itself is a 'factor' (kārakaṃ); thus the factor-hood of the state should be seen. However, since the characteristic of a factor is precisely being a cause for the action, in the case of nominals, in the definition of a factor, grammarians abandon the usage 'state-factor' and make use of the terms 'agent-factor,' 'object-factor,' 'instrument-factor,' 'dative-factor,' 'ablative-factor,' and 'locative-factor' for the six things. Thus, based on the method of grammar, there are three factors: the aforementioned state-factor, and the two factors of object and agent. And the finite verb which indicates them is three-factored.

Imamatthañhi sandhāya, vuttamācariyehipi;

Mahāveyyākaraṇehi, niruttinayadassibhi.

Indeed, with reference to this meaning, it has been said by the teachers, the great grammarians, who discern the method of grammar.

“Yaṃ tikālaṃ tipurisaṃ, kriyāvāci tikārakaṃ;

Atiliṅgaṃ dvivacanaṃ, tadākhyātanti vuccatī”ti.

"That which has three tenses, three persons, expresses action, has three factors, is beyond gender, and has two numbers—that is called a finite verb."

Idha bhāvakammesu attanopaduppattiṃ keci akkharacintakā avassamicchantīti tesaṃ mativibhāvanatthamamhehi bhāvakammānaṃ kriyāpadāni attanopadavasenuddiṭṭhāni ceva niddiṭṭhāni ca. Sabbānipi panetāni tikārakāni kriyāpadāni kriyāpadamālamicchatā parassapadattanopadavasena yojetabbāni. Pāḷiādīsu hi tikārakāni kriyāpadāni parassapadattanopadavasena dvidhā ṭhitāni. Seyyathidaṃ? Bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati. Samādhijjhānakusalā, vandanti lokanāyakaṃ. Monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ. Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccati. Kathaṃ paṭipannassa puggalassa rūpaṃ vibhoti vibhaviyyati. So [M 0.0015] pahīyissati. Paṇḍukambale nikkhittaṃ bhāsate tapate. Pūjako labhate pūjaṃ. Puttakāmā thiyo yācaṃ, labhante tādisaṃ sutaṃ. Asito tādi vuccate sabrahmā. Aggijādi pubbeva bhūyate. So pahīyethāpi no pahīyethāti evaṃ dvidhā ṭhitāni. Atridaṃ pāḷivavatthānaṃ –

Here, some grammarians insist on the occurrence of the attanopada in bhāva and kamma constructions; to clarify their view, we have both indicated and explained the verbs of bhāva and kamma by way of the attanopada. However, all these three-factored verbs should be construed by way of parassapada and attanopada by one who desires the complete collection of verbs. For in the Pāḷi and other texts, three-factored verbs exist in two ways, namely, by way of parassapada and attanopada. As follows: 'The Blessed One dwells in Sāvatthī.' 'Skilled in concentration and meditation, they venerate the leader of the world.' 'Wisdom is called silence.' 'The wise one, through comprehension of the meaning, is called learned.' 'How for a person who practices does form vanish, is it made to vanish?' 'It will be abandoned.' 'Placed on a yellow wool blanket, it shines and glows.' 'The worshiper obtains worship.' 'Women desiring sons, praying, obtain such a son.' 'Such a one is called Asita, one with Brahmā.' 'Fire and so on is produced from the start.' 'It might be abandoned or it might not be abandoned'—thus they exist in two ways. Herein is this arrangement of the Pāḷi:

Tikārakāni sabbāni, kriyāpadāni pāyato;

Parassapadayogena, dissanti piṭakattaye.

All three-factored verbs, for the most part, are seen in the three Piṭakas with the use of the parassapada.

Attanopadayuttāni, cuṇṇiyesu padesu hi;

Atīvappāni gāthāsu, padānīti bahūni tu.

Words connected with the attanopada, indeed, are very few in prose passages, but in verses, they are many.

Gāthāsu cevitarāni, cuṇṇiyesu padesu ca;

Subahūneva hutvāna, dissantīti pakāsaye.

One should declare that the others, both in verses and in prose passages, having become very many, are seen.

Padānaṃ niddeso panati antiādīnaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ vacanānamanurūpena yojetabbo. Evaṃ tikārakakriyāpadāni sarūpato vavatthānato niddesato ca veditabbāni.

The explanation of the endings, such as 'ti', 'anti', and so on, should be applied in accordance with their respective numbers. Thus, the three-factored verbs should be understood according to their form, arrangement, and explanation.

Idāni nopasaggākammikādivasena bhavatissa dhātussa vinicchayaṃ vadāma –

Now, we will state the analysis of the root of 'bhavati' by way of being non-prefixed, intransitive, and so on.

Nopasaggā akammā ca, sopasaggā akammikā;

Sopasaggā sakammā ca, iti bhūti vibhāvitā.

Non-prefixed and intransitive, prefixed and intransitive, and prefixed and transitive—thus is the root 'bhū' distinguished.

Idaṃ tu vacanaṃ “dhamma-bhūto bhutvā”tiādisu;

Pattānubhavanatthaṃ me, vivajjetvā udīritaṃ.

This statement, however, was spoken by me having avoided the meaning of attaining and experiencing found in examples such as 'dhamma-bhūto bhutvā'.

Etena pana atthena, nopasaggasakammikaṃ;

Gahetvā catudhā hoti, iti ñeyyaṃ visesato.

But with this meaning, taking the non-prefixed transitive, it becomes fourfold—this should be distinctly understood.

Nopasaggā akammā ca, sopasaggā akammikā;

Bhūdhātu kārite sante, ekakammā bhavanti hi.

The non-prefixed intransitive and prefixed intransitive root 'bhū', when in the causative, indeed become single-object.

“Bhāveti [M 0.0016] kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, vibhāvetī”timānidha;

Dassetabbāni viññūhi, sāsanaññūhi sāsane.

'He cultivates a wholesome state,' 'he develops it'—these examples should be shown here in the Dispensation by the wise, those who know the Dispensation.

Sopasaggā sakammā tu, kāritappaccaye sati;

Dvikammāyeva hotīti, ñātabbaṃ viññunā kathaṃ.

The prefixed transitive, however, when the causative suffix is present, becomes ditransitive—how should this be known by the wise?

Abhibhāventi purisā, purise pāṇajātikaṃ;

Anubhāveti puriso, sampattiṃ purisaṃ iti.

Men cause a living being to overcome men. A man causes a man to experience success—thus.

Idaṃ sakammakaṃ nāma, akammakamidaṃ iti;

Kathamamhehi ñātabbaṃ, vitthārena vadetha no.

This is called transitive, that is intransitive—how should we know this? Explain it to us in detail.

Vitthāreneva kiṃ vattuṃ, sakkomi ekadesato;

Kathayissāmi sakkaccaṃ, vadato me nibodhatha.

Why should I speak at length? I can explain it in part; I will tell it attentively, listen to me as I speak.

Ākhyātikapadaṃ nāma, duvidhaṃ samudīritaṃ;

Sakammakamakammañca, iti viññū vibhāvaye.

The term 'verb' is said to be twofold: transitive and intransitive—so the wise should discern.

Tatra yassa payogamhi, padassa kattunā kriyā;

Nipphāditā vinā kammaṃ, na hoti taṃ sakammakaṃ.

Therein, that is a transitive word whose action, when performed by an agent in usage, is not accomplished without an object.

“Pacatī”ti hi vutte tu, yena kenaci jantunā;

Odanaṃ vā panaññaṃ vā, kiñci vatthunti ñāyati.

For when 'he cooks' is said by any person, it is understood that rice, or something else, or some object is being cooked.

Yassa pana payogamhi, kammena rahitā kriyā;

Padassa ñāyate etaṃ, akammakanti tīraye.

But when in usage, the action of a word is understood to be devoid of an object—this one should conclude is intransitive.

“Tiṭṭhati devadatto”ti, vutte kenaci jantunā;

Ṭhānaṃva buddhivisayo, kammabhūtaṃ na kiñcipi.

When 'Devadatta stands' is said by any person, only the standing is within the scope of understanding; there is no object whatsoever.

Sakammakapadaṃ tattha, kattāraṃ kammameva ca;

Pakāseti yathāyoga-miti viññū vibhāvaye.

Therein, a transitive word reveals both the agent and the object, as appropriate—so the wise should discern.

“Odanaṃ pacati poso, odano paccate sayaṃ”;

Iccudāharaṇā ñeyyā, avuttepi ayaṃ nayo.

Examples such as, "A person cooks rice," and "The rice is cooked by itself," should be known. Even if unstated, this is the principle.

Akammakapadaṃ [M 0.0017] nāma, kattāraṃ bhāvameva ca;

Yathārahaṃ pakāseti, iti dhīropalakkhaye.

An intransitive word reveals the agent and the state of being, as is fitting—thus the discerning one should recognize.

Kattāraṃ “tiṭṭhati”ccatra, sūceti bhāvanāmakaṃ;

“Upaṭṭhīyati” iccatra, avuttepi ayaṃ nayo.

Here, 'stands' indicates the agent; 'is present' indicates what is called the state of being. Even if unstated, this is the principle.

Evaṃ sakammakākammaṃ, ñatvā yojeyya buddhimā;

Tikammakañca jāneyya, karādo kārite sati.

Thus, knowing the transitive and intransitive, the wise person should apply them. And one should know the tri-objective when a causative of roots like 'kar' is present.

“Suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ poso, kāreti purisa”nti ca;

“Puriso purise gāmaṃ, rathaṃ vāheti”iccapi.

"A person causes a man to make a golden bracelet," and also, "A person leads men to the village, or drives a chariot."

Ettha bhavatidhātumhi, nayo eso na labbhati;

Tasmā dvikammakaññeva, padamettha vibhāvitaṃ.

Here, this principle is not found with the root 'bhū'. Therefore, only the di-objective word is explained here.

Ediso ca nayo nāma, pāḷiyaṃ tu na dissati;

Ekaccānaṃ mateneva, mayā evaṃ pakāsito.

Such a principle, however, is not seen in the Pāli Canon; it has been thus explained by me only according to the opinion of some.

Ettha ca “tamenaṃ rājā, vividhā kammakāraṇā;

Kārāpetī”ti yo pāṭho, niddese taṃ suniddise.

And here, the reading, "The king causes him to perform various tasks"—that one should explain well in the commentary.

“Manussehī”ti āharitvā, pāṭhasesaṃ sumedhaso;

“Sunakhehipi khādāpenti”, iti pāṭhassa dassanā.

Having supplied 'by people,' the wise one should complete the rest of the passage, from seeing the reading, "they cause [them] to be eaten even by dogs."

Etaṃ nayaṃ vidū ñatvā, yoje pāṭhānurūpato;

“Suvaṇṇaṃ kaṭakaṃ poso, kāreti puriseni”ti.

The wise one, understanding this principle, should apply it according to the text: "A person causes a golden bracelet to be made by a man."

Vikaraṇappaccayāva, vuttā ettha sarūpato;

Sagaṇe sagaṇe tesaṃ, vuttiṃ dīpetumeva ca.

The conjugational sign suffixes have been stated here according to their form, and also to show their usage in each respective group.

“Asmiṃ gaṇe ayaṃ dhātu, hotī”ti tehi viññuno;

Viññāpetuñca aññehi, ñāpanā paccayehi na.

And to make it known to the wise by them that 'this root is in this group,' and not by other knowledge-indicating suffixes.

Tathā hi bhāvakammesu, vihito paccayo tu yo;

Aṭṭhavidhepi dhātūnaṃ, gaṇasmiṃ sampavattati.

For indeed, the suffix that is prescribed in the case of the state and the passive applies in the group of all eight kinds of roots.

Bhūdhātujesu [M 0.0018] rūpesu, asammohāya sotunaṃ;

Nānāvidho nayo evaṃ, mayā ettha pakāsito.

Regarding forms derived from the root 'bhū', for the sake of the non-confusion of listeners, various principles have thus been explained by me here.

Ye loke appayuttā vividhavikaraṇākhyātasaddesvachekā,

Te patvākhyātasadde avigatavimatī honti ñāṇīpi tasmā;

Accantaññeva dhīro saparahitarato sāsane daḷhapemo,

Yogaṃ tesaṃ payoge paṭutaramatitaṃ patthayāno kareyya.

Those in the world who are unpracticed and unskilled in the words of various conjugational signs and verbs, even the wise, upon encountering the words of verbs, are not free from doubt. Therefore, the wise one, ever devoted to the welfare of self and others, with firm love for the Teaching, desiring surpassing skill, should make an effort in their application.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu

Thus, in the ninefold Dispensation with its commentary, in the three Piṭakas, in the modes of expression,

Viññūnaṃ kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

In the treatise on the science of grammar, composed for the proficiency of the wise,

Savikaraṇākhyātavibhāgo nāma

The Section on Verbs with Conjugational Signs,

Paṭhamo paricchedo.

The First Chapter.

2. Bhavatikriyāpadamālāvibhāga

2. The Division of the Series of Verb Forms of 'Bhavati'

Ito paraṃ pavakkhāmi, sotūnaṃ mativaḍḍhanaṃ;

Kriyāpadakkamaṃ nāma, vibhattādīni dīpayaṃ.

Henceforth I shall explain, to increase the wisdom of listeners, what is called the 'Sequence of Verb Forms,' elucidating the endings and so forth.

Tatra ākhyātikassa kriyālakkhaṇattasūcikā tyādayo vibhattiyo, tā aṭṭhavidhā vattamānāpañcamīsattamīparokkhāhiyyattanajjatanībhavissantī kālātipattivasena.

Herein, the endings such as 'ti' and so forth are indicators of the characteristic of action for the verb. They are of eight kinds, by way of: present, imperative, optative, perfect, imperfect, aorist, future, and conditional.

Tatthati anti, si tha, mi ma, te ante, se vhe, e mhe iccetā vattamānāvibhattiyo nāma.

Herein, 'ti, anti,' 'si, tha,' 'mi, ma,' 'te, ante,' 'se, vhe,' 'e, mhe'—these are called the present tense endings.

Tu antu, hi tha, mi ma, taṃ antaṃ, su vho, e āmase iccetā pañcamīvibhattiyo nāma.

'Tu, antu,' 'hi, tha,' 'mi, ma,' 'taṃ, antaṃ,' 'su, vho,' 'e, āmase'—these are called the imperative (pañcamī) endings.

Eyya [M 0.0019] eyyuṃ, eyyāsi eyyātha, eyyāmi eyyāma, etha eraṃ, etho eyyāvho, eyyaṃ eyyāmhe iccetā sattamīvibhattiyo nāma.

'Eyya, eyyuṃ,' 'eyyāsi, eyyātha,' 'eyyāmi, eyyāma,' 'etha, eraṃ,' 'etho, eyyāvho,' 'eyyaṃ, eyyāmhe'—these are called the optative (sattamī) endings.

A u, e ttha, aṃ mha, ttha re, ttho vho, iṃ mhe iccetā parokkhāvibhattiyo nāma.

'A, u,' 'e, ttha,' 'aṃ, mha,' 'ttha, re,' 'ttho, vho,' 'iṃ, mhe'—these are called the perfect (parokkhā) endings.

Ā ū, o ttha, aṃ mhā, ttha tthuṃ, se vhaṃ, iṃ mhase iccetā hiyyattanīvibhattiyo nāma.

'Ā, ū,' 'o, ttha,' 'aṃ, mhā,' 'ttha, tthuṃ,' 'se, vhaṃ,' 'iṃ, mhase'—these are called the imperfect (hiyyattanī) endings.

Ī uṃ, o ttha, iṃ mhā, ā ū, se vhaṃ, aṃ mhe iccetā ajjatanīvibhattiyo nāma.

'Ī, uṃ,' 'o, ttha,' 'iṃ, mhā,' 'ā, ū,' 'se, vhaṃ,' 'aṃ, mhe'—these are called the aorist (ajjatanī) endings.

Ssati ssanti, ssasi ssatha, ssāmi ssāma, ssate ssante, ssase ssavhe, ssaṃ ssāmhe iccetā bhavissantīvibhattiyo nāma.

'Ssati, ssanti,' 'ssasi, ssatha,' 'ssāmi, ssāma,' 'ssate, ssante,' 'ssase, ssavhe,' 'ssaṃ, ssāmhe'—these are called the future (bhavissantī) endings.

Ssā ssaṃsu, sse ssatha, ssaṃ ssāmhā, ssatha ssisu, ssase ssavhe, ssiṃ ssāmhase iccetā kālātipattivibhattiyo nāma.

'Ssā, ssaṃsu,' 'sse, ssatha,' 'ssaṃ, ssāmhā,' 'ssatha, ssisu,' 'ssase, ssavhe,' 'ssiṃ, ssāmhase'—these are called the conditional (kālātipatti) endings.

Sabbāsametāsaṃ vibhattīnaṃ yāni yāni pubbakāni cha padāni, tāni tāni parassapadāni nāma. Yāni yāni pana parāni cha padāni, tāni tāni attanopadāni nāma. Tattha parassapadāni vattamānā cha, pañcamiyo cha, sattamiyo cha, parokkhā cha, hiyyattaniyo cha, ajjataniyo cha, bhavissantiyo cha, kālātipattiyo chāti aṭṭhacattālīsavidhāni honti, tathā itarāni, sabbāni tāni piṇḍitāni channavutividhāni.

Of all these endings, the first six forms are called the parassapada. The latter six forms are called the attanopada. Among these, the parassapada includes six forms for the present tense, six for the imperative (pañcamī), six for the optative (sattamī), six for the perfect, six for the imperfect, six for the aorist, six for the future, and six for the conditional—thus totaling forty-eight forms. Similarly, the others also total forty-eight forms. Combined, all these amount to ninety-six forms.

Parassapadānamattanopadānañca dve dve padāni paṭhamamajjhimuttamapurisā nāma. Te vattamānādīsu cattāro cattāro, aṭṭhannaṃ vibhattīnaṃ vasena dvattiṃsa, piṇḍitāni parimāṇāneva.

Of the parassapada and attanopada, the pairs of forms are called the first, middle, and ultimate persons. These are four each in the present and so forth, totaling thirty-two by way of the eight endings. The counted forms are precisely these.

Dvīsu [M 0.0020] dvīsu padesu paṭhamaṃ paṭhamaṃ ekavacanaṃ, dutiyaṃ dutiyaṃ bahuvacanaṃ.

In each pair of forms, the first is singular, and the second is plural.

Tatra vattamānavibhattīnanti anti, si tha, mi ma iccetāni parassapadāni. Te ante, se vhe, e mhe iccetāni attanopadāni. Parassapadattanopadesupiti anti iti paṭhamapurisā, sitha iti majjhimapurisā, mi ma iti uttamapurisā, te ante iti paṭhamapurisā, se vhe iti majjhimapurisā, e mhe iti uttamapurisā.

Herein, of the present tense endings, 'ti, anti,' 'si, tha,' 'mi, ma'—these are the parassapada (active voice). 'Te, ante,' 'se, vhe,' 'e, mhe'—these are the attanopada (middle voice). In both the parassapada and attanopada, 'ti, anti' are the first person; 'si, tha' are the middle person; 'mi, ma' are the ultimate person. Likewise, 'te, ante' are the first person; 'se, vhe' are the middle person; 'e, mhe' are the ultimate person.

Paṭhamamajjhimuttamapurisesupi ti-iti ekavacanaṃ, anti-iti bahuvacananti evaṃ ekavacanabahuvacanāni kamato ñeyyāni. Evaṃ sesāsu vibhattīsu parassapadattanopadapaṭhamamajjhimuttamapurisekavacanabahuvacanāni ñeyyāni.

In the first, middle, and ultimate persons, 'ti' is the singular and 'anti' is the plural; thus, the singular and plural forms should be understood sequentially. Likewise, in the remaining endings, the singular and plural forms of the first, middle, and ultimate persons in both parassapada and attanopada should be understood.

Tattha vibhattīti kenaṭṭhena vibhatti? Kālādivasena dhātvatthaṃ vibhajatīti vibhatti, syādīhi nāmikavibhattīhi saha sabbasaṅgāhakavasena pana sakatthaparatthādibhede atthe vibhajatīti vibhatti, kammādayo vā kārake ekavacanabahuvacanavasena vibhajatīti vibhatti, vibhajitabbā ñāṇenātipi vibhatti, vibhajanti atthe etāyātipi vibhatti, atha vā satipi jinasāsane avibhattikaniddese sabbena sabbaṃ vibhattīhi vinā atthassā’niddisitabbato visesena vividhena vā ākārena bhajanti sevanti naṃ paṇḍitātipi vibhatti. Tattha avibhattikaniddesalakkhaṇaṃ vadāma saha payoganidassanādīhi.

Herein, by what meaning is it 'vibhatti' (inflection)? It divides the meaning of the root according to time and so forth; therefore it is 'vibhatti.' Or, together with nominal inflections such as 'sya,' by way of comprehensively including all, it divides meanings into distinctions such as one's own purpose and another's purpose; therefore it is 'vibhatti.' Or, it divides the agents (kāraka) such as the object and so forth, by way of singular and plural; therefore it is 'vibhatti.' Or, because it is to be distinguished by knowledge, it is also 'vibhatti.' Or, because they distinguish meanings by means of it, it is also 'vibhatti.' Alternatively, even though indeclinable expressions exist in the Dispensation of the Conqueror, since the meaning cannot be fully indicated in every respect without inflections, the wise resort to or cultivate it in a special or diverse manner; therefore it is 'vibhatti.' Herein, we will explain the characteristic of an indeclinable expression, along with examples of usage and so forth.

Avibhattikaniddeso, nāmikesupalabbhati;

Nākhyātesūti viññeyya-midamettha nidassanaṃ.

The indeclinable expression is found among nominal forms; it should be understood as not found among verbs. This is the illustration here.

Nigrodhova mahārukkho, thera vādānamuttamo;

Anūnaṃ anadhikañca, kevalaṃ jinasāsanaṃ.

Like a great banyan tree, the Elder's doctrine is the foremost of doctrines; the Victor's Teaching is complete, lacking nothing and exceeding nothing.

Tatra [M 0.0021] thera-iti avibhattiko niddeso, therānaṃ ayanti thero. Ko so? Vādo. Theravādo aññesaṃ vādānaṃ uttamoti ayamattho veditabbo.

Herein, 'thera' is an indeclinable expression. The derivation is 'this of the elders' (therānaṃ ayaṃ). What is that? A doctrine. The meaning to be understood is that 'Theravāda' is the foremost among other doctrines.

“Kāyo te sabba sovaṇṇo”, iccādimhipi nāmike;

Avibhattikaniddeso, gahetabbo nayaññunā.

In nominal phrases like 'Kāyo te sabba sovaṇṇo' (Your body is all golden), the indeclinable expression should be understood by one skilled in method.

Avibhattikaniddeso, nanvākhyātepi dissati;

“Bho khāda piva”iccatra, vade yo koci codako.

Is the indeclinable expression not seen even in verbs? An objector might say, 'Bho, eat, drink' here.

Yadi evaṃ matenassa, bhaveyya avibhattikaṃ;

“Bhikkhu, bho purisi”ccādi, padampi, na hidaṃ tathā.

If this were his view, then even a word such as 'Bhikkhu, bho, purisa' would be indeclinable; but this is not so.

“Bhikkhu, bho purisi”ccādi, si ga lopena vuccati;

Tathā “khādā”tiādīni, hi lopena pavuccare.

Words like 'Bhikkhu, bho, purisa' and so forth are said to be formed by the elision of 'si' or 'ga'; similarly, 'khāda' and so forth are said to be expressed by the elision of 'hi'.

Evaṃ avibhattikaniddeso ākhyātesu na labbhati, nāmesuyeva labbhati. Tatrāpi “aṭṭha ca puggala dhammadasā te”ti ettha chandavasena puggala iti rassakaraṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, na “kakusandha koṇāgamano ca kassapo”ti ettha kakusandha iti avibhattikaniddeso viya avibhattikaniddeso daṭṭhabbo. “Bhikkhu nisinne mātugāmo upanisinno vā hoti upanipanno vā”ti ettha pana bhikkhūti idaṃ bhikkhumhīti vattabbatthattā bhumme paccattantipi adiṭṭhavibhattikaniddesotipi vattuṃ yujjati. Tattha pana chandavasena katarassattā tāni padāni avibhattikaniddesapakkhampi bhajantīti vattuṃ na yujjati.

Thus, the indeclinable expression is not found in verbs, but is found only in nouns. Moreover, in 'aṭṭha ca puggala dhammadasā te' (these eight persons, seers of the Dhamma), the shortening of 'puggala' should be seen as due to metrical necessity, and it is not to be viewed as an indeclinable expression like 'kakusandha' in 'kakusandha koṇāgamano ca kassapo.' However, in 'Bhikkhu nisinne mātugāmo upanisinno vā hoti upanipanno vā' (When a bhikkhu is seated, a woman is seated near or lying near), it is appropriate to say that 'bhikkhu' here is an indeclinable expression in the locative case, or an indeclinable expression of an unseen ending, because it has the meaning that should be expressed as 'bhikkhumhi' (when a bhikkhu). However, it is not appropriate to say that those words, being shortened due to metrical necessity, also fall into the category of indeclinable expressions.

Tattha parassapadānīti parassa atthabhūtāni padāni parassapadāni. Etthuttamapurisesu attano atthesupi attanopadavohāro na kariyati.

Herein, 'parassapadāni' are words that are for the purpose of another. In this context, for the ultimate person, the designation 'attanopada' is not used, even when the meaning pertains to oneself.

Kiñcāpi [M 0.0022] attano atthā, purisā uttamavhayā;

Tathāpi itaresāna-mussannattāva tabbasā;

Tabbohāro imesānaṃ, porāṇehi niropito.

Although the persons called ultimate are for their own purpose, nevertheless, because of the prevalence of use for others, by that power, this usage for them was established by the ancients.

Attanopadānīti attano atthabhūtāni padāni attanopadāni. Ettha pana paṭhamamajjhimapurisesu parassatthesupi parassapadavohāro na kariyati.

'Attanopadāni' are words that are for the purpose of oneself. Here, however, for the first and middle persons, the designation 'parassapada' is not used, even when the meaning pertains to another.

Paṭhamamajjhimā cete, parassatthā tathāpi ca;

Itaresaṃ nirūḷhattā, tabbohārassa saccato.

And these first and middle persons, though for another's purpose, nevertheless, because of the firm establishment of that usage for the others, truly...

Imassa panimesānaṃ, pubbavohāratāya ca;

Tathā saṅkaradosassa, haraṇatthāya so ayaṃ;

Attanopadavohāro, esamāropito dhuvaṃ.

And for these, because of this prior usage, and for the purpose of removing the fault of confusion, this 'attanopada' usage is surely imposed upon them.

Parassapadasaññādi-saññāyo bahukā idha;

Porāṇehi katattātā, saññā porāṇikā matā.

Many designations here, such as the designation of parassapada, are considered ancient designations because they were made by the ancients.

Tasmā idha paṭhamapurisādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ purisānaṃ vacanatthaṃ na pariyesāma. Rūḷhiyā hi porāṇehi tyādīnaṃ purisasaññā vihitā.

Therefore, here we do not seek the literal meaning of the three persons, beginning with the first person. For, by convention, the ancients have assigned the designation 'person' to 'ti' and so forth.

Ekavacanabahuvacanesu pana ekassatthassa vacanaṃ ekavacanaṃ. Bahūnamatthānaṃ vacanaṃ bahuvacanaṃ. Atha vā bahuttepi sati samudāyavasena jātivasena vā cittena sampiṇḍetvā ekīkatassatthassa ekassa viya vacanampi ekavacanaṃ, bahutte nissitassa nissayavohārena vuttassa nissayavasena ekassa viya vacanampi ekavacanaṃ, ekattalakkhaṇena bavhatthānaṃ ekavacanaṃ viya vacanampi ekavacanaṃ. Abahuttepi sati attagarukārāparicchedamātikānusandhinayapucchāsabhāgaputhucitta- samāyogaputhuārammaṇavasena ekatthassa bahūnaṃ viya vacanaṃ bahuvacanaṃ, tathā ye ye bahavo tannivāsataṃputtasaṅkhātassekassatthassa rūḷhīvasena bahūnaṃ viya vacanampi bahuvacanaṃ, ekassatthassa aññenatthena ekābhidhānavasena bahūnaṃ [M 0.0023] viya vacanampi bahuvacanaṃ, ekassatthassa nissitavasena bahūnaṃ viya vacanampi bahuvacanaṃ, ekassatthassa ārammaṇabhedakiccabhedavasena bahūnaṃ viya vacanampi bahuvacanaṃ. Evamimehi ākārehi ekamhi vattabbe, ekamhi viya ca vattabbe ekavacanaṃ, bahumhi vattabbe, bahumhi viya ca vattabbe bahuvacanaṃ hotīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Puthuvacanaṃ, anekavacananti ca imasseva nāmaṃ.

Now, regarding the singular and plural, the expression of a single meaning is the singular. The expression of many meanings is the plural. Alternatively, even when there is multiplicity, the expression of a meaning that has been unified by being mentally condensed by way of a collective or a class is also the singular, as if it were one. The expression of something dependent on multiplicity, spoken of by way of its dependence, is also the singular, as if it were one. The expression of many meanings characterized by unity is also the singular, as if it were one. Conversely, even when there is no multiplicity, the expression of a single meaning is the plural, as if it were many, by way of respect for self, indefiniteness, the method of following a matrix, the nature of a question, association with diverse minds, and diverse objects. Likewise, the expression of a single meaning designated as its many inhabitants or children is also the plural, as if it were many, by way of convention. The expression of a single meaning through a single designation with another meaning is also the plural, as if it were many. The expression of a single meaning by way of what is dependent on it is also the plural, as if it were many. The expression of a single meaning by way of a difference in object or function is also the plural, as if it were many. Thus, it should be understood that in these ways, the singular is used when one is to be expressed or when something is to be expressed as if it were one; and the plural is used when many are to be expressed or when something is to be expressed as if it were many. 'Diverse expression' and 'multiple expression' are also its names.

Vacanesu ayaṃ attho, nāmākhyātavibhattinaṃ;

Vasena adhigantabbo, sāsanatthagavesinā.

This meaning in expressions should be understood by one seeking the purpose of the Dispensation, by means of the inflections of nouns and verbs.

Tasmā tadatthaviññāpanatthaṃ idha nāmikapayogehi sahevākhyātapayoge pavakkhāma – “rājā āgacchati, sahāyo me āgacchati, ekaṃ citta” miccevamādayo ekassatthassa ekavacanapayogā. “Rājāno āgacchanti, sahāyā me āgacchanti, na me dessā ubho puttā, dve tīṇi” iccevamādayo bavhatthānaṃ bahuvacanapayogā.

Therefore, to clarify that meaning here, we shall explain the use of verbal forms together with the use of nominal forms: ‘The king comes; my friend comes; one thought,’ and so forth, are examples of singular usage for a single meaning. ‘The kings come; my friends come; both sons are not hateful to me; two, three,’ and so forth, are examples of plural usage for many meanings.

“Sā senā mahatī āsi, bahujjano pasannosi, sabbo taṃ jano ojināyatu, itthigumbassa pavarā, buddhassāhaṃ vatthayugaṃ adāsiṃ, dvayaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmi, pemaṃ mahantaṃ ratanattayassa, kare pasādañca naro avassaṃ, bhikkhusaṅgho, balakāyo, devanikāyo, ariyagaṇo”- iccevamādayo, “dvikaṃ tika”miccādayo ca samudāyavasena bavhatthānaṃ ekavacanapayogā.

‘That army was great; many people were devoted; may all that populace attend to you; the foremost of the group of women; I gave a pair of robes to the Buddha; Bhikkhus, I shall teach you a dyad; a person should certainly generate great love and faith for the Triple Gem; the community of bhikkhus; the host of forces; the assembly of deities; the noble group’—and so forth, and ‘a dyad, a triad,’ and so forth, are examples of singular usage for many meanings by way of a collective.

Katthaci pana īdisesu ṭhānesu bahuvacanapayogāpi dissanti. Tathā hi “pūjitā ñātisaṅghehi, devakāyā samāgatā, sabbete devanikāyā, dve devasaṅghā, tīṇi [M 0.0024] dukāni, cattāri navakāni” iccevamādayo payogāpi dissanti. Ime ekavacanavasena vattabbassa samudāyassa bahusamudāyavasena bahuvacanapayogāti gahetabbā, saṅgayhamānā ca bavhatthabahuvacane saṅgahaṃ gacchanti visuṃyeva vā, tasmā bahusamudāyāpekkhabahuvacananti etesaṃ nāmaṃ veditabbaṃ.

However, in some such instances, plural usages are also seen. For example: ‘Honored by assemblies of relatives; hosts of devas gathered; all these groups of devas; two assemblies of devas; three dyads; four nines’—such usages are also seen. These should be understood as plural usages by way of many collectives for a collective that should be expressed in the singular. And being included, they are included in the plural for many meanings, or else separately. Therefore, their name should be known as ‘the plural with reference to many collectives’.

“Pāṇaṃ na hane, sasso sampajjati” iccevamādayo jātivasena bavhatthānaṃ ekavacanapayogā, tabbhāvasāmaññena bavhatthānaṃ ekavacanapayogātipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

‘One should not kill a living being; the crop prospers’—and so forth are examples of singular usage for many meanings by way of class. It is also possible to say that this is singular usage for many meanings due to the commonality of their nature.

“Nāgaṃ raṭṭhassa pūjitaṃ, sāvatthī saddhā ahosi pasannā” iccevamādayo nissayavasena pavattānaṃ nissayavohārena vuttānamekavacanapayogā.

‘The elephant, honored by the kingdom; Sāvatthī was faithful and devoted’—and so forth are examples of singular usages for terms that proceed by way of dependence and are expressed through the language of dependence.

“Tilakkhaṇaṃ, kusalākusalaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ, dhammavinayo, cittaseno ca gandhabbo, natiyā asati āgatigati na hoti, āgatigatiyā asati cutūpapāto na hoti” iccevamādayo ekattalakkhaṇe bavhatthānaṃ ekavacanapayogā.

‘The three characteristics; the wholesome and unwholesome; from consciousness as condition, name-and-form; from name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; the Dhamma and the Discipline; Cittasena and the gandhabba; when there is no inclination, there is no coming and going; when there is no coming and going, there is no decease and rebirth’—and so forth are examples of singular usage for many meanings characterized by unity.

“Evaṃ mayaṃ gaṇhāma, amhākaṃ pakati, padhānanti kho meghiya vadamānaṃ kinti vadeyyāma” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa attavasena bahuvacanapayogā.

‘Thus we grasp, it is our nature, our striving—Meghiya, what could we say to one speaking thus?’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for a single meaning by way of self-reference.

“Te manussā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavocuṃ ‘bhuñjatha bhante’ti, ahaṃ manussesu manussabhūtā, abbhāgatānā’sanakaṃ adāsiṃ” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa garukāravasena bahuvacanapayogā.

‘Those people said to that bhikkhu, “Eat, venerable sir.”’; ‘I, being a human among humans, gave a seat to the newly arrived ones’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for a single meaning by way of respect.

“Appaccayā [M 0.0025] dhammā, asaṅkhatā dhammā” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa aparicchedavasena bahuvacanapayogā, aniyamitasaṅkhāvasena bahuvacanapayogā vā.

‘Phenomena without causal condition; unconditioned phenomena’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for a single meaning by way of indefiniteness, or by way of unspecified quantity.

Keci pana “desanāsotapātavasena bahuvacanapayogā”tipi vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi tathāgato satisampajaññarahito dhammaṃ deseti, yutti ca na dissati “mātikāyaṃ pucchāyaṃ vissajjane cāti tīsupi ṭhānesu appaccayādidhamme desento satthā punappunaṃ bahuvacanavasena desanāsote patitvā dhammaṃ desetī”ti.

Some, however, say that this is ‘plural usage by way of falling into the stream of the teaching,’ but that should not be accepted. For the Tathāgata does not teach the Dhamma devoid of mindfulness and clear comprehension, and no reason is seen for the view that ‘In the three instances—the matrix, the question, and the answer—the Teacher, when teaching about phenomena without causal condition and so on, repeatedly falls into the stream of the teaching and teaches the Dhamma by way of the plural.’

“Katame dhammā appaccayā” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa mātikānusandhinayena bahuvacanapayogā.

‘Which phenomena are without causal condition?’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for a single meaning by the method of following the matrix.

“Ime dhammā appaccayā” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa pucchānusandhinayena bahuvacanapayogā.

‘These phenomena are without causal condition’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for a single meaning by the method of following the question.

“Katame dhammā no parāmāsā, te dhamme ṭhapetvā avasesā kusalākusalābyākatā dhammā” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa pucchāsabhāgena bahuvacanapayogā.

‘Which phenomena are not objects of grasping? Setting aside those phenomena, the remaining phenomena are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for a single meaning by way of the nature of the question.

“Atthi bhikkhave aññeva dhammā gambhīrā duddasā duranubodhā santā paṇītā atakkāvacarā nipuṇā paṇḍitavedanīyā, ye tathāgato sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedetī”ti ayamekassatthassa puthucittasamāyogaputhuārammaṇavasena bahuvacanapayogo.

‘Bhikkhus, there are other phenomena that are profound, difficult to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, to be experienced by the wise, which the Tathāgata, having realized them for himself with direct knowledge, makes known.’ This is an example of plural usage for a single meaning by way of association with diverse minds and diverse objects.

“Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ mahāvane,

‘At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in Kapilavatthu, in the Great Wood,

Santi [M 0.0026] puttā videhānaṃ, dīghāvu raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Te rajjaṃ kārayissanti, mithilāyaṃ pajāpati” –

There are sons of the Videhans, O Dīghāvu, enhancer of the kingdom! They will rule the kingdom in Mithilā, O lord of the people!’—

Iccevamādayo saddā ye ye bahavo, tannivāsataṃputtasaṅkhātassekatthassa rūḷhīvasena bahuvacanapayogā.

Such words and so forth, which are plural, are examples of plural usage by way of convention for a single meaning designated as ‘its inhabitants’ or ‘its children’.

“Sāriputtamoggallāne āmantesi ‘gacchatha tumhe sāriputtā kīṭāgiriṃ gantvā assajipunabbasukānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kīṭāgirismā pabbājanīyakammaṃ karotha, tumhākaṃ ete saddhivihārino’ti”, “kacci vo kulaputtā, etha byagghā nivattavho” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa aññenatthena ekābhidhānavasena bahuvacanapayogā.

‘He addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna: “Go, you Sāriputtas, to Kīṭāgiri and perform the act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri upon the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasu. These are your co-residents.”’; ‘Well, clansmen, have you tigers turned back?’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for one meaning by way of designating it along with another by a single name.

“Mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karonti” iccevamādayo ekassatthassa nissitavasena bahuvacanapayogā.

‘The couches make an outcry’—and so forth are examples of plural usage for the dependent things, by way of that on which they depend.

“Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti ayamārammaṇabhedena ekassatthassa bahuvacanapayogo.

‘The four establishments of mindfulness’ is a plural usage for a single meaning, based on the difference of objects.

“Cattāro sammappadhānā”ti ayaṃ pana kiccabhedena ekassatthassa bahuvacanapayogo.

‘The four right strivings’ is, however, a plural usage for a single meaning, based on the difference of function.

Tattha ekatthekavacanaṃ, samudāyāpekkhekavacanaṃ, jātyāpekkhekavacanaṃ, tannissayāpekkhekavacanaṃ, ekattalakkhaṇekavacananti pañcavidhaṃ ekavacanaṃ bhavati. Ettha pana jātyāpekkhekavacanaṃ atthato sāmaññāpekkhekavacanamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Therein, the singular is of five kinds: singular in the sense of one, singular with respect to an aggregate, singular with respect to a genus, singular with respect to dependence on that, and singular characterized by oneness. Here, however, the singular with respect to a genus should be understood as being, in meaning, a singular with respect to generality.

Bavhatthabahuvacanaṃ, bahusamudāyāpekkhabahuvacanaṃ, attabahuvacanaṃ, garukārabahuvacanaṃ, aparicchedabahuvacanaṃ, mātikānusandhinayabahuvacanaṃ, pucchānusandhinayabahuvacanaṃ, pucchāsabhāgabahuvacanaṃ, puthucittasamāyogaputhuārammaṇabahuvacanaṃ, tannivāsabahuvacanaṃ, taṃputtabahuvacanaṃ, ekābhidhānabahuvacanaṃ, tannissitāpekkhabahuvacanaṃ[M 0.0027], ārammaṇabhedabahuvacanaṃ, kiccabhedabahuvacananti pannarasavidhaṃ bahuvacanaṃ bhavati. Iccevaṃ vīsadhā sabbāni ekavacanabahuvacanāni saṅgahitāni. Atridaṃ pāḷivavatthānaṃ –

The plural is of fifteen kinds: plural in the sense of many, plural with respect to a large collection, plural for oneself, plural for respect, plural for indefiniteness, plural by the method of connection to the matrix, plural by the method of connection to the question, plural sharing the nature of the question, plural for the association of various minds and various objects, plural for its inhabitants, plural for its children, plural by a single designation, plural with respect to dependence on that, plural due to difference of object, and plural due to difference of function. Thus, all singulars and plurals are included in twenty types. Herein is the analysis of the Pāli.

Ekatthe dekavacana-ñcitarasmitarampi ca;

Samudāyajātiekatta-lakkhaṇekavacopi ca;

Sāṭṭhakathe piṭakamhi, pāṭhe pāyena dissare.

The singular in the sense of one, and the other number in the other sense; also the singulars characterized by aggregation, genus, and oneness; are generally seen in the text of the Piṭaka with its commentaries.

Garumhi cattanekasmiṃ, bahuvacanakaṃ pana;

Pāḷiyaṃ appakaṃ aṭṭha-kathāṭīkāsu taṃ bahuṃ.

However, the plural form for a venerable person or for oneself is rare in the Pāli; but in the commentaries and sub-commentaries, it is abundant.

Tathā hi bahukaṃ deka-vacanaṃyeva pāḷiyaṃ;

Garumhi cattanekasmiṃ, idamettha nidassanaṃ.

For indeed, in the Pāli, the singular is abundant even for a venerable person or for oneself. Herein is an example:

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Tava sāsanamāgamma, pattomhi amataṃ padaṃ”.
