‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O highest of men; having come to your teaching, I have attained the deathless state.’

Iccevamādayo pāṭhā, bahudhā jinasāsane;

Dissantīti vijāneyya, vidvā akkharacintako.

The wise one, the grammarian, should understand that such and similar passages appear in many ways in the Victor’s Dispensation.

Sātisayaṃ garukārā-rahassāpi mahesino;

Ekavacanayogena, niddeso dissate yato.

Since, even for the Great Sage, who is worthy of extreme reverence, the designation is seen by way of singular usage.

Tato vohārakusalo, kareyyatthānurūpato;

Ekavacanayogaṃ vā, itaraṃ vā sumedhaso.

Therefore, the intelligent one skilled in expression should use either the singular or the other form, according to the meaning.

Pāyena tannivāsamhi, bahuvacanakaṃ ṭhitaṃ;

Taṃputte appakaṃ tanni-ssayekavacanampi ca.

Generally, the plural is established for its inhabitants; for its children it is rare, and also the plural referring to dependence on that.

Puthucittāpariccheda-mātikāsandhiādisu;

Bahuvacanakañcāpi, appakanti pakāsaye.

In cases of diverse minds, indefiniteness, matrix-connection, and so forth, the plural is also declared to be rare.

Ekābhidhānato kiccā, tathā gocaratopi ca;

Bahuvacanakaṃ tanni-ssitāpekkhañca appakaṃ.

The plural arising from a single designation, from function, and also from range of objects, as well as the plural with respect to dependence on that, is rare.

Iccevaṃ [M 0.0028] sappayogaṃ tu, ñatvāna vacanadvayaṃ;

Kātabbo pana vohāro, yathāpāḷi vibhāvinā.

Thus, having understood the two numbers together with their proper application, the discerning one should make use of language according to the Pāli.

Idāni kālādivasena ākhyātappavattiṃ dīpayissāma – kālakārakapurisaparidīpakaṃ kriyālakkhaṇaṃ ākhyātikaṃ. Tatra kālanti atītānāgatapaccuppannavasena tayo kālā, atītānāgatapaccuppannāṇattiparikappakālātipattivasena pana cha, te ekekā tipurisakā.

Now, we shall explain the occurrence of verbs according to time, etc. The verb is characterized by action and illuminates time, kāraka, and person. Therein, time is threefold: past, future, and present. Alternatively, by way of past, future, present, imperative, optative, and conditional, it is sixfold—each of these has three persons.

Vuttappakārakālesu, yadidaṃ vattate yato;

Ākhyātikaṃ tato tassa, kāladīpanatā matā.

Since this verb functions in the tenses of the kind described, its nature of illuminating time is therefore acknowledged.

Kārakanti kammakattubhāvā. Te hi upacāramukhyasabhāvavasena karonti karaṇanti ca “kārakā”ti vuccanti. Teva yathākkamaṃ kriyānimitta taṃsādhaka taṃsabhāvāti veditabbā.

Kāraka means object, agent, and state. For they are called 'kārakas' because, by way of their figurative, primary, and intrinsic nature, they 'do' or are the 'means of doing'. They should be understood, in order, as the cause of the action, its accomplisher, and its intrinsic nature.

Kammaṃ kattā ca bhāvo ca, iccevaṃ kārakā tidhā;

Vibhattipaccayā ettha, vuttā nāññatra saccato.

Object, agent, and state—thus, the kārakas are threefold; Herein, the verbal inflections are stated for these, in truth, and for nothing else.

“Paribhaviyyati”ccādī, kamme sijjhanti kārake;

“Sambhavatī”tiādīni, sijjhare kattukārake.

‘Is overcome,’ etc., are formed in the object-kāraka; ‘arises,’ etc., are formed in the agent-kāraka.

“Vibhaviyyati”iccādī, bhāve sijjhanti kārake;

Tividhesvevametesu, vibhattipaccayā matā.

‘Is destroyed,’ etc., are formed in the state-kāraka; thus, in these three, the verbal inflections are held to apply.

Kārakattayamuttaṃ yaṃ, ākhyātaṃ natthi sabbaso;

Tasmā taddīpanattampi, tassākhyātassa bhāsitaṃ.

There is no verb whatsoever that is devoid of the triad of kārakas; therefore, its nature of illuminating them is also spoken of for that verb.

Kārakattaṃ tu bhāvassa, sacepi na samīritaṃ;

Kārakalakkhaṇe tena, bhāvena ca avatthunā.

Although the kāraka-nature of the bhāva is not stated in the definition of kāraka, and on account of that bhāva being without an object,

Kriyānipphatti [M 0.0029] natthīti, yuttitopi ca natthi taṃ;

Tathāpākhyātike tassa, tabbohāro niruttiyaṃ;

Patiṭṭhitanayovāti, mantvā amhehi bhāsito.

and since there is no accomplishment of action, and logically that kāraka-nature does not exist, nevertheless, considering that in grammar its usage in a verb is an established method, it has been stated by us.

Purisoti ekavacanabahuvacanakā paṭhamamajjhimuttamapurisā. Tattha paṭhamapuriso ākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇe sādhakavācake vā kammavācake vā tumhā’mhasaddavajjite paccattavacanabhūte nāmamhi “abhinīhāro samijjhati, bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesuñāṇa”ntiādīsu viya payujjamānepi, taṭṭhāniyatte sati “bhāsati vā karoti vā, pīḷiyakkhoti maṃ vidū, vuccatīti vacana”ntiādīsu viya appayujjamānepi sabbadhātūhi paro hoti. Katthaci pana pāḷippadese nāmassa appayuttattā paṭhamapurisapayogattho duranubodho bhavati, yathā “dukkhaṃ te vedayissāmi, tattha assāsayantu ma”nti. Tathā hi ettha “pādā”ti pāṭhaseso, tasmiṃ dukkhasāsanārocane vattuṃ avisahanavasena kilamantaṃ maṃ devassa ubho pādā assāsentu, vissaṭṭho kathehīti maṃ vadathāti adhippāyo ca bhavati.

By 'person' are meant the first, middle, and last persons, in singular and plural forms. Therein, the first person is used after all roots, whether the noun with which the verb agrees is expressed or not, when that noun expresses the agent or the object, is other than the words 'tumha' and 'amha', and is the subject—as in 'the aspiration succeeds' and 'enlightenment is called the knowledge in the four paths', or as in 'he speaks or acts', 'they know me as Pīḷiyakkha', and 'it is called speech'. However, in some Pāli passages, because the noun is not used, the meaning of the first person usage becomes difficult to understand, as in 'I will proclaim suffering to you; may they comfort me there.' Indeed, here 'pādā' (feet) is the textual remainder, and the intended meaning is: 'May the two feet of the deity comfort me, who am weary from being unable to speak in that proclamation of suffering,' and 'Tell me, "Speak freely."

Adhippāyo sudubbodho, yasmā vijjati pāḷiyaṃ;

Tasmā upaṭṭhahaṃ gaṇhe, garuṃ garumataṃ vidū.

Since the intended meaning in the Pāli is very difficult to understand, therefore the wise one should attend upon a revered teacher.

Tatrimāni bhūdhātādhikārattā bhūdhātuvasena nidassanapadāni. So paribhavati, te paribhavanti, paribhavati, paribhavanti. Sapatto abhibhaviyate, sabbā vityā’nubhūyate, abhibhaviyate, anubhūyateti. Yattha satipi nāmassa sādhakavācakatte apaccattavacanattā ākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇatā na labbhati, tattha kammavācakaṃ paccattavacanabhūtaṃ tulyādhikaraṇapadaṃ paṭicca paṭhamapurisādayo tayo labbhanti. Taṃ [M 0.0030] yathā? Paribhaviyyate puriso devadattena, paribhaviyyase tvaṃ devadattena, paribhaviyyamhe mayaṃ akusalehi dhammehi. Ettha panidaṃ vacanaṃ na vattabbaṃ “nindanti tuṇhimāsina’ntiādīsu satipi nāmassa kammavācakatte apaccattavacanattā ākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇatā na labbhatīti paṭhamapurisuppatti na siyā”ti. Kasmāti ce? “Nindanti tuṇhimāsina”ntiādīsu “janā”ti ajjhāharitabbassa sādhakavācakassa nāmassa saddhimākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇabhāvassa icchitattā. Evamuttaratrāpi nayo.

Here, because this is the section on the root 'bhū', are these illustrative examples based on the root 'bhū': 'He overcomes,' 'they overcome'; 'he overcomes,' 'they overcome.' 'The enemy is overcome,' 'all is experienced'; 'he is overcome,' 'it is experienced.' In a passive construction, although there is a noun expressing the agent, it does not agree with the verb because it is not the grammatical subject. There, the three persons are obtained based on the word which expresses the object and which functions as the grammatical subject in agreement with the verb. How so? 'The man is overcome by Devadatta,' 'you are overcome by Devadatta,' 'we are overcome by unwholesome states.' Here, however, this objection should not be raised: 'In cases like "they blame the silent one," since the noun, though expressing the object, is not the grammatical subject, there is no agreement with the verb, and therefore the first person verb cannot arise.' Why? Because in cases like 'they blame the silent one,' agreement with the verb is intended with the noun 'people,' which expresses the agent and must be supplied. This method also applies elsewhere.

Majjhimapuriso ākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇe sādhakavācake vā kammavācake vā paccattavacanabhūte tumhasadde payujjamānepi, taṭṭhāniyatte sati appayujjamānepi sabbadhātūhi paro hoti. Tvaṃ atibhavasi, tumhe atibhavatha, atibhavasi, atibhavatha. Tvaṃ paribhaviyase devadattena, tumhe paribhaviyavhe. Yattha satipi tumhasaddassa sādhakavācakatte apaccattavacanattā ākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇatā na labbhati, na tattha majjhimapuriso hoti. Itare pana dve honti kammavācakaṃ paccattavacanabhūtaṃ tulyādhikaraṇapadaṃ paṭicca. Taṃ yathā? Tayā abhibhaviyate sapatto, tayā abhibhaviye ahaṃ.

The second person occurs after all roots, even when the word 'tumha'—which is in the nominative case and expresses either the agent or the object—is used in agreement with the verb, or even when it is not used but is implied in that position. For example: Tvaṃ atibhavasi (You overcome), tumhe atibhavatha (you all overcome); or without the pronoun: atibhavasi, atibhavatha. Tvaṃ paribhaviyase devadattena (You are overcome by Devadatta), tumhe paribhaviyavhe (you all are overcome). But where, even though the word 'tumha' expresses the agent, agreement with the verb is not obtained because it is not in the nominative case, there the second person does not occur. However, the other two persons occur, depending on the word in agreement, which is in the nominative case and expresses the object. For example: Tayā abhibhaviyate sapatto (By you, the enemy is overcome); tayā abhibhaviye ahaṃ (by you, I am overcome).

Uttamapuriso ākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇe sādhakavācake vā kammavācake vā paccattavacanabhūte amhasadde payujjamānepi, taṭṭhāniyatte sati appayujjamānepi sabbadhātūhi paro hoti. Ahaṃ paribhavāmi, mayaṃ paribhavāma, paribhavāmi, paribhavāma. Ahaṃ paribhaviyyāmi akusalehi dhammehi, mayaṃ paribhaviyyāma, paribhaviyyāmi, paribhaviyyāma. Yattha satipi amhasaddassa sādhakavācakatte apaccattavacanattā ākhyātapadena tulyādhikaraṇatā na labbhati, na tattha [M 0.0031] uttamapuriso hoti. Itare pana dve honti kammavācakaṃ paccattavacanabhūtaṃ tulyādhikaraṇapadaṃ paṭicca. Taṃ yathā? Mayā anubhaviyate sampatti, mayā abhibhaviyase tvaṃ. Evaṃ yattha yattha sādhakavācakānaṃ vā kammavācakānaṃ vā nāmādīnaṃ paccattavacanabhūtānaṃ ākhyātapadehi tulyādhikaraṇatte laddhe tattha tattha paṭhamapurisādayo labbhanti, tasmā nāmādīnaṃ paccattavacanabhūtānaṃ tulyādhikaraṇabhāvoyeva paṭhamapurisādīnamuppattiyā kāraṇaṃ.

The first person occurs after all roots, even when the word 'amha'—which is in the nominative case and expresses either the agent or the object—is used in agreement with the verb, or even when it is not used but is implied in that position. For example: Ahaṃ paribhavāmi (I overcome), mayaṃ paribhavāma (we overcome); or without the pronoun: paribhavāmi, paribhavāma. Ahaṃ paribhaviyyāmi akusalehi dhammehi (I am overcome by unwholesome states), mayaṃ paribhaviyyāma (we are overcome); or without the pronoun: paribhaviyyāmi, paribhaviyyāma. But where, even though the word 'amha' expresses the agent, agreement with the verb is not obtained because it is not in the nominative case, there the first person does not occur. However, the other two persons occur, depending on the word in agreement, which is in the nominative case and expresses the object. For example: Mayā anubhaviyate sampatti (By me, prosperity is experienced); mayā abhibhaviyase tvaṃ (by me, you are overcome). Thus, wherever agreement with verbs is obtained for nouns and so forth, which are in the nominative case and express either the agent or the object, there the first, second, and third persons are obtained. Therefore, the state of being in the nominative case and in agreement with the verb, for nouns and so forth, is the very cause for the arising of the first, second, and third persons.

Dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā purisānamekābhidhāne paro puriso gahetabbo. Ettha ekābhidhānaṃ nāma ekato abhidhānaṃ ekakālābhidhānañca. Tañca kho casaddapayogeyeva, acasaddapayoge bhinnakālābhidhāne taggahaṇābhāvato. “Tumhe atthakusalā bhavatha, mayamatthakusalā bhavāma” iccevamādayo tappayogā. Tattha tumhe atthakusalā bhavatha – iccetasmiṃ vohāre “so ca atthakusalo bhavati, tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, tumhe atthakusalā bhavathā”ti evaṃ dvinnamekābhidhāne paro puriso gahetabbo. “Mayamatthakusalā bhavāma” iccetasmiṃ pana “so ca atthakusalo bhavati, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi, mayamatthakusalā bhavāmā”ti vā “tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi, mayamatthakusalā bhavāmā”ti vā evampi dvinnamekābhidhāne paro puriso gahetabbo. “So ca atthakusalo bhavati, tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi, mayamatthakusalā bhavāmā”ti vā “so ca atthakusalo bhavati, te ca atthakusalā bhavanti, tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, tumhe ca atthakusalā bhavatha, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi, mayamatthakusalā bhavāmā”ti vā evaṃ tiṇṇamekābhidhāne paro puriso gahetabbo.

When two or three persons are denoted by a single expression, the latter person should be taken. Here, 'single expression' means a unified denotation and a simultaneous denotation. And this occurs only with the use of the word 'ca'; without the use of the word 'ca', if the denotation is at different times, that latter person is not taken. Examples of such usage are: “Tumhe atthakusalā bhavatha” (Be ye skilled in the meaning), “mayamatthakusalā bhavāma” (Let us be skilled in the meaning), and so forth. Therein, in the expression “Tumhe atthakusalā bhavatha,” which is composed of “so ca atthakusalo bhavati, tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi” (He is skilled in the meaning, and you are skilled in the meaning), thus, when two are denoted by a single expression, the latter person should be taken, resulting in “tumhe atthakusalā bhavatha.” In the expression “Mayamatthakusalā bhavāma,” which is composed of “so ca atthakusalo bhavati, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi” (He is skilled in the meaning, and I am skilled in the meaning), or “tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi” (You are skilled in the meaning, and I am skilled in the meaning), thus also, when two are denoted by a single expression, the latter person should be taken, resulting in “mayamatthakusalā bhavāma.” And when composed of “so ca atthakusalo bhavati, tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi” (He is skilled in the meaning, and you are skilled in the meaning, and I am skilled in the meaning), or “so ca atthakusalo bhavati, te ca atthakusalā bhavanti, tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, tumhe ca atthakusalā bhavatha, ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi, mayamatthakusalā bhavāma” (He is skilled..., and they are skilled..., and you are skilled..., and you all are skilled..., and I am skilled..., and we are skilled...), thus, when three are denoted by a single expression, the latter person should be taken.

Aparopi [M 0.0032] atthanayo vuccati – “tvañca atthakusalo bhavasi, so ca atthakusalo bhavati, tumhe atthakusalā bhavathā”ti vā “ahañca atthakusalo bhavāmi, so ca atthakusalo bhavati, mayamatthakusalā bhavāmā”ti vā iminā nayena anekappabhedo atthanayo. Evaṃ sesāsu vibhattīsu pañcamīsattamiyādīsu paropuriso gahetabbo. Sabbesu ca kriyāpadesu bavhatthavācakesu bahuvacanantesu, na pana bahuvacanantesupi ekassattano vācakesu garukātabbassekassatthassa vācakesu ca kriyāpadesu. Ettha codanāsandīpaniyo imā gāthā –

Another method of interpretation is also stated: “You are skilled in the meaning, and he is skilled in the meaning; therefore, ‘tumhe atthakusalā bhavatha’ (be ye skilled in the meaning),” or “I am skilled in the meaning, and he is skilled in the meaning; therefore, ‘mayamatthakusalā bhavāma’ (let us be skilled in the meaning).” By this method, the way of interpretation has many variations. Similarly, in the remaining verbal endings—such as the imperative (fifth) and optative (seventh)—the latter person should be taken. And this applies to all verb forms ending in the plural that express a plural subject, but not, however, to verb forms that, though ending in the plural, express a single self or express a single revered entity. Herein, these verses serve for questioning and clarification:

“Tvañca bhavasi so cāpi, bhavati”ccādibhāsane;

“Tumhe bhavatha” iccādi, paroposo kathaṃ siyā?;

“In an expression such as, ‘You are, and he also is,’ how can ‘You all are,’ etc., be the latter person?”

“Ahaṃ bhavāmi so cāpi, bhavati”ccādibhāsane;

“Mayaṃ bhavāma”iccādi, uttamo ca kathaṃ siyā?;

“In an expression such as, ‘I am, and he also is,’ how can ‘We are,’ etc., be the first person?”

Ettha ca vuccate –

To this, it is said:

Pacchā vutto paro nāma, saññāya paṭipāṭiyā;

Evaṃ pana gahetabbo, paropurisanāmako.

What is stated later is called 'latter' (para), according to the established sequence. Thus should that which is named the 'latter person' be understood.

Paṭhamamhā paro nāma, majjhimo uttamopi ca;

Majjhimamhā paro nāma, uttamo puriso ruto.

Latter than the third person are the second and also the first; latter than the second person, the first person is declared.

Evaṃ tu gahaṇañhettha, vohārassānulomakaṃ;

Doso tadanulomamhi, gahaṇasmiṃ na vijjati.

Indeed, this understanding here conforms to usage; no fault is found in an understanding that is in such conformity.

“Tvañca bhadde sukhī hohi, eso cāpi mahāmigo”;

Iti pāṭho yato diṭṭho, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

“Be thou happy, good lady, and this great deer also”; since this text is seen, therefore we speak thus.

“Tumhe dve sukhitā hotha”, iccattho tattha dissati;

Evaṃpyayaṃ nayo vutto, attanomatiyā mama.

“Be ye two happy”—this is the meaning seen there. Even so, this method is stated according to my own opinion.

Attanomati [M 0.0033] kiñcāpi, kathitā sabbadubbalā;

Tathāpi nayamādāya, kathitattā akopiyā.

Although one's own opinion is said to be the weakest of all, nevertheless, since this is stated having adopted a method, it is irrefutable.

“Dhammena rajjaṃ kārentaṃ, raṭṭhā pabbājayittha maṃ;

Tvañca jānapadā ceva, negamā ca samāgatā”.

“You, and the country-folk, and the town-folk, having gathered together, banished me from the kingdom, though I was ruling righteously.”

“Ahañca maddidevī ca, jālīkaṇhājinā cubho;

Aññamaññaṃ sokanudā, vasāma assame tadā”.

“I and Queen Maddī, and both Jālī and Kaṇhājinā, mutually dispelling sorrow, lived then in the hermitage.”

Etā gāthāpi etassa, atthassa pana sādhikā;

Tāsu vuttanayeneva, attho supākaṭo siyā;

Evaṃ viññūhi viññeyyaṃ, bahunā bhāsitena kiṃ.

These verses, too, are corroborative of this meaning. By the method stated in them, the meaning should become very clear. Thus it should be understood by the wise; what is the use of much speech?

Ākārena manāpena, kathane yena kenaci;

Na virujjhati ce attho, taṃ pamāṇaṃ sudhīmataṃ.

In the speech of anyone whatsoever, if the meaning is not contradicted by a pleasing manner of expression, that is an authority for the wise.

Purisattayato eso, paropurisanāmako;

Nupalabbhati paccekaṃ, tadantogadhatova yaṃ.

This so-called 'latter person' is from the triad of persons; it is not found individually, since it is included within that triad.

Pāṭavatthāya sotūnaṃ, vohāratthesu sabbaso;

Visuṃ alabbhamānopi, labbhamānova uddhaṭo.

For the sake of the listeners' study, in all matters of usage, though not found separately, it is extracted as if it were found.

Saṅkhepatopettha purisappavatti evaṃ upalakkhitabbā “amhavacanatthe uttamo, tumhavacanatthe majjhimo, aññesaṃ vacanatthe paṭhamo”ti.

In brief, the application of the persons should be understood here thus: in the meaning of the word 'amha', the first person; in the meaning of the word 'tumha', the second person; in the meaning of others, the third person.

Tyādīnaṃ purisasaññā, yasmā vuttā tato idaṃ;

Tabbantākhyātikaṃ ñeyyaṃ, purisaparidīpakaṃ.

Since the designation 'person' is given to the verbal endings 'ti' and so forth, therefore this verbal form ending in them should be known as that which illuminates the person.

Evaṃ sabbathāpi ākhyātikassa kālakārakapurisaparidīpanatā vuttā.

Thus, in all respects, the verbal form's function of illuminating time, agent, and person has been stated.

Kriyālakkhaṇanti ettha kathaṃ ākhyātikassa kriyālakkhaṇatā veditabbā?

Regarding the phrase 'the characteristic of action,' how is the verbal form's nature as a characteristic of action to be understood?

Lakkhiyati [M 0.0034] kriyāyetaṃ, kriyā vā assa lakkhaṇaṃ;

Kriyālakkhaṇatā evaṃ, veditabbā tathā hi ca.

Action is characterized by this, or action is its characteristic; thus its nature as the characteristic of action should be understood, for so it is.

“Gacchati”ccādikaṃ sutvā, kriyāsandīpanaṃ padaṃ;

“Ākhyātika”nti dhīrehi, ākhyātaññūhi saññitaṃ.

Having heard a word like “gacchati,” which illuminates action, it is designated as “ākhyātika” by the wise who are knowers of verbal forms.

Lakkhaṇaṃ hoti nāmassa, yathā satvābhidhānatā;

Kriyābhidhānatā evaṃ, ākhyātasseva lakkhaṇaṃ.

Just as the characteristic of a noun is the designation of an entity, so the designation of action is the characteristic of the verbal form.

Atthato pana etassa, kriyāvācakatā idha;

Lakkhaṇaṃ iti viññeyyaṃ, lakkhaṇaññūhi lakkhitaṃ.

However, with respect to meaning, its expression of action here is to be understood as the characteristic defined by those who know characteristics.

“Kiṃ karosī”ti puṭṭhassa, “pacāmi”ccādinā “ahaṃ”;

Paṭivācāya dānena, kriyāvācakatā matā.

When one is asked, “What are you doing?”, by the giving of a reply such as, “I am cooking,” it is considered an expression of action.

Evamākhyātikassa kriyālakkhaṇatā veditabbā;

Idāni kālesu vibhattippavatti evaṃ veditabbā –

Thus, the characteristic of action in the verb (ākhyātika) should be understood. Now, the application of the verbal endings in the tenses should be understood as follows:

Paccuppannamhi kālasmiṃ, vattamānā pavattati;

Āsiṭṭhāṇāpanatthesu, paccuppannamhi pañcamī.

In the present time, the present tense (vattamānā) occurs. In the meanings of command and entreaty, the fifth [inflection] (pañcamī) is used in the present.

Paccuppanne parikappā-numatyatthesu sattamī;

Appaccakkhe atītamhi, parokkhā sampavattati.

In the present, the seventh [inflection] (sattamī) is used in the meanings of supposition and permission. In the past not directly perceived, the perfect (parokkhā) occurs.

Hiyyo pabhuti kālasmiṃ, atītamhi pavattati;

Paccakkhe vā apaccakkhe, hiyyattanī niruttitā.

In the past time beginning from yesterday, it occurs. Whether directly perceived or not directly perceived, it is called the aorist (hiyyattanī).

Ajjappabhuti kālasmiṃ, atītamhi pavattati;

Paccakkhe vā apaccakkhe, samīpejjatanavhayā.

In the past time beginning from today, it occurs. Whether directly perceived or not, it is called the imperfect (ajjatanī).

Anāgate bhavissantī, kālasmiṃ sampavattati;

Kriyātipannamattamhi, tīte kālātipattikā;

Anāgatepi hotīti, niruttaññūhi bhāsitā.

In the future time, the future tense (bhavissantī) occurs. In the past, in the case of the non-completion of an action, the conditional (kālātipattikā) occurs; it also occurs in the future—thus it has been said by those who know etymology.

Evaṃ kālesu vibhattippavattiṃ ñatvā ye te suttantesu vicittā suvisadavipulatikhiṇabuddhivisayabhūtā payogā dissanti, tesu pāṭavamicchantehi tyādikkamena vuccamānā kriyāpadamālā [M 0.0035] sallakkhitabbā – bhavati, bhavanti. Bhavasi, bhavatha. Bhavāmi, bhavāma. Bhavate, bhavante. Bhavase, bhavavhe. Bhave, bhavāmhe. Ayaṃ aññayogādirahitā kriyāpadamālā.

Having thus understood the occurrence of the verbal endings in the tenses, those who desire proficiency in the varied, very clear, extensive applications which are the domain of a sharp intellect and are seen in the suttas, should note the series of verbal forms spoken in the order beginning with 'ti'—bhavati, bhavanti; bhavasi, bhavatha; bhavāmi, bhavāma; bhavate, bhavante; bhavase, bhavavhe; bhave, bhavāmhe. This is the series of verbal forms without connection to another word.

Dissanti ca suttantesu atthasambhavepi aññayogādirahitāni kriyāpadāni. Seyyathidaṃ? “Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccāti, yadā paññāya passati. Yaṃ maṃ bhaṇasi sārathi. Aññaṃ sepaṇṇi gacchāmi” iccevamādīni etassatthassa paridīpaniyā kriyāpadamālā.

And in the suttas, verbal forms without connection to another word are seen, even when the meaning is present. For example: “When one sees with wisdom that ‘all formations are impermanent’”; “What you say to me, charioteer”; “I will go to another Sepaṇṇi tree.” These and others are a series of verbal forms that illustrate this meaning.

Ettha tividho kriyāpadesu yogo tayogo, mayogo, aññayogo ca. Tattha majjhimapurisā tayogavasena gahetabbā, uttamapurisā mayogavasena. Paṭhamapurisā aññayogavasena. Tyādīnamettha paṭipāṭiyā ayaṃ anugīti –

Herein, the connection (yoga) in verbal forms is threefold: ta-connection, ma-connection, and añña-connection. Therein, the middle person is to be understood by way of the ta-connection, the first person by way of the ma-connection, and the third person by way of the añña-connection. For these, beginning with 'ti', this is the verse in order:

Aññayogena paṭhamā, tayogena tu majjhimā;

Mayogenuttamā honti, gahetabbā vibhāvinā.

The third person is with the añña-connection, the middle person with the ta-connection, and the first person with the ma-connection; thus they should be understood by the discerning.

Sotūnaṃ payogesu kosallatthaṃ aññayogādisahitamaparampi kriyāpadamālaṃ vadāma – so bhavati, te bhavanti. Tvaṃ bhavasi, tumhe bhavatha. Ahaṃ bhavāmi, mayaṃ bhavāma. So bhavate, te bhavante. Tvaṃ bhavase, tumhe bhavavhe. Ahaṃ bhave, mayaṃ bhavāmhe. Ayaṃ aññayogādisahitā kriyāpadamālā.

For the sake of the listeners’ skill in usages, we state another series of verbal forms, together with the añña-connection, etc.—so bhavati, te bhavanti (he is, they are); tvaṃ bhavasi, tumhe bhavatha (you are, you all are); ahaṃ bhavāmi, mayaṃ bhavāma (I am, we are); so bhavate, te bhavante (he is, they are); tvaṃ bhavase, tumhe bhavavhe (you are, you all are); ahaṃ bhave, mayaṃ bhavāmhe (I am, we are). This is the series of verbal forms with the añña-connection, etc.

Dissanti ca suttantesu aññayogādisahitānipi kriyāpadāni. Seyyathidaṃ? “Yaṃpāyaṃ deva kumāro suppatiṭṭhitapādo, idampimassa mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati, tassimāni satta ratanāni bhavanti. Yo dandhakāle tarati[M 0.0036], taraṇīye ca dandhati, tvaṃsi ācariyo mama, ahampi daṭṭhukāmosmi, pitaraṃ me idhāgataṃ” iccevamādīni etassatthassa paridīpaniyā kriyāpadamālā.

And in the suttas, verbal forms with the añña-connection, etc., are also seen. For example: “That this prince, O deva, has well-established feet, this also is a great man’s mark of a great man”; “For him there are these seven treasures”; “He who hurries when it is time to be slow, and is slow when it is time to hurry”; “You are my teacher”; “I too am desirous of seeing my father who has come here.” These and others are a series of verbal forms that illustrate this meaning.

Yo tumhasaddena vattabbe atthe nipatati, na pana hoti tumhatthavācako, neso saddo kriyāpadassa tayogasahitattaṃ sādheti, aññadatthu aññayogasahitattaññeva sādheti. Yo ca amhasaddena vattabbe atthe nipatati, na pana hoti amhatthavācako, na sopi saddo kriyāpadassa mayogasahitattaṃ sādheti, aññadatthu aññayogasahitattaññeva sādheti.

Whatever word is used in a meaning to be expressed by the word 'tumha' but is not a word that expresses the meaning of 'tumha', that word does not establish a ta-connection with the verbal form; on the contrary, it establishes only an añña-connection. And whatever word is used in a meaning to be expressed by the word 'amha' but is not a word that expresses the meaning of 'amha', that word also does not establish a ma-connection with the verbal form; on the contrary, it establishes only an añña-connection.

Tatra tumhasaddena tāva vattabbatthe – “na bhavaṃ eti puññatthaṃ, sivirājassa dassanaṃ. Māyasmā samaggassa saṅghassa bhedāya parakkami. Idha bhante bhagavā paṃsukūlaṃ dhovatū”ti iccevamādayo payogā. Amhasaddena pana vattabbatthe “upāli taṃ mahāvīra, pāde vandati satthuno. Sāvako te mahāvīra, saraṇo vandati satthuno”ti ca iccevamādayo payogā. Idametthupalakkhitabbaṃ “tvaṃ tumhe ahaṃ maya”nti atthadīpaka tayoga mayogato añño aññatthadīpano payogoyeva aññayogo nāma, tattha paṭhamapuriso bhavatīti.

Here, first, regarding the meaning to be expressed by the word 'tumha', are usages such as: 'The venerable one does not come for merit, for the sight of King Sivi'; 'Let the venerable one not strive to break the harmonious Saṅgha'; 'Here, venerable sir, let the Blessed One wash the rag-robe.' As for the meaning to be expressed by the word 'amha', are usages such as: 'Upāli, O great hero, worships the feet of the Teacher'; 'Your disciple, O great hero, having gone for refuge, worships the Teacher.' Herein, this should be noted: other than the ta-connection and ma-connection which illuminate the meaning of 'tvaṃ, tumhe, ahaṃ, mayaṃ', any other usage which illuminates another meaning is called 'añña-yoga'; therein, the third person occurs.

Yajjevaṃ “sabbāyasaṃ kūṭamatippamāṇaṃ, paggayha so tiṭṭhasi antalikkhe. Esa sutvā pasīdāmi, vaco te isisattamā”tiādīsu kathaṃ. Ettha hi majjhimuttamapurisasambhavoyeva dissati, na tu paṭhamapurisasambhavoti? Vuccate – “sabbāyasaṃ kūṭamatippamāṇaṃ, paggayha so tiṭṭhasi antalikkhe”tiādīsu “so”tiādikassa nāmasaddassa tumha’mhasaddassatthavācakasaddehi“tiṭṭhasī”tiādīnaṃ syādyantānaṃ padānaṃ dassanato accantamajjhāharitabbehi [M 0.0037] samānādhikaraṇattā tagguṇabhūtattā ca majjhimuttamapurisasambhavo samadhigantabbo. Īdisesu payogesu syādyantānaṃ dassanavasena avijjamānānipi ajjhāharitabbāni “tvamaha”miccādīni padāni bhavanti. Katthaci pana paripuṇṇāni dissanti “sātvaṃ vaṅkamanuppattā, kathaṃ maddi karissasi. So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā pura”nti iccevamādīsu.

If so, how is it in passages such as, 'Having taken up the all-iron, immeasurable club, you, that one, stand in the sky,' and 'Hearing your words, O supreme sage, I, this one, am pleased'? Here, indeed, only the occurrence of the middle and first persons is seen, not the occurrence of the third person, is it not? It is said: in passages such as '...you, that one, stand in the sky,' the occurrence of the middle and first persons should be understood because the noun 'so' and so on has co-reference with, and takes on the quality of, the words expressing the meaning of 'tumha' and 'amha' which must absolutely be supplied along with the finite verb forms such as 'tiṭṭhasi'. In such usages, even if they are not present, words such as 'tvaṃ' and 'ahaṃ' are to be supplied based on the appearance of the finite verb forms. In some places, however, they are seen in full, as in: 'You, that one, having gone astray, how will you act, Maddī?' and 'I, that one, will wander from village to village, from city to city.'

Ākhyātikassa kriyālakkhaṇattā aliṅgabhedattā ca tiṇṇaṃ liṅgānaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvaparidīpanatthaṃ aparampi kriyāpadamālaṃ vadāma –

Because the verb (ākhyāta) is characterized by action and has no distinction of gender, for the purpose of clarifying its state of being common to the three genders, we state another series of verbal forms:

Puriso bhavati, kaññā bhavati, cittaṃ bhavati, purisā bhavanti, kaññāyo bhavanti, cittāni bhavanti. Bho purisa tvaṃ bhavasi, bhoti kaññe tvaṃ bhavasi, bho citta tvaṃ bhavasi, bhavanto purisā tumhe bhavatha, bhotiyo kaññāyo tumhe bhavatha, bhavanto cittāni tumhe bhavatha. Ahaṃ puriso bhavāmi, ahaṃ kaññā bhavāmi, ahaṃ cittaṃ bhavāmi, mayaṃ purisā bhavāma, mayaṃ kaññāyo bhavāma, mayaṃ cittāni bhavāma.

A man is, a maiden is, a mind is. Men are, maidens are, minds are. O man, you are. O maiden, you are. O mind, you are. O men, you are. O maidens, you are. O minds, you are. I am a man. I am a maiden. I am a mind. We are men. We are maidens. We are minds.

Esa nayo attanopadesu, sesavibhattīnaṃ sabbapadesupi. Ayamākhyātikassa tiṇṇaṃ liṅgānaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvaparidīpanī kriyāpadamālāva.

This is the method for the middle voice (attanopada), and also for all forms of the remaining inflections. This is indeed the series of verbal forms that clarifies the common nature of the verb with respect to the three genders.

Vuttañhetaṃ niruttipiṭake “kriyālakkhaṇamākhyātikamaliṅgabheda”miti. Tatra aliṅgabhedamiti ko attho? Itthipumanapuṃsakānaṃ avisesattho vuccate “aliṅgabheda”miti. Yathā “puriso gacchati, kaññā gacchati, cittaṃ gacchatī”ti. Catudhā uddiṭṭhakriyāpadesu yathā “bhavatī”ti akārānantaratyantapadaṃ gahetvā “bhavati bhavanti bhavasī”tiādinā kriyāpadamālā sabbathā katā, evaṃ “ubbhavati”ccādīnipi akārānantaratyantapadāni gahetvā “ubbhavati ubbhavanti ubbhavasī”tiādinā [M 0.0038] kriyāpadamālā sabbathā kātabbā. “Bhoti sambhotī”tiādīni pana okārānantaratyantapadāni, “bhāveti vibhāvetī”tiādīni ca ekārānantaratyantapadāni gahetvā pāḷinayānusāreneva padamālā kātabbā, nayidha vuttanayānusārena. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu duranubodhā kriyāpadagati. Ato labbhamānavasena kriyāpadamālā kātabbā. Na hi loke lokiyā sabbe dhātusadde paccekaṃ sabbehipi channavutiyā vacanehi yojetvā vadanti, evaṃ avadantānampi nesaṃ kathā aparipuṇṇā nāma na hoti, tasmā vajjetabbaṭṭhānaṃ vajjetvā yathāsambhavaṃ padamālā kātabbā. Evaṃ pañcamiyādīsupi vibhattīsu. Ayaṃ vattamānavibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

This is stated in the Niruttipiṭaka: 'A verb is characterized by action and is without gender distinction.' Here, what is the meaning of 'without gender distinction'? It means there is no distinction among feminine, masculine, and neuter; this is called 'aliṅgabheda.' For example: 'A man goes, a woman goes, the mind goes.' Among the fourfold indicated verb-forms, just as with 'bhavati,' taking the word ending in 'ti' preceded by the vowel 'a,' the entire paradigm of verb-forms—'bhavati, bhavanti, bhavasi,' etc.—has been fully formed. Similarly, for verbs like 'ubbhavati,' taking those words ending in 'ti' preceded by the vowel 'a,' the entire paradigm—'ubbhavati, ubbhavanti, ubbhavasi,' etc.—should be fully formed. For words like 'bhoti, sambhoti,' etc., which end in 'ti' preceded by the vowel 'o,' and 'bhāveti, vibhāveti,' etc., which end in 'ti' preceded by the vowel 'e,' the paradigm of verb-forms should be constructed strictly following the Pāli method, and not the method described here. In such cases, the derivation of verb-forms is difficult to comprehend. Therefore, the paradigm of verb-forms should be formed according to what is available. Indeed, in the world, worldly people do not use every verbal root with all ninety-six endings individually when speaking. Even when they do not speak in this way, their speech is not considered incomplete. Hence, avoiding what should be avoided, the paradigm of verb-forms should be formed as is possible. The same applies to the fifth and other inflections. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the present tense inflection.

Ito paṭṭhāya pana yathuddiṭṭhapadāneva pariṇāmetvā pariṇāmetvā pañcamiyādīnaṃ mātikābhāvena gahetabbāni. Idāni pana tayogādisahitāsahitavasena dvidhā kriyāpadamālāyo dassessāma kvacādesavasena sambhūtāni ca rūpantarāni sotūnaṃ sukhadhāraṇatthañceva purisappayoge asammohatthañca.

From this point onward, however, the previously indicated words, having been repeatedly transformed, should be taken as the matrix for the fifth and other inflections. Now, we will present the paradigms of verb-forms in two ways—with and without the pronouns for the three persons—along with other forms that have arisen through occasional substitution, for the sake of the listeners' easy retention and to prevent confusion in the application of the persons.

Bhavatu, bhavantu. Bhavāhi, bhava, bhavatha. Bhavāmi, bhavāma. Bhavataṃ, bhavantaṃ. Bhavassu, bhavavho. Bhave, bhavāmase. So bhavatu, te bhavantu. Tvaṃ bhavāhi, bhava, tumhe bhavatha. Ahaṃ bhavāmi, mayaṃ bhavāma. So bhavataṃ, te bhavantaṃ. Tvaṃ bhavassu, tumhe bhavavho. Ahaṃ bhave, mayaṃ bhavāmase. Ayaṃ pañcamīvibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

Let him be, let them be. Be, be, you all be. Let me be, let us be. Let him be, let them be. Be, you all be. Let me be, let us be. He, let him be; they, let them be. You, be, be; you all, you all be. I, let me be; we, let us be. He, let him be; they, let them be. You, be; you all, you all be. I, let me be; we, let us be. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the fifth inflection.

Bhaveyya, bhave, bhaveyyuṃ. Bhaveyyāsi, bhaveyyātha. Bhaveyyāmi, bhaveyyāma, bhavemu. Bhavetha, bhaveraṃ. Bhavetho, bhaveyyāvho. Bhaveyyaṃ, bhaveyyāmhe iti vā, so bhaveyya[M 0.0039], bhave, te bhaveyyuṃ. Tvaṃ bhaveyyāsi, tumhe bhaveyyātha. Ahaṃ bhaveyyāmi, mayaṃ bhaveyyāma, bhavemu. So bhavetha, te bhaveraṃ. Tvaṃ bhavetho, tumhe bhaveyyāvho. Ahaṃ bhaveyyaṃ, mayaṃ bhaveyyāmhe iti vā. Ayaṃ sattamīvibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

He might be, he might be, they might be. You might be, you all might be. I might be, we might be, we might be. He might be, they might be. You might be, you all might be. I might be, or we might be. He, he might be, he might be; they, they might be. You, you might be; you all, you all might be. I, I might be; we, we might be, we might be. He, he might be; they, they might be. You, you might be; you all, you all might be. I, I might be; or we, we might be. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the seventh inflection.

Babhūva, babhūvu. Babhūve, babhūvittha. Babhūvaṃ, babhūvimha. Babhūvittha, babhūvire. Babhūvittho, babhūvivho. Babhūviṃ, babhūvimhe iti vā, so babhūva, te babhūvu. Tvaṃ babhūve, tumhe babhūvittha. Ahaṃ babhūvaṃ, mayaṃ babhūvimha. So babhūvittha, te babhūvire. Tvaṃ babhūvittho, tumhe babhūvivho. Ahaṃ babhūviṃ, mayaṃ babhūvimhe iti vā. Ayaṃ parokkhāvibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

He became, they became. You became, you all became. I became, we became. He became, they became. You became, you all became. I became, or we became. He, he became; they, they became. You, you became; you all, you all became. I, I became; we, we became. He, he became; they, they became. You, you became; you all, you all became. I, I became; or we, we became. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the perfect tense inflection.

Abhavā, abhavū. Abhavo, abhavattha. Abhavaṃ, abhavamhā. Abhavattha, abhavatthuṃ. Abhavase, abhavavhaṃ. Abhaviṃ, abhavamhase iti vā, so abhavā, te abhavū. Tvaṃ abhavo, tumhe abhavattha. Ahaṃ abhavaṃ, mayaṃ abhavamhā. So abhavattha, te abhavatthuṃ. Tvaṃ abhavase, tumhe abhavavhaṃ. Ahaṃ abhaviṃ, mayaṃ abhavamhase iti vā. Ayaṃ hiyyattanīvibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, we were. He was, they were. You were, you all were. I was, or we were. He, he was; they, they were. You, you were; you all, you all were. I, I was; we, we were. He, he was; they, they were. You, you were; you all, you all were. I, I was; or we, we were. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the imperfect tense inflection.

Abhavi, abhavuṃ. Abhavo, abhavittha. Abhaviṃ, abhavimhā. Abhavā, abhavū. Abhavase, abhavivhaṃ. Abhavhaṃ, abhavimhe iti vā, so abhavi, te abhavuṃ. Tvaṃ abhavo, tumhe abhavittha. Ahaṃ abhaviṃ, mayaṃ abhavimhā. So abhavā, te abhavū. Tvaṃ abhavase, tumhe abhavivhaṃ. Ahaṃ abhavaṃ, mayaṃ abhavimhe iti vā. Ayaṃ ajjatanīvibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

He became, they became. You became, you all became. I became, we became. He became, they became. You became, you all became. I became, or we became. He, he became; they, they became. You, you became; you all, you all became. I, I became; we, we became. He, he became; they, they became. You, you became; you all, you all became. I became, or we became. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the aorist inflection.

Ettha panajjataniyā uṃvacanassa iṃsumādesavasena bhavatino rūpantarānipi veditabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ? Te bhaviṃsu, samubbhaviṃsu, pabhaviṃsu, parābhaviṃsu, sambhaviṃsu, pātubhaviṃsu, pātubbhaviṃsu[M 0.0040], imāni akammakapadāni. Paribhaviṃsu, abhibhaviṃsu, adhibhaviṃsu, atibhaviṃsu, anubhaviṃsu, samanubhaviṃsu, abhisambhaviṃsu.

Here, however, other forms of the root bhū should also be known, arising from the substitution of iṃsu for the aorist plural ending uṃ. As follows: They were, they arose, they originated, they were defeated, they came to be, they appeared, they manifested—these are intransitive words. They treated with contempt, they overcame, they overpowered, they surpassed, they experienced, they fully experienced, they fully realized.

“Adhibhosu”nti rūpampi, yasmā dissati pāḷiyaṃ;

Tasmā hi nayato ñe yyaṃ, “paribhosu”ntiādikaṃ.

The form 'adhibhosu' also exists, since it is seen in the Pāli Canon; therefore, by this method, 'paribhosu' and the like are to be known.

Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi – “evaṃvihāriñcāvuso bhikkhuṃ rūpā adhibhosuṃ, na bhikkhu rūpe adhibhosī”ti. Imāni sakammakapadāni, evamajjataniyā uṃvacanassa iṃsumādesavasena bhavatino rūpantarāni bhavanti. Apica

Herein, this is the Pāli text: 'Friends, forms overpowered a monk dwelling thus; the monk did not overpower forms.' These are intransitive words. Thus, in the aorist, by way of the substitution of iṃsu for the uṃ-ending, other forms of the root bhū exist. Moreover,

“Anvabhi” itirūpampi, ajjatanyā padissati;

Tasmā hi nayato ñeyyaṃ, “ajjhabhi”ccādikampi ca.

The form 'anvabhi' also is seen in the aorist; therefore, by this method, 'ajjhabhi' and the like should also be known.

Tatrāyaṃ pāḷi – so tena kammena divaṃ samakkami, sukhañca khiḍḍāratiyo ca anvabhīti. Tattha anvabhīti anu abhīti chedo. Anūti upasaggo. Abhīti ākhyātikapadanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, this is the Pāli text: 'By that deed, he proceeded to heaven, and experienced happiness, sport, and delight.' Therein, 'anvabhī' is to be analyzed as 'anu' and 'abhī'. 'Anu' is a prefix. 'Abhī' is to be understood as the verbal form.

Bhavissati, bhavissanti. Bhavissasi, bhavissatha. Bhavissāmi, bhavissāma. Bhavissate, bhavissante. Bhavissase, bhavissavhe. Bhavissaṃ, bhavissāmhe iti vā, so bhavissati, te bhavissanti. Tvaṃ bhavissasi, tumhe bhavissatha. Ahaṃ bhavissāmi, mayaṃ bhavissāma. So bhavissate, te bhavissante. Tvaṃ bhavissase, tumhe bhavissavhe. Ahaṃ bhavissaṃ, mayaṃ bhavissāmhe iti vā. Ayaṃ bhavissantīvibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

He will be, they will be. You will be, you all will be. I will be, we will be. He will be, they will be. You will be, you all will be. I will be, or we will be. He, he will be; they, they will be. You, you will be; you all, you all will be. I, I will be; we, we will be. He, he will be; they, they will be. You, you will be; you all, you all will be. I, I will be; or we, we will be. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the future tense inflection.

Abhavissā, abhavissaṃsu. Abhavisse, abhavissatha. Abhavissaṃ, abhavissāmhā. Abhavissatha, abhavissisu. Abhavissase, abhavissavhe. Abhavissiṃ, abhavissāmhase iti vā, so abhavissā, te abhavissaṃsu. Tvaṃ abhavisse, tumhe [M 0.0041] abhavissatha. Ahaṃ abhavissaṃ, mayaṃ abhavissāmhā. So abhavissatha, te abhavissisu. Tvaṃ abhavissase, tumhe abhavissavhe. Ahaṃ abhavissiṃ, mayaṃ abhavissāmhase iti vā. Ayaṃ kālātipattivibhattivasena kriyāpadamālāniddeso.

He would have been, they would have been. You would have been, you all would have been. I would have been, we would have been. He would have been, they would have been. You would have been, you all would have been. I would have been, or we would have been. He, he would have been; they, they would have been. You, you would have been; you all, you all would have been. I, I would have been; we, we would have been. He, he would have been; they, they would have been. You, you would have been; you all, you all would have been. I, I would have been; or we, we would have been. This is the exposition of the paradigm of verb-forms by way of the conditional tense inflection.

Vohārabhedakusalena subuddhinā yo,

Kaccāyanena kathito jinasāsanatthaṃ;

Tyādikkamo tadanugaṃ kiriyāpadānaṃ,

Katvā kamo bhavatidhātuvasena vutto.

That sequence beginning with ti, which was expounded by the wise Kaccāyana, skilled in distinguishing conventional speech, for the sake of the Victor's Dispensation—that sequence of verbal forms, following that order, has been stated here by way of the root bhavati.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the proficiency of the wise who are skilled in the modes of expression within the ninefold Canon with its commentary and the three Piṭakas,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise that was composed,

Bhavatino kriyāpadamālāvibhāgo nāma

this is the section called 'The Verb Paradigm of Bhavati',

Dutiyo paricchedo.

the Second Chapter.

3. Pakiṇṇakavinicchaya

3. Miscellaneous Determinations

Ito paraṃ pavakkhāmi, pakiṇṇakavinicchayaṃ;

Sappayogesu atthesu, viññūnaṃ pāṭavatthayā.

Hereafter, I shall explain the miscellaneous determinations for the proficiency of the discerning in applicable matters.

Tattha atthuddhāro, atthasaddacintā, atthātisayayogo, samānāsamānavasenavacanasaṅgaho, āgamalakkhaṇavasena vibhattivacanasaṅgaho, kālavasena vibhattivacanasaṅgaho, kālasaṅgaho, pakaraṇasaṃsandanā, vattamānādīnaṃ vacanatthavibhāvanā cāti navadhā vinicchayo veditabbo.

Herein, the determination should be understood in nine ways: extraction of meaning, consideration of meaning and sound, connection with exceeding meaning, collection of expressions by way of similarity and dissimilarity, collection of inflections and expressions by way of scriptural characteristics, collection of inflections and expressions by way of time, temporal collection, contextual correlation, and differentiation of the meaning of expressions such as the present tense, etc.

Atthuddhāre tāva samānasutikapadānamatthuddhāraṇaṃ karissāma. Etthākhyātapadasaññitānaṃ bhotisadda bhavesaddānamattho uddharitabbo. Tathā hete nāmikapadasaññitehi aparehi bhotisadda bhavesaddehi samānasutikāpi asamānatthā ceva honti asamānavibhattikā ca. Sāsanasmiñhi [M 0.0042] keci saddā aññamaññaṃ samānasutikā samānāpi asamānatthā asamānapavattinimittā asamānaliṅgā asamānavibhattikā asamānavacanakā asamānantā asamānakālikā asamānapadajātikā ca bhavanti.

First, in the extraction of meaning, we shall extract the meaning of words that are homophonous. Here, the meaning of the words 'bhoti' and 'bhave', which are designated as verbal forms, must be extracted. For these words, though homophonous with other words designated as nominal forms, they are indeed dissimilar in meaning and dissimilar in inflection. Indeed, in the Dispensation, some words, though homophonous with each other, are dissimilar in meaning, dissimilar in the cause of their occurrence, dissimilar in gender, dissimilar in inflection, dissimilar in number, dissimilar in ending, dissimilar in tense, and dissimilar in word class.

Tesamasamānatthatte “sabbañhi taṃ jīrati dehanissitaṃ. Appassutāyaṃ puriso, balibaddova jīrati. Santo tasito. Pahu santo na bharati. Santo ācikkhate muni. Santo sappurisā loke. Santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmi”nti evamādayo payogā. Ettha jīratisaddadvayaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ navabhāvāpagamavaḍḍhanavācakaṃ. Santosaddapañcakaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ parissamappattasamānopasantopalabbhamānavācakanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding their dissimilarity in meaning, there are such usages as: 'For all that is body-dependent decays. This person of little learning decays like an ox.' 'The weary one is thirsty.' 'The capable one, being present, does not support.' 'The sage, being calm, declares.' 'Good people exist in the world.' 'Existing ones are found in the world.' Here, the two words 'jīrati' should be understood, as appropriate, as expressing the passing away of newness or growth. The five words 'santo' should be seen as conveying, as appropriate, having attained weariness, equality, tranquility, and being found.

Asamānapavattinimittatte pana “akataññū mittadubbhī, assaddho akataññūcā”tievamādayo. Ettha ca akataññūsaddadvayaṃ katākatājānanajānanapavattinimittaṃ paṭicca sambhūtattā asamānapavattinimittakanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But regarding dissimilarity in the cause of occurrence, there are such usages as: 'ungrateful, betraying friends; faithless and ungrateful,' and so on. Here, the two words 'akataññū' should be understood as having dissimilar causes of occurrence, since they arise dependent on knowing or not knowing what has been done.

Asamānaliṅgatte “sukhī hotu pañcasikha sakko devānamindo. Tvañca bhadde sukhī hohi. Yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti. Mātā me atthi, sā mayā posetabbā”ti evamādayo. Ettha sukhīsaddadvayaṃ sāsaddadvayañca pumitthiliṅgavasena asamānaliṅganti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding dissimilarity in gender, there are such usages as: 'May Pañcasikha be happy, Sakka, lord of the devas. And you, good lady, be happy. Wherever she is present. I have a mother; she should be supported by me,' and so on. Here, the two words 'sukhī' and the two words 'sā' should be understood as having dissimilar genders by way of masculine and feminine forms.

Asamānavibhattikatte “āhāre udare yato. Yato pajānāti sahetudhamma”nti evamādayo. Ettha yatosaddadvayaṃ [M 0.0043] paṭhamāpañcamīvibhattisahitattā asamānavibhattikanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding dissimilarity in inflection, there are such usages as: 'Restrained in food, in the belly.' 'Because one understands conditioned phenomena,' and so on. Here, the two words 'yato' should be understood as having dissimilar inflections, being accompanied by the first and fifth inflections respectively.

Asamānavacanakatte ime payogā –

Regarding dissimilarity in number, these are the usages:

“Yāya mātu bhato poso, imaṃ lokaṃ avekkhati;

Tampi pāṇadadiṃ santiṃ, hanti kuddho puthujjano”ti

“The man, fed by his mother, looks upon this world; yet an angry commoner kills even that peaceful life-giver.”

Ādīsu hantisaddo ekavacano.

In these examples, the word 'hanti' is singular.

“Ime nūna araññasmiṃ, migasaṅghāni luddakā;

Vākurāhi parikkhippa, sobbhaṃ pātetvā tāvade;

Vikkosamānā tibbāhi, hanti nesaṃ varaṃ vara”nti.

“Surely these hunters in the forest, having surrounded herds of deer with snares and immediately caused them to fall into a pit, screaming loudly, kill the best among them one by one.”

Ādīsu pana bahuvacano. “Sīlavā vattasampanno. Etha tumhe āyasmanto sīlavā hotha. Santo danto niyato brahmacārī. Santo have sabbhi pavedayanti. Mahārājā yasassī so. Cattāro mahārājā”ti evamādīsu sīlavāsaddādayo ekavacanabahuvacanakā.

In these examples, however, it is plural. 'The virtuous one, accomplished in conduct. Come, venerable ones, be virtuous. Calm, tamed, restrained, a celibate. The calm ones indeed make known to the good. That great king is glorious. The four great kings'—in such examples, words like 'sīlavā' and so on are singular and plural.

Asamānantatte pana yattha samānasutikānaṃ asamānavibhattikattaṃ vā asamānavacanattaṃ vā upalabbhati. Teyeva payogā. Taṃ yathā? “Sataṃ sampajānaṃ, sataṃ dhammo, santo danto, santo sappurisā” iccevamādayo.

But regarding dissimilarity in ending, where dissimilarity in inflection or dissimilarity in number is found among homophonous words, those very usages apply. How is that? For example: 'Mindful, clearly knowing; the Dhamma of the good; calm, tamed; good people'—and so on.

Asamānakālatte “nanu te sutaṃ brāhmaṇa bhaññamāne, devā na issanti purisaparakkamassa. Te janā pāramissanti, maccudheyyaṃ suduttara”nti evamādayo. Ettha issantisaddadvayaṃ vattamānābhavissantīkālavasena asamānakālanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vattamānābhavissantīvibhattivasena pana asamānavibhattikantipi.

Regarding dissimilarity in tense, there are such usages as: 'Have you not heard, Brahmin, it being spoken, that the devas do not envy human effort? Those people will cross over the realm of death, so hard to traverse,' and so on. Here, the two words 'issanti' should be understood as dissimilar in tense by way of present and future tenses. But also, by way of present and future inflections, they are dissimilar in inflection.

Asamānapadajātikatte [M 0.0044] “sayaṃ samāhito nāgo, sayaṃ abhiññāya kamuddiseyyaṃ. Pathe dhāvantiyā pati, ekaṃsaṃ ajinaṃ katvā, pādesu sirasā pati. Giriṃ caṇḍoraṇaṃ patī”ti evamādayo. Ettha sayaṃsaddadvayaṃ nāmanipātavasena patisaddattayaṃ nāmākhyātopasaggavasena asamānapadajātikanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Regarding dissimilarity in word class, there are such usages as: 'The self-composed elephant; having understood by himself, to whom would he declare? The husband of one running on the path; having made a deer-skin cloak on one shoulder, he falls at her feet with his head. Towards the fierce mountain,' and so on. Here, the two words 'sayaṃ' should be understood as having dissimilar word classes by way of noun and indeclinable, and the three words 'pati' by way of noun, verb, and prefix.

Iminā nayena sabbattha vitthāretabbaṃ. Evaṃ sāsanasmiṃ keci saddā aññamaññaṃ samānasutikā samānāpi asamānatthā asamānapavattinimittā asamānaliṅgā asamānavibhattikā asamānavacanakā asamānantā asamānakālikā asamānapadajātikā ca bhavanti. Etādisesu saddesu yo kriyāpadattaṃ pakāseti, na so nāmikapadattaṃ. Yo ca nāmikapadattaṃ pakāseti, na so kriyāpadattaṃ. Evaṃ santepi sutisāmaññato ekattena gahetvā atthuddhāro karaṇīyoti yathāvuttakriyāpadānaṃ nāmapadehi samānasutikānaṃ bhotisadda bhave saddānamatthuddhāraṃ vadāma.

In this way, it should be elaborated everywhere. Thus, in the Dispensation, some words, though homophonous with each other, are dissimilar in meaning, dissimilar in the cause of occurrence, dissimilar in gender, dissimilar in inflection, dissimilar in number, dissimilar in ending, dissimilar in tense, and dissimilar in word class. Among such words, that which expresses the verbal nature does not express the nominal nature, and that which expresses the nominal nature does not express the verbal nature. Even so, because of the similarity in sound, the extraction of meaning should be done by taking them as one. Thus, we shall declare the extraction of meaning of the words 'bhoti' and 'bhave', which are verbal forms homophonous with nominal forms as stated.

Kathaṃ? Bhotisaddo kattuyoge kriyāpadaṃ, kriyāyoge nāmikapadaṃ, tasmā so dvīsu atthesu vattati kriyāpadatthe nāmikapadatthe ca. Tattha kriyāpadatthe vattamānavasena, nāmikapadatthe panālapanavasena. Kriyāpadatthe tāva “eko bhoti”, nāmikapadatthe “mā bhoti paridevesi”. Atridaṃ vuccati –

How? The word 'bhoti' is a verb in the active construction, and a nominal form when used with a verb; therefore, it functions in two meanings: in the verbal meaning and in the nominal meaning. Therein, in the verbal meaning, it functions by way of the present tense, while in the nominal meaning, it functions by way of address. First, in the verbal meaning, 'eko bhoti' (one is); in the nominal meaning, 'mā bhoti paridevesi' (do not lament, sir). Here, this is said:

Bhāve nāmapadatthe ca, ālapanavisesite;

Imesu dvīsu atthesu, bhotisaddo pavattati.

In the sense of being and in the meaning of a nominal form, specifically in address; in these two meanings, the word 'bhoti' occurs.

Bhavesaddo [M 0.0045] pana “bhavāmī”timassa vattamānāvibhattiyuttassa saddassatthepi vattati. “Bhavāmī”timassa pañcamīvibhattiyuttassa saddassa āṇatyāsīsanatthesupi vattati. “Bhaveyyāmī”timassa sattamīvibhattisahitassa saddassa anumatiparikappatthesupi vattati. Tatridaṃ paṭhamatthassa sādhakaṃ āhaccavacanaṃ –

The word 'bhave', however, also functions in the meaning of the word 'bhavāmi' (I am), which is connected with the present tense inflection. It also functions in the meanings of command and wish for the word 'bhavāmi' (may I be), which is connected with the fifth inflection. It also functions in the meanings of approval and supposition for the word 'bhaveyyāmi' (may I be), which is accompanied by the seventh inflection. Herein, this direct statement supports the first meaning:

“Devānaṃ adhiko homi, bhavāmi manujādhipo;

Rūpalakkhaṇasampanno, paññāya asamo bhave”ti.

“May I be superior to the devas, may I become the lord of men; endowed with marks of beauty, may I be unequaled in wisdom.”

Ayaṃ pana sabbesaṃ tesamatthānaṃ sādhikā amhākaṃ gāthāracanā –

And this verse composition of ours supports all those meanings:

“Sukhī bhavati eso ca, ahañcāpi sukhī bhave;

Sukhī bhavatu eso ca, ahañcāpi sukhī bhave.

“This one is happy, and may I also be happy; may this one be happy, and may I also be happy.”

Imāya buddhapūjāya, bhavantu sukhitā pajā;

Bhave’hañca sukhappatto, sāmacco saha ñātibhi.

By this offering to the Buddha, may beings be happy; and may I attain happiness, together with my ministers and relatives.

Sukhī bhaveyya eso ca, ahañcāpi sukhī bhave;

Sukhī bhaveyya ce eso, ahañcāpi sukhī bhave”ti.

“May this one be happy, and may I also be happy; if this one were to be happy, then I too would be happy.”

Iccevaṃ –

Thus—

Vattamānāya pañcamyaṃ, sattamyañca vibhattiyaṃ;

Etesu tīsu ṭhānesu, bhavesaddo pavattati.

In the present, fifth, and seventh inflections, in these three instances, the word 'bhave' occurs.

Ekadhā vattamānāyaṃ, pañcamīsattamīsu ca;

Dvedhā dvedhātimassatthaṃ, pañcadhā paridīpaye.

In one way in the present tense, and in two ways each in the fifth and seventh [inflections]; its meaning should be explained in five ways.

Dvedhā vā vattamānāya-mādipurisavācako;

Attho “bhave”ti etassa, “bhavatī”tipiyujjati.

Alternatively, in the present tense, the meaning of this word 'bhave' is twofold: expressing the first person, and it is also used for 'bhavati'.

Idāni pana etassa, vuttassatthassa sādhakaṃ;

Ettha pāḷippadesaṃ tu, āharissaṃ suṇātha me.

Now, however, in support of the meaning of what has been said, I shall cite a Pāli passage here; listen to me.

Ko’yaṃ [M 0.0046] majjhesamuddasmiṃ, apassaṃ tīramāyuhe;

Kaṃ tvaṃ atthavasaṃ ñatvā, evaṃ vāyamase bhusaṃ.

“Who is this in the middle of the ocean, struggling without seeing the shore? Knowing what purpose do you strive so intensely in this way?”

Nisamma vattaṃ lokassa, vāyāmassa ca devate;

Tasmā majjhesamuddasmiṃ, apassaṃ tīramāyuhe.

“Having considered the way of the world and the fruit of effort, O deity, therefore I strive in the middle of the ocean, though not seeing the shore.”

Assaṃ purimagāthāyaṃ, “āyuhe”tipadassa hi;

“Āyūhatī”ti atthoti, viññātabbo vibhāvinā.

Indeed, in the former verse, the word 'āyuhe' should be understood by the discerning as having the meaning 'āyūhati' (he strives).

Vibhattiyā vipallāsa-vasenāyaṃ samīrito;

Vattamāne sattamīti, tissekāravasena vā.

This is stated by way of an interchange of inflection; or by the rule 'the seventh inflection for the present tense'; or by way of the substitution of 'e' for 'ti'.

Pacchimāya ca gāthāyaṃ, “āyuhe”tipadassa tu;

“Āyūhāmī”ti atthoti, saddatthaññū vibhāvaye.

And in the latter verse, the knower of word-meanings should discern that the meaning of the word 'āyuhe' is 'āyūhāmi' (I strive).

Tathā “bhave”tietassa, vattamānāvibhattiyaṃ;

“Bhavatī”ti, “bhavāmī”ti, catthaṃ dvedhā vibhāvaye.

Similarly, regarding 'bhave' in the present tense inflection, one should discern its meaning in two ways: as 'bhavati' (he is) and 'bhavāmi' (I am).

Evaṃvidhesu aññesu, pāṭhesupi ayaṃ nayo;

Netabbo nayadakkhena, nayasāgarasāsane.

In other similar passages too, this method should be applied by one skilled in method, in this Dispensation, which is an ocean of methods.

Evamayaṃ bhavesaddo pañcasu chasu vā kriyāpadatthesu pavattati. Tathā sattamīvibhatyantanāmikapadassa vuddhisaṃsārakammabhavūpapattibhavasaṅkhātesu atthesupi. Tathā hi “abhave nandati tassa, bhave tassa na nandatī”tiādīsu vuddhimhi. “Bhave vicaranto”tiādīsu saṃsāre. “Bhave kho sati jāti hoti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”ntiādīsu kammabhave. “Evaṃ bhavevijjamāne”tiādīsu upapattibhaveti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iminā nayena bhūdhātuto nipphannānaṃ aññatopi aññesaṃ kriyāpadānaṃ yathāsambhavamattho uddharitabbo.

Thus this word 'bhava' occurs with five or six verbal meanings. Similarly, as a nominal word ending in the seventh inflection (i.e., 'bhave'), it also has meanings designated as growth, saṃsāra, kamma-bhava, and upapatti-bhava. For instance, in phrases like ‘delights in non-becoming... does not delight in becoming,’ it refers to growth. In phrases like ‘wandering in becoming,’ it refers to saṃsāra. In phrases like ‘when there is becoming, there is birth; conditioned by birth, there is aging and death,’ it refers to kamma-bhava. In phrases like ‘when becoming is present in this way,’ it should be understood as referring to upapatti-bhava. By this method, the meanings of other verbal forms derived from the root ‘bhū’ should also be extracted as is appropriate.

Ākhyātatthamhime [M 0.0047] atthā, na lātabbā kudācanaṃ;

Atthuddhāravasenete, uddhaṭā nāmato yato.

These meanings are never to be obtained from the verb, since they are extracted from the noun by way of meaning-extraction.

Idamettha saṅkhepato atthuddhāranayanidassanaṃ.

This, here, is a brief illustration of the method of extracting meaning.

Atthasaddacintāyaṃ pana evamupalakkhetabbaṃ – “bhavante, parābhavante, parābhave”iccādayo gacchati gacchaṃ gacchatosaddādayo viya visesasaddā, na yācanopatāpanatthādivācako nāthatisaddo viya, na ca rājadevatādivācako devasaddo viya sāmaññasaddā. Ye cettha visesasaddā, te sabbakālaṃ visesasaddāva. Ye ca sāmaññasaddā, tepi sabbakālaṃ sāmaññasaddāva.

However, in the consideration of words and meanings, it should be noted thus: words like ‘bhavante, parābhavante, parābhave,’ and so on, like the words ‘gacchati, gacchaṃ, gacchato,’ and so on, are specific words. They are not general words, like the word ‘nāthati,’ which expresses meanings such as begging or tormenting, nor like the word ‘deva,’ which refers to kings or deities. And those here which are specific words are always specific words. And those which are general words are always general words.

Tatra gacchatītiādīnaṃ visesasaddatā evaṃ daṭṭhabbā – gacchatīti ekaṃ nāmapadaṃ, ekamākhyātaṃ. Tathā gacchanti ekaṃ nāmapadaṃ, ekamākhyātaṃ. Gacchatoti eko kitanto, aparo rūḷhīsaddo. Satipi visesasaddatte sadisattā sutisāmaññato tabbisayaṃ buddhiṃ nuppādeti vināva’tthappakaraṇasaddantarābhisambandhena. Tathā hi saddantarābhisambandhena “gacchati patiṭṭhita”nti vutte sattamyantaṃ nāmapadanti viññāyati. “Gacchati tisso”ti vutte panākhyātanti. Tathā “sa gacchaṃ na nivattatī”ti vutte paṭhamantaṃ nāmapadanti viññāyati. “Gacchaṃ puttanivedako”ti vutte ākhyātanti viññāyati. “Gacchato hayato patito”ti vutte kitantoti viññāyati. “Gacchato paṇṇapupphāni patantī”ti vutte rukkhavācako rūḷhīsaddoti. Iti visesasaddānaṃ ākhyātanāmānaṃ nāmākhyātehi samānasutikānaṃ atthābhisambandhādīsu yo koci atthavisesañāpako sambandho avassamicchitabbo. Evaṃ “gacchatī”tiādīnaṃ ākhyātanāmattādivasena paccekaṃ ṭhitānaṃ ekekatthavācakānaṃ visesasaddatā daṭṭhabbā.

Herein, the specific nature of words like ‘gacchati’ and so on should be understood thus: ‘gacchati’ is one nominal word and one verbal word. Similarly, ‘gacchanti’ is one nominal word and one verbal word. ‘Gacchato’ is one participle, and another is a conventional word. Although they are specific words, due to their similarity and commonality of sound, they do not produce an understanding of their specific meaning without a connection to meaning, context, and other words. For example, when connected with other words, if ‘gacchati patiṭṭhita’ is said, it is understood as a nominal word in the locative case. But when ‘gacchati tisso’ is said, it is understood as a verb. Similarly, when ‘sa gacchaṃ na nivattatī’ is said, it is understood as a nominal word in the nominative case. When ‘Gacchaṃ puttanivedako’ is said, it is understood as a verb. When ‘Gacchato hayato patito’ is said, it is understood as a participle. When ‘Gacchato paṇṇapupphāni patantī’ is said, it is understood as a conventional word referring to a tree. Thus, for specific words—verbs and nouns that are homophonous with nouns and verbs—some connection that indicates a specific meaning, through association with meaning and so on, is necessarily required. In this way, the specific nature of words like ‘gacchati,’ etc., each standing individually and conveying a single meaning according to its nature as a verb or noun, should be seen.

“Nāthati [M 0.0048] devo”tiādīnaṃ pana ākhyātanāmānaṃ nāmākhyātehi asamānasutikānaṃ anekatthavācakānaṃ sāmaññasaddatā eva daṭṭhabbā. Atthasambandhādīsu hi vinā yena kenaci sambandhena “nāthatī”ti vutte “yācatī”ti vā “upatāpetī”ti vā “issariyaṃ karotī”ti vā “āsīsatī”ti vā attho paṭibhāti, tathā “devo”ti vutte “megho”ti vā “ākāso”ti vā “rājā”ti vā “devatā”ti vā “visuddhidevo”ti vā attho paṭibhāti. Yadā pana saddantarābhisambandhena “nāthati suppaṭipatti”nti vutte tadā “nāthatī”ti kriyāpadassa “yācatī”ti attho viññāyati, “nāthati sabbakilese”ti vutte “upatāpetī”ti attho viññāyati. “Nāthati sakacitte”ti vutte “issariyaṃ karotī”ti attho viññāyati. “Nāthati lokassa hita”nti vutte “āsīsatī”ti attho viññāyati. Tathā “devo gajjatī”ti vutte “devo”ti nāmapadassa “megho”ti attho viññāyati. “Viddho vigatavalāhako devo”ti vutte “ākāso”ti attho viññāyati. “Pivatu devo pānīya”nti vutte “rājā”ti attho viññāyati. “Devo devakāyā cavati āyusaṅkhayā”ti vutte “devatā”ti attho viññāyati. “Devātidevo satapuññalakkhaṇo”ti vutte “visuddhidevo”ti attho viññāyati. Iminā nayena aññepi sāmaññasaddā ñātabbā.

However, the general nature of verbs and nouns like ‘nāthati’ and ‘deva,’ and so on—which are not homophonous with other nouns and verbs but convey multiple meanings—should be understood. For indeed, when ‘nāthati’ is said without any connection to meaning, context, and so on, meanings such as ‘begs,’ or ‘torments,’ or ‘exercises lordship,’ or ‘wishes for’ arise. Similarly, when ‘deva’ is said, meanings such as ‘cloud,’ or ‘sky,’ or ‘king,’ or ‘deity,’ or ‘a pure deity’ arise. However, when connected with other words, if ‘nāthati suppaṭipatti’ is said, the verb ‘nāthati’ is understood to mean ‘begs.’ If ‘nāthati sabbakilese’ is said, it is understood to mean ‘torments.’ If ‘nāthati sakacitte’ is said, it is understood to mean ‘exercises lordship.’ If ‘nāthati lokassa hita’ is said, it is understood to mean ‘wishes for.’ Likewise, if ‘devo gajjatī’ is said, the nominal word ‘devo’ is understood to mean ‘cloud.’ If ‘viddho vigatavalāhako devo’ is said, it is understood to mean ‘sky.’ If ‘pivatu devo pānīya’ is said, it is understood to mean ‘king.’ If ‘devo devakāyā cavati āyusaṅkhayā’ is said, it is understood to mean ‘deity.’ If ‘devātidevo satapuññalakkhaṇo’ is said, it is understood to mean ‘a pure deity.’ In this way, other general words should also be understood.

Sabbametaṃ ñatvā yathā attho saddena, saddo catthena na virujjhati, tathātthasaddā cintanīyā. Tatridaṃ upalakkhaṇamattaṃ cintākāranidassanaṃ – “atthakusalā bhavante”ti vā “kiccāni bhavante”ti vā vutte “bhavante”ti idaṃ “bhavantī”timinā samānatthamākhyātapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Bhavante passāmī”ti vā “icchāmī”ti vā vutte upayogatthavaṃ [M 0.0049] nāmapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Bhavante jane pasaṃsatī”ti vā “kāmetī”ti vā vutte paccattopayogatthavantāni dve nāmapadānīti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Corā parābhavante”ti vutte “parābhavante”ti idaṃ “parābhavantī”timinā samānatthamākhyātikapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Parābhavante janā icchanti amittāna”nti vutte “parābhavante”ti imāni upayogapaccattatthavantāni dve nāmapadānīti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Eso parābhave”ti vutte “parābhave”ti idaṃ “parābhaveyyā”timinā samānatthamākhyātapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Ete parābhave loke, paṇḍito samavekkhiyā”ti vutte “parābhave”ti idaṃ upayogatthavaṃ bahuvacanaṃ nāmapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Parābhave satī”ti vutte bhāvalakkhaṇabhummatthekavacanakaṃ nāmapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Tumhe me pasādā sambhave”ti vutte “sambhave”ti idaṃ “sambhavathā”timinā samānatthamākhyātapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Ehi tvaṃ sambhavavhe”ti vutte “sambhavavhe”ti idaṃ sambhavāya nāma itthiyā vācakaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ sālapanaṃ nāmikapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Ehi tvaṃ sambhavavhepatiṭṭhita”nti vutte sambhavanāmakassa purisassa vācakaṃ pulliṅgaṃ bhummavacananti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo.

Having understood all this, meaning and words should be considered such that the meaning does not conflict with the word, nor the word with the meaning. Thus, meaning and word should be considered. Here is merely an illustration of the method of reflection: When it is said, ‘atthakusalā bhavante’ or ‘kiccāni bhavante,’ this ‘bhavante’ is a verb synonymous with ‘bhavantī.’ Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Bhavante passāmī’ or ‘icchāmī,’ ‘bhavante’ is a nominal in the objective case. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Bhavante jane pasaṃsatī’ or ‘kāmetī,’ these are two nominals with subjective and objective meaning. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Corā parābhavante,’ this ‘parābhavante’ is a verb synonymous with ‘parābhavantī.’ Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Parābhavante janā icchanti amittāna,’ these ‘parābhavante’ are two nominals with objective and subjective meaning. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Eso parābhave,’ this ‘parābhave’ is a verb synonymous with ‘parābhaveyyā.’ Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Ete parābhave loke, paṇḍito samavekkhiyā,’ this ‘parābhave’ is a plural nominal in the objective case. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Parābhave satī,’ it is a singular nominal in the locative case denoting a state. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Tumhe me pasādā sambhave,’ this ‘sambhave’ is a verb synonymous with ‘sambhavathā.’ Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Ehi tvaṃ sambhavavhe,’ this ‘sambhavavhe’ is a feminine nominal in the vocative case, denoting a woman named Sambhavā. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When it is said, ‘Ehi tvaṃ sambhavavhepatiṭṭhita,’ this is a masculine nominal in the locative case, denoting a man named Sambhava. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered.

“Varuṇo brahmadevo ca, ahesuṃ aggasāvakā;

Sambhavo nāmupaṭṭhāko, revatassa mahesino”ti –

Varuṇa and Brahmadeva were the chief disciples; Sambhava was the attendant of the great seer Revata.

Hi pāḷi. “Dhammā pātubhavante”ti vutte “pātubhavante”ti idaṃ “pātubhavantī”timinā samānatthaṃ sanipātamākhyātapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Pātu bhavante jane”ti vutte “te jane bhavaṃ rakkhatū”ti atthavācakāni ākhyātakitantasabbanāmikapadānīti [M 0.0050] evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Pātubhavase tvaṃ guṇehī”ti vutte “pātubhavase”ti idaṃ “pātubhavasī”timinā samānatthamākhyātapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Pātubhavase guṇe yo tva”nti vutte “pātubhavāhi attano guṇahetu tva”nti atthavācakāninipātayuttākhyātanāmapadānīti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Ahamattano guṇehi pātubhave”ti vutte “pātubhave”ti idaṃ “pātubhavāmī”timinā samānatthaṃ sanipātamākhyātapadanti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. “Maṃ pātu bhave idaṃ puññakamma”nti vutte “maṃ rakkhatu saṃsāre idaṃ puññakamma”nti atthavācakāni ākhyātanāmapadānīti evamattho ca saddo ca cintanīyo. Iminā nayena sabbattha yathārahamatthasaddā cintanīyā. Tattha samānasutikānaṃ kesañci saddānaṃ “na tesaṃ koṭṭhe openti. Na tesaṃ antarā gacche. Satta vo licchavī aparihānīye dhamme desessāmi, ime te deva sattavo, tvañca uttamasattavo”tiādīsu samānasutikānaṃ viya uccāraṇaviseso icchanīyo. Uccāraṇavisese hi sati padāni paribyattāni, padesu paribyattesu attho paribyatto hoti, atthapariggāhakānaṃ atthādhigamo akiccho hoti, suparisuddhādāsatale paṭibimbadassanaṃ viya, so ca gahitapubbasaṅketassa atthasambandhādīsu aññatarasmiṃ ñāteyeva hoti, na itarathā. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

Indeed, in the Pāli. When 'Dhammā pātubhavante' is said, 'pātubhavante' here is a verb with a particle, synonymous with 'pātubhavantī.' Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When 'Pātu bhavante jane' is said, meaning 'may that being protect those people,' these are words expressing meaning, being verbs, participles, and pronominal words. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When 'Pātubhavase tvaṃ guṇehī' is said, 'pātubhavase' here is a verb synonymous with 'pātubhavasī.' Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When 'Pātubhavase guṇe yo tva' is said, meaning 'reveal yourself for the sake of your own virtue,' these are words expressing meaning, being nominals and verbs joined with particles. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When 'Ahamattano guṇehi pātubhave' is said, 'pātubhave' here is a verb with a particle, synonymous with 'pātubhavāmī.' Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. When 'Maṃ pātu bhave idaṃ puññakamma' is said, meaning 'may this meritorious action protect me in saṃsāra,' these are words expressing meaning, being verbs and nominals. Thus, both the meaning and the word should be considered. In this way, meanings and words should be considered appropriately everywhere. Among some words that sound alike, such as in 'they do not put them in a compartment,' 'one should not go between them,' 'I shall teach you, O Licchavis, seven conditions of non-decline,' 'these, O deva, are your seven enemies (sattavo),' and 'you are the supreme being (sattavo),' a distinction in pronunciation is desirable for such similar-sounding words. For when there is a distinction in pronunciation, the words become clear; when the words are clear, the meaning becomes clear. For those who grasp meanings, the attainment of meaning becomes effortless, like seeing a reflection in a perfectly clean mirror. And this is known only by one who has previously grasped the convention concerning one or another of these, such as the meaning or the connection, and not otherwise. For this has been said by the ancients—

“Visayattamanāpannā, saddā nevatthabodhakā;

Na padamattato atthe, te aññātā pakāsakā”ti.

Sounds that have not reached their proper domain do not convey meaning. Not from the mere word do they illuminate the meaning; unknown, they are mere declarers.

Yadidamettha vuttamamhehi “uccāraṇaviseso icchanīyo”ti. Atrāyamuccāraṇavisesadīpanī gāthā sahatthappakāsananayadānagāthāya.

Herein, what has been stated by us is: 'A distinction in pronunciation is desirable.' Here, this verse elucidates the distinction in pronunciation, by way of the verse illustrating the method of giving by pointing with one's own hand.

“Na [M 0.0051] te saṃ koṭṭhe openti”, iti pāṭhe sumedhaso;

Padaṃ “na te”ti chinditvā, “saṃ koṭṭhe”ti paṭheyya ve.

In the reading 'Na te saṃ koṭṭhe openti,' a wise person should indeed separate the word as 'na te' and read 'saṃ koṭṭhe'.

“Saṃ na openti koṭṭhe te, bhikkhū”ti atthamīraye;

Evamimesu aññesu, pāṭhesupi ayaṃ nayo.

One should explain the meaning as: 'Those bhikkhus do not store them in a compartment.' Similarly, in these other readings too, this is the method.

Atha yaṃ panidampi vuttaṃ “kesañcī”ti, taṃ kimatthaṃ? “Gacchati patiṭṭhitaṃ, gacchati tisso, bhavante passāmi, atthakusalā bhavante, vadantaṃ ekapokkharā, vadantaṃ paṭivadatī”tiādīsu samānasutikānamuccāraṇaviseso na labbhatīti dassanatthaṃ. Tasmā idamettha sallakkhetabbaṃ – yattha samānasutikānamuccāraṇaviseso labbhati atthaviseso ca padānaṃ vibhāgavasena vā avibhāgavasena vā, tattha payoge samānasutikamekaccaṃ padaṃ vicchinditvā uccāretabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ? “Hetu hetusampayuttakānaṃ dhammānaṃ taṃsamuṭṭhānānañca rūpānaṃ hetupaccayena paccayo. So tena saddhiṃ bhāsati, sotena vuyhati. Bhavante jane pasaṃsati, bhavante passāmī”ti evamādayo payogā. Ettha “hetū”ti īsakaṃ vicchinditvā “hetusampayuttāna”nti uccāretabbaṃ. Tathā “so”ti vicchinditvā “tena saddhi”nti uccāretabbaṃ. “Bhava”nti vicchinditvā “te jane”ti uccāretabbaṃ.

Now, what is the purpose of what was also said here, 'for some'? It is to show that in cases such as 'gacchati patiṭṭhitaṃ' (he goes, established), 'gacchati tisso' (he goes, three), 'bhavante passāmi' (I see the venerable ones), 'atthakusalā bhavante' (skilled in meaning, venerable ones), 'vadantaṃ ekapokkharā' (speaking, one lotus), 'vadantaṃ paṭivadatī' (speaking, he replies), and so on, a distinction in pronunciation for words that sound alike is not found. Therefore, this should be noted here: where a distinction in pronunciation for words that sound alike is found, and a distinction in meaning either by way of division or non-division of words, there, in application, a particular word that sounds alike should be pronounced by separating it. For example: 'The root (hetu) is a condition by way of root-condition for the phenomena associated with the root and for the material forms arisen from them.' (Here, 'hetu' is to be pronounced slightly separated from 'hetusampayuttānaṃ'.) 'He speaks with him (so tena); he is carried by the stream (sotena).' (Here, 'so' is to be pronounced separated from 'tena saddhiṃ'.) 'O venerable one, he praises those people' (bhavaṃ te jane pasaṃsati); 'I see the venerable ones' (bhavante passāmi). (Here, 'bhavaṃ' is to be pronounced separated from 'te jane'.)

Sesaṃ pana samānasutikaṃ vicchinditvā na uccāretabbaṃ. Avicchindanīyasmiñhi ṭhāne vicchinditvā paṭhitassa attho duṭṭho hoti. Evaṃ padavibhāgāvibhāgavasena samānasutikānamatthuccāraṇaviseso veditabbo. Ettha hi “so tenā”tiādīsu dvipadatthaggahaṇaṃ vibhāgo, ekapadatthaggahaṇamavibhāgoti adhippeto. Ettha ca visuṃ vavatthitānaṃ asamānasutikānaṃ ekato katvā samānasutikabhāvaparikappanaṃ atthantaraviññāpanatthañceva uccāraṇavisesadassanatthañca. Na hi etāni [M 0.0052] “sappo sappo”tiādīsu viya ekasmiṃyevatthe samānasutikāni. Evaṃ santepi ekajjhakaraṇena laddhaṃ samānasutilesaṃ gahetvā atthantaraviññāpanatthaṃ uccāraṇavisesadassanatthañca “samānasutikānī”ti vuttāni. Esa nayo aññatrāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu. Idamettha sallakkhetabbaṃ –

However, the remaining words that sound alike should not be pronounced by separating them. For if one reads by separating in a place where it should not be separated, the meaning becomes corrupted. Thus, the distinction in pronunciation for words that sound alike should be understood by way of word division and non-division for their meaning. For here, in cases like 'so tena' and so on, grasping the meaning of two words is intended as division, and grasping the meaning of one word is intended as non-division. And here, the imagining of dissimilar-sounding words, separately situated, as having a similar-sounding status by combining them into one, is both for the purpose of making known a different meaning and for showing a distinction in pronunciation. For these are not similar-sounding in the same sense as in 'sappo sappo' (snake, snake) and so on, which are in one meaning only. Even so, having taken the trace of similar sounds acquired by combining them into one, they are called 'similar-sounding words' both for the purpose of making known a different meaning and for showing a distinction in pronunciation. This is the method elsewhere in similar instances. This should be noted here—

Yattha samānasutikānaṃ aṭṭhārasākāresu yena kenaci ākārena atthaviseso labbhati, vicchinditvā pana uccāraṇe saddavilāso na hoti, attho vā duṭṭho hoti, na tādisesu payogesu samānasutikāni padāni vicchinditvā uccāretabbāni. Tatra katamena cākārena atthavisesalābho bhavati?
