Padānaṃ vibhāgavasena vā avibhāgavasena vā akkharasannidhānavasena vā padasannidhānavasena vā padakkharasannidhānavasena vā vicchāvasena vā kammappavacanīyavasena vā bhayakodhādīsu uppannesu kathitāmeḍitavacanavasena vā guṇavācakasaddassa dviruttavasena vā kriyāpadassa dviruttavasena vā saṃhitāpadacchedavasena vā agāravatthaparidīpanavasena vā nirantaratthaparidīpanavasena vā nanirantaratthaparidīpanavasena vā “punappuna”miccatthaparidīpanavasena vā upamāne iva saddavasena vā itisaddaṃ paṭicca saddapadatthavācakatthaparidīpanavasena vā tathāpavattacittaparidīpanavasena vāti imesuṭṭhārasākāresu, vitthārato pana chabbīsāya ākāresu tato vādhikesu yena kenaci ākārena atthavisesalābho bhavati.

Where, in the case of words that sound alike, a distinction in meaning is obtained through any one of the eighteen modes, but when pronounced separately, there is no elegance of sound, or the meaning is corrupted, then in such instances, words that sound alike should not be pronounced separately. And by which mode is the distinction in meaning obtained? By way of dividing words or not dividing them, by proximity of syllables or proximity of words, by proximity of word and syllable, by way of distributive repetition, by way of kammappavacaniya particles, by repetition of words spoken when fear, anger, etc. arise, by repetition of a word expressing quality, by repetition of a verb, by dividing a compound word, by clarifying matters of disrespect, by clarifying continuous meaning, by clarifying non-continuous meaning, by clarifying the meaning of 'again and again,' by the use of the word 'iva' in a simile, by clarifying the meaning of a word or phrase that expresses sound with reference to the word 'iti,' or by clarifying the mind as it thus arises—in these eighteen modes, or in detail, in twenty-six modes or even more, a distinction in meaning is obtained through any one mode.

Ettha padānaṃ tāva vibhāgavasena vā avibhāgavasena vā samānasutikānamatthavisesalābhe “sā naṃ saṅgati pāleti, abhikkamo sānaṃ paññāyati. Mā no deva avadhi, māno mayhaṃ na vijjatī”ti evamādayo payogā.

Here, in obtaining a distinction in meaning for words that sound alike by way of word division or non-division, there are usages such as: 'She protects his association (sā naṃ saṅgati pāleti); his advancement is evident to them (sānaṃ paññāyati).' 'O deva, do not kill us (mā no deva avadhi); conceit does not exist in me (māno mayhaṃ na vijjatī),' and so forth.

Akkharasannidhānavasena [M 0.0053] pana atthavisesalābhe “santehi mahito hito. Saṅgā saṅgāmajiṃ muttaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ. Dāṭhī dāṭhīsu pakkhandi, maññamāno yathā pure. Sabbābhibhuṃva sirasāsirasā namāmi. Bhūmito uṭṭhitā yāva, brahmalokā vidhāvati. Acci accimato loke, ḍayhamānamhi tejasā”ti evamādayo payogā.

However, in obtaining a distinction in meaning by way of proximity of syllables, there are usages such as: 'Honored by the peaceful, beneficial.' 'Released from attachments, victorious in battle, him I call a brahmin.' 'The fanged one rushed among the fanged ones, imagining as before.' 'I bow to the all-conquering one with my head, as if headless.' 'Having risen from the earth, it runs up to the Brahma-world.' 'The flame in the flaming world, burning with energy'—such are the applications.

Padasannidhānavasena atthavisesalābhe “āpo āpogataṃ. Rājarājamahāmattādayo, sukho’lokassa lokassa, kārako ñāṇacakkhudo, nirāpade pade ninno, anantañāṇaṃ karuṇālayaṃ layaṃ, malassa buddhaṃ susamāhitaṃ hitaṃ. Namāmi dhammaṃ bhavasaṃvaraṃ varaṃ, guṇākarañceva niraṅgaṇaṃ gaṇa”nti evamādayo payogā.

In obtaining a distinction in meaning by way of proximity of words, there are usages such as: 'Water has gone to water.' 'Kings, royal ministers, and so on.' 'The happiness of light for the world.' 'The doer, the giver of the eye of wisdom.' 'Inclined to the state free from danger.' '(To him who is of) infinite knowledge, the abode of compassion, the destroyer of defilement; the Buddha, well-composed and beneficial.' 'I bow to the Dhamma, the excellent restraint of existence, and to the Sangha, the source of virtues and spotless.' Such are the applications.

Padakkharasannidhānavasena atthavisesalābhe “pamāṇarahitaṃ hitaṃ, siddhattho sabbasiddhattho, tilokamahito hito. Upagantvāna sambuddho, idaṃ vacanamabravī”ti evamādayo payogā. Tatrimā akkharasannidhānādīsu adhippāyaviññāpaniyo gāthā –

In obtaining a distinction in meaning by way of proximity of words and syllables, there are usages such as: 'Beneficial, without measure.' 'Siddhattha, the one who has accomplished all.' 'Beneficial, honored in the three worlds.' 'Having approached, the Perfectly Awakened One spoke these words.' Herein are these verses that reveal the intention regarding proximity of syllables and so on—

Mahitoiti saddamhā, makāro ce vivecito;

Saddo niratthako ettha, “akkhara”nti vade budho.

If the syllable 'ma' is separated from the word 'mahito,' the word here becomes meaningless; the wise call it an 'akkhara' (syllable).

Ñeyyā akkharayogena,

“Santehi mahito hito”;

Iccādīsu sarūpānaṃ,

Hoti atthavisesatā.

It should be known that by the combination of syllables, in cases like 'Honored by the peaceful, beneficial,' a distinction in meaning arises for words of similar form.

Upasaggā nipātā ca, yañcaññaṃ atthajotakaṃ;

Ekakkharampi viññūhi, taṃ “pada”nti samīritaṃ.

Prefixes and particles, and whatever else illuminates meaning—even a single syllable, by the discerning, is called a 'word'.

Padānaṃ [M 0.0054] sannidhānañca, padakkharānameva ca;

Samāse labbhamānattaṃ, sandhāya lapitaṃ mayā.

The proximity of words, and of words and syllables, has been spoken of by me with reference to their being found in compounds.

Vicchāvasena atthavisesalābhe “gāme gāme sataṃ kumbhā, gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo”ti evamādayo payogā. Ettha hi vicchāvasena sabbepi gāmā pariggahitā.

In obtaining a distinction in meaning by way of distributive repetition, there are usages such as: 'In every village, a hundred pots; every village is delightful.' For here, by way of distributive repetition, all villages are included.

Nānādhikaraṇānaṃ tu, vattumekakkhaṇamhi yā;

Icchato byāpituṃ icchā, sā vicchāti pakittitā.

When one wishes to express many subjects at once, the desire to pervade them is known as 'vicchā'.

Kammappavacanīyavasena atthavisesalābhe “rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate cando, rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ pari vijjotate cando”ti payogā, rukkhānaṃ upari upari vijjotateti attho.

In obtaining a distinction in meaning by means of kammappavacanīya particles, there are usages such as: 'The moon shines upon tree after tree; the moon shines all around tree after tree'—the meaning is that it shines above and around the trees.

Bhayakodhādīsu uppannesu kathitāmeḍitavacanavasena pana atthavisesalābhe ime payogā – bhaye tāva “coro coro, sappo sappo”iccādayo. Kodhe “vasala vasala, caṇḍāla caṇḍāla, vijjha vijjha, pahara pahara”iccādayo. Pasaṃsāyaṃ “sādhu sādhu sāriputta, abhikkantaṃ bhante abhikkantaṃ bhante”iccādayo. Turite “abhikkama vāseṭṭha abhikkama vāseṭṭha, gaccha gaccha, lunāhi lunāhi”iccādayo. Kotūhale “āgaccha āgaccha”iccādayo. Acchariye “aho buddho aho buddho”iccādayo. Hāse “aho sukhaṃ aho sukhaṃ, aho manāpaṃ aho manāpaṃ”iccādayo. Soke “kahaṃ ekaputtaka kahaṃ ekaputtaka”iccādayo. Pasāde “bhavissanti vajjī bhavissanti vajjī”iccādayo. Evaṃ bhayakodhādīsu uppannesu kathitāmeḍitavacanavasena atthavisesalābho bhavati. Ettha pana atthantarābhāvepi daḷhīkammavasena padānamatthajotakabhāvoyeva atthavisesalābho.

In cases of fear, anger, and so on, when they have arisen, a distinction in meaning is obtained through repeated and emphasized speech. For fear, for instance: 'Thief! Thief! Snake! Snake!' and so on. For anger: 'Wretch! Wretch! Outcaste! Outcaste! Shoot! Shoot! Strike! Strike!' and so on. For praise: 'Well done! Well done, Sāriputta! Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir!' and so on. For urgency: 'Go forth, Vāseṭṭha! Go forth, Vāseṭṭha! Go! Go! Cut! Cut!' and so on. For curiosity: 'Come! Come!' and so on. For wonder: 'Ah, the Buddha! Ah, the Buddha!' and so on. For joy: 'Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness! Ah, delightful! Ah, delightful!' and so on. For sorrow: 'Where is my only son? Where is my only son?' and so on. For confidence: 'The Vajjis will prosper! The Vajjis will prosper!' and so on. Thus, when fear, anger, and so on have arisen, a distinction in meaning is obtained through repeated and emphasized speech. Here, even when there is no other meaning, the distinction in meaning obtained is simply the meaning-illuminating quality of the words by way of reinforcement.

Bhaye [M 0.0055] kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ,

Turite kotūhala’cchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca,

Kare āmeḍitaṃ budho.

In fear, anger, praise, in urgency, curiosity, and wonder, in joy, sorrow, and confidence—the wise one should make repetition.

Casaddo avuttasamuccayattho, tena garahāasammānādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. “Pāpo pāpo”tiādīsu hi garahāyaṃ. “Abhirūpaka abhirūpakā”tiādīsu asammāne. “Kvāyaṃ abalabalo viyā”tiādīsu atisayatthe āmeḍitaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Guṇavācakassa dviruttavasena atthavisesalābhe “kaṇho kaṇho ca ghoro cā”ti evamādayo. “Kaṇho kaṇho”ti hi atīva kaṇhoti attho. Kriyāpadassa dviruttavasena atthavisesalābhe “dhame dhame nātidhame”ti evamādayo. Tattha dhame dhameti dhameyya no na dhameyya. Nātidhameti pamāṇātikkantaṃ pana na dhameyya. Saṃhitāpadacchedavasena atthavisesalābhe “narānarā, surāsurā, katākatakusalākusalavisayaṃ vippaṭisārākārena pavattaṃ anusocanaṃ kukkucca”nti evamādayo. Ettha pana viññūnaṃ paramakosallajananatthaṃ silokaṃ racayāma –

The particle 'ca' has the meaning of including what is unsaid; thereby, the inclusion of blame, disrespect, and so on, should be understood. For instance, in phrases like 'Pāpo pāpo' (wicked, wicked), blame is implied. In phrases like 'Abhirūpaka abhirūpakā' (handsome, handsome), disrespect is implied. In phrases like 'Kvāyaṃ abalabalo viyā' (where is this weakling?), repetition should be understood in the sense of excess. In the gaining of special meaning by means of the reduplication of a word denoting a quality, there are usages such as 'kaṇho kaṇho ca ghoro cā' (black, black and fierce). Here, 'kaṇho kaṇho' means 'extremely black.' In the gaining of special meaning by means of the reduplication of a verb, there are usages such as 'dhame dhame nātidhame' (chastise, chastise, but not excessively). Here, 'dhame dhame' means 'one should chastise; one should not fail to chastise.' 'Nātidhame' means 'one should not chastise beyond measure.' In the gaining of special meaning by means of the analysis of connected words, there are usages such as 'narānarā' (men and non-men), 'surāsurā' (gods and non-gods), 'katākatakusalākusalavisayaṃ' (the sphere of what is done and not done, skillful and unskillful), and 'vippaṭisārākārena pavattaṃ anusocanaṃ kukkuccaṃ' (worry is regret arising in the form of remorse). Here, to generate the highest skill in the wise, we compose a verse:

Hitāhitā hitaṃhitaṃ, ānubhāvena te jina;

Pavarāpavarāhacca, bhavāmā’nāmayā mayanti.

By your power, O Victor, may the beneficial and the harmful be [known as] beneficial and harmful. Having left behind the excellent and the inferior, may we be free from affliction.

Agāravatthaparidīpanavasena atthavisesalābhe “tuvaṃtuvaṃ pesuññakalahaviggahavivādā”ti evamādayo. Nirantaratthaparidīpanavasena atthavisesalābhe “divase divase paribhuñjatī”ti evamādayo. Nanirantaratthaparidīpanavasena atthavisesalābhe [M 0.0056] “khaṇe khaṇe pīti uppajjatī”ti evamādayo. “Punappuna”miccatthaparidīpanavasena atthavisesalābhe “muhuṃ muhuṃ bhāyayate kumāre”ti evamādayo. Upamāne ivasaddavasena atthavisesalābhe “rājā rakkhatu dhammena, attanova pajaṃ paja”nti evamādayo. Itisaddaṃ paṭicca saddapadatthavācakattaparidīpanavasena atthavisesalābhe “buddho buddhoti kathayanto, somanassaṃ pavedayi”nti evamādayo. Tathāpavattacittaparidīpanavasena atthavisesalābhe “buddho buddhoti cintento, maggaṃ sodhemahaṃ tadā”ti evamādayo. Evaṃ īdisesu payogesu samānasutikapadaṃ vicchinditvā na uccāretabbaṃ. Vicchinditvā hi uccāraṇe sati saddavilāso na bhavati, katthaci pana “katākatākusalākusalavisaya”nti evamādīsu vicchinditvā uccāritassa attho duṭṭho hoti, tasmā vicchinditvā na uccāretabbaṃ, ekābaddhaṃyeva katvā uccāretabbaṃ. Iti samānasutikesu vinicchayo chabbīsāya ākārehi adhikehi ca maṇḍetvā dassito.

In gaining a special meaning by explaining a matter of disrespect, there are examples such as: 'You, you! Slander, quarrels, disputes,' and so on. In gaining a special meaning by explaining the sense of 'uninterrupted,' there are examples such as: 'Day by day, he enjoys,' and so on. In gaining a special meaning by explaining the sense of 'non-uninterrupted,' there are examples such as: 'Moment by moment, joy arises,' and so on. In gaining a special meaning by explaining the meaning of 'again and again,' there are examples such as: 'Again and again, the prince is frightened,' and so on. In gaining a special meaning by means of the word 'iva' in a simile, there are examples such as: 'May the king protect by Dhamma, his own people as a father,' and so on. In gaining a special meaning by relying on the word 'iti' and explaining its function of denoting a word as a sound, there are examples such as: 'Saying 'Buddha, Buddha,' he expressed joy,' and so on. In gaining a special meaning by explaining a mind that has arisen in that way, there are examples such as: 'Thinking 'Buddha, Buddha,' I then purified the path,' and so on. Thus, in such usages, a word with a similar sound should not be split when recited. For if it is split and recited, the beauty of the sound is lost. In some cases, like 'katākatākusalākusalavisaya' (the sphere of what is done and not done, skillful and unskillful), the meaning is corrupted if it is split and recited. Therefore, it should not be split but recited as one continuous phrase. Thus, the analysis of words with similar sounds is presented, adorned with twenty-six and more modes.

Yasmā pana samānasutikesu vinicchaye dassite asamānasutikesupi vinicchayo dassetabbo hoti, tasmā tampi dassessāma – yattha niggahītamhā parākāralopopi pāṭho paññāyati, saṃyogabyañjanassa visaṃyogattampi. Tesu payogesu niggahītapadaṃ anantarapadena saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃyeva katvā uccāretabbaṃ. Katamāni tāni? “Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ-sā’jīvo garahito mama. Pupphaṃ’sā uppajji. Khayamattaṃ na nibbānaṃ’sa gambhīrādivācato”ti evamādayo. Ettha hi “sace bhutto bhaveyyāha”ntiādinā vicchedamakatvā [M 0.0057] anantare dvīsu gāthāpadesu antarībhūtānaṃ dvinnaṃ samānasutikapadānaṃ ekato uccāraṇamiva anantarapadehi saddhiṃ ekābaddhuccāraṇavasena “sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ-sā’jīvo garahito mamā”tiādinā uccāretabbaṃ. Evarūpoyeva hi uccāraṇaviseso sakalehipi porāṇehi viññūhi anumato uccārito ca “assa ājīvo garahito mama, assā uppajji, assa gambhīrādivācato”tievamādiatthappaṭipādanassānurūpattā.

Since, after showing the analysis in cases of similar-sounding words, it is also necessary to show the analysis in cases of dissimilar-sounding words, we will now explain that too—where a reading is found with the elision of a following letter 'a' after a niggahīta, as well as the separation of a conjunct consonant. In these usages, the word ending in a niggahīta should be pronounced as if bound together with the immediately following word. What are these? Examples include: 'Sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ-sā’jīvo garahito mama. Pupphaṃ’sā uppajji. Khayamattaṃ na nibbānaṃ’sa gambhīrādivācato' and so on. Here, without making a break after phrases like 'sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ', it should be pronounced bound together with the following words—as in 'sace bhutto bhaveyyāhaṃ-sā’jīvo garahito mamā'—just like two similar-sounding words that appear between two lines of verse are pronounced as one. Indeed, this particular manner of pronunciation has been approved and employed by all the ancient wise ones because it appropriately conveys the intended meaning, such as 'his livelihood is blameworthy to me,' 'hers arose,' and 'from his profound speech,' and so on.

Yattha pana yādise uccāraṇe kariyamāne attho paribyatto hoti, tesu payogesu kvaci casadda panasaddādiyogaṭṭhāne īsakaṃ vicchinditvā padamuccāretabbaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ? “Vāḷā ca lapasakkharā. Accantasantā pana yā, ayaṃ nibbānasampadā, “idaṃ dukkha”nti vācaṃ bhāsato “idaṃ dukkha”nti ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti? Āmantā. Iti ca danti ca duti ca khanti ca ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti? Na hevaṃ vattabbe”ti evamādayo payogā.

Where, however, the meaning becomes clear with a certain pronunciation, in such usages, a word should be pronounced by slightly pausing at places where particles like 'ca' or 'pana' are joined. For example: 'Vāḷā ca lapasakkharā. Accantasantā pana yā, ayaṃ nibbānasampadā, 'idaṃ dukkha'nti vācaṃ bhāsato 'idaṃ dukkha'nti ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti? Āmantā. Iti ca danti ca duti ca khanti ca ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti? Na hevaṃ vattabbe'—these are examples of such usages.

Etesu hi paṭhamapayoge “vāḷā cā”ti īsakaṃ vicchinditvā “lapasakkharā”ti uccāretabbaṃ. Tattha lapasakkharāti sakkharasadisamadhuravacanā. Jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “niratthakavacanehi sakkharā viya madhurā”ti vuttaṃ, tasmātra bahubbīhitappurisavasena dvidhā samāso daṭṭhabbo “lapā sakkharā viya yāsaṃ tā lapasakkharā, lapehi vā sakkharā viyāti lapasakkharā”ti.

In this first usage, in the phrase 'vāḷā cā,' one should pause slightly and then utter 'lapasakkharā.' Here, 'lapasakkharā' means sweet speech resembling sugar. However, in the Jātaka commentary, it is said, 'sweet like sugar with meaningless words.' Therefore, here the compound should be understood in two ways, as a bahubbīhi and a tappurisa compound: 'Those whose speech is like sugar—they are lapasakkharā,' or 'like sugar through speech—that is lapasakkharā.'

Dutiyapayoge “accantasantā pana”iti īsakaṃ vicchinditvā “yā”ti uccāretabbaṃ. Yā pana ayaṃ nibbānasampadā accantasantāti hi attho.

In the second usage, after 'accantasantā pana,' one should pause slightly and then pronounce 'yā.' The meaning is: 'And this attainment of Nibbāna, which is ultimately peaceful...'

Tatiyapayoge [M 0.0058] iti ca danti ca duti ca khanti cāti etesu catūsu ṭhānesu ikārañca daṃkārañca dukārañca khaṃkārañca īsakaṃ vicchinditvā tadanantaraṃ ti ca saddā uccāretabbā.

In the third usage, in these four instances of 'iti ca,' 'danti ca,' 'duti ca,' and 'khanti ca,' the 'i' sound, the 'daṃ' sound, the 'du' sound, and the 'khaṃ' sound should be slightly separated, and immediately after that, the words 'ti ca' should be uttered.

Ettha hi avicchinditvā uccāraṇe sati aññathā gahetabbattā attho duṭṭho bhavati. Kathaṃ? Īdisesu ṭhānesu avicchinditvā uccāraṇe sati itisaddo evanti atthavācako nipāto siyā, sandhivasena pana ikāratthavācako rūḷhīsaddo na siyā. Dantisaddo damanattho siyā, daṃkāravācako na siyā. Dutisaddo niratthako siyā, dukāravācako na siyā. Khantisaddo khamanattho siyā, khaṃkāravācako na siyā. Tasmā ikāra daṃkāra dukāra khaṃkārāni īsakaṃ vicchinditabbāni.

Here, if uttered without a break, the meaning becomes corrupted due to being understood differently. How? In such instances, if uttered without separation, the word 'iti' could become the particle 'evaṃ' (thus), signifying meaning, but the conventional word denoting the sound 'i' would not be present. The word 'danti' could mean 'taming,' but not express the sound 'daṃ.' The word 'duti' could be meaningless, but not express the sound 'du.' The word 'khanti' could mean 'forbearance,' but not express the sound 'khaṃ.' Therefore, the 'i' sound, the 'daṃ' sound, the 'du' sound, and the 'khaṃ' sound should be slightly separated.

Ettha hi iiti daṃiti duiti khaṃitītiādinā saṃhitāpadacchedo veditabbo, parabhūtassa ca ikārassa lopo. Na panettha idaṃ vattabbaṃ “sarūpasarānaṃ visaye parabhūtassa sarūpasarassa lopo na hoti, pubbasarasseva lopo hoti tatrāyanti ettha viyā”ti “akilāsuno vaṇṇapathe khaṇantā, udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avindu”nti pāḷiyaṃ sarūpaparasarassa lopadassanato. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathācariyehi “pavaddhaṃ āpaṃ papa”nti attho saṃvaṇṇito. Tasmā “iti cā”ti etthāpi iiti cāti chedaṃ katvā dvīsu ikāresu parassa ikārassa lopo kātabbo, na pubbassa.

Here, the division of connected words should be understood as 'i-iti,' 'daṃ-iti,' 'du-iti,' 'khaṃ-iti,' etc., with the elision of the subsequent 'i'. However, it should not be said here that "in the case of similar vowels, the elision of a subsequent similar vowel does not occur; only the preceding vowel is elided, as in 'tatrāyaṃ' here," because in the Pāli phrase 'akilāsuno vaṇṇapathe khaṇantā, udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avindu,' the elision of a subsequent similar vowel is observed. Indeed, the commentary teachers have explained the meaning as 'pavaddhaṃ āpaṃ papa.' Therefore, here too, in 'iti cā,' having made the division as 'i-iti cā,' the elision of the subsequent 'i' should be made from the two 'i's, not the preceding one.

Pubbasmiñhi ikāravācake ikāre naṭṭhe sati nipātabhūtena itisaddena ikārasaṅkhāto attho na viññāyeyya, nipātabhūtassa pana itisaddassa ikāre naṭṭhepi so attho viññāyateva “devadattoti me suta”nti ettha [M 0.0059] devadattapadattho viya. Tasmā itisaddassa parabhūtassa ikārasseva lopo kātabbo, na pubbassa ikāravācakassa ikārassa. Kaccāyane pana yebhuyyappavattiṃ sandhāya asarūpasarato parasseva asarūpasarassa lopo vutto, na sarūpasarato parassa sarūpasarassa. Mahāpadesasuttehi vā sarūpassa parasarassa lopo vuttoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

For if the preceding 'i', which denotes 'i', were to be elided, the meaning designated by 'i', which is the particle 'iti', would not be understood. But even if the 'i' of the particle 'iti' were to be elided, that meaning is still understood, just as the meaning of the word 'Devadatta' is understood in the phrase 'devadattoti me sutaṃ'. Therefore, only the subsequent 'i' of the particle 'iti' should be elided, not the preceding 'i' that denotes 'i'. In the Kaccāyana grammar, however, with reference to general usage, the elision of a dissimilar vowel following a dissimilar vowel is stated, not of a similar vowel following a similar vowel. Or, it should be understood that the elision of a subsequent similar vowel is stated by the Mahāpadesa Suttas.

“Antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷanda”ntiādīsu pana casaddādiyogaṭṭhānepi sati vicchinditvā padaṃ na uccāretabbaṃ. Yattha ca āgamakkharādīni dissanti, tesu payogesu pubbapadāni vicchinditvā na uccāretabbāni, āgamakkharavantehi parapadehi saddhiṃyeva uccāretabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ? “Nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca”iccevamādayo payogā. Yattha yesaṃ visuṃ visuṃ sambandho dissati, attho ca yujjati, tattha tāni atthānurūpaṃ vicchinditvā uccāretabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ? “Nahāne ussukkaṃ akāsi, ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā khādanīye bhattasmiṃ” iccevamādayo payogā. Ettha hi “nahāne ussukkaṃ akāsī”ti vicchinditvā “ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā khādanīye bhattasmi”nti uccāretabbaṃ. Evañhi sati na kevalaṃ so bhikkhu nahāneyeva ussukkaṃ akāsi, atha kho yāguyāpi khādanīyepi bhattasmimpi ussukkaṃ akāsīti atthappakāsane samattho bhavati, aṭṭhānappayutto samuccayatthavācako apisaddo.

However, in cases like 'Antarā ca rājagahaṃ antarā ca nāḷandaṃ', even when there is a connection with the particle 'ca' and so on, the words should not be recited separately. And wherever augment letters and the like are seen, in those usages, the preceding words should not be recited separately; they should be recited together with the following words that have augment letters. For example: 'Nakkhattarājāriva tārakānaṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca'—such are the usages. Wherever a separate connection is seen for each word, and the meaning is coherent, there they should be recited separately according to the meaning. For example: 'Nahāne ussukkaṃ akāsi, ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā khādanīye bhattasmiṃ'—such are the usages. Here, indeed, it should be recited separately as 'nahāne ussukkaṃ akāsi', and then 'ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā khādanīye bhattasmiṃ'. For in this way, it becomes capable of expressing the meaning that 'not only did that bhikkhu show eagerness for bathing, but he also showed eagerness for gruel, for solid food, and for the meal', and the particle 'api', which denotes accumulation, is not used in the wrong place.

Yattha pana yesamitarena vā itarena vā ekekapadena ubhayapadehi vā sambandho dissati sahevatthayuttiyā, tattha tāni yathārahaṃ vicchinditvā uccāretabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ? “So dhammaṃ desetiādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ [M 0.0060] pakāseti. Paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmi, taṃ suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasikarotha. Ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāva”nti evamādayo payogā. Tatrimā adhippāyaviññāpikā gāthā –

Where, however, a connection is seen with one word or another, or with both words, along with a coherent meaning, there they should be recited separately as is appropriate. For example: 'So dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti. Paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmi, taṃ suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasikarotha. Ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ'—such are the usages. Here are these verses that make the intention known:

Dhammasaddena vā brahma-cariyasaddena vā padaṃ;

Yojetvā īraye viññū, “sātthaṃ sabyañjana”ntidaṃ.

The wise person should utter this phrase, 'sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ', connecting it with the word 'dhamma' or with the word 'brahmacariya'.

“Sādhuka”nti padaṃ viññū, “suṇāthā”ti padena vā;

Tathā “manasikarotha”, iti vuttapadena vā;

Īraye yojayitvāna, ubhayehi padehi vā.

The wise person should utter the word 'sādhukaṃ', having connected it with the word 'suṇātha', or likewise with the word spoken as 'manasikarotha', or with both words.

Ekamekena sambandho, sambandho ubhayehi vā;

Dissatīti vijāneyya, saddhimevatthayuttiyā.

One should understand that a connection with each one is seen, or a connection with both, together with the coherence of meaning.

Nattanomatiyā eso, attho ettha mayā ruto;

Pubbācariyasīhānaṃ, nayaṃ nissāya me ruto.

This meaning has been uttered by me here not according to my own opinion; it has been uttered by me relying on the method of the former teachers, who were like lions.

Evaṃvidhesu aññesu, pāṭhesupi ayaṃ nayo;

Netabbo nayadakkhena, sāsanatthagavesinā.

In other such passages too, this method should be applied by one skilled in method, who seeks the meaning of the Teaching.

Atthānurūpato saddaṃ, atthaṃ saddānurūpato;

Cintayitvāna medhāvī, vohare na yathā tathāti.

The wise person, having reflected on the word according to the meaning, and on the meaning according to the word, should speak, not haphazardly.

Ayamettha atthasaddacintā.

Herein is the consideration of meaning and words.

Atthātisayayoge evaṃ upalakkhetabbaṃ – bhūdhātuatthātisayayogato vaḍḍhane diṭṭhā “ekamantaṃ nisinno kho mahānāmo licchavī udānaṃ udānesi ‘bhavissanti vajjī bhavissanti vajjī’ti” iti vā “ahameva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassā”ti vā “vedā na tāṇāya bhavantidassa, mittadduno bhūnahuno narassā”ti vā “bhūnahaccaṃ kataṃ mayā”ti vā evaṃ vaḍḍhane diṭṭhā.

In the context of an excess of meaning, it should be understood thus: from the connection with an excess of meaning of the root `bhū-`, it is seen in the sense of 'growth,' as in: 'The Licchavi Mahānāma, sitting to one side, uttered an inspired utterance: "The Vajjis will prosper, the Vajjis will prosper!"' or 'I alone am ruined, a destroyer of beings, by King Mahāpatāpa.' or 'The Vedas are no protection for that man, the friend-betrayer, the destroyer of beings.' or 'An act of destroying beings has been done by me'—thus it is seen in the sense of 'growth.'

Vacanasaṅgahe [M 0.0061] evaṃ upalakkhetabbaṃ – vattamānāya vibhattiyā parassapadaṃ majjhimapurisabahuvacanaṃ pañcamiyā parassapadena majjhimapurisabahuvacanena sadisaṃ. Tumhe bhavatha.

In the collection of verbal forms, it should be understood thus: the second person plural of the active voice of the present tense is similar to the second person plural of the active voice of the imperative mood. 'Tumhe bhavatha.'

Vattamānapañcamīnaṃ parassapade uttamapurisacatukke ekavacanaṃ ekavacanena, bahuvacanampi bahuvacanena sadisaṃ. Ahaṃ bhavāmi, mayaṃ bhavāma.

In the active voice of the present and imperative tenses, in the four forms of the first person, the singular is similar to the singular, and the plural is also similar to the plural. 'Ahaṃ bhavāmi,' 'mayaṃ bhavāma.'

Vattamānāya attanopadaṃ majjhimapurisekavacanaṃ hiyyattanajjatanīnaṃ attanopadehi dvīhi majjhimapurisekavacanehi sadisaṃ katthaci vaṇṇasamudāyavasena kiñci visesaṃ vajjetvā, esa nayo uttaratrāpi yojetabbo. Tvaṃ bhavase, idaṃ vattamānāya rūpaṃ. Tvaṃ abhavase, idaṃ hiyyattanajjatanīnaṃ rūpaṃ.

The second person singular of the middle voice of the present tense is similar to the two second person singular forms of the middle voice of the imperfect and aorist tenses, with the exception of some difference in the collection of letters; this method should be applied in what follows as well. 'Tvaṃ bhavase,' this is the present tense form. 'Tvaṃ abhavase,' this is the form of the imperfect and aorist tenses.

Vattamānāya attanopadaṃ uttamapurisekavacanaṃ pañcamiyā attanopadenuttamapurisekavacanena ca parokkhāya parassapadena majjhimapurisekavacanena cāti dvīhi vacanehi sadisaṃ. Ahaṃ bhave, idaṃ vattamānapañcamīnaṃ rūpaṃ. Tvaṃ babhūve, idaṃ parokkhāya rūpaṃ.

The first person singular of the middle voice of the present tense is similar to two verbal forms: the first person singular of the middle voice of the imperative mood, and the second person singular of the active voice of the perfect tense. 'Ahaṃ bhave,' this is the form of the present and imperative tenses. 'Tvaṃ babhūve,' this is the form of the perfect tense.

Vattamānāya attanopadaṃ uttamapurisabahuvacanaṃ parokkhajjatanīnaṃ attanopadehi dvīhi uttamapurisabahuvacanehi sadisaṃ. Mayaṃ bhavāmhe, idaṃ vattamānāya rūpaṃ. Mayaṃ babhūvimhe, idaṃ parokkhāya rūpaṃ. Mayaṃ abhavimhe, idamajjataniyā rūpaṃ.

The first person plural of the middle voice of the present tense is similar to the two first person plural forms of the middle voice of the perfect and aorist tenses. 'Mayaṃ bhavāmhe,' this is the present tense form. 'Mayaṃ babhūvimhe,' this is the perfect tense form. 'Mayaṃ abhavimhe,' this is the aorist tense form.

Pañcamiyā attanopadaṃ majjhimapurisabahuvacanaṃ parokkhāya attanopadena majjhimapurisabahuvacanena sadisaṃ. Tumhe bhavavho, idaṃ pañcamiyā rūpaṃ. Tumhe babhūvivho, idaṃ parokkhāya rūpaṃ.

The second person plural of the middle voice of the imperative mood is similar to the second person plural of the middle voice of the perfect tense. 'Tumhe bhavavho,' this is the imperative mood form. 'Tumhe babhūvivho,' this is the perfect tense form.

Parokkhāya parassapadaṃ paṭhamapurisabahuvacanaṃ hiyyattaniyā parassapadena paṭhamapurisabahuvacanena ca ajjataniyā attanopadena paṭhamapurisabahuvacanena cāti dvīhi vacanehi sadisaṃ. Te babhūvu, idaṃ parokkhāya rūpaṃ. Te abhavu, idaṃ hiyyattanajjatanīnaṃ rūpaṃ.

The third person plural of the active voice of the perfect tense is similar to two verbal forms: the third person plural of the active voice of the imperfect tense, and the third person plural of the middle voice of the aorist tense. 'Te babhūvu,' this is the perfect tense form. 'Te abhavu,' this is the form of the imperfect and aorist tenses.

Parokkhāya [M 0.0062] parassapadaṃ majjhimapurisabahuvacanaṃ attanopadena paṭhamapurisekavacanena ca hiyyattaniyā parassapadena majjhimapurisabahuvacanena ca attanopadena paṭhamapurisekavacanena ca ajjataniyā parassapadena majjhimapurisabahuvacanena cāti catūhi vacanehi sadisaṃ. Tumhe babhūvittha, so babhūvittha, imāni parokkhāya rūpāni. Tumhe abhavattha, so abhavattha, imāni hiyyattaniyā rūpāni. Tumhe abhavittha, idamajjataniyā rūpaṃ.

The second person plural of the active voice of the perfect tense is similar to four verbal forms: the third person singular of the middle voice of the perfect tense, the second person plural of the active voice of the imperfect tense, the third person singular of the middle voice of the imperfect tense, and the second person plural of the active voice of the aorist tense. 'Tumhe babhūvittha,' 'so babhūvittha'—these are perfect tense forms. 'Tumhe abhavattha,' 'so abhavattha'—these are imperfect tense forms. 'Tumhe abhavittha,' this is the aorist tense form.

Parokkhāya parassapadaṃ uttamapurisekavacanaṃ hiyyattaniyā parassapadenuttamapurisekavacanena ca ajjataniyā attanopadenuttamapurisekavacanena cāti dvīhi vacanehi sadisaṃ. Ahaṃ babhūvaṃ, idaṃ parokkhāya rūpaṃ. Ahaṃ abhavaṃ, idaṃ hiyyattanajjatanīnaṃ rūpaṃ.

The first person singular of the active voice in the perfect tense is similar to two forms: the first person singular of the active voice in the imperfect tense, and the first person singular of the middle voice in the aorist tense. 'Ahaṃ babhūvaṃ' is the perfect tense form. 'Ahaṃ abhavaṃ' is the form for the imperfect and aorist tenses.

Parokkhāya parassapadaṃ uttamapurisabahuvacanaṃ hiyyattaniyā parassapadenuttamapurisabahuvacanena sadisaṃ. Mayaṃ babhūvimha, idaṃ parokkhāya rūpaṃ. Mayaṃ abhavamha, idaṃ hiyyattaniyā rūpaṃ.

The first person plural of the active voice of the perfect tense is similar to the first person plural of the active voice of the imperfect tense. 'Mayaṃ babhūvimha' is the perfect tense form. 'Mayaṃ abhavamha' is the imperfect tense form.

Parokkhāya attanopadauttamapurisekavacanaṃ hiyyattaniyā attanopadenuttamapurisekavacanena ca ajjataniyā parassapadenuttamapurisekavacanena cāti dvīhi vacanehi sadisaṃ. Ahaṃ babhūviṃ, idaṃ parokkhāya rūpaṃ. Ahaṃ abhaviṃ, idaṃ hiyyattanajjatanīnaṃ rūpaṃ.

The perfect tense, middle voice, first person singular is similar to two forms: the imperfect tense, middle voice, first person singular, and the aorist tense, active voice, first person singular. 'Ahaṃ babhūviṃ' is the perfect tense form. 'Ahaṃ abhaviṃ' is the form for the imperfect and aorist tenses.

Hiyyattaniyā parassapadaṃ paṭhamapurisekavacanaṃ ajjataniyā attanopadena paṭhamapurisekavacanena sadisaṃ. So abhavā.

The imperfect tense, active voice, third person singular is similar to the aorist tense, middle voice, third person singular, as in 'So abhavā'.

Hiyyattaniyā parassapadaṃ majjhimapurisekavacanaṃ ajjataniyā parassapadena majjhimapurisekavacanena sadisaṃ. Tvaṃ abhavo.

The imperfect tense, active voice, second person singular is similar to the aorist tense, active voice, second person singular, as in 'Tvaṃ abhavo'.

Bhavissantiyā parassapadaṃ majjhimapurisabahuvacanaṃ kālātipattiyā parassapadena majjhimapurisabahuvacanena attanopadena paṭhamapurisekavacanena cāti dvīhi vacanehi sadisaṃ. Tumhe [M 0.0063] bhavissatha, idaṃ bhavissantiyā rūpaṃ. Tumhe abhavissatha, so abhavissatha, imāni kālātipattiyā rūpāni.

The future tense, active voice, second person plural is similar to two forms: the conditional tense, active voice, second person plural, and the conditional tense, middle voice, third person singular. 'Tumhe bhavissatha' (You will be) is the future tense form. 'Tumhe abhavissatha' (You would have been) and 'so abhavissatha' (he would have been) are the conditional tense forms.

Bhavissantiyā attanopadaṃ majjhimapurisekavacanaṃ kālātipattiyā attanopadena majjhimapurisekavacanena sadisaṃ. Tvaṃ bhavissase, idaṃ bhavissantiyā rūpaṃ. Tvaṃ abhavissase, idaṃ kālātipattiyā rūpaṃ.

The future tense, middle voice, second person singular is similar to the conditional tense, middle voice, second person singular. 'Tvaṃ bhavissase' (You will be) is the future tense form. 'Tvaṃ abhavissase' (You would have been) is the conditional tense form.

Bhavissantiyā attanopadaṃ majjhimapurisabahuvacanaṃ kālātipattiyā attanopadena majjhimapurisabahuvacanena sadisaṃ. Tumhe bhavissavhe, idaṃ bhavissantiyā rūpaṃ. Tumhe abhavissavhe, idaṃ kālātipattiyā rūpaṃ.

The future tense, middle voice, second person plural is similar to the conditional tense, middle voice, second person plural. 'Tumhe bhavissavhe' (You will be) is the future tense form. 'Tumhe abhavissavhe' (You would have been) is the conditional tense form.

Bhavissantiyā attanopadaṃ uttamapurisekavacanaṃ kālātipattiyā parassapadenuttamapurisekavacanena sadisaṃ. Ahaṃ bhavissaṃ, idaṃ bhavissantiyā rūpaṃ. Ahaṃ abhavissaṃ, idaṃ kālātipattiyā rūpaṃ. Sesāni sabbāsamaṭṭhannaṃ vibhattīnaṃ vacanāni aññamaññaṃ visadisānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhavanti catra –

The future tense, middle voice, first person singular is similar to the conditional tense, active voice, first person singular. 'Ahaṃ bhavissaṃ' (I will be) is the future tense form. 'Ahaṃ abhavissaṃ' (I would have been) is the conditional tense form. It should be understood that the remaining forms of all eight inflections are mutually dissimilar. And here are the verses:

Vattamānāpañcamīsu, thadvayaṃ samudīritaṃ;

“Tumhe bhavatha”iccatra, udāharaṇakaṃ dvidhā.

In the present and imperative tenses, two 'tha' forms are declared. 'Tumhe bhavatha' (You are/be) is a twofold example here.

Midvayaṃ madvayañceva, tāsu vuttaṃ dvidhā dvidhā;

“Bhavāmī”ti “bhavāmā”ti, cettha rūpāni niddise.

The two 'mi' forms and the two 'ma' forms are stated in those tenses in two ways each. 'Bhavāmi' (I am) and 'bhavāma' (we are)—here these forms are indicated.

Vattamānakahiyyatta-najjatanīvibhattisu;

Settayaṃ “bhavase tva”nti, vattamānāvibhattito;

“Abhavase”ti hiyyatta-najjatanīvibhattito.

In the present, imperfect, and aorist inflections, there are three 'se' forms. 'Tvaṃ bhavase' (You are) is from the present inflection; 'Abhavase' (You were) is from the imperfect and aorist inflections.

Vattamānāpañcamikā-parokkhāsu vibhattisu;

Ettayaṃ lapitaṃ tattha, ādo dvinnaṃ vasena tu.

In the present, imperative, and perfect inflections, the three 'e' forms are spoken of there, initially in terms of two.

Jaññā “ahaṃ bhave”ti “tvaṃ, babhūve”ti parokkhato;

Vattamānāparokkhajja-tanīsu tīsu sadditaṃ.

One should know 'ahaṃ bhave' (let me be), and 'tvaṃ babhūve' (you were) from the perfect tense. In the three tenses—present, perfect, and aorist—it is sounded:

Mhettayaṃ [M 0.0064] kamato rūpaṃ, mayaṃsaddavisesiyaṃ;

“Sambhavāmhe babhūvimhe, abhavimhe”ti niddise.

The three 'mhe' forms are the forms in order, specified by the word 'mayaṃ' (we). 'Sambhavāmhe' (we are), 'babhūvimhe' (we were), and 'abhavimhe' (we were) are indicated.

Pañcamikāparokkhāsu, vhodvayaṃ rūpamettha hi;

“Bhavavho babhūvivho”ti, tumhesaddavisesiyaṃ.

In the imperative and perfect tenses, indeed, two 'vho' forms are here. 'Bhavavho' (You be) and 'babhūvivho' (you were) are specific to the word 'tumhe' (you).

Parokkhamhi vā hiyyatta-najjatanīvibhattisu;

Uttayaṃ “te babhūvū”ti, rūpaṃ jaññā parokkhato;

In the perfect, or in the imperfect and aorist inflections, there are three 'ū' forms. The form 'te babhūvū' (they were) should be known as being from the perfect;

Hiyyattanajjatanito, jaññā “te abhavū”iti.

and from the imperfect and aorist, one should know 'te abhavū' (they were).

Parokkhamhi vā hiyyatta-najjatanīvibhattisu;

Sadditaṃ tathasaṃyoga- pañcakaṃ iti niddise.

In the perfect, or in the imperfect and aorist inflections, the five forms with the conjunct consonant 'tth' are indicated thus:

Babhūvitthadvayaṃ tattha, rūpaṃ jaññā parokkhajaṃ;

Bavhattekattato vuttaṃ, majjhimapaṭhamavhayaṃ.

There, the two 'babhūvittha' forms should be known as arising from the perfect tense. They are stated as plural and singular, designated as second and third person respectively.

Abhavatthadvayaṃ ñeyyaṃ, hiyyattanīvibhattijaṃ;

Bavhattekattato vuttaṃ, majjhimo paṭhamo ca so;

“Abhavitthā”tidaṃ rūpaṃ, ajjatanīvibhattijaṃ.

The two 'abhavattha' forms should be known as arising from the imperfect inflection. They are stated as plural and singular, and are second and third person respectively. The form 'Abhavitthā' arises from the aorist inflection.

Tañca kho bahukattamhi, tumhesaddena yojaye;

Parokkhāvhayahiyyatta-najjatanīsu kittitaṃ.

And indeed, that form, being plural, should be joined with the word 'tumhe'. It is stated in the perfect, imperfect, and aorist tenses:

Aṃtayaṃ tattha ādiyaṃ, “babhūvaṃ”rūpamīritaṃ;

Duvinnaṃ abhavaṃrūpaṃ, ahaṃsaddena yojaye.

There, regarding the three 'aṃ' forms: firstly, the form 'babhūvaṃ' (I became) is mentioned. The 'abhavaṃ' form, common to the other two tenses, should be joined with the word 'ahaṃ'.

Parokkhakāhiyyattanī-vasena mhadukaṃ “mayaṃ;

Babhūvimha abhavimha”, iti rūpadvayaṃ kamā.

By way of the perfect and imperfect tenses, the pair of 'mha' forms with 'mayaṃ' (we) are, in order, the two forms: 'Babhūvimha' (we were) and 'abhavimha' (we were).

Parokkhāvhayahiyyatta-najjatanīvibhattisu;

Iṃtayaṃ tu tahiṃ rūpaṃ, “babhūvi”nti parokkhajaṃ;

“Abhavi”ntītarāsaṃ tu, ahaṃsaddayutākhilaṃ.

In the perfect, imperfect, and aorist inflections, there are three 'iṃ' forms. The form 'babhūviṃ' (I became) is from the perfect. 'Abhaviṃ' (I became) is from the others, all of them joined with the word 'ahaṃ'.

Hiyyattanajjatanīsu[M 0.0065], ādvayaṃ matamettha hi;

“Abhavā” iti ekatte, rūpaṃ paṭhamaporisaṃ.

In the imperfect and aorist tenses, indeed, two 'ā' forms are considered here. 'Abhavā' is the singular, third person form.

Hiyyattanajjatanīsu, odvayaṃ vuttamettha tu;

“Abhavo”iti ekatte, rūpaṃ majjhimaporisaṃ.

In the imperfect and aorist tenses, however, two 'o' forms are stated here. 'Abhavo' is the singular, second person form.

Bhavissantiyakālāti-pattīsu dvīsu bhāsitaṃ;

Bavhatte bahuekatte, sasaṃyogaṃ ssathattayaṃ.

In the two tenses, future and conditional, it is spoken: in the plural and singular, there are three 'ssatha' forms with a conjunct 's'.

“Tumhe bhavissathi”ccetaṃ, bhavissantiyato mataṃ;

“Abhavissatha tumhe”ti, “abhavissatha so”ti ca;

Kālātipattito vuttaṃ, etañhi vacanadvayaṃ.

'Tumhe bhavissatha' (You will be) is considered to be from the future tense. 'Tumhe abhavissatha' (You would have been) and 'so abhavissatha' (he would have been)—these two expressions are stated to be from the conditional tense.

Bhavissantiyakālāti-pattīsu samudīritaṃ;

Majjhimapurisaṭṭhāne, sasaṃyogaṃ ssaseyugaṃ.

In the future and conditional tenses, it is declared: in the place of the second person, the pair of 'ssase' forms with a conjunct 's'.

“Bhavissase tva”miccetaṃ, “tvaṃ abhavissase”ti ca;

Imāni tu payogāni, tattha viññū pakāsaye.

“‘You will be’ (bhavissase tvaṃ), and ‘you would be’ (tvaṃ abhavissase); these applications a wise person should explain therein.

Ssavhedvayaṃ sena yutaṃ, ssaṃdvayañca catukkakaṃ;

Idampi kathitaṃ dvīsu, yathārutavibhattisu.

The two ‘ssavhe’ forms, joined with ‘se’, and the two ‘ssaṃ’ forms, making a set of four; this too is stated for the two inflections known from tradition.

“Bhavissavhe”ti bavhatte, bhavissantikamajjhimo;

Bavhatte “abhavissavhe”, kālātipattimajjhimo.

‘You will be’ (bhavissavhe) in the plural, is the future tense, second person, middle voice; in the plural, ‘you would be’ (abhavissavhe), is the conditional tense, second person, middle voice.

“Bhavissaṃ” iti ekatte, bhavissantikamuttamo;

“Abhavissa”nti ekatte, kālātipattikuttamo.

‘I will be’ (bhavissaṃ) in the singular, is the future tense, first person; ‘I would be’ (abhavissaṃ) in the singular, is the conditional tense, first person.

Iti vuttāni vuttehi, vacanehi samānataṃ;

Yante’kaccehi taṃ sabbaṃ, ekatālīsadhā ṭhitaṃ.

Thus the spoken forms attain similarity with those previously mentioned. Some hold that all of this is established in forty-one ways.

Sesāni pañcapaññāsa, asamānāni sabbathā;

Etaṃ nayaṃ gahetvāna, vade sabbattha sambhavāti.

The remaining fifty-five are in every way dissimilar. Having grasped this method, one should speak appropriately in all instances.

Ayamettha samānāsamānavasena vacanasaṅgaho.

Herein is the compilation of verbal forms according to similarity and dissimilarity.

Āgamalakkhaṇavasena [M 0.0066] vibhattivacanasaṅgahe evaṃ upalakkhetabbaṃ –

In the compilation of inflections and verbal forms, according to the characteristics of augments, it should be understood thus:

Bhavissantīparokkhajja-tanīkālātipattisu;

Niccaṃ kvaci kvacā’niccaṃ, ikārāgamanaṃ bhave.

In the future, perfect, aorist, and conditional tenses, the augment ‘i’ may occur, sometimes regularly and sometimes irregularly.

Ikārāgamanaṃ tañhi, parokkhāyaṃ vibhattiyaṃ;

Bavhatte majjhimaṭṭhāne, bavhatte cuttame siyā;

Parassapadaṃ sandhāya, idaṃ vacanamīritaṃ.

Indeed, that augment ‘i’ in the perfect inflection may occur in the plural second person and in the plural first person. This statement is made with reference to the active voice.

Uttamekavaco cāpi, netassa attanopade;

Hotīti avagantabbaṃ, bhavissantimhi sabbaso.

And it should be understood that for the first person singular, this [augment] does not occur in the middle voice; it occurs entirely in the future tense.

Hiyyattanajjatanika-kālātipattīsu pana;

Akārāgamanaṃ hoti, sabbaso iti lakkhaye.

However, in the aorist and conditional tenses, the augment ‘a’ occurs without exception; thus it should be noted.

Ajjatanimhi bavhatte, majjhime uttame tathā;

Bavhattamhi akārena, ikārāgamanaṃ bhave.

In the aorist, for the plural second and first persons, the augment ‘i’ may occur along with the augment ‘a’.

Ikārāgamanaṃ niccaṃ, kālātipattiyaṃ bhave;

Akārāgamanaṃ tattha, anekantikamīritaṃ.

In the conditional tense, the augment ‘i’ is regular, while the augment ‘a’ there is said to be irregular.

Akārāgamanaṃyeva, hiyyattanyaṃ pakāsati;

Parokkhāyaṃ bhavissantya-ñcikāroyeva dissati.

The augment ‘a’ alone appears in the aorist; in the perfect and future, only the augment ‘i’ is seen.

Akārāgamanañceva, ikārāgamanampi ca;

Ajjatanikakālāti-pattīsu pana dissati.

However, both the augment ‘a’ and the augment ‘i’ are seen in the aorist and conditional tenses.

Tīsu sesavibhattīsu, nā’kārattayamīritaṃ;

Vattamānāya pañcamyaṃ, sattamiyanti sabbaso.

In the three remaining inflections—the present, imperative, and optative—the triad of augments is not mentioned at all.

Ikāreneva sahitā, dve bhavanti vibhattiyo;

Satta dvādasa hontettha, vacanānīti lakkhaye.

Two inflections occur accompanied only by the augment ‘i’. One should note that in these, there are seven and twelve verbal forms respectively.

Akāreneva sahitā, ekāyeva vibhatti tu;

Dvādasa vacanānettha, bhavantīti ca lakkhaye.

However, there is only one inflection accompanied by the augment ‘a’ alone. And one should note that in this, twelve verbal forms occur.

Akārikārasahitā[M 0.0067], duveyeva vibhattiyo;

Cattāri dvādasañceva, vacanāni bhavantidha.

There are indeed two inflections accompanied by both the augment ‘a’ and the augment ‘i’. Herein, there are four and twelve verbal forms respectively.

Ākārattayamuttā tu, tissoyeva vibhattiyo;

Vacanānettha chattiṃsa, hontīti paridīpaye.

However, there are three inflections free from the triad of augments. One should declare that in these, there are thirty-six verbal forms.

Parokkhāajjatanīsu, pañcaṭṭha ca yathākkamaṃ;

Ikārato vimuttāni, vacanāni bhavantiti.

In the perfect and aorist, five and eight forms respectively, free from the augment ‘i’, occur thus.

Evamettha vibhattīnaṃ, channavutividhāna ca;

Saṅgaho vacanānanti, viññātabbo vibhāvināti.

Thus, this compilation of the ninety-six types of verbal forms according to their inflections is to be understood by the discerning.

Ayamettha āgamalakkhaṇavasena vibhattivacanasaṅgaho.

Herein is the compilation of inflections and verbal forms according to the characteristics of augments.

Kālavasena pana vibhattivacanasaṅgahe duvidho saṅgaho kālattayavasena saṅgaho, kālachakkavasena saṅgaho cāti. Tattha vattamānāpañcamīsattamīvibhattiyo paccuppannakālikā, vattamānāpañcamīsattamīvibhatyantāni padāni paccuppannavacanāni. Parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanīvibhattiyo atītakālikā, parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanīvibhatyantāni padāni atītavacanāni. Bhavissantīvibhatti anāgatakālikā, bhavissantīvibhatyantāni padāni anāgatavacanāni. Kālātipattivibhatti pana katthaci atītakālikā katthaci anāgatakālikā, tasmā tadantāni padāni atītavacanānipi anāgatavacanānipi honti. Ayaṃ kālattayavasena vibhattivacanasaṅgaho.

However, regarding the compilation of verbal inflections and expressions according to time, there are two types of compilation: compilation according to the three times, and compilation according to the wheel of time. Therein, the present, imperative, and optative verbal inflections pertain to the present time; words ending in the present, imperative, and optative inflections are present expressions. The perfect, hiyyattanī, and ajjatanī verbal inflections pertain to the past time; words ending in the perfect, hiyyattanī, and ajjatanī inflections are past expressions. The future verbal inflection pertains to the future time; words ending in the future inflection are future expressions. The conditional verbal inflection, however, pertains sometimes to the past time and sometimes to the future time; therefore, words ending in it are both past expressions and future expressions. This is the compilation of verbal inflections and expressions according to the three times.

Ayaṃ pana kālachakkavasena vibhattivacanasaṅgaho – parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanīvibhattiyo atītakālikā, parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanīvibhatyantāni padāni atītavacanāni. Bhavissantīvibhatti anāgatakālikā, bhavissantīvibhatyantāni padāni anāgatavacanāni. Vattamānāvibhatti paccuppannakālikā, vattamānāvibhatyantāni padāni paccuppannavacanāni. Pañcamīvibhatti āṇattikālikā[M 0.0068], pañcamīvibhatyantāni padāni āṇattivacanāni. Sattamīvibhatti parikappakālikā, sattamīvibhatyantāni padāni parikappavacanāni. Ettha pana “āṇattivacanānī”ti ca “parikappavacanānī”ti ca idaṃ tathāsīsamattaṃ āsiṭṭhānumatyādīsu pañcamyādīnaṃ dissanato. Kālātipattivibhatti kālātipattikālikā, kālātipattivibhatyantāni padāni kālātipattivacanāni. Evaṃ kālachakkavasena vibhattivacanasaṅgaho veditabbo.

This, however, is the compilation of verbal inflections and expressions according to the wheel of time: the perfect, hiyyattanī, and ajjatanī verbal inflections pertain to the past time; words ending with these inflections are past expressions. The future verbal inflection pertains to the future time; words ending with the future verbal inflection are future expressions. The present verbal inflection pertains to the present time; words ending with the present verbal inflection are present expressions. The imperative verbal inflection pertains to the time of command; words ending with the imperative verbal inflection are expressions of command. The optative verbal inflection pertains to the time of supposition; words ending with the optative verbal inflection are expressions of supposition. Herein, however, the terms ‘expressions of command’ and ‘expressions of supposition’ are merely headings, since the imperative and other inflections are seen in the sense of blessing, permission, and so forth. The conditional (kālātipatti) verbal inflection pertains to the conditional time; words ending with the conditional verbal inflection are conditional expressions. Thus the compilation of verbal inflections and expressions according to the wheel of time should be understood.

Kālasaṅgahe tividho kālasaṅgaho kālattayasaṅgaho kālacatukkasaṅgaho kālachakkasaṅgaho cāti.

In the compilation of time, the compilation is threefold: a compilation of three times, a compilation of four times, and a compilation of six times.

Paccuppanne vattamānā, pañcamī sattamī cimā;

Hontātīte parokkhādī, saha kālātipattiyā.

These—the present, imperative, and optative—are in the present time. The perfect and others, together with the conditional, are in the past time.

Anāgate bhavissantī, kālātipattikāpi vā;

Evaṃ kālattayaṃ ñeyyaṃ, ākhyātaṃ tappakāsakaṃ.

In the future is the future tense, and also optionally the conditional. Thus the threefold time should be known, with the finite verb as its indicator.

Nanu kaccāyane ganthe, kālo vutto catubbidho;

Paccuppannenuttakāle, atītenāgate iti.

But is it not said in the Kaccāyana treatise that time is fourfold: present, unspoken time, past, and future?

Saccaṃ vutto nuttakālo, paccuppannoti icchito;

Samīpe vuttakāloti, atthasambhavato pana.

Truly, 'nuttakāla' is spoken, and it is intended as 'present'; or, 'time spoken of as near,' due to the possibility of meaning.

Tathā hi “yaṃ tikāla”nti, vuttamācariyehipi;

Na kālato vinimuttaṃ, ākhyātaṃ kiñci dissati.

For thus, “that which is threefold in time” is said by the teachers. No finite verb is seen that is freed from time.

Nanu cāvuttakāleti, attho tatra tu yujjati;

Tathā hi chabbidho kālo, niruttimhi pakāsito.

Surely, the meaning 'avuttakāla' (unspoken time) is fitting there; for six kinds of time are explained in grammar.

Atītānāgato paccu-ppanno āṇattimeva ca;

Parikappo ca kālassa, atipattīti chabbidho.

Past, future, present, and also imperative, potential, and lapse of time—thus it is sixfold.

Duve vibhattiyo tattha, āṇattiparikappikā;

Kālamanāmasitvāpi, niruttaññūhi bhāsitā.

Among them, two inflections—the imperative and the potential—are spoken by grammarians even without designating them as time.

“Gacchatu [M 0.0069] gaccheyyi”ccādi-vacane kathite na hi;

Kriyā nipphajjati niṭṭhaṃ, nāgatā nātipannikā.

Indeed, when expressions like “gacchatu” (let him go) or “gaccheyya” (he should go) are spoken, the action is not accomplished, concluded, future, nor past.

Kālātipattikā saddā, atītenāgatepi ca;

Bhavantīti yathāvuttā, niruttimhi vidūhi ve.

Indeed, words of kālātipatti occur in both the past and the future; thus it has been stated by the wise in grammar.

Pañcamīsattamīvhitā, āṇattiparikappikā;

Paccuppanne bhavantīti, na tathā tattha bhāsitā.

The fifth and seventh inflections, the imperative and potential, are not spoken of in that way as being in the present.

Tasmā kaccāyane ganthe, “nuttakāle”ti yaṃ padaṃ;

Attho “avuttakāle”ti, tassa ñāyatimevidaṃ.

Therefore, in the Kaccāyana treatise, regarding the word “nuttakāle,” its meaning is to be understood as “avuttakāle” (unspoken time).

Saccamevaṃ tu santepi, āṇattiparikappikā;

Paccuppannepi daṭṭhabbā, paṇḍitena nayaññunā.

Even though this is truly so, the imperative and potential forms should be seen as present by the wise who understand the method.

Kasmāti ce āṇāpanaṃ, parikappo ca saccato;

Paccuppanne yato atthā, nipphannā dissare ime.

If it is asked, 'Why?'; because these things, command and potential, are in truth seen as accomplished in the present.

“Anuttakāle”ti padaṃ, etassatthassa jotakaṃ;

“Samīpe vuttakāle”ti, atthadīpanatotha vā.

The word “anuttakāle” illuminates this meaning; or alternatively, it is an elucidation of the meaning 'time spoken of as near'.

Atthānaṃ gamanādīnaṃ, nipphatti na tu dissati;

“Gacchatu gaccheyyi”ccādi, vuttakāle yato tato;

Avuttakāle niddiṭṭhā, taddīpakavibhattiyo.

Indeed, the accomplishment of actions such as going is not seen at the time of speaking words like 'gacchatu' or 'gaccheyya'; therefore, the inflections that indicate them are designated as 'unspoken time'.

Kālo vā vuttakāloti, iccevaṃ gahito idha;

Dakkhiṇāsuddhipāṭhamhi, katāva tatiyā ayaṃ;

Kāladīpanatā tāsaṃ, iti yujjati nāññathā.

Or, time is understood here as 'vuttakāla' (spoken time). This third explanation is indeed made in the Dakkhiṇāsuddhipāṭha. That their nature is to indicate time is fitting, and not otherwise.

Atthadvayaṃ pakāsetuṃ, ganthe kaccāyanavhaye;

Thero kaccāyano “nutta-kāle”ti padamabravi.

To clarify the two meanings in the treatise called Kaccāyana, the elder Kaccāyana uttered the word “nuttakāle.”

Evaṃ tidhā catudhāpi, vutto kālāna saṅgaho;

Chadhā idāni kālānaṃ, saṅgaho nāma niyyate.

Thus, the classification of times has been stated in three or even four ways; now, a sixfold classification of times is set forth.

Vibhattiyo [M 0.0070] parokkhā ca, hiyyattanīvibhattiyo;

Atha ajjatanī cāti, tisso’tīte pakāsitā.

The inflections—the perfect, the aorist, and the immediate past—these three are explained as being in the past.

Anāgate bhavissantī, bhavatīti pakittitā;

Paccuppanne vattamānā, tikāle pañcadhā katā.

In the future, the bhavissantī is declared. In the present, the vattamānā. Thus, in the three times, five inflections are made.

Pañcamīsattamīvhitā, āṇattiparikappikā;

Saṅgayhamānā tā yanti, paccuppannamhi saṅgahaṃ.

The fifth and seventh inflections, the imperative and potential, when included, come under the classification of the present.

Yasmā pañcamibhūtāya, vattamānāya ṭhānato;

Samānā pañcamī hoti, tasmā sā pañcamī matā.

Because the fifth (imperative) is similar in position to the present, therefore it is considered the fifth.

Sattamī pana kiñcāpi, samānā tāhi sattamā;

Hoti yasmā tato vuttā, sattamītveva no mati.

But as for the seventh (optative), although it is similar to them, it is called the seventh simply because it is the seventh; this is our view.

Kālātipattiyādīhi, yajjevaṃ vattamānikā;

Chaṭṭhī bhaveyya kālāti-pattikātītavācikā.

If it were so, with kālātipatti and so on, the present would be the sixth inflection, expressing kālātipatti and the past.

Pañcamī tāya chaṭṭhassa, tulyattā ṭhānato nanu;

Tāhi sattavibhattīhi, sattamī aṭṭhamī siyā.

Is not the imperative (pañcamī) equivalent to that sixth inflection in position? Then, with those seven inflections, the optative (sattamī) would be the eighth.

Iti ce koci bhāseyya, “tannā”ti paṭisedhaye;

Atītenāgate cāpi, kālātipattisambhavā.

If anyone should speak thus, one should reject it, saying, 'That is not so,' because kālātipatti occurs in both the past and the future.

Tathā hi bhāsitā cūḷa-niruttimhi visuṃ ayaṃ;

Kālātipatyatītamhā-nāgate cāti dīpaye.

Indeed, this is separately explained in the Cūḷanirutti; it clarifies that kālātipatti occurs in the past and in the future.

Kriyātipannetīteti, kasmā kaccāyane rutaṃ;

Athāpi ce vadeyyatra, “pāyenā”ti pakāsaye.

Why is 'kriyātipanna' (lapsed action) said to be past in Kaccāyana? If one should say here, it clarifies by saying 'pāyena' (mostly).

Yebhuyyena hi lokasmiṃ, atītamhi pavattati;

Kālātipattisaṃyutto, vohāro iti lakkhaye.

For one should recognize that, in the world, the usage connected with kālātipatti mostly occurs in the past.

Atridaṃ kālātipattiyā atītavacanaṃ – “sacāyaṃ bhikkhave rājā pitaraṃ dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ jīvitā na voropessatha, imasmiṃyevassa āsane virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhu [M 0.0071] uppajjissathā”ti. “Passānanda imaṃ mahādhanaseṭṭhiputtaṃ imasmiṃyeva nagare dveasītikoṭidhanaṃ khepetvā bhariyaṃ ādāya bhikkhāya carantaṃ. Sace hi ayaṃ paṭhamavaye bhoge akhepetvā kammante payojayissā, imasmiṃyeva nagare aggaseṭṭhi abhavissā. Sace pana nikkhamitvā pabbajissā, arahattaṃ pāpuṇissā, bhariyāpissa anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahissā. Sace majjhimavaye bhoge akhepetvā kammante payojayissā, dutiyaseṭṭhi abhavissā. Nikkhamitvā pabbajanto anāgāmī abhavissā, bhariyāpissa sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahissā. Sace pacchimavaye bhoge akhepetvā kammante payojayissā, tatiyaseṭṭhi abhavissā. Nikkhamitvā pabbajanto sakadāgāmī abhavissā, bhariyāpissa sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahissā” iti vā, “sace satthā agāraṃ ajjhāvasissā, cakkavattirājā abhavissā. Rāhulasāmaṇero pariṇāyakaratanaṃ, therī itthiratanaṃ, sakalacakkavāḷarajjaṃ etesaññeva abhavissā” iti vā evaṃ kālātipattiyā atītavacanaṃ bhavati.

Herein, this is an example of kālātipatti expressing the past: “If this king, monks, had not deprived his righteous father, the righteous king, of life, the dust-free, stainless eye of the Dhamma would have arisen in him even on this very seat.” Or: “See, Ānanda, this son of a wealthy merchant in this very city, who, after squandering eighty crores of wealth, takes his wife and wanders for alms. If he had engaged in business without squandering his wealth in his youth, he would have become the foremost merchant in this very city. If he had gone forth and renounced, he would have attained arahantship, and his wife would have been established in the fruit of non-returning. If he had engaged in business without squandering his wealth in middle age, he would have become the second merchant. Having gone forth and renounced, he would have become a non-returner, and his wife would have been established in the fruit of once-returning. If he had engaged in business without squandering his wealth in his later years, he would have become the third merchant. Having gone forth and renounced, he would have become a once-returner, and his wife would have been established in the fruit of stream-entry.” Or: “If the Teacher had remained a householder, he would have become a wheel-turning monarch. The novice Rāhula would have been the jewel of an advisor, the elder nun the jewel of a woman, and the sovereignty of the entire universe would have belonged to them.” Thus, this is an example of kālātipatti expressing the past.

Kathaṃ kālātipattiyā anāgatavacanaṃ bhavati? “Cirampi bhakkho abhavissā, sace na vivadāmase. Asīsakaṃ anaṅguṭṭhaṃ, siṅgālo harati rohitaṃ”itivā, “sace ānanda nālabhissā mātugāmo tathāgatappavedite dhammavinaye agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajjaṃ, ciraṭṭhitikaṃ ānanda brahmacariyaṃ abhavissā”ti iti vā, “ayaṃ aṅgulimālassa mātā ‘aṅgulimālaṃ ānessāmī’ti gacchati, sace samāgamissati, aṅgulimālo ‘aṅgulisahassaṃ pūressāmī’ti mātaraṃ māressati. Sacāhaṃ na gamissāmi, mahājāniko abhavissā” iti vā evaṃ kālātipattiyā anāgatavacanaṃ bhavati[M 0.0072]. Kaccāyane pana yebhuyyena atītappavattiṃ sandhāya kālātipattivibhattiyā atītakālikatā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

How does kālātipatti express the future? “The food would have lasted long, if we had not quarreled. The jackal carries away the rohita fish, headless and tailless.” Or: “Ānanda, if women had not obtained the going forth from the household life into homelessness in the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, the holy life, Ānanda, would have lasted long.” Or: “This mother of Aṅgulimāla is going, thinking, 'I will bring Aṅgulimāla.' If she meets him, Aṅgulimāla will kill his mother, thinking, 'I will complete the thousand fingers.' But if I do not go, there would be a great loss of life.” In this way, kālātipatti expresses the future. In Kaccāyana, however, it should be understood that the kālātipatti inflection is stated as being of the past time with reference to what mostly occurs.

Kaccāyanepi vā esā, kālātipattikā pana;

Anāgatepi hotīti, ayamatthopi dissati.

Or, even in Kaccāyana, this meaning is also seen: that this kālātipatti inflection also occurs in the future.

Appaccakkhe parokkhāya-tīte iti hi lakkhaṇe;

Santepyatītaggahaṇe, anapekkhiya taṃ idaṃ.

Not directly perceived, beyond sight, past—such indeed are its characteristics; even when the matter is present, in grasping the past, this present is not regarded.

Anāgate bhavissantī, iti suttassanantaraṃ;

Kālātipattivacanā, anāgatānukaḍḍhanaṃ;

Tasmā aniyataṃ kālaṃ, kālātipattikaṃ vinā.

‘In the future, they will be’—thus, following the Sutta; from the statement concerning the time-transcending tense, there is an inclusion of the future. Therefore, the time is indefinite, without the time-transcending tense.

Atītānāgatapaccu-ppannikāhi vibhattihi;

Sattamī sattamīyeva, bhavate na tu aṭṭhamī.

By the inflections pertaining to the past, future, and present, the seventh is indeed the seventh, and not the eighth.

Pañcamīsattamīnaṃ tu, paccuppannavibhattiyaṃ;

Saṅgaṇhanatthametāsaṃ, majjhe chaṭṭhī na vuccati.

But as for the fifth and seventh, among the present-time inflections, for the purpose of including them, the sixth is not stated in the middle.

Tathā pañca upādāya, bhavitabbañca chaṭṭhiyā;

Pañcamiyā tu sā esā, “chaṭṭhī”ti na samīritā.

Similarly, taking the fifth, there should also be a sixth; but this one is the fifth, it is not referred to as ‘sixth’.

Chaṭṭhībhāvamhi santepi, “pañcamī”ti vaco pana;

Pañcamiyā vibhattiyā, paccuppannavibhattiyaṃ.

Even though it is in the state of being the sixth, the word ‘fifth’, however, is for the fifth inflection among the present-time inflections.

Saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ vuttanti, viññātabbā vibhāvinā;

Pañcamiṃ tu upādāya, sattamiyā vibhattiyā.

It is said for the purpose of inclusion, which is to be understood by the discerning one. But taking the fifth, with regard to the seventh inflection,

Chaṭṭhiyā ca bhavitabbaṃ, na sā “chaṭṭhī”ti īritā;

Chaṭṭhiṃ pana upādāya, “sattamī”tveva īritā.

there should also be a sixth, but it is not called ‘sixth’; but having taken the sixth, it is indeed called ‘seventh’.

Majjhe chaṭṭhiṃ adassetvā, evaṃ tu kathanampi ca;

Sattamiyā vibhattiyā, paccuppannavibhattiyaṃ;

Saṅgaṇhanatthaṃ vuttanti, adhippāyaṃ vibhāvaye.

And by not showing the sixth in the middle, this statement is also made; one should discern the intention that it is spoken for the purpose of including the seventh inflection among the present-time inflections.

Sabhāvo hesa vatthūnaṃ, gambhīratthesu attano;

Yena kenacākārena, adhippāyassa ñāpanaṃ.

For this is the nature of things in their own profound meanings: that by whatever means, there is a making known of the intended meaning.

Yajjevaṃ [M 0.0073] paṭhamaṃtīte-nāgate ca vibhattiyo;

Vatvā tato paccuppanne, kathetabbā vibhattiyo.

If it is so that first the inflections for the past and future should be stated, and having stated them, then the inflections for the present should be spoken,

Kaccāyanavhaye ganthe, kasmā evaṃ na bhāsitā;

Paccuppannavibhatyova, kasmā ādimhi bhāsitā?

why in the treatise called Kaccāyana was it not stated thus? Why were only the present-time inflections stated at the beginning?

Yasmā vadanti vohāra-pathe etāva pāyato;

Tasmā bahuppayogattaṃ, hotetāsaṃ vibhattinaṃ.

Because these inflections are mostly spoken in the path of conventional usage, therefore, for these inflections there is frequent use.

Ādobahuppayogova, kathetabboti ñāyato;

Paccuppannamhi sambhūtā, vibhatyovādito matā.

From the principle that what is frequently used should be stated at the beginning, the inflections that arise in the present are indeed considered to be stated first.

Atītānāgataṃ vatvā, paccuppanne tato paraṃ;

Yasmā vuttamhi lokasmiṃ, hoti vācāsiliṭṭhatā.

Because, when one has spoken of the past and future, and then subsequently of the present, there is smoothness of speech in the world.

Tasmā siliṭṭhakathane, atītādimapekkhiya;

Pañcamī sattamī cetā, vattamānāyanantaraṃ;

Saṅgaṇhanatthamakkhātā, paccuppannavibhattisu.

Therefore, for the sake of smooth speech, considering the past and so forth, these fifth and seventh inflections are declared after the present inflection for the purpose of inclusion among the present-time inflections.

Ettha hi yathā “mātāpitaro”ti vutte siliṭṭhakathanaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva vacane vipariyayaṃ katvā samāsavasena “pitāmātaro”ti vutte siliṭṭhakathanaṃ na hoti, tasmā tādisī saddaracanā apūjanīyā, “pitā mātā ca me dajju”nti pāṭho pana byāsavasena yathicchitappayogattā pūjanīyo, evameva “atītānāgatapaccuppanna”nti vutte siliṭṭhakathanaṃ hoti, “atītapaccuppannānāgata”nti evamādinā vutte siliṭṭhakathanaṃ na hoti, tasmā tādisī saddaracanā apūjanīyā siyā. “Atītārammaṇā paccu-ppannānāgatagocarā”ti vacanaṃ pana gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ yathicchitappayogattā pūjanīyameva. Ayamettha pāḷi veditabbā –

Here, for example, when ‘mātāpitaro’ (mother and father) is said, the phrasing is smooth. But if, in that very statement, the order is reversed and ‘pitāmātaro’ (father and mother) is said by way of a compound, the phrasing is not smooth. Therefore, such a word construction is not commendable. However, the reading ‘pitā mātā ca me dajju’ (may my father and mother give me) is commendable because, being an expanded form, its usage is as desired. Similarly, when ‘atītānāgatapaccuppanna’ (past, future, and present) is said, the phrasing is smooth. But when ‘atītapaccuppannānāgata’ (past, present, and future) and so on is said, the phrasing is not smooth. Therefore, such a word construction would not be commendable. Yet, the statement ‘atītārammaṇā paccuppannānāgatagocarā’ (having the past as object, with the present and future as its range) is indeed commendable because, for the sake of ease in composing verse, its usage is as desired. This Pāli here is to be understood:

“Yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppanna”nti ca,

‘Whatever form, whether past, future, or present…’ and,

“Ekāyanaṃ [M 0.0074] jātikhayantadassī,

Maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena ataṃsu pubbe,

Tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha”nti ca,

‘The one who sees the end of birth, compassionate for the welfare of others, knows the one-going path. By this path, those of the past crossed over; and by it they will cross, and are now crossing the flood.’ and,

“Ye cabbhatītā sambuddhā, ye ca buddhā anāgatā;

Ye cetarahi sambuddhā, bahūnaṃ sokanāsakā.

‘And those Fully Enlightened Ones who have passed, and those Buddhas who are to come in the future, and those Fully Enlightened Ones who are now, the removers of sorrow for many.

Sabbe saddhammagaruno, vihaṃsu viharanti ca;

Athopi viharissanti, esā buddhāna dhammatā”ti ca

All, revering the True Dhamma, have dwelt, are dwelling, and will also dwell thus; this is the nature of the Buddhas.’ and,

Evamanekesu saddappayogesu. Idha yathicchitappayogavasena atītānāgatapaccuppannakālikāsu aṭṭhasu vibhattīsu tisso paccuppannakālikā vibhattiyo ādimhi kathitā, tañca kathanaṃ tāsaññeva vohārapathe yebhuyyena pavattito bahuppayogatāñāpanatthaṃ. Tāsu pana dvinnaṃ vibhattīnaṃ “pañcamīsattamī”tisaññā siliṭṭhakathanicchāyaṃ kamena vattabbā, atītānāgatakālikā vibhattiyo apekkhitvā katā. Iccevaṃ

Thus it is in many such applications of words. Here, by way of desired usage, among the eight inflections pertaining to past, future, and present times, the three present-time inflections are stated at the beginning. And that statement is for the purpose of making known their frequent use, since they occur mostly in the path of conventional usage. But among those, the designations ‘fifth’ and ‘seventh’ for two of the inflections, which should be stated in order out of a desire for smooth expression, were made with consideration to the inflections of past and future time. Thus,

Yathicchitappayogena, paccuppannavibhattiyo;

Tidhā katvāna ādimhi, kaccānena udīritā.

According to desired usage, the present-time inflections, having been made threefold, were declared at the beginning by Kaccāyana.

Ādimhi kathanaṃ tañca, tāsaṃ pāyena vuttito;

Bahuppayogabhāvassa, ñāpanatthanti niddise.

And one should point out that this statement at the beginning is for the purpose of making known their state of frequent use, because they are generally spoken.

Atītādimapekkhitvā, siliṭṭhakathane dhuvaṃ;

“Pañcamī sattami”cceva, dvinnaṃ nāmaṃ katanti ca;

Kālātipattiṃ vajjetvā, idaṃ vacanamīritaṃ.

And one should point out that the naming of the two as ‘fifth’ and ‘seventh’ was certainly done for the sake of smooth speech, with consideration to the past and so forth. This statement was uttered excluding the time-transcending tense.

Yadi evaṃ ayaṃ doso, āpajjati na saṃsayo;

Iti ce koci bhāseyya, atthe akusalonaro.

‘If it is so, this fault arises without a doubt’—if some person unskilled in the meaning should speak thus,

Tekālikākhyātapade[M 0.0075], kālātipattiyā pana;

Asaṅgahova hotīti, “tannā”ti paṭisedhaye.

if he should say that in the verbal forms pertaining to the three times there is a non-inclusion of the time-transcending tense, one should refute it with ‘That is not so’.

Tekālikākhyātapade, na no kālātipattiyā;

Iṭṭho asaṅgaho tattha, saṅgahoyeva icchito.

For us, in the verbal forms pertaining to the three times, non-inclusion of the time-transcending tense is not desired; there, inclusion is indeed desired.

Pañcamīsattamīsaññā, kālātipattikaṃ pana;

Vibhattimanapekkhitvā, katā icceva no mati.

But the designations ‘fifth’ and ‘seventh’ were made without considering the time-transcending inflection; such indeed is our view.

Nānānayaṃ gahetvāna,

Paccetabbaṃ tu sārato;

Yāya eso ruto attho,

Tasmā esā na dubbalā.

Having grasped the various methods, the essence should be understood. By whichever method this meaning is expressed, that method is therefore not weak.

Attho labbhati pāsaṃso,

Yattha yattha yathā yathā;

Tathā tathā gahetabbo,

Tattha tattha vibhāvinā.

Wherever and however a praiseworthy meaning is obtained, in that very way should it be grasped in each case by the discerning one.

Vuttañhetaṃ abhidhammaṭīkāyaṃ “yattha yattha yathā yathā attho labbhati, tattha tattha tathā tathā gahetabbo”ti.

Indeed, this was stated in the Abhidhamma Sub-commentary: 'Wherever and however a meaning is obtained, there and in that way it should be grasped.'

Pañcamīsattamīsaññā, rūḷhīsaññāti kecana;

Na panevaṃ gahetabbaṃ, ajānitvā vadanti te.

Some say that the designations 'fifth' and 'seventh' are conventional designations. But it should not be taken thus; they speak without knowing.

Nesā purisasaññādi, jhala saññādayo viya;

Rūḷhiyā bhāsitā saññā, bhūtenatthena bhāsitā.

This designation is not spoken by convention, like the designations 'person', 'flame', and so forth; it is spoken with a factual meaning.

Upanidhāya paññatti, esā saññā yato tato;

Anvatthasaññā ṭhapitā, porāṇehīti lakkhaye.

This designation is a concept based on comparison, arising from various sources. One should discern that it is an etymological designation established by the ancients.

Iccevaṃ kālachakkaṃ tu, saṅkhepena tidhā mataṃ;

Etamatthañhi sandhāya, “yaṃ tikāla”nti bhāsitaṃ.

Thus, the wheel of time, in brief, is considered threefold; indeed, referring to this very meaning, it is said, 'that which is of three times'.

Ayamettha kālachakkasaṅgaho.

Herein is the compendium of the wheel of time.

Evaṃ [M 0.0076] tidhā catudhā vā, chadhā vāpi sumedhaso;

Kālabhedaṃ vibhāveyya, kālaññūhi vibhāvitaṃ.

Thus, the wise one should discern the divisions of time, whether threefold, fourfold, or even sixfold, as distinguished by those who know time.

Atītānāgataṃ kālaṃ, visuṃ kālātipattikaṃ;

Gahetvā pañcadhā hoti, evañcāpi vibhāvaye.

Taking the past and future time, and separately the time-transcending, it becomes fivefold; thus should one also discern.

Ettha nayova “ajjhatta-bahiddhā vā”ti pāḷiyaṃ;

Atītānāgatakālī, vibhatti samudīritā.

Herein, the method is just as in the Pāli passage 'internally or externally'; the inflections for past and future time are declared.

Iccevaṃ sabbathāpi kālasaṅgaho samatto.

Thus, the compendium concerning time is complete in every respect.

Idāni viññūnaṃ atthaggahaṇe kosallajananatthaṃ pakaraṇantaravasenapi imasmiṃ pakaraṇe vattamānānantaraṃ vuttānaṃ āṇattiparikappakālikānaṃ “pañcamīsattamī”tisaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnaṃ vibhattīnaṃ paṭipāṭiṭṭhapane pakaraṇasaṃsandanaṃ kathayāma – kātantappakaraṇasmiñhi sakkatabhāsānurūpena dasadhā ākhyātavibhattiyo ṭhapitā, kaccāyanappakaraṇe pana māgadhabhāsānurūpena aṭṭhadhā ṭhapitā, niruttiyañca pana māgadhabhāsānurūpeneva atītānāgatapaccuppannāṇattiparikappakālātipattivasena chadhā ṭhapitā. Tesu hi kātante vattamānā, sattamī, pañcamī, hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, parokkhā, svātanī, āsī, bhavissantī, kriyātipatti cāti dasadhā vibhattā. Kaccāyane pana vattamānā, pañcamī, sattamī, parokkhā, hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, bhavissantī, kālātipatti cāti aṭṭhadhā vibhattā. Iti etesu dvīsu kātantakaccāyanesu vibhattiyo visadisāya paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapitā. Kiñcāpettha visadisā paṭipāṭi, tathāpetā niruttiyaṃ vuttātītādikālavibhāgavasena ekato saṃsandanti samenti kiñci visesaṃ ṭhapetvā.

Now, for the purpose of generating skill in grasping the meaning for the discerning, and also by way of other treatises, we will explain the comparison of treatises regarding the arrangement of the two inflections called 'fifth' and 'seventh', which are mentioned immediately after the present in this treatise, pertaining to the imperative and potential moods. Indeed, in the Kātantra treatise, ten verbal inflections are established in accordance with the Sanskrit language. In the Kaccāyana treatise, however, eight are established in accordance with the Māgadhī language. And in the Nirutti, moreover, six are established also in accordance with the Māgadhī language, by way of past, future, present, imperative, potential, and conditional tenses. Among these, in the Kātantra, they are divided into ten: present, seventh, fifth, imperfect, aorist, perfect, future, benedictive, future, and conditional. In the Kaccāyana, however, they are divided into eight: present, fifth, seventh, perfect, imperfect, aorist, future, and conditional. Thus, in these two, Kātantra and Kaccāyana, the inflections are established in a dissimilar order. Although there is a dissimilar order here, nevertheless, they converge and agree in the Nirutti by way of the division of tenses—past, etc.—as stated, except for some minor distinction.

Kathaṃ[M 0.0077]? Kātante tāva hiyyattanī ajjatanī parokkhā cāti imā tisso ekantena atītakālikā, svātanī āsī bhavissanti cāti imā tisso ekantena anāgatakālikā, vattamānā ekāyeva paccuppannakālikā, sattamī pana pañcamī ca paccuppannānāgatakālavasena dvikālikā “ajja puññaṃ kareyya, svepi kareyya. Ajja gacchatu, sve vā gacchatū”ti payogārahattā. Kriyātipatti aniyatakālikā “so ce hiyyo yānaṃ alabhissā, agacchissā. So ce ajja anatthaṅgate sūriye yānaṃ alabhissā, agacchissā. So ce sve yānaṃ alabhissā, agacchissā”ti payogārahattā. Evaṃ asaṅkarato vavatthapetabbaṃ.

How? In the Kātantra system, first, these three—the hiyyattanī (imperfect), ajjatanī (aorist), and parokkhā (perfect)—are exclusively of past time. These three—the svātanī (future), āsī (benedictive), and bhavissantī (future)—are exclusively of future time. The vattamānā (present) is solely of present time. However, the sattamī (optative) and pañcamī (imperative) are of two times, pertaining to both present and future, due to their suitability for use, as in: “May he do merit today, and may he do it tomorrow.” “Let him go today, or let him go tomorrow.” The kriyātipatti (conditional) is of indefinite time, due to its suitability for use, as in: “If he had obtained a vehicle yesterday, he would have gone.” “If he obtained a vehicle today before the sun set, he would go.” “If he obtains a vehicle tomorrow, he would go.” Thus, it should be distinguished without confusion.

Evaṃ vavatthapetvā ayamamhehi vuccamāno nayo sādhukaṃ sallakkhetabbo. Kathaṃ? Hiyyattanajjatanīparokkhāsvātanyāsībhavissantivasena ekantātītānāgatakālikā vibhattiyo cha, vattamānavasena ekantapaccuppannakālikā vibhatti ekāyeva, sā paṭipāṭiyā gaṇiyamānā sattamaṃ ṭhānaṃ bhajati. Evaṃ etasmiṃ vattamānāsaṅkhāte sattamaṭṭhāne pakkhipituṃ niruttinayena “parikappakālikā”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ satthanayena “paccuppannānāgatakālikā”tivattabbaṃ ekaṃ vibhattiṃ sattamībhūtāya vattamānāya samānaṭṭhānattā sattamīsaññaṃ katvā ṭhapesi. Tato punadeva svātanyāsībhavissantivasena ekantānāgatakālikā tisso vibhattiyo gaṇetvā taṃ paccuppannānāgatakālikaṃ “sattamī”ti laddhasaññaṃ vibhattiṃ anāgatakālikabhāvena tāhi tīhi saddhiṃ samānaṭṭhānattā catutthaṃ katvā niruttinayena “āṇattikālikā”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ satthanayena “paccuppannānāgatakālikā”ti vattabbaṃ ekaṃ vibhattiṃ pañcannaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ pūraṇena pañcamīsaññaṃ katvā ṭhapesi.

Having thus established this, the method we are explaining should be carefully considered. How? There are six inflections—hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, parokkhā, svātanī, āsī, and bhavissanti—which are exclusively of past and future time. There is only one inflection, the vattamānā, which is exclusively of present time; when counted in sequence, it occupies the seventh position. Thus, to place in this seventh position, designated as the present, one inflection—which, according to the etymological method, is called “the potential tense” (parikappakālikā), but according to the grammatical method, should be called “the present-future tense” (paccuppannānāgatakālikā)—he established with the designation “seventh” (sattamī), because it shares the same position as the vattamānā, which has become the seventh.
