Then again, counting the three inflections that are exclusively of future time—svātanī, āsī, and bhavissanti—and making that present-future inflection, which had acquired the designation “seventh,” the fourth, because of its future-time nature and its sharing the same position with those three, he established one inflection—which, according to the etymological method, is called “the imperative tense” (āṇattikālikā), but according to the grammatical method, should be called “the present-future tense” (paccuppannānāgatakālikā)—with the designation “fifth” (pañcamī) by completing the count of five.

Kriyātipattiyā [M 0.0078] pana aniyatakālikattā taṃ vajjetvā ayaṃ vinicchayo kato, so ca kho niruttinayaṃyeva nissāya. Ayaṃ tāva kātante vattamānānantaraṃ vuttānaṃ sattamīpañcamīnaṃ anvatthasaññaṃ icchantānaṃ amhākaṃ ruci, esā saddhammavidūhi garūhi appaṭikkositā anumatā sampaṭicchitā “evamevaṃ āvuso, evamevaṃ āvuso”ti. Veyyākaraṇehipi appaṭikkositā anumatā sampaṭicchitā “evamevaṃ bhante, evamevaṃ bhante”ti. Evaṃ sabbehipi tehi pubbācariyehi abbhanumoditā appaṭikkositā.

However, because the kriyātipatti (conditional) is of indefinite time, this decision has been made excluding it, and it is based solely on etymological principles. This, indeed, is our preference for the etymological designation of the sattamī and pañcamī, which are mentioned in the Kātantra immediately after the vattamānā, for those who desire it. This has not been rejected, but approved and accepted by the venerable ones who know the true Dhamma, who say, “Yes, friend, it is just so; yes, friend, it is just so.” It has also not been rejected, but approved and accepted by grammarians, who say, “Yes, venerable sir, it is just so; yes, venerable sir, it is just so.” Thus, it has been fully approved and not rejected by all those ancient teachers.

Kaccāyanappakaraṇe pana buddhavacanānurūpena aṭṭhadhā vibhattīnaṃ vuttattā vattamānāvibhatti pañcamaṭṭhāne ṭhitā. Kathaṃ? Parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanībhavissantivasena ekantātītānāgatakālikā catasso vibhattiyo, vattamānavasena ekantapaccuppannakālikā vibhatti ekāyeva, sā paṭipāṭiyā gaṇiyamānā pañcamaṃ ṭhānaṃ bhajati. Evaṃ etasmiṃ vattamānāsaṅkhāte pañcamaṭṭhāne pakkhipituṃ niruttinayena “āṇattikālikā”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ “anuttakālikā”ti vuttaṃ vibhattiṃ pañcamībhūtāya vattamānāya samānaṭṭhānattā pañcamīsaññaṃ katvā ṭhapesi. Tato paraṃ taṃ pañcamaṃ chaṭṭhiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā parokkhā hiyyattanī ajjatanī bhavissantī vattamānā pañcamīti evaṃ gaṇanāvasena cha vibhattiyo upādāya niruttinayena “parikappakālikā”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ “anuttakālikā”ti vuttaṃ vibhattiṃ sattannaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ pūraṇena sattamīsaññaṃ katvā ṭhapesi.

In the Kaccāyana treatise, however, because the eightfold classification of inflections is stated in accordance with the Buddha’s words, the vattamānā inflection is situated in the fifth place. How so? The four inflections—parokkhā, hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, and bhavissanti—are exclusively of past or future time. The vattamānā inflection is solely of present time; when counted in sequence, it occupies the fifth position. Thus, to place in this fifth position, designated as the present, the inflection called “non-past tense” (anuttakālikā), which has obtained the designation “imperative tense” (āṇattikālikā) according to the etymological method, he established with the designation “fifth” (pañcamī), because it shares the same position as the vattamānā, which has become the fifth. Thereafter, having placed that fifth in the sixth place, and taking the six inflections by way of counting—parokkhā, hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, bhavissanti, vattamānā, and pañcamī—he established the inflection called “non-past tense” (anuttakālikā), which has obtained the designation “potential tense” (parikappakālikā) according to the etymological method, with the designation “seventh” (sattamī) by completing the count of seven.

Kālātipattiyā pana atītānāgatakālikattā taṃ vajjetvā ayaṃ vinicchayo kato, so ca kho niruttinayaṃyeva nissāya. Ayaṃ kaccāyane vattamānānantaraṃ vuttānaṃ pañcamīsattamīnaṃ anvatthasaññaṃ icchantānaṃ amhākaṃ ruci, esā ca saddhammavidūhi garūhi appaṭikkositā anumatā sampaṭicchitā [M 0.0079] “evamevaṃ āvuso, evamevaṃ āvuso”ti. Veyyākaraṇehipi appaṭikkositā anumatā sampaṭicchitā “evamevaṃ bhante, evamevaṃ bhante”ti. Evaṃ sabbehipi tehi pubbācariyehi abbhanumoditā appaṭikkositā.

However, because the kālātipatti pertains to past and future time, this decision has been made excluding it, and that too is based solely on linguistic principles. This is our preference for the meaningful designation of the pañcamī and sattamī, which are mentioned immediately after the vattamānā in Kaccāyana, for those who desire it. And this has not been rejected, but approved and accepted by the wise elders who know the true Dhamma, saying, “So it is, friend, so it is.” It has also not been rejected, but approved and accepted by the grammarians, saying, “So it is, venerable sir, so it is.” Thus, it has been fully approved and not rejected by all those ancient teachers.

Yasmā hi kātantakaccāyanāni aññamaññaṃ visadisavibhattikkamānipi antarena kiñci visesaṃ niruttiyaṃ vuttātītādikālavibhāgavasenekajjhaṃ saṃsandanti samenti, tasmā niruttinayaññeva sārato gahetvā pañcamīsattamīvibhattīnaṃ anvatthasaññāparikappane amhākaṃ ruci pubbācariyehi abbhanumoditā appaṭikkositā, tasmā eva yo koci imaṃ vādaṃ madditvā aññaṃ vādaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ sakkhissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Ayañhi nayo atīva sukhumo duddaso ca paramāṇuriva, dukkhogāḷho ca mahāgahanamiva, atigambhīro ca mahāsamuddo viya, tasmā imissaṃ saddanītiyaṃ saddhāsampannehi kulaputtehi sāsanopakāratthaṃ yogo suṭṭhu karaṇīyo. Tathā hi idha katayogehi nāmākhyātādīsu catūsu padesu uppannavādā paravādino jitāva honti.

For since the Kātantra and Kaccāyana grammars, though their sequences of inflections differ from each other, nevertheless converge and agree in linguistic expression without any real distinction, especially in the divisions of time such as past and future, therefore, our preference for the meaningful designation of the pañcamī and sattamī inflections, taking linguistic principles as essential, has been approved and not rejected by the ancient teachers. Hence, it is not possible for anyone to refute this doctrine and establish another. For this method is exceedingly subtle and hard to perceive like an atom, difficult to fathom like a great forest, and profoundly deep like the great ocean. Therefore, in this science of language, sons of good family endowed with faith should diligently apply themselves for the benefit of the Dispensation. Indeed, those who have applied themselves herein will always overcome opponents in debates concerning the four topics—nouns, verbs, and the rest—where disputes arise.

Muninā munināgena, duṭṭhā pabbajitā jitā;

Yathā yathā asaddhamma-pūraṇā pūraṇādayo.

By the Sage, the Sage-elephant, were wicked renunciants conquered, just as Pūraṇa and others, who were full of false doctrine.

Tathā tathāgatādāyā-nugāyaṃ saddanītiyaṃ;

Katayogehipi jitā, savanti paravādinoti.

So too, in this science of language which follows the Tathāgata’s tradition, are opponents conquered and dispersed by those who have made effort herein.

Ayaṃ pañcamīsattamīnaṃ paṭipāṭiṭṭhapane pakaraṇasaṃsandanā.

This is the harmonization of treatises regarding the establishment of the sequence of the pañcamī and sattamī.

Atha vattamānādīnaṃ vacanatthaṃ kathayāma – tattha vattamānāti kenaṭṭhena vattamānā? Vattamānakālavacanaṭṭhena. Paccuppannabhāvena hi vattatīti vattamāno, paccuppannakriyāsaṅkhāto kālo. Tabbācakavasena vattamāno kālo etissā atthīti ayaṃ ti antiādivibhatti vattamānā. Tathā [M 0.0080] hi “gacchati devadatto”ti ettha devadattassa paccuppannaṃ gamanakriyaṃ vibhattibhūto tisaddoyeva vadati, tasmā tabbācakavasena vattamāno kālo etissā atthīti vattamānāti vuccati. Pañcamīti kenaṭṭhena pañcamī? Pañcamaṃ vattamānaṭṭhānaṃ gamanaṭṭhena, pañcannañca saṅkhyānaṃ pūraṇaṭṭhena. Tathā hi niyogā atītānāgatapaccuppannakālikānaṃ parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanībhavissantīvattamānāsaṅkhātānaṃ pañcannaṃ vibhattīnamantare pañcamībhūtāya vattamānāya sayampi paccuppannakālikabhāvena samānaṭṭhānattā pañcamaṃ vattamānaṭṭhānaṃ gacchatīti pañcamī. Yathā nadantī gacchatīti nadī. Tathā niyogā atītānāgatakālikā parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanībhavissantīsaṅkhātā catasso vibhattiyo upādāya sayampi vattamānāvibhatti viya pañcannaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ pūraṇīti pañcamī. Sattamīti kenaṭṭhena sattamī? Sattannaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ pūraṇaṭṭhena. Tathā hi atītānāgatapaccuppannakālikā parokkhāhiyyattanajjatanībhavissantīvattamānāpañcamīsaṅkhātā cha vibhattiyo upādāya sayampi paccuppannakālikā hutvā sattannaṃ saṅkhyānaṃ pūraṇīti sattamī.

Now, we shall explain the meaning of terms such as 'vattamānā'. Herein, in what sense is it 'vattamānā'? In the sense of expressing the present time. For it is called 'vattamāna' because it exists in the present state; it is time characterized by present action. This inflection ending in 'ti,' 'anti,' etc., is called 'vattamānā' because it possesses the present time by way of being its indicator. For example, in the phrase 'Devadatta goes,' the sound 'ti,' which is the inflection, expresses Devadatta’s present action of going; hence, it is called 'vattamānā' because it possesses the present time by way of being its indicator. In what sense is it 'pañcamī'? In the sense of going to the fifth position of the vattamānā, and in the sense of completing the number five. For, among the five inflections pertaining to the past, future, and present, reckoned as parokkhā, hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, bhavissantī, and vattamānā, because it, being of the present time, shares the same position as the vattamānā, which has become the fifth, it goes to the fifth position of the vattamānā; hence 'pañcamī.' Just as 'nadī' (river) means 'that which goes sounding.' Similarly, taking the four inflections pertaining to the past and future, reckoned as parokkhā, hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, and bhavissantī, it itself, like the vattamānā inflection, completes the number five; hence 'pañcamī.' In what sense is it 'sattamī'? In the sense of completing the number seven. For, taking the six inflections pertaining to the past, future, and present, reckoned as parokkhā, hiyyattanī, ajjatanī, bhavissantī, vattamānā, and pañcamī, it itself, being of the present time, completes the number seven; hence 'sattamī.'

Parokkhāti kenaṭṭhena parokkhā? Parokkhe bhavāti atthena. Tathā hi cakkhādindriyasaṅkhātassa akkhassa paro tirobhāvo parokkhaṃ, tabbācakabhāvena parokkhe bhavāti parokkhā. Hiyyattanīti kenaṭṭhena hiyyattanī? Hiyyo pabhuti atīte kāle bhavā tabbācakabhāvenāti atthena. Ajjatanīti kenaṭṭhena ajjatanī? Ajja pabhuti atīte kāle bhavā tabbācakabhāvenāti atthena. Bhavissantīti kenaṭṭhena bhavissantī? “Evaṃ anāgate bhavissatī”ti atthaṃ pakāsentī eti gacchatīti atthena. Kālātipattīti kenaṭṭhena kālātipatti? Kālassātipatanavacanaṭṭhena. Tathā hi kālassa atipatanaṃ accayo atikkamitvā pavatti kālātipatti, labhitabbassa atthassa nipphattirahitaṃ kriyātikkamanaṃ[M 0.0081]. Kāloti cettha kriyā adhippetā. Karaṇaṃ kāro, kāro eva kālo rakārassa lakāraṃ katvā uccāraṇavasena. Ayaṃ pana vibhatti tabbācakattā kālātipattīti. Ayaṃ pana vattamānādīnaṃ vacanatthavibhāvanā.

In what sense is it 'parokkhā'? In the sense that it occurs in what is beyond the senses. For 'parokkhaṃ' is what is beyond, concealed from the faculty called the eye; because it occurs in that which signifies this, it is 'parokkhā'. In what sense is it 'hiyyattanī'? In the sense that it occurs in past time from yesterday onwards, by its nature of signifying this. In what sense is it 'ajjatanī'? In the sense that it occurs in past time from today onwards, by its nature of signifying this. In what sense is it 'bhavissantī'? In the sense that it proceeds, clarifying the meaning, 'Thus it will be in the future.' In what sense is it 'kālātipatti'? In the sense of stating the transgression of time. For 'kālātipatti' is the transgression of time, the passing beyond, the proceeding by having transgressed; it is the transgression of an action devoid of the accomplishment of the purpose to be achieved. Here, by 'kāla' action is intended. 'Doing' is 'kāro', and 'kāro' itself is 'kālo' by pronouncing 'l' in place of 'r'. This verbal ending, however, is called 'kālātipatti' because it signifies that. This, then, is the explanation of the meaning of the terms for the present and other tenses.

Vippakiṇṇavividhanaye, saṃkiṇṇalakkhaṇadharavarasāsane;

Sumatimativaḍḍhanatthaṃ, kathito pakiṇṇakavinicchayo.

Concerning the various scattered methods in the excellent teaching that bears mixed characteristics, for the purpose of increasing the wisdom of the wise, the Analysis of Miscellaneous Points has been expounded.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the paths of exposition of the nine-limbed teaching with its commentaries and the Tipiṭaka,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the purpose of their skill,

Pakiṇṇakavinicchayo nāma

the Analysis of Miscellaneous Points, named

Tatiyo paricchedo.

the Third Chapter.

4. Bhūdhātumayanāmikarūpavibhāga

4. The Division of Nominal Forms Derived from the Root bhū

“Bhū sattāya”nti dhātussa, rūpamākhyātasaññitaṃ;

Tyādyantaṃ lapitaṃ nāna-ppakārehi anākulaṃ.

Of the root 'bhū in the sense of existence,' the form called the finite verb, ending in 'ti' and so on, has been explained in various ways, without confusion.

Syādyantaṃ, dāni tasseva, rūpaṃ nāmikasavhayaṃ;

Bhāsissaṃ bhāsitatthesu, paṭubhāvāya sotunaṃ.

Now of that same root, the form called the nominal, ending in 'si' and so on, I shall explain, for the proficiency of the listeners in the meanings that have been stated.

Yadatthe’ttani nāmeti, para’matthesu vā sayaṃ;

Namatīti tadāhaṃsu, nāmaṃ iti vibhāvino.

Because it bends itself towards a meaning, or itself bends towards other meanings, the discerning have said that it is a 'name' (nāma), because it bends (namati).

Nāmaṃ nāmikamiccatra, ekamevetthato bhave;

Tadevaṃ nāmikaṃ ñe yyaṃ, saliṅgaṃ savibhattikaṃ.

Here, 'name' and 'nominal' are one and the same. Thus the nominal should be understood as possessing gender and a case-ending.

Satvābhidhānaṃ liṅganti, itthipumanapuṃsakaṃ;

Vibhattītidha satteva, tattha caṭṭha pavuccare.

Gender is the denotation of a substance: feminine, masculine, and neuter. Here there are just seven case-endings, but eight are spoken of in that connection.

Paṭhamā dutiyā tatiyā, catutthī pañcamī tathā;

Chaṭṭhī ca sattamī cāti, honti satta vibhattiyo.

First, second, third, fourth, and fifth, as well as sixth and seventh—thus there are seven case-endings.

Liṅgatthe paṭhamā sāyaṃ, bhinnā dvedhā siyo iti;

Kammatthe dutiyā sāpi, bhinnā aṃ yo iti dvidhā.

The first case, in the sense of the nominal stem, is divided in two as 'si' and 'yo'. The second, in the sense of the object, is also divided in two as 'aṃ' and 'yo'.

Karaṇe [M 0.0082] tatiyā sāpi, bhinnā nā hi iti dvidhā;

Sampadāne catutthī sā, bhinnā dvedhā sa naṃ iti.

The third case, in the sense of the instrument, is also divided in two as 'nā' and 'hi'. The fourth, in the sense of the recipient, is divided in two as 'sa' and 'naṃ'.

Apādāne pañcamī sā, bhinnā dvedhā smā hi iti;

Chaṭṭhī sāmimhi sā cāpi, bhinnā dvedhā sa naṃ iti.

The fifth case, in the sense of the point of departure, is divided in two as 'smā' and 'hi'. The sixth, in the sense of the owner, is also divided in two as 'sa' and 'naṃ'.

Okāse sattamī sāpi, bhinnā dvedhā smiṃsu iti;

Āmantanaṭṭhamī sāyaṃ, siyoyevāti cuddasa.

The seventh case, in the sense of location, is also divided in two as 'smiṃ' and 'su'. The vocative is the eighth; its endings are just 'si' and 'yo'. Thus there are fourteen.

Vacanadvayasaṃyuttā, ekekā tā vibhattiyo;

Satvamitiha viññeyyo, attho so dabbasaññito.

Each of those case-endings is connected with the two numbers. Here the meaning should be known as 'being,' which is designated as 'substance.'

Yo karotisa kattātu, taṃ kammaṃ yaṃ karoti vā;

Kubbate yena vā tantu, karaṇaṃ iti saññitaṃ.

He who acts is the agent; what he does is the object. That by which something is done is designated as the instrument.

Deti rocati vā yassa, sampadānanti taṃ mataṃ;

Yatopeti bhayaṃ vā taṃ, apādānanti kittitaṃ.

The one to whom something is given or is pleasing, that is considered the recipient; that from which one departs or from which there is fear, is declared the point of departure.

Yassāyatto samūhovā, taṃ ve sāmīti desitaṃ;

Yasmiṃ karoti kiriyaṃ, tadokāsanti sadditaṃ.

He on whom a group is dependent is taught to be the 'owner.' That in which one performs an action is called the 'location.'

Yadālapati taṃ vatthu, āmantanamudīritaṃ;

Saddenābhimukhīkāro, vijjamānassa vā pana.

That which one addresses is called the 'vocative.' It is the act of turning someone to face one by means of a word, whether they are present or not.

Vinā ālapanatthaṃ liṅgatthādīsu paṭhamādivibhattuppatti upalakkhaṇavasena vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It should be understood that, apart from the sense of the vocative, the arising of the first and other case-endings in the sense of the nominal stem and so on is stated by way of illustration.

Idamettha niruttilakkhaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ – paccattavacane paṭhamā vibhatti bhavati, upayogavacane dutiyā vibhatti bhavati, karaṇavacane tatiyā vibhatti bhavati, sampadānavacane catutthī vibhatti bhavati, nissakkavacane pañcamī vibhatti bhavati, sāmivacane chaṭṭhī vibhatti bhavati, bhummavacane sattamī vibhatti bhavati, āmantanavacane aṭṭhamī vibhatti bhavati. Tatruddānaṃ –

Herein, the characteristic definitions should be noted—the first case-ending occurs in the sense of the subject, the second case-ending occurs in the sense of the object, the third case-ending occurs in the sense of the instrument, the fourth case-ending occurs in the sense of the recipient, the fifth case-ending occurs in the sense of separation, the sixth case-ending occurs in the sense of the possessor, the seventh case-ending occurs in the sense of the location, the eighth case-ending occurs in the sense of address. Here is the summary:

Paccattamupayogañca, karaṇaṃ sampadāniyaṃ;

Nissakkaṃ sāmivacanaṃ, bhummamālapanaṭṭhamaṃ.

Subject and object, instrument, recipient, separation, possessor, location, and address as the eighth.

Tatra [M 0.0083] paccattavacanaṃ nāma tividhaliṅgavavatthānagatānaṃ itthipumanapuṃsakānaṃ paccattasabhāvaniddesattho. Upayogavacanaṃ nāma yo yaṃ karoti, tena tadupayuttaparidīpanattho. Karaṇavacanaṃ nāma tajjāpakatanibbattakaparidīpanattho. Sampadānavacanaṃ nāma tappadānaparidīpanattho. Nissakkavacanaṃ nāma tannissaṭatadapagamaparidīpanattho. Sāmivacanaṃ nāma tadissaraparidīpanattho. Bhummavacanaṃ nāma tappatiṭṭhāparidīpanattho. Āmantanavacanaṃ nāma tadāmantanaparidīpanattho. Evaṃ ñatvā payogāni asammuyhantena yojetabbāni.

Herein, the sense of the subject is for the purpose of indicating the inherent nature of the feminine, masculine, and neuter, established in the threefold division of gender. The sense of the object is for the purpose of clarifying that which is utilized by one who performs an action. The sense of the instrument is for the purpose of clarifying that which indicates and accomplishes it. The sense of the recipient is for the purpose of clarifying the giving of that. The sense of separation is for the purpose of clarifying departure and removal from that. The sense of the owner is for the purpose of clarifying the lord of that. The sense of location is for the purpose of clarifying the foundation of that. The sense of address is for the purpose of clarifying the addressing of that. Having understood thus, the usages should be applied without confusion.

Bhūto, bhāvako, bhavo, abhavo, bhāvo, abhāvo, sabhāvo, sabbhāvo, sambhavo, pabhavo, pabhāvo, anubhavo, ānubhāvo, parābhavo, vibhavo, pātubhāvo, āvibhāvo, tirobhāvo, vinābhāvo, sotthibhāvo, atthibhāvo, natthibhāvoti okārantapulliṅgaṃ.

Being, producer, becoming, non-becoming, state, non-state, own-nature, true nature, arising, source, power, experiencing, influence, ruin, disappearance, appearance, manifestation, concealment, separation, well-being, existence, non-existence—these are masculine nouns ending in -o.

Abhibhavitā, paribhavitā, anubhavitā, samanubhavitā, bhāvitā, paccanubhavitāti ākārantapulliṅgaṃ.

Overcomer, one who treats with contempt, experiencer, one who fully experiences, developer, one who experiences for oneself—these are masculine nouns ending in -ā.

Bhavaṃ, parābhavaṃ, paribhavaṃ, abhibhavaṃ, anubhavaṃ, samanubhavaṃ, paccanubhavaṃ, pabhavaṃ, appabhavanti niggahītantapulliṅgaṃ.

Existence, decline, contempt, overpowering, experiencing, fully experiencing, re-experiencing, source, lack of source—these are masculine nouns ending in niggahīta.

Dhanabhūti, siribhūti, sotthibhūti, suvatthibhūtīti ikārantapulliṅgaṃ.

Dhanabhūti, Siribhūti, Sotthibhūti, Suvatthibhūti—these are masculine nouns ending in -i.

Bhāvī, vibhāvī, sambhāvī, paribhāvīti īkārantapulliṅgaṃ.

One who is to become, one who discerns, one who esteems, one who despises—these are masculine nouns ending in -ī.

Sayambhū, pabhū, abhibhū, vibhū, adhibhū, patibhū, gotrabhū, vatrabhū, parābhibhū, rūpābhibhū, saddābhibhū, gandhābhibhū, rasābhibhū, phoṭṭhabbābhibhū, dhammābhibhū, sabbābhibhūti ūkārantapulliṅgaṃ.

Self-existent, lord, conqueror, ruler, sovereign, surety, one who transcends the lineage, Vatrabhū, one who overcomes others, one who overcomes form, one who overcomes sound, one who overcomes smell, one who overcomes taste, one who overcomes touch, one who overcomes mental objects, one who overcomes all—these are masculine nouns ending in -ū.

Imānettha chabbidhāni pulliṅgāni bhūdhātumayāni uddiṭṭhāni.

Herein, these six kinds of masculine nouns derived from the root bhū have been specified.

Ukārantaṃ [M 0.0084] pulliṅgaṃtu bhūdhātumayamappasiddhaṃ, aññadhātumayaṃ panukārantapulliṅgaṃ pasiddhaṃ “bhikkhu, hetu”iti. Tena saddhiṃ sattavidhāni pulliṅgāni honti, sabbānetāni sabhāvatoyeva pulliṅgānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Ettha sattoti atthavācako bhūtasaddoyeva niyogā pulliṅgantipi daṭṭhabbo.

Masculine nouns ending in -u derived from the root bhū are uncommon, but masculine nouns ending in -u derived from other roots are common, such as 'bhikkhu' and 'hetu.' Together with this, there are seven kinds of masculine nouns, all of which should be understood as masculine by their very nature. Herein, the word satta (being), which denotes a thing, just like the word bhūta, should also be understood as masculine by application.

Ye pana “yo dhammo bhūto, yā dhammajāti bhūtā, yaṃ dhammajātaṃ bhūta”nti evaṃ liṅgattaye yojanārahattā aniyataliṅgā aññepi bhūtaparābhūtasambhūtasaddādayo sandissanti pāvacanavare, tepi nānopasagganipātapadehi yojanavasena saddaracanāyaṃ sukhumatthaggahaṇe ca viññūnaṃ kosallajananatthaṃ niyatapulliṅgesu pakkhipitvā dassessāma.

However, as for other words such as bhūta, parābhūta, and sambhūta, which are found in the excellent teaching and are of unfixed gender due to their suitability for application in the three genders—as in 'that phenomenon which has become,' 'that species of phenomenon which has become,' 'that kind of phenomenon which has become'—these too we will demonstrate by including them among the fixed masculine nouns, for the purpose of generating skill for the wise in word formation by means of application with various prefixes, particles, and terms, and in the grasping of subtle meanings.

Seyyathidaṃ? Bhūto, parābhūto, sambhūto, vibhūto, pātubhūto, āvibhūto, tirobhūto, vinābhūto, bhabbo, paribhūto, abhibhūto, adhibhūto, addhabhūto, anubhūto, samanubhūto, paccanubhūto, bhāvito, sambhāvito, vibhāvito, paribhāvito, anuparibhūto, paribhavitabbo, paribhotabbo, paribhavanīyo, abhibhavitabbo, abhibhotabbo, abhibhavanīyo, adhibhavitabbo, adhibhotabbo, adhibhavanīyo, anubhavitabbo, anubhotabbo, anubhavanīyo, samanubhavitabbo, samanubhotabbo, samanubhavanīyo, paccanubhavitabbo, paccanubhotabbo, paccanubhavanīyo, bhāvetabbo, bhāvanīyo, sambhāvetabbo, sambhāvanīyo, vibhāvetabbo, vibhāvanīyo, paribhāvetabbo, paribhāvanīyo, bhavamāno, vibhavamāno, paribhavamāno, abhibhavamāno, anubhavamāno, samanubhavamāno, paccanubhavamāno, anubhonto, samanubhonto, paccanubhonto, sambhonto, abhisambhonto, bhāvento, sambhāvento, vibhāvento[M 0.0085], paribhāvento, paribhaviyamāno, paribhuyyamāno, abhibhaviyamāno, abhibhūyamāno, anubhaviyamāno, anubhuyyamāno, samanubhaviyamāno, samanubhuyyamāno, paccanubhaviyamāno, paccanubhuyyamānoti imāni niyatapulliṅgesu pakkhittaliṅgāni. Evamokārantādivasena chabbidhāni pulliṅgāni bhūdhātumayāni pakāsitāni. Ayaṃ tāva pulliṅgavasena udāharaṇuddeso.

That is: become, overcome, arisen, manifest, appeared, evident, disappeared, separated, capable, despised, overwhelmed, overpowered, certainly become, experienced, experienced together, experienced in return; developed, esteemed, made clear, pervaded, despised; to be despised, to be despised, fit to be despised; to be overwhelmed, to be overwhelmed, fit to be overwhelmed; to be overpowered, to be overpowered, fit to be overpowered; to be experienced, to be experienced, fit to be experienced; to be experienced together, to be experienced together, fit to be experienced together; to be experienced in return, to be experienced in return, fit to be experienced in return; to be developed, fit to be developed; to be esteemed, fit to be esteemed; to be made clear, fit to be made clear; to be pervaded, fit to be pervaded; becoming, ceasing to be, despising, overwhelming, experiencing, experiencing together, experiencing in return; experiencing, experiencing together, experiencing in return; arising, fully arising; developing, esteeming, making clear, pervading; being despised, being despised; being overwhelmed, being overwhelmed; being experienced, being experienced; being experienced together, being experienced together; being experienced in return, being experienced in return—these are nouns of variable gender included among the fixed masculine nouns. Thus, the sixfold masculine nouns derived from the root 'bhū' by way of those ending in 'o', etc., have been explained. This, for now, is the indication of examples by way of the masculine gender.

Bhāvikā, bhāvanā, vibhāvanā, sambhāvanā, paribhāvanāti ākārantaitthiliṅgaṃ.

A female developer, development, elucidation, esteeming, suffusing: these are the feminine nouns ending in 'ā'.

Bhūmi, bhūti, vibhūti. Ikārantaitthiliṅgaṃ.

Earth, prosperity, splendour: these are the feminine nouns ending in 'i'.

Bhūrī, bhūtī, bhotī, vibhāvinī, parivibhāvinī, sambhāvinī, pātubhavantī, pātubhontī, paribhavantī, paribhontī, abhibhavantī, abhibhontī, adhibhavantī, adhibhontī, anubhavantī, anubhontī, samanubhavantī, samanubhontī, paccanubhavantī, paccanubhontī, abhisambhavantī, abhisambhontīti īkārantaitthiliṅgaṃ.

Abundant, prosperity, lady; a discerning woman, a woman who thoroughly discerns, a woman who esteems; appearing, appearing; despising, despising; overwhelming, overwhelming; overpowering, overpowering; experiencing, experiencing; experiencing together, experiencing together; experiencing in return, experiencing in return; fully arising, fully arising: these are the feminine nouns ending in 'ī'.

Bhū, abhū. Ūkārantaitthiliṅgaṃ.

Earth, non-existence: these are the feminine nouns ending in 'ū'.

Imānettha catubbidhāni itthiliṅgāni bhūdhātumayāni uddiṭṭhāni.

Herein, these four kinds of feminine nouns derived from the root 'bhū' have been indicated.

Ukārantitthiliṅgaṃ bhūdhātumayamappasiddhaṃ, aññadhātumayaṃ pana ukārantitthiliṅgaṃ pasiddhaṃ “dhātu, dhenu”iti. Tena saddhiṃ pañcavidhāni itthiliṅgāni honti, okārantassa vā gosaddassa itthiliṅgabhāve tena saddhiṃ chabbidhānipi honti, sabbānetāni sabhāvatoyevitthiliṅgānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Etthāpi aniyataliṅgā bhūtaparābhūtasambhūtasaddādayo itthiliṅgavasena yujjante.

A feminine noun ending in 'u' derived from the root 'bhū' is uncommon, but a feminine noun ending in 'u' derived from another root is common, such as 'dhātu' (element) and 'dhenu' (cow). With this, there are five kinds of feminine nouns. Or, if the word 'go', ending in 'o', is taken as feminine, with it there are even six kinds. All these should be understood as being feminine by their very nature. Here too, words of variable gender such as 'bhūta' (become), 'parābhūta' (overcome), and 'sambhūta' (arisen) are used in the feminine gender.

Kathaṃ? Bhūtā, parābhūtā, sambhūtāti sabbaṃ vitthārato gahetabbaṃ “anubhonto samanubhonto”tiādīni nava padāni [M 0.0086] vajjetvā. Tāni hi īkārantavasena yojitāni. Imāni niyataliṅgesu pakkhittaliṅgāni. Evaṃ ākārantādivasena catubbidhāni itthiliṅgāni bhūdhātumayāni pakāsitāni. Ayaṃ itthiliṅgavasena udāharaṇuddeso.

How? 'Bhūtā,' 'parābhūtā,' 'sambhūtā'—the entire list should be understood in detail, excluding the nine words beginning with 'anubhonto,' 'samanubhonto,' and so on. For these are formed with an 'ī'-ending. These are nouns of variable gender included among the fixed nouns. Thus, the four kinds of feminine nouns derived from the root 'bhū' by way of those ending in 'ā', etc., have been explained. This is the indication of examples by way of the feminine gender.

Bhūtaṃ, mahābhūtaṃ, bhavittaṃ, bhūnaṃ, bhavanaṃ, parābhavanaṃ, sambhavanaṃ, vibhavanaṃ, pātubhavanaṃ, āvibhavanaṃ, tirobhavanaṃ, vinābhavanaṃ, sotthibhavanaṃ, paribhavanaṃ, abhibhavanaṃ, adhibhavanaṃ, anubhavanaṃ, samanubhavanaṃ, paccanubhavananti niggahītantanapuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

A being, a great element, the state of being, a being; becoming, ruin, origin, annihilation, appearance, manifestation, disappearance, separation, well-being, contempt, overcoming, overpowering, experiencing, experiencing together, experiencing in return: these are the neuter nouns ending in 'ṃ'.

Atthavibhāvi, dhammavibhāvi. Ikārantanapuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

Elucidating the meaning, elucidating the Dhamma. These are the neuter nouns ending in 'i'.

Gotrabhu, cittasahabhu, nacittasahabhu. Ukārantanapuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

One who overcomes the lineage, arising together with consciousness, not arising together with consciousness. These are the neuter nouns ending in 'u'.

Sabbānetāni sabhāvatoyeva napuṃsakaliṅgānīti daṭṭhabbāni. Ettha sattabhūtarūpavācako bhūtasaddoyeva niyogā napuṃsakaliṅgotipi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthāpi aniyataliṅgā bhūta parābhūta sambhūtasaddādayo napuṃsakaliṅgavasena yujjante.

All these should be understood as being neuter by their very nature. Here it should also be understood that the word 'bhūta', when denoting the elemental form of a being, is neuter by application. Here too, words of variable gender such as 'bhūta', 'parābhūta', and 'sambhūta' are used in the neuter gender.

Kathaṃ? Bhūtaṃ, parābhūtaṃ, sambhūtaṃ, vibhūtaṃ. Peyyālo. Samanubhavamānaṃ, paccanubhavamānaṃ, anubhontaṃ, anubhavantaṃ, samanubhontaṃ, samanubhavantaṃ, paccanubhontaṃ, paccanubhavantaṃ, sambhontaṃ, sambhavantaṃ, abhisambhontaṃ, abhisambhavantaṃ, pātubhontaṃ, pātubhavantaṃ, paribhontaṃ, paribhavantaṃ, abhibhontaṃ, abhibhavantaṃ, adhibhontaṃ, adhibhavantaṃ, bhāventaṃ, sambhāventaṃ, vibhāventaṃ, paribhāventaṃ, paribhāviyamānaṃ, paribhuyyamānaṃ, peyyālo. Paccanubhaviyamānaṃ, paccanubhuyyamānanti imāni niyatanapuṃsakaliṅgesu pakkhittaliṅgāni. Evaṃ niggahītantādivasena tividhāni napuṃsakaliṅgāni bhūdhātumayāni pakāsitāni[M 0.0087]. Ayaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgavasena udāharaṇuddeso, evaṃ pulliṅgādivasena liṅgattayaṃ bhūdhātumayamuddiṭṭhaṃ.

How? Become, overcome, arisen, manifest. (Repetition.) Experiencing together, experiencing in return; experiencing, experiencing; experiencing together, experiencing together; experiencing in return, experiencing in return; arising, arising; fully arising, fully arising; appearing, appearing; despising, despising; overwhelming, overwhelming; overpowering, overpowering; developing, esteeming, making clear, pervading; being despised, being despised. (Repetition.) Being experienced in return, being experienced in return—these are nouns of variable gender included among the fixed neuter nouns. Thus, by way of those ending in 'ṃ' and so on, the three kinds of neuter nouns derived from the root 'bhū' have been explained. This is the indication of examples by way of the neuter gender; thus the threefold gender—masculine and so on—derived from the root 'bhū' has been indicated.

Ettha me appasiddhāti, ye ye saddā pakāsitā;

Te te pāḷippadesesu, maggitabbā vibhāvinā.

Should any words explained herein not be specified in detail, they are to be sought in the passages of the Pāḷi by a discerning person.

O, ā, bindu, i, ī, u, ū-antime sattadhā ṭhitā;

Ñe yyā pulliṅgabhedāti, niruttaññūhi bhāsitā.

O, ā, bindu, i, ī, u, ū—these seven stand as endings; they should be known as the divisions of the masculine gender, as stated by those skilled in etymology.

Ā ivaṇṇo cuvaṇṇo ca, pañca antā sarūpato;

Itthibhedāti viññeyyā, okārantena chāpi vā.

Ā, the 'i'-vowel group, and the 'u'-vowel group—these five endings in their own form should be known as the divisions of the feminine; or with the 'o'-ending, there are even six.

Bindu, i, u-ime antā, tayo ñeyyā vibhāvinā;

Napuṃsakappabhedāti, niruttaññūhi bhāsitā.

Bindu, i, and u—these three endings should be known by a discerning person as the divisions of the neuter gender, as stated by those skilled in etymology.

Antā satteva pulliṅge, itthiyaṃ pañca vā cha vā;

Napuṃsake tayo evaṃ, dasa pañcahi chabbidhā.

There are seven endings in the masculine, five or six in the feminine, and three in the neuter.

Yasmā panettha “bhūto”tiādayo saddā nibbacanābhidheyyakathanatthasādhakavacanapariyāyavacanatthuddhāravasena vuccamānā pākaṭā honti suviññeyyā ca, tasmā imesaṃ nibbacanādīni yathāsambhavaṃ vakkhāma viññūnaṃ tuṭṭhijananatthañceva sotārānamatthesu paṭutarabuddhipaṭilābhāya ca. Tatra bhūtoti khandhapātubhāvena bhavatīti bhūto, idaṃ tāva nibbacanaṃ. “Bhūto”ti sabbasaṅgāhakavasena satto vuccati, idamabhidheyyakathanaṃ. “Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto. Sabbeva nikkhipissanti, bhūtā loke samussaya”nti ca idametassa atthassa sādhakavacanaṃ. Atha vā bhūtoti evaṃnāmako amanussajātiyo sattaviseso, idamabhidheyyakathanaṃ. “Bhūtavijjā, bhūtavejjo, bhūtaviggahito”ti ca idametassa atthassa sādhakavacanaṃ. Yañca pana “satto macco pajā”tiādikaṃ tattha tattha āgataṃ vacanaṃ, idaṃ sattoti [M 0.0088] atthavācakassa bhūtasaddassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Yañca niddesapāḷiyaṃ “maccoti satto naro mānavo poso puggalo jīvo jagu jantu hindagu manujo”ti āgataṃ, idampi pariyāyavacanameva. Tāni sabbāni piṇḍetvā vuccante –

Since the words such as 'bhūta' become clear and easily understood when they are explained by way of derivation, statement of meaning, supporting statements, synonyms, and extraction of meaning, we will therefore explain their derivations and so on as is possible, both for the delight of the wise and for the listeners to acquire a sharper intellect regarding the meanings. Therein, 'bhūta' is so called because it 'becomes' (bhavati) through the appearance of the aggregates; this is the derivation. 'Bhūta' is said to be a 'being' in an all-inclusive sense; this is the statement of meaning. 'Whatever being is devoured by time...' and 'All beings in the world will lay down their composite bodies' are supporting statements for this meaning. Alternatively, 'bhūta' is a particular kind of being of a non-human species; this is the statement of meaning. 'The science of spirits,' 'a spirit-doctor,' and 'possessed by a spirit' are supporting statements for this meaning. Furthermore, whatever statements such as 'a being, a mortal, a creature' are found here and there, this is a synonym for the word 'bhūta' which denotes the meaning 'being'. And what is found in the Pāḷi of the Niddesa, 'A mortal means a being, a man, a human, a person, an individual, a living thing, a creature, a sentient being, a human being,' this too is a synonym. Collecting them all, they are stated:

Satto macco jano bhūto, pāṇo hindagu puggalo;

Jantu jīvo jagu yakkho, pāṇī dehī tathāgato.

A being, a mortal, a person, a creature, a living thing, a sentient being, an individual; a creature, a living being, a creature, a yakkha, a breathing one, an embodied one, a Tathāgata.

Sattavo mātiyo loko, manujo mānavo naro;

Poso sarīrīti pume, bhūtamiti napuṃsake.

The words for 'being' such as `satta`, `loka`, `manuja`, `mānava`, `nara`, `posa`, and `sarīrī` are masculine; `bhūtaṃ` is neuter.

Pajāti itthiyaṃ vutto, liṅgato, na ca atthato;

Evaṃ tiliṅgikā honti, saddā sattābhidhānakā.

The word 'pajā' (creature) is said to be feminine by gender, not by meaning. Thus, words that denote a being can be of three genders.

Yo so jaṅghāya ulati, so satto jaṅghalo idha;

Pāṇadehābhidhānehi, sattanāmaṃ papañcitaṃ.

He who moves by his shanks, that being is called 'jaṅghala' here. With terms for 'life' and 'body,' the name 'being' is elaborated.

Imasmiṃ pakaraṇe “pariyāyavacana”nti ca “abhidhāna”nti ca “saṅkhā”tiādīni ca ekatthāni adhippetāni, atthuddhāravasena pana bhūtasaddo pañcakkhandhāmanussadhātusassatavijjamānakhīṇāsavasattarukkhādīsu dissati, tappayogo upari atthattikavibhāge āvibhavissati. Bhāvakoti bhāvetīti bhāvako, idaṃ nibbacanaṃ. Yo bhāvanaṃ karoti, so bhāvako. Idamabhidheyyakathanaṃ. “Bhāvako nipako dhīro”ti idametassa atthassa sādhakavacanaṃ. “Bhāvako bhāvanāpasuto bhāvanāpayutto bhāvanāsampanno”ti idaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ. Imāni “bhūto bhāvako”ti dve padāni suddhakattuhetukattuvasena vuttānīti. Ito paraṃ nayānusārena suviññeyyattā “idaṃ nibbacana”nti ca ādīni [M 0.0089] avatvā katthaci atthasādhakavacanaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ atthuddhārañca yathārahaṃ dassessāma. Tesu hi sabbattha dassitesu ganthavitthāro siyā, tasmā yesamattho uttāno, tesampi padānamabhidheyyaṃ na kathessāma, nibbacanamattameva nesaṃ kathessāma. Yesaṃ pana gambhīro attho, tesamabhidheyyaṃ kathessāma.

In this treatise, the terms 'pariyāyavacana' (synonym), 'abhidhāna' (designation), 'saṅkhā' (term), and so on, are intended to have a single meaning. By way of extracting the meaning, however, the word 'bhūta' is seen in reference to the five aggregates, a non-human being, the elements, the eternal, what is existent, one whose taints are destroyed, a being, a tree, and so on. Its application will become manifest above in the analysis of the triad of meanings. 'Bhāvako' is so called because one 'develops' (bhāveti); this is the etymological derivation. One who undertakes development is a 'developer' (bhāvako); this is the statement of the designated meaning. 'A developer, skillful and wise' is a statement that supports this meaning. 'A developer devoted to development, engaged in development, accomplished in development' are synonymous expressions. These two terms, 'bhūta' and 'bhāvako,' are stated in the sense of a simple agent and a causative agent. From here on, so that it may be easily understood according to the method, we will not state 'this is the etymological derivation,' and so on, but will show, as is suitable, a supporting statement for the meaning, a synonymous expression, and the extraction of meaning. For if these were shown in every case, the text would become prolix. Therefore, for those terms whose meaning is plain, we will not state their designated meaning but only their derivation. But for those whose meaning is profound, we will state their designated meaning.

Bhavanaṃ bhavo, bhavo vuccati vuddhi. Bhūsaddassa atthātisayayogato vaḍḍhanepi dissamānattā bhavanaṃ vaḍḍhananti katvā. “Bhavo ca rañño abhavo ca rañño”ti idaṃ vuddhiatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Atha vā bhavoti vuccati sassataṃ. “Sassato attā ca loko cā”ti hi sassatavasena pavattā diṭṭhi sassatadiṭṭhi, tasmā bhavadiṭṭhī”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Tathā bhavoti bhavadiṭṭhi, bhavati sassataṃ tiṭṭhatīti pavattanato sassatadiṭṭhi bhavadiṭṭhi nāma. Bhavadiṭṭhi hi uttarapadalopena bhavoti vuccati. “Bhavena bhavassa vippamokkhamāhaṃsū”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Etthāyaṃ pāḷivacanattho – ekacce samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhavadiṭṭhiyā vā kāmabhavādinā vā sabbabhavato vimuttiṃ saṃsāravisuddhiṃ kathayiṃsūti. Atha vā bhavanti vaḍḍhanti sattā etenāti bhavoti atthena sampattipuññāni bhavoti ca vuccanti. “Itibhavābhavatañca vītivatto”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Ettha panāyaṃ pāḷivacanattho – bhavoti sampatti, abhavoti vipatti. Tathā bhavoti vuddhi, abhavoti hāni. Bhavoti sassataṃ, abhavoti ucchedo. Bhavoti puññaṃ, abhavoti pāpaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ vītivattoti.

Coming to be (bhavanaṃ) is becoming (bhavo); becoming is called growth (vuddhi). Since the word 'bhū' is also seen in the sense of 'to increase' due to its connection with an abundance of meaning, 'coming to be' is taken as 'growth.' The statement, 'Prosperity for the king and decline for the king,' supports this meaning of growth. Alternatively, 'becoming' (bhava) is called the eternal (sassata). For the view that proceeds in an eternalistic way, 'The self and the world are eternal,' is the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi); therefore, it is called the 'view of becoming' (bhavadiṭṭhi). This statement supports this meaning. Thus 'becoming' (bhava) is the view of becoming. Because it proceeds as 'it becomes, it exists eternally,' the eternalist view is named the 'view of becoming.' Indeed, 'view of becoming' (bhavadiṭṭhi) is called 'becoming' (bhava) by elision of the final member of the compound. 'They declared liberation from becoming by means of becoming' is a statement that supports this meaning. Here the meaning of the Pāli passage is this: some ascetics and brahmins declared liberation from all becoming—purification from saṃsāra—by means of the view of becoming or by means of sensual becoming and so on. Alternatively, in the sense that 'beings come to be and grow through this,' both attainments and merit are also called 'becoming.' 'He has overcome both becoming and non-becoming' is a statement that supports this meaning. Here the meaning of the Pāli passage is this: 'becoming' is attainment, 'non-becoming' is misfortune; likewise, 'becoming' is growth, 'non-becoming' is decline; 'becoming' is eternalism, 'non-becoming' is annihilationism; 'becoming' is merit, 'non-becoming' is demerit—he has overcome all that.

Sahokāsā [M 0.0090] khandhāpi bhavo. “Kāmabhavo rūpabhavo” iccevamādi etassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Ettha pana khandhā “yo paññāyati, so sarūpaṃ labhatī”ti katvā “bhavati avijjātaṇhādisamudayā nirantaraṃ samudetī”ti atthena vā “bhavā”ti vuccanti. Okāso pana “bhavanti jāyanti ettha sattā nāmarūpadhammā cā”ti atthena “bhavo”ti. Apica kammabhavopi bhavo, upapattibhavopi bhavo. “Upādānapaccayā bhavo duvidhena atthi kammabhavo, atthi upapattibhavo”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Tattha kammameva bhavo kammabhavo. Tathā upapatti eva bhavo upapattibhavo. Etthūpapatti bhavatīti bhavo, kammaṃ pana yathā sukhakāraṇattā “sukho buddhānamuppādo”ti vutto. Evaṃ bhavakāraṇattā phalavohārena bhavoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā bhāvanalakkhaṇattā bhāvetīti bhavo. Kiṃ bhāveti? Upapattiṃ. Iti upapattiṃ bhāvetīti bhavoti vuccati. Bhāvetītimassa ca nibbattetīti hetukattuvasenattho. Atha vā “bhavapaccayā jātī”ti vacanato bhavati etenāti bhavoti kammabhavo vuccati.

The aggregates together with their location are also becoming. The statement, 'Sensual becoming, form becoming,' and so on, supports this meaning. Here, the aggregates are called 'becoming' either on the grounds that 'what is cognized acquires its own nature,' or in the sense that 'it comes to be, it arises continuously from the origination of ignorance, craving, and so on.' The location, however, is 'becoming' in the sense that 'beings and name-and-form phenomena come to be and are born here.' Furthermore, kamma-becoming is also becoming, and rebirth-becoming is also becoming. The statement, 'With clinging as condition, becoming; becoming is twofold: there is kamma-becoming and there is rebirth-becoming,' supports this meaning. Therein, kamma itself is becoming as kamma; similarly, rebirth itself is becoming as rebirth. Here, rebirth 'comes to be' (bhavati), thus it is 'becoming' (bhavo). As for kamma, just as it is said, 'The arising of the Buddhas is happiness,' because it is a cause of happiness, so too kamma should be seen as 'becoming' by designation based on the fruit. Alternatively, because it has the characteristic of producing, 'it produces' (bhāveti), thus it is 'becoming' (bhavo). What does it produce? Rebirth. Thus, because it produces rebirth, it is called 'becoming.' And the meaning of 'it produces' is 'it generates' in the sense of a causative agent. Or, based on the statement, 'With becoming as condition, birth,' that through which one comes to be is called kamma-becoming.

“Khandhānañca paṭipāṭi, dhātuāyatanāna ca;

Abbocchinnaṃ vattamānā, saṃsāroti pavuccatī”ti

“The succession of the aggregates, and of the elements and sense bases, proceeding uninterruptedly, is called saṃsāra.”

Vuttalakkhaṇo saṃsāropi bhavo. “Bhave dukkhaṃ bhavadukkhaṃ, bhave saṃsaranto”ti imānetassatthassa sādhakāni vacanāni. Tatra kenaṭṭhena saṃsāro bhavoti kathīyati? Bhavati ettha sattasammuti khandhādipaṭipāṭisaṅkhāte dhammapuñjasminti atthena[M 0.0091]. Idaṃ bhavasaddassa bhāvakattukaraṇādhikaraṇasādhanavasenatthakathanaṃ.

Saṃsāra, which has the characteristic just stated, is also 'becoming.' The statements, 'In becoming there is suffering, the suffering of becoming,' and 'wandering in becoming,' support this meaning. Therein, in what sense is saṃsāra said to be 'becoming'? In the sense that 'herein—in this mass of phenomena designated as the succession of aggregates, etc.—what is conventionally called a "being" comes to be.' This is the explanation of the word 'bhava' by way of its derivation in the sense of state, agent, instrument, and location.

Ettha bhavasaddassa atthuddhāraṃ vadāma –

Here we state the extraction of meanings for the word 'bhava':

Vuddhisampattipuññāni, khandhā sokāsasaññitā;

Saṃsāro sassatañcetaṃ, bhavasaddena sadditaṃ.

Growth, attainment, and merit, the aggregates designated with their location, saṃsāra, and the eternal—these are expressed by the word 'bhava'.

Bhavataṇhā bhavadiṭṭhi, upapattibhavo tathā;

Kammabhavo ca sabbantaṃ, bhavasaddena sadditaṃ.

Craving for becoming, the view of becoming, likewise rebirth-becoming, and kamma-becoming—all this is expressed by the word 'bhava'.

Bhavataṇhābhavadiṭṭhi-dvayaṃ katthaci pāḷiyaṃ;

Uttarapadalopena, bhavasaddena sadditaṃ.

The pair—craving for becoming and the view of becoming—are somewhere in the Pāli canon, by elision of the final member, expressed by the word 'bhava'.

Abhavoti na bhavo abhavo.

'Non-becoming' (abhava) means 'not becoming'.

Vipatti hāni ucchedo, pāpañceva catubbidhā;

Ime abhavasaddena, atthā vuccanti sāsane.

Misfortune, decline, annihilation, and demerit—these fourfold meanings are stated in the Dispensation by the word 'abhava'.

Bhāvoti ajjhāsayo, yo “adhippāyo”tipi vuccati. “Thīnaṃbhāvo durājāno. Nāmacco rājabhariyāsu, bhāvaṃ kubbetha paṇḍito. Hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetī”ti evamādi etassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Apica vatthudhammopi bhāvo. “Bhāvasaṅketasiddhīna”nti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ, cittampi bhāvo. “Accāhitaṃ kammaṃ karosi luddaṃ, bhāve ca te kusalaṃ natthi kiñcī”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Kriyāpibhāvo. “Bhāvalakkhaṇaṃ bhāvasattamī”ti ca idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Apica bhāvoti sattavevacananti bhaṇanti, dhātu vā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha ajjhāsayo ca vatthudhammo ca cittañca satto cāti ime bhavatīti bhāvo. Tathā pana bhāvetīti bhāvo, kriyā [M 0.0092] tu bhavananti bhāvo. Sā ca bhavanagamanapacanādivasenānekavidhā. Apica bhāvarūpampi bhāvo, yaṃ itthibhāvo pumbhāvo itthindriyanti ca vuccati. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – “itthī”ti vā “puriso”ti vā bhavati etena cittaṃ abhidhānañcāti bhāvo.

'Bhāva' is disposition, which is also called 'intention.' The following statements, and others, support this meaning: 'The nature (bhāva) of women is hard to know'; 'A wise minister should not form an intimacy (bhāva) with the king's wives'; 'He reveals the state (bhāva) that has gone to the heart.' Furthermore, an objective phenomenon is also 'bhāva.' 'Of the accomplishment of states and conventions' is a statement that supports this meaning. Mind, too, is 'bhāva.' 'You do a terrible, cruel deed, and in your nature (bhāve) there is no good whatsoever' is a statement that supports this meaning. An action, too, is 'bhāva.' 'The characteristic of a state' and 'the locative of state' are statements that support this meaning. Moreover, some say 'bhāva' is a synonym for 'being,' or it is a term for a root (dhātu). Herein, disposition, objective phenomenon, mind, and being—these 'are' (bhavati), thus they are 'bhāva.' Similarly, 'it produces' (bhāveti), thus it is 'bhāva'; an action, however, 'is a coming to be' (bhavanaṃ), thus it is 'bhāva.' And this is of many kinds, such as coming to be, going, cooking, etc. Furthermore, the material form that is a state is also 'bhāva,' which is called 'the female state,' 'the male state,' and 'the femininity faculty.' Here the meaning of the word is: that by which the mind and the designation 'woman' or 'man' come to be (bhavati) is 'bhāva'.

Nattanomatiyā etaṃ, nibbacanamudāhaṭaṃ;

Pubbācariyasīhānaṃ, mataṃ nissāya māhaṭaṃ.

This is not from my own opinion, not adduced by myself; relying on the view of the lion-like teachers of the past, it has been brought by me.

Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi “itthiyā bhāvo itthibhāvo, itthīti vā bhavati etena cittaṃ abhidhānañcāti itthibhāvo”ti, tasmā pumbhāvoti etthāpi pumassa bhāvo pumbhāvo, pumāti vā bhavati etena cittaṃ abhidhānañcāti pumbhāvoti nibbacanaṃ samadhigantabbaṃ. Idaṃ bhāvasaddassa kattubhāvakaraṇasādhanavasenatthakathanaṃ.

This was said by the ancients: 'The state (bhāvo) of a woman is the female state (itthibhāvo); or, that by which the mind and the designation become "woman" is the female state.' Therefore, in the case of 'male state' (pumbhāvo) too, the etymological derivation should be understood as: 'The state of a man is the male state; or, that by which the mind and the designation become "man" is the male state.' This is the explanation of the word 'bhāva' by way of its derivation in the sense of agent, state, and instrument.

Abhāvoti na bhāvoti abhāvo, ko so? Suññatā natthitā. Sabhāvoti attano bhāvo sabhāvo, attano pakati iccevattho. Atha vā sabhāvoti dhammānaṃ sati atthasambhave yo koci sarūpaṃ labhati, tassa bhāvo lakkhaṇamiti saññito namanaruppanakakkhaḷaphusanādiākāro iccevattho. “Sāmaññaṃ vā sabhāvo vā, dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ mata”nti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Apica sabhāvoti salakkhaṇo paramatthadhammo. Kenaṭṭhena? Saha bhāvenāti atthena. Sabbhāvoti sataṃ bhāvo sabbhāvo, sappurisadhammo iccevattho. Atha vā attano bhāvo sabbhāvo. “Gāhāpayanti sabbhāva”nti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Saṃvijjamāno vā bhāvo sabbhāvo. “Evaṃ gahaṇasabbhāvo”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ [M 0.0093] vacanaṃ. Idaṃ sabhāva sabbhāvasaddānaṃ bhāvasādhanavasenatthakathanaṃ.

'Non-state' (abhāva) means 'not a state.' What is that? Voidness, non-existence. 'Own-nature' (sabhāva) is one's own state; the meaning is simply one's own nature. Alternatively, 'own-nature' is this: when there is a possible occurrence of meaning for phenomena, whatever acquires an own-form, its state—designated as its characteristic—is the mode of bending, breaking up, hardness, contact, etc. This is the meaning. 'The general characteristic or the individual nature is considered the characteristic of phenomena' is a statement that supports this meaning. Furthermore, 'own-nature' is an ultimate reality together with its characteristic. In what sense? In the sense of 'together with its state.' 'Good-nature' (sabbhāva) is the state of the good; the meaning is simply the quality of a true person. Alternatively, one's own state is 'good-nature.' 'They make one grasp the good state' is a statement that supports this meaning. Or, an existing state is 'good-nature.' 'Thus the real nature of grasping' is a statement that supports this meaning. This is the explanation of the words 'sabhāva' and 'sabbhāva' by way of their derivation in the sense of 'state'.

Sambhavoti sambhavanaṃ sambhavo, sambhavanakriyā, yutti vā. Yutti hi sambhavoti vuccati “sambhavo gahaṇassa kāraṇa”ntiādīsu. Atha vā sambhavati etasmāti sambhavo. Yato hi yaṃ kiñci sambhavati, so sambhavo. Pabhavoti pabhavanaṃ pabhavo, acchinnatā, pabhavati etasmāti vā pabhavo. Yato hi yaṃ kiñci pabhavati, so pabhavo. Ime pana sambhavapabhavasaddā katthaci samānatthā katthaci bhinnatthāti veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Sambhavasaddo hi bhavanakriyampi vadati yuttimpi paññattimpi sambhavarūpampi paccayatthampi, pabhavasaddo pana bhavanakriyampi vadati nadippabhavampi paccayatthampi, tasmā paccayatthaṃ vajjetvā bhinnatthāti gahetabbā, paccayatthena pana samānatthāti gahetabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “paccayo hetu nidānaṃ kāraṇaṃ sambhavo pabhavotiādi atthato ekaṃ, byañjanato nāna”nti.

Origination (sambhavo) is the act of originating (sambhavanaṃ), the action of originating, or suitability (yutti). For suitability is called 'origination' in such contexts as 'origination is the cause of grasping.' Or, 'that from which something originates' is its origination (sambhava). For whatever originates from something, that is its origination. Production (pabhavo) is the act of producing (pabhavanaṃ), continuity (acchinnatā); or 'that from which something is produced' is its production (pabhava). For whatever is produced from something, that is its production. But these words, 'origination' and 'production,' should be understood as sometimes having the same meaning and sometimes different meanings. How so? The word 'origination' (sambhava) signifies the act of becoming, suitability, designation, the form of origination, and the meaning of 'condition.' The word 'production' (pabhava), however, signifies the act of becoming, the source of a river, and the meaning of 'condition.' Therefore, they should be taken as having different meanings except in the sense of 'condition'; but in the sense of 'condition,' they should be taken as having the same meaning. For it has been said: 'Condition, cause, source, reason, origination, production, etc., are one in meaning but different in expression.'

“Mūlaṃ hetu nidānañca, sambhavo pabhavo tathā;

Samuṭṭhānāhārārammaṇaṃ, paccayo samudayena cā”ti

“Root, cause, and source, origination and production as well; arising, nutriment, object, condition, and origin too.”

Ayampi gāthā etassatthassa sādhikā. Idaṃ sambhavapabhavasaddānaṃ bhāvāpādānasādhanavasenatthakathanaṃ.

This verse also establishes this meaning. This is the explanation of the words 'origination' and 'production' by way of their grammatical functions as verbal nouns and as ablatives.

Evamettha bhāvakattukammakaraṇāpādānādhikaraṇavasena cha sādhanāni pakāsitāni. Tāni sampadānasādhanena sattavidhāni bhavanti, taṃ pana uttari āvibhavissati “dhanamassa bhavatūti dhanabhūtī”tiādinā. Iccevaṃ kitakavasena sabbathāpi sattavidhāni sādhanāni honti, yāni “kārakānī”tipi vuccati, ito aññaṃ sādhanaṃ natthi. Idha payogesvatthesu ca viññūnaṃ [M 0.0094] pāṭavatthaṃ sādhananāmaṃ pakāsitaṃ. Tathā hi dunnikkhittasādhanehi padehi yojitā saddappayogā dubbodhatthā honti, sunikkhittasādhanehi pana padehi yojitā subodhatthā honti, tasmā payogāsādhanamūlakā, attho ca payogamūlako. Payogānurūpañhi aviparītaṃ katvā atthaṃ kathanasīlā “yācitova bahulaṃ cīvaraṃ paribhuñjati, appaṃ ayācito”ti evamādīsu sādhanavasena gahetabbesu atthesu, aññesu catthesu paṭutarabuddhino paṇḍitāyeva ekantena bhagavato pariyattisāsanadharā nāma hontīti veditabbaṃ. Ito paraṃ nayānusārena suviññeyyattā “idaṃ nāma sādhana”nti na vakkhāma, kevalamidha dassitesu payogesu viññūnaṃ bahumānuppādanatthañceva vividhavicittapāḷigatike vividhatthasāre jinavaravacane sotūnaṃ buddhivijambhanatthañca atthasādhakavacanāniyeva yathārahaṃ suttageyyaveyyākaraṇagāthādīsu tato tato āharitvā dassessāma.

Thus, six grammatical functions (sādhanāni) have been explained here: verbal noun (bhāva), agent (kattu), object (kamma), instrument (karaṇa), source (apādāna), and location (adhikaraṇa). These become sevenfold with the inclusion of the dative function (sampadānasādhana), which will become clear later in such phrases as 'may there be wealth for him' (dhanamassa bhavatūti). Thus, by way of primary derivation (kitaka), there are in every way seven grammatical functions, which are also called 'case relations' (kārakāni); there is no other grammatical function besides these. Here, the term 'grammatical function' (sādhana) has been explained for the acumen of the wise in regard to usage and meaning. Indeed, verbal expressions constructed with poorly applied grammatical functions are difficult to comprehend, whereas those constructed with well-applied grammatical functions are easy to comprehend. Therefore, usage is rooted in the grammatical function, and meaning is rooted in usage. It should be understood that only the wise with keen intellect—who are accustomed to explaining the meaning without distortion, in conformity with usage, in meanings that are to be grasped by way of grammatical function (as in 'being requested, he uses the robe often; unrequested, seldom'), and in other meanings—are truly called bearers of the Blessed One’s scriptural teaching. Henceforth, since it will be easily understood according to the method, we will not state 'this is such-and-such a grammatical function.' We will only adduce from here and there—from suttas, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, etc.—statements that establish the meaning, in order to generate great esteem in the wise for the usages shown here, and to expand the intelligence of the listeners regarding the word of the supreme Conqueror, which is found in the varied and intricate Pāli scriptures and is rich in diverse and essential meanings.

Pabhāvoti pakārato bhavatīti pabhāvo, soyamānubhāvoyeva. “Pabhāvaṃ te na passāmi, yena tvaṃ mithilaṃ vaje”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Anubhavoti anubhavanaṃ anubhavo, kiṃ taṃ? Paribhuñjanaṃ. Ānubhāvoti tejussāhamantapabhūsattiyo. “Tejasaṅkhato ussāhamantapabhūsattisaṅkhāto vā mahanto ānubhāvo etassāti mahānubhāvo”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ.

Power (pabhāvo) is so called because 'it comes to be (bhavati) in a special way (pakārato)'; this is majesty (ānubhāva) itself. 'I do not see your power by which you might go to Mithilā'—this statement establishes its meaning. Experience (anubhavo) is the act of experiencing (anubhavanaṃ). What is that? It is enjoying. Majesty (ānubhāvo) consists of energy, effort, counsel, and sovereign power. 'He has great majesty (mahānubhāvo) because his majesty (ānubhāvo)—defined as energy, or as effort, counsel, and sovereign power—is great'—this statement establishes its meaning.

Tejo ussāhamantā ca, pabhūsattīti pañcime;

Ānubhāvāti vuccanti, pabhāvāti ca te vade.

Energy, effort, counsel, and sovereign power—these five are called 'majesties' (ānubhāvā), and they are also spoken of as 'powers' (pabhāvā).

Tejādivācakattamhi, ānubhāvapadassa tu;

Atthanibbacanaṃ dhīro, yathāsambhavamuddise.

But when the word 'majesty' (ānubhāva) denotes energy and so on, the wise one should set forth the explanation of its meaning as is appropriate.

Atha [M 0.0095] vā ānubhāvoti anubhavitabbaphalaṃ. “Anubhavitabbassa phalassa mahantatāya mahānubhāvo”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Parābhavoti parābhavanaṃ parābhavo, atha vā parābhavatīti parābhavo. “Suvijāno parābhavo”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Apica “dhammadessī parābhavo”ti pāṭhānurūpato parābhavissatīti parābhavoti anāgatakālavasenapi nibbacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā parābhavanti etenāti parābhavo. Kiṃ taṃ? Dhammadessitādi. “Paṭhamo so parābhavo”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Vibhavoti nibbānaṃ. Tañhi bhavato vigatattā bhavato vigatoti vibhavo, bhavassa ca taṃhetu vigatattā vigato bhavo etasmāti vibhavo. Vibhavanti ucchijjanti vinassanti ito ariyadhanavilomakā kilesamahācorātipi vibhavo. Vibhavasaddassa nibbānābhidhānatte “evaṃ bhave vijjamāne, vibhavo icchitabbako”ti idamettha sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Imāni pana nibbānassa pariyāyavacanāni –

Or, 'majesty' (ānubhāva) is the result to be experienced. 'He has great majesty (mahānubhāvo) because of the greatness of the result to be experienced'—this statement establishes its meaning. Decline (parābhavo) is the act of declining (parābhavanaṃ), or 'one declines' (parābhavati), thus it is 'decline.' 'Decline is easily known'—this statement establishes its meaning. Moreover, in accordance with the reading 'one who hates the Dhamma is a person in decline,' the derivation should also be seen in a future sense: 'one will decline' (parābhavissati), thus it is 'decline' (parābhava). Or, 'one declines by means of this,' thus it is 'decline.' What is that? Hating the Dhamma, etc. 'That is the first decline'—this statement establishes its meaning. Non-becoming (vibhava) means Nibbāna. For since it is devoid of becoming, 'devoid of becoming' (bhavato vigato) is 'non-becoming' (vibhava). And since becoming is absent because of it, 'becoming is absent from it' (vigato bhavo etasmā) is 'non-becoming.' Also, because the great thieves, the defilements, which are contrary to the noble wealth, are annihilated (vibhavanti), cut off (ucchijjanti), and perish from it, it is 'non-becoming.' Regarding the word 'non-becoming' denoting Nibbāna, 'Thus, while becoming exists, non-becoming should be wished for'—this statement here establishes the meaning. And these are synonyms for Nibbāna:

Nibbānaṃ vibhavo mokkho, nirodho amataṃ samaṃ;

Saṅkhārūpasamo dukkha-nirodho accuta’kkhayo.

Nibbāna, non-becoming, liberation, cessation, the deathless, the calm; the stilling of formations, the cessation of suffering, the unfallen, the unperishing.

Vivaṭṭa’makataṃ atthaṃ, santipada’masaṅkhataṃ;

Pāraṃ taṇhākkhayo dukkha-kkhayo saññojanakkhayo.

The unrolling, the unmade, the goal, the state of peace, the unconditioned; the further shore, the destruction of craving, the destruction of suffering, the destruction of the fetters.

Yogakkhemo virāgo ca,

Lokanto ca bhavakkhayo;

Apavaggo visaṅkhāro,

Sabbhi suddhi visuddhi ca.

Security from bondage and dispassion, the end of the world and the destruction of existence; release, the unconditioned, the state of the virtuous, purity, and purification.

Vimutyā’pacayo mutti, nibbuti upadhikkhayo;

Santi asaṅkhatā dhātu, disā ca sabbatopabhaṃ.

Release, non-accumulation, liberation, extinguishment, the destruction of the substrata; peace, the unconditioned element, the refuge, and the light radiant on all sides.

Vināpetāni [M 0.0096] nāmāni, visesakapadaṃ idha;

Nibbānavācakānīti, sallakkheyya sumedhaso.

The wise should mark that these names, and other special terms besides, are here designators of Nibbāna.

“Tāṇaṃ leṇa”ntiādīni-pekkhikāni bhavanti hi;

Visesakapadānanti, etthetāni pakāsaye.

'Protection,' 'shelter,' and so on are indeed relative terms; as they are special terms, I will declare them here.

Tāṇaṃ leṇa’marūpañca, santaṃ sacca’manālayaṃ;

Sududdasaṃ saraṇañca, parāyaṇa’manītikaṃ.

Protection, shelter, and the formless, the peaceful, truth, the non-abode; the very hard to see, and the refuge, the final goal, the unafflicted.

Anāsavaṃ dhuvaṃ niccaṃ, viññāṇa’manidassanaṃ;

Abyāpajjaṃ sivaṃ khemaṃ, nipuṇaṃ apalokikaṃ.

The taintless, the firm, the constant, consciousness that is non-manifesting; the non-afflictive, the blissful, the secure, the subtle, the supramundane.

Ananta’makkharaṃ dīpo, accantaṃ kevalaṃ padaṃ;

Paṇītaṃ accutañcāti, bahudhāpi vibhāvaye.

The endless, the imperishable, the island-refuge, the absolute, the sole state; the excellent and the unfallen—thus may one understand it in many ways.

Gotrabhūti padassatthaṃ, vadantehi garūhi tu;

Gottaṃ vuccati nibbāna-miti gottanti bhāsitaṃ.

But by the venerable teachers who state the meaning of the word 'gotrabhū,' it is said that Nibbāna is called 'lineage' (gotta); thus it is spoken of as 'lineage.'

Vibhavoti vā vināsasampattidhanucchedadiṭṭhiyopi vuccanti. Tattha vināso vibhavanaṃ ucchijjanaṃ nassananti atthena vibhavo. “Vibhavo sabbadhammānaṃ, ittheke sato sattassa ucchedaṃ vināsaṃ vibhavaṃ paññapentī”ti ca idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Sampatti pana visesato bhavatīti vibhavo. “Rañño sirivibhavaṃ daṭṭhukāmā”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Dhanaṃ pana bhavanti vaḍḍhanti vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjanti sattā etenāti vibhavo. “Asītikoṭivibhavassa brāhmaṇassa putto hutvā nibbattī”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Idaṃ pana pariyāyavacanaṃ –

Or, by 'vibhava' are also meant destruction, attainment, wealth, and the annihilationist view. Therein, destruction (vināsa) is 'vibhava' in the sense of annihilation (vibhavanaṃ), being cut off (ucchijjanaṃ), and perishing (nassanaṃ). 'Annihilation of all things,' and 'some proclaim the cutting off, destruction, and annihilation of an existing being'—this statement establishes its meaning. Attainment (sampatti), however, is 'vibhava' because 'one becomes (bhavati) in a special way (visesato).' 'Desiring to see the king’s glorious prosperity (sirivibhavaṃ)'—this statement establishes its meaning. Wealth (dhana) is 'vibhava' because by means of it beings become (bhavanti), grow (vaḍḍhanti), and attain increase, growth, and abundance. 'He was reborn as the son of a brahmin possessing a fortune (vibhava) of eighty crores'—this statement establishes its meaning. And this is a synonymous expression:

Dhanaṃ saṃ vibhavo dabbaṃ, sāpateyyaṃ pariggaho;

Oḍḍaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sakaṃ attho, iccete dhanavācakā.

Wealth, treasure, riches, substance, property, possessions; bullion, goods, one's own, benefit—these are designators of wealth.

Ucchedadiṭṭhi pana vibhavati ucchijjati “attā ca loko ca puna cutito uddhaṃ na jāyatī”ti gahaṇato vibhavoti. “Vibhavataṇhā”ti [M 0.0097] idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Vibhavataṇhāti hi ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatāya taṇhāya nāmaṃ. Ettha atthuddhāro vuccati –

The annihilationist view, however, is 'vibhava' because of the holding that 'the self and the world are annihilated (vibhavati), are cut off (ucchijjati), and do not arise again after passing away.' 'Craving for annihilation' (vibhavataṇhā) is a statement that establishes this meaning. For 'craving for annihilation' is the name for craving accompanied by the annihilationist view. Herein, a summary of the meanings is stated:

Dhananibbānasampatti-vināsucchedadiṭṭhiyo;

Vuttā vibhavasaddena, iti viññū vibhāvaye.

Wealth, Nibbāna, attainment, destruction, and the annihilationist view: these are stated by the word 'vibhava.' Thus the wise should understand.

Pātubhāvoti pātubhavanaṃ pātubhāvo. Āvibhāvoti āvibhavanaṃ āvibhāvo, ubhinnametesaṃ pākaṭatā iccevattho. Tirobhāvoti tirobhavanaṃ tirobhāvo, paṭicchannabhāvo. Vinābhāvoti vinābhavanaṃ vinābhāvo, viyogo. Sotthibhāvoti sotthibhavanaṃ sotthibhāvo, suvatthibhāvo sukhassa atthitā, atthato pana nibbhayatā nirupaddavatā eva. Atthibhāvoti atthitā vijjamānatā avivittatā. Natthibhāvoti natthitā avijjamānatā vivittatā rittatā tucchatā suññatā. Okārantapulliṅganiddeso.

Manifestation (pātubhāvo) is the act of becoming manifest. Becoming evident (āvibhāvo) is the act of becoming evident; the meaning of both of these is simply conspicuousness. Disappearance (tirobhāvo) is the act of disappearing, the state of being concealed. Separation (vinābhāvo) is the act of being separated, disjunction. Well-being (sotthibhāvo) is the act of being well, a state of welfare, the existence of happiness; but in meaning, it is just fearlessness and freedom from affliction. Existence (atthibhāvo) is being, presence, non-remoteness. Non-existence (natthibhāvo) is non-being, absence, remoteness, emptiness, hollowness, voidness. This is the exposition of masculine nouns ending in -o.

Abhibhavatīti abhibhavitā, paraṃ abhibhavanto yo koci. Evaṃ paribhavitā, anubhavatīti anubhavitā, sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā anubhavanto yo koci. Evaṃ samanubhavitā. Paccanubhavitā, ettha pana yathā “amatassa dātā. Anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā”tiādīsu “dātā”ti padānaṃ kattuvācakānaṃ “amatassā”tiādīhi padehi kammavācakehi chaṭṭhiyantehi saddhiṃ yojanā dissati, tathā imesampi padānaṃ “paccāmittassa abhibhavitā”tiādinā yojanā kātabbā. Evaṃ aññesampi evarūpānaṃ padānaṃ. Ākārantapulliṅganiddeso.

He overcomes, thus he is an overcomer—whoever overcomes another. Similarly, an oppressor. He experiences, thus he is an experiencer—whoever experiences pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain. Similarly, one who fully experiences, one who undergoes. Here, just as in such phrases as 'giver of the deathless' and 'producer of the unarisen path,' the agent nouns like 'giver' are seen to be connected with words in the genitive case denoting the object, such as 'of the deathless,' so too these words should be connected in phrases like 'overcomer of the enemy.' It is the same for other such words. This is the exposition of masculine nouns ending in -ā.

Bhavatīti bhavaṃ. Bhavissatīti vā bhavaṃ, vaḍḍhamāno puggalo. “Suvijāno bhavaṃ hoti, suvijāno parābhavo. Dhammakāmo [M 0.0098] bhavaṃ hoti, dhammadessī parābhavo”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Atha vā yena saddhiṃ katheti, so “bhava”nti vattabbo, “bhavaṃ kaccāyano. Bhavaṃ ānando. Maññe bhavaṃ patthayati, rañño bhariyaṃ patibbata”ntiādīsu. Ettha pana dhātuatthe ādaro na kātabbo, sammutiattheyevādaro kātabbo “saṅketavacanaṃ saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇa”nti vacanato. Vohāravisayasmiñhi lokasammuti eva padhānā avilaṅghanīyā. Parābhavatīti parābhavaṃ. Evaṃ paribhavaṃ. Abhibhavaṃ. Anubhavaṃ. Pabhavati pahoti sakkotīti pabhavaṃ, pahonto yo koci. Na pabhavaṃ appabhavaṃ, “appabhava”nti ca idaṃ jātake diṭṭhaṃ –

'He prospers,' thus he is a prospering one (bhavaṃ). Or, 'he will prosper,' thus he is a prospering one, a person who is growing. This statement is proof of this meaning: 'Easily known is the prospering one; easily known is the one who declines. One who loves the Dhamma prospers; one who hates the Dhamma declines.' Alternatively, the one being addressed is designated 'bhavaṃ' (sir), as in: 'Venerable Kaccāyana,' 'Venerable Ānanda,' and 'I think your reverence desires the king's faithful wife.' Here, however, one should not pay attention to the root meaning but only to the conventional meaning, in accordance with the saying: 'A conventional term is true, being a cause of worldly convention.' For in the sphere of common usage, worldly convention is paramount and not to be transgressed. 'He declines,' thus he is a declining one (parābhavaṃ). Similarly, a contemptuous one (paribhavaṃ), an overpowering one (abhibhavaṃ), an experiencing one (anubhavaṃ). 'He is powerful, he is able, he is capable,' thus he is a capable one (pabhavaṃ)—whoever is capable. Not a capable one is an incapable one (appabhavaṃ), and this 'appabhavaṃ' is seen in the Jātaka:

“Chinnabbhamiva vātena, ruṇṇo rukkhamupāgamiṃ;

Sohaṃ appabhavaṃ tattha, sākhaṃ hatthehi aggahi”nti

"Like a cloud rent by the wind, weeping I approached a tree; there, powerless, I grasped a branch with my hands."

Tattha sādhakavacanamidaṃ. Niggahītantapulliṅganiddeso.

This is the illustrative statement for that. This is the exposition of masculine nouns ending in a niggahīta (ṃ).

Dhanabhūtīti dhanamassa bhavatūti dhanabhūti. Siribhūtīti sobhāya ceva paññāpuññānañca adhivacanaṃ. Sā assa bhavatūti siribhūti. Evaṃ sotthibhūti, suvatthibhūti. Ikārantapulliṅganiddeso.

Dhanabhūti means 'may wealth be his.' Siribhūti is a designation for splendor and for wisdom and merit; it means 'may glory be his.' Similarly, Sotthibhūti means 'may he be safe,' and Suvatthibhūti means 'may he be well.' This is the exposition of masculine nouns ending in -i.

Bhāvīti bhavanasīlo bhāvī, bhavanadhammo bhāvī, bhavane sādhukārī bhāvī. Evaṃ vibhāvī. Sambhāvī. Paribhāvīti. Tatra vibhāvīti atthavibhāvane samattho paṇḍito vuccati. Ettha vidvā, vijjāgato, ñāṇītiādi pariyāyavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhavanti catra –

A 'bhāvī' is one whose character is to develop, whose nature is to develop, or who is skilled in developing. Similarly, a 'vibhāvī' (one who clarifies), a 'sambhāvī' (one who esteems), and a 'paribhāvī' (one who despises). Therein, a 'vibhāvī' is said to be a wise person capable of clarifying the meaning. Here, synonymous terms such as 'the learned one,' 'one who has attained knowledge,' and 'the knowing one' should be understood. And on this there are these verses:

Vidvā vijjāgato ñāṇī, vibhāvī paṇḍito sudhī;

Budho visārado viññū, dosaññū viddasu vidū.

The learned, one who has attained knowledge, the knowing one, the discerning, the scholar, the very wise; the awakened, the expert, the intelligent, the fault-knower, the experienced, the wise.

Vipassī [M 0.0099] paṭibhāṇī ca, medhāvī nipako kavi;

Kusalo viduro dhīmā, gatimā mutimā cayaṃ.

One with insight and ready wit, intelligent, prudent, a sage; skilled, learned, resolute, astute, and intelligent is this one.

Cakkhumā kaṇṇavā dabbo, dhīro bhūri vicakkhaṇo;

Sappañño buddhimā pañño, evaṃnāmā vibhāvinoti.

One with vision, one who listens, accomplished, firm, of vast wisdom, discerning; sagacious, intelligent, wise—by such names is the discerning one known.

Īkārantapulliṅganiddeso.

This is the exposition of masculine nouns ending in -ī.

Sayambhūti sayameva bhavatīti sayambhū. Ko so? Antarena paropadesaṃ sāmaṃyeva sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ paṭivijjhitvā sabbaññutaṃ patto sakyamuni bhagavā. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Sayambhū means 'he becomes by himself.' Who is that? Without instruction from another, having himself penetrated all knowable phenomena and attained omniscience, he is the Blessed One, the Sage of the Sakyans. This was said by the Blessed One:

“Na me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati;

Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi me paṭipuggalo.

"I have no teacher; one like me does not exist. In this world with its devas, there is no one to rival me."

Ahañhi arahā loke, ahaṃ satthā anuttaro;

Ekomhi sammāsambuddho, sītībhūtosmi nibbuto”ti.

"For I am the Arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed Teacher; I alone am the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, I have become cool, I am extinguished."

Atthato pana pāramitāparibhāvito sayambhūñāṇena saha vāsanāya vigataviddhastaniravasesakileso mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimeyyaguṇagaṇādhāro khandhasantāno sayambhū. So evaṃbhūto khandhasantāno loke aggapuggaloti vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “ekapuggalo bhikkhave loke uppajjamāno uppajjati acchariyamanusso, katamo ekapuggalo? Tathāgato bhikkhave arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti. So ekapuggalo etarahi “sabbaññū, sugato”tiādīhi yathābhuccaguṇādhigatanāmehi ca pasiddho, “gotamo ādiccabandhū”ti gottato ca pasiddho, sakyaputto sakko sakyamuni sakyasīho sakyapuṅgavoti kulato ca pasiddho, suddhodanimāyādevīsutoti [M 0.0100] mātāpitito ca pasiddho, siddhatthoti gahitanāmena ca pasiddho. Bhavanti catra –

In meaning, however, the 'Sayambhū' is the continuum of aggregates that has been perfected by the perfections; which, along with self-originated knowledge, is devoid of all defilements, with their latent tendencies completely eradicated and destroyed; and which is the repository for the host of immeasurable qualities such as great compassion, omniscient knowledge, and so on. Such a continuum of aggregates is called the foremost individual in the world. For this has been said by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, one individual, arising in the world, arises as a wonderful person. What one individual? The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.' That one individual is now renowned by names acquired through his actual qualities, such as 'the Omniscient One,' 'the Well-Farer,' and so on. He is renowned by his clan name as 'Gotama' and 'Kinsman of the Sun.' He is renowned by his lineage as 'Son of the Sakyans,' 'the Sakyan,' 'the Sakyan Sage,' 'the Lion of the Sakyans,' and 'the Bull of the Sakyans.' He is renowned by his parents as 'the son of Suddhodana and Queen Māyā.' And he is renowned by his given name, 'Siddhattha.' And on this there are these verses:

Yo ekapuggalo āsi, buddho so vadataṃ varo;

Gottato gotamo nāma, tathevādiccabandhu ca.

That one individual who was, the Buddha, best of speakers; by clan he was named Gotama, and also Kinsman of the Sun.

Sakyakule pasūtattā, sakyaputtoti vissuto;

Sakko iti ca avhito, tathā sakyamunīti ca.

Because he was born in the Sakyan clan, he was famed as 'Son of the Sakyans'; he was also called 'the Sakyan,' and likewise 'the Sakyan Sage.'

Sabbattha seṭṭhabhāvena, sakye ca seṭṭhabhāvato;

Sakyasīhoti so sakya-puṅgavoti ca sammato.

Because of his excellence in all things, and his excellence among the Sakyans, he is deemed 'the Lion of the Sakyans' and 'the Bull of the Sakyans.'

Suddhodanīti pitito, nabhe candova vissuto;

Mātitopi ca saññāto, māyādevīsuto iti.

From his father, he is Suddhodani, famed like the moon in the sky; from his mother, too, he is known as 'the son of Queen Māyā.'

Sabbaññū sugato buddho, dhammarājā tathāgato;

Samantabhaddo bhagavā, jino dasabalo muni.

The Omniscient, the Well-Farer, the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, the Tathāgata; the All-Auspicious, the Blessed One, the Victor, the Ten-Powered One, the Sage.

Satthā vināyako nātho,

Munindo lokanāyako;

Narāsabho lokajino,

Sambuddho dvipaduttamo.

The Teacher, the Guide, the Protector, the Lord of Sages, the Leader of the World; the Bull of Men, the World-Victor, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Supreme among Bipeds.

Devadevo lokagaru, dhammassāmī mahāmuni;

Samantacakkhu purisa-dammasārathi māraji.

God of gods, Teacher of the World, Master of the Dhamma, the Great Sage; the All-Seeing Eye, the Trainer of persons to be tamed, the Māra-Victor.

Dhammissaro ca advejjha-vacano satthavāhako;

Visuddhidevo devāti-devo ca samaṇissaro.

Lord of Dhamma, of Incontrovertible Speech, the Caravan Leader; the God of Purity, God beyond gods, and Lord of Ascetics.

Bhūripañño’nadhivaro, narasīho ca cakkhumā;

Munimuni naravaro, chaḷabhiñño jane suto.

Of Vast Wisdom, Unsurpassed, the Lion of Men, and the One with Vision; Sage of Sages, Best of Men, possessing the six higher knowledges, famed among the people.

Aṅgīraso yatirājā, lokabandhu’matandado;

Vattā pavattā saddhamma-cakkavattī yatissaro.

Aṅgīrasa, King of Ascetics, Kinsman of the World, Giver of the Deathless; the Speaker, the Expounder, Turner of the Wheel of the Good Dhamma, the Lord of Ascetics.

Lokadīpo [M 0.0101] sirīghano, samaṇindo naruttamo;

Lokattayavidū loka-pajjoto purisuttamo.

Lamp of the World, a Mass of Glory, Chief of Ascetics, Noblest of Men; Knower of the Three Worlds, Light of the World, Foremost of Men.

Saccadaso satapuñña-lakkhaṇo saccasavhayo;

Ravibandhā’samasamo, pañcanetta’ggapuggalo.

Seer of Truth, with the hundred marks of merit, named 'Truth'; Kinsman of the Sun, the Unequalled, the foremost person with the five eyes.

Sabbābhibhū sabbavidū, saccanāmo ca pāragū;

Purisātisayo sabba-dassāvī narasārathi.

All-Conqueror, All-Knower, Truly Named, and Gone Beyond; Supreme among Men, All-Seeing, Charioteer of Men.

Sammāsambuddho iti so, ñāto sattuttamoti ca;

Tādī vibhajjavādīti, mahākāruṇikoti ca.

The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is he, known also as the Supreme among Beings; as the Suchlike One, the Analyst, and as the Greatly Compassionate One.

Cakkhubhūto dhammabhūto, ñāṇabhūtoti vaṇṇito;

Brahmabhūtoti purisā-jañño iti ca thomito.

He is described as 'Become Vision,' 'Become Dhamma,' 'Become Knowledge'; he is extolled as 'Become Brahma' and as the 'Thoroughbred among Men.'

Lokajeṭṭho sayambhū ca, mahesi mārabhañjano;

Amoghavacano dhamma-kāyo mārābhibhū iti.

Eldest in the World, Self-Become, the Great Seer, Crusher of Māra; of Infallible Speech, the Dhamma-Body, and Conqueror of Māra.

Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Nāmaṃ guṇehi nissitaṃ, ko kavindo kathessati.

Incalculable are the names of the Great Sage, according to his qualities. What lord of poets could relate all the names that are based on his virtues?

Tatra sabbaññu iccādi-nāmaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ bhave;

Sabbesānampi buddhānaṃ, gotamo itiādi na.
