Therein, names such as 'the Omniscient One' are common to all Buddhas, but names like 'Gotama' and so on are not.

Buddho paccekabuddho ca, “sayambhū”iti sāsane;

Keci “brahmā sayambhū”ti, sāsanāvacaraṃ na taṃ.

In the Dispensation, both a Buddha and a Paccekabuddha are called 'Sayambhū' (Self-Become). Some say, 'Brahmā is Sayambhū,' but that is not a statement of the Dispensation.

“Buddho tathāgato satthā, bhagavā”ti padāni tu;

Ṭhānenekasahassamhi, sañcaranti abhiṇhaso.

But the terms 'the Buddha,' 'the Tathāgata,' 'the Teacher,' 'the Blessed One' occur frequently in many thousands of places.

Tatra cādipadaṃ anta-padañceva imāni tu;

Ekatopi carantīti, vibhāveyya visārado.

But the wise one should discern that these terms, from the first to the last, also occur by themselves.

Visesakapadānaṃ tu, apekkhakapadāni ca;

Anapekkhapadānīti, padāni duvidhā siyuṃ.

Epithets, however, are of two kinds: dependent terms and independent terms.

Tathā [M 0.0102] hi satthavāho naravaro chaḷabhiññoti evaṃpakārāni abhidhānapadāni visesakapadāpekkhakāni. Kathaṃ?

For such appellations as 'Caravan Leader,' 'Best of Men,' and 'Possessor of the Six Higher Knowledges' are dependent qualifying terms. How so?

“Evaṃ vijitasaṅgāmaṃ, satthavāhaṃ anuttaraṃ;

Sāvakā payirupāsanti, tevijjā maccuhāyino.

"The disciples with the threefold knowledge, who have left death behind, wait upon the one who has thus conquered in battle, the unsurpassed Caravan Leader."

Yaṃ loko pūjayate,

Salokapālo sadā namassati ca;

Tasseta sāsanavaraṃ,

Vidūhi ñeyyaṃ naravarassā”ti,

"He whom the world reveres, and to whom the world-guardian always pays homage—this supreme teaching of that Best of Men should be known by the wise."

“Chaḷabhiññassa sāsana”nti ca evaṃ visesakapadāpekkhakāni bhavanti. Buddho jino bhagavāti evaṃpakārāni pana no visesakāpekkhānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

And 'the teaching of the one with the six higher knowledges'—in this way they are dependent qualifying terms. However, it should be understood that such terms as 'Buddha,' 'Victor,' and 'Blessed One' are not dependent on qualifiers.

Keci panettha evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “munindo samaṇindo samaṇissaro yatissaro ādiccabandhu ravibandhūti evaṃpakārānaṃ idha vuttānamabhidhānānaṃ visesatthābhāvato punaruttidoso atthī”ti. Tanna, abhidhānānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇīyānabhisaṅkharaṇīyavasena abhisaṅkhatābhidhānāni anabhisaṅkhatābhidhānānīti dvedhā dissanato. Tathā hi katthaci keci “sakyasīho”ti abhidhānaṃ paṭicca “sakyakesarī sakyamigādhipo”tiādinā nānāvividhamabhidhānamabhisaṅkharonti, pāvacanepi hi “dviduggamavarahanutta’malatthā”ti pāṭho dissati. Tathā keci “dhammarājā”ti abhidhānaṃ paṭicca “dhammadisampatī”tiādīni abhisaṅkharonti. “Sabbaññū”ti abhidhānaṃ paṭicca “sabbadassāvī sabbadassī”tiādīni abhisaṅkharonti, “sahassakkho”ti abhidhānaṃ paṭicca “dasasatalocano”tiādīni abhisaṅkharonti. “Ādiccabandhū”ti abhidhānaṃ paṭicca “aravindasahāyabandhū”tiādīni abhisaṅkharonti. “Ambuja”nti abhidhānaṃ paṭicca “nīrajaṃ kuñja”ntiādīni abhisaṅkharonti. Pāvacanepi hi [M 0.0103] yaṃ padumaṃ, taṃ jalajaṃ nāmāti mantvā paṭisambhidāppattehi ariyehi desanāvilāsavasena vutto “padumuttaranāmino”ti vattabbaṭṭhāne “jalajuttaranāmino”ti pāṭho dissati. Evaṃ abhisaṅkhatābhidhānāni dissanti.

But some might argue here: "Terms such as 'Lord of Sages,' 'Chief of Ascetics,' 'Lord of Ascetics,' 'Lord of Ascetics,' 'Kinsman of the Sun,' 'Kinsman of the Sun'—since these, as stated here, do not have distinct meanings, there is the fault of repetition." This is not so, for designations are seen to be of two kinds: elaborated designations and unelaborated designations, depending on whether they are to be elaborated or not. For instance, regarding the designation "Sakyan Lion," some elaborate various terms such as "Sakyan Lion," "Sakyan Lord of Beasts," and so on. Indeed, in the scriptures, the reading "twice-difficult-to-go, supreme, having attained the spotless" is found. Similarly, some, regarding the designation "Dhamma King," elaborate "Lord of the Dhamma's Domain" and so on. Regarding the designation "All-Knowing," they elaborate "All-Seeing, All-Perceiving," and so on. Regarding the designation "Thousand-Eyed," they elaborate "Ten-Hundred-Eyed" and so forth. Regarding the designation "Kinsman of the Sun," they elaborate "Kinsman, Friend of the Lotus" and suchlike. Regarding the designation "Lotus," they elaborate "Water-Born, Thicket" and so forth. Indeed, in the scriptures, understanding that what is called "paduma" (lotus) is "jalaja" (water-born), the noble ones who have attained analytical knowledge, for the sake of elegant teaching, instead of what should be said, "named Padumuttara," the reading "named Jalajuttara" is found. Thus, elaborated designations are seen.

“Buddho bhagavā”ti abhidhānāni pana anabhisaṅkhatābhidhānāni. Vuttañhetaṃ dhammasenāpatinā āyasmatā sāriputtena “buddhoti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ, na pitarā kataṃ, na bhaginiyā kataṃ, na ñātisālohitehi kataṃ, na devatāhi kataṃ, vimokkhantikametaṃ buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ buddho”ti, tathā “bhagavāti netaṃ nāmaṃ mātarā kataṃ…pe… sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ bhagavā”ti. Evaṃ “buddho bhagavā”ti abhidhānāni anabhisaṅkhatābhidhānāni. Na hi tāni abhidhānāni ceva “satthā sugato jino”tiādīni ca aññaṃ kiñci abhidhānaṃ paṭicca abhisaṅkhatāni, nāpi aññāni abhidhānāni etāni paṭicca abhisaṅkhatāni dissanti. Tathā hi “buddho”ti abhidhānaṃ paṭicca “bujjhitā bodhetā bodhako”tiādīni nāmābhidhānāni na abhisaṅkharonti. Tathā “bhagavā satthā sugato”tiādīni nāmābhidhānāni paṭicca “sampannabhago anusāsako sundaravacano”tiādīni nāmābhidhānāni nābhisaṅkharonti. Evaṃ imaṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “munindo samaṇindo samaṇissaro yatissaro ādiccabandhu ravibandhū”tiādinā nayena punarutti amhehi katāti daṭṭhabbā. Evamaññatrāpi nayo netabbo. Atridaṃ vuccati –

The designations 'Buddha' and 'Blessed One' are, however, unelaborated designations. For this was said by the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta: "'Buddha'—this is not a name made by a mother, nor by a father, nor by a sister, nor by relatives or kin, nor by deities. This is a designation truly realized by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, at the root of enlightenment, together with the attainment of all-knowing knowledge, a designation culminating in liberation; that is, ‘Buddha.’" Similarly, "'Blessed One'—this is not a name made by a mother… but a designation truly realized; that is, ‘Blessed One.’" Thus, the designations "Buddha" and "Blessed One" are unelaborated designations. For these designations, such as "Teacher," "the Well-gone," "the Victor," and others, are not elaborated in dependence on any other designation, nor are other designations seen to be elaborated in dependence on these. Indeed, the designation "Buddha" does not elaborate other name-designations such as "one who awakens, one who causes to awaken, an awakener," and so forth. Similarly, name-designations such as "Blessed One," "Teacher," "the Well-gone," and so on, do not elaborate other name-designations like "endowed with fortune, the instructor, the speaker of beautiful words," and so forth. Thus, to show this distinction, the repetition made by us—'Lord of Sages,' 'Chief of Ascetics,' 'Lord of Ascetics,' 'Lord of Ascetics,' 'Kinsman of the Sun,' 'Kinsman of the Sun,' and so on—should be understood as having been done. The same method should be applied elsewhere as well. Here it is said:

“Abhisaṅkhatanāmañca, nāmañcānabhisaṅkhataṃ;

Dviduggamavaro buddho, iti nāmaṃ dvidhā bhave”ti.

The elaborated name and the unelaborated name; The Buddha, supreme in two ways of difficult going—thus the name is twofold.

Pabhūti paraṃ pasayha bhavatīti pabhū, issaro. “Araññassa pabhū ayaṃ luddako”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Abhibhūti [M 0.0104] abhibhavatīti abhibhū, asaññasatto. Kiṃ so abhibhavi? Cattāro khandhe arūpino. Iti cattāro khandhe arūpino abhibhavīti abhibhū. So ca kho niccetanattā abhibhavanakriyāyāsati pubbevā’saññuppattito jhānalābhikāle attanā adhigatapañcamajjhānaṃ saññāvirāgavasena bhāvetvā cattāro arūpakkhandhe asaññibhave appavattikaraṇena abhibhavitumārabhi, tadabhibhavanakiccaṃ idāni siddhanti abhibhavīti abhibhūti vuccati. Apica niccetanabhāvena abhibhavanabyāpāre asatipi pubbe sacetanakāle sabyāpārattā sacetanassa viya niccetanassāpi sato tassa upacārena sabyāpāratāvacanaṃ yujjateva. Dissati hi loke sāsane ca sacetanassa viya acetanassapi upacārena sabyāpāratāvacanaṃ. Taṃ yathā? Kūlaṃ patitukāmaṃ, evaṃ loke. Sāsane pana –

Pabhū is one who becomes (bhavati) by overpowering (pasayha) others (paraṃ); a lord (issaro). 'This hunter is the lord of the forest'—this statement serves to illustrate this meaning. Abhibhū is one who overcomes (abhibhavati); the non-percipient being (asaññasatto). What did he overcome? The four formless aggregates. Thus, he is called Abhibhū because he overcame the four formless aggregates. And yet, due to his being without consciousness, the act of overcoming is not present in him. But because he previously—before the arising of non-perception, at the time of attaining jhāna—having developed the fifth jhāna attained by himself through the fading away of perception, began to overcome the four formless aggregates by causing their non-occurrence in the non-percipient state, and since that act of overcoming is now accomplished, he is called 'Abhibhū' because he overcame. Moreover, even though the activity of overcoming is not present due to his being without consciousness, it is indeed appropriate to speak of him as active by way of figurative expression, just as one would a conscious being, because he was active in the past when he was conscious. Indeed, in the world and in the Dispensation, it is seen that even unconscious things are spoken of as active by way of figurative expression, just as conscious things are. How so? For example, in the world: 'The bank is about to collapse.' In the Dispensation, however—

“Rodante dārake disvā, ubbiggā vipulā dumā;

Sayamevonamitvāna, upagacchanti dārake”ti ca

Seeing the children crying, the vast trees were agitated; of their own accord bending down, they approached the children.

“Aṅgārino dāni dumā bhadante, phalesino chadanaṃ vippahāyā”ti ca “phalaṃ toseti kassaka”nti ca ādi. Abhibhūsaddassa asaññasattābhidhānatte “abhibhuṃ abhibhuto maññatī”ti idamettha sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Atha vā abhibhavatīti abhibhū, paresamabhibhavitā yo koci. Visesato pana tathāgatoyeva abhibhū. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “tathāgato bhikkhave abhibhū anabhibhūto aññadatthudaso vasavattī”ti. Keci pana “abhibhū nāma sahasso brahmā”ti vadanti.

'The trees are now like embers, venerable sir, seeking fruit, having cast off their foliage,' and also 'the fruit pleases the farmer,' and so on. Regarding the term 'Abhibhū' as a designation for the non-percipient being, this statement is the proof here: 'He perceives Abhibhū as Abhibhū.' Alternatively, 'Abhibhū' means one who overcomes, any conqueror of others. Specifically, however, the Tathāgata alone is the Abhibhū. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, the Tathāgata is the overcomer, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power.' Some, however, say that 'Abhibhū' is the name for the thousand-fold Brahmā.

Vibhūti visesabhūtoti vibhū, “bhavasotaṃ sace buddho, tiṇṇo lokantagū vibhū”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ [M 0.0105] vacanaṃ. Vibhūti hettha rūpakāyadhammakāyasampattiyā visesabhūtoti attho. Āha ca –

Vibhū is one who is distinguished (visesabhūta), hence Vibhū. 'If the Buddha has crossed the stream of existence, gone to the end of the world, he is distinguished (vibhū)'—this statement serves to illustrate this meaning. Here, 'Vibhū' signifies being distinguished by the attainment of the form-body and the Dhamma-body. And it is said:

“Dissamānopi tāvassa, rūpakāyo acintiyo;

Asādhāraṇañāṇaṭṭhe, dhammakāye kathāva kā”ti.

Even his visible form-body is inconceivable; when he is established in the state of uncommon knowledge, what can be said of the Dhamma-body?

Adhibhūti adhibhavatīti adhibhū, issaro.

Adhibhū is one who overcomes (adhibhavati); a lord (issaro).

“Tadā maṃ tapatejena, santatto tidivādhibhū;

Dhārento brāhmaṇaṃ vaṇṇaṃ, bhikkhāya maṃ upāgamī”ti –

Then, scorched by the heat of his asceticism, the lord of the heavens, bearing the appearance of a brahmin, came to me for alms.

Idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Patibhūti patibhūtoti patibhū, “goṇassa patibhū”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Gotrabhūti gottasaṅkhātaṃ amatamahānibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā bhūtoti gotrabhū, sotāpattimaggassa anantarapaccayena sikhāppattabalavavipassanācittena samannāgato puggalo. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “katamo ca puggalo gotrabhū? Yesaṃ dhammānaṃ samanantarā ariyadhammassa avakkanti hoti, tehi dhammehi samannāgato puggalo gotrabhū”ti, idamevettha atthasādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Apica samaṇoti gottamattamanubhavamāno kāsāvakaṇṭhasamaṇopi gotrabhū. So hi “samaṇo”ti gottamattaṃ anubhavati vindati, na samaṇadhamme attani avijjamānattāti “gotrabhū”ti vuccati, “bhavissanti kho panānanda anāgatamaddhānaṃ gotrabhuno kāsāvakaṇṭhā dussīlā pāpadhammā”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Vatrabhūti sakko. So hi mātāpitibharaṇādīhi sattahi vattehi sakkattaṃ labhitvā aññe deve vattena abhibhavatīti vatrabhū. Āgamaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana bhūdhātumhi labbhamānaṃ pattiatthampi gahetvā “vattena aññe abhibhavitvā devissariyaṃ pattoti vatrabhū”ti [M 0.0106] vuttaṃ, “vatranāmakaṃ vā asuraṃ abhibhavatīti vatrabhū”ti ca, “vatrabhū jayataṃpitā”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Ettha hi vatrabhūti vatranāmakassa asurassa abhibhavitā. Jayataṃ pitāti jayantānaṃ pitā. “Sakko indo purindado” iccādi pariyāyavacanaṃ. Idaṃ tu dhātādhikāre pakāsessāma. Parābhibhūti paramabhibhavatīti parābhibhū. Evaṃ rūpābhibhūtiādīsupi. Sabbābhibhūti sabbamabhibhavitabbaṃ abhibhavatīti sabbābhibhū. Sabbābhibhūti ca idaṃ nāmaṃ tathāgatasseva yujjati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

This statement serves to illustrate this meaning. Patibhū is one who stands as surety (patibhūta), hence Patibhū. 'The surety for the ox'—this statement serves to illustrate this meaning. Gotrabhū is one who has become (bhūta) by making the deathless great Nibbāna, which is called 'lineage' (gotta), his object, hence Gotrabhū. It refers to a person endowed with a powerful insight consciousness that has reached its peak, which is the immediate condition for the path of stream-entry. For this, the Blessed One has said: 'And what person is a gotrabhū? A person endowed with those states immediately after which there is the descent of the noble path is a gotrabhū.' This very statement serves to prove the meaning here. Furthermore, even a mere nominal ascetic (samaṇo) who experiences only the lineage, an ascetic with a yellow robe around his neck, is also a gotrabhū. For he merely experiences or partakes of the lineage of 'ascetic,' but since the qualities of an ascetic are not present in him, he is called 'gotrabhū.' 'In the future, Ānanda, there will be gotrabhūs wearing yellow robes around their necks, immoral and of evil character'—this statement serves to illustrate this meaning. Vatrabhū is Sakka. For he, having attained the state of Sakka by fulfilling the seven vows such as supporting his parents, overcomes other devas by his vows (vatta), hence he is called 'Vatrabhū.' In the Āgama commentary, however, taking also the meaning 'attainment' (patti) found in the root 'bhū,' it is said: 'Having overcome others by his vows and attained lordship over the devas, he is called 'Vatrabhū.'' And also, 'he overcomes the asura named Vatra, hence he is called 'Vatrabhū.'' 'Vatrabhū, the father of the victorious'—this statement serves to illustrate this meaning. Here, 'Vatrabhū' means the conqueror of the asura named Vatra. 'Father of the victorious' means the father of those who are victorious. 'Sakka, Indra, Purindada'—these are synonymous terms. We will explain this further in the section on roots. Parābhibhū is one who overcomes another (paraṃ abhibhavati), hence Parābhibhū. Similarly in cases like 'rūpābhibhū,' etc. Sabbābhibhū is one who overcomes all that is to be overcome (sabbaṃ abhibhavitabbaṃ abhibhavati), hence Sabbābhibhū. And this name 'Sabbābhibhū' is fitting only for the Tathāgata. For this, the Blessed One has said—

“Sabbābhibhū sabbavidūhamasmi,

Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitto;

Sabbañjaho taṇhakkhaye vimutto,

Sayaṃ abhiññāya kamuddiseyya”nti.

All-vanquishing, all-knowing am I, untainted by all things; all-relinquishing, released in the destruction of craving, having directly known for myself, whom should I point to as my teacher?

Ūkārantapulliṅganiddeso. Niyatapulliṅganiddesoyaṃ.

The exposition of masculine nouns ending in -ū. This is the exposition of the fixed masculine gender.

Idāni aniyataliṅgānaṃ niyataliṅgesu pakkhittānaṃ bhūtaparābhūta sambhūtasaddādīnaṃ niddeso vuccati. Tatra bhūtoti attano paccayehi abhavīti bhūto, bhūtoti jāto sañjāto nibbatto abhinibbatto pātubhūto, bhūtoti vā laddhasarūpo yo koci saviññāṇako vā aviññāṇako vā. Atha vā tathākārena bhavatīti bhūto, bhūtoti sacco tatho avitatho aviparīto yo koci, ettha yo bhūtasaddo saccattho, tassa “bhūtaṭṭho”ti idamettha sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Parābhūtoti parābhavīti parābhūto. Suṭṭhu bhūtoti sambhūto. Visesena bhūtoti vibhūto. Vissuto bhūtoti vā vibhūto, “vibhūtārammaṇa”nti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Vibhavīti vā vibhūto, vinaṭṭhoti attho, “rūpe vibhūte na phusanti phassā”ti [M 0.0107] idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Pākaṭo bhūtoti pātubhūto. Āvi bhavatīti āvibhūto. Evaṃ tirobhūto. Vinābhūto. Bhavitumanucchavikoti bhabbo. Paribhaviyate soti paribhūto. Yena kenaci yo pīḷito hīḷito vā, so paribhūto. Gamyamānattho yathākāmacārī. Abhibhaviyyate soti abhibhūto. Adhibhaviyate soti adhibhūto. Evaṃ addhabhūto. Ettha adhisaddena samānattho addhasaddo, “cakkhu bhikkhave addhabhūtaṃ, rūpā addhabhūtā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ addhabhūta”nti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ, tathā “idha bhikkhave bhikkhu na heva anaddhabhūtaṃ attānaṃ na addhabhāvetī”ti padampi. Tattha anaddhabhūtanti dukkhena anadhibhūtaṃ. Dukkhena anadhibhūto nāma manussattabhāvo vuccati, taṃ na addhabhāveti nābhibhavatīti suttapadattho.

Now, the explanation of terms like 'bhūta,' 'parābhūta,' 'sambhūta,' and others, which are of indeterminate gender but are included among those of fixed gender, is stated. Here, 'bhūta' means that which has come into being through its own conditions; thus, it is 'bhūta.' 'Bhūta' also means born, produced, arisen, manifested, or come into existence. Alternatively, 'bhūta' refers to anything that has acquired its own nature, whether sentient or insentient. Or, 'bhūta' means that which comes into being in such a way; 'bhūta' means whatever is true, real, not false, not contrary. Here, where the word 'bhūta' has the meaning of truth, the phrase 'bhūtaṭṭho' is the statement that proves this meaning. 'Parābhūta' means that which has been ruined or overcome. 'Sambhūta' means well-formed or well-produced. 'Vibhūta' means distinctly manifest or distinguished. Alternatively, 'vibhūta' means widely known, as in the phrase 'vibhūtārammaṇa,' which serves to illustrate this meaning. Or, 'vibhūta' means that which has perished, the meaning being 'destroyed,' as in the phrase 'when form has perished, contacts do not touch,' which serves to illustrate this meaning. 'Pātubhūta' means manifest or evident. 'Āvibhūta' means openly existing. Similarly, 'tirobhūta' (concealed) and 'vinābhūta' (separated or absent). 'Bhabbo' means suitable to become. 'Paribhūta' means that which is despised or oppressed; whoever is harassed or humiliated by anyone is 'paribhūta.' The meaning to be understood is one who is subject to another's will. 'Abhibhūta' means that which is overpowered. 'Adhibhūta' means that which is overpowered. Similarly, 'addhabhūta.' Here, the word 'addha' has the same meaning as 'adhi,' as in the phrase 'Monks, the eye is overpowered, forms are overpowered, eye-consciousness is overpowered,' which serves to illustrate this meaning. Likewise, there is also the passage: 'Here, monks, a bhikkhu does not overpower a self that is not overpowered.' There, 'anaddhabhūta' means not overpowered by suffering. The human state is called 'not overpowered by suffering,' and the meaning of the sutta passage is that one does not overpower it.

Anubhaviyate soti anubhūto. Evaṃ samanubhūto. Paccanubhūto. Bhāvito. Ettha bhāvitoti iminā samānādhikaraṇaṃ “satisambojjhaṅgo kho kassapa mayā sammadakkhāto bhāvito”tiādīsu guṇīvācakaṃ padhānapadaṃ sāsane daṭṭhabbaṃ. Titthiyasamaye pana bhāvitoti kāmaguṇo vuccati. Vuttañhetaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “na bhāvitamāsīsatī”ti. Tatra bhāvitā nāma pañca kāmaguṇā, te na āsīsati na sevatīti suttapadattho. Sambhāviyate soti sambhāvito. Evaṃ vibhāvito. Paribhāvito. Anuparibhūto. Manaṃparibhūtoti manaṃ paribhaviyittha soti manaṃparibhūto. Ettha manaṃparibhūtoti īsakaṃ appattaparibhavano vuccati. Mananti hi nipātapadaṃ. “Atipaṇḍitena puttena, manamhi upakūlito, devadattena attano abuddhabhāvena ceva khantimettādīnañca [M 0.0108] abhāvena kumārakassapatthero ca therī ca manaṃ nāsito, manaṃ vuḷho ahosī”tiādīsu cassa payogo veditabbo. Atra manaṃsaddassa kiñci yuttiṃ vadāma.

That which is experienced is 'anubhūta.' Similarly, 'samanubhūta' (thoroughly experienced) and 'paccanubhūta' (repeatedly experienced). 'Bhāvita' (developed). Here, 'bhāvita' is a principal word denoting a quality, which should be seen in the Dispensation in apposition with this, as in phrases like 'Kassapa, the mindfulness enlightenment factor has been well expounded and developed by me.' However, in the doctrine of the sectarians, 'bhāvita' is said to refer to sensual pleasure. This was stated in the Pāli: 'He does not long for what is cultivated.' There, 'bhāvitā' refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure; the meaning of the sutta passage is that one does not long for them, does not indulge in them. That which is esteemed is 'sambhāvita.' Similarly, 'vibhāvita' (well-esteemed), 'paribhāvita' (fully esteemed), and 'anuparibhūta' (somewhat despised). 'Manaṃparibhūta' means that which was slightly despised, because it was slightly despised. Here, 'manaṃparibhūta' refers to one who has not quite reached the state of being despised. For 'manaṃ' is an indeclinable particle. Its usage should be understood in phrases such as: 'By an overly clever son, he was slightly troubled in mind (manamhi upakūlito).' 'By Devadatta, due to his own lack of enlightenment and his lack of patience, loving-kindness, and so forth, Kumārakassapa Thera and the Therī were slightly ruined (manaṃ nāsito) and were slightly carried away (manaṃ vuḷho ahosī).' Here, let us speak of some reasoning concerning the word 'manaṃ'.

Manaṃsaddo dvidhā bhinno, nāmaṃ nepātikañciti;

Santaṃ tassa manaṃ hoti, manamhi upakūlitoti.

The word 'manaṃ' is divided in two ways: as a noun and as an indeclinable particle. As in: 'His mind is peaceful,' and 'in mind he was troubled.'

Paribhavitabboti aññena paribhavituṃ sakkuṇeyyoti paribhavitabbo. Evaṃ paribhottabbo paribhavanīyo. Tabbapaccayaṭṭhāne hi sakkuṇeyyapadayojanā dissati “aladdhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ laddhabbaṃ labhanīyaṃ laddhuṃ vā sakkuṇeyya”nti. Atha vā paribhavanamarahatīti paribhavitabbo. Evaṃ paribhottabbo paribhavanīyo. Tathā hi tabbapaccayaṭṭhāne arahatipadayojanā dissati “parisakkuṇeyyaṃ lābhamarahatīti laddhabba”nti. Ettha pana paribhottabboti padassa atthibhāve “khattiyo kho mahārāja daharoti na uññātabbo na paribhottabbo”ti pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Abhiadhipubbā bhūdhātuyo samānatthā. Sesāni dukāni nayānusārena ñeyyāni. Bhamānoti bhavatīti bhamāno, majjhe vakāralopo daṭṭhabbo. Atridaṃ vattabbaṃ –

'Paribhavitabba' means one whom another is able to despise—thus, he is 'paribhavitabba.' Similarly, 'paribhottabba' and 'paribhavanīya.' For in the context of the suffix '-tabba,' the interpretation with the word 'able' is seen, as in 'What is not obtained should be obtained, should be attainable, or should be able to be obtained.' Alternatively, 'paribhavitabba' means one who deserves contempt. Similarly, 'paribhottabba' and 'paribhavanīya.' Thus, in the context of the suffix '-tabba,' the interpretation with the word 'deserves' is seen, as in 'That which deserves a gain that can be obtained is 'laddhabba' (to be obtained).' Here, moreover, regarding the existence of the word 'paribhottabba,' the Pāli passage 'O great king, a young noble should not be disdained, should not be despised' is an illustration. The verbal root bhū with the prefixes abhi- and adhi- have similar meanings. The remaining difficult points should be understood according to the method. 'Bhamāno' means 'becoming' (bhavati); the elision of the middle 'v' sound should be noted. Here this should be said:

“Kiṃ so bhamāno saccako”, iccatra pāḷiyaṃ pana;

Rūpaṃ bhavatidhātussa, valopeneva dissati.

'What is that Saccaka raving?'—in that Pāli passage, the form of the root 'bhavati' appears with the elision of 'v'.

Atrāyaṃ pāḷi “kiṃ so bhamāno saccako nigaṇṭhaputto, yo bhagavato vādaṃ āropessatī”ti. Vibhavamānoti vibhavatīti vibhavamāno. Evaṃ paribhavamānotiādīsu. Tattha “abhisambhonto”timassa karonto nipphādento iccevattho. “Sabbāni abhisambhonto, sa rājavasatiṃ vase”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Yasmā panimāni [M 0.0109] “bhavamāno”tiādīni vippakatapaccattavacanāni, tasmā saramāno rodati, gacchanto gaṇhāti, “gacchanto so bhāradvājo, addasa accutaṃ isi”ntiādīni viya paripuṇṇuttarakriyāpadāni katvā rājā bhavamāno sampattimanubhavatītiādinā yojetabbāni. “Saramāno gacchanto”tiādīni hi “yāto gato patto”tiādīhi sadisāni na honti, uttarakriyāpadāpekkhakāni honti tvāpaccayantapadāni viyāti.

Here is that Pāli passage: 'What is this Saccaka, the Nigaṇṭha’s son, raving, that he would challenge the Blessed One’s doctrine?' 'Vibhavamāno' means 'flourishing' (vibhavati). Similarly, in cases like 'paribhavamāno,' etc. Here, 'abhisambhonto' means 'doing' or 'accomplishing'—that is the meaning. The phrase 'accomplishing all things, he should dwell in the royal residence' supports this meaning. Moreover, since these terms—'bhavamāno,' etc.—are incomplete present participles, they should be construed with complete subsequent verbs, just like 'saramāno rodati' (remembering, he weeps), 'gacchanto gaṇhāti' (going, he takes), or 'gacchanto so Bhāradvājo, addasa accutaṃ isi' (going, that Bhāradvāja saw the deathless sage), etc. For example, they should be connected in the way 'the king, becoming, experiences prosperity,' etc. For terms like 'saramāno gacchanto' are not equivalent to 'yāto gato patto' (gone, gone, arrived), as they depend on subsequent verbs, similar to words ending in the '-tvā' suffix.

Paribhaviyamānoti paribhaviyate soti paribhaviyamāno. Evaṃ paribhuyyamānotiādīsupi. Imānipi vippakatapaccattavacanāni, tasmā “rājapurisehi nīyamāno coro evaṃ cintesī”tiādīni viya paripuṇṇuttarakriyāpadāni katvā aññehi paribhaviyamāno tāṇaṃ gavesati. Bhogo puggalenānubhaviyamāno parikkhayaṃ gacchatītiādinā yojetabbāni. Evaṃ sabbatra īdisesu vippakatavacanesu yojetabbāni. Ayaṃ aniyataliṅgānaṃ niyataliṅgesu pakkhittānaṃ bhūta parābhūta sambhūtasaddānaṃ niddeso. Iccevaṃ pulliṅgānaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ yathārahaṃ nibbacanādivasena niddeso vibhāvito.

That which is being despised is 'paribhaviyamāna,' because it is being despised. Similarly, with 'paribhuyyamāna,' etc. These, too, are incomplete passive participles. Therefore, just as in the example, 'The thief, being led by the king’s men, thought thus,' and so on, they should be construed with complete subsequent verbs, such as 'being despised by others, he seeks protection.' Similarly, 'Wealth, being enjoyed by a person, dwindles away,' and so on—these should be connected accordingly. Thus, in all such cases of incomplete participles, they should be construed appropriately. This is an explanation concerning the words 'bhūta,' 'parābhūta,' and 'sambhūta,' which, though of indeterminate gender, are included among those of fixed gender. Thus, the explanation of masculine nouns derived from the root 'bhū,' along with their appropriate exposition, etc., has been elucidated.

Idāni itthiliṅganiddeso vuccati – tatra bhāvikāti bhāvetīti bhāvikā. Yā bhāvanaṃ karoti, sā bhāvikā. Bhāvanāti vaḍḍhanā brūhanā phātikaraṇaṃ āsevanā bahulīkāro. Vibhāvanāti pakāsanā sandassanā. Atha vā vibhāvanāti abhāvanā antaradhāpanā. Sambhāvanāti ukkaṃsanā thomanā. Paribhāvanāti vāsanā, samantato vā vaḍḍhanā. Ākārantitthiliṅganiddeso.

Now the explanation of the feminine gender is stated. Here, 'bhāvikā' means 'one who develops' (bhāveti); thus, she is 'bhāvikā.' She who performs development is 'bhāvikā.' 'Bhāvanā' means growth, increase, expansion, cultivation, and frequent practice. 'Vibhāvanā' means clarification or showing. Alternatively, 'vibhāvanā' means non-development or causing to disappear. 'Sambhāvanā' means exaltation or praising. 'Paribhāvanā' means perfuming or complete growth. This is the explanation of feminine nouns ending in '-ā'.

Bhūmīti sattāyamānā bhavatīti bhūmi, atha vā bhavanti jāyanti vaḍḍhanti cettha thāvarā ca jaṅgamā cāti bhūmi. Bhūmi vuccati [M 0.0110] pathavī. “Paṭhamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā”tiādīsu pana lokuttaramaggo bhūmīti vuccati. Yā panandhabālamahājanena viññātā pathavī, tassimāni abhidhānāni –

'Bhūmi' is so called because beings exist and come into being on it. Alternatively, it is called 'bhūmi' because stationary and moving beings come into existence, are born, and grow here. 'Bhūmi' is also called 'pathavī' (earth). However, in phrases such as 'attaining the first bhūmi,' the supramundane path is called 'bhūmi.' Now, these are the synonyms for the earth as known by the blind, foolish masses:

“Pathavī medanī bhūmi, bhūrī bhū puthuvī mahī;

Chamā vasumatī ubbī, avanī ku vasundharā;

Jagatī khiti vasudhā, dharaṇī go dharā”iti.

Pathavī, Medanī, Bhūmi, Bhūrī, Bhū, Puthuvī, Mahī; Chamā, Vasumatī, Ubbī, Avanī, Ku, Vasundharā; Jagatī, Khiti, Vasudhā, Dharaṇī, Go, Dharā.

Atra bhū ku gosaddā pathavīpadatthe vattantīti kutra diṭṭhapubbāti ce?

If it is asked, 'Where has it ever been seen that the words 'bhū,' 'ku,' and 'go' are used in the sense of 'earth'?'

Vidvā bhūpāla kumuda-gorakkhādipadesu ve;

Bhū ku goiti pathavī, vuccatīti vibhāvaye.

The wise should discern that in words like 'bhūpāla' (earth-protector), 'kumuda' (earth-joy), 'gorakkha' (earth-protector), etc., 'bhū,' 'ku,' and 'go' are indeed said to mean 'earth'.

Bhūtīti bhavanaṃ bhūti. Vibhūtīti vināso, visesato bhavanaṃ vā, atha vā visesato bhavanti sattā etāyāti vibhūti, sampattiyeva, “rañño vibhūti. Pihanīyā vibhūtiyo”ti ca idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Ikārantitthiliṅganiddeso.

'Bhūti' means 'becoming' (bhavanaṃ); thus, it is 'bhūti.' 'Vibhūti' means destruction, or alternatively, a special kind of becoming. Or, 'vibhūti' is so called because beings particularly come into being through it; it is indeed prosperity, as in 'the king's prosperity' and 'desirable prosperities.' This statement supports this meaning. This is the explanation of feminine nouns ending in '-i'.

Bhūrīti pathavī. Sā hi bhavanti etthāti bhūrīti vuccati, bhavati vā paññāyati vaḍḍhati cāti bhūrī, atha vā bhūtābhūtā tannissitā sattā ramanti etthāti bhūrī. Pathavīnissitā hi sattā pathaviyaṃyeva ramanti, tasmā sā imināpi atthena bhūrīti vuccati. Bhūrīsaddassa pathavīvacane “bhūripañño”ti atthasādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Apica bhūrī viyāti bhūrī, paññā, bhūrīti pathavīsamāya vitthatāya paññāya nāmaṃ, “yogā ve jāyatī bhūrī, ayogā bhūrisaṅkhayo”ti ettha aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ imassatthassa sādhakaṃ. Atha vā bhūte atthe ramatīti bhūrī, paññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ, “bhūrī medhā pariṇāyikā”ti ettha [M 0.0111] aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ imassatthassa sādhakaṃ. Atha vā paññāyeva rāgādayo dhamme abhibhavatīti bhūrī, rāgādiarayo abhibhavatītipi bhūrī. Tathā hi paṭisambhidāmagge āyasmatā sāriputtena vuttaṃ “rāgaṃ abhibhūyatīti bhūrī, paññā. Dosaṃ mohaṃ…pe… rāgo ari, taṃ ariṃ maddatīti bhūrī, paññā. Doso. Moho…pe… sabbe bhavagāmino kammā ari, taṃ ariṃ maddatīti bhūrī, paññā”. Ettha pana “gotrabhū”ti padamiva “aribhū”ti vattabbepi bhūsaddaṃ pubbanipātaṃ katvā sandhivasena bhūrīti padamuccāritanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Apica īdisesu nāmikapadesu vināpi upasaggena abhibhavanādiatthā labbhantiyeva, nākhyātikapadesūti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idaṃ pana paññāya pariyāyavacanaṃ –

Bhūrī is the earth. For it is called 'bhūrī' because beings exist here; or it is 'bhūrī' because it exists, is known, and grows; or alternatively, beings, both existent and non-existent, dependent on it, delight here—thus it is called 'bhūrī'. Indeed, beings dependent on the earth delight in the earth itself; therefore, for this reason too, it is called 'bhūrī'. In the sense of earth for the word 'bhūrī', the statement 'bhūripañño' (one of vast wisdom) supports the meaning. Furthermore, wisdom is called 'bhūrī' because it is like the earth; 'bhūrī' is a name for wisdom, which is vast like the earth. The commentary statement, 'Wisdom indeed arises through application; through non-application, there is a decline of wisdom'—this supports this meaning. Alternatively, it is called 'bhūrī' because it delights in true matters—this is a name for wisdom. The commentary statement, 'Bhūrī is understanding, the guide'—this supports this meaning. Alternatively, because wisdom itself overcomes states like lust, it is 'bhūrī'. Because it overcomes foes like lust, it is also 'bhūrī'. Thus, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the Venerable Sāriputta said: 'Because it overcomes lust, it is 'bhūrī,' that is, wisdom. It overcomes hatred, delusion... Lust is a foe; because it crushes that foe, it is 'bhūrī,' that is, wisdom. Hatred, delusion... All actions leading to becoming are foes; because it crushes those foes, it is 'bhūrī,' that is, wisdom.' Here, however, it should be understood that just as there is the word 'gotrabhū', although 'aribhū' could have been said, the word 'bhūrī' is uttered by placing the word 'bhū' first and through sandhi. Moreover, it should be understood that in such nominal expressions, meanings like 'overcoming' can be obtained even without a prefix, but not in verbal expressions. This, however, is a synonym for wisdom—

Paññā pajānanā cintā, vicayo upalakkhaṇā;

Pavicayo ca paṇḍiccaṃ, dhammavicayameva ca.

Wisdom, understanding, thinking, investigation, discernment; thorough investigation, sagacity, and indeed investigation of the Dhamma.

Sallakkhaṇā ca kosallaṃ, bhūrī paccupalakkhaṇā;

Nepuññañceva vebhabyā, medhā cupaparikkhakā.

Observation and skill; wisdom and thorough discernment; expertise and comprehensiveness; intelligence and thorough examination.

Sampajaññañca pariṇā-yikā ceva vipassanā;

Paññindriyaṃ paññābalaṃ, amoho sammādiṭṭhi ca;

Patodo cābhidhammasmā, imāni gahitāni me.

And clear comprehension, and indeed the guide, insight; the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, non-delusion, and right view; and the goad from the Abhidhamma—these have been taken by me.

Ñāṇaṃ paññāṇamummaṅgo, sattho soto ca diṭṭhi ca;

Mantā bodho buddhi buddhaṃ, paṭibhānañca bodhiti.

Knowledge, understanding, ingenuity; guidance, the stream, and the view; counsel, awakening, intelligence, the awakened state; and inspiration—this is enlightenment.

Dhammo vijjā gati monaṃ, nepakkaṃ go matī muti;

Vīmaṃsā yoni dhonā ca, paṇḍā paṇḍiccayampi ca;

Vedo paṇḍitiyañceva, cikicchā miriyāpi ca.

Dhamma, knowledge, course, sagehood; discretion, intellect, understanding, thought; investigation, origin, and cleansing; wisdom, and also sagacity; knowledge, and indeed sagacity; investigation and also miriyā.

“Soto bodhī”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, ñāṇanāmadvayaṃ idaṃ;

Buddhapaccekasambuddha-sāvakānampi rūhati.

What is called 'stream' and 'enlightenment'—this is a twofold name for knowledge. It applies also to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples.

“Abhisambodhi [M 0.0112] sambodhi”, iti nāmadvayaṃ pana;

Paccekabuddhasabbaññu-buddhānaṃyeva rūhati.

However, these two names, 'Abhisambodhi' and 'Sambodhi,' apply only to Paccekabuddhas and All-Knowing Buddhas.

Abhisambodhisaṅkhātā, paramopapadā pana;

Ñāṇapaṇṇatti sabbaññu-sambuddhasseva rūhati.

However, the supreme attainment, known as supreme enlightenment, the designation of knowledge, applies only to the All-Knowing, Fully Awakened Buddha.

Sammāsambodhisaṅkhātā, anuttarapadādikā;

Buddhā vā ñāṇapaṇṇatti, sabbaññusseva rūhati.

The unsurpassed state and so on, designated as perfect enlightenment, or the Buddhas' designation of knowledge, applies only to the Omniscient One.

“Sabbaññutā”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, ñāṇaṃ sabbaññunova taṃ;

Yujjate avasesā tu, ñāṇapaññatti sabbagā.

What is called 'omniscience'—that knowledge indeed belongs to the Omniscient One. The remaining designations of knowledge, however, are all-encompassing.

Ñāṇabhāvamhi santepi, dhammacakkhādikaṃ pana;

Payojanantarābhāvā, nātra sandassitaṃ mayāti.

However, even though there is the state of knowledge, such as the Dhamma-eye and the like, due to the absence of another purpose, it was not shown here by me.

Bhūtīti bhūtassa bhariyā. Yathā hi petassa bhariyā “petī”ti vuccati, evameva bhūtassa bhariyā “bhūtī”ti vuccati. Bhotīti yāya saddhiṃ kathentena sā itthī “bhotī” iti vattabbā, tasmā iminā padena itthī vohariyatīti ca daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathā hi purisena saddhiṃ kathentena puriso “bhavaṃ” iti vohariyati, evameva itthiyā saddhiṃ kathentena itthī “bhotī”iti vohariyati. “Kuto nu bhavaṃ bhāradvājo, ime ānesi dārake”ti, “ahaṃ bhotiṃ upaṭṭhissaṃ, mā bhotī kupitā ahū”ti cettha nidassanaṃ. Atha vā idhekacco satto itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmo, so “bhotī”iti vattabbo, tasmā iminā padena itthīpi itthiliṅgena laddhanāmā anitthīpi vohariyatīti ca daṭṭhabbā. Tathā hi devaputtopi “devatā”ti itthiliṅgavasena voharitabbattā devatāsaddamapekkhitvā “bhotī”iti voharito, pageva devadhītā. Tathā hi “bhotī carahi jānāti, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchitā”ti ettha pana devatāsaddamapekkhitvā “bhotī”iti itthi liṅgavohāro kato. Atrāyaṃ [M 0.0113] suttapadattho “yadi so kuhako dhanatthiko tāpaso na jānāti, bhotī devatā pana jānāti ki”nti. Apica –

Bhūtī is the wife of a bhūta (being). Just as the wife of a peta (departed one) is called 'petī,' so too the wife of a bhūta is called 'bhūtī.' Bhotī is so called because a woman, when conversed with, should be addressed as 'bhotī.' Therefore, it should be understood that this term is used to address a woman. Just as a man conversing with another man addresses him as 'bhavaṃ,' similarly, when conversing with a woman, one addresses her as 'bhotī.' For example: 'From where, bhavaṃ Bhāradvāja, have you brought these children?' and 'I will serve you, bhotī; may bhotī not be angry'—here is an illustration. Alternatively, a certain being here has acquired a name in accordance with the feminine gender, and so should be addressed as 'bhotī.' Therefore, it should be understood that by this term, both a woman and a non-woman with a feminine name are addressed. For instance, even a devaputta, because he should be addressed with the feminine term 'devatā,' is called 'bhotī' with reference to the term 'devatā,' how much more so a devadhītā. Thus: 'Bhotī, if you know, tell me when asked'—here, with reference to the term 'devatā,' the feminine form of address 'bhotī' is used. Here the meaning of the sutta passage is: 'If that deceitful, greedy ascetic does not know, does bhotī, the devatā, perhaps know?' Furthermore—

“Atthakāmosi me yakkha, hitakāmāsi devate;

Karomi te taṃ vacanaṃ, tvaṃsi ācariyo mamā”ti –

‘You desire my welfare, O yakkha; you desire my good, O deity. I shall do that word of yours; you are my teacher.’

Maṭṭhakuṇḍalīvatthusmiṃ pulliṅgayakkhasaddamapekkhitvā “atthakāmo”ti pulliṅgavasena itthiliṅgañca devatāsaddamapekkhitvā “hitakāmā”ti itthiliṅgavasena purisabhūto maṭṭhakuṇḍalī voharito. Aññatrāpi devatāsaddamapekkhitvā devaputto itthiliṅgavasena voharito –

In the story of Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, Maṭṭhakuṇḍalī, who was a male, was addressed in the masculine gender as 'atthakāmo', with reference to the masculine word 'yakkha', and in the feminine gender as 'hitakāmā', with reference to the feminine word 'devatā'. Elsewhere also, with reference to the word 'devatā', a devaputta was addressed in the feminine gender—

“Na tvaṃ bāle vijānāsi, yathā arahataṃ vaco”ti;

“Atthakāmāsi me amma, hitakāmāsi devate”ti.

‘O fool, you do not understand the word of the Arahants.’ And: ‘You desire my welfare, O mother; you desire my good, O deity.’

Ettha pana “ehi bāle khamāpehi, kusarājaṃ mahabbala”nti ettha ca itthīyeva itthiliṅgavasena voharitā, tasmā katthaci itthipurisapadatthasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ anapekkhitvā liṅgamattamevāpekkhitvā bhotī devatā, bhotī silā, bhotī jambū, bhotiṃ devatantiādīhi saddhiṃ paccattavacanādīni yojetabbāni. Katthaci pana liṅgañca atthañca apekkhitvā “bhotī itthī, bhotiṃ deva”ntiādinā yojetabbāni. Vibhāvinīti vibhāvetīti vibhāvinī. Evaṃ paribhāvinītiādīsupi. Īkārantitthiliṅganiddeso.

Here, however, in the phrase, ‘Come, O fool, ask forgiveness from the mighty Kosala king,’ a woman indeed is addressed in the feminine gender. Therefore, in some cases, disregarding the meaning of the word as male or female and considering only the grammatical gender, singular pronouns and the like should be used with terms such as 'bhotī devatā,' 'bhotī silā,' 'bhotī jambū,' 'bhotiṃ devataṃ,' and so on. In other cases, however, considering both the gender and the meaning, they should be used with terms such as 'bhotī itthī,' 'bhotiṃ devaṃ,' and so on. 'Vibhāvinī' means 'she who makes clear,' thus 'vibhāvinī.' The same applies to 'paribhāvinī' and so on. This is the explanation of feminine nouns ending in 'ī'.

Bhūti sattāyamānā bhavatīti bhū. Atha vā bhavanti jāyanti vaḍḍhanti cettha sattasaṅkhārāti bhū. Bhū vuccati pathavī. Abhūti vaḍḍhivirahitā kathā, na bhūtapubbāti vā abhū, abhūtapubbā kathā. Na bhūtāti vā abhū, abhūtā kathā. “Abhuṃ me kathaṃ nu bhaṇasi, pāpakaṃ vata bhāsasī”ti idametesamatthānaṃ [M 0.0114] sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. Ūkārantitthiliṅganiddeso. Niyatitthiliṅganiddesoyaṃ.

'Bhū' is so called because it exists as an entity. Alternatively, it is called 'bhū' because beings and formations are born, exist, and grow here. 'Bhū' is called the earth. 'Abhū' is speech devoid of growth; or 'abhū' is what has never been before, a story that has never existed before. Or 'abhū' is what is not true, a false story. 'Why do you speak to me of what never was? Surely, you speak evil words!'—this statement serves to illustrate these meanings. This is the explanation of feminine nouns ending in 'ū.' This is the explanation of the fixed feminine gender.

Aniyataliṅgānaṃ pana niyatitthiliṅgesu pakkhittānaṃ bhūtaparābhūtasambhūtasaddādīnaṃ niddeso nayānusārena suviññeyyova. Iccevaṃ itthiliṅgānaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ yathārahaṃ nibbacanādivasena niddeso vibhāvito.

However, the explanation of words of unfixed gender, such as 'bhūta,' 'parābhūta,' and 'sambhūta,' when they are included among the fixed feminine genders, should be easily understood according to the method. Thus, the explanation of feminine-gendered terms derived from the root 'bhū' has been clarified appropriately by way of analysis and so on.

Idāni napuṃsakaliṅganiddeso vuccati – tatra bhūtanti catubbidhaṃ pathavīdhātuādikaṃ mahābhūtarūpaṃ. Tañhi aññesaṃ nissayabhāvena bhavatīti bhūtaṃ, bhavati vā tasmiṃ tadadhīnavuttitāya upādārūpanti bhūtaṃ. Atha vā bhūtanti satto bhūtanāmako vā. Bhūtanti hi napuṃsakavasena sakalo satto evaṃnāmako ca yakkhādiko vuccati. “Kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā. Yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatāni, ujjhāpetvāna bhūtāni, tamhā ṭhānā apakkamī”ti evamādīsu napuṃsakappayogo veditabbo. Gātābandhasukhatthaṃ liṅgavipallāsoti ce? Tanna, “yakkhādīni mahābhūtāni yaṃ gaṇhanti, neva tesaṃ tassa anto, na bahi ṭhānaṃ upalabbhatī”ti cuṇṇiyapadaracanāyampi bhūtasaddassa napuṃsakaliṅgattadassanatoti avagantabbaṃ. Mahābhūtanti vuttappakāraṃ catubbidhaṃ mahābhūtarūpaṃ. Tassa mahantapātubhāvādīhi kāraṇehi mahābhūtatā veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Mahantaṃ bhūtanti mahābhūtaṃ, māyākārasaṅkhātena mahābhūtena samantipi mahābhūtaṃ, yakkhādīhi mahābhūtehi samantipi mahābhūtaṃ, mahantehi ghāsacchādanādipaccayehi bhūtaṃ pavattantipi mahābhūtaṃ, mahāvikārabhūtantipi mahābhūtaṃ. Evaṃ mahantapātubhāvādīhi kāraṇehi mahābhūtatā veditabbā. Atridaṃ suṭṭhupalakkhitabbaṃ –

Now the explanation of the neuter gender is stated. Herein, 'bhūta' refers to the fourfold great primary material form, such as the earth element. For it is called 'bhūta' because it exists as a basis for others, or because derived material form exists in it, having its subsistence dependent on it. Alternatively, 'bhūta' means a being, or one named 'bhūta.' Indeed, in the neuter sense, every being is called thus, as are yakkhas and the like. In such passages as, 'Time devours beings, all of them, along with their self. Whatever beings are gathered here... having driven out the beings, departed from that place,' the neuter usage should be understood. If it is asked whether this is a gender alteration for the sake of metrical ease, it is not so. For it should be understood from the fact that the word 'bhūta' is also seen in the neuter gender in prose compositions, such as: 'That which great beings, such as yakkhas, seize, no place for it is found inside or outside of them.' 'Mahābhūta' refers to the fourfold great primary material form as described. Its quality of being 'great' should be understood for reasons such as its vast manifestation. How so? 'Mahābhūta' means 'great bhūta'; it is also 'mahābhūta' because it is connected with the great being designated as a magician; it is also 'mahābhūta' because it is connected with great beings such as yakkhas; it is also 'mahābhūta' because it is a being that subsists on great requisites such as food and clothing; it is also 'mahābhūta' because it is a being of great transformation. Thus, its quality of being 'great' should be understood for reasons such as its vast manifestation. Herein, this should be well noted:

Punnapuṃsakaliṅgo [M 0.0115] ca, bhūtasaddo pavattati;

Paṇṇattiyaṃ guṇe ceva, guṇeyevitthiliṅgako.

The word 'bhūta' occurs in the masculine and neuter genders; in designation, in quality, and in that which possesses quality, it is feminine.

Bhūta sambhūtasaddādi-naye paṇṇattivācakā;

Yojetabbā tiliṅge te, iti ñe yyaṃ visesato.

Words that denote a concept, in the manner of 'bhūta,' 'sambhūta,' and so forth, should be applied in the three genders; this should be known in particular.

“Bhūto tiṭṭhati, bhūtāni, tiṭṭhanti, samaṇo ayaṃ;

Idāni bhūto, cittāni, bhūtāni vimalāni tu.

‘A being stands,’ ‘beings stand,’ ‘this ascetic has now become,’ ‘thoughts, indeed, have become pure.’

Vañjhā bhūtā vadhū esā”, iccudāharaṇānime;

Vuttāni suṭṭhu lakkheyya, sāsanatthagavesako.

‘This young woman has become barren’—these are the examples stated. A seeker of the meaning of the Dispensation should note them well.

Bhavittanti vaḍḍhitaṭṭhānaṃ. Tañhi bhavanti vaḍḍhanti etthāti bhavittanti vuccati, “janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ me, iti paṅke avassayi”nti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ.

‘Bhavittaṃ’ means a place of growth. For it is called ‘bhavittaṃ’ because beings come into existence and grow there. The statement, ‘My birthplace, my place of growth, thus he sank into the mire,’ is a saying that proves this meaning.

“Bhavittaṃ” iti “bhāvitta”-nti ca pāṭho dvidhā mayā;

Rassattadīghabhāvena, diṭṭho bhaggavajātake.

The two readings, ‘bhavittaṃ’ and ‘bhāvittaṃ,’ due to the shortness and length of the vowel, have been seen by me in the Bhaggava Jātaka.

Bhūnanti bhavanaṃ bhūnaṃ vaddhi. “Ahameva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassā”ti, “bhūnahaccaṃ kataṃ mayā”ti ca idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ.

‘Bhūnaṃ’ means existence; ‘bhūnaṃ’ means growth. The statements, ‘I, a corrupted woman, have destroyed the embryo of the king of great majesty,’ and ‘The killing of an embryo has been committed by me,’ are sayings that prove this meaning.

Bhavananti bhavanakriyā. Atha vā bhavanti vaḍḍhanti ettha sattā puttadhītāhi nānāsampattīhi cāti bhavanaṃ vuccati geho, “pettikaṃ bhavanaṃ mamā”ti idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. “Geho gharañca āvāso, bhavanañca niketana”nti idaṃ pariyāyavacanaṃ. Parābhavananti avaddhimāpajjanaṃ. Sambhavananti suṭṭhu bhavanaṃ. Vibhavananti ucchedo vināso vā. Pātubhavananti pākaṭatā sarūpalābho iccevattho. Āvibhavananti paccakkhabhāvo. Tirobhavananti paṭicchannabhāvo. Vinābhavananti vinābhāvo. Sotthibhavananti suvatthitā. Paribhavananti pīḷanā hīḷanā vā. Abhibhavananti vidhamanaṃ. Adhibhavananti ajjhottharaṇaṃ[M 0.0116]. Anubhavananti paribhuñjanaṃ. Samanubhavananti suṭṭhu paribhuñjanaṃ. Paccanubhavananti adhipatibhāvenapi suṭṭhu paribhuñjanaṃ. Niggahītantanapuṃsakaliṅganiddeso.

‘Bhavana’ means the act of becoming. Alternatively, because beings exist and grow here with sons, daughters, and various kinds of prosperity, ‘bhavana’ is called a house. The statement, ‘My paternal house,’ is a saying that proves this meaning. The terms ‘geha,’ ‘ghara,’ ‘āvāsa,’ ‘bhavana,’ and ‘niketana’ are synonyms. ‘Parābhavana’ means reaching a state of decline. ‘Sabhavana’ means coming to be well. ‘Vibhavana’ means annihilation or destruction. ‘Pātubhavana’ means manifestation, the attainment of one's own form; this is the meaning. ‘Āvibhavana’ means the state of being manifest. ‘Tirobhavana’ means the state of being concealed. ‘Vinābhavana’ means separation. ‘Sotthibhavana’ means well-being. ‘Paribhavana’ means oppression or contempt. ‘Abhibhava’ means vanquishing. ‘Adhibhava’ means overpowering. ‘Anubhavana’ means experiencing. ‘Samanubhavana’ means experiencing well. ‘Paccanubhavana’ means experiencing well even by way of mastery. The explanation of neuter gender words ending in niggahīta is finished.

Atthavibhāvīti atthassa vibhāvanasīlaṃ cittaṃ vā ñāṇaṃ vā kulaṃ vā atthavibhāvi. Evaṃ dhammavibhāvi. Ikārantanapuṃsakaliṅganiddeso.

‘Atthavibhāvī’ means a mind, knowledge, or family that has the nature of clarifying the meaning. Similarly, ‘dhammavibhāvī.’ This is the explanation of neuter gender words ending in ‘i’.

Gotrabhūti paññattārammaṇaṃ mahaggatārammaṇaṃ vā gotrabhucittaṃ. Tañhi kāmāvacaragottamabhibhavati, mahaggatagottañca bhāveti nibbattetīti “gotrabhū”ti vuccati. Apica gotrabhūti nibbānārammaṇaṃ maggavīthiyaṃ pavattaṃ gotrabhuñāṇaṃ vā saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ vā phalasamāpattivīthiyaṃ pavattaṃ gotrabhuñāṇaṃ. Tesu hi paṭhamaṃ puthujjanagottamabhibhavati, ariyagottañca bhāveti, gottābhidhānā ca nibbānato ārammaṇakaraṇavasena bhavatīti “gotrabhū”ti vuccati, dutiyaṃ pana saṅkhārārammaṇampi samānaṃ āsevanapaccayabhāvena sasampayuttāni phalacittāni gottābhidhāne nibbānamhi bhāvetīti “gotrabhū”ti vuccati. Idaṃ pāḷivavatthānaṃ –

‘Gotrabhū’ refers to the change-of-lineage consciousness (gotrabhucitta) which has a concept or a sublime state as its object. For it overcomes the sense-sphere lineage and develops or produces the sublime lineage; thus, it is called ‘gotrabhū.’ Moreover, ‘gotrabhū’ refers to the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhuñāṇa) that occurs in the path process with Nibbāna as its object, or the change-of-lineage knowledge that occurs in the fruition attainment process with formations as its object. Among these, the first overcomes the worldling’s lineage and develops the noble lineage, and it is called ‘gotrabhū’ because it arises by way of taking as its object Nibbāna, which is designated as the lineage. The second, however, although having formations as its object, is called ‘gotrabhū’ because, by way of the repetition condition, it develops the associated fruition consciousnesses in Nibbāna, which is designated as the lineage. This is the determination in the Pāli:

“Gotrabhu”iti rassatta-vasena kathitaṃ padaṃ;

Napuṃsakanti viññeyyaṃ, ñāṇacittādipekkhakaṃ.

The word ‘gotrabhu,’ when spoken with a short vowel, should be understood as neuter, in reference to knowledge, consciousness, and so on.

“Gotrabhū”iti dīghatta-vasena kathitaṃ pana;

Pulliṅgamiti viññeyyaṃ, puggalādikapekkhakaṃ.

But the word ‘gotrabhū,’ when spoken with a long vowel, should be understood as masculine, in reference to a person and so on.

Dīghabhāvena vuttaṃ tu, napuṃsakanti no vade;

Binduvantī’tare bhedā, tayo iti hi bhāsitā.

But what is spoken with a long vowel, one should not call neuter. For the distinctions other than ‘binduvantī’ are said to be three.

Īkārantā ca ūdantā, rassattaṃ yanti sāsane;

Napuṃsakattaṃ patvāna, sahabhu sīghayāyiti.

Words ending in ‘ī’ and ‘ū’ in the Dispensation become short, having attained the neuter gender, like ‘sahabhu’ and ‘sīghayāyi’.

Cittena saha bhavatīti cittasahabhu, cittena saha na bhavatīti nacittasahabhu, rūpaṃ. Ukārantanapuṃsakaliṅganiddeso. Niyatanapuṃsakaliṅganiddesoyaṃ.

That which arises together with consciousness is ‘consciousness-concomitant’ (cittasahabhu); that which does not arise together with consciousness is ‘not-consciousness-concomitant’ (nacittasahabhu), which is material form. This is the explanation of neuter gender words ending in ‘u.’ This is the explanation of invariably neuter gender words.

Aniyataliṅgānaṃ [M 0.0117] niyatanapuṃsakaliṅgesu pakkhittānaṃ bhūtaparābhūtasaddādīnaṃ niddeso nayānusārena suviññeyyova. Iccevaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ yathārahaṃ nibbacanādivasena niddeso vibhāvito. Iccevaṃ sabbathāpi liṅgattayaniddeso samatto.

The explanation of words of variable gender, such as ‘bhūta’ and ‘parābhūta,’ when included among the invariably neuter gender words, is easily understood according to the method. Thus, the explanation of neuter gender words derived from the root ‘bhū’ has been clarified by way of what is appropriate here and so forth. Thus, in every way, the explanation of the three genders is completed.

Ulliṅganena vividhena nayena vuttaṃ,

Bhūdhātusaddamayaliṅgatikaṃ yadetaṃ;

Āliṅgiyaṃ piyatarañca sutaṃ suliṅgaṃ,

Poso kare manasi liṅgaviduttamicchaṃ.

This triad of genders, consisting of words from the root ‘bhū,’ which has been stated by various methods of indication, is worthy of being embraced, most dear, well-learned, and of good form. A person desiring expertise in gender should hold it in mind.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the paths of expression within the nine-limbed Dispensation with its commentaries and the three Piṭakas,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the treatise Saddanīti, composed for the purpose of acquiring skill,

Bhūdhātumayānaṃ tividhaliṅgikānaṃ nāmikarūpānaṃ vibhāgo

the analysis of the nominal forms of the three genders derived from the root ‘bhū’,

Catuttho paricchedo.

is the Fourth Chapter.

5. Okārantapulliṅganāmikapadamālā

5. Declension of Masculine Nouns Ending in -o

Bhū dhātuto pavattānaṃ, nāmikānamito paraṃ;

Nāmamālaṃ pakāsissaṃ, nāmamālantarampi ca.

Henceforth, I shall set forth the declension of nominals derived from the root ‘bhū,’ and other nominal declensions as well.

Vippakiṇṇakathā ettha, evaṃ vutte na hessati;

Pabhedo nāmamālānaṃ, paripuṇṇova hehiti.

When this is stated, there will be no miscellaneous discussion here; the classification of nominal declensions will indeed be complete.

Pubbācariyasīhānaṃ, tasmā idha mataṃ sutaṃ;

Purecaraṃ karitvāna, vakkhāmi savinicchayaṃ.

Therefore, having first set forth here what is thought and heard from the lion-like teachers of the past, I shall speak with decisiveness.

Puriso, purisā. Purisaṃ, purise. Purisena, purisehi, purisebhi. Purisassa, purisānaṃ. Purisā, purisasmā, purisamhā, purisehi, purisebhi. Purisassa, purisānaṃ. Purise, purisasmiṃ, purisamhi, purisesu. Bho purisa, bhavanto purisā.

Puriso, purisā (Nominative). Purisaṃ, purise (Accusative). Purisena, purisehi, purisebhi (Instrumental). Purisassa, purisānaṃ (Dative). Purisā, purisasmā, purisamhā, purisehi, purisebhi (Ablative). Purisassa, purisānaṃ (Genitive). Purise, purisasmiṃ, purisamhi, purisesu (Locative). Bho purisa, bhavanto purisā (Vocative).

Ayamāyasmatā mahākaccānena pabhinnapaṭisambhidena katasmā niruttipiṭakato uddharito purisaiccetassa pakatirūpassa [M 0.0118] nāmikapadamālānayo. Tatra purisavacanaekavacanaputhuvacanesu paccattavacanādīni bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? Puriso tiṭṭhati, purisā tiṭṭhanti. Tatra purisoti purisavacane ekavacane paccattavacanaṃ bhavati, purisāti purisavacane puthuvacane paccattavacanaṃ bhavati.

This is the method of nominal declension for the natural form of the word 'purisa' (man), extracted from the Nirutti Piṭaka composed by the venerable Mahākaccāna, who possessed the analytical knowledges. Herein, in the masculine gender, singular and plural forms, the nominative case and so on occur. How so? 'Puriso' stands, 'purisā' stand. Herein, 'puriso' is the nominative case in the masculine gender, singular number; 'purisā' is the nominative case in the masculine gender, plural number.

Purisaṃ passati, purise passati. Tatra purisanti purisavacane ekavacane upayogavacanaṃ bhavati, puriseti purisavacane puthuvacane upayogavacanaṃ bhavati.

He sees a man, he sees men. Herein, 'purisaṃ' is the accusative case in the masculine gender, singular number; 'purise' is the accusative case in the masculine gender, plural number.

Purisena kataṃ, purisehi kataṃ, purisebhi kataṃ. Tatra purisenāti purisavacane ekavacane karaṇavacanaṃ bhavati, purisehi, purisebhīti purisavacane puthuvacane karaṇavacanaṃ bhavati.

Done by a man, done by men, done by men. Herein, 'purisena' is the instrumental case in the masculine gender, singular number; 'purisehi' and 'purisebhi' are the instrumental case in the masculine gender, plural number.

Purisassa dīyate, purisānaṃ dīyate. Tatra purisassāti purisavacane ekavacane sampadānavacanaṃ bhavati, purisānanti purisavacane puthuvacane sampadānavacanaṃ bhavati.

To a man it is given, to men it is given. Herein, 'purisassa' is the dative case in the masculine gender, singular number; 'purisānaṃ' is the dative case in the masculine gender, plural number.

Purisā nissaṭaṃ, purisasmā nissaṭaṃ, purisamhā nissaṭaṃ, purisehi nissaṭaṃ, purisebhi nissaṭaṃ. Tatra purisāti purisavacane ekavacane nissakkavacanaṃ bhavati. Purisasmāti…pe… purisamhāti purisavacane ekavacane nissakkavacanaṃ bhavati, purisehi, purisebhīti purisavacane puthuvacane nissakkavacanaṃ bhavati.

Departed from a man, departed from a man, departed from a man, departed from men, departed from men. Herein, 'purisā' is the ablative case in the masculine gender, singular number. 'Purisasmā' and 'purisamhā' are also the ablative case in the masculine gender, singular number. 'Purisehi' and 'purisebhi' are the ablative case in the masculine gender, plural number.

Purisassa pariggaho, purisānaṃ pariggaho. Tatra purisassāti purisavacane ekavacane sāmivacanaṃ bhavati, purisānanti purisavacane puthuvacane sāmivacanaṃ bhavati.

A man's possession, men's possession. Herein, 'purisassa' is the genitive case in the masculine gender, singular number; 'purisānaṃ' is the genitive case in the masculine gender, plural number.

Purise patiṭṭhitaṃ, purisasmiṃ patiṭṭhitaṃ, purisamhi patiṭṭhitaṃ, purisesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Tatra puriseti purisavacane ekavacane bhummavacanaṃ bhavati, purisasminti…pe… purisamhīti…pe… purisesūti purisavacane puthuvacane bhummavacanaṃ bhavati.

Established on a man, established in a man, established in a man, established among men. Herein, 'purise' is the locative case in the masculine gender, singular number. 'Purisasmiṃ' and 'purisamhi' are also the locative case in the masculine gender, singular number. 'Purisesu' is the locative case in the masculine gender, plural number.

Bho [M 0.0119] purisa tiṭṭha, bhavanto purisā tiṭṭhatha. Tatra bho purisaiti purisavacane ekavacane ālapanaṃ bhavati, bhavanto purisāiti purisavacane puthuvacane ālapanaṃ bhavatīti iminā nayena sabbattha nayo vitthāretabbo.

O man, stand; Sirs, stand. Herein, 'bho purisa' is the vocative case in the masculine gender, singular number; 'bhavanto purisā' is the vocative case in the masculine gender, plural number. In this way, the method should be extended everywhere.

Yamakamahātherena katāya pana cūḷaniruttiyaṃ “bho purisa”iti rassavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ vatvā “bho purisā”iti dīghavasena ālapanabahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi tādiso nayo niruttipiṭake natthi, tathāpi bahūnamālapanavisaye “bho yakkhā”itiādīnaṃ ālapanabahuvacanānaṃ jātakaṭṭhakathādīsu dissanato pasatthatarova hoti viññūnaṃ pamāṇañca, tasmā iminā yamakamahātheramatenapi “puriso purisā purisa”ntiādīni vatvā āmantane “bho purisa, bho purisā, bhavanto purisā”ti nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

However, in the Cūḷanirutti composed by the Elder Yamaka, 'bho purisa' is stated as the vocative singular with a short vowel, and 'bho purisā' is stated as the vocative plural with a long vowel. Although such a method is not found in the Nirutti Piṭaka, nevertheless, since many vocative plurals like 'bho yakkhā' and so on are seen in the Jātakaṭṭhakathā and other texts, it is indeed more commendable and authoritative for the wise. Therefore, according to this opinion of the Elder Yamaka, after stating 'puriso, purisā, purisa,' and so on, in addressing, the nominal declension 'bho purisa, bho purisā, bhavanto purisā' should be applied.

Tattha purisoti paṭhamāya ekavacanaṃ. Purisāti bahuvacanaṃ. Purisanti dutiyāya ekavacanaṃ. Puriseti bahuvacanaṃ. Purisenāti tatiyāya ekavacanaṃ. Purisehi, purisebhīti dve bahuvacanāni. Purisassāti catutthiyā ekavacanaṃ. Purisānanti bahuvacanaṃ. Purisā, purisasmā, purisamhāti tīṇi pañcamiyā ekavacanāni. Purisehi, purisebhīti dve bahuvacanāni. Purisassāti chaṭṭhiyā ekavacanaṃ. Purisānanti bahuvacanaṃ. Purise, purisasmiṃ, purisamhīti tīṇi sattamiyā ekavacanāni. Purisesūti bahuvacanaṃ. Bho purisāti aṭṭhamiyā ekavacanaṃ. Bho purisā, bhavanto purisāti dve bahuvacanāni.

Herein, 'puriso' is the nominative singular. 'Purisā' is the nominative plural. 'Purisaṃ' is the accusative singular. 'Purise' is the accusative plural. 'Purisena' is the instrumental singular. 'Purisehi, purisebhī' are the two instrumental plurals. 'Purisassa' is the dative singular. 'Purisānaṃ' is the dative plural. 'Purisā, purisasmā, purisamhā' are the three ablative singulars. 'Purisehi, purisebhī' are the two ablative plurals. 'Purisassa' is the genitive singular. 'Purisānaṃ' is the genitive plural. 'Purise, purisasmiṃ, purisamhi' are the three locative singulars. 'Purisesu' is the locative plural. 'Bho purisa' is the vocative singular. 'Bho purisā, bhavanto purisā' are the two vocative plurals.

Kiñcāpetesu “purisā”ti idaṃ paṭhamāpañcamīaṭṭhamīnaṃ, “purise”ti idaṃ dutiyāsattamīnaṃ, “purisehi, purisebhī”ti tatiyāpañcamīnaṃ, “purisāna”nti catutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ ekasadisaṃ, tathāpi atthavasena asaṅkarabhāvo veditabbo. Kathaṃ? “Puriso [M 0.0120] tiṭṭhati, purisā tiṭṭhanti. Purisaṃ passati, purise passatī”tiādinā.

Moreover, among these, 'purisā' is identical for the nominative, ablative, and vocative; 'purise' for the accusative and locative; 'purisehi, purisebhī' for the instrumental and ablative; and 'purisānaṃ' for the dative and genitive. Nevertheless, non-confusion in meaning should be understood based on context. How? 'Puriso' stands, 'purisā' stand. He sees 'purisaṃ', he sees 'purise', and so on.

Tattha ca bhoti āmantanatthe nipāto. So na kevalaṃ ekavacanaṃyeva hoti, atha kho bahuvacanampi hotīti “bho purisā”iti bahuvacanappayogopi gahito. “Bhavanto”tidaṃ pana bahuvacanameva hotīti “purisā”ti puna vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iti yamakamahātherena “bho purisa”iti rassavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ vatvā “bho purisā”iti dīghavasena ālapanabahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu ca nipātabhūto bhosaddo ekavacanabahuvacanavasena dvidhā bhijjati. Atrimāni nidassanapadāni – “api nu kho sapariggahānaṃ tevijjānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ apariggahena brahmunā saddhiṃ saṃsandati sametīti, no hidaṃ bho gotama. Acchariyaṃ bho ānanda, abbhutaṃ bho ānanda, ehi bho samaṇa, bho pabbajita”iccādipāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca bhosaddassa ekavacanappayoge pavattinidassanaṃ, “tena hi bho mamapi suṇātha. Yathā mayameva arahāma taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamituṃ, nāhaṃ bho samaṇassa gotamassa subhāsitaṃ subhāsitato nābbhanumodāmi, passatha bho imaṃ kulaputtaṃ. Bho yakkhā ahaṃ imaṃ tumhākaṃ bhājetvā dadeyyaṃ. Aparisuddho panamhi, bho dhuttā tumhākaṃ kriyā mayhaṃ na ruccati. So te purise āha bho tumhe maṃ mārentā rañño dassetvāva mārethā”ti iccādi pana pāḷito aṭṭhakathāto ca bhosaddassa bahuvacanappayoge pavattinidassanaṃ. Kaccāyanappakaraṇe pana “bho purisa, bho purisā”ti padadvayaṃ ālapanekavacanavasena vuttaṃ. Taṃ yathā āgamehi na virujjhati, tathā gahetabbaṃ.

Herein, 'bho' is a particle used for addressing. It is not only singular but also plural, hence the plural usage 'bho purisā' is also accepted. However, 'bhavanto' is exclusively plural, so the repetition of 'purisā' should be understood accordingly. Thus, the Elder Yamaka first used the vocative singular 'bho purisa' with a short vowel and then the vocative plural 'bho purisā' with a long vowel. Indeed, in the Pāli texts and commentaries, the particle 'bho' is distinguished in two ways, according to singular and plural usage. Here are illustrative examples: From the Pāli texts and commentaries, instances of 'bho' used in the singular include: 'api nu kho sapariggahānaṃ tevijjānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ apariggahena brahmunā saddhiṃ saṃsandati sametīti, no hidaṃ bho gotama. Acchariyaṃ bho ānanda, abbhutaṃ bho ānanda, ehi bho samaṇa, bho pabbajita.' From the Pāli texts and commentaries, instances of 'bho' used in the plural include: 'tena hi bho mamapi suṇātha. Yathā mayameva arahāma taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ dassanāya upasaṅkamituṃ, nāhaṃ bho samaṇassa gotamassa subhāsitaṃ subhāsitato nābbhanumodāmi, passatha bho imaṃ kulaputtaṃ. Bho yakkhā ahaṃ imaṃ tumhākaṃ bhājetvā dadeyyaṃ. Aparisuddho panamhi, bho dhuttā tumhākaṃ kriyā mayhaṃ na ruccati. So te purise āha bho tumhe maṃ mārentā rañño dassetvāva mārethā.' In the Kaccāyana grammar, however, the two phrases 'bho purisa' and 'bho purisā' are stated as vocative singular. This should be understood in such a way that it does not contradict the canonical texts.

Keci [M 0.0121] pana adūraṭṭhassālapane “bho purisa”iti rassavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ icchanti, dūraṭṭhassālapane pana “bho purisā”iti dīghavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ icchanti. Adūraṭṭhānaṃ dūraṭṭhānañca purisānaṃ itthīnañca ālapane na kiñci vadanti. Tathā adūraṭṭhāya dūraṭṭhāya ca itthiyā ālapane te pucchitabbā “adūraṭṭhānaṃ dūraṭṭhānañca purisānamālapane kathaṃ vattabba”nti. Addhā te evaṃ puṭṭhā uttari kiñci vattuṃ na sakkhissanti. Evampi te ce vadeyyuṃ “bhavanto purisāti imināva adūraṭṭhānaṃ dūraṭṭhānañca purisānamālapanaṃ bhavatī”ti. Tadā te vattabbā “yadi bhavanto purisā”ti iminā advejjhena vacanena adūraṭṭhānaṃ dūraṭṭhānañca purisānamālapanaṃ bhavati, evaṃ sante “bho purisa”iti rassapadenapi dūraṭṭhassa ca purisassālapanaṃ vattabbaṃ, evaṃ avatvā kimatthaṃ adūraṭṭhassālapane “bho purisa”iti rassavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ icchatha, kimatthañca dūraṭṭhassālapane “bho purisā”iti dīghavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ icchatha.

Some, however, wish for the vocative singular 'bho purisa' with a short vowel when addressing someone near, but for addressing someone at a distance, they wish for the vocative singular 'bho purisā' with a long vowel. They say nothing about addressing men and women, whether near or far. Then, they should be asked concerning the addressing of a woman who is near or far: 'How should one address men who are near and far?' Surely, when questioned thus, they will be unable to say anything further. Even if they were to say, 'By 'bhavanto purisā' one can address men who are near and far,' then they should be told: 'If by the unambiguous phrase 'bhavanto purisā,' both men who are near and men who are far can be addressed, this being so, it should be stated that a distant man can also be addressed with the short-vowel word 'bho purisa'. Not stating this, for what reason do you wish for the vocative singular 'bho purisa' with a short vowel for someone near, and for what reason do you wish for the vocative singular 'bho purisā' with a long vowel for someone at a distance?'

Nanu “taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā, taggha sugata bojjhaṅgā”tiādīsu ālapanapadabhūtaṃ “bhagavā”iti dīghapadaṃ samīpe ṭhitakālepi dūre ṭhitakālepi buddhassālapanapadaṃ bhavitumarahateva, tathā ālapanapadabhūtaṃ “sugata”iti rassapadampi. Yasmā panetesu “bhagavā”ti ālapanapadassa na katthacipi rassattaṃ dissati, “sugatā”ti ālapanapadassa ca na katthacipi dīghattaṃ dissati, tasmā dīgharassamattābhedaṃ acintetvā “purisa”iti rassavasena vuttapadaṃ pakatissaravasena samīpe ṭhitassa purisassa āmantanakāle adūraṭṭhassālapanapadaṃ bhavati, āyatassaravasena dūre ṭhitapurisassa āmantanakāle dūraṭṭhassālapanapadaṃ bhavatīti gahetabbaṃ. Tathā “bhavanto purisā, bho yakkhā, bho dhuttā”tiādīni [M 0.0122] dīghavasena vuttāni ālapanabahuvacanapadānipi pakatissaravasena samīpe ṭhitapurisānaṃ āmantanakāle adūraṭṭhānamālapanapadāni bhavanti, āyatassaravasena dūre ṭhitapurisādīnaṃ āmantanakāle dūraṭṭhānamālapanapadāni bhavantīti gahetabbāni. Tathā hi brāhmaṇā katthaci katthaci rassaṭṭhānepi dīghaṭṭhānepi āyatena sarena majjhimāyatena sarena accāyatena ca sarena vedaṃ paṭhanti likhitumasakkuṇeyyena gītassarena viya. Iti sabbakkharesupi āyatena sarenuccāraṇaṃ labbhateva likhitumasakkuṇeyyaṃ, tasmā asampathamanotaritvā “bho purisa”iti vacanena dūraṭṭhassa ca adūraṭṭhassa ca purisassālapanaṃ bhavati, “bho purisā, bhavanto purisā”ti imehi vacanehipi dūraṭṭhānañca adūraṭṭhānañca purisānamālapanaṃ bhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iti dūraṭṭhassa adūraṭṭhānañca āyatena sarena āmantanameva pamāṇaṃ, na dīgharassamattāviseso, tasmā “bho sattha, bho rāja, bho gaccha, bho muni, bho daṇḍi, bho bhikkhu, bho sayambhu, bhoti kaññe, bhoti patti, bhoti itthi, bhoti yāgu, bhoti vadhu, bho kula, bho aṭṭhi, bho cakkhu”iccevamādīhi padehi adūraṭṭhassālapanañca dūraṭṭhassālapanañca bhavati. “Bhavanto satthā, satthāro, bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo”ti evamādīhipi padehi adūraṭṭhānañcālapanaṃ bhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Indeed, in phrases like 'taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā, taggha sugata bojjhaṅgā,' the vocative word 'bhagavā' is long; whether the Buddha is standing near or far, it is fitting that it remains a vocative. Similarly, the vocative word 'sugata' is short. However, in these instances, the vocative 'bhagavā' is nowhere seen as short, nor is the vocative 'sugata' ever seen as long. Therefore, without considering the distinction between long and short quantity, it should be understood that the word 'purisa,' spoken with a short vowel, when used to address a man standing nearby with its natural intonation, becomes a vocative for one who is not far. When addressing a man standing far away, it is spoken with a lengthened tone, and it becomes a vocative for one who is far. Similarly, vocative plural words like 'bhavanto purisā, bho yakkhā, bho dhuttā,' spoken with long vowels, when addressing men standing nearby with their natural intonation, become vocatives for those who are not far, but when addressing men and others standing far away with a lengthened tone, they become vocatives for those who are far. For instance, Brahmins sometimes recite the Vedas with elongated, medium-elongated, and highly-elongated sounds, in places where the sounds are short and in places where the sounds are long, like a sung tone that cannot be written down. Thus, the utterance of all syllables with a lengthened sound is always possible, even though it cannot be written down. Therefore, without entering a wrong path, it should be understood that with the expression 'bho purisa,' there is addressing of a man who is far and a man who is not far; with these expressions, 'bho purisā, bhavanto purisā,' there is addressing of men who are far and men who are not far. Thus, with respect to those who are far and those who are not far, addressing with a lengthened tone is the criterion, not the distinction of long and short quantity. Therefore, phrases like 'bho sattha, bho rāja, bho gaccha, bho muni, bho daṇḍi, bho bhikkhu, bho sayambhu, bhoti kaññe, bhoti patti, bhoti itthi, bhoti yāgu, bhoti vadhu, bho kula, bho aṭṭhi, bho cakkhu' can serve as vocatives for those who are not far and for those who are far. Similarly, it should be understood that phrases like 'bhavanto satthā, satthāro, bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo' can also function as vocatives for those who are not far.

Idaṃ panettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ –

This is the conclusion here.

Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, rañño puttaṃ adassayuṃ;

Putto ca pitaraṃ disvā, dūratovajjhabhāsatha.

Having heard his words, they showed him the king's son; and the son, seeing his father, addressed him from afar.

Āgacchu dovārikā khaggabandhā,

Kāsāviyā hantu mamaṃ janinda;

Akkhāhi me pucchito etamatthaṃ,

Aparādho ko nvidha mamajja atthi.

Let the gatekeepers with girded swords come, clad in yellow robes, to slay me, O lord of men! Tell me, I who ask, this matter: What fault of mine is here today?

Evaṃ [M 0.0123] saddhammarājena, vohārakusalena ve;

Sudesite somanassa-jātake sabbadassinā.

Thus, by the king of the true Dhamma, skilled in discourse, the All-Seeing One, in the well-expounded Somanassa Jātaka.

Dūraṭṭhānepi rassattaṃ, “janinda”iti dissati;

Na katthacipi dīghattaṃ, iti nīti mayā matā.

Even when addressing one who is far, shortness is seen in 'janinda'; nowhere is length seen. Thus, this principle is held by me.

Idampettha vattabbaṃ “kuto nu bho idamāyātaṃ ‘dūraṭṭhassālapanaṃ adūraṭṭhassālapanami’ti”? Saddasatthato. Saddasatthaṃ nāma na sabbaso buddhavacanassopakārakaṃ, ekadesena pana hoti.

This should also be stated here: 'From where, indeed, friend, has this come—"the vocative for one who is far and the vocative for one who is not far"?' From grammar. Grammar is not entirely helpful for the Buddha's word, but it is so in part.

Imasmiṃ pakaraṇe “bahuvacana”nti vā “puthuvacana”nti vā “anekavacana”nti vā atthato ekaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ, tasmā sabbattha “bahuvacana”nti vā “puthuvacana”nti vā “anekavacana”nti vā vohāro kātabbo, puthuvacanaṃ anekavacananti ca idaṃ sāsane niruttaññūnaṃ vohāro, itaraṃ saddasatthavidūnaṃ.

In this treatise, 'plural' or 'multiple' or 'many-fold' are one in meaning; only the expression differs. Therefore, in all cases, the terms 'plural,' 'multiple,' or 'many-fold' should be used. The usage of 'multiple' and 'many-fold' is common among those skilled in the language of the Teaching, while the other is used by those versed in grammar.

Kasmā pana imasmiṃ pakaraṇe dvivacanaṃ na vuttanti? Yasmā buddhavacane dvivacanaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā na vuttanti. Nanu buddhavacane vacanattayaṃ atthi, tathā hi “āyasmā”ti idaṃ ekavacanaṃ, “āyasmantā”ti idaṃ dvivacanaṃ, “āyasmanto”ti idaṃ bahuvacananti? Tanna, yadi “āyasmantā”ti idaṃ vacanaṃ dvivacanaṃ bhaveyya, “puriso purisā”tiādīsu kataraṃ dvivacananti vadeyyātha, tasmā buddhavacane dvivacanaṃ nāma natthi. Teneva hi si yo aṃ yo nā hītiādinā ekavacanabahuvacanāneva dassitānīti.

Why then is the dual number not mentioned in this treatise? Because in the Buddha's word, there is no such thing as a dual number; therefore it is not mentioned. But is there not a threefold number in the Buddha's word? For example, 'āyasmā' is singular, 'āyasmantā' is dual, and 'āyasmanto' is plural? That is not so. If 'āyasmantā' were a dual number, then in cases like 'puriso, purisā,' which would you call the dual? Therefore, in the Buddha's word, there is no such thing as a dual number. For that very reason, only the singular and plural numbers are shown by 'si, yo, aṃ, yo, nā, hi,' and so on.

Nanu ca bho “suṇantu me āyasmantā, ajja uposatho pannaraso. Yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kareyyāmā”ti pāḷiyaṃ dve sandhāya “āyasmantā”ti vuttaṃ, “uddiṭṭhā kho āyasmanto cattāro pārājikā dhammā”tiādīsu pana pāḷīsu bahavo sandhāya “āyasmanto”ti vuttaṃ, na ca sakkā vattuṃ “yathā tathā vutta”nti[M 0.0124], parivāsādiārocanepi aṭṭhakathācariyehi viññātasugatādhippāyehi “dvinnaṃ ārocentena ‘āyasmantā dhārentū’ti, tiṇṇaṃ ārocentena ‘āyasmanto dhārentū’ti vattabba”nti vuttattāti? Saccaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ pana vinayavohāravasena vuttanti. Nanu vinayo buddhavacanaṃ, kasmā “buddhavacane dvivacanaṃ nāma natthī”ti vadathāti? Saccaṃ vinayo buddhavacanaṃ, tathāpi vinayakammavasena vuttattā upalakkhaṇamattaṃ, na sabbasādhāraṇabahuvacanapariyāpannaṃ. Yadi hi “āyasmantā”ti idaṃ dvivacanaṃ siyā, tappayogānipi kriyāpadāni dvivacanāneva siyuṃ, tathārūpānipi kriyāpadāni na santi. Na hi akkharasamayakovido jhānalābhīpi dibbacakkhunā vassasatampi vassasahassampi samavekkhanto buddhavacane ekampi kriyāpadaṃ dvivacananti passeyya, evaṃ kriyāpadesu dvivacanassābhāvā nāmikapadesu dvivacanaṃ natthi. Nāmikapadesu tadabhāvāpi kriyāpadesu tadabhāvo veditabbo. Sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ dvīsupi dvivacanāni santi, māgadhabhāsāyaṃ pana natthi.

But, sir, in the Pāli text, 'suṇantu me āyasmantā, ajja uposatho pannaraso. Yadāyasmantānaṃ pattakallaṃ, mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ kareyyāmā'—there, 'āyasmantā' is used referring to two. But in passages like 'uddiṭṭhā kho āyasmanto cattāro pārājikā dhammā,' 'āyasmanto' is used referring to many, and it cannot be said that it is used arbitrarily. Even in the case of announcing parivāsa, etc., the commentary masters, understanding the Sugata's intention, have stated: 'When announcing to two, one should say, "āyasmantā dhārentū"; when announcing to three, one should say, "āyasmanto dhārentū."' That is truly stated, but it is said in accordance with Vinaya usage. But is not the Vinaya the word of the Buddha? Why do you say, 'In the Buddha’s words, the dual number does not exist'? It is true that the Vinaya is the word of the Buddha, yet because it is spoken in connection with Vinaya procedures, it is merely a designation and not included under the general plural. If 'āyasmantā' were a dual form, then the corresponding verbal forms would also be dual; however, such verbal forms do not exist. Not even an expert in grammatical convention, who has attained jhāna and possesses the divine eye, examining for a hundred or a thousand years, would find a single verbal form in the Buddha’s words that is dual. Thus, since the dual number does not exist in verbal forms, the dual number does not exist in nominal forms. From its absence in nominal forms, its absence in verbal forms should also be understood. In the Sanskrit language, dual forms exist in both, but in the Māgadhī language, they do not.

Apica “puthuvacana”nti niruttivohāropi “buddhavacane dvivacanaṃ natthī”ti etamatthaṃ dīpeti. Tañhi sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ vuttā dvivacanato bahuvacanato ca visuṃbhūtaṃ vacanaṃ, tattha vā vuttehi atthehi visuṃbhūtassa atthassa vacanaṃ “puthuvacana”nti vuccati. Kathamidaṃ sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ vuttā dvivacanato bahuvacanato ca visuṃbhūtaṃ vacananti ce? Yasmā sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ “puthuvacana”nti vohāro natthi, tasmā idaṃ tehi sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ vuttehi dvivacanabahuvacanehi visuṃbhūtaatthassa vacananti vuccati. Kathañca pana sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ vuttehi visuṃbhūtassa atthassa vacananti puthuvacananti ce? Yasmā sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ dve upādāya dvivacanaṃ vuttaṃ, na ticatupañcādike [M 0.0125] bahavo upādāya, bahavo pana upādāya bahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ, na dve upādāya, ayaṃ sakkaṭabhāsāya viseso. Māgadhabhāsāyaṃ pana dviticatupañcādike bahavo upādāya puthuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ vuttehi atthehi visuṃbhūtassa atthassa vacananti puthuvacananti vuccati. Ayaṃ māgadhabhāsāya viseso. Tasmātra puthubhūtassa, puthuno vā atthassa vacanaṃ “puthuvacana”nti attho samadhigantabbo.

Moreover, the linguistic term 'puthuvacana' also illuminates this meaning: 'in the Buddha's words, there is no dual number.' For this is a term distinct from the dual and plural spoken of in the Sanskrit language; or, it is called 'puthuvacana' because it is a term for a meaning distinct from the meanings expressed there. If it is asked how this is a term distinct from the dual and plural spoken of in the Sanskrit language: because in the Sanskrit language the term 'puthuvacana' does not exist, it is therefore said to be a term for a meaning distinct from the dual and plural spoken of in that Sanskrit language.
