And if it is asked how 'puthuvacana' is a term for a meaning distinct from those expressed in the Sanskrit language: because in the Sanskrit language the dual is used with reference to two, not with reference to many such as three, four, five, etc., whereas the plural is used with reference to many, not with reference to two—this is a special feature of the Sanskrit language. In the Māgadhī language, however, 'puthuvacana' is used with reference to many, such as two, three, four, five, etc. Therefore, it is called 'puthuvacana' because it is a term for a meaning distinct from the meanings expressed in the Sanskrit language. This is a special feature of the Māgadhī language. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: 'puthuvacana' is a term for a meaning that is manifold or diverse.

Idāni “puriso, purisā, purisa”nti niruttipiṭakato uddharitanayaṃ nissāya pakatirūpabhūtassa bhūtasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, relying on the method extracted from the Niruttipiṭaka concerning 'puriso, purisā, purisa,' the paradigm of nominal forms for the word 'bhūta,' which is the base form, is stated:

Bhūto, bhūtā. Bhūtaṃ, bhūte. Bhūtena, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūtā, bhūtasmā, bhūtamhā, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūte, bhūtasmiṃ, bhūtamhi, bhūtesu. Bho bhūta, bhavanto bhūtā.

A being, beings. A being, beings. By a being, by beings, by beings. For a being, of beings. From a being, from a being, from a being, from beings, from beings. Of a being, of beings. In a being, in a being, in a being, in beings. O being, O beings.

Atha vā “bho bhūtā”iti bahuvacanaṃ viññeyyaṃ. Yathā panettha bhūtaiccetassa pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā purisanayena yojitā, evaṃ bhāvakādīnañca aññesañca taṃsadisānaṃ nāmikapadamālā purisanayena yojetabbā. Etthaññāni taṃsadisāni nāma “buddho”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ buddhaiccādīni pakatirūpāni.

Alternatively, 'bho bhūtā' should be understood as the plural. Just as the nominal paradigm of the base form 'bhūta' is applied here according to the model of 'purisa,' so too the nominal paradigms of 'bhāvaka' and other similar words should be applied according to the model of 'purisa.' Here, other similar words are the base forms, such as 'buddha' and so on, of words such as 'buddho.'

Buddho dhammo saṅgho maggo,

Khandho kāyo kāmo kappo;

Māso pakkho yakkho bhakkho,

Nāgo megho bhogo yāgo.

The Buddha, the Dhamma, the Sangha, the path; The aggregates, the body, desire, the eon; The month, the fortnight, the yakkha, the food; The nāga, the cloud, possessions, the offering.

Rāgo doso moho māno,

Makkho thambho kodho lobho;

Hāso vero dāho tejo,

Chando kāso sāso rogo.

Lust, hatred, delusion, conceit; Contempt, obstinacy, anger, greed; Laughter, enmity, burning, splendor; Desire, cough, panting, disease.

Asso [M 0.0126] sasso isso sisso,

Sīho byaggho rukkho selo;

Indo sakko devo gāmo,

Cando sūro ogho dīpo.

A horse, a crop, a lord, a pupil; A lion, a tiger, a tree, a rock; Indra, Sakka, a god, a village; The moon, the sun, a flood, an island.

Passo yañño cāgo vādo,

Hattho patto soso gedho;

Somo yodho gaccho accho,

Geho māḷo aṭṭo sālo.

The side, the sacrifice, renunciation, speech; The hand, the bowl, dryness, greed; The moon, the warrior, the plant, the bear; The house, the pavilion, the watchtower, the sāl tree.

Naro nago migo saso,

Suṇo bako ajo dijo;

Hayo gajo kharo saro,

Dumo talo paṭo dhajo.

The man, the serpent, the deer, the hare; The dog, the heron, the goat, the bird; The horse, the elephant, the donkey, the arrow; The tree, the palm, the cloth, the flag.

Urago paṭago vihago bhujago,

Kharabho sarabho pasado gavajo;

Mahiso vasabho asuro garuḷo,

Taruṇo varuṇo baliso paligho.

The serpent, the winged one, the bird, the snake; The camel, the sarabha deer, the spotted deer, the wild ox; The buffalo, the bull, the asura, the garuḍa; The youth, Varuṇa, the fishhook, the crossbar.

Sālo dhavo ca khadiro,

Godhumo saṭṭhiko yavo;

Kaḷāyo ca kulattho ca,

Tilo muggo ca taṇḍulo.

The sāl tree, the dhava tree, and the khadira tree; Wheat, sixty-day rice, and barley; The chickpea, and the horse gram; Sesame, mung bean, and husked rice.

Khattiyo brāhmaṇo vesso,

Suddo dhutto ca pukkuso;

Caṇḍālo patiko paṭṭho,

Manusso rathiko ratho.

The warrior, the brahmin, the merchant; The śūdra, the rogue, and the pukkusa; The caṇḍāla, the patika, the paṭṭha; The human, the charioteer, the chariot.

Pabbajito [M 0.0127] gahaṭṭho ca,

Goṇo oṭṭho ca gadrabho;

Mātugāmo ca orodho,

Iccādīni vibhāvaye.

The one who has gone forth and the householder; The ox, the camel, and the donkey; A woman and the women's quarters— These and others should be considered.

Kecettha vadeyyuṃ “nanu bho ‘orodhā ca kumārā cā’ti pāṭhassa dassanato orodhasaddo itthiliṅgo”ti? Tanna, tattha hi “orodhā”ti idaṃ okārantapulliṅgameva, nā’kārantitthiliṅgaṃ, tumhe pana “ākārantitthiliṅga”nti maññamānā evaṃ vadatha, na panidaṃ ākārantitthiliṅgaṃ, atha kho “mātugāmā”tipadaṃ viya bahuvacanavasena vuttamākārantapadanti. Nanu ca bho sammohavinodaniyādīsu orodhasaddassa itthiliṅgatā pākaṭā, kathanti ce? “Rukkhe adhivatthā devatā therassa kuddhā paṭhamameva manaṃ palobhetvā ‘ito te sattadivasamatthake upaṭṭhāko rājā marissatī’ti supine ārocesi. Thero taṃ kathaṃ sutvā rājorodhānaṃ ācikkhi. Tā ekappahāreneva mahāviravaṃ viraviṃsū”ti. Ettha hi “rājorodhāna”nti vatvā “tā”ti vuttattāva orodhasaddassa itthiliṅgatā pākaṭāti? Tanna, atthassa duggahaṇato. Duggahito hi ettha tumhehi attho, ettha pana orodhasaddena itthipadatthassa kathanato itthipadatthaṃ sandhāya “tā”ti vuttattā “tā itthiyo”ti ayamevattho. Tumhe pana amātāpitarasaṃvaddhattā ācariyakule ca anivuṭṭhattā etaṃ sukhumatthamajānantā yaṃ vā taṃ vā mukhārūḷhaṃ vadatha.

Some might argue here: "But, sir, according to the reading 'orodhā ca kumārā ca,' is not the word 'orodha' feminine?" That is not so. For here, the word 'orodhā' is in fact a masculine noun with a nominative singular in -o, not a feminine noun with a nominative singular in -ā. You, however, speak thus because you mistakenly think it is a feminine noun ending in -ā. But this is not a feminine noun ending in -ā; rather, like the word 'mātugāmā,' it is a word ending in -ā by way of the plural. But, sir, in texts like the Sammohavinodanī, is not the feminine gender of the word 'orodha' made clear? How so? 'A deity dwelling in a tree, angered at the elder, first captivated his mind and then announced in a dream, “Seven days from now, the king who is your supporter will die.” Hearing this account, the elder informed the royal women's quarters. They all cried out with a great wail at once.' Here, since it says 'rājorodhānaṃ' and then refers to them as 'tā,' is not the feminine gender of the word 'orodha' made clear? That is not so; it is due to a misapprehension of the meaning. For the meaning here has been misapprehended by you. Here, since the word 'orodha' is used to express the meaning of 'women,' the pronoun 'tā' is used with reference to that meaning, so the meaning is precisely 'those women.' But you, not having been brought up by mother and father and not having lived in a teacher's family, do not understand this subtle meaning and say whatever comes to your lips.

Bhuñjanatthaṃ kathanatthaṃ, mukhaṃ hotīti no vade;

Yaṃ vā taṃ vā mukhārūḷhaṃ, vacanaṃ paṇḍito naroti.

One should not say: 'The mouth is for eating and speaking; whatever comes to the mouth is the speech of a wise person.'

Na mayaṃbho yaṃ vā taṃ vā mukhārūḷhaṃ vadāma, aṭṭhakathācariyānaññeva vacanaṃ gahetvā vadāma, aṭṭhakathāyeva amhākaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ[M 0.0128], na mayaṃ tumhākaṃ saddahāmāti. Amhākaṃ saddahatha vā mā vā, mā tumhe “aṭṭhakathācariyānaññeva vacanaṃ gahetvā vadāmā”ti aṭṭhakathācariye abbhācikkhatha. Na hi aṭṭhakathācariyehi “orodhasaddo itthiliṅgo”ti vuttaṭṭhānamatthi, tasmāpi aṭṭhakathācariye abbhācikkhatha, na yuttaṃ buddhādīnaṃ garūnamabbhācikkhanaṃ mahato anatthassa lābhāya saṃvattanato. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “attanā duggahitena amhe ceva abbhācikkhati, bahuñca apuññaṃ pasavati, tato attānañca khaṇatī”ti.

We do not, good sir, say just whatever comes to our lips. We speak only after taking the words of the commentary teachers. The commentary is our refuge; we do not believe you. Whether you believe us or not, do not misrepresent the commentary teachers by saying, 'We speak only after taking the words of the commentary teachers.' For there is no place where the commentary teachers have stated that the word 'orodha' is of feminine gender. Therefore, you are misrepresenting the commentary teachers, and it is not proper to misrepresent venerable ones like the Buddha, as it leads to the obtaining of great harm. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'By poorly grasping it oneself, one both misrepresents us and generates much demerit, and thereby uproots oneself.'

Evaṃ abbhācikkhanassa ayuttataṃ sāvajjatañca dassetvā punapi te idaṃ vattabbā – jātakaṭṭhakathāyampi tumhehi āhaṭaudāharaṇasadisaṃ udāharaṇamatthi, taṃ suṇātha. Kosiyajātakaṭṭhakathāyañhi “satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ mātugāmaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kirekassa saddhassa pasannassa upāsakabrāhmaṇassa brāhmaṇī dussīlā pāpadhammā”ti pāṭho dissati. Ettha hi “mātugāmaṃ ārabbha kathesī”ti vatvā “sā”ti vuttattā tumhākaṃ matena mātugāmasaddo itthiliṅgoyeva siyā, na pulliṅgo, kimidaṃ aṭṭhakathāvacanampi na passatha, tadeva pana aṭṭhakathāvacanaṃ passatha, kiṃ sā eva aṭṭhakathā tumhākaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ, na tadaññāti.

Having thus shown the inappropriateness and blameworthiness of misrepresentation, we should further say this to them: In the Jātaka commentary too, there is an example similar to the one you have brought forward; listen to it. In the Kosiyajātaka commentary, the passage is found: 'While the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, he spoke concerning a certain woman in Sāvatthī. She, it seems, was the wife of a devout lay-follower brahmin, but she was immoral and of evil character.' Here, having said, 'he spoke concerning a certain woman,' it then says, 'she.' According to your view, the word 'mātugāma' should be of feminine gender only, not masculine. What is this? Do you not see this statement from the commentary, yet you see that other one? Is that commentary alone your refuge, and not any other?

Yadi tāsaddaṃ apekkhitvā orodhasaddassa itthiliṅgattamicchatha, etthāpi sāsaddamapekkhitvā mātugāmasaddassa itthiliṅgattamicchathāti. Evaṃ vuttā te niruttarā appaṭibhānā maṅkubhūtā pattakkhandhā adhomukhā pajjhāyeyyuṃ. Etthāpi mātugāmasaddena itthipadatthassa kathanato itthipadatthaṃ sandhāya “sā”ti vuttattā “sā itthī”ti ayamevattho. Katthaci [M 0.0129] hi padhānavācakena pulliṅgena napuṃsakaliṅgena vā samānādhikaraṇassa guṇasaddassa abhidheyyaliṅgānuvattittāpulliṅgavasena vā napuṃsakaliṅgavasena vā niddisitabbattepi liṅgamanapekkhitvā itthipadatthamevāpekkhitvā itthiliṅganiddeso dissati. Taṃ yathā? “Idha visākhe mātugāmo susaṃvihitakammantā hoti saṅgahitaparijanā bhattumanāpaṃ carati, sambhataṃ anurakkhatī”ti ca, “ko nu kho bhante hetu ko paccayo, yena midhekacco mātugāmo dubbaṇṇā ca hoti durūpā supāpikā dassanāya, daliddā ca hoti appassakā appabhogā appesakkhā ca. Idha mallike ekacco mātugāmo kodhanā hoti upāyāsabahulā, appampi vuttā samānā abhisajjati kuppati byāpajjati patitthiyati kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātukarotī”ti ca, “taṃ kho pana bhikkhave itthiratanaṃ rañño cakkavattissa pubbuṭṭhāyinī pacchānipātinī kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī”ti ca ime payogā.

If you wish for the word 'orodha' to be feminine by considering the word 'tā', then here too you should wish for the word 'mātugāma' to be feminine by considering the word 'sā'. Thus addressed, they would be speechless, unable to reply, humbled, with shoulders drooping, heads down, brooding. Here too, since the term 'mātugāma' is used to denote the meaning of 'woman,' and because 'sā' is said with reference to the meaning of 'woman,' the meaning is simply: 'she is a woman.' For in some cases, even when a term denoting a quality is syntactically connected with a masculine or neuter noun as its subject and should be described in the masculine or neuter gender accordingly, the feminine gender is still indicated by disregarding the grammatical gender and focusing solely on the meaning of 'woman.' For example: 'Here, Visākhā, a woman is well-managed in her duties, attentive to her household, behaves agreeably to her husband, and preserves what has been gathered.' And: 'What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here a certain woman is ugly, ill-favored, of bad appearance, poor, with little wealth and few possessions, and of little influence? Here, Mallikā, a certain woman is angry, full of resentment; even when spoken to mildly, she takes offense, becomes irritated, hostile, and stubborn, displaying anger, hatred, and ingratitude.' And: 'Then, monks, that woman-jewel of the wheel-turning king rises before him, retires after him, and is responsive to what needs to be done.' These are the instances.

Katthaci pana padhānavācakena napuṃsakaliṅgena samānādhikaraṇassa guṇasaddassa abhidheyyaliṅgānuvattittā napuṃsakaliṅgavasena niddisitabbattepi liṅgamanapekkhitvā purisapadatthamevāpekkhitvā pulliṅganiddeso dissati. Taṃ yathā? “Pañca paccekabuddhasatāni imasmiṃ isigilismiṃ pabbate ciranivāsino ahesuṃ. Taṃ kho pana rañño cakkavattissa pariṇāyakaratanaṃ ñātānaṃ pavesetā aññātānaṃ nivāretā”ti. Katthaci padhānavācakena liṅgattayena samānādhikaraṇassa guṇasaddassa abhidheyyaliṅgānurūpaṃ niddeso dissati. Taṃ yathā? Sā itthī “sīlavatī kalyāṇadhammā. Aṭṭhahi kho nakulamāte dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā parammaraṇā manāpakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ [M 0.0130] sahabyataṃ upapajjati. Saddho purisapuggalo, saddhaṃ kulaṃ, cittaṃ dantaṃ sukhāvaha”nti.

In some cases, however, even though a quality-word in the same grammatical relation with a principal neuter word is to be indicated by the neuter gender due to conformity with its gender, the masculine gender is described by disregarding the grammatical gender and considering only the meaning of the word 'man'. For example: 'Five hundred Paccekabuddhas dwelt long on this Isigili mountain.' And: 'Moreover, the counselor-jewel of the wheel-turning king admitted the known and excluded the unknown.' In some cases, the description is given in conformity with the gender of the thing denoted for a quality-word in the same grammatical relation with a principal word in any of the three genders. For example: That woman is 'virtuous, endowed with good qualities.' 'A woman endowed with the eight qualities of Nakula’s mother, upon the breakup of the body after death, is reborn in the company of the delightful gods.' 'A faithful man, a faithful family, a tamed mind brings happiness.'

Seyyaiti saddo pana yebhuyyena okārantabhāve ṭhatvā liṅgattayānukūlo bhavati ekākāreneva tiṭṭhanato. Kathaṃ? Seyyo amitto matiyā upeto. Esāva pūjanā seyyo, ekāhaṃ jīvitaṃ seyyo.

The word 'seyya', however, generally standing with an -o ending, accords with all three genders because it remains in a single form. How so? 'Better is an enemy endowed with wisdom.' 'This very reverence is better.' 'A single day of life is better.'

“Dhammena ca alābho yo,

Yo ca lābho adhammiko;

Alābho dhammiko seyyo,

Yañce lābho adhammiko.

"The loss that is by the Dhamma, and the gain that is unrighteous; a righteous loss is better than the gain that is unrighteous."

Yaso ca appabuddhīnaṃ, viññūnaṃ ayaso ca yo;

Ayasova seyyo viññūnaṃ, na yaso appabuddhinaṃ.

Honor from the foolish and disgrace from the wise—disgrace from the wise is better than honor from the foolish.

Dummedhehi pasaṃsā ca, viññūhi garahā ca yā;

Garahāva seyyo viññūhi, yañce bālappasaṃsanā.

Praise from fools and blame from the wise—blame from the wise is better than the praise of fools.

Sukhañca kāmamayikaṃ, dukkhañca pavivekikaṃ;

Pavivekaṃ dukkhaṃ seyyo, yañce kāmamayaṃ sukhaṃ.

Sensual pleasure and the pain of seclusion—the pain of seclusion is better than the pleasure born of sensual desires.

Jīvitañca adhammena, dhammena maraṇañca yaṃ;

Maraṇaṃ dhammikaṃ seyyo, yañce jīve adhammika”nti.

Life by unrighteousness and death by righteousness—a righteous death is better than an unrighteous life.

Evamayaṃ seyya iti saddo okārantabhāve ṭhatvā liṅgattayānukūlo bhavati. Katthaci pana ākārantabhāve ṭhatvā itthiliṅgānukūlo dissati “itthīpi hi ekacciyā, seyyā posa janādhipā”ti. Niggahītanto pana hutvā napuṃsakaliṅgānukūlo apasiddho. Evaṃpakāre payoge kiṃ tumhe na passathāti. Evaṃ vuttā ca te niruttarāva bhavissanti.

Thus, this word 'seyya', standing as an 'o'-ending, agrees with all three genders. However, in some cases, it stands as an 'ā'-ending and appears agreeing with the feminine gender, as in the example: 'For a certain woman, O lord of people, is superior to a man.' But when it ends with a niggahīta, its agreement with the neuter gender is unestablished. Do you not see usages of this kind? And when this is said, they will remain without reply.

Sacepi [M 0.0131] te ettha evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “tattha tattha suttappadese aṭṭhakathādīsu ca ‘mātugāmo’ti vā ‘mātugāmenā’ti vā okārantapulliṅgabhāvena mātugāmasaddassa dassanato pulliṅgabhūtaṃ mātugāmasaddaṃ anapekkhitvā itthipadatthameva apekkhitvā “sā itthī”ti itthīsaddena sāsaddassa sambandhaggahaṇaṃ mayaṃ sampaṭicchāma, ‘orodho’ti vā ‘orodhenā’ti vā okārantapulliṅgabhāvena ṭhitassa orodhasaddassa adassanato pana tumhehi vuttaṃ purimatthaṃ na sampaṭicchāmā”ti. Tadā tesaṃ imāni vinayapāḷiyaṃ āgatapadāni dassetabbāni “tena kho pana samayena rājā udeno uyyāne paricāresi saddhiṃ orodhena, atha kho rañño udenassa orodho rājānaṃ udenaṃ etadavocā”ti. Evaṃ imāni suttapadāni dassetvā suttanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “rāmo nāma rājā kuṭṭharogī orodhehi ca nāṭakehi ca jigucchamāno”ti vacanañca dassetvā “gacchatha tumhe garukulamupagantvā bhagavato saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ sādhukaṃ padabyañjanāni uggaṇhathā”ti uyyojetabbā.

If they should say here thus: "In various places in the suttas and commentaries, the word 'mātugāmo' or 'mātugāmena' appears as a masculine-gender word ending in 'o.' Therefore, we accept the connection of the word 'sā' (she) with the word 'itthī' (woman), considering only the meaning of the word 'itthī' (woman) without regard to the masculine-gender form of the word 'mātugāma.' However, since the word 'orodho' or 'orodhena' is not seen to exist as a masculine-gender word ending in 'o,' we do not accept the previous argument you made." Then, these words found in the Vinaya Piṭaka should be shown to them: "At that time, King Udena was enjoying himself in the park together with his harem. Then King Udena's harem said this to King Udena." Having shown these sutta passages, the commentary on the Sutta Nipāta should also be cited: "A king named Rāma, afflicted with leprosy, was disgusted with his harem and actors." Then, they should be dismissed with the words: "Go, approach a qualified teacher and thoroughly learn the words and syllables of the Blessed One’s true Dhamma for its long-lasting benefit."

Idāni mātugāmasaddādīsu kiñci vinicchayaṃ vadāma – mātugāmasaddo ca orodhasaddo ca dārasaddo cāti ime itthipadatthavācakāpi samānā ekantena pulliṅgā bhavanti. Tesu dārasaddassa ekasmiṃ atthe vattamānassāpi bahuvacanakattameva saddasatthavidū icchanti, na ekavacanakattaṃ. Mayaṃ pana dārasaddassa ekasmiṃ atthe ekavacanakattaṃ, yebhuyyena pana bahuvacanakattaṃ anujānāma, bavhatthe vattabbameva natthi. Pāḷiyañhi dārasaddo yebhuyyena bahuvacanako bhavati, ekavacanako appo. Tatrime payogā –

Now we shall discuss some distinctions regarding words such as 'mātugāma'—the words 'mātugāma', 'orodha', and 'dāra', though signifying the meaning of 'woman', are invariably masculine in gender. Among these, even when the word 'dāra' has a singular meaning, grammarians prefer its plural form, not its singular form. We, however, permit the word 'dāra' to have a singular form when it has a singular meaning, but generally its plural form; and when it has a plural meaning, there is nothing to say. For in the Pāli canon, the word 'dāra' generally occurs in the plural, rarely in the singular. Here are the usages:

“Dāsā [M 0.0132] ca dāsyo anujīvino ca,

Puttā ca dārā ca mayañca sabbe;

Dhammañcarāmapparalokahetu,

Tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na miyyare”ti ca,

"Servants and female servants, dependents, sons and wives, and all of us—we practice the Dhamma for the sake of the next world, therefore our young ones do not die."

“Yo ñātīnaṃ sakhīnaṃ vā, dāresu paṭidissati;

Sahasā sampiyāyena, taṃ jaññāvasalo itī”ti ca,

"He who is seen among the wives of relatives or friends, associating intimately or forcibly—know him as an outcast."

“Sehi dārehi’santuṭṭho, vesiyāsu padissati;

Dissati paradāresu, taṃ parābhavato mukha”nti ca,

"Dissatisfied with his own wives, he is seen among courtesans; he is seen with the wives of others—that is a cause of downfall."

“Puttesu dāresu ca yā apekkhā”ti ca byāse, samāse pana “puttadārā disā pacchā, puttadārehi mattano”ti ca evamādayo bahuvacanappayogā bahavo bhavanti.

And 'the attachment that is to sons and wives' in the expanded form; but in the condensed form, such as 'sons and wives are the western direction,' and 'with regard to one's sons and wives,' and so on—such plural usages are numerous.

Ekavacanappayogā pana appā. Seyyathidaṃ? “Garūnaṃ dāre, dhammaṃ care yopi samuñjakaṃ care, dārañca posaṃ dadamappakasmi”nti ca,

Singular usages, however, are few. For example: 'Towards the wife of elders, one should behave righteously; even if one lives on gleanings, and gives support to a wife, even if little.'

“Ye gahaṭṭhā puññakarā, sīlavanto upāsakā;

Dhammena dāraṃ posenti, te namassāmi mātalī”ti ca,

"Those householders who are doers of merit, virtuous lay followers, who support their wife according to the Dhamma—them I salute, Mātali!"

“Paradāraṃ na gaccheyyaṃ, sadārapasuto siya”nti ca,

"One should not go to another's wife; one should be devoted to one's own."

“Yo icche puriso hotuṃ, jātiṃ jātiṃ punappunaṃ;

Paradāraṃ vivajjeyya, dhotapādova kaddama”nti ca

"If a man wishes to be born as a man again and again, he should avoid another's wife as one with washed feet avoids mud."

Evamādayo ekavacanappayogā appā.

Such singular usages are few.

Samāhāralakkhaṇavasena panesa dārasaddo napuṃsakaliṅgekavacanopi katthaci bhavati. “Ādāya puttadāraṃ. Puttadārassa saṅgaho”iti evaṃ idha vuttappakārena liṅgañca atthañca sallakkhetvā “puriso purisā”ti pavattaṃ purisasaddanayaṃ nissāya [M 0.0133] sabbesaṃ “bhūto bhāvako bhavo”tiādīnaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ aññesañcokārantapadānaṃ nāmikapadamālāsu saddhāsampannehi kulaputtehi saddhammaṭṭhitiyā kosallamuppādetabbaṃ.

However, by way of its characteristic of collective meaning, this word 'dāra' sometimes occurs in the neuter gender and singular number. For instance: 'Taking along children and wife,' 'the support of children and wife.' In this way, having considered the gender and meaning as explained here, and relying on the method of the word 'purisa', which proceeds as 'puriso' and 'purisā', skill should be developed by faithful sons of good families for the stability of the true Dhamma in the nominal paradigms of all other 'o'-ending words derived from the root 'bhū', such as 'bhūto', 'bhāvako', 'bhavo', and so on.

Kiṃ pana sabbāni okārantapadāni purisanaye sabbappakārena ekasadisāneva hutvā paviṭṭhānīti? Na paviṭṭhāni. Kānici hi okārantapadāni purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭhāni ca honti, ekadesena paviṭṭhāni ca, kānici okārantapadāni purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhāni ca honti, ekadesena na paviṭṭhāni ca, kānici okārantapadāni purisanaye sabbathā appaviṭṭhāneva. Tatra katamāni kānici okārantapadāni purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭhāni ca honti, ekadesena paviṭṭhāni ca? “Saro vayo ceto”tiādīni. Saroiti hi ayaṃsaddo ususaddasaravanaakārādisaravācako ce, purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭho. Rahadavācako ce, manogaṇapakkhikattā purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭho. Vayoiti saddo parihānivācako ce, purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭho. Āyukoṭṭhāsavācako ce, manogaṇapakkhikattā purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭho. Ceto iti saddo yadi paṇṇattivācako, purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭho. Yadi pana cittavācako, manogaṇapakkhikattā purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭho. Manogaṇo ca nāma –

But are all 'o'-ending words included in the purisa paradigm, being entirely uniform in every way? They are not included. For some 'o'-ending words are fully included in the purisa paradigm in all respects, and partially included; some 'o'-ending words are partially included in the purisa paradigm, and partially not included; and some 'o'-ending words are not included in the purisa paradigm at all. Among these, which are those 'o'-ending words that are fully included in the purisa paradigm in all respects, and partially included? Such as 'saro', 'vayo', 'ceto', and so on. For if this word 'saro' signifies sound—the sound of arrows, the sound of wind, the sound of the letter 'a', and so on—it is fully included in the purisa paradigm. But if it signifies a lake, being connected to the 'mano-group', it is partially included in the purisa paradigm. If the word 'vayo' signifies decline, it is fully included in the purisa paradigm. But if it signifies a division of age, being connected to the 'mano-group', it is partially included in the purisa paradigm. If the word 'ceto' signifies a concept, it is fully included in the purisa paradigm. But if it signifies the mind, being connected to the 'mano-group', it is partially included in the purisa paradigm. And what is the 'mano-group'?

Mano vaco vayo tejo,

Tapo ceto tamo yaso;

Ayo payo siro chando,

Saro uro raho aho –

Mind, speech, age, heat, Austerity, thought, darkness, fame; Iron, milk, head, will, Lake, chest, secret, day –

Ime soḷasa.

These are sixteen.

Idāni yathāvuttassa pākaṭīkaraṇatthaṃ manasaddādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālaṃ kathayāma –

Now, to clarify what has been stated, we will explain the nominal paradigm of the word 'mano' and so on.

Mano[M 0.0134], manā. Manaṃ, mano, mane. Manasā, manena, manehi, manebhi. Manaso, manassa, manānaṃ. Manā, manasmā, manamhā, manehi, manebhi. Manaso, manassa, manānaṃ. Manasi, mane, manasmiṃ, manamhi, manesu. Bho mana, bhavanto manā.

Mano, manā. Manaṃ, mano, mane. Manasā, manena, manehi, manebhi. Manaso, manassa, manānaṃ. Manā, manasmā, manamhā, manehi, manebhi. Manaso, manassa, manānaṃ. Manasi, mane, manasmiṃ, manamhi, manesu. Bho mana, bhavanto manā.

Atha vā “bho manā”iti bahuvacanampi ñeyyaṃ. Evaṃ vaco, vacā. Vacaṃ, vaco, vace. Vacasātiādinā nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Ahasaddassa pana bhummekavacanaṭṭhāne ahasi, ahe, ahasmiṃ, ahamhi, ahu, ahanīti yojetabbā.

Or alternatively, 'bho manā' should also be understood as plural. Similarly, 'vaco', 'vacā'. 'Vacaṃ', 'vaco', 'vace'. The nominal paradigm beginning with 'vacasā' should be constructed. However, for the word 'aha', in place of the singular locative, 'ahasi', 'ahe', 'ahasmiṃ', 'ahamhi', 'ahu', and 'ahanī' should be constructed.

Idāni rūpantaravisesadassanatthaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgassa manasaddassapi nāmikapadamālaṃ vadāma, aṭṭhāne ayaṃ kathitāti na codetabbaṃ.

Now, for the purpose of showing the distinctions in the transformations of form, we will explain the nominal paradigm of the word 'mana' in the neuter gender as well. It should not be criticized that this has been stated out of place.

Manaṃ, manāni, manā. Manaṃ, manāni, mane. Manena, manehi, manebhi. Manassa, manaso, manānaṃ. Manā, manasmā, manamhā, manehi, manebhi. Manassa, manaso, manānaṃ. Mane, manasmiṃ, manamhi, manesu. Bho mana, bhavanto manā. Atha vā “bho manāni, bho manā”evampi bahuvacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evamuttaratrāpi nayo.

Manaṃ, manāni, manā. Manaṃ, manāni, mane. Manena, manehi, manebhi. Manassa, manaso, manānaṃ. Manā, manasmā, manamhā, manehi, manebhi. Manassa, manaso, manānaṃ. Mane, manasmiṃ, manamhi, manesu. Bho mana, bhavanto manā. Or alternatively, 'bho manāni, bho manā'—thus the plural should be understood. The same method applies to the rest.

Ettha ca pulliṅgassa manasaddassa paccattakaraṇasampadānasāmibhummavacanāni mano manasā manaso manasīti rūpāni ṭhapetvā yāni sesāni, napuṃsakaliṅgassa ca manasaddassa paccattavacanāni “manaṃ manānī”ti rūpāni ca, aṭṭhamyopayogavacanānaṃ “manaṃ manānī”ti rūpadvayañca ṭhapetvā yāni sesāni, tāni sabbāni kamato samasamāni.

Here, for the masculine word 'mano', having set aside the forms of the nominative, instrumental, dative, genitive, and locative cases—'mano, manasā, manaso, manasi'—whatever remains; and for the neuter word 'mana', having set aside the forms of the nominative case—'manaṃ, manāni'—and having set aside the two forms 'manaṃ, manāni' for the vocative case (the eighth case in usage)—whatever remains, all those are sequentially identical.

Keci okāranto manoiti saddo napuṃsakaliṅgoti vadanti, te vattabbā – yadi so napuṃsakaliṅgo siyā, tassadisehi vaco vayotiādisaddehipi napuṃsakaliṅgeheva bhavitabbaṃ, na “te napuṃsakaliṅgā”ti garū vadanti, “pulliṅgā”icceva vadanti. Yasmā ca pāḷiyaṃ “kāyo anicco; mano [M 0.0135] anicco”ti ca “kāyo dukkho, mano dukkho”ti ca “nicco vā anicco vāti anicco bhante”ti ca evamādayo pulliṅgappayogā bahavo diṭṭhā. Tena ñāyati manosaddo ekantena pulliṅgoti. Yadi pana napuṃsakaliṅgosiyā, “anicco dukkho”ti evamādīni taṃsamānādhikaraṇāni anekapadasatānipi napuṃsakaliṅgāneva siyuṃ. Na hi tāni napuṃsakaliṅgāni, atha kho abhidheyyaliṅgānuvattakāni vāccaliṅgāni. Evaṃ manosaddassa pulliṅgatā paccetabbāti, sace manosaddo napuṃsakaliṅgo na hoti, kathaṃ “manānī”ti napuṃsakarūpaṃ dissatīti? Saccaṃ “manānī”ti napuṃsakaliṅgameva, tathāpi manogaṇe pamukhabhāvena gahitassokārantassa manasaddassa rūpaṃ na hoti. Atha kiñcarahīti ce? Cittasaddena samānaliṅgassa samānasutittepi manogaṇe apariyāpannassa niggahītantasseva manasaddassa rūpaṃ. Manasaddo hi punnapuṃsakavasena dvidhā bhijjati “mano manaṃ”iti yathā “ajjavoajjava”nti. “Mano ce nappadussati. Santaṃ tassa manaṃ hotī”ti hi pāḷi. Yadi ca so manosaddo napuṃsakaliṅgo na hoti.

Some say that the word 'mano,' ending in 'o,' is of the neuter gender. They should be told: If it were of the neuter gender, then similar words like 'vaco,' 'vayo,' and so forth should also be of the neuter gender. But the teachers do not say, 'They are of the neuter gender'; they say only, 'They are of the masculine gender.' And because in the Pāli canon many masculine usages are seen, such as 'The body is impermanent; the mind is impermanent,' and 'The body is suffering; the mind is suffering,' and 'Is it permanent or impermanent? It is impermanent, venerable sir,' and so on. By this it is known that the word 'mano' is exclusively masculine. If, however, it were of the neuter gender, then hundreds of words in apposition with it, such as 'impermanent, suffering,' would also be of the neuter gender. But they are not of the neuter gender; rather, their gender follows the gender of the thing signified. Thus, the masculinity of the word 'mano' is to be understood. If the word 'mano' is not of the neuter gender, how is the neuter form 'manāni' seen? It is true that 'manāni' is indeed of the neuter gender. Nevertheless, it is not a form of the word 'mano' ending in 'o' which is taken as the primary one in the 'mano' group. Then what is it? It is the form of the word 'manaṃ' ending in a niggahīta, which is of the same gender as the word 'citta' and has the same meaning, but is not included in the 'mano' group. For the word 'mana' is divided in two ways, as masculine and neuter, as 'mano' and 'manaṃ', just as 'ajjavo' and 'ajjavaṃ'. For the Pāli says: 'If the mind is not corrupted,' and 'His mind is at peace.' And if that word 'mano' were not of the neuter gender.

“Garu cetiyapabbatavattaniyā,

Pamadā pamadā pamadā vimadaṃ;

Samaṇaṃ sunisamma akā hasitaṃ,

Patitaṃ asubhesu munissa mano”ti

A venerable woman, following the customs of Cetiyapabbata, yet heedless, infatuated the one free from intoxication. Having carefully observed the ascetic, she smiled, and the mind of the sage fell upon impure things.

Ettha manosaddena samānādhikaraṇo “patita”nti saddo napuṃsakaliṅgabhāvena kasmā sannihito. Yasmā ca samānādhikaraṇapadaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgabhāvena sannihitaṃ, tasmā saddantarasannidhānavasena manosaddo napuṃsakaliṅgoti ñāyatīti? Tanna, samānādhikaraṇapadassa sabbattha liṅgavisesājotanato. Yadi hi samānādhikaraṇapadaṃ sabbattha liṅgavisesaṃ joteyya, “cattāro indriyānī”ti etthāpi “cattāro”ti [M 0.0136] padaṃ indriyasaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ kareyya, na ca kātuṃ sakkoti. Indriyasaddo hi ekantena napuṃsakaliṅgo. Yadi tumhe “patita”nti samānādhikaraṇapadaṃ nissāya manosaddassa napuṃsakaliṅgattamicchatha, “cattāro indriyānī”ti etthapi “cattāro”ti samānādhikaraṇapadaṃ nissāya indriyasaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ icchathāti. Na mayaṃ bho indriyasaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ icchāma, atha kho napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃyeva icchāma, “cattāro”ti padaṃ liṅgavipallāsavasena ṭhitattā “cattārī”ti gaṇhāma, tasmā “cattāri indriyānī”ti atthaṃ dhāremāti. Yadi evaṃ “patitaṃ asubhesu munissa mano”ti etthāpi “patita”nti padaṃ liṅgavipallāsavasena ṭhitanti mantvā “patito”ti atthaṃ dhārethāti. Na dhārema ettha liṅgavipallāsassa anicchitabbato. Yadi hi manosaddo pulliṅgo siyā, taṃsamānādhikaraṇapadaṃ “patito”ti vattabbaṃ siyā. Kimācariyo evaṃ vattuṃ na jāni, jānamāno eva so “patito”ti nāvoca, “patita”nti panāvoca, tena ñāyati “manosaddo napuṃsakaliṅgo”ti. Mā tumhe evaṃ vadetha, samānādhikaraṇapadaṃ nāma katthaci padhānaliṅgamanuvattati, katthaci nānuvattati, tasmā na taṃ liṅgavisesajotane ekantato pamāṇaṃ. “Mātugāmo, orodho, āvuso visākha, ehi visākhe, cittāni aṭṭhīnī”ti evamādirūpavisesoyeva pamāṇaṃ. Yadi samānādhikaraṇapadeyeva liṅgaviseso adhigantabbo siyā, “cattāro ca mahābhūtā”tiādīsu liṅgavavatthānaṃ na siyā. Yasmā evamādīsupi ṭhānesu liṅgavavatthānaṃ hotiyeva. Kathaṃ? “Cattāro”ti pulliṅgaṃ “mahābhūtā”ti napuṃsakanti, tasmā “patitaṃ asubhesu munissa mano”ti etthāpi “patita”nti napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ “mano”ti pulliṅganti vavatthānaṃ bhavatīti. Idaṃ sutvā te tuṇhī bhavissanti. Tato [M 0.0137] tesaṃ tuṇhībhūtānaṃ idaṃ vattabbaṃ – yasmā manogaṇe pavattānaṃ padānaṃ samānādhikaraṇapadāni katthaci napuṃsakavasena yojetabbāni, tasmā manogaṇe pamukhassa manosaddassapi samānādhikaraṇapadāni katthaci napuṃsakavasena yojitāni. Tathā hi pubbācariyā “saddhammatejavihataṃ vilayaṃ khaṇena, veneyyasattahadayesu tamo’payāti. Dukkhaṃ vaco etasminti dubbaco. Avanataṃ siro yassa soyaṃ avaṃsiro, appakaṃ rāgādi rajo yesaṃ paññāmaye akkhimhi te apparajakkhā”tiādinā saddaracanaṃ kubbiṃsu, na pana tehi vaco siro rajosaddādīnaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃ vibhāvetuṃ īdisī saddaracanā katā, atha kho siromanosaddānaṃ manogaṇe pavattānaṃ pulliṅgasaddānaṃ katthacipi īdisānipi liṅgavipallāsavasena ṭhitāni samānādhikaraṇapadāni hontīti paresaṃ jānāpanādhippāyavatiyā anukampāya viracitā. Etthāpi tumhākaṃ matena manosaddassa napuṃsakaliṅgatte sati vaco siro iccādayopi napuṃsakaliṅgattamāpajjanti napuṃsakaliṅgavasena samānādhikaraṇapadānaṃ niddiṭṭhattā. Kiṃ panetesampi napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃ icchathāti. Addhā te idampi sutvā nibbeṭhetumasakkontā tuṇhī bhavissanti. Kiñcāpi te aññaṃ gahetabbakāraṇaṃ apassantā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “yadi bho mano saddo napuṃsakaliṅgona hoti, kasmā veyyākaraṇā ‘manosaddo napuṃsakaliṅgo’ti vadantī”ti? Te vattabbā – yadi tumhe veyyākaraṇamataṃ gahetvā manosaddassa napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃ rocetha, nanu bhagavāyeva loke asadiso mahāveyyākaraṇo mahāpuriso visārado parappavādamaddano. Bhagavantañhi padakā veyyākaraṇā ambaṭṭhamāṇavapokkharasātisoṇadaṇḍādayo ca brāhmaṇā saccakanigaṇṭhādayo ca paribbājakā [M 0.0138] vādena na sampāpuṇiṃsu, aññadatthu bhagavāyeva mattavāraṇagaṇamajjhe kesarasīho viya asambhīto nesaṃ nesaṃ vādaṃ maddesi, mahante ca ne atthe patiṭṭhāpesi, evaṃvidhena bhagavatā vohārakusalena yasmā “kāyo anicco”ti ca “kāyo dukkho, mano anicco, mano dukkho”ti ca evamādinā vuttā manosaddassa pulliṅgabhāvasūcanikā bahū pāḷiyo dissanti, tasmā manosaddo pulliṅgoyevāti sārato paccetabboti. Evaṃ vuttā te niruttarā appaṭibhānā maṅkubhūtā pattakkhandhā adhomukhā pajjhāyissanti.

Here, why is the word 'patita,' which is in apposition with the word 'mano,' placed in the neuter gender? Is it that because the appositional word is placed in the neuter gender, therefore, by the proximity of the other word, the word 'mano' is known to be neuter? That is not so, because an appositional word does not everywhere indicate a specific gender. For if an appositional word were to indicate a specific gender everywhere, then in 'cattāro indriyānī,' the word 'cattāro' would make the word 'indriya' masculine, but it is not able to do so. For the word 'indriya' is exclusively neuter. If you desire the word 'mano' to be neuter by relying on the appositional word 'patita,' then in 'cattāro indriyānī' you should also desire the word 'indriya' to be masculine by relying on the appositional word 'cattāro.' 'We, sir, do not desire the word 'indriya' to be masculine; rather, we desire it to be neuter. We take 'cattāro' as standing by way of a gender change for 'cattāri,' and therefore we hold the meaning to be 'cattāri indriyānī.' If so, then in 'patitaṃ asubhesu munissa mano,' you should also hold that the word 'patitaṃ' stands by way of a gender change and understand the meaning to be 'patito.' 'We do not hold that, because a gender change is not to be desired here. For if the word 'mano' were masculine, its appositional word should be stated as 'patito.' Did the teacher not know to say it thus? Knowing, he did not say 'patito,' but rather said 'patitaṃ.' By this it is known that the word 'mano' is neuter.' Do not say so. An appositional word sometimes follows the gender of the principal word, and sometimes it does not. Therefore, it is not an absolute authority for indicating a specific gender. Only specific forms such as 'mātugāmo,' 'orodho, āvuso Visākha,' 'ehi Visākhe,' 'cittāni aṭṭhīnī' are the authority. If a specific gender were to be ascertained only by an appositional word, there would be no determination of gender in cases such as 'cattāro ca mahābhūtā.' Because even in such cases there is indeed a determination of gender. How? 'Cattāro' is masculine, 'mahābhūtā' is neuter. Therefore, in 'patitaṃ asubhesu munissa mano' also, there can be the determination that 'patitaṃ' is neuter and 'mano' is masculine. Hearing this, they will become silent. Then, to those who have become silent, this should be said: Since appositional words for words occurring in the 'mano'-group are sometimes to be construed in the neuter, therefore, for the word 'mano' itself, which is chief in the 'mano'-group, appositional words are also sometimes construed in the neuter. For thus the ancient teachers made word-compositions such as 'saddhammatejavihataṃ vilayaṃ khaṇena, veneyyasattahadayesu tamo’payāti. Dukkhaṃ vaco etasminti dubbaco. Avanataṃ siro yassa soyaṃ avaṃsiro, appakaṃ rāgādi rajo yesaṃ paññāmaye akkhimhi te apparajakkhā,' but such word-compositions were not made by them to demonstrate the neuter gender of words like 'vaco,' 'siro,' 'rajo,' etc. Rather, they were composed out of compassion, with the intention of informing others that for masculine words occurring in the 'mano'-group, such as 'siro' and 'mano', there are sometimes such appositional words standing by way of a gender change. Here too, according to your view, if the word 'mano' were neuter, then 'vaco,' 'siro,' and so on would also become neuter, because their appositional words are indicated in the neuter. Do you then desire these also to be neuter? Surely, hearing this too, being unable to refute it, they will become silent. And even if they, seeing no other reason to grasp, should say this: 'Sir, if the word 'mano' is not neuter, why do the grammarians say 'the word mano is neuter'?' They should be told: If you, taking the grammarians' view, approve of the word 'mano' being neuter, is not the Blessed One himself the incomparable great grammarian in the world, the great person, confident, the subduer of others' doctrines? For grammarians who are masters of words, Brahmins such as Ambaṭṭha, Māṇava, Pokkharasāti, and Soṇadaṇḍa, and wanderers such as Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha, could not match the Blessed One in debate; on the contrary, the Blessed One, like a lion with a mane amidst a herd of intoxicated elephants, fearlessly crushed their respective doctrines and established them in great matters. Since many Pāli passages indicative of the masculine nature of the word 'mano' are seen, spoken by such a Blessed One, skilled in expression, such as 'the body is impermanent,' and 'the body is suffering, the mind is impermanent, the mind is suffering,' therefore, it should be accepted in essence that the word 'mano' is indeed masculine. Having been told this, they will be without reply, without resource, bewildered, with drooping shoulders, downcast, and lost in thought.

Idāni sarasaddādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālā visesato vuccate –

Now, the declension of words beginning with 'sara' is specifically stated.

Saro, sarā. Saraṃ, sare. Sarena, sarehi, sarebhi. Sarassa, sarānaṃ. Sarā, sarasmā, saramhā, sarehi, sarebhi. Sarassa, sarānaṃ. Sare, sarasmiṃ, saramhi, saresu. Bho sara, bhavanto sarā.

An arrow, arrows. An arrow, arrows. By an arrow, by arrows. To/of an arrow, to/of arrows. From an arrow, from arrows. To/of an arrow, to/of arrows. In an arrow, in arrows. O arrow, O arrows.

Ayaṃ purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭhassa ususaddasaravanaakārādisaravācakassa sarasaddassa nāmikapadamālā.

This is the declension of the word 'sara,' which, denoting 'arrow,' 'sound,' 'vowel,' and so on, has fully entered the masculine paradigm.

Ayaṃ pana purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhassa manogaṇapakkhikassa rahadavācakassa sarasaddassa nāmikapadamālā –

This, however, is the declension of the word 'sara,' denoting 'lake,' which has partially entered the masculine paradigm, belonging to the mind-group.

Saro, sarā. Saraṃ, saro, sare. Sarasā, sarena, sarehi, sarebhi. Saraso, sarassa, sarānaṃ. Sarā, sarasmā, saramhā, sarehi, sarebhi. Saraso, sarassa, sarānaṃ. Sarasi, sare, sarasmiṃ, saramhi, saresu. Bho sara, bhavanto sarā, bho sarā iti vā.

A lake, lakes. A lake, a lake, lakes. By a lake, by a lake, by lakes. To/of a lake, to/of lakes. From a lake, from lakes. To/of a lake, to/of lakes. In a lake, in lakes. O lake, O venerable lakes, or O lakes.

Vayo, vayā. Vayaṃ, vaye. Vayena, vayehi, vayebhīti purisanayena ñe yyo. Ayaṃ purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭhassa parihānivācakassa vayasaddassa nāmikapadamālā.

Age, ages. Age, ages. By age, by ages—thus it should be understood according to the masculine paradigm. This is the declension of the word 'vaya,' denoting decline, which has fully entered the masculine paradigm.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0139] pana purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhassa manogaṇapakkhikassa āyukoṭṭhāsavācakassa vayasaddassa nāmikapadamālā – vayo, vayā. Vayaṃ, vayo, vaye. Vayasā, vayena, vayehi, vayebhīti mananayena ñeyyo. Tassa ceto paṭissosi, araññe luddagocaro. Cetā haniṃsu vedabbaṃ.

This, however, is the nominal paradigm of the word 'vayas,' denoting a portion of life, which belongs to the 'mano' group and is partially included in the masculine declension: vayo, vayā. Vayaṃ, vayo, vaye. Vayasā, vayena, vayehi, vayebhīti—this should be understood according to the 'mano' method. His mind assented; his hunting ground was in the forest. The minds killed Vedabba.

Ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, cete. Cetena, cetehi, cetebhīti purisanayena ñeyyo. Ayaṃ purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭhassa paṇṇattivācakassa cetasaddassa nāmikapadamālā.

Ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, cete. Cetena, cetehi, cetebhīti—this should be understood according to the masculine declension. This is the nominal paradigm of the word 'cetas,' which denotes a concept and is fully included in the masculine declension.

Ayaṃ pana purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhassa cittavācakassa cetasaddassa nāmikapadamālā – ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, ceto, cete. Cetasā, cetena, cetehi, cetebhīti mananayena ñeyyo. Yaso kulaputto, yasaṃ kulaputtaṃ, yasena kulaputtenāti ekavacanavasena purisanayena yojetabbā, ekavacanaputhuvacanavasena vā. Evaṃ kānici okārantapadāni purisanaye sabbathā paviṭṭhāni ca honti, ekadesena paviṭṭhāni cāti iminā nayena sabbapadāni paññācakkhunā upaparikkhitvā viseso veditabbo. Avisesaññuno hi evamādivibhāgaṃ ajānantā yaṃ vā taṃ vā byañjanaṃ ropentā yathādhippetaṃ atthaṃ virādhenti, tasmā yo ettha amhehi pakāsito vibhāgo, so saddhāsampannehi kulaputtehi sakkaccamuggahetabbo. Katamāni kānici okārantapadāni purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhāni ca ekadesena na paviṭṭhāni ca? Mano vaco tejosaddādayo ceva ayyasaddo ca, tatra manasaddādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālā heṭṭhā vibhāvitā.

This, however, is the nominal paradigm of the word 'cetas,' denoting 'citta' (mind), which is partially included in the masculine declension: ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, ceto, cete. Cetasā, cetena, cetehi, cetebhīti—this should be understood according to the 'mano' method. 'Yaso kulaputto,' 'Yasaṃ kulaputtaṃ,' 'Yasena kulaputtena'—these should be construed according to the masculine declension in the singular form, or according to singular and plural forms. Thus, some words ending in '-o' are fully included in the masculine declension, and some are partially included. By examining all words with the eye of wisdom according to this method, the distinctions should be understood. For those who do not know the distinctions, being ignorant of such classifications, distort the intended meaning by arbitrarily applying inflections. Therefore, the classification explained here by us should be carefully learned by faithful noble sons. Which are some words ending in '-o' that are partially included and partially not included in the masculine declension? The words mano, vaco, tejo, and others, as well as the word 'ayya.' Among these, the nominal paradigm of 'mano' and similar words has been explained below.

Ayyasaddassa [M 0.0140] pana nāmikapadamālāyaṃ “ayyo, ayyā. Ayyaṃ, ayye”ti purisanayena vatvā ālapanaṭṭhāne “bho ayya, bho ayyo”ti dve ekavacanāni, “bhavanto ayyā, bhavanto ayyo”ti dve bahuvacanāni ca vattabbāni. Ettha ayyo iti saddo paccattavacanabhāve ekavacanaṃ, ālapanavacanabhāve ekavacanañceva bahuvacanañca. Tatrime payogā “ayyo kira sāgato ambatitthikena nāgena saṅgāmesi, pivatu bhante ayyo sāgato kāpotikaṃ pasanna”nti evamādīni ayyosaddassa paccattekavacanappayogāni, “atha kho sā itthī taṃ purisaṃ etadavoca ‘nāyyo so bhikkhu maṃ nippāṭesi, apica ahameva tena bhikkhunā gacchāmi, akārako so bhikkhu, gaccha khamāpehī’ti” evamādīni ayyosaddassa ālapanekavacanappayogāni, “etha’yyo rājavasatiṃ, nisīditvā suṇātha me. Etha mayaṃ ayyo samaṇesu sakyaputtiyesu pabbajissāmā”ti evamādīni ayyosaddassa ālapanabahuvacanappayogāni. Bhavati catra –

In the nominal paradigm of the word 'ayya,' however, having stated 'ayyo, ayyā. Ayyaṃ, ayye' according to the masculine declension, in the vocative case, two singular forms, 'bho ayya, bho ayyo,' and two plural forms, 'bhavanto ayyā, bhavanto ayyo,' should be stated. Here, the word 'ayyo' is singular in the nominative case, and both singular and plural in the vocative case. These are the usages: 'Ayyo, it is said, Sāgata fought with the Nāga Ambatitthika. May the venerable Sāgata drink the dove-coloured liquor'—such are the examples of the word 'ayyo' used in the nominative singular. 'Then that woman said to the man, “No, venerable, that monk did not strike me. Rather, I myself went with that monk. That monk is not the doer; go and ask his forgiveness”'—such are the examples of the word 'ayyo' used in the vocative singular. 'Come, venerable ones, to the royal residence. Sit and listen to me. Come, venerable ones, let us go forth among the ascetics, the Sakyan sons'—such are the examples of the word 'ayyo' used in the vocative plural. And here it is stated—

Ayyo iti ayaṃ saddo, paccattekavaco bhave;

Ālapane bahuvaco, bhave ekavacopi ca –

This word 'ayyo' is a nominative singular; in the vocative, it is plural and also singular.

Evaṃ kānici okārantapadāni purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhāni ca honti ekadesena na paviṭṭhāni ca.

Thus, some words ending in '-o' are included in the masculine declension in part, and in part are not included.

Katamāni kānici okārantapadāni purisanaye sabbathā appaviṭṭhāni? Gosaddoyeva. Gosaddassa hi ayaṃ nāmikapadamālā –

Which are some words ending in '-o' that are entirely not included in the masculine declension? Only the word 'go.' For the word 'go,' this is the nominal paradigm:

Go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvo, gavo. Gāvena, gavena, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāvā, gāvasmā, gāvamhā, gavā, gavasmā, gavamhā, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāve, gāvasmiṃ, gāvamhi, gave, gavasmiṃ[M 0.0141], gavamhi, gāvesu, gavesu, gosu. Bho go, bhavanto gāvo, gavo. Ayaṃ purisanaye sabbathā appaviṭṭhassa gosaddassa nāmikapadamālā.

Go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvo, gavo. Gāvena, gavena, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāvā, gāvasmā, gāvamhā, gavā, gavasmā, gavamhā, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāve, gāvasmiṃ, gāvamhi, gave, gavasmiṃ, gavamhi, gāvesu, gavesu, gosu. Bho go, bhavanto gāvo, gavo. This is the nominal paradigm of the word 'go,' which is entirely not included in the masculine declension.

Nanu ca bho gosaddo attanā sambhūtagoṇasaddamālāvasena purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭho ceva ekadesena na paviṭṭho cāti? Saccaṃ. Goṇasaddo gosaddavasena sambhūtopi “vatticchānupubbikā saddapaṭipattī”ti vacanato gosaddato visuṃ amhehi gahetvā purisanaye pakkhitto. Tassa hi visuṃ gahaṇe yutti dissati syādīsu ekākāreneva tiṭṭhanato, tasmā gosaddato sambhūtampi goṇasaddaṃ anapekkhitvā suddhaṃ gosaddameva gahetvā purisanaye sabbathā gosaddassa appaviṭṭhatā vuttā.

But, venerable sirs, is not the word 'go,' through the paradigm of the word 'goṇa' (bull) which arises from it, partially included in the masculine declension and partially not included? It is true. Although the word 'goṇa' arises from the word 'go,' according to the maxim 'the application of words follows convention,' it is taken by us separately from the word 'go' and placed in the masculine declension. For appropriateness is seen in its separate treatment, as it maintains a single form before the case endings; therefore, disregarding the word 'goṇa' which arises from the word 'go,' and taking only the pure word 'go,' the complete non-inclusion of the word 'go' in the masculine declension is stated.

Nanu ca bho paccattavacanabhūto goiti saddo purisoti saddena sadisattā purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhoti? Tanna, gosaddo hi niccamokāranto, na purisasaddādayo viya paṭhamaṃ akārantabhāve ṭhatvā pacchā paṭiladdhokārantaṭṭho. Teneva hi paccattavacanaṭṭhānepi ālapanavacanaṭṭhānepi goicceva tiṭṭhati. Yadi paccattavacanattaṃ paṭicca gosaddassa purisanaye ekadesena paviṭṭhatā icchitabbā, “kānici okārantapadānī”ti evaṃ vuttā okārantakathā kamatthaṃ dīpeyya, nipphalāva sā kathā siyā, tasmā amhehi yathāvutto nayoyeva āyasmantehi manasi kātabbo. Evaṃ gosaddassa purisanaye sabbathā appaviṭṭhatā daṭṭhabbā.

But, venerable sirs, is not the word 'go,' being in the nominative singular form, partially included in the masculine declension due to its similarity with the word 'puriso'? That is not so, for the word 'go' is always o-final, unlike words such as 'purisa,' which first exist with an a-final stem and later acquire an o-final state. For that very reason, it remains as 'go' in both the nominative singular and the vocative positions. If, on account of its being the nominative singular, the partial inclusion of the word 'go' in the masculine declension were to be accepted, then what purpose would the discussion of 'some words ending in -o' serve? That discussion would be entirely fruitless. Therefore, the method stated by us should be kept in mind by the venerable sirs. Thus, the complete non-inclusion of the word 'go' in the masculine declension should be understood.

Kecettha evaṃ puccheyyuṃ “gosaddassa tāva ‘go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ’ iccādinā nayena purisanaye sabbathā appaviṭṭhatā amhehi ñātā, jaraggava puṅgavādisaddā pana kutra naye [M 0.0142] paviṭṭhā”ti? Tesaṃ evaṃ byākātabbaṃ “jaraggava puṅgavādisaddā sabbathāpi purisanaye paviṭṭhā”ti. Tathā hi tesaṃ gosaddato ayaṃ viseso, jaranto ca so go cāti jaraggavo. Ettha nakāralopo takārassa ca gakārattaṃ bhavati samāsapadattā, samāse ca simhi pare gosaddassokārassa avādeso labbhati, tasmā pāḷiyaṃ “visāṇena jaraggavo”ti ekavacanarūpaṃ dissati. Tathā hi aññattha anupapadattā gavoiti bahuvacanapadaṃyeva dissati. Idha pana sopapadattā samāsapadabhāvamāgamma “jaraggavo”ti ekavacanapadaṃyeva dissati. Tathā hi jaraggavoti ettha jarantā ca te gavo cāti evaṃ bahuvacanavasena nibbacanīyatā na labbhati lokasaṅketavasena ekasmiṃ atthe nirūḷhattāti. “Jaraggavo, jaraggavā. Jaraggavaṃ, jaraggave. Jaraggavenā”ti purisanayena nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Esa nayo puṅgavo sakyapuṅgavotiādīsupi.

Some here might ask: 'Regarding the word 'go,' we have understood that, according to the method shown by 'go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ,' and so forth, it is entirely not included in the masculine declension. But in which declension are words like 'jaraggava,' 'puṅgava,' and others included?' To them, it should be explained thus: 'Words like 'jaraggava,' 'puṅgava,' and others are entirely included in the masculine declension.' Indeed, this is their distinction from the word 'go': 'jaranto ca so go cāti jaraggavo' (an old bull). Here, the elision of 'na' and the change of 'ta' to 'ga' occurs because it is a compound word. And in a compound, when 'si' follows, the substitution of 'ava' for the 'o' of the word 'go' is found. Therefore, in the Pāli language, the singular form 'visāṇena jaraggavo' is seen. Indeed, elsewhere, because it is not preceded by another word, only the plural form 'gavo' is seen. Here, however, because it is preceded by another word, having become a compound, only the singular form 'jaraggavo' is seen. Indeed, here in 'jaraggavo,' a derivation in the plural sense as 'jarantā ca te gavo ca' (old bulls) is not obtained, because by worldly convention it is established in a singular meaning. The nominal paradigm should be constructed according to the masculine declension: 'Jaraggavo, jaraggavā. Jaraggavaṃ, jaraggave. Jaraggavena.' This same method applies to 'puṅgavo,' 'sakyapuṅgavo,' and other such words.

Tatra puṅgavoti gunnaṃ yūthapati nisabhasaṅkhāto usabho. Yo pāḷiyaṃ “muhuttajātova yathā gavaṃpati, samehi pādehi phusī vasundhara”nti ca “gavañce taramānānaṃ, ujuṃ gacchati puṅgavo”ti ca āgato. Īdisesu pana ṭhānesu keci “pumā ca so go cāti puṅgavo”ti vacanatthaṃ bhaṇanti. Mayaṃ pana padhāne nirūḷho ayaṃ saddoti vacanatthaṃ na bhaṇāma. Na hi puṅkokilotiādisaddānaṃ kokilādīnaṃ pumbhāvappakāsanamatte samatthatā viya imassa pumbhāvappakāsanamatte samatthatā sambhavati, atha kho padhānabhāvappakāsane ca samatthatā sambhavati. Tena “sakyapuṅgavo”tiādīsu nisabhasaṅkhāto puṅgavo viyāti puṅgavo, sakyānaṃ, sakyesu [M 0.0143] vā puṅgavo sakyapuṅgavotiādinā samāsapadattho gahetabbo. Atha vā uttarapadatte ṭhitānaṃ sīhabyagghanāgādisaddānaṃ seṭṭhavācakattā “sakyapuṅgavo”tiādīnaṃ “sakyaseṭṭho”tiādinā attho gahetabbo. Iti sabbathāpi purisanaye pavattanato jaraggava puṅgavādisaddānaṃ gosaddassa padamālato visadisapadamālatā vavatthapetabbā. Gosaddassa pana purisanaye sabbathā appaviṭṭhatā ca vavatthapetabbā.

There, 'puṅgava' means the bull, the leader of the herd, known as the foremost bull. In the Pāli texts, it is mentioned: "Just after birth, like the lord of cattle, he touched the earth with even feet," and "When cattle are hurrying, the bull goes straight." However, in such contexts, some say the meaning is "a male and a cow, hence 'puṅgava'." But we do not say that this is the meaning of the word, for this word is established as referring to what is foremost. For unlike words such as 'puṅkokila' (male cuckoo), which are capable only of indicating the maleness of the cuckoo and so on, this word is not capable only of indicating maleness; rather, it is also capable of indicating the state of being foremost. Therefore, in phrases like 'Sakyapuṅgavo' (the foremost one of the Sakyans), 'puṅgavo' should be understood as the foremost one, like a bull known as a leader; the compound 'Sakyapuṅgavo' should be understood as 'the foremost one of the Sakyans' or 'the foremost one among the Sakyans'. Alternatively, since words like 'sīha' (lion), 'byaggha' (tiger), and 'nāga' (elephant) when in the final position of compounds denote excellence, the meaning of phrases like 'Sakyapuṅgavo' should be taken as 'the best of the Sakyans' and so on. Thus, in all respects, because it functions in the masculine paradigm, the words 'jaraggava' (old bull), 'puṅgava' (bull), and such should be established as having a declension distinct from the word 'go' (cow). Moreover, it should be established that the word 'go' is in no way included in the masculine paradigm.

Āpasadde ācariyānaṃ liṅgavacanavasena matibhedo vijjati, tasmā taṃmatena tassa purisanaye sabbathā appaviṭṭhatā bhavati. “Aṅguttarāpesū”ti pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “mahiyā pana nadiyā uttarena āpo”ti vuttaṃ, ṭīkāyaṃ pana taṃ ulliṅgitvā “mahiyā nadiyā āpo tassa janapadassa uttarena honti, tāsaṃ avidūrattā so janapado uttarāpo”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ āpasaddassa ekantena itthiliṅgatā bahuvacanatā ca ācariyehi icchitā, tesaṃ mate āpoiti itthiliṅge paṭhamābahuvacanarūpe honte dutiyātatiyāpañcamīsattamīnaṃ bahuvacanarūpāni kīdisāni siyuṃ. Tathā hi “purise, purisehi purisebhi purisesū”ti rūpavato pulliṅgassa viya okārantitthiliṅgassa ekāraehi kārādiyuttāni rūpāni katthacipi na dissanti. Ato tesaṃ mate padamālānayo atīva dukkaro.

Regarding the word 'āpo', there is a difference of opinion among teachers concerning its gender and number; hence, according to their view, it is completely inapplicable to the masculine paradigm. In the commentary on the Pāli phrase "Aṅguttarāpesu," it is stated, "north of the Mahī river is water," but in the sub-commentary, elaborating on this, it is said, "the waters are north of the Mahī river, and because they are not far from it, that region is called Uttarāpo." Thus, the teachers hold that the word "āpo" is exclusively feminine in gender and plural in number. According to their view, if "āpo" were a feminine plural form in the nominative case, what would the plural forms in the accusative, instrumental, ablative, and locative cases be like? For instance, forms like "purise, purisehi, purisebhi, purisesu" are seen for masculine nouns, but similar forms for feminine nouns ending in -o with endings such as -e, -ehi, are nowhere to be found. Therefore, according to their view, the system of declension is exceedingly difficult.

Āpasaddassa garavo, saddasatthanayaṃ pati;

Bahuvacanatañcitthi-liṅgabhāvañca abravuṃ.

The venerable teachers, with regard to the system of grammar, declared the plurality and feminine gender of the word 'āpo'.

Iccāpasaddassa [M 0.0144] itthiliṅgabahuvacanantatā veyyākaraṇānaṃ mataṃ nissāya anumatāti veditabbā. Aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ pana āpo iti saddassa napuṃsakaliṅgekavacanavasena vutto payogo diṭṭho “omattaṃ pana āpo adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jāta”nti. Jātakapāḷiyaṃ tu tassekavacanantatā diṭṭhā. Tathā hi “suciṃ sugandhaṃ salilaṃ, āpo tatthābhisandatī”ti. Imasmiṃ padese āpo iti saddo ekavacanaṭṭhāne ṭhito diṭṭho. Kecettha vadeyyuṃ “āpoti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ salilaṃ suci sugandhaṃ hutvā tattha abhisandatīti salilaṃsaddavasena ekavacanappayogo kato, na nāmasaddavasena. Āpasaddo hi ekantenitthiliṅgo ceva bahuvacananto ca. Tathā hi ‘āpo tatthābhisandantī’ti bahuvacanavasena tappayogo vattabbopi chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ vacanavipallāsavasena niddiṭṭho”ti. Tanna, “āpo tatthābhisandare”ti vattuṃ sakkuṇeyyattā “tāni ajja padissare”ti bahuvacanappayogā viya. Yasmā evaṃ na vuttaṃ, yasmā ca pana pāḷiyaṃ “āpo labbhati, tejo labbhati, vāyo labbhatī”ti ekavacanappayogo dissati, tasmā “āpo”ti saddassa ekavacanantatā paccakkhato diṭṭhāti.

Thus, the state of the word 'āpo' as being feminine and plural should be understood as accepted based on the opinion of grammarians. However, in the Aṭṭhasālinī, the usage of the word 'āpo' is seen in the neuter gender and singular number, as in the phrase, "but the water, having become excessive, has become possessed of an excessive earth element." In the Jātaka Pāli, its singular number is seen. For example: "Clear, fragrant water, the water flows there." In this passage, the word 'āpo' is seen standing in the place of a singular noun. Some might argue here: "The word 'āpo' refers to water that has attained the designation 'salila' (water), which, being clear and fragrant, flows there—thus, the singular usage is made on account of the word 'salila,' not on account of the noun 'āpo.' For the word 'āpo' is exclusively feminine in gender and plural in number. Thus, although the plural usage 'āpo tatthābhisandantī' should be stated, for the sake of preserving the meter, it is presented with a change in number." That is not so, since it could be said "āpo tatthābhisandare," like the plural usage in "tāni ajja padissare." Because it is not stated thus, and because in the Pāli, singular usages like "āpo labbhati, tejo labbhati, vāyo labbhati" are seen, therefore, the singular number of the word 'āpo' is directly observed.

Athāpi ce vadeyyuṃ – nanu pāḷiyaṃyeva tassa bahuvacanantatā paccakkhato diṭṭhā “āpo ca devā pathavī ca, tejo vāyo tadāgamu”nti? Tampi na. Ettha hi “devā”ti saddaṃ apekkhitvā “āgamu”nti bahuvacanappayogo kato, na “āpo”ti saddaṃ. Yadi “āpo”ti saddaṃ sandhāya bahuvacanappayogo kato siyā, “pathavī”ti “tejo”ti “vāyo”ti ca saddampi sandhāya bahuvacanappayogo kato siyā[M 0.0145]. Evaṃ sante pathavī tejo vāyosaddāpi bahuvacanakabhāvamāpajjeyyuṃ, na pana āpajjanti. Na hete bahuvacanakā, atha kho ekavacanakā eva. Rūḷhīvasena te pavattā pakatiāpādīsu atthesu appavattanato. Tathā hi āpokasiṇādīsu parikammaṃ katvā nibbattā devā ārammaṇavasena “āpo”tiādināmaṃ labhantīti. Evaṃ vuttāpi te evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “nanu ca bho ‘aṅguttarāpesū’ti bahuvacanapāḷi dissatī”ti? Te vattabbā – asampathamavatiṇṇā tumhe, na hi tumhe saddappavattiṃ jānātha, “aṅguttarāpesū”ti bahuvacanaṃ pana “kurūsu aṅgesu aṅgānaṃ magadhāna”ntiādīni bahuvacanāni viya rūḷhīvasena ekassāpi janapadassa vuttaṃ, na āpasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ sandhāya. “Aṅguttarāpesū”ti ettha hi āpasaṅkhāto attho upasajjanībhūto, pulliṅgabahuvacanena pana vutto janapadasaṅkhāto atthoyeva padhāno “āgatasamaṇo saṅghārāmo”ti ettha samaṇasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ upasajjanakaṃ katvā pavattassa āgatasamaṇasaddassa saṅghārāmasaṅkhāto attho viya, tasmā āpasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā yo aṅguttarāpo nāma janapado, tasmiṃ aṅguttarāpesu janapadeti attho veditabbo. Tathā hi “aṅguttarāpesu viharati āpaṇaṃ nāma aṅgānaṃ nigamo”ti pāḷi dissati. Tattha uttarena mahāmahiyā nadiyā āpo yesaṃ te uttarāpā, aṅgā ca te uttarāpā cāti aṅguttarāpā, tesu aṅguttarāpesu. Evaṃ ekasmiṃ janapadeyeva bahuvacanaṃ na āpasaṅkhāte atthe, tena aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “tasmiṃ aṅguttarāpesu janapade”ti. Evaṃ vuttā te niruttarā bhavissanti.

And if they were to say, "But is not its plural form directly seen in the Pāli itself—'āpo ca devā pathavī ca, tejo vāyo tadāgamu' (Water and gods, earth, fire, and air came then)?" That too is not so. For here, the plural form 'āgamu' is used with reference to the word 'devā,' not the word 'āpo.' If the plural form were used with reference to the word 'āpo,' then it would also have been used with reference to the words 'pathavī,' 'tejo,' and 'vāyo.' In that case, the words 'pathavī,' 'tejo,' and 'vāyo' would also become plural, but they do not. They are not plural, but rather singular. They are used conventionally, as they do not apply in the sense of natural water and so on. For instance, the deities born through preliminary practice involving the water-kasiṇa, etc., receive the name 'āpo,' etc., by way of the object of meditation. Even when this is said, they might say, "But, venerable sirs, is not the plural Pāli form 'aṅguttarāpesu' seen?" They should be told: "You have not entered the proper path; indeed, you do not understand the usage of words. The plural form 'aṅguttarāpesu' is used conventionally for a single country, like the plurals 'kurūsu,' 'aṅgesu,' 'aṅgānaṃ,' 'magadhānaṃ,' etc., not with reference to the meaning of 'āpa' (water). In 'aṅguttarāpesu,' the meaning of 'āpa' is secondary, while the primary meaning, expressed in the masculine plural, is the country—just as in 'āgatasamaṇo saṅghārāmo,' the meaning of 'samaṇa' is made secondary to the meaning of 'saṅghārāma' for the word 'āgatasamaṇo.' Therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'in the country of Aṅguttarāpesu,' which is the country named Aṅguttarāpa, a name derived from the meaning of 'āpa.' For the Pāli is seen: 'He dwells in Aṅguttarāpa, in a market town of the Aṅgas named Āpaṇa.' There, 'uttarāpā' are those whose waters (āpo) are north of the great Mahī River, and 'aṅguttarāpā' are 'the Aṅgas and those Uttarāpas'; 'tesu aṅguttarāpesu' means 'in those Aṅguttarāpas.' Thus, the plural is used for a single country, not for the meaning of 'āpa'; therefore, in the commentary it is said, 'in that country of Aṅguttarāpesu.' When this is said, they will be without reply.

Tathāpi ye evaṃ vadanti “āpasaddo itthiliṅgo ceva bahuvacanakocā”ti. Te pucchitabbā “kiṃ paṭicca tumhe āyasmanto ‘āpasaddo itthiliṅgo ceva bahuvacanako cā’ti vadathā”ti[M 0.0146]? Te evaṃ puṭṭhā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “aṅgāyeva so janapado, mahiyā pana nadiyā uttarena āpo, tāsaṃ avidūrattā uttarāpoti vuccatī”ti ca “mahiyā pana nadiyā āpo tassa janapadassa uttarena honti, tāsaṃ avidūrattā so janapado uttarāpoti vuccatī”ti ca evaṃ pubbācariyehi abhisaṅkhato saddaracanāviseso dissati, tasmā itthiliṅgo ceva bahuvacanako cā”ti vadāmāti. Saccaṃ dissati, so pana saddasatthe veyyākaraṇānaṃ mataṃ gahetvā abhisaṅkhato, saddasatthañca nāma na sabbathā buddhavacanassopakārakaṃ, ekadesena pana hoti, tasmā kaccāyanappakaraṇe icchitānicchitasaṅgahavivajjanaṃ kātuṃ “jinavacanayuttañhi, liṅgañca nippajjate”ti lakkhaṇāni vuttāni.

Yet those who say thus: 'The word āpa is feminine and plural.' They should be asked: 'On what basis do you, venerable ones, say that the word āpa is feminine and plural?' When asked thus, they would reply: 'That country is indeed Aṅga; to the north of the Mahī river, however, are the waters (āpo), and because of their proximity, it is called Uttarāpa.' And also: 'The waters (āpo) are to the north of the Mahī river of that country, and because of their proximity, that country is called Uttarāpa.' Thus a special rule of word formation, fashioned by the ancient teachers, is seen; therefore we say it is feminine and plural.' It is true that this is seen, but it is fashioned by adopting the view of grammarians in the science of grammar, and the science of grammar is not entirely beneficial for the word of the Buddha, but only in part. Therefore, in the Kaccāyana treatise, in order to include the desired and exclude the undesired, the rules have been stated: 'For gender is produced in accordance with the Jina's word.'

Yadi ca āpasaddo itthiliṅgabahuvacanako, kathaṃ āpoti padaṃ sijjhatīti? Āpasaddato paṭhamāyovacanaṃ katvā tassokārādesañca katvā āpoti padaṃ sijjhati “gāvo”ti padamivāti. Visamamidaṃ nidassanaṃ, “gāvo”ti padañhi niccokārantena gosaddena sambhūtaṃ. Tathā hi yomhi pare gosaddantassāvādesaṃ katvā tato yonamokārādesaṃ katvā “gāvo”ti nipphajjati, āpasadde pana dve ādesā na santi. Buddhavacanañhi patvā āpasaddo akārantatāpakatiko jāto, na aññathāpakatikoti.

And if the word 'āpa' is feminine and plural, how is the form 'āpo' accomplished? The form 'āpo' is accomplished from the word 'āpa' by taking the nominative plural ending and substituting the letter 'o' for it, like the form 'gāvo.' This is an unsuitable example, for the form 'gāvo' arises from the word 'go,' which is always o-final. For when 'yo' follows, 'gāvo' is formed by substituting 'āva' for the end of the word 'go,' and then substituting the letter 'o' for 'yo.' In the case of the word 'āpa,' however, there are not two substitutions. For in the context of the word of the Buddha, the word 'āpa' has become one whose nature is to be a-final, and not of another nature.

Evaṃ vuttāpi te “idameva saccaṃ, nāñña”nti cetasi sannidhāya ādhānaggāhiduppaṭinissaggibhāve, “na vacanapaccanīkasātena suvijānaṃ subhāsita”nti evaṃ vuttapaccanīkasātabhāve ca ṭhatvā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “yatheva gāvosaddo, tatheva āposaddo kiṃ itthiliṅgo na bhavissati bahuvacanako cā”ti? Tato tesaṃ imāni suttapadāni dassetabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ? “Āpaṃ āpato sañjānāti, āpaṃ āpato [M 0.0147] saññatvā āpaṃ maññati, āpasmiṃ maññati, āpaṃ meti maññati, āpaṃ abhinandatī”ti evaṃ suttapadāni dassetvā “āpanti idaṃ kataravacana”nti pucchitabbā. Addhā te āpasaddassa bahuvacanantabhāvameva icchamānā vakkhanti “dutiyābahuvacana”nti. Te vattabbā “nanu yovacanaṃ na suyyatī”ti? Te vadeyyuṃ “yovacanaṃ kataamādesattā na suyyatī”ti. Yaṃ yaṃ bhonto icchanti, taṃ taṃ mukhārūḷhaṃ vadanti.

Even when told thus, they, having determined in their minds, 'This alone is true, nothing else,' and abiding in a state of stubborn grasping and difficult relinquishing, and in a state of sharp opposition to what is said, as in 'A well-spoken statement is not easily known through sharp opposition to the words,' might say: 'Just as the word 'go' is, so too the word 'āpa'—why should it not be feminine and plural?' Then, these passages from the suttas should be shown to them. Namely: 'One perceives water as water. Having perceived water as water, one conceives water, conceives in water, conceives 'water is mine,' and delights in water.' Having shown these sutta passages, they should be asked: 'This "āpaṃ," what number is it?' Surely, desiring only that the word 'āpa' be plural, they will say, 'The accusative plural.' They should be told: 'But surely the plural ending 'yo' is not heard?' They might reply: 'The plural ending 'yo' is not heard because a substitution has been made for it.' Whatever these gentlemen desire, that they say as it comes to their mouths.

“Āpato”ti idaṃ pana kiṃ bhonto vadantīti? “Āpato”ti idampi “bahuvacanakaṃ topaccayanta”nti vadāma topaccayassa ekatthe ca bavhatthe ca pavattanato. Iti tumhe bahuvacanakattaṃyeva icchamānā “āposaddo ca yovacananto”ti bhaṇatha, “āpato”ti idampi “bahuvacanakaṃ topaccayanta”nti bhaṇatha, “āpasmiṃ maññatī”ti ettha pana “āpasmi”ntidaṃ kataravacanantaṃ katarādesena sambhūtanti? Addhā te evaṃ puṭṭhā niruttarā bhavissanti. Tathā yesaṃ evaṃ hoti “āpasaddo itthiliṅgo ceva bahuvacanako cā”ti, te pucchitabbā “yaṃ ācariyehi veyyākaraṇamataṃ gahetvā ‘yā āpo’ti ca ‘tāsa’nti ca vuttaṃ, tattha ‘kiṃ tāsa’nti vacane ‘āpāna’nti padaṃ ānetvā attho vattabbo, udāhu āpassā”ti? “Āpāna’nti padamānetvā attho vattabbo”ti ce, evañca sati “yā āpā”ti vattabbaṃ “yā kaññā tiṭṭhantī”ti padamiva. Atha “āpā”ti padaṃ nāma natthi, “āpo”ti padaṃyeva bahuvacanakanti ce, evaṃ sati “tāsa”nti etthāpi “āpassā”ti padaṃ ānetvā attho veditabbo. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā “āpo”ti paccattekavacanassa tumhākaṃ matena bahuvacanatte sati “āpassā”ti padampi bahuvacananti katvā tāsaṃsaddena yojetvā vattuṃ yuttitoti. Evaṃ sati “āpāna”nti [M 0.0148] padassa abhāveneva bhavitabbaṃ. Yathā pana “puriso, purisā. Purisaṃ, purise”ti ca, “go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvu”nti ca ekavacanabahuvacanāni bhavanti, evaṃ “āpo, āpā. Āpaṃ, āpe”ti ekavacanabahuvacanehi bhavitabbaṃ. Evañca sati “āpasaddo bahuvacanakoyeva hotī”ti na vattabbaṃ.

And this 'āpato,' what do you gentlemen say it is? 'We say that this "āpato" is also plural, ending in the suffix "to," because the suffix "to" occurs in both the singular and the plural sense.' Thus, desiring only its plurality, you say that the word 'āpo' ends in the plural ending 'yo,' and you say that this 'āpato' is also plural, ending in the suffix 'to.' But here in 'āpasmiṃ maññati,' this 'āpasmiṃ,' what number does it end in, and by what substitution has it arisen? Surely, when asked thus, they will be speechless. Likewise, those who hold that 'the word āpa is feminine and plural' should be asked: 'Regarding what was said by the teachers, adopting the view of the grammarians, namely "yā āpo" (which waters) and "tāsaṃ" (of them), in that statement "tāsaṃ," should the meaning be explained by supplying the word "āpānaṃ" (of the waters), or "āpassa"?' If you say, 'The meaning should be explained by supplying the word "āpānaṃ,"' in that case, one would have to say 'yā āpā,' like the phrase 'yā kaññā tiṭṭhanti' (which girls are standing). But if you say, 'There is no such word as "āpā"; only the word "āpo" is plural,' in that case, here too with "tāsaṃ," the meaning should be understood by supplying the word "āpassa." If asked why, it is because, since according to your view the singular form 'āpo' is plural, it is also proper to consider the word 'āpassa' as plural and thus construe it with the word 'tāsaṃ.' In that case, the word 'āpānaṃ' must simply not exist. Just as there are singular and plural forms like 'puriso, purisā' and 'purisaṃ, purise,' and 'go, gāvo, gavo, gāvuṃ,' so too there should be singular and plural forms like 'āpo, āpā' and 'āpaṃ, āpe.' And if this is so, it should not be said that 'the word āpa is only plural.'

Ye evaṃ vadanti, tesaṃ vacanaṃ sadosaṃ duppariharaṇīyaṃ mūlapariyāyasutte “āpaṃ maññati āpasmi”nti ekavacanapāḷīnaṃ dassanato, visuddhimaggādīsu ca “vissandanabhāvena taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ āpoti appotīti āpo”tiādikassa ekavacanavasena vuttanibbacanassa dassanato. Yathā pana pāḷiyaṃ itthiliṅgepi pariyāpanno gosaddo “tā gāvo tato tato daṇḍena ākoṭeyyā”ti ca “annadā baladā cetā”ti ca ādinā bavhatthadīpakehi itthiliṅgabhūtehi sabbanāmikapadehi ca asabbanāmikapadehi ca samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vutto dissati, na tathā pāḷiyaṃ bavhatthadīpakehi itthiliṅgabhūtehi sabbanāmikapadehi vā asabbanāmikapadehi vā samānādhikaraṇabhāvena vutto āpasaddo dissati. Yadi hi āpasaddo itthiliṅgo siyā, kaññasaddato āpaccayo viya āpasaddato āpaccayo vā siyā, nadasaddato viya ca īpaccayo vā siyā, ubhayampi natthi, ubhayābhāvato itthiliṅge vuttaṃ sabbampi vidhānaṃ tattha na labbhati, tena ñāyati “āpasaddo anitthiliṅgo”ti. Nanu ca bho gosaddatopi āpaccayo natthi, tadabhāvato itthiliṅge vuttavidhānaṃ na labbhati, evaṃ sante kasmā soyeva itthiliṅgo hoti, na panāyaṃ āpasaddoti?

The statement of those who speak thus is flawed and untenable, because of the appearance in the Mūlapariyāya Sutta of the singular Pāḷi forms 'āpaṃ maññati āpasmiṃ,' and because of the appearance in the Visuddhimagga and other texts of the etymology given in the singular, such as 'Because it flows (āpoti) or reaches (appoti) from place to place with a flowing nature, it is āpo.' Just as in the Pāḷi, the word 'go,' though included in the feminine gender, is seen used in apposition with feminine pronominal and non-pronominal words indicating plurality, such as in 'tā gāvo tato tato daṇḍena ākoṭeyyā' and 'annadā baladā cetā,' the word 'āpa' is not seen in the Pāḷi used in apposition with feminine pronominal or non-pronominal words indicating plurality. If the word 'āpa' were indeed feminine, there would be an 'ā' suffix from the word 'āpa' like from the word 'kaññā,' or an 'ī' suffix like from the word 'nadī.' But neither is found. Due to the absence of both, no rule stated for the feminine gender is obtained for it. From this it is known that 'the word āpa is not feminine.' But, sir, from the word 'go' also there is no 'ā' suffix, and due to its absence, the rule stated for the feminine gender is not obtained. This being so, why is that very word feminine, but not this word 'āpa'?

Ettha vuccate – gosaddo na niyogā itthiliṅgo, atha kho pulliṅgova. Itthiliṅgabhāve pana tamhā āpaccaye [M 0.0149] ahontepi īpaccayo vikappena hoti, aññampi itthiliṅge vuttavidhānaṃ labbhati. So hi niccamokārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā “go, gāvī”tiādinā attano itthiliṅgarūpānaṃ nibbattikāraṇabhūto, tena so itthiliṅgo bhavati. Āpasadde pana īpaccayādi na labbhati. Tena so itthiliṅgoti na vattabbo. Yathā vā gosaddassa avisadākāravohārataṃ paṭicca itthiliṅgabhāvo upapajjati, na tathā āpasaddassa. Āpasaddassa hi anākularūpakkamattā avisadākāravohāratā na dissati, yāya eso itthiliṅgo siyā. Evaṃ vuttā te niruttarā bhavissanti.

Here it is said: The word 'go' is not feminine by rule, but rather masculine. However, in its feminine sense, even without the 'ā' suffix, the 'ī' suffix optionally occurs; other feminine formations are also obtained according to the stated rules. For this word, while remaining in its natural state of always ending in 'o,' is the cause for the production of its own feminine forms, such as 'go, gāvī,' and thus it becomes feminine. But for the word 'āpa,' the 'ī' suffix and so on are not obtained. Therefore, it should not be called feminine. Just as the feminine state of the word 'go' is justified on account of its indistinct form of usage, it is not so for the word 'āpa.' For the word 'āpa,' because of its unambiguous formal process, an indistinct form of usage is not seen, by which it could be feminine. Thus spoken to, they will be without reply.

Tathā yesaṃ evaṃ hoti “āpasaddo sabbadā itthiliṅgo ceva bahuvacanako cā”ti, te vattabbā – yathā itthiliṅgabhūtassa kaññāsaddassa paṭhamaṃ kaññaiti rassavasena ṭhapitassa āpaccayato paraṃ smiṃvacanaṃ sarūpato na tiṭṭhati, yaṃbhāvena ca yābhāvena ca tiṭṭhati “kaññāyaṃ, kaññāyā”ti, na tathā “itthiliṅga”nti tumhehi gahitassa āposaddassa paṭhamaṃ āpaiti rassavasena ṭhapitassa paraṃ smiṃvacanaṃ yaṃbhāvena ca yābhāvena ca tiṭṭhati, atha kho sarūpatoyeva tiṭṭhati “āpasmiṃ maññatī”ti. Yadi pana āpasaddo itthiliṅgo siyā, smiṃvacanaṃ sarūpato na tiṭṭheyya. Yasmā ca smiṃvacanaṃ sarūpato tiṭṭhati, tasmā āpasaddo na itthiliṅgo. Na hi caturāsītidhammakkhandhasahassasaṅgahesu anekakoṭisatasahassesu pāḷippadesesu ekasmimpi pāḷippadese paṭhamaṃ akārantabhāvena ṭhapetabbānaṃ itthiliṅgasaddānaṃ parato ṭhitaṃ smiṃvacanaṃ sarūpato tiṭṭhatīti. Evaṃ vuttā te niruttarā bhavissanti.

Likewise, for those who hold that 'the word "āpa" is always feminine and plural,' they should be told: Just as for the feminine word 'kaññā,' when first established with the short vowel as 'kañña,' the locative case ending following the 'ā' suffix does not remain in its original form but exists as the forms 'yaṃ' and 'yā', as in 'kaññāyaṃ, kaññāyā'; it is not so for the word 'āpa,' which you take to be feminine. When it is first established with the short vowel as 'āpa,' the locative case ending that follows does not exist as the forms 'yaṃ' and 'yā', but rather remains in its original form, as in 'āpasmiṃ maññati.' If, however, the word 'āpa' were feminine, the locative case ending would not remain in its original form. Because the locative case ending does remain in its original form, the word 'āpa' is not feminine. Indeed, among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dhamma, in countless hundreds of thousands of Pāli passages, there is not a single Pāli passage where, for feminine words that are to be established as ending in '-a', the locative case ending that follows remains in its original form. Thus addressed, they will be left without reply.

Keci panettha evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “āpasaddo napuṃsakaliṅgo, tathā hi aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ ‘omattaṃ pana āpo adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ [M 0.0150] jāta’nti napuṃsakaliṅgabhāvena taṃsamānādhikaraṇapadāni niddiṭṭhānī”ti? Tanna, manogaṇe pavattehi tama vaca sirasaddādīhi viya āpasaddenapi samānādhikaraṇapadānaṃ katthaci napuṃsakaliṅgabhāvena niddisitabbattā. Pubbācariyānañhi saddaracanāsu “saddhammatejavihataṃ vilayaṃ khaṇena, veneyyasattahadayesu tamo payātī”ti ettha “tamo”tipadena samānādhikaraṇaṃ “vihata”nti napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ dissati, tathā “dukkhaṃ vaco etasmiṃ vipaccanīkasāte puggaleti dubbaco”ti ettha “vaco”ti padena samānādhikaraṇaṃ “dukkha”nti napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, “avanataṃ siro yassa so avanatasiro”ti ettha “siro”ti padena samānādhikaraṇaṃ “avanata”nti napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, “appaṃ rāgādirajo yesaṃ paññāmaye akkhimhi te apparajakkhā”ti ettha “rajo”ti padena samānādhikaraṇaṃ “appa”nti napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ dissati. Na te ācariyā tehi samānādhikaraṇapadehi tamavacasirasaddādīnaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgattaviññāpanatthaṃ tathāvidhaṃ saddaracanaṃ kubbiṃsu, atha kho “sobhanaṃ mano tassāti sumano”ti ettha viya manogaṇe pavattapulliṅgānaṃ payoge napuṃsakaliṅgabhāvenapi samānādhikaraṇapadāni katthaci hontīti dassanatthaṃ kubbiṃsu.
