Yathā ca “vihata”ntiādikā saddaracanā tamavacasirasaddādīnaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgattaviññāpanatthaṃ na katā, tathā “omatta”nti ca “adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jāta”nti ca saddaracanāpi āpasaddassa napuṃsakaliṅgattaviññāpanatthaṃ na katā. Yasmā pana manogaṇe pavattehi manasaddādīhi ekadesena samānagatikattā āpasaddenapi napuṃsakaliṅgassa samānādhikaraṇatā yujjati, tasmā aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ “omattaṃ pana āpo adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jāta”nti napuṃsakaliṅgassa āpasaddena samānādhikaraṇatā katā. Tathāpi āpasaddo [M 0.0151] manasaddādīhi ekadesena samānagatiko samāsapadatte majjhokārassa “āpokasiṇaṃ, āpogata”ntiādippayogassa dassanato, tasmā “omatta”ntiādivacanaṃ āpasaddassa napuṃsakaliṅgattaviññāpanatthaṃ vuttanti na gahetabbaṃ, liṅgavipariyayavasena pana katthaci evampi saddagati hotīti ñāpanatthaṃ vuttanti gahetabbaṃ. “Omatto”ti ca “adhimattapathavīgatiko jāto”ti ca liṅgaṃ parivattetabbaṃ. Yadi hi āpasaddo napuṃsakaliṅgo siyā, sanikārāni’ssa paccattopayogarūpāni buddhavacanādīsu vijjeyyuṃ, na tādisāni santi. Kiñci bhiyyo – okārantaṃ nāma napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ katthacipi natthi, niggahītantaikāranta ukārantavasena hi tividhāniyeva napuṃsakaliṅgāni. Tena āpasaddassa napuṃsakaliṅgatā nupapajjatīti. Evaṃ vuttā te niruttarā bhavissanti. Iccokārantavasena gahitassa āpasaddassa itthiliṅgatā ca napuṃsakaliṅgatā ca ekantato natthi, niggahītantavasena pana gahitassa katthaci napuṃsakaliṅgatā siyā “bhante nāgasena samuddo samuddoti vuccati, kena kāraṇena āpaṃ udakaṃ samuddoti vuccatī”ti payogadassanato. Ettha paneke vadeyyuṃ “yadi bho okārantavasena gahitassa āpasaddassa itthinapuṃsakaliṅgavasena dviliṅgatā natthi, okāranto āpasaddo kataraliṅgo”ti? Pulliṅgoti mayaṃ vadāmāti.

Some might say here: "The word 'āpa' is of neuter gender, for in the Aṭṭhasālinī, words in apposition to it are stated in the neuter gender, as in 'But water (āpo) is excessive (omattaṃ), born from the predominance of the earth element (adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jātaṃ).'" That is not so. For just as with words like 'tamo' (darkness), 'vaca' (speech), 'sira' (head), and 'sadda' (sound), etc., which belong to the 'mano' group, so too with the word 'āpa,' words in apposition are sometimes stated in the neuter gender. For in the grammatical compositions of the ancient teachers, in the phrase 'Struck by the radiance of the True Dhamma, the darkness (tamo) vanishes (vihataṃ) instantly from the hearts of beings capable of being taught,' here 'tamo' is seen in apposition with 'vihataṃ,' which is neuter. Similarly, in 'Painful (dukkhaṃ) is speech (vaco) for this hostile and disagreeable person, hence he is called 'dubbaco' (difficult to speak to),' here 'vaco' is in apposition with 'dukkhaṃ,' which is neuter. In 'One whose head (siro) is bowed (avanataṃ) is 'avanatasiro' (one with a bowed head),' here 'siro' is in apposition with 'avanataṃ,' which is neuter. And in 'Those in whom the dust (rajo) of lust and so on is little (appaṃ) in the eye of wisdom are 'apparajakkhā' (those with little dust in their eyes),' here 'rajo' is seen in apposition with 'appaṃ,' which is neuter. Those teachers did not make such grammatical compositions to indicate that words like 'tamo,' 'vaco,' 'sira,' and 'sadda' are neuter, but rather to show that words in apposition can sometimes be neuter even when used with masculine words of the 'mano' group, as in 'One whose mind (mano) is beautiful (sobhanaṃ) is 'sumano' (of beautiful mind).' Just as grammatical compositions like 'vihataṃ' were not made to indicate that words like 'tamo,' 'vaco,' 'sira,' and 'sadda' are neuter, so too the grammatical compositions 'omattaṃ' and 'adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jātaṃ' were not made to indicate that the word 'āpa' is neuter. However, since the word 'āpa' shares a partial similarity in nature with words like 'mano' and others belonging to the 'mano' group, it is appropriate for a neuter word to be in apposition with the word 'āpa.' Therefore, in the Aṭṭhasālinī, a neuter word is placed in apposition with 'āpa' in the phrase 'But water (āpo) is excessive (omattaṃ), born from the predominance of the earth element (adhimattapathavīgatikaṃ jātaṃ).' Nevertheless, since the word 'āpa' is partially similar in nature to words like 'mano,' and since in compound words like 'āpokasiṇaṃ' and 'āpogata' the vowel 'o' is seen in the middle, the statement 'omattaṃ' and so on should not be taken as indicating that the word 'āpa' is neuter. Rather, it should be taken as stated to show that sometimes such a word-formation occurs by way of gender variation. The gender should be changed to 'omatto' and 'adhimattapathavīgatiko jāto.' If the word 'āpa' were neuter, its forms for individual use with a nasal ending would be found in the Buddha's words and elsewhere, but no such forms exist. Furthermore, there is no neuter noun ending in '-o' anywhere. For neuter nouns are of only three kinds: those ending in a nasal consonant, those ending in '-i,' and those ending in '-u.' Therefore, the neuter gender of 'āpa' is not established. Thus spoken to, they will be without reply. Thus, the word 'āpa,' when taken as ending in '-o,' is definitely not feminine or neuter. However, when taken as ending in a nasal consonant, it could sometimes be neuter, as seen in the usage: 'Venerable Nāgasena, the ocean is called 'samudda'; for what reason is water (āpaṃ, udakaṃ) called 'samudda'?' Here, some might say: 'If, sir, the word 'āpa,' when taken as ending in '-o,' is neither feminine nor neuter, then what gender is the '-o'-ending word 'āpa'?' We say it is masculine.

Yadi ca bho āpasaddo pulliṅgo. Yathā āpasaddassa pulliṅgatā paññāyeyya, nijjhānakkhamatā ca bhaveyya, tathā suttaṃ āharathāti. “Āharissāmisuttaṃ, na no suttāharaṇe bhāro atthī”ti evañca pana vatvā tesaṃ imāni suttapadāni dassetabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ? “Āpo upalabbhatīti? Āmantā. Āpassa kattā kāretā upalabbhatīti? Na [M 0.0152] hevaṃ vattabbe. Atīto āpo atthīti? Āmantā. Tena āpena āpakaraṇīyaṃ karotīti? Na hevaṃ vattabbe. Āpaṃ maññati āpasmiṃ maññatī”ti imāni suttapadāni.

And if, sir, the word 'āpa' is masculine, then bring forth a sutta so that the masculinity of the word 'āpa' may be evident and acceptable upon reflection. Having said, 'We will bring a sutta; for us there is no burden in bringing a sutta,' these sutta passages should be shown to them. Namely: 'Is water found?' 'Yes.' 'Is a doer or maker of water found?' 'It should not be said thus.' 'Was there water in the past?' 'Yes.' 'Does one perform with that water what is to be done with water?' 'It should not be said thus.' 'One conceives water, one conceives in water'—these are the sutta passages.

Ettha ca “upalabbhatī”tiādinā āpasaddassa ekavacanatā siddhā, tāya siddhāya bahuvacanatāpi siddhāyeva. Ekavacanatāyeva hi saddasatthe paṭisiddhā, na bahuvacanatā, tena “āpenā”ti iminā pana āpasaddassa itthiliṅgabhāvavigamo siddho itthiliṅge enādesābhāvato. “Āpassa, āpasmi”nti imināpi itthiliṅgabhāvavigamoyeva itthiliṅge sarūpato nā smā smiṃ vacanānamabhāvā. “Atīto”ti iminā itthiliṅganapuṃsakaliṅgabhāvavigamo okārantanapuṃsakaliṅgassa abhāvato, okārantassa guṇanāmabhūtassa itthiliṅgassa ca abhāvato.

Here, by 'is found' and so on, the singular form of the word 'āpa' is established; and with that established, the plural form is also established. For in the science of grammar, only the singular form is refuted, not the plural. Therefore, by 'āpena', the absence of the feminine gender in the word 'āpa' is established, because there is no 'enā' substitution in the feminine gender. By 'āpassa' and 'āpasmiṃ', the absence of the feminine gender is likewise established, due to the absence in the feminine gender of the endings `nā`, `smā`, and `smiṃ` as such. By 'atīto', the absence of the feminine and neuter genders is established, due to the absence of a neuter gender noun ending in '-o', and the absence of a feminine quality-noun ending in '-o'.

Apica buddhavacanādīsu “cittāni, rūpānī”tiādīni viya sanikārānaṃ rūpānaṃ adassanato okārantabhāvena gahitassa napuṃsakaliṅgabhāvavigamo atīva pākaṭo. Aparampettha vattabbaṃ – “atīto āpo atthīti? Āmantā”ti ettha “atīto”ti iminā āpasaddassa visadākāravohāratāsūcakena okārantapadena tassa avisadākāravohāratāya ca ubhayamuttākāravohāratāya ca abhāvo siddho. Tassa ca avisadākāravohāratāya abhāve siddhe itthiliṅgabhāvo dūrataro. Ubhayamuttākāravohāratāya ca abhāve siddhe napuṃsakaliṅgabhāvopi dūrataroyeva. Iti na katthacipi okārantabhāvena gahito āpasaddo itthiliṅgo vā napuṃsakaliṅgo vā bhavati. Milindapañhe pana niggahītantavasena āgato napuṃsakaliṅgoti veditabbo, na cettha vattabbaṃ “atīto”ti “tenā”ti [M 0.0153] ca imāni liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttānīti vāccaliṅgānamanuvattāpakassa abhidheyyaliṅgabhūtassa āpasaddassa “kaññāya cittānī”tiādīnaṃ viya itthinapuṃsakaliṅgarūpānaṃ abhāvato. Apica vohārakusalā tathāgatā tathāgatasāvakā ca, tehiyeva uttamapurisehi vohārakusalehi “atīto āpo”tiādinā vuttattāpi “atīto”ti “tenā”ti ca imāni liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttānīti na cintetabbāni, tasmā taṃsamānādhikaraṇo okārantabhāvena gahito āpasaddo ekavacananto pulliṅgo ceva yathāpayogaṃ ekavacanabahuvacanako cāti veditabbo “āpo, āpā. Āpaṃ, āpe”tiādinā yojetabbattā. Evaṃ vuttāni suttapadāni savinicchayāni sutvā addhā te āpasaddassa itthiliṅgabahuvacanatāvādino niruttarā bhavissanti.

Moreover, in the words of the Buddha and elsewhere, the absence of the neuter gender for the word 'āpa' when taken as ending in '-o' is very evident, due to the non-perception of forms with a nasal ending, like 'cittāni' and 'rūpāni'. Furthermore, it should be stated here: In the phrase 'Was there water (āpo) in the past (atīto)? Yes,' the word 'atīto,' which ends in '-o' and indicates a clear form of usage for the word 'āpa,' establishes the absence of its unclear usage and its usage free from both genders. When the absence of its unclear usage is established, the feminine gender is far removed. And when the absence of its usage free from both genders is established, the neuter gender is also far removed. Thus, the word 'āpa,' when taken as ending in '-o,' is not found anywhere as feminine or neuter. However, in the Milindapañha, it should be understood as neuter gender when it occurs with a nasal ending. And here it should not be said that 'atīto' and 'tena' are stated by way of gender inversion, because the word 'āpa,' which is the gender of the expressed meaning that dictates the gender of the words in apposition, lacks feminine or neuter forms like 'kaññāya cittāni'. Moreover, the Tathāgatas and the disciples of the Tathāgatas are skilled in usage. Since these excellent persons, skilled in usage, have themselves stated 'atīto āpo' and so on, 'atīto' and 'tena' should not be considered as stated by way of gender inversion. Therefore, the word 'āpa,' when taken as ending in '-o' and in apposition with it, should be understood as masculine in the singular, and as having singular and plural forms according to usage, to be construed as 'āpo,' 'āpā,' 'āpaṃ,' 'āpe,' and so on. Having heard these sutta passages with their analysis, those who assert the feminine plural gender of the word 'āpa' will surely be left without a reply.

Ettha koci vadeyya – pāḷiyaṃ pulliṅganayo ekavacananayo ca kiṃ aṭṭhakathāṭīkācariyehi na diṭṭho, ye āpasaddassa itthiliṅgabahuvacanattaṃ vaṇṇesunti? No na diṭṭho, diṭṭhoyeva so nayo tehi. Yasmā pana te na kevalaṃ sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacaneyeva visāradā, atha kho sakalepi saddasatthe visāradā, tasmā saddasatthe attano paṇḍiccaṃ pakāsetuṃ, “saddasatthe ca īdiso nayo vutto”ti viññāpetuñca saddasatthanayaṃ gahetvā āpasaddassa itthiliṅgabahuvacanakattaṃ vaṇṇesunti natthi tesaṃ doso. Tathā hi mūlapariyāyasuttantaṭṭhakathāyaṃ tehiyeva vuttaṃ āpasaddassa pulliṅgekavacanakattasūcanakaṃ “lakkhaṇasasambhārārammaṇasammutivasena catubbidho āpo, tesū”tiādi, tasmā natthi tesaṃ doso. Pūjārahā hi te āyasmanto, namoyeva tesaṃ [M 0.0154] karoma, na tesaṃ vacanaṃ codanābhājanaṃ. Ye pana ujuvipaccanīkavādā daḷhameva āpasaddassa itthiliṅgabahuvacanattaṃ mamāyanti, tesaṃyeva vacanaṃ codanābhājanaṃ. Yasmā pana mayaṃ pāḷinayānusārena antadvayavato āpasaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgattañca vidadhāma, tasmā yo koci idaṃ vādaṃ madditvā aññaṃ vādaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ sakkhissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, idañca pana ṭhānaṃ mahāgahanaṃ duppaṭivijjhanaṭṭhena, paramasukhumañca katañāṇasambhārehi paramasukhumañāṇehi paṇḍitehi vedanīyattā. Sabbamidañhi vacanaṃ tesu tesu ṭhānesu atthabyañjanapariggahaṇe sotūnaṃ paramakosallajananatthañceva sāsane ādaraṃ akatvā saddasatthamatena kālaṃ vītināmentānaṃ sāthalikānaṃ pamādavihāranisedhanatthañca sāsanassātimahantabhāvadīpanatthañca vuttaṃ, na attukkaṃsanaparavambhanatthanti imissaṃ nītiyaṃ saddhāsampannehi kulaputtehi yogo karaṇīyo bhagavato sāsanassa ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ.

Here someone might say: 'Was the principle of masculine gender and singular number in the Pāli not seen by the teachers of the commentaries and sub-commentaries, that they describe the word 'āpa' as being feminine gender and plural number?' No, it was not unseen; they indeed saw that principle. However, since they are experts not only in the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries—the words of the Buddha—but also in the entire science of grammar, they describe the word 'āpa' as being feminine and plural by adopting the principles of grammar, in order to demonstrate their own erudition in grammar and to make known that 'such a principle is stated in the science of grammar.' There is no fault in them. Indeed, in the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, they themselves have stated, indicating the masculine gender and singular number of the word 'āpa': 'Water is fourfold by way of characteristic, substance, object, and convention—among these,' and so on. Therefore, there is no fault in them. Those venerable ones are indeed worthy of reverence; we pay homage to them, and their words are not subject to censure. But the words of those who are directly contrary in their assertions and firmly cling to the feminine gender and plural number of the word 'āpa'—their words alone are subject to censure. Since we, following the principles of the Pāli, establish both the masculine and neuter genders for the word 'āpa', which has two endings, it is not possible that anyone could refute this view and establish another. Moreover, this matter is very profound, being difficult to penetrate, and extremely subtle, to be known by the wise with extremely subtle knowledge, through the accumulation of developed wisdom. All these words, in their respective contexts, are spoken for the purpose of generating supreme skill in listeners in thoroughly grasping the meaning and expression, for preventing the negligent dwelling of those indolent individuals who spend their time according to the views of grammar without reverence for the Teaching, and for illuminating the immense greatness of the Dispensation—not for self-praise or disparagement of others. In accordance with this principle, faithful sons of good family should make an effort for the long-lasting stability of the Blessed One's Dispensation.

Yasmā pana pāḷito aṭṭhakathā balavatī nāma natthi, tasmā pāḷinayānurūpeneva āpasaddassa nāmikapadamālaṃ yojessāma sotūnamasammohatthaṃ, kimettha saddasatthanayo karissati. Atrāyaṃ udānapāḷi “kiṃ kayirā udapānena, āpā ce sabbadā siyu”nti.

Since no commentary is stronger than the Pāli text itself, we will accordingly construct the nominal declension of the word 'āpa' in accordance with the Pāli method, for the sake of preventing bewilderment in the listeners—what can the science of grammar accomplish here? Here is this Pāli passage from the Udāna: "What should one do with a well, if water is always available?"

Āpo, āpā. Āpaṃ, āpe. Āpena, āpehi, āpebhi. Āpassa, āpānaṃ. Āpā, āpasmā, āpamhā, āpehi, āpebhi. Āpassa, āpānaṃ. Āpe, āpasmiṃ, āpamhi, āpesu. Bho āpa, bhavanto āpā.

Āpo, āpā (water, waters). Āpaṃ, āpe (water, waters). Āpena, āpehi, āpebhi (by water, by waters). Āpassa, āpānaṃ (of water, of waters). Āpā, āpasmā, āpamhā, āpehi, āpebhi (from water, from waters). Āpassa, āpānaṃ (of water, of waters). Āpe, āpasmiṃ, āpamhi, āpesu (in water, in waters). Bho āpa, bhavanto āpā (O water, O waters).

Sabbanāmādīhipi yojessāma – yo āpo, ye āpā. Yaṃ āpaṃ, ye āpe. Yena āpena, sesaṃ neyyaṃ[M 0.0155], so āpo, te āpā. Atīto āpo, atītā āpā. Sesaṃ neyyaṃ. Iccevaṃ –

We will also apply pronouns and so forth: yo āpo, ye āpā (which water, which waters); yaṃ āpaṃ, ye āpe (which water, which waters); yena āpena (by which water), the rest should be inferred. So āpo, te āpā (that water, those waters). Atīto āpo, atītā āpā (past water, past waters). The rest should be inferred. Thus:

Purisena samā āpa-saddādī sabbathā matā;

Na sabbathāva gosaddo, purisena samo mato.

The word 'āpa' and others are considered in all respects similar to 'purisa';

The word 'go' is not considered in all respects similar to 'purisa'.

Manādī ekadesena, purisena samā matā;

Sarādī ekadesena, sabbathā vā samā matā.

Words like 'mana' are regarded as partly similar to 'purisa';

Words like 'sara' are regarded as partly or wholly similar.

Ye panettha saddā “manogaṇo”ti vuttā, kathaṃ tesaṃ manogaṇabhāvo sallakkhetabboti? Vuccate tesaṃ manogaṇabhāvasallakkhaṇakāraṇaṃ –

Regarding those words here said to be of the 'mind-group' (manogaṇa), how is their nature as the mind-group to be understood? The reason for understanding their nature as the mind-group is stated:

Manogaṇo manogaṇā-

Dikā cevā’manogaṇo;

Iti saddā tidhā ñeyyā,

Manogaṇavibhāvane.

The mind-group, those like the mind-group, and the non-mind-group;

Thus, in the analysis of the mind-group, words are to be known in three ways.

Ye te nā sa smiṃvisaye,

Sā so syantā bhavanti ca;

Samāsataddhitantatte,

Majjhokārā ca honti hi.

Those which, in the domain of the case endings `nā`, `ssa`, and `smiṃ`, take the forms ending in `-sā` and `-so`;

and which, at the end of compounds and derivatives, indeed have 'o' in the middle.

Sokārantapayogā ca, kriyāyogamhi dissare;

Evaṃvidhā ca te saddā, ñeyyā “manogaṇo”iti.

And usages ending in '-so' are seen in connection with verbs;

Such words are to be known as 'the mind-group'.

Atra tassatthassa sādhakāni payogāni sāsanato ca lokato ca yathārahamāharitvā dassessāma – manasā ce pasannena, bhāsati vā karoti vā. Na mayhaṃ manaso piyo. Sādhukaṃ manasi karotha. Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā. Manoramaṃ, manodhātu, manomayena kāyena, iddhiyā upasaṅkami. Yo ve “dassa”nti vatvāna, adāne kurute mano. Vacasā paricitā. Vacaso vacasi.

Here, to demonstrate the examples that prove that meaning, we will present them appropriately from the Teaching and from the world: 'If one speaks or acts with a serene mind...'; 'Not pleasing to my mind'; 'Attend carefully in mind'; 'Mind precedes all mental states'; 'Delightful'; 'the mind-element'; '...with a mind-made body, he approached by psychic power'; 'Whoever, having said, "I shall give," then sets his mind on not giving'; 'Familiar in speech'; 'Of speech, in speech.'

Vacorasmīhi [M 0.0156] bodhesi, veneyyakumudañcidaṃ;

Rāgo sārāgarahito, visuddho buddhacandimā.

With rays of speech, you awaken this lotus of those to be guided; He, passionless, devoid of attachment, pure, the Buddha-moon.

Kassapassa vaco sutvā, alāto etadabravi;

Esa bhiyyo pasīdāmi, sutvāna munino vaco.

Hearing Kassapa's words, Alāta said this: "I am even more pleased, having heard the words of the sage."

Sakhā ca mitto ca mamāsi sīvika, susikkhito sādhu karohi me vaco. Ekūnatiṃso vayasā subhadda. Vayaso, vayasi, vayovuddho, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahanti. Jalantamiva tejasā. Tejaso, tejasi, tejodhātukusalo. Tejokasiṇaṃ. Tapasā uttamo, tapaso, tapasi, tapodhano, tapojigucchā. Kasmā bhavaṃ vijanamaraññanissito, tapo idha krubbasi brahmapattiyā. Cetasā aññāsi, evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi, etamatthaṃ cetasi sannidhāya, cetoparivitakkamaññāya. Cetopariyañāṇaṃ, ceto paricchindati, so parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca jānāti. Tamasā, tamaso, tamasi, tamonudo, tamoharo. Navāhametaṃ yasasā dadāmi. Yasaso, yasasi, yaso bhogasamappito. Yasoladdhākho panasmākaṃ bhogā. Yasodharā devī, yaso laddhā na majjeyya. Ayasāva malaṃ samuṭṭhitaṃ. Ayaso, ayasi, ayopākārapariyantaṃ, ayasā paṭikujjitaṃ. Seyyo ayoguḷo bhutto, ayopatto[M 0.0157], ayomayaṃ, ayo kantatīti ayokanto. Ghatena vā bhuñjassu payasā vā, sādhu khalu payaso pānaṃ yaññadattena, payasi ojā, payodharā, payonidhi. Sahassanetto sirasā paṭiggahi. Siraso, sirasi añjaliṃ katvā, vanditabbaṃ isiddhajaṃ. Siroruhā, siro chindati. Yo kāme parivajjeti, sappasseva padāsiro. Siro te vajjhayitvāna. Sarasā, saraso, tīṇi uppalajātāni, tasmiṃ sarasi brāhmaṇa. Saroruhaṃ. Yaṃ etā upasevanti, chandasāvā dhanenavā. Sāvittī chandaso mukhaṃ. Chandasi, chandoviciti, chandobhaṅgo, urasā panudahissāmi, uraso, urasi jāyati, urasilomo, uromajjhe vijjhi. Rahasā, rahaso, rahasi, rahogato nisīditvā, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā. Ahasā, ahasi. Jāyanti tattha pārohā, ahorattānamaccayeti imāni payogāni. Ettha ca “manena, manassa, mane, manasmiṃ, manamhī”tiādīni ca “manaāyatanaṃ tamaparāyano ayapatto chandahānī”tiādīni ca “na manaṃ aññāsi. Yasaṃ laddhāna dummedho. “Siraṃ chindatī”tiādīni ca rūpāni manogaṇabhāvappakāsakāni na hontīti na dassitāni, na alabbhamānavasena, tasmātra imā ādito paṭṭhāya manogaṇabhāvavibhāvinī gāthāyo bhavanti –

A friend and a companion you were, Sivika, well-trained; fulfill my word well. Twenty-nine years old, Subhadda. Of age, in age, aged, the qualities of age gradually fade away. Blazing, as if with splendor. Of splendor, in splendor, skilled in the element of splendor. The fire kasina. Supreme through austerity, of austerity, in austerity, rich in austerity, loathing austerity. Why, sir, having gone forth to the lonely forest, do you practice austerity here for the attainment of Brahma? He knew with his mind; thus, a reflection arose in his mind, having placed this meaning in his mind, knowing the reflection of the mind. Knowledge of others' minds; the mind discerns. He, with his mind, knows the minds of other beings, other persons. By darkness, of darkness, in darkness, dispeller of darkness, remover of darkness. I do not give this for the sake of fame. Of fame, in fame, fame endowed with wealth. The wealth we have is acquired through fame. Queen Yasodhara; having gained fame, one should not be intoxicated. From iron, rust has arisen. Of iron, in iron, bounded by an iron wall, covered with iron. Better to eat an iron ball, an iron pot, made of iron, iron cuts – therefore, an iron cutter. Eat with ghee or drink with milk; indeed, drinking milk is good when given by Yaññadatta. In milk there is essence; milk-bearing (clouds), the ocean of milk. The thousand-eyed one received it with his head. Of the head, on the head, having made a gesture of reverence, the banner of the sage should be worshipped. Hair of the head; he cuts off the head. Whoever avoids sensual pleasures, as a snake avoids its head from a foot. Having severed your head. By a lake, of a lake, three kinds of lotuses, in that lake, O Brahmin. A lotus. Those who resort to it, with meter or with wealth. Savitri is the mouth of the Vedas. In meter, metrical analysis, metrical break. With the chest I will push away; of the chest, on the chest, born on the chest, hairy-chested, pierced in the middle of the chest. By secret, of secret, in secret, having gone into seclusion and sat down, thus I reflected then. By day, in day. There, sprouts grow; by the passing of days and nights – these are the usages. And here, too, "by mind, of mind, in mind, from mind," etc., and "mind-sphere, devoted to that, iron bowl, loss of meter," etc., and "he did not know the mind. Having gained fame, the fool." "He cuts off the head," etc., and such forms do not reveal the nature of the mind-group – thus, they are not shown, not because they are unavailable. Therefore, from the beginning here, these verses reveal the nature of the mind-group.

“Manasā [M 0.0158] manaso manasi”,

Itiādivasā ṭhitā;

Sā so syantā saddarūpā,

Vuttā “manogaṇo”iti.

"By mind, of mind, in mind," and so forth, thus they stand; Those word-forms ending in 'sā', 'so', 'si', are called 'the mind-group'.

Manodhātu vacorasmi,

Vayovuddho tapoguṇo;

Tejodhātu tamonāso,

Yasobhogasamappito.

Mind-element, ray of speech; Aged, the quality of austerity; Element of splendor, destruction of darkness; Endowed with fame and wealth.

Cetoparivitakko ca, ayopatto payodharā;

Siroruhā saroruhaṃ, uromajjhe rahogato.

And mental reflection, iron bowl, clouds; Hair of the head, lotus; in the middle of the chest, gone into seclusion.

Chandobhaṅgo ahorattaṃ, manomaya’mayomayaṃ;

Evaṃvidho viseso yo, lakkhaṇantaṃ manogaṇe.

Breaking of meter, day and night, mind-made, iron-made; Such is the distinctive attribute, the characteristic in the mind-group.

“Vaco sutvā, siro chindi, ayo kantati” iccapi;

Upayogassa saṃsiddhi, lakkhaṇantaṃ manogaṇe.

"Having heard the word, he cut off the head, 'Iron cuts'," and so on; The perfect application, the characteristic in the mind-group.

Manogaṇe vuttanayo, itthiliṅge na labbhati;

Punnapuṃsakaliṅgesu, labbhateva yathārahaṃ.

The rule stated for the mind-group is not found in the feminine gender; but in the masculine and neuter genders, it is indeed found as is fitting.

Iccevaṃ sabbathāpi –

Thus, in all ways—

Sā so syantāni rūpāni, sandissanti manogaṇe;

Majjhokārantarūpā ca, sokārantūpayogatā.

Those forms ending in 'sā', 'so', 'si' are seen in the mind-group; and forms with a middle 'o' vowel, and those applicable with an ending in 'so'.

Idaṃ manogaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Evaṃ manogaṇalakkhaṇaṃ anākulaṃ niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ samuddiṭṭhaṃ.

This is the characteristic of the mind-group. Thus is the characteristic of the mind-group clearly, without confusion, without thickets, and without entanglements, explained.

Atha manogaṇādilakkhaṇaṃ kathayāma –

Now, we will explain the defining characteristics of the mind-group and so on.

Ye te nā sasmiṃvisaye,

Sā so syantā yathārahaṃ;

Samāsataddhitantatte,

Majjhokāro na honti tu.

Those which are not in this domain, those ending in 'sā', 'so', 'si' as is appropriate; in compounds and derivatives, the middle 'o' vowel does not occur.

Sokārantūpayogā [M 0.0159] ca,

Kriyāyoge na honti te;

Saddā evaṃvidhā sabbe;

Manogaṇādikā matā.

And usages of words ending in 'so' do not occur in conjunction with verbs; all such words are regarded as belonging to the mind-group, etc.

Seyyathidaṃ? “Bilaṃ padaṃ mukha”miccādayo. Tesaṃ rūpāni bhavanti – bilasā, bilaso, bilasi, bilagato, bilaṃ pāvisi. Padasāva agamāsi, tīṇi padavārāni, mākāsi mukhasā pāpaṃ, mukhagataṃ bhojanaṃ chaḍḍāpeti. Saccena danto damasā upeto. Rasavaraṃ rasamayaṃ rasaṃ pivīti. Idaṃ manogaṇādikalakkhaṇaṃ.

For example: "Bilaṃ, padaṃ, mukha," and so on. Their forms are: bilasā, bilaso, bilasi, bilagato, bilaṃ pāvisi. Padasāva agamāsi, tīṇi padavārāni, mākāsi mukhasā pāpaṃ, mukhagataṃ bhojanaṃ chaḍḍāpeti. Tamed by truth, endowed with self-control. He drank the excellent flavor, the flavor made of flavor. This is the characteristic of the mind-group and so on.

Aparampi bhavati –

Furthermore, it is said:

Ye samāsādibhāvamhi, majjhokārāva honti tu;

Nā sa smiṃvisaye sāso-syantā pana na hontihi.

Those which, in compounds and so forth, have the middle vowel 'o'; in that domain, the endings 'sā,' 'so,' and 'si' do not occur.

Sokārantūpayogā ca,

Kriyāyoge na honti te;

Saddā evaṃvidhā cāpi,

Manogaṇādikā matā.

And usages of words ending in 'so' do not occur in conjunction with verbs. Such words as these are also considered to belong to the mind-group and so on.

Seyyathidaṃ? “Āpo vāyo sarado”iccevamādayo. Tesaṃ rūpāni bhavanti – āpodhātu, vāyodhātu, āpokasiṇaṃ, vāyokasiṇaṃ, āpomayaṃ, vāyomayaṃ, jīva tvaṃ saradosataṃ, saradakālo. Āpena, āpassa, āpe, āpasmiṃ, āpamhi. Vāyena, vāyassa, vāye, vāyasmiṃ, vāyamhi. Saradena, saradassa, sarade, saradasmiṃ, saradamhi. Āpaṃ āpato sañjānāti. Vāyaṃ vāyato sañjānāti. Saradaṃ pattheti, saradaṃ ramaṇīyā nadī.

For example: "Water, air, autumn," and so on. Their forms are: āpodhātu (water element), vāyodhātu (air element), āpokasiṇaṃ (water kasina), vāyokasiṇaṃ (air kasina), āpomayaṃ (made of water), vāyomayaṃ (made of air), jīva tvaṃ saradosataṃ (live for a hundred autumns), saradakālo (autumn time). Āpena (by water), āpassa (of water), āpe (in water), āpasmiṃ (in water), āpamhi (in water). Vāyena (by air), vāyassa (of air), vāye (in air), vāyasmiṃ (in air), vāyamhi (in air). Saradena (by autumn), saradassa (of autumn), sarade (in autumn), saradasmiṃ (in autumn), saradamhi (in autumn). He perceives water as water. He perceives air as air. He desires autumn. In autumn, the river is delightful.

Keci [M 0.0160] panettha vadeyyuṃ “nanu sāsane vāyasaddo viya vāyusaddopi manogaṇādīsu icchitabbo”ti? Ettha vuccate –

Some here might say: "Surely in the Dispensation, should not the word 'vāyu,' like 'vāya,' also be included among the mind-group and so on?" Here it is said:

“Vāyu vāyo”ti etesu, pacchimoyeva icchito;

Manogaṇādīsu nādi, ādiggahavasenidha.

Among "Vāyu" and "Vāyo," only the latter is intended. In the mind-group and so on, the former is not, here, by way of taking the first form.

“Manodhātu vāyodhātu”, iccādīni padāni hi;

Akārantavaseneva, majjhokārāni sijjhare.

Indeed, words such as "Manodhātu" and "Vāyodhātu" are formed with a medial 'o' sound precisely by virtue of being a-final.

Vāyusaddamhi gahite, ādiggahavasenidha;

“Vāyodhātū”ti omajjhaṃ, rūpameva na hessati.

When the word 'vāyu' is taken, here, by way of taking the first form, the form with a medial 'o' like "Vāyodhātu" will simply not occur.

Yathā hi āyusaddassa, rūpaṃ dissati sāgamaṃ;

“Āyusā ekaputta”nti, manasādipadaṃ viya.

Just as the form of the word 'āyu' is seen with its augment, as in "Āyusā ekaputta," like the word 'manas' and so on.

Na tathā vāyusaddassa, rūpaṃ dissati sāgamaṃ;

Tasmā manogaṇādimhi, tasso’kāso na vijjati.

Not so is the form of the word 'vāyu' seen with its augment. Therefore, in the mind-group and so on, there is no scope for it.

Tathā hi “vāyati iti, vāyo” iti garū vaduṃ;

“Vāyodhātū”ti etassa, padassatthaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ.

For indeed, the teachers have said, "It blows, thus it is wind," explaining the meaning of the word "Vāyodhātu" in various places.

Yattha pathavī ca āpo ca, tejo vāyo na gādhati;

Ettha āpādikaṃ sadda-ttikaṃ manogaṇādike.

Where earth, water, fire, and air gain no footing; here, the triad of words beginning with 'āpa' belong to the mind-group and so on.

Idampi manogaṇādikalakkhaṇaṃ. Ettha manogaṇādikā dvidhā bhijjanti bila padādito āpādito ca. Evaṃ manogaṇādikalakkhaṇaṃ anākulaṃ niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ samuddiṭṭhaṃ.

This is also a characteristic of the mind-group and so on. Here, the mind-group and so on are divided in two: those beginning with 'bila' and 'pada', and those beginning with 'āpa'. Thus, the characteristic of the mind-group and so on has been clearly expounded as unconfused, free from thickets, and untangled.

Atha amanogaṇalakkhaṇaṃ kathayāma –

Now we shall explain the characteristic of the non-mind-group:

Ye ca nāvisaye sontā, ye ca smāvisaye siyuṃ;

Saddā evaṃpakārā te, amanogaṇasaññitā.

Those words which are in the domain of 'nā', and those which would be in the domain of 'smā'—such words are designated as the non-mind-group.

Ke [M 0.0161] te? Atthabyañjanakkharasaddādayo ceva dīghorasaddā ca. Etesu hi atthasaddādīnaṃ nāvacanaṭṭhāne “atthaso byañjanaso akkharaso suttaso upāyaso sabbaso ṭhānaso”tiādīni sontāni rūpāni bhavanti. Dīghorasaddānaṃ pana smāvacanaṭṭhāne “dīghaso oraso”ti sontāni rūpāni bhavanti. Idaṃ amanogaṇalakkhaṇaṃ.

What are they? The words 'attha', 'byañjana', 'akkhara', and so on, and also the words 'dīgha' and 'ora'. Among these, for the words 'attha' and so on, in place of the 'nā' inflection, forms such as "atthaso, byañjanaso, akkharaso, suttaso, upāyaso, sabbaso, ṭhānaso" occur. But for the words 'dīgha' and 'ora', in place of the 'smā' inflection, forms such as "dīghaso, oraso" occur. This is the characteristic of the non-mind-group.

Aparampi bhavati –

Furthermore, it is said:

Sabbathā vinimuttā ye, sā so syantādibhāvato;

Evaṃvidhāpi te saddā, amanogaṇasaññitā.

Those which are entirely free from the state of having 'sā', 'so', 'sya' endings and so on—even such words are designated as the non-mind-group.

Ke te? “Puriso kaññā citta”miccādayo. Idampi amanogaṇalakkhaṇaṃ. Evaṃ amanogaṇalakkhaṇaṃ anākulaṃ niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ samuddiṭṭhaṃ.

What are they? "Purisa" (man), "kaññā" (maiden), "citta" (mind), and so on. This, too, is a characteristic of the non-mind-group. Thus, the characteristic of the non-mind-group has been clearly expounded as unconfused, free from thickets, and untangled.

Evaṃ dassitesu manogaṇalakkhaṇādīsu koci vadeyya “yadidaṃ tumhehi vuttaṃ ‘ye samāsādibhāvamhi, majjhokārāva honti tū’tiādinā manogaṇādikalakkhaṇaṃ, tena “parosataṃ gomayaṃ godhano”iccādīsu goparasaddādayopi manogaṇādikabhāvaṃ āpajjantīti? Nāpajjanti. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā –

When the characteristics of the mind-group and so on have been shown in this way, someone might say: “By that which you have stated as the characteristic of the mind-group and so on, beginning with ‘those which, in compounds and so forth, have the middle vowel ‘o’,’ would not the words ‘go,’ ‘para,’ and so on, in examples like ‘parosataṃ,’ ‘gomayaṃ,’ and ‘godhano,’ also acquire the nature of the mind-group and so on?” They do not. And why? Because—

Ettha manogaṇādīnaṃ, antassottaṃ paṭiccidaṃ;

“Majjhokārā”ti vacanaṃ, vuttaṃ na tvāgamādikaṃ.

Here, for the mind-group and so on, the internal source is specified; the statement 'having a middle o' was made, but not concerning an augment or the like.

“Parosataṃ gomaya”nti-ādīsu amanogaṇo;

Pubbabhūtaṃ padaṃ ossā-gamattā’niccatāya ca.

In examples like 'parosataṃ' and 'gomayaṃ', the preceding word belongs to the non-mind-group, because its 'o' is an augment and is not a constant feature.

Tasmā nāpajjanti. Iti sabbathāpi amanogaṇalakkhaṇaṃ nissesato dassitaṃ. Iccevaṃ manogaṇavibhāvanāyaṃ manogaṇo manogaṇādiko amanogaṇo cāti tidhā bhedo veditabbo.

Therefore, they do not acquire that nature. Thus, in every way, the characteristic of the non-mind-group has been shown completely. In this explanation of the mind-group, the division should be understood as threefold: the mind-group, the mind-group-etc., and the non-mind-group.

Tattha [M 0.0162] manogaṇe pariyāpannasaddānaṃ samāsaṃ patvā “abyaggamanaso naro, thiracetasaṃ kulaṃ, saddheyyavacasā upāsikātiādinā liṅgattayavasena aññathāpi rūpāni bhavanti. Ettha pana keci evaṃ vadanti “yadā manasaddo sakatthe avattitvā ‘abyaggo mano yassa soyaṃ abyaggamanaso, alīno mano yassa soyaṃ alīnamanaso’ti evaṃ aññatthe vattati, tadā purisanayeneva nāmikapadamālā labbhati, na manogaṇanayenā”ti. Taṃ na gahetabbaṃ ubhinnampi yathārahaṃ labbhanato. Tathā hi visuddhimagge puggalāpekkhanavasena “khantisoraccamettādi-guṇabhūsitacetaso. Ajjhesanaṃ gahetvānā”ti ettha manogaṇanayo dissati. Taṭṭīkāyampi “ajjhesito dāṭhānāga-ttherena thiracetasā”ti manogaṇanayo dissati, tasmā tesaṃ vacanaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ vadantā ca te abyaggamanasaddādīnaṃ abyaggamanasaiccādinā sakārantapakatibhāvena ṭhapetabbabhāvaṃ vibbhantamativasena cintetvā sabbāsu vibhattīsu, dvīsu ca vacanesu purisanayena yojetabbataṃ maññanti. Evañca sati “guṇabhūsitacetaso, thiracetasā”ti chaṭṭhīcatutthītatiyārūpāni nasiyuṃ, aññāniyeva anabhimatāni rūpāni siyuṃ. Yasmā siyuṃ, tasmā evaṃ aggahetvā ayaṃ viseso gahetabbo.

Therein, words included in the mind-group, when in a compound, take forms such as “abyaggamanaso naro” (a man with an undistracted mind), “thiracetasaṃ kulaṃ” (a family with a steadfast mind), and “saddheyyavacasā upāsikā” (a female lay follower with trustworthy speech), varying according to the three genders. Some, however, argue thus: “When the word ‘manas’ is not used in its own sense but in another sense—as in ‘abyaggo mano yassa so’yaṃ abyaggamanaso’ (he whose mind is undistracted) or ‘alīno mano yassa so’yaṃ alīnamanaso’ (he whose mind is unattached)—then the nominal declension follows the pattern of ‘purisa’, not the pattern of the mind-group.” This should not be accepted, as both patterns are found where appropriate. For instance, in the Visuddhimagga, with reference to a person, the mind-group pattern is seen: “khantisoraccamettādi-guṇabhūsitacetaso. Ajjhesanaṃ gahetvānā” (having accepted the request of him whose mind was adorned with the qualities of patience, gentleness, loving-kindness, and so on). In its commentary as well, the mind-group pattern is seen: “ajjhesito dāṭhānāga-ttherena thiracetasā” (requested by the elder Dāṭhānāga, of steadfast mind). Therefore, their statement should not be accepted. Those who say this, thinking erroneously that words like ‘abyaggamanasa’ should be kept in their natural form ending in ‘sa’, believe they should be declined according to the pattern of ‘purisa’ in all cases and both numbers. If this were so, the sixth, fourth, and third case forms like ‘guṇabhūsitacetaso’ and ‘thiracetasā’ would not exist, and other, unintended forms would arise. Since this would be the case, this view should not be accepted; instead, this distinction should be understood.

Yattha hi samāsavasena manasaddo cetasaddādayo ca sakatthe avattitvā aññatthe vattanti, tattha sakārāgamānaṃ padānaṃ nāmikapadamālā purisanayena ca manogaṇe mananayena ca yathārahaṃ labbhati. Nissakārāgamānaṃ pana purisanayeneva labbhati. Yattha pana samāsavisayeyeva manādisaddā sakatthe vattanti, tattha nissakārāgamānaṃ nāmikapadamālā purisanayena ca manogaṇe mananayena ca labbhati.

Indeed, where, by means of compounding, words like ‘manas’, ‘cetas’, and so on do not occur in their own sense but in another sense, there the nominal declension of words with the ‘sa’ augment is obtained, as appropriate, by both the pattern of ‘purisa’ and the pattern of the mind-group. For those without the ‘sa’ augment, however, it is obtained only by the pattern of ‘purisa’. But where, in the context of a compound, words like ‘manas’ and so on do occur in their own sense, there the nominal declension of those without the ‘sa’ augment is obtained by both the pattern of ‘purisa’ and the pattern of the mind-group.

Idāni [M 0.0163] imassatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ, saddagatīsu ca viññūnaṃ kosalluppādanatthaṃ yathāvuttānaṃ padānaṃ padamālā tidhā katvā dassayissāma – “byāsatto mano yassa soyaṃ byāsattamanaso naro”ti evamaccantaṃ puggalāpekkhakassa imassa padassa –

Now, to make this meaning clear, and to produce skill in the wise regarding the ways of words, we will show the declension of the aforementioned words, having divided it into three. For this word, which is entirely with reference to a person, as in “byāsatto mano yassa so’yaṃ byāsattamanaso naro” (he whose mind is attached is a man called byāsattamanaso):

Byāsattamanaso naro, byāsattamanasā narā. Byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ, byāsattamanase nare. Byāsattamanasā, byāsattamanena narena, byāsattamanehi, byāsattamanebhi narehi. Byāsattamanaso, byāsattamanassa narassa, byāsattamanānaṃ narānaṃ. Byāsattamanā, byāsattamanasmā, byāsattamanamhā narā, byāsattamanehi, byāsattamanebhi narehi. Byāsattamanaso, byāsattamanassa narassa, byāsattamanānaṃ narānaṃ. Byāsattamanasi, byāsattamane, byāsattamanasmiṃ, byāsattamanamhi nare, byāsattamanesu naresu. Bho byāsattamanasa nara, bhavanto byāsattamanasā narāti nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

The nominal declension is as follows: Nominative: Byāsattamanaso naro, byāsattamanasā narā. Accusative: Byāsattamanasaṃ naraṃ, byāsattamanase nare. Instrumental: Byāsattamanasā, byāsattamanena narena; byāsattamanehi, byāsattamanebhi narehi. Genitive: Byāsattamanaso, byāsattamanassa narassa; byāsattamanānaṃ narānaṃ. Ablative: Byāsattamanā, byāsattamanasmā, byāsattamanamhā narā; byāsattamanehi, byāsattamanebhi narehi. Genitive: Byāsattamanaso, byāsattamanassa narassa; byāsattamanānaṃ narānaṃ. Locative: Byāsattamanasi, byāsattamane, byāsattamanasmiṃ, byāsattamanamhi nare; byāsattamanesu naresu. Vocative: Bho byāsattamanasa nara; bhavanto byāsattamanasā narā.

Evaṃ sakārāgamassa labbhamānālabbhamānatā vavatthapetabbā. Ettha hi paṭhamādutiyāvibhattīnaṃ ekavacanabahuvacanaṭṭhāne ca tatiyācatutthīchaṭṭhīsattamīnaṃ ekavacanaṭṭhāne ca yathārahaṃ sāgamo bhavati ādesasaravibhattisaraparattā. Ayañca nayo sukhumo sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

Thus, the presence or absence of the ‘sa’ augment should be determined. Here, the ‘sa’ augment occurs where appropriate in the singular and plural of the first and second inflections, and in the singular of the third, fourth, sixth, and seventh inflections, because of a following vowel of a substitute or a following vowel of an inflection. This subtle principle should be carefully kept in mind.

Aparo nayo – “byāsatto mano yassa soyaṃ byāsattamano”ti evampi puggalāpekkhakassa imassa padassa “byāsattamano naro, byāsattamanā narā. Byāsattamanaṃ nara”ntiādinā purisanayeneva nāmikapadamālā bhavati. Ettha pana sabbathāpi sāgamo natthi. Aparopi nayo – “byāsatto ca so mano cāti byāsattamano”ti evaṃ cittāpekkhakassapi imassa padassa “byāsattamano, byāsattamanā. Byāsattamanaṃ, byāsattamane. Byāsattamanasā, byāsattamanenā”tiādinā manogaṇe mananayena nāmikapadamālā bhavati, ettha pana tatiyācatutthīchaṭṭhīsattamīnaṃ [M 0.0164] ekavacanaṭṭhāneyeva sāgamo bhavati ādesasaraparattā. Yathā ca ettha, evaṃ “alīnamanaso naro”tiādīsupi ayaṃ tividho nayo veditabbo.

Another way: For the word ‘byāsattamano’, also with reference to a person, as in “he whose mind is attached is byāsattamano,” the nominal declension is only according to the pattern of ‘purisa’, as in “byāsattamano naro, byāsattamanā narā, byāsattamanaṃ nara,” and so on. Here, however, there is no ‘sa’ augment in any instance. Still another way: For the word ‘byāsattamano’, with reference to the mind itself, as in “it is an attached mind, thus byāsattamano,” the nominal declension is according to the pattern of the mind-group, as in “byāsattamano, byāsattamanā, byāsattamanaṃ, byāsattamane, byāsattamanasā, byāsattamanenā,” and so on. Here, however, the ‘sa’ augment occurs only in the singular of the third, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases, because of a following vowel of a substitute. And just as here, so also in examples like “alīnamanaso naro,” this threefold way should be understood.

Napuṃsakaliṅge pana vattabbe “byāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, byāsattamanāni kulāni. Byāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, byāsattamanāni kulāni. Byāsattamanasā kulenā”tiādinā nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Ettha pana paṭhamādutiyātatiyācatutthīchaṭṭhīsattamīnaṃ ekavacanaṭṭhāneyeva yathārahaṃ sāgamo bhavati ādesasaravibhattisaraparattā, ayampi nayo sukhumo sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbo.

But when the neuter gender is to be expressed, the nominal declension should be formed as follows: “byāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, byāsattamanāni kulāni. Byāsattamanasaṃ kulaṃ, byāsattamanāni kulāni. Byāsattamanasā kulenā,” and so on. Here, however, the ‘sa’ augment occurs where appropriate only in the singular of the first, second, third, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases, because of a following vowel of a substitute or a following vowel of an inflection. This subtle principle, too, should be carefully kept in mind.

Itthiliṅge pana vattabbe “byāsattamanasā itthī”ti evaṃ paṭhamekavacanaṭṭhāneyeva sāgamaṃ vatvā tato “byāsattamanā, byāsattamanāyo itthiyo. Byāsattamanaṃ itthi”nti kaññānayena yojetabbā. “Evaṃ saddheyyavacasā upāsikā, saddheyyavacāyo upāsikāyo. Saddheyyavacaṃ upāsika”ntiādināpi. “Byāsattamanaṃ kulaṃ, byāsattamanā itthī”tiādinā pana cittakaññānayena yojetabbā. Ettha pana sabbathāpi sāgamo natthi.

id

Sotūnaṃ ñāṇappabhedajananatthaṃ aparāpi nāmikapadamālāyo dassayissāma sahanibbacanena – mano eva mānasaṃ, samussāhitaṃ mānasaṃ yassa soyaṃ samussāhitamānaso. “Samussāhitamānaso, samussāhitamānasā. Samussāhitamānasaṃ, samussāhitamānase. Samussāhitamānasenā”ti purisanayena yojetabbā. Sundarā medhā assa atthīti sumedhaso. “Sumedhaso, sumedhasā. Sumedhasaṃ, sumedhase. Sumedhasenā”ti purisanayena, evaṃ “bhūrimedhaso”tiādīnampi. Tatrime payogā –

id

“Yaṃ [M 0.0165] vadanti sumedhoti, bhūripaññaṃ sumedhasaṃ;

Kiṃ nu tamhā vippavasi, muhuttamapi piṅgiya;

Gotamā bhūripaññāṇā, gotamā bhūrimedhasā.

id

Nāhaṃ tamhā vippavasāmi, muhuttamapi brāhmaṇa;

Gotamā bhūripaññāṇā, gotamā bhūrimedhasā”ti.

id

Itthiliṅge vattabbe “samussāhitamānasā sumedhasā”ti rūpāni, napuṃsake vattabbe “samussāhitamānasaṃ sumedhasa”nti rūpāni, kaññā cittanayena etesaṃ padamālā yojetabbā. Okārantapulliṅgaṭṭhāne itthiliṅgādivinicchayo nayappakāsanatthaṃ kato. Visesato hi okārantakathāyeva idhādhippetā. Apica loke nīti nāma nānappakārehi kathitā eva sobhati, ayañca sāsane nīti, tasmā nānappakārehi kathitāti.

id

Sabbāni nayato evaṃ, okārantapadānime;

Pulliṅgāni pavuttāni, sāsanatthaṃ mahesino.

id

Viseso tesu kesañci, pāḷiyaṃ yo padissati;

Paccattavacanaṭṭhāne, pakāsessāmi taṃ’dhunā.

id

“Vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge”, itiādinayena hi;

Katthacodantapulliṅga-rūpāni aññathā siyuṃ.

id

Paccattavacanicceva, tañca rūpaṃ pakāsaye;

“Paccatte bhummaniddeso”, iti bhāsanti kecana.

id

Tatra kānici suttapadāni dassessāma – natthi attakāre, natthi parakāre, natthi purisakāre, pariyantakate saṃsāre, jīve sattame, na hevaṃ vattabbe, bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantīti. Imāni [M 0.0166] ekavacanabahuvacanavasena dvidhā gahetabbāni. Paccattekavacanabahuvacanānañca ekārādeso veditabbo.

id

Ye pana “vanappagumbeti paccattavacanassa bhummavacananiddeso”ti vadanti, te vattabbā “yadi vanappagumbeti paccattavacanassa bhummavacananiddeso, evañca sati ‘thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacatī’ti ettha viya ādhārasutisambhavato ‘gimhāna māse paṭhamasmiṃ gimhe’ti idaṃ kataratthaṃ jotetī”ti? Te vadeyyuṃ “na mayaṃ bho ‘vanappagumbeti idaṃ bhummavacana’nti vadāma, atha kho ‘paccattavacanassa bhummavacananiddeso’ti vadāmā”ti. Evampi dosoyeva tumhākaṃ, nanu “saṅghe gotami dehī”ti etthāpi sampadānavacanassa bhummavacananiddesoti vuttepi saṅghassa dānakriyāya ādhārabhāvato “saṅghe”ti vacanaṃ suṇantānaṃ ādhārasuti ca ādhāraparikappo ca hotiyeva. Na hi sakkā evaṃ pavattaṃ cittaṃ nivāretuṃ, tasmā ettha evaṃ pana viseso gahetabbo “paccattavacanassapi katthaci bhummavacanassa viya rūpaṃ hotī”ti. Evañhi gahite na koci virodho. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu niruttippabhedakusalo lokānukampako bhagavā paccattavacanavasena niddisitabbe sati evaṃ aniddisitvā lokassa sammohamuppādayanto viya kathaṃ bhummavacananiddesaṃ karissati, tasmā saddasāmaññalesamattaṃ gahetvā “bhummavacananiddeso”ti na vattabbaṃ. Yadi saddasāmaññaṃ gahetvā bhummavacananiddesaṃ icchatha, “paccattekavacanassa upayogabahuvacananiddeso”tipi icchitabbaṃ siyā.

id

Apica tatheva “attakāre”ti paccattavacanassa bhummavacananiddese sati ādhārasutisambhavato “attakārasmiṃ kiñci vatthu natthī”ti anadhippeto attho siyā, na pana “attakāro natthī”ti adhippeto attho. “Upayogabahuvacananiddeso”ti gahaṇepi upayogatthassa natthisaddena [M 0.0167] avattabbattā dosoyeva siyā, atthisaddādīnaṃ viya pana natthisaddassapi paṭhamāya yogato “attakāre”ti idaṃ paccattavacanamevāti viññāyati. “Bāle ca paṇḍite ca sandhāvitvā saṃsaritvā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī”ti etthāpi paccattavacanassa “bhummavacananiddeso”ti vā “upayogavacananiddeso”ti vā gahaṇe sati “bālā ca paṇḍitā cā”ti ettakampi vattuṃ ajānanadoso siyā, “karissantī”ti padayogato pana “bāle cā”tiādi paccattavacanamevāti viññāyati. Yathā pana niggahītāgamavasenuccārite “cakkhuṃ udapādī”ti pade paccattavacanassa “cakkhuṃ me dehi yācito”ti ettha upayogavacanena sutivasena samānattepi paccattavacanatthoyeva sotāre paṭibhāti “udapādī”tiākhyātena kathitattā, na pana vibhattivipallāsatthabhūto upayogavacanattho “udapādī”tiākhyātena avacanīyattā, “cakkhuṃ udapādī”ti hi bhagavatā vuttakāle ko “cakkhuṃ udapādī”ti padaṃ parivattitvā atthamācikkhati, tathā “bāle paṇḍite”tiādīnampi paccattavacanānaṃ aparehi “bāle paṇḍite”tiādīhi bhummopayogavacanehi sutivasena samānattepi paccattavacanatthoyeva sotāre paṭibhāti, na itaravacanattho yathāpayogaṃ atthassa gahetabbattā. Iti “vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite”tiādīnaṃ suddhapaccattavacanattaññeva sārato paccetabbaṃ, na sutisāmaññena bhummopayogavacanattaṃ.

id

Yaṃ panācariyena jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ –

id

“Tayo giriṃ tiantaraṃ kāmayāmi,

Pañcālā kuruyo kekake ca;

Tatuttariṃ brāhmaṇa kāmayāmi,

Tikiccha maṃ brāhmaṇa kāmanīta”nti –

“I desire the three mountains and what is between them, the Pañcālas, the Kurus, and the Kekakas. Beyond that, brahmin, I desire more—heal me, brahmin, I am led by desire.”

Imassa [M 0.0168] kāmanītajātakassa saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “kekake cāti paccatte upayogavacanaṃ, tena kekakassa raṭṭhaṃ dassetī”ti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ vadanto ca so “purise passati, purise patiṭṭhita”nti, “passāmi loke sadhane manusse”ti ca ādīsu yebhuyyena “purise, loke, sadhane, manusse”tiādīnaṃ upayogabahuvacanabhummekavacanabhāvena āgatattā paccattekavacanabahuvacanabhāvassa pana apākaṭattā yebhuyyappavattiṃ sandhāya “idampi tādisamevā”ti maññamāno vadati maññe. Ācariyā hi katthaci attano ruciyāpi visuṃ visuṃ kathenti. Ayaṃ pana amhākaṃ ruci – “kekake”ti idaṃ paccattavacanameva “pañcālā, kuruyo”ti sahajātapadāni viya, raṭṭhavācakattā pana “kuruyo”ti padamiva bahuvacanavasena vuttaṃ. Na hi bhagavā “khattiyo, brāhmaṇo, vesso”tiādīsu viya samānavibhattīhi niddisitabbesu sahajātapadesu pacchimaṃ upayogavacanavasena niddiseyya, yutti ca na dissati “pañcālā”ti, “kuruyo”ti paccattavacanaṃ vatvā “kekake”ti upayogavacanassa vacane, tasmā “kekake”ti idaṃ paccattavacanameva. Tathā hi sandhivisodhanavidhāyako ācariyo tādisānaṃ padānaṃ paccattavacanattaññeva vibhāvento sāmaṃ kate pakaraṇe “vanappagumbo vanappagumbe, sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ jīvo, sukhe dukkhe jīve”ti āha, ṭīkāyampi ca tesaṃ paccattavacanabhāvameva vibhāvento “vanappagumbo, sukhaṃ, dukkhaṃ, jīvo”ti sādhanīyaṃ rūpaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā niggahītalopavasena akārokārānañca ekārādesavasena “vanappagumbe, sukhe, dukkhe, jīve”ti rūpanipphattimāha. Sā pāḷinayānu kūlā. Kaccāyanācariyenapi pāḷinayaṃ nissāya “dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe”ti paccattabahuvacanapadaṃ vuttaṃ. Tenāha vuttiyaṃ “dve padāni tulyādhikaraṇānī”ti. “Dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe”ti [M 0.0169] ca idaṃ “aṭṭha nāgāvāsasatānī”ti vattabbe “aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate”ti padamiva vuccatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the commentary on the Kāmanīta Jātaka, it is said: “‘Kekake ca’ is an accusative with a locative sense; thereby it indicates the country of the Kekakas.” And he who says this, seeing that in phrases such as “he sees men (purise), he is established among men (purise)” and “I see in the world (loke) wealthy people (sadhane manusse),” the words “purise, loke, sadhane, manusse,” and so on, mostly occur as plural accusatives with a locative sense or as locative singulars, while their nature as nominative/accusative singular or plural is not evident, he thinks, I suppose, “This too is just like that,” and speaks thus, considering the general usage. For teachers sometimes explain things differently according to their own preference. This, however, is our preference: this word ‘kekake’ is indeed a nominative/accusative, like the coordinate terms ‘pañcālā’ and ‘kuruyo’; but because it denotes a country, it is stated in the plural, like the word ‘kuruyo.’ For the Blessed One would not, in the case of coordinate terms that should be specified with the same case ending, such as ‘khattiyo, brāhmaṇo, vesso,’ specify the last one as an accusative with a locative sense. And no reason is seen for saying ‘pañcālā’ and ‘kuruyo’ as nominative/accusatives and then stating ‘kekake’ as an accusative with a locative sense. Therefore, ‘kekake’ is indeed a nominative/accusative. Thus, the teacher who composed the Sandhivisodhana, analyzing the very nominative/accusative nature of such terms, stated in the treatise he himself composed: “vanappagumbo vanappagumbe, sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ jīvo, sukhe dukkhe jīve.” And in the sub-commentary, explaining their very nominative/accusative nature, he establishes the derivable forms as “vanappagumbo, sukhaṃ, dukkhaṃ, jīvo,” and then, by eliding the niggahīta and substituting ‘e’ for ‘a’ and ‘o,’ he states the derivation of the forms “vanappagumbe, sukhe, dukkhe, jīve.” This is in accordance with the Pāli method. Teacher Kaccāyana also, relying on the Pāli method, stated the nominative/accusative plural term in the rule “dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe.” Thus he says in the commentary: “two terms in the same case.” And this phrase “dvipade tulyādhikaraṇe” should be understood as being like the word `aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate` which is said when `aṭṭha nāgāvāsasatāni` should be said.

Keci pana tesaṃ bhummekavacanattaṃ icchanti. Tattha yadi “vanappagumbe”ti paccatte bhummavacanaṃ, “kekake”ti ca paccatte upayogavacanaṃ, “esese eke ekaṭṭhe”ti ettha “esese”ti imānipi paccatte bhummavacanāni vā siyuṃ, upayogavacanāni vā. Yathetāni evaṃvidhāni na honti, suddhapaccattavacanāniyeva honti, tathā “vanappagumbe, kekake”tiādīnipi tathāvidhāni na honti, suddhapaccattavacanāniyeva honti. Iccevaṃ sabbathāpi “vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite, kekake”ti, “viratte kosiyāyane, aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate, ke purise, esese”ti evamādīnaṃ anekesaṃ purisaliṅgaitthiliṅganapuṃsakaliṅgasabbanāmaekavacanaanekavacanavasena sāsanavare ṭhitānaṃ padānaṃ nipphatti paccattekavacanaputhuvacanānamekārādesavaseneva bhavatīti avassamidaṃ sampaṭicchitabbaṃ. Evaṃ “vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite”tiādīnaṃ suddhapaccattavacanatā atīva sukhumā dubbiññeyyā, saddhena kulaputtena ācariye payirupāsitvā tadupadesaṃ sakkaccaṃ gahetvā jānitabbā. Buddhavacanasmiñhi saddato ca atthato ca adhippāyato ca akkharacintakānaṃ ñāṇacakkhusammuyhanaṭṭhānabhūtā pāḷinayā vividhā dissanti.

Some, however, wish for them to be locative singulars. In that case, if ‘vanappagumbe’ were a locative singular, and ‘kekake’ an accusative with a locative sense, then in ‘esese eke ekaṭṭhe,’ these words ‘esese’ could also be either locative singulars or accusatives with a locative sense. Just as these are not of such a kind, but are purely nominative/accusatives, so too ‘vanappagumbe,’ ‘kekake,’ and so on are not of that kind, but are purely nominative/accusatives. Thus, in every case, the formation of the many words standing in the excellent Dispensation—such as ‘vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite, kekake,’ ‘viratte kosiyāyane, aṭṭha nāgāvāsasate, ke purise, esese,’ in masculine, feminine, and neuter genders, as pronouns, in singular and plural numbers—must necessarily be accepted as occurring solely through the substitution of ‘e’ for the nominative/accusative singular and plural endings. This must certainly be accepted. In this way, the purely nominative/accusative nature of words like ‘vanappagumbe, bāle, paṇḍite,’ and so on, is extremely subtle and difficult to discern; it should be known by a faithful clansman after attending upon a teacher and carefully receiving their instruction. For in the word of the Buddha, various Pāli methods are seen which are places of confusion for the eye of wisdom of those who analyze letters, with respect to sound, meaning, and intention.

Tattha saddato tāva idaṃ sammuyhanaṭṭhānaṃ – “virattā kosiyāyanī”ti vattabbe “viratte kosiyāyane”ti itthiliṅgapaccattavacanaṃ dissati, “ko puriso”ti vattabbe “ke purise”ti sabbanāmikapaccattavacanaṃ dissati, “kinnāmo te upajjhāyo”ti vattabbe “konāmo te upajjhāyo”ti samāsapadaṃ pulliṅgavisayaṃ dissati. Kiṃ nāmaṃ etassāti [M 0.0170] konāmoti hi samāso. Tena “konāmā itthī, konāmaṃ kula”nti ayampi nayo gahetabbo. “Kva te balaṃ mahārājā”ti vattabbe “ko te balaṃ mahārājā”ti ettha kvasaddena īsakaṃ samānasutiko sattamiyanto kosaddo dissati, kva kosaddā hi aññamaññamīsakasamānasutikā. Tathā “idha hemantagimhesu, idha hemantagimhisu, na tenatthaṃ abandhi so, na tenatthaṃ abandhisū”ti aññānipi yojetabbāni.

Therein, with respect to sound, this is a place of confusion: when “virattā kosiyāyanī” (Kosiyāyanī is detached) should be said, the feminine nominative/accusative “viratte kosiyāyane” is seen. When “ko puriso” (which man?) should be said, the pronominal nominative/accusative “ke purise” is seen. When “kinnāmo te upajjhāyo” (what is your preceptor’s name?) should be said, the compound word “konāmo te upajjhāyo,” pertaining to the masculine, is seen. For ‘konāmo’ is a compound of ‘kiṃ nāmaṃ etassa’ (what is its name?). By this, the method for “konāmā itthī” (what is the woman’s name?) and “konāmaṃ kulaṃ” (what is the family’s name?) should also be taken. When “kva te balaṃ mahārājā” (where is your army, great king?) should be said, here in “ko te balaṃ mahārājā,” the word ‘ko’ is seen, which is slightly similar in sound to the word ‘kva’ and has a locative sense. For the words ‘kva’ and ‘ko’ are indeed slightly similar in sound to each other. Similarly, other examples should be applied: “idha hemantagimhesu, idha hemantagimhisu” (here in winter and summer), “na tenatthaṃ abandhi so, na tenatthaṃ abandhisū” (he did not bind the meaning with that, they did not bind the meaning with that).

Atthato pana idaṃ sammuyhanaṭṭhānaṃ – “yaṃ na kañcanadvepiñcha, andhena tamasā gata”nti ettha nakāro “kata”nti iminā sambandhitabbo. Na katanti kataṃ viyāti attho. Ettha hi nakāro upamāne vattati, na paṭisedhe.

With respect to meaning, this is a place of confusion: in the phrase “yaṃ na kañcanadvepiñcha, andhena tamasā gata,” the particle ‘na’ should be connected with ‘kataṃ.’ The meaning of ‘na kataṃ’ is ‘as if done.’ For here the particle ‘na’ is used in the sense of a simile, not in negation.

“Assaddho akataññū ca,

Sandhicchedo ca yo naro;

Hatāvakāso vantāso,

Sa ve uttamaporiso”ti

“The faithless, the ungrateful, the breaker of connections, one who has destroyed opportunity, who has given up hope—he is indeed the highest person.”

Evamādīnipi aññāni yojetabbāni.

Similarly, other such examples should be applied.

Adhippāyato idaṃ sammuyhanaṭṭhānaṃ – “taṇhaṃ asmimānaṃ sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyo dvādasāyatananissitaṃ nandirāgañca hantvā brāhmaṇo anīgho yātī”ti vattabbepi tathā avatvā tamevatthaṃ gahetvā aññena pariyāyena

With respect to intention, this is a place of confusion: although it should be said, “Having destroyed craving, the conceit ‘I am,’ the views of eternalism and annihilationism, and the delight and lust dependent on the twelve sense bases, the brahmin proceeds untroubled,” it is not stated thus, but taking that very meaning, it is expressed by another method:

“Mātaraṃ pitaraṃ hantvā, rājāno dve ca khattiye;

Raṭṭhaṃ sānucaraṃ hantvā, anīgho yāti brāhmaṇo”ti

“Having slain mother and father, two warrior kings, and the kingdom with its follower, the brahmin proceeds untroubled.”

Vuttaṃ.

It is said.

“Vanaṃ [M 0.0171] chindatha mā rukkhaṃ, vanato jāyate bhayaṃ;

Chetvā vanañca vanathaṃ, nibbanā hotha bhikkhavo”ti

“Cut down the forest, but not a tree; from the forest fear is born. Having cut down the forest and its undergrowth, be free from the forest, O bhikkhus.”

Evamādīnipi aññāni yojetabbāni. Evaṃ buddhavacane saddato ca atthato ca adhippāyato ca akkharacintakānaṃ ñāṇacakkhusammuyhanaṭṭhānabhūtā pāḷinayā vividhā dissanti. Yathāha –

Similarly, other such examples should be applied. Thus, in the word of the Buddha, various Pāli methods are seen which are places of confusion for the eye of wisdom of those who analyze letters, with respect to sound, meaning, and intention. As it is said:

“Jānantā api saddasatthamakhilaṃ muyhanti pāṭhakkame,

Yebhuyyena hi lokanītividhurā pāṭhe nayā vijjare;

Paṇḍiccampi pahāya bāhiragataṃ ettheva tasmā budho,

Sikkheyyāmaladhammasāgaratare nibbānatitthūpage”ti.

“Even those who know the entire science of grammar become confused in the textual method, for methods are found in the text that are mostly devoid of worldly convention. Therefore, abandoning external erudition, the wise should train right here in this stainless ocean of Dhamma, approaching the ford of Nibbāna.”

Evaṃ pāḷinayānaṃ dubbiññeyyattā “vanappagumbe, bāle ca, paṇḍite cā”tiādīnaṃ suddhapaccattavacanattaññeva sārato paccetabbaṃ, na sutisāmaññena bhummopayogavacanattaṃ bhummopayogavacanehi tesaṃ samānasutikattepi paccattajotakattā. Samānasutikāpi hi saddā atthappakaraṇaliṅgasaddantarābhisambandhādivasena atthavisesajotakā bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? “Sīho gāyatī”ti vutte “evaṃnāmako puriso”ti attho viññāyati. “Sīho naṅguṭṭhaṃ cāletī”ti vutte pana “migarājā”ti viññāyati. Evaṃ atthavasena samānasutikānaṃ atthavisesajotanaṃ bhavati. Saṅgāme ṭhatvā “sindhavamānehī”ti vutte “asso”ti viññāyati. Rogisālāyaṃ pana “sindhavamānehī”ti vutte “lavaṇa”nti viññāyati. Evaṃ pakaraṇavasena samānasutikānaṃ atthavisesajotanaṃ bhavati. “Issā”ti vutte “evaṃnāmikā dhammajātī”ti viññāyati. “Isso”ti vutte pana “acchamigo”ti viññāyati. Evaṃ liṅgavasena ekadesasamānasutikānaṃ atthavisesajotanaṃ bhavati. Ettha pana kiñcāpi “devadattaṃ pakkosa ghaṭadhārakaṃ [M 0.0172] daṇḍadhāraka”ntiādīsupi ghaṭadaṇḍādīni liṅgaṃ, tathāpi samānasutikādhikārattā na taṃ idhādhippetaṃ.

Thus, due to the difficulty of understanding the Pāli system, it should be accepted in essence that words such as 'vanappagumbe', 'bāle', and 'paṇḍite' are purely nominative case words, not locative usage words by mere similarity of sound. For even though they sound similar to locative usage words, they indicate the nominative case. For indeed, even words with similar sounds convey distinct meanings based on meaning, context, gender, and connection with other words. How so? When it is said, "Sīho gāyati," the meaning understood is "a man of that name." But when it is said, "Sīho naṅguṭṭhaṃ cāleti," the meaning understood is "the king of beasts." Thus, words with similar sounds convey distinct meanings based on their meaning. Standing in battle, if it is said, "Bring the Sindhava," it is understood as "a horse." But in a sickroom, if it is said, "Bring the Sindhava," it is understood as "salt." Thus, words with similar sounds convey distinct meanings based on the context. When it is said, "Issā," it is understood as "a mental state of that name." But when it is said, "Isso," it is understood as "a bear." Thus, words with partially similar sounds convey distinct meanings based on gender. Here, although in phrases like "Summon Devadatta, the pot-bearer, the staff-bearer," the pot and staff are also characteristics (liṅga), because the topic concerns words of similar sound, that is not the intended meaning here.

“Issā uppajjatī”ti ca “issā purisamanubandhiṃsū”ti ca vutte pana sabbathā samānasutikānaṃ saddantarābhisambandhavasena yathāvuttaatthavisesajotanaṃ bhavati. Tathā “sīho bhikkhave migarājā sāyanhasamayaṃ āsayā nikkhamatī”ti vutte “migādhipo kesarasīho”ti viññāyati. “Sīho samaṇuddeso, sīho senāpatī”ti ca vutte pana “sīho nāma sāmaṇero, sīho nāma senāpatī”ti viññāyati. Evampi saddantarābhisambandhavasena samānasutikānaṃ atthavisesajotanaṃ bhavati. “Addasaṃsu kho chabbaggiyā bhikkhū sattarasavaggiye bhikkhū vihāraṃ paṭisaṅkharonte”ti evampi saddantarābhisambandhavasena samānasutikānaṃ paccattopayogatthasaṅkhātaatthavisesajotanaṃ bhavati. Tathā “siñca bhikkhu imaṃ nāvaṃ, aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavocā”ti evampi saddantarābhisambandhavasena samānasutikānaṃ ālapanatthapaccattatthasaṅkhātaatthavisesajotanaṃ bhavati, tasmā “vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge”tiādīni bhummopayogavacanehi sadisattepisaddantarābhisambandhavasena suddhapaccattavacanānīti gahetabbāni. Paccattekavacanabahuvacanānaṃ eva hi ekārādesavasena evaṃvidhāni rūpāni bhavanti bhummopayogavacanāni viyāti. Nanu ca bho evaṃvidhānaṃ rūpānaṃ pāḷiyaṃ dissanato ‘ekārantampi pulliṅgaṃ atthī’ti vattabbanti? Na vattabbaṃ, okārantabhāvogadharūpavisesattā tesaṃ rūpānaṃ. Ādesavasena hi siddhattā visuṃ ekārantapulliṅgaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā pulliṅgānaṃ yathāvuttasattavidhatāyeva gahetabbāti.

When it is said, "Issā uppajjati" (Envy arises), and "Issā purisamanubandhiṃsu" (Envy followed the men), for words of completely identical sound, the clarification of the specific meaning occurs through association with other words, as stated before. Similarly, when it is said, "Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, emerges from his lair in the evening," it is understood as "the lord of beasts, the maned lion." But when it is said, "Sīha the novice, Sīha the general," it is understood as "a novice named Sīha, a general named Sīha." In this way, too, the specific meaning of words of identical sound is clarified through association with other words. Again, when it is said, "The group-of-six monks saw the group-of-seventeen monks repairing the monastery," here too, for words of identical sound, the specific meaning, known as the meaning of nominative usage, is clarified through association with other words. Similarly, when it is said, "O monk, bail out this boat," and "a certain monk said this to the Blessed One," here too, for words of identical sound, the specific meaning, known as the meaning of the vocative and the nominative, is clarified through association with other words. Therefore, expressions like "vanappagumbe yatha phussitagge" should be taken as purely nominative case words through association with other words, despite their similarity to locative usage words. For it is for the nominative singular and plural that such forms arise through the substitution of the vowel 'e', appearing like locative usage words. Now, good sirs, since such forms are seen in the Pāli texts, should it be said that "there is also a masculine gender ending in -e"? It should not be said, because those forms are a special type of form that is fundamentally of the -o stem. Since they are established through substitution, there is no separate masculine gender ending in -e. Therefore, the sevenfold classification of masculine words, as previously stated, should be accepted.

Keci [M 0.0173] pana vadeyyuṃ “yāyaṃ purisasaddanayaṃ gahetvā ‘bhūto, bhūtā. Bhūta’ntiādinā sabbesamokārantapadānaṃ nāmikapadamālā vibhattā, tattha catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitāni rūpāni kimatthaṃ na vuttānī”ti? Visesadassanatthaṃ. Tādisāni hi catutthekavacanarūpāni pāḷinaye porāṇaṭṭhakathānaye ca upaparikkhiyamāne “gatyatthakammani, nayanatthakammani, vibhattivipariṇāme, tadatthe cā”ti saṅkhepato imesu catūsuyeva ṭhānesu, pabhedato pana sattasu ṭhānesu dissanti. Dānarocanadhāraṇanamoyogādibhede pana yattha katthaci sampadānavisaye na dissanti, iti imaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ na vuttānīti. Nanu dānakriyāyoge “abhirūpāya kaññā deyyā”ti catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitarūpadassanato imasmimpi saddanītippakaraṇe “purisāya, bhūtāyā”tiādīni vattabbāni, evaṃ sante kasmā “dānarocanadhāraṇanamoyogādibhede pana yattha katthaci sampadānavisaye na dissantī”ti vuttanti? Apāḷinayattā. “Abhirūpāya kaññā deyyā”ti ayañhi saddasatthato āgato nayo, na buddhavacanato. Buddhavacanañhi patvā “abhirūpassa kaññā deyyā”ti padarūpaṃ bhavissatīti. Nanu ca bho namoyogādīsupi catutthekavacanassa āyādeso dissatīti. Sāsanāvacarāpi hi nipuṇā paṇḍitā “namo buddhāyā”tiādīni vatvā ratanattayaṃ vandanti. Keci pana –

But some might say: "Taking the masculine noun 'purisa' as the model, the nominal declension for all nouns ending in -o, such as 'bhūto, bhūtā, bhūta,' has been presented. Why then are the forms for the dative singular, together with the 'āya' substitution, not mentioned there?" It is to show a distinction. For upon examination in the Pāli system and the ancient commentaries, such forms of the dative singular are found only in these four contexts in brief—namely, as the object of verbs of motion, as the object of verbs of purpose, in the change of case-ending, and in the sense of 'for the sake of that'. When analyzed in detail, they are seen in seven contexts. However, in the various instances of the dative case, such as in connection with giving, pleasing, owing, and homage, they are not found anywhere. Thus, to show this distinction, they were not mentioned. But is it not so that in the context of the act of giving, the appearance of the dative singular form with the 'āya' substitution is seen in "abhirūpāya kaññā deyyā" (a girl should be given to a handsome man)? Therefore, in this grammatical treatise too, forms like 'purisāya', 'bhūtāya', and so on should be stated. If so, why was it said that 'in the various instances of the dative case, such as in connection with giving, pleasing, owing, and homage, they are not found anywhere'?" Because it is not in accordance with the Pāli system. The usage "abhirūpāya kaññā deyyā" comes from the science of grammar, not from the word of the Buddha. In the word of the Buddha, the form of the word would be "abhirūpassa kaññā deyyā." But is it not so, good sirs, that even in connection with homage and so on, the 'āya' substitution for the dative singular is seen? For even skilled and learned scholars within the Dispensation, when venerating the Triple Gem, say things like "namo buddhāya". Yet some say—

“Namo buddhāya buddhassa,

Namo dhammāya dhammino;

Namo saṅghāya saṅghassa,

Namokārena sotthi me”ti ca,

Homage to the Buddha, and to the Buddha; Homage to the Dhamma, and to the possessor of Dhamma; Homage to the Saṅgha, and to the Saṅgha; Through this act of homage, may there be well-being for me.

“Mukhe [M 0.0174] sarasi samphulle, nayanuppalapaṅkaje;

Pādapaṅkajapūjāya, buddhāya satataṃ dade”ti ca,

Upon the face like a blossoming lake, upon the eyes like a pond of lotuses; for the worship of the lotus-feet, I constantly make an offering to the Buddha.

“Naro naraṃ yācati kiñci vatthuṃ, narena dūto pahito narāyā”ti ca gāthāracanampi kubbantīti? Saccaṃ, sāsanāvacarāpi nipuṇā paṇḍitā “namo buddhāyā”tiādīnivatvā ratanattayaṃ vandanti, gāthāracanampi kubbanti, evaṃ santepi te saddasatthe kataparicayavasena saddasatthato nayaṃ gahetvā tathārūpā gāthāpi cuṇṇiyapadānipi abhisaṅkharonti, “namo buddhāyā”tiādīni vatvā ratanattayaṃ vandanti. Ye pana saddasatthe akataparicayā antamaso bāladārakā, tepi aññesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā kataparicayavasena “namo buddhāyā”tiādīni vatvā ratanattayaṃ vandanti, “namo buddhassā”ti vadantā pana appakatarā. Katthaci hi padese kumārake akkharasamayaṃ uggaṇhāpentā garū akkharānamādimhi “namo buddhāyā”ti sikkhāpenti, na pana “namo buddhassā”ti, evaṃ santepi pāḷinaye porāṇaṭṭhakathānaye ca upaparikkhiyamāne ṭhapetvā gatyatthakammādiṭṭhānacatukkaṃ, pabhedato sattaṭṭhānaṃ vā dānarocanadhāraṇanamoyogādibhede yattha katthaci sampadānavisaye catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitāni rūpāni na dissanti, tasmā kehici abhisaṅkhatāni “namo buddhāya, buddhāya dānaṃ dentī”ti padāni pāḷiṃ patvā “namo buddhassa, buddhassa dānaṃ dentī”ti aññarūpāni bhavantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana pāḷinayaaṭṭhakathānayānurūpena āyādesassa payogaracanā – “buddhāya saraṇaṃ gacchati, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchatī”ti vā, “buddhāya nagaraṃ nenti, buddhaṃ nagaraṃ nentī”ti vā, “buddhāya sakkato dhammo, buddhena sakkato dhammo”ti vā, “buddhāya jīvitaṃ pariccajati, buddhassa atthāya jīvitaṃ pariccajatī”ti vā, “buddhāya apenti aññatitthiyā, buddhasmā apenti aññatitthiyā”ti vā[M 0.0175], “buddhāya dhammatā, buddhassa dhammatā”ti vā, “buddhāya pasanno, buddhe pasanno”ti vā iti pabhedato imaṃ sattaṭhānaṃ vivajjetvā aññattha āyādeso na dissati. Tathā hi –

id

Pāṭhe mahānamakkāra-saṅkhāte sādhunandane;

Sampadāne namoyoge, āyādeso na dissati.

id

Ettha mahānamakkārapāṭho nāma “namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti pāṭho. Atrāpi āyādeso na dissati. Vammikasuttepi “namo karohi nāgassā”ti evaṃ āyādeso na dissati. Ambaṭṭhasuttepi “sotthi bhadante hotu rañño, sotthi janapadassa”. Evaṃ āyādeso na dissati.

id

“Suppabuddha”nti pāṭhassa, atthasaṃvaṇṇanāyapi;

Sampadāne namoyoge, āyādeso na dissati.

id

Tathā hi

id

“Suppabuddhaṃ pabujjhanti, sadā gotamasāvakā;

Yesaṃ divā ca ratto ca, niccaṃ buddhagatā satī”ti

id

Imissā pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “sammādiṭṭhikassa putto guḷaṃ khipamāno buddhānussatiṃ āvajjetvā ‘namo buddhassā’ti vatvā guḷaṃ khipatī”ti āyādesavajjito saddaracanāviseso dissati. Sagāthāvaggavaṇṇanāyampi dhanañjānīsuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tvaṃ ṭhitāpi nisinnāpi khipitvāpi kāsetvāpi ‘namo buddhassā’ti tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa namakkāraṃ karosī”ti āyādesavajjito saddaracanāviseso dissati. Tathā tattha tattha “buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ deti. Tassa [M 0.0176] purisassa bhattaṃ na ruccati. Samaṇassa rocate saccaṃ, buddhassa chattaṃ dhāreti, buddhassa silāghate”tiādinā āyādesavivajjito saddaracanāviseso dissati. Evaṃ dānarocanādīsu bahūsu sampadānavisayesu catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitaṃ rūpaṃ na dissati.

id

Gatyatthakammādīsu pana catūsu ṭhānesu dissati. Tathā hi “mūlāya paṭikasseyya, appo saggāya gacchatī”ti cettha gatyatthakammani dissati. Ettha hi “mūlaṃ paṭikasseyya, appo saggaṃ gacchatī”ti ca attho. “Paṭikasseyyā”ti cettha kasa gatiyanti dhātussa patiupasaggena visesitattā “ākaḍḍheyyā”ti attho bhavati. “Ayaṃ puriso mama atthakāmo, yo maṃ gahetvāna dakāya netī”ti ettha nayanatthakammani dissati. Ettha hi maṃ udakaṃ neti, attano vasanakasobbhaṃ pāpetīti attho. “Viramathāyasmanto mama vacanāyā”ti ettha vibhattivipariṇāme dissati. Mama vacanato viramathāti hi nissakkavacanavasena attho. “Mahāgaṇāya bhattā me”ti etthāpi vibhattivipariṇāme dissati. Mama mahato haṃsagaṇassa bhattāti hi sāmivacanavasena attho. Mama haṃsarājāti cettha adhippāyo. “Asakkatā casma dhanañcayāyā”ti etthāpi vibhattivipariṇāme dissati. Mayaṃ dhanañcayassa rañño asakkatā ca bhavāmāti hi kattutthe sāmivacanaṃ. Tathā hi “dhanañcayassā”ti vā “dhanañcayenā”ti vā vattabbe evaṃ avatvā “dhanañcayāyā”ti sampadānavacanaṃ dānakriyādikassa sampadānavisayassa abhāvato vibhattivipariṇāmeyeva yujjati, tasmā dhanañcayarājena mayaṃ asakkatā ca bhavāmāti attho gahetabbo. Aññampi vibhattivipariṇāmaṭṭhānaṃ maggitabbaṃ.

id

“Virāgāya [M 0.0177] upasamāya nirodhāyā”tiādīni pana anekasahassāni āyādesasahitāni saddarūpāni tadatthe pavattanti. Aṭṭhakathācariyāpi hi dhammavinayasaddatthaṃ vaṇṇentā “dhammānaṃ vinayāya. Anavajjadhammatthañhesa vinayo, na bhavabhogādiattha”nti tadatthavaseneva āyādesasahitaṃ saddarūpaṃ payuñjiṃsu, evaṃ catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitāni rūpāni gatyatthakammani nayanatthakammani vibhattivipariṇāme tadatthe cāti imesu catūsuyeva ṭhānesu dissanti, na pana dānarocanādibhede yattha katthaci sampadānavisaye. Tathā hi niruttipiṭake “atthāyāti sampadānavacana”nti āyādesasahitaṃ saddarūpaṃ vuttaṃ, purisasaddādivasena pana tādisāni rūpāni na vuttāni tādisānaṃ saddarūpānaṃ yattha katthaci appavattanato. Kaccāyanappakaraṇepi hi “āya catutthekavacanassa tū”ti lakkhaṇassa vuttiyaṃ “atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna”nti vuttaṃ. “Purisāyā”ti vā “samaṇāyā”ti vā “brāhmaṇāyā”ti vā na vuttanti.

"For dispassion, for appeasement, for cessation"—these and many thousands of sound-forms accompanied by the āya-substitution are used in that sense. Indeed, the commentary teachers, explaining the meaning of the words of the Dhamma and Vinaya, used the sound-form accompanied by the āya-substitution in that very sense, saying: "for the discipline of qualities. For this discipline is for the sake of blameless qualities, not for the sake of worldly enjoyments, etc." Thus, forms of the dative singular accompanied by the āya-substitution are seen only in these four instances: in the object of verbs of motion, in the object of verbs of leading, in case transformation, and in the sense of 'for the sake of'; but not in the context of any dative case, such as giving or pleasing. For in the Nirutti Piṭaka, the sound-form accompanied by the āya-substitution is mentioned as: "'atthāya' is a dative expression." However, such forms are not mentioned with nouns like 'purisa' (man), etc., because such sound-forms do not occur anywhere. Indeed, in Kaccāyana's grammar, in the explanation of the rule 'āya for the dative singular,' it is said: 'for the welfare, for the benefit, for the happiness of gods and humans.' But it is not said: 'for a man,' or 'for an ascetic,' or 'for a brahmin.'

Ettha siyā – nanu bho tasseva vuttiyaṃ “catutthīti kimatthaṃ purisassa mukhaṃ. Ekavacanassāti kimatthaṃ purisānaṃ dadāti. Vāti kimatthaṃ dātā hoti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā”ti vuttattā “purisāya samaṇāya brāhmaṇāyā”tiādīni padarūpāni nayato dassitāni, kevalaṃ pana mukhasaddayogato bahuvacanabhāvato vikappanato ca “purisāyā”tiādīni na sijjhanti, mukhasaddayogādivirahite pana ṭhāne avassaṃ sijjhantīti? Ettha vuccate – “catutthīti kimatthaṃ purisassa mukha”nti vadanto “sace āyādeso bhaveyya[M 0.0178], catutthiyā eva bhavati, na chaṭṭhiyā”ti dassento “mukha”nti padaṃ dassesi, na ca tena “mukhasaddaṭṭhāne detītiādike sampadānavisayabhūte kriyāpade ṭhite āyādeso hotī”ti dasseti. “Ekavacanassāti kimatthaṃ purisānaṃ dadātī”ti vadantopi “ekavacanasseva āyādeso hoti, na bahuvacanassā”ti dasseti. “Dadātī”ti idaṃ padaṃ “purisāna”nti padassa sampadānavacanattaṃ ñāpetuṃ avoca, na ca “detītiādike sampadānavisayabhūte kriyāpade sati catutthekavacanassa āyādeso hotī”ti imamatthaṃ viññāpeti. “Vāti kimatthaṃ dātā hoti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā”ti ca vadantopi “sampadāneyeva vikappena āyādeso hotī”ti viññāpeti, na dānādikriyaṃ paṭicca āyādesavidhānaṃ ñāpeti.

Here it may be asked: "But, sir, in that very explanation, since it was stated: 'Why the dative? The man's mouth. Why the singular? He gives to men. Why 'or'? One is a giver to an ascetic or a brahmin,' were not forms such as 'purisāya,' 'samaṇāya,' and 'brāhmaṇāya' thus shown by implication? However, forms like 'purisāya' are not accomplished merely due to the connection with the word 'mouth,' the plural form, or the optionality. But in places devoid of such connections with 'mouth,' etc., they must surely be accomplished, must they not?" To this it is replied: When saying, "Why the dative? The man's mouth," he showed the word 'mouth' to demonstrate that "if the āya-substitution were to occur, it would be in the dative only, not the genitive." However, this does not demonstrate that "the āya-substitution occurs when a verb like 'deti' (gives), etc., which is in the context of the dative, is present in the place of the word 'mukha'." Also, when saying, "Why the singular? He gives to men," he demonstrates that "the āya-substitution occurs only for the singular, not the plural." He uttered the word 'gives' to make known that the word 'purisānaṃ' is a dative expression, but he does not make known the meaning that "when verbs like 'gives,' which are in the context of the dative, are present, the āya-substitution occurs for the dative singular." And when saying, "Why 'or'? One is a giver to an ascetic or a brahmin," he makes known that "the āya-substitution occurs optionally in the dative," but does not make known that the āya-substitution is prescribed dependent on an action such as giving.

Yadi pana dānādikriyaṃ paṭicca āyādesavidhānaṃ siyā, vuttikārakena lakkhaṇassa vuttiyaṃ mūlodāharaṇeyeva “atthāya hitāyā”ti tadatthapayogāni viya “purisāya dīyate”tiādi vattabbaṃ siyā, na ca vuttaṃ. Kasmāti ce? Buddhavacane porāṇaṭṭhakathāsu ca tādisassa payogassa abhāvā. Niruttipiṭake hi pabhinnapaṭisambhido so āyasmā mahākaccāno “purisassa dīyate”ti āyādesarahitāniyeva rūpāni dasseti, “atthāyāti sampadānavacana”nti bhaṇantopi ca thero dānādikriyāpekkhaṃ akatvā catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitaṃ rūpameva niddisi. Tena so payogo tadatthappayogoti viññāyati. Iti imehi kāraṇehi jānitabbaṃ “dānādikriyaṃ paṭicca āyādesavidhānaṃ na kata”nti. Yajjevaṃ “atthāya hitāyā”tiādīniyeva tadatthappayogāni “āya catutthekavacanassa tū”ti lakkhaṇassa visayā bhaveyyuṃ, nāññānīti? Tanna, aññānipi visayāyeva tassa. Katamāni? “Mūlāya paṭikasseyya, appo [M 0.0179] saggāya gacchati, dakāya neti, viramathāyasmanto mamavacanāya, gaṇāya bhattā”tiādīni. “Saggassa gamanena vā”tiādīni pana vādhikārattā avisayāvāti.

If, however, the āya-substitution were prescribed dependent on actions like giving, then the commentator, when illustrating the rule in his explanation with the root example 'for welfare, for benefit,' should have mentioned usages like 'is given to a man' as examples of its application, just as those usages exemplify the sense of 'for the sake of,' but this was not done. Why? Because such usages are absent in the Buddha's words and in the ancient commentaries. Indeed, in the Nirutti Piṭaka, that Venerable Mahākaccāna, skilled in analytical knowledge, presents forms devoid of the āya-substitution, such as 'purisassa dīyate.'
