Even when the Elder explains "'atthāya' is a dative expression," he, without considering actions like giving, etc., pointed out only the form of the dative singular accompanied by the āya-substitution. Therefore, that usage is understood as a usage in the sense of 'for the sake of.' Thus, for these reasons, it should be known that 'the āya-substitution is not prescribed dependent on actions like giving.' If that is so, would only examples like 'for welfare, for benefit,' etc., which are usages in the sense of 'for the sake of,' be within the scope of the rule 'āya for the dative singular,' and no others? That is not the case; others are also within its scope. Which ones? Examples like 'he should pull back to the root,' 'few go to heaven,' 'he leads to water,' 'desist, venerable ones, from my words,' 'food for the assembly.' However, usages like 'saggassa gamanena' (by going to heaven) are outside its scope due to the option (indicated by 'vā').

Nanu ca bho evaṃ sante vuttikārakena mūlodāharaṇesu “atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna”nti vatvā “mūlāya paṭikasseyyā”tiādīnipi vattabbāni, kimudāharaṇe pana “vāti kimatthaṃ saggassa gamanena vā”ti vattabbanti? Saccaṃ, avacane kāraṇamatthi, taṃ suṇātha – “mūlāya paṭikasseyya, appo saggāya gacchatī”ti ettha hi “mūlāya, saggāyā”ti padāni suddhasampadānavacanāni na honti gatyatthakammani vattanato, tasmā mūlodāharaṇesu na vuttāni. Tathā “dakāya netī”ti ettha “dakāyā”ti padaṃ nayanatthakammani vattanato suddhasampadānavacanaṃ na hotīti na vuttaṃ. “Viramathāyasmanto mama vacanāyā”ti ettha pana “vacanāyā”ti padaṃ nissakkavacanatthe vattanato, “gaṇāya bhattā”ti ettha “gaṇāyā”ti padaṃ sāmivacanatthe vattanato, “asakkatā casma dhanañcayāyā”ti ettha “dhanañcayāyā”ti padaṃ kattuvasena sāmiatthe vattanato suddhasampadānavacanaṃ na hotīti na vuttaṃ. Kimudāharaṇepi “saggassā”ti padaṃ gamanasaddasannidhānato gatyatthakammani vattanato suddhasampadānavacanaṃ na hotīti “vāti kimatthaṃ saggassa gamanena vā”ti na vuttaṃ. Evañhettha vuttanayena buddhavacanaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathānayañca patvā catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitāni rūpāni gatyatthakammādīsu catūsuyeva ṭhānesu dissanti, na pana dānarocanādibhede yattha katthaci sampadānavisayeti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

"But, sir, if this is so, then the commentator should have said in the root examples, 'for the welfare, for the benefit, for the happiness of gods and humans,' and also, 'he should pull back to the root,' etc. So why, in the counter-example, is it said: 'Why 'or'? By going to heaven'?" "True, there is a reason for not saying so. Listen: In the phrase 'he should pull back to the root; few go to heaven,' the words 'to the root' and 'to heaven' are not pure dative expressions because they function as the object of verbs of motion. Therefore, they are not mentioned in the root examples. Similarly, in 'he leads to water,' the word 'to water' is not a pure dative expression because it functions as the object of a verb of leading, so it is not mentioned. In 'Venerable ones, desist from my words,' the word 'from my words' functions in the sense of the ablative case, so it is not a pure dative expression. In 'food for the assembly,' the word 'for the assembly' functions in the sense of the possessive case, so it is not a pure dative expression. In 'and we are not honored by Dhanañcaya,' the word 'by Dhanañcaya' functions in the sense of the possessive case for the agent, so it is not a pure dative expression, and therefore is not mentioned. Likewise, in the counter-example, the word 'of heaven' is not a pure dative expression because, due to the proximity of the word 'going,' it functions as the object of a verb of motion, and therefore it is not said: 'Why 'or'? By going to heaven.' Thus, in this way, having considered the Buddha's words and the method of the ancient commentaries, the forms of the dative singular accompanied by the āya-substitution are seen only in these four instances: as the object of verbs of motion, etc., but not in the context of any dative case, such as giving or pleasing. This should be understood."

Nanu ca bho “candanasāraṃ jeṭṭhikāya adāsi suvaṇṇamālaṃ kaniṭṭhāyā”ti dānappayoge catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitarūpadassanato “rājakaññāya dīyate, rājakaññāya [M 0.0180] ruccati alaṅkāro, rājakaññāya chattaṃ dhāreti, rājakaññāya namo karohi, rājakaññāya sotthi bhavatu, rājakaññāya silāghate”tiādīhipi payogehi bhavitabbaṃ, atha kasmā “buddhavacanaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathānayañca patvā catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitāni rūpāni gatyatthakammādīsu catūsuyeva ṭhānesu dissanti, na pana dānarocanādibhede yattha katthaci sampadānavisaye”ti vadathāti? Uppathamavatiṇṇo bhavaṃ, na hi bhavaṃ amhākaṃ vacanatthaṃ jānāti. Ayañhettha amhākaṃ vacanattho – sabbānipi itthiliṅgāni ekavacanavasena tatiyācatutthīpañcamīchaṭṭhīsattamīṭhānesu samasamāni honti, appāni asamāni, tasmā tāni ṭhapetvā pulliṅganapuṃsakaliṅgesu purisādi cittādisaddānaṃ akārantapakatibhāve ṭhitānaṃ catutthekavacanassa āyādesasahitāni rūpāni buddhavacanādīsu dānarocanādibhede yattha katthaci sampadānavisaye na dissanti. Teneva hi “mūlāya, saggāya, dakāya, vacanāya, gaṇāyā”tiādīni gatyatthakammādīsu tīsu “abhiññāya, sambodhāya, nibbānāyā”ti evamādīni pana anekasatāni tiliṅgapadāni tadattheyevāti imesu catūsu ṭhānesu dissanti. “Deti, rocati, dhāretī”tiādīsu pana suddhasampadānavisayesu na dissanti. Bhavanti catra –

But, good sir, since in the usage of giving, the form with the āya substitution for the dative singular is seen in 'He gave sandalwood essence to the eldest (jeṭṭhikāya) and a golden garland to the youngest (kaniṭṭhāya)', should it not also be so in usages such as 'it is given to the princess (rājakaññāya)', 'the ornament pleases the princess (rājakaññāya)', 'he holds a parasol for the princess (rājakaññāya)', 'pay homage to the princess (rājakaññāya)', 'may there be well-being for the princess (rājakaññāya)', 'he praises the princess (rājakaññāya)', and so on? Then why do you say, 'Having considered the word of the Buddha and the method of the ancient commentaries, the forms of the dative singular with the āya substitution are seen only in four places—such as in the object of verbs of motion—but not in any dative context in the categories of giving, pleasing, and so on'? You have gone astray, good sir; indeed, you do not understand the meaning of our words. Herein, this is the meaning of our words: all feminine nouns in the singular are identical in the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh cases; a few are not identical. Therefore, setting those aside, in the masculine and neuter genders, for words such as purisa and citta which stand in their natural form ending in -a, the forms of the dative singular with the substitution of āya are not seen in the Buddha's words and so on, in any dative context in the categories of giving, pleasing, etc. For that very reason, forms such as mūlāya, saggāya, dakāya, vacanāya, gaṇāyā, etc., are seen in three of the four places, namely in the object of verbs of motion, etc., and hundreds of such words of the three genders, such as abhiññāya, sambodhāya, nibbānāya, are seen in these four places, that is, in the sense of 'for the purpose of'. But they are not seen in purely dative contexts with verbs such as deti, rocati, dhāreti, etc. And here there are these verses:

Catutthekavacanassa, āyādesena saṃyutaṃ;

Rūpaṃ anitthiliṅgānaṃ, ṭhānesu catusuṭṭhitaṃ.

The form of the dative singular, combined with the substitution of āya, for non-feminine genders, stands in four places.

Gatyatthakammani ceva, nayanatthassa kammani;

Vibhattiyā vipallāse, tadatthe cāti niddise.

One should point out that it occurs in the object of verbs with the sense of motion, in the object of verbs with the sense of leading, in the interchange of case endings, and in the sense of 'for the purpose of'.

“Mūlāya paṭikasseyya, appo saggāya gacchati”;

Evaṃ gatyatthakammasmiṃ, diṭṭhamamhehi sāsane.

‘One should revert to the root; few go to heaven.’ Thus, in the Teaching, it has been seen by us in the object of verbs of motion.

“Dakāya [M 0.0181] neti” iccevaṃ, nayanatthassa kammani;

“Vacanāyā”ti nissakke, viramaṇappayogato.

‘He leads to water’—thus, in the object of verbs with the sense of leading. ‘Vacanāya’ is in the sense of removal, from its usage with cessation.

“Gaṇāya”iti sāmismiṃ, “bhattā”ti saddayogato;

“Dhanañcayāyā”ti padaṃ, kattutthe sāmisūcakaṃ.

‘Gaṇāya’ is in the genitive sense, due to its connection with the word ‘bhattā’. The word ‘Dhanañcayāya’ indicates the genitive in the sense of the agent.

“Asakkatā”ti saddassa, yogatoti viniddise;

Añño cāpi vipallāso, maggitabbo vibhāvinā.

One should specify it from the connection with the word ‘asakkatā’; and another interchange, too, should be sought by the discerning one.

“Abhiññāya sambodhāya, nibbānāyā”timāni tu;

Liṅgattayavaseneva, tadatthasmiṃ viniddise.

But as for ‘for higher knowledge, for full enlightenment, for Nibbāna’—these one should specify in the sense of ‘for the purpose of that’, according to the three genders.

Evaṃ pāṭhānulomena, kathito āyasambhavo;

Idantu sukhumaṃ ṭhānaṃ, cintetabbaṃ punappunaṃ.

Thus, following the order of the text, the occurrence of āya has been explained; but this is a subtle point, to be reflected upon again and again.

Okārantavaseneva, nānānayasumaṇḍitā;

Padamālā mahesissa, sāsanatthaṃ pakāsitā.

By way of the o-ending, the paradigm of the Great Sage, well-adorned with various methods, has been declared for the benefit of the Teaching.

Imamatimadhurañce cittikatvā suṇeyyuṃ,

Vividhanayavicittaṃ sādhavo saddanītiṃ;

Jinavaravacanete saddato jātakaṅkhaṃ,

Kumudamiva’sinā ve suṭṭhu chindeyyumettha.

If good people would listen attentively to this Saddanīti, which is exceedingly sweet and variegated with diverse methods, then, regarding the words of the Supreme Conqueror, they would surely cut off well the doubt born from grammar, as one cuts a water lily with a sword.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise who are skilled in the paths of exposition in the nine-limbed teaching with its commentaries and in the three Piṭakas,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise composed for the purpose of skill,

Savinicchayo okārantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa

The Determination of the Natural Form of Masculine Nouns Ending in -o

Nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo nāma

Named the Division of the Nominal Paradigm.

Pañcamo paricchedo.

Fifth Chapter.

Akārantokārantatāpakatikaokārantapulliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Here ends the section on masculine nouns ending in -a, ending in -o, and those with a natural form ending in -o.

6. Ākārantapulliṅganāmikapadamālā

6. The Nominal Paradigm of Masculine Nouns Ending in -ā

Atha pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā ākārantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpesu abhibhavitu iccetassa pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālaṃ [M 0.0182] vakkhāma – satthā, satthā, satthāro. Satthāraṃ, satthāro. Satthārā, satthārehi, satthārebhi. Satthu, satthussa, satthuno, satthānaṃ, satthārānaṃ. Satthārā, satthārehi, satthārebhi. Satthu, satthussa, satthuno, satthānaṃ, satthārānaṃ. Satthari, satthāresu. Bho sattha, bho satthā, bhavanto satthāro.

Now, having placed the opinion of the former teachers at the forefront, among the natural forms of masculine nouns ending in -ā, we will explain the nominal paradigm of the natural form of this word for 'teacher': The teacher, the teacher, the teachers. The teacher, the teachers. By the teacher, by the teachers, by the teachers. To the teacher, to the teacher, to the teacher, to the teachers, to the teachers. From the teacher, from the teachers, from the teachers. Of the teacher, of the teacher, of the teacher, of the teachers, of the teachers. In the teacher, in the teachers. O teacher, O teacher, O venerable teachers.

Ayaṃ yamakamahātherena katāya cūḷaniruttiyā āgato nayo. Ettha ca niruttipiṭake ca kaccāyane ca “satthunā”ti padaṃ anāgatampi gahetabbameva “dhammarājena satthunā”ti dassanato. “Satthārā, satthunā, satthārehi, satthārebhī”ti kamo ca veditabbo. Ettha ca asatipi atthavisese byañjanavisesavasena, byañjanavisesābhāvepi atthanānatthatāvasena saddantarasandassanaṃ niruttikkamoti “satthā”ti padaṃ ekavacanabahuvacanavasena dvikkhattuṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Niruttipiṭakādīsu pana “satthā”ti paṭhamābahuvacanaṃ na āgataṃ. Kiñcāpi na āgataṃ, tathāpi “avitakkitā maccumupabbajantī”ti pāḷiyaṃ “avitakkitā”ti paṭhamābahuvacanassa dassanato “satthā”ti padassa paṭhamābahuvacanattaṃ avassamicchitabbaṃ. Tathā vattā, dhātā, gantādīnampi taggatikattā. Tathā niruttipiṭake “satthāre”ti dutiyābahuvacanañca “satthussa, satthāna”nti catutthīchaṭṭhekavacanabahuvacanāni ca āgatāni, cūḷaniruttiyaṃ pana na āgatāni. Tattha “mātāpitaro poseti. Bhātaro atikkamatī”ti dassanato “satthāre”ti dutiyābahuvacanarūpaṃ ayuttaṃ viya dissati. Kaccāyanādīsu “bho sattha, bho satthā” iti rassadīghavasena ālapanekavacanadvayaṃ vuttaṃ. Niruttipiṭake “bho sattha” itirassavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ vatvā “bhavanto satthāro”ti ārādesavasena ālapanabahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ [M 0.0183] “bho sattha” iti rassavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ vatvā “bho satthā” iti dīghavasena ālapanabahuvacanaṃ lapitaṃ. Sabbametaṃ āgame upaparikkhitvā yathā na virujjhati, tathā gahetabbaṃ.

This is the method that comes from the Cūḷanirutti composed by the great elder Yamaka. Here, in the Niruttipiṭaka and in Kaccāyana, the word ‘satthunā’ should be taken even though it is not given, because of the example ‘dhammarājena satthunā’ (by the Teacher, the King of Dhamma). The sequence ‘satthārā, satthunā, satthārehi, satthārebhi’ should also be understood. Here, it is the method of grammar to show another word form by way of a difference in expression even when there is no difference in meaning, and by way of a difference in meaning even when there is no difference in expression; thus it should be understood that the word ‘satthā’ is stated twice, as a singular and as a plural. However, in the Niruttipiṭaka and so on, the nominative plural ‘satthā’ is not found. Although it is not found, nevertheless, because the nominative plural ‘avitakkitā’ is seen in the Pāli text ‘avitakkitā maccumupabbajantī,’ the status of the word ‘satthā’ as a nominative plural must necessarily be accepted. The same applies to ‘vattā,’ ‘dhātā,’ ‘gantā,’ etc., because they follow the same course. Furthermore, in the Niruttipiṭaka, the accusative plural ‘satthāre’ and the dative-genitive singular and plural forms ‘satthussa’ and ‘satthānaṃ’ are found, but they are not found in the Cūḷanirutti. There, because of seeing examples like ‘mātāpitaro poseti’ (he nourishes his parents) and ‘bhātaro atikkamatī’ (he surpasses his brothers), the accusative plural form ‘satthāre’ appears to be incorrect. In Kaccāyana and other texts, two vocative singular forms, ‘bho sattha’ and ‘bho satthā,’ are stated by way of short and long vowels. In the Niruttipiṭaka, having stated the vocative singular with a short vowel, ‘bho sattha,’ the vocative plural ‘bhavanto satthāro’ is stated by way of the āra substitution. In the Cūḷanirutti, having stated the vocative singular with a short vowel, ‘bho sattha,’ the vocative plural ‘bho satthā’ is stated with a long vowel. All this should be examined in accordance with the tradition and accepted in such a way that it is not contradictory.

Idāni satthusaddassa yaṃ rūpantaraṃ amhehi diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ dassessāma – tathā hi “imesaṃ mahānāma tiṇṇaṃ satthūnaṃ ekā niṭṭhā udāhu puthu niṭṭhā”ti pāḷiyaṃ “satthūna”nti padaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, tasmā ayampi kamo veditabbo “satthu, satthussa, satthuno, satthānaṃ, satthārānaṃ, satthūna”nti. Abhibhavitā, abhibhavitā, abhibhavitāro. Abhibhavitāraṃ, abhibhavitāro. Abhibhavitārā, abhibhavitunā, abhibhavitārehi, abhibhavitārebhi. Abhibhavitu, abhibhavitussa, abhibhavituno, abhibhavitānaṃ, abhibhavitārānaṃ, abhibhavitūnaṃ. Abhibhavitārā, abhibhavitārehi, abhibhavitārebhi. Abhibhavitu, abhibhavitussa, abhibhavituno, abhibhavitānaṃ, abhibhavitārānaṃ. Abhibhavitari, abhibhavitāresu. Bho abhibhavita, bho abhibhavitā, bhavanto abhibhavitāro. Yathā panettha abhibhavitu iccetassa pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā satthunayena yojitā, evaṃ paribhavituādīnañca aññesañca taṃsadisānaṃ nāmikapadamālā satthunayena yojetabbā. Etthaññāni taṃsadisāni nāma “vattā, dhātā”iccādīnaṃ padānaṃ vattudhātu iccādīni pakatirūpāni.

Now, regarding the other form of the word ‘teacher’ that we have seen, we shall explain it—for in the Pāli, the word ‘satthūnaṃ’ is seen in the phrase, ‘Mahānāma, for these three teachers is there one final attainment or are there separate final attainments?’ Therefore, this sequence should also be understood: ‘satthu, satthussa, satthuno, satthānaṃ, satthārānaṃ, satthūnaṃ.’ Conqueror, conqueror, conquerors. The conqueror, the conquerors. By the conqueror, by the conqueror, by the conquerors, by the conquerors. Of/to the conqueror, of/to the conqueror, of/to the conqueror, of/to the conquerors, of/to the conquerors, of/to the conquerors. From the conqueror, from the conquerors, from the conquerors. Of/to the conqueror, of/to the conqueror, of/to the conqueror, of/to the conquerors, of/to the conquerors. In the conqueror, in the conquerors. O conqueror, O conqueror, O venerable conquerors. Just as here the nominal word-series of the natural form ‘abhibhavitu’ is joined according to the method of ‘satthu,’ so too should the nominal word-series of ‘paribhavitu’ and other similar words be joined according to the method of ‘satthu.’ Here, other similar words are the natural forms like ‘vattu,’ ‘dhātu,’ etc., of words like ‘vattā,’ ‘dhātā,’ etc.

Vattā dhātā gantā netā,

Dātā kattā cetā tātā;

Chettā bhettā hantā metā,

Jetā boddhā ñātā sotā.

The speaker, the maintainer, the goer, the guide; the giver, the doer, the thinker, the protector; the cutter, the breaker, the slayer, the measurer; the conqueror, the enlightened one, the knower, the listener.

Gajjitā vassitā bhattā, mucchitā paṭisedhitā;

Bhāsitā pucchitā khantā, uṭṭhātokkamitā tatā.

The roarer, the rainer, the nourisher; the deluded one, the preventer; the speaker, the questioner, the patient one; the one who rises, the one who departs, the stretcher.

Nattā [M 0.0184] panattā akkhātā, sahitā paṭisevitā;

Netā vinetā iccādī, vattare suddhakattari.

The grandson, the great-grandson, the explainer; the endurer, the one who attends; the leader, the trainer, and so forth, are spoken of as other such words.

Uppādetā viññāpetā, sandassetā pabrūhetā;

Bodhetādī caññe saddā, ñeyyā hetusmiṃ atthasmiṃ.

The producer, the one who makes known, the one who shows, the one who develops; the enlightener and other such words should be known in the causal sense.

Kattā khattā nettā bhattā, pitā bhātātime pana;

Kiñci bhijjanti suttasmiṃ, taṃ pabhedaṃ kathessahaṃ.

The doer, the warrior, the leader, the nourisher, the father, and the brother—these indeed differ somewhat according to the rule; I shall explain that distinction.

Satthātiādīsu keci, upayogena sāminā;

Saheva niccaṃ vattanti, neva vattanti keci tu.

Some words, such as ‘teacher’ and the like, always occur together with the possessor by usage, while some do not.

Tatra kattusaddādayo rūpantaravasena satthusaddato kiñci bhijjanti. Tathā hi “uṭṭhehi katte taramāno, gantvā vessantaraṃvadā”ti ettha “katte”ti idaṃ ālapanekavacanarūpaṃ, evañhi “bho kattā”ti rūpato rūpantaraṃ nāma. “Tena hi bho khatte yena campeyyakā brāhmaṇagahapatikā tenupasaṅkamā”ti ettha “khatte”ti idañcālapanekavacanarūpaṃ. Evampi “bho khattā”ti rūpato rūpantaraṃ nāma. “Nette ujuṃ gate satī”ti ettha “nette”ti idaṃ sattamiyā ekavacanarūpaṃ, etampi “nettarī”ti rūpato rūpantaraṃ. “Ārādhayati rājānaṃ, pūjaṃ labhati bhattusū”ti ettha “bhattūsū”ti idaṃ sattamiyā bahuvacanarūpaṃ. “Bhattāresū”ti rūpato rūpantaraṃ, atra “bhattūsū”ti dassanato, “mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā”ti ettha “pitūsū”ti dassanato ca “vattūsu dhātūsu gantūsu netūsu dātūsu kattūsū”ti evamādinayopi gahetabbo. Ayaṃ nayo satthusaddepi icchitabbo viya amhe paṭibhāti.

Here, words like 'kattu' and others differ somewhat from the word 'satthu' by way of a different form. For example, in the phrase “Arise, O doer, quickly, go and tell Vessantara,” the word 'katte' is in the vocative singular form. Indeed, it is a different form from 'bho kattā.' Similarly, in “Therefore, O charioteer, approach the brahmin householders of Campeyya,” the word 'khatte' is also in the vocative singular form. Here too, it is a different form from 'bho khattā.' In “when the eye is straight,” the word 'nette' is in the locative singular form. This too is a different form from 'nettarī.' In “He pleases the king, he receives honor from the masters,” the word 'bhattūsū' is in the locative plural form. It is a different form from 'bhattāresū.' Here, from seeing 'bhattūsū' and from seeing 'pitūsū' in 'mātāpitūsu paṇḍitā' (wise among mothers and fathers), the method of 'vattūsu, dhātūsu, gantūsu, netūsu, dātūsu, kattūsū' and so on should also be understood. This method, it appears to us, should also be desired for the word 'satthu'.

Pitā, pitā, pitaro. Pitaraṃ, pitaro. Pitarā, pitunā, petyā, pitarehi, pitarebhi, pitūhi, pitūbhi. Pitu, pitussa, pituno[M 0.0185], pitānaṃ, pitarānaṃ, pitūnaṃ. Pitarā, petyā, pitarehi, pitarebhi, pitūhi, pitūbhi. Pitu, pitussa, pituno, pitānaṃ, pitarānaṃ, pitūnaṃ. Pitari, pitaresu, pitūsu. Bho pita, bho pitā, bhavanto pitaro. Ettha pana “petyā, pitūna”nti imaṃ nayadvayaṃ vajjetvā bhātusaddassa ca padamālā yojetabbā. Tattha “matyā ca petyā ca kataṃ susādhu, anuññātosi mātāpitūhi, mātāpitūnaṃ accayenā”ti ca dassanato pitusaddassa “petyā, pitūhi, pitūbhi. Pitūna”nti rūpabhedo ca, “pitaro” iccādīsu rassattañca satthusaddato viseso. Tattha ca “petyā”ti idaṃ “jantuyo, hetuyo, hetuyā, adhipatiyā”ti padāni viya acinteyyaṃ pulliṅgarūpanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Father (Nom. Sg.), father (Nom. Sg.), fathers (Nom. Pl.). Father (Acc. Sg.), fathers (Acc. Pl.). By the father (Inst. Sg.: pitarā, pitunā, petyā); by the fathers (Inst. Pl.: pitarehi, pitarebhi, pitūhi, pitūbhi). Of/to the father (Gen./Dat. Sg.: pitu, pitussa, pituno); of/to the fathers (Gen./Dat. Pl.: pitānaṃ, pitarānaṃ, pitūnaṃ). From the father (Abl. Sg.: pitarā, petyā); from the fathers (Abl. Pl.: pitarehi, pitarebhi, pitūhi, pitūbhi). Of/to the father (Gen./Dat. Sg.: pitu, pitussa, pituno); of/to the fathers (Gen./Dat. Pl.: pitānaṃ, pitarānaṃ, pitūnaṃ). In the father (Loc. Sg.: pitari); in the fathers (Loc. Pl.: pitaresu, pitūsu). O father (Voc. Sg.: bho pita, bho pitā), O venerable fathers (Voc. Pl.: bhavanto pitaro). Here, however, excluding these two forms, 'petyā' and 'pitūna,' the word paradigm of 'bhātu' (brother) should be applied. There, from seeing 'matyā ca petyā ca kataṃ susādhu' (what is well done by mother and father), 'anuññātosi mātāpitūhi' (you are permitted by mother and father), and 'mātāpitūnaṃ accayena' (after the passing of mother and father), the variations in form of the word 'pitu' (father) such as 'petyā, pitūhi, pitūbhi, pitūna,' and the shortening in 'pitaro' and so on, are a distinction from the word 'satthu.' And there, 'petyā' should be regarded as an inconceivable masculine form, like the words 'jantuyo, hetuyo, hetuyā, adhipatiyā.'

Codanā sodhanā cātra bhavati – satthā pitā iccevamādīni nipphannattamupādāya ākārantānīti ca, paṭhamaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ pakatirūpamupādāya ukārantānīti ca tumhe bhaṇatha, “hetu satthāradassanaṃ. Amātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho. Kattāraniddeso”tiādīsu pana satthāra iccādīni kathaṃ tumhe bhaṇathāti? Etānipi mayaṃ pakatirūpamupādāya ukārantānīti bhaṇāmāti. Nanu ca bho etāni akārantānīti? Na, ukārantāniyeva tāni. Nanu ca bho yo aṃ nādīni parabhūtāni vacanāni na dissanti yehi ukārantasaddānamantassa ārādeso siyā, tasmā akārantānīti? Na, īdise ṭhāne parabhūtānaṃ yo aṃ nādīnaṃ vacanānamanokāsattā. Tathā hi samāsavisayo eso. Samāsavisayasmiñhi acinteyyānipi rūpāni dissantīti. Evaṃ santepi bho “gāmato nikkhamatī”ti payogassa viya asamāsavisaye “satthārato satthāraṃ gacchatī”ti niddesapāḷidassanato “hetu [M 0.0186] satthāradassana”ntiādīsu satthāra iccādīni akārantānīti cintetabbānīti? Na cintetabbāni “satthārato satthāraṃ gacchatī”ti etthāpi ukārantattā. Ettha hi asamāsattepi topaccayaṃ paṭicca satthusaddassa ukāro ārādesaṃ labhati. Yāni pana tumhe ukārassa ārādesanimittāni yo aṃnādīni vacanāni icchatha, tāni īdise ṭhāne viññūnaṃ pamāṇaṃ na honti. Kāni pana hontīti ce? Asamāsavisaye topaccayo ca samāsavisaye parapadāni ca parapadābhāve syādivibhattiyo cāti imāneva īdise ṭhāne ekantena pamāṇaṃ honti. Tathā hi dhammapadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yāvadeva anatthāya, ñattaṃ bālassa jāyatī”ti imissā pāḷiyā atthasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “ayaṃ nimmātāpitaroti imasmiṃ pahaṭe daṇḍo natthī”ti ettha nimmātāpitaroti imassa samāsavisayattā simhi pare ukāro ārādesaṃ labhati, tato sissa okārādeso, iccetaṃ padaṃ pakatirūpavasena ukārantaṃ bhavati. Nipphannattamupādāya “puriso, urago”ti padāni viya okārantañca bhavati. Ayaṃ panettha samāsaviggaho “mātā ca pitā ca mātāpitaro, natthi mātāpitaro etassāti nimmātāpitaro”ti. Pakatirūpavasena hi “nimmātāpitu” iti ṭhite sivacanasmiṃ pare ukārassa ārādeso hoti. Katthaci pana dhammapadaṭṭhakathāpotthake “ayaṃ nimmātāpitiko”ti pāṭho dissati, eso pana “ayaṃ nimmātāpitaro”ti padassa ayuttataṃ maññamānehi ṭhapitoti maññāma, na so ayutto aṭṭhakathāpāṭho. So hi umaṅgajātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ ekapitaroti simhi ārādesapayogena sameti. Tathā hi –

Here arises an objection and a rectification. You say that 'satthā,' 'pitā,' and so on, are 'ā'-ending by virtue of their derived state, and that, to begin with, their natural form should be established as 'u'-ending. But how do you explain 'satthāra' and so on in phrases like 'hetu satthāradassanaṃ' (the cause is the sight of the teacher), 'amātāpitarasaṃvaḍḍho' (one raised without mother or father), 'kattāraniddeso' (the designation of the doer)? We say that these too are 'u'-ending by virtue of their natural form. But, sir, are these not 'a'-ending? No, they are indeed 'u'-ending. But, sir, since the subsequent case endings 'yo,' 'aṃ,' and so on, are not seen, by which the 'ā' substitution for the final 'u' of 'u'-ending words could occur, therefore, are they not 'a'-ending? No, because in such a place, there is no occasion for subsequent case endings like 'yo,' 'aṃ,' and so on. For this is the domain of a compound. Indeed, in the domain of compounds, even inconceivable forms are seen. Even so, sir, just as in the usage 'gāmato nikkhamati' (he leaves the village), considering the statement in the text 'satthārato satthāraṃ gacchati' (he goes from the teacher to the teacher) in a non-compound context, should not 'satthāra' and so on in 'hetu satthāradassanaṃ' and so forth be considered as 'a'-ending words? They should not be so considered, for even in 'satthārato satthāraṃ gacchati,' they are 'u'-ending. For here, even though it is not a compound, due to the suffix '-to,' the 'u' of the word 'satthu' obtains an 'ā' substitution. But the case endings 'yo,' 'aṃ,' and so on, which you desire as the cause for the 'ā' substitution of 'u,' are not authoritative for the wise in such cases. What, then, is authoritative? In a non-compound context, the suffix '-to,' and in a compound context, the subsequent words, or in the absence of subsequent words, case endings like 'si' and so on—these alone are definitively authoritative in such cases. Thus, in the Dhammapada commentary, in the explanation of the meaning of this verse, 'yāvadeva anatthāya, ñattaṃ bālassa jāyatī' (Only to his harm does the fool gain knowledge), in the phrase 'ayaṃ nimmātāpitaroti imasmiṃ pahaṭe daṇḍo natthī' (this one is without mother or father—for striking this one, there is no punishment), here, because 'nimmātāpitaro' is in the domain of a compound, when 'si' follows, the 'u' obtains 'ā' substitution, then the 'si' ending is substituted by 'o'; thus, this word becomes 'u'-ending in its natural form. By virtue of its derived state, it also becomes 'o'-ending, like the words 'puriso' (man) and 'urago' (snake). Here, the analysis of the compound is: 'mātā ca pitā ca' (mother and father) is 'mātāpitaro'; 'natthi mātāpitaro etassāti' (he has no mother or father) is 'nimmātāpitaro.' Indeed, in its natural form, when 'nimmātāpitu' stands and the 'si' case ending follows, the 'u' obtains 'ā' substitution. However, in some Dhammapada commentary books, the reading 'ayaṃ nimmātāpitiko' is found. But we think this was inserted by those who considered the word 'ayaṃ nimmātāpitaro' inappropriate. That commentary reading is not incorrect, for it agrees with the usage of `ā` substitution before the `si` ending in `ekapitaro` in the Umaṅga Jātaka commentary. Thus –

“Yathāpi [M 0.0187] niyako bhātā,

Saudariyo ekamātuko;

Evaṃ pañcālacando te,

Dayitabbo rathesabhā”ti

“Just as one’s own brother, born of the same womb, of one mother; even so, O chief of charioteers, the Pañcāla moon should be given to you.”

Imissā pāḷiyā atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇentehi pāḷinayaññūhi garūhi “niyakoti ajjhattiko ekapitaro ekamātuyā jāto”ti simhi ārādesapayogaracanā katā. Na kevalañca simhi ārādese pulliṅgappayogoyevamhehi diṭṭho, atha kho itthiliṅgappayogopi sāsane diṭṭho. Tathā hi vinayapiṭake cūḷavagge “assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā”ti padaṃ dissati. Ayaṃ panettha samāsaviggaho “sakyakule uppannattā sakyassa bhagavato dhītā sakyadhītarā, na sakyadhītarā asakyadhītarā”ti. Idhāpi simhi pare ukārassa ārādeso kato, itthiliṅgabhāvassa icchitattā āpaccayo, tato silopo ca daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ samāsapadatte satthu pitu kattusaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālāyaṃ vuttarūpato koci koci rūpaviseso dissati. Aññesampi rūpaviseso nayaññunā maggitabbo suttantesu. Ko hi nāma samattho nissesato buddhavacanasāgare saṃkiṇṇāni vicitrāni paṇḍitajanānaṃ hadayavimhāpanakarāni padarūparatanāni samuddharitvā dassetuṃ, tasmā amhehi appamattakāniyeva dassitāni.

The venerable experts in the Pāḷi method, in explaining the meaning of this Pāḷi passage, made the formulation 'niyako (one’s own) means internal, born of one father and one mother' with the application of 'ārādesa' when 'si' is present. Not only has the masculine gender usage with 'ārādesa' in relation to 'si' been seen by us, but also the feminine gender usage has been seen in the Dispensation. Thus, in the Cūḷavagga of the Vinaya Piṭaka, the word 'assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā' (she is a non-ascetic, not a daughter of the Sakyans) is seen. Here, the analysis of the compound is: 'sakyadhītarā' is 'a daughter of the Sakyan, the Blessed One, because she was born in the Sakyan clan'; 'asakyadhītarā' is 'not a daughter of the Sakyan.' Here too, when 'si' follows, the 'u' obtains 'ārādesa,' and because the feminine gender is desired, the suffix 'ā' is added, and then the elision of 'si' should be understood. Thus, in compound words, some variations in form are seen from the forms stated in the nominal paradigms of the words 'satthu,' 'pitu,' and 'kattu.' Other variations in form should also be sought by the wise in the Suttas. For who, indeed, is capable of fully extracting and presenting the diverse and marvelous word-form gems, scattered throughout the ocean of the Buddha’s words, which astonish the hearts of the learned? Therefore, only a very few have been shown by us.

Adandhajātiko viññu-jātiko satataṃ idha;

Yogaṃ karoti ce satthu, pāḷiyaṃ so na kaṅkhati.

The one not of a sluggish nature, of a wise nature, constantly here; if he practices the Teacher’s discipline, he has no doubt in the Pāḷi text.

Ye panidha amhehi “satthā, abhibhavitā, vattā, kattā”dayo saddā pakāsitā, tesu keci upayogavacanena saddhiṃ niccaṃ vattanti “pucchitā, okkamitā”iccādayo. Tathā hi “abhijānāsi [M 0.0188] no tvaṃ mahārāja imaṃ pañhaṃ aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā. Niddaṃ okkamitā”tiādipayogā bahū dissanti. Keci sāmivacanena saddhiṃ niccaṃ vattanti “abhibhavitā, vattā”iccādayo. Tathā hi “paccāmittānaṃ abhibhavitā, tassa bhavanti vattāro. Amatassa dātā. Parissayānaṃ sahitā. Anuppannassa maggassa, uppādetā naruttamo”tiādipayogā bahū dissanti. Keci pana upayogavacanenapi saddhiṃ neva vattanti niyogā paññattiyaṃ pavattanato. Taṃ yathā? “Satthā, pitā, bhātā, nattā”iccādayo. Ettha pana “upayogavacanena saddhiṃ niccaṃ vattantī”tiādivacanaṃ kammabhūtaṃ atthaṃ sandhāya katanti veditabbaṃ.

But here, among the words such as 'satthā' (teacher), 'abhibhavitā' (conqueror), 'vattā' (speaker), 'kattā' (doer), and others, which have been explained by us, some always occur together with an accusative case, such as 'pucchitā' (questioner), 'okkamitā' (enterer), and so on. Thus, many usages like 'abhijānāsi no tvaṃ mahārāja imaṃ pañhaṃ aññe samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchitā' (Do you remember, O great king, having asked this question of other ascetics and brahmins?) and 'niddaṃ okkamitā' (having entered sleep) are seen. Some always occur together with a genitive case, such as 'abhibhavitā' (conqueror), 'vattā' (speaker), and so on. Thus, many usages like 'paccāmittānaṃ abhibhavitā' (conqueror of enemies), 'tassa bhavanti vattāro' (they are his speakers), 'amatassa dātā' (giver of the Deathless), 'parissayānaṃ sahitā' (endurer of dangers), 'anuppannassa maggassa, uppādetā naruttamo' (the supreme man, the producer of the unarisen path) are seen. However, some do not occur even with an accusative case, due to their functioning as designations or definitions. Such as? 'Satthā' (teacher), 'pitā' (father), 'bhātā' (brother), 'nattā' (grandson), and so on. Here, however, the statement 'always occur together with an accusative case' and so on, should be understood as made with reference to the meaning that becomes the object.

Evaṃ ukārantatāpakatikānaṃ ākārantapadānaṃ pavattiṃ viditvā saddesu atthesu ca kosallamicchantehi puna liṅgaantavasena “satthā, sattho, sattha”nti tikaṃ katvā padānamattho ca pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā ca padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā ca vavatthapetabbā. Tatra hi “satthā”ti idaṃ paṭhamaṃ ukārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchā ākārantabhūtaṃ pulliṅgaṃ, “sattho”ti idaṃ paṭhamaṃ akārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchā okārantabhūtaṃ pulliṅgaṃ, “sattha”ntidaṃ pana paṭhamaṃ akārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchā niggahītantabhūtaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ. Tatra satthāti sadevakaṃ lokaṃ sāsati anusāsatīti satthā, ko so? Bhagavā. Satthoti saha atthenāti sattho, bhaṇḍamūlaṃ gahetvā vāṇijjāya desantaraṃ gato janasamūho. Satthanti sāsati ācikkhati atthe etenāti satthaṃ, byākaraṇādigantho, atha vā sasati hiṃsati satte etenāti satthaṃ, asiādi. “Satthā, satthā, satthāro. Satthāraṃ, satthāro”ti pure viya [M 0.0189] padamālā. “Sattho, satthā. Satthaṃ, satthe”ti purisanayena padamālā. “Satthaṃ, satthāni, satthā. Satthaṃ, satthāni, satthe”ti napuṃsake vattamāna cittanayena padamālā yojetabbā. Evaṃ tidhā bhinnāsu nāmikapadamālāsu padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā vavatthapetabbā.

Having thus understood the formation of words ending in -ā from those with an original -u ending, those desiring skill in both words and meanings should further, by way of the gender and ending, form the triad 'satthā, sattho, sattha,' and the meaning of the words, the nominal paradigm of the original form, and the similarities and differences of the words should be determined. Herein, 'satthā' first stands with an original -u ending, later becoming a masculine word ending in -ā. 'Sattho' first stands with an original -a ending, later becoming a masculine word ending in -o. 'Satthaṃ,' however, first stands with an original -a ending, later becoming a neuter word ending in a niggahīta. Therein, 'satthā' is one who instructs and admonishes the world with its devas; thus, 'satthā.' Who is that? The Blessed One. 'Sattho' is 'with goods'; thus, 'sattho,' a group of people who, having taken merchandise, have gone to another country for trade. 'Satthaṃ' is that by which one instructs or explains the meaning; thus, 'satthaṃ,' a text on grammar and so forth. Alternatively, it is that by which one injures or harms beings; thus, 'satthaṃ,' a sword and so forth. The paradigm 'Satthā, satthā, satthāro. Satthāraṃ, satthāro' is as before. The paradigm 'Sattho, satthā. Satthaṃ, satthe' is according to the paradigm of 'purisa'. The paradigm 'Satthaṃ, satthāni, satthā. Satthaṃ, satthāni, satthe' should be applied in the neuter according to the paradigm of 'citta'. Thus, in these three distinct nominal paradigms, the similarities and differences among the words should be determined.

Satthā tiṭṭhati sabbaññū, satthā yanti dhanatthikā;

Satthā apeti puriso, bhonto satthā dadātha saṃ.

The Teacher, the all-knowing one, stands. The caravans, seekers of wealth, depart. O man, the weapons depart. O sirs, caravan leaders, give your own.

Evaṃ sutisāmaññavasena sadisatā bhavati.

Thus, similarity arises by way of common sound.

Satthaṃ yaṃ tikhiṇaṃ tena, sattho katvāna kappiyaṃ;

Phalaṃ satthussa pādāsi, satthā taṃ paribhuñjati.

With that sharp weapon, the caravan leader, having prepared it suitably, offered the fruit to the Teacher; the Teacher partakes of it.

Evaṃ asutisāmaññavasena asadisatā bhavati, tathā liṅgaantavasena. “Cetā ceto”ti ca “tātā tāto”ti ca dukaṃ katvā padānamattho ca pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā ca padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā ca vavatthapetabbā.

Thus, dissimilarity arises by way of non-common sound, and likewise by way of the gender and ending. And by forming the pairs 'cetā, ceto' and 'tātā, tāto,' the meaning of the words, the nominal paradigm of the original form, and the similarities and differences of the words should be determined.

Tatra hi “cetā”ti paṭhamaṃ ukārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchā ākārantabhūtaṃ pulliṅgaṃ, tathā “tātā”ti padampi. “Ceto”ti idaṃ pana paṭhamaṃ akārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchā okārantabhūtaṃ pulliṅgaṃ, tathā “tāto”ti padampi. Tatra cetāti cinoti rāsiṃ karotīti cetā, pākāracinanako puggalo, iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakīti attho. Cetoti cittaṃ, evaṃnāmako vā luddo. Ettha ca cittaṃ “cetayati cintetī”ti atthavasena ceto, luddo pana paṇṇattivasena. Tātāti tāyatīti tātā. “Aghassa tātā hitassa vidhātā”tissa payogo. “Tāto”ti etthāpi tāyatīti tāto, puttānaṃ pitūsu, pitarānaṃ puttesu, aññesañca aññesu piyapuggalesu vattabbavohāro [M 0.0190] eso. “So nūna kapaṇo tāto, ciraṃ ruccati assame. Kicchenādhigatā bhogā, te tāto vidhamaṃ dhamaṃ. Ehi tātā”tiādīsu cassa payogo veditabbo. “Cetā, cetā, cetāro. Cetāraṃ, cetāro”ti satthunayena padamālā. “Ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, cete. Cetasā, cetenā”ti manogaṇanayena ñeyyā. Ayaṃ cittavācakassa cetasaddassa nāmikapadamālā. “Ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, cete. Cetenā”ti purisanayena ñeyyā. Ayaṃ paṇṇattivācakassa cetasaddassa nāmikapadamālā. “Tātā, tātā, tātāro. Tātāra”nti satthunayena ñeyyā. “Tāto, tātā, tāta”nti purisanayena ñeyyā. Evamimāsupi nāmikapadamālāsu padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā vavatthapetabbā, tathā liṅgaantavasena “ñātā, ñāto, ñātaṃ, ñātā”ti catukkaṃ katvā padānamattho ca pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā ca padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā ca vavatthapetabbā.

Herein, 'cetā' first stands with an original -u ending, later becoming a masculine word ending in -ā; similarly also the word 'tātā'. 'Ceto,' however, first stands with an original -a ending, later becoming a masculine word ending in -o; similarly also the word 'tāto'. Therein, 'cetā' is one who gathers or makes a heap; thus, 'cetā,' meaning a person who builds walls, that is, a bricklayer. 'Ceto' means 'mind,' or a hunter of that name. Here, 'ceto' as 'mind' is derived by way of meaning from 'it thinks, it reflects,' while as 'hunter' it is by way of designation. 'Tātā' is one who protects. Its usage is 'a protector from misfortune, a provider of welfare.' In 'tāto' also, it means one who protects; this is an expression to be used by sons towards fathers, by fathers towards sons, and by others towards other beloved individuals. Its usage should be understood in such phrases as: 'Surely that poor dear one delights long in the hermitage. Wealth acquired with difficulty, that dear one wastes away. Come, dear one!' The paradigm for 'cetā' is 'Cetā, cetā, cetāro. Cetāraṃ, cetāro,' according to the paradigm of 'satthar'. 'Ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, cete. Cetasā, cetenā' should be known according to the paradigm of the 'manas' group. This is the nominal paradigm for the word 'ceto' that signifies mind. 'Ceto, cetā. Cetaṃ, cete. Cetenā' should be known according to the paradigm of 'purisa'. This is the nominal paradigm for the word 'ceto' that signifies by designation. The paradigm for 'tātā' is 'Tātā, tātā, tātāro. Tātāraṃ,' which should be known according to the paradigm of 'satthar'. 'Tāto, tātā, tāta' should be known according to the paradigm of 'purisa'. Thus, in these nominal paradigms also, the similarities and differences of the words should be determined. Likewise, by way of the gender and ending, forming the quartet 'ñātā, ñāto, ñātaṃ, ñātā,' the meaning of the words, the nominal paradigm of the original form, and the similarities and differences of the words should be determined.

Tatra hi “ñātā”ti idaṃ paṭhamaṃ ukārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchā ākārantabhūtaṃ pulliṅgaṃ. “Ñāto ñāta”nti imāni yathākkamaṃ paṭhamaṃ akārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchokārantaniggahītantabhūtāni vāccaliṅgesu punnapuṃsakaliṅgāni. Tathā hi “ñāto attho sukhāvaho. Ñātametaṃ kuraṅgassā”ti nesaṃ payogā dissanti. “Ñātā”ti idaṃ pana paṭhamaṃ ākārantatāpakatiyaṃ ṭhatvā pacchāpi ākārantabhūtaṃ vāccaliṅgesu itthiliṅgaṃ. Tathā hi “esā itthimayā ñātā”ti payogo. Tatra pulliṅgapakkhe “jānātīti ñātā”ti kattukārakavattamānakālavasena attho gahetabbo. Itthiliṅgādipakkhe “ñāyitthāti ñātā ñāto [M 0.0191] ñāta”nti kammakārakātītakālavasena attho gahetabbo. Esa nayo aññatthāpi yathāsambhavaṃ daṭṭhabbo. “Ñātā, ñātā, ñātāro. Ñātāra”nti satthunayena ñeyyā. “Ñāto, ñātā. Ñāta”nti purisanayena ñeyyā. “Ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñātā. Ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñāte”ti vakkhamānacittanayena ñeyyā. “Ñātā, ñātā, ñātāyo. Ñātaṃ, ñātā, ñātāyo”ti vakkhamānakaññānayena ñeyyā. Evamimāsupi nāmikapadamālāsu padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā vavatthapetabbā. Aññesupi ṭhānesu yathārahaṃ iminā nayena sadisāsadisatā upaparikkhitabbā. Vattā dhātā gantādīnampi “vadatīti vattā, dhāretīti dhātā, gacchatīti gantā”tiādinā yathāsambhavaṃ nibbacanāni ñeyyāni.

Herein, 'ñātā' first stands with an original -u ending, later becoming a masculine word ending in -ā. 'Ñāto' and 'ñātaṃ' first stand with an original -a ending, later becoming, respectively, masculine and neuter words ending in -o and a niggahīta, in their expressed genders. Thus, their usages are seen as 'a known meaning brings happiness' and 'this is known to the deer.' 'Ñātā,' however, first stands with an original -a ending, and remains a feminine word ending in -ā in its expressed gender. Thus, its usage is 'this woman is known by me.' Therein, in the masculine case, the meaning 'one who knows—thus, ñātā' should be taken by way of the agent in the present tense. In the feminine and other cases, the meaning 'she/it which was known—thus, ñātā, ñāto, ñātaṃ' should be taken by way of the patient in the past tense. This method should be seen elsewhere as is possible. 'Ñātā, ñātā, ñātāro. Ñātāraṃ' should be known according to the paradigm of 'satthar'. 'Ñāto, ñātā. Ñātaṃ' should be known according to the paradigm of 'purisa'. 'Ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñātā. Ñātaṃ, ñātāni, ñāte' should be known according to the paradigm of 'citta' which will be described. 'Ñātā, ñātā, ñātāyo. Ñātaṃ, ñātā, ñātāyo' should be known according to the paradigm of 'kaññā' which will be described. Thus, in these nominal paradigms also, the similarities and differences of the words should be determined. In other places as well, similarities and differences should be examined appropriately by this method. For words such as 'vattā,' 'dhātā,' and 'gantā,' the derivations 'one who speaks—thus, vattā,' 'one who bears—thus, dhātā,' and 'one who goes—thus, gantā' should be known as is possible.

Yaṃ panettha amhehi pakiṇṇakavacanaṃ kathitaṃ, taṃ “aṭṭhāne idaṃ kathita”nti na vattabbaṃ. Yasmā ayaṃ saddanīti nāma saddānamatthānañca yuttāyuttipakāsanatthaṃ katārambhattā nānappakārena sabbaṃ māgadhavohāraṃ saṅkhobhetvā kathitāyeva sobhati, na itarathā, tasmā nānappabhedena vattumicchāya sambhavato “aṭṭhāne idaṃ kathita”nti na vattabbaṃ. Nānāupāyehi viññūnaṃ ñāpanatthaṃ katārambhattā ca pana punaruttidosopettha na cintetabbo, aññadatthu saddhāsampannehi kulaputtehi ayaṃ saddanīti piṭakattayopakārāya sakkaccaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbā.

Whatever miscellaneous discourse has been spoken here by us, it should not be said of it, 'This has been spoken out of place.' Because this work, called the Saddanīti, has been undertaken for the purpose of clarifying the appropriate and inappropriate aspects of words and meanings, it shines only when it is presented by thoroughly stirring up all Magadhan usage in various ways, and not otherwise. Therefore, because of the desire to speak with various distinctions where possible, it should not be said, 'This has been spoken out of place.' Furthermore, since it was undertaken for the purpose of instructing the wise through various means, the fault of repetition should not be considered here either. On the contrary, this Saddanīti should be diligently studied by sons of good families endowed with faith for the benefit of the three Piṭakas.

Iti abhibhavitāpadasadisāni vattā, dhātā, gantādīni padāni dassitāni. Idāni ataṃsadisāni dassessāma. Seyyathidaṃ –

Thus have words similar to the word 'abhibhavitā' been shown, such as 'vattā,' 'dhātā,' 'gantā,' and others. Now we will show words similar to 'ataṃ.' Namely:

Guṇavā gaṇavā ceva, balavā yasavā tathā;

Dhanavā sutavā vidvā, dhutavā katavāpi ca.

One endowed with virtue and one with a following, one who is strong and one who is famous too; one who is wealthy, learned, and wise, one who has shaken off (defilements), and also one who has done (his duty).

Hitavā [M 0.0192] bhagavā ceva, dhitavā thāmavā tathā;

Yatavā cāgavā cātha, himaviccādayo ravā.

One who is beneficial, and the Blessed One; one who is resolute and one who is strong too; one who strives, and one who is generous; and then the words 'Himavā' and so forth.

Punnapuṃsakaliṅgehi, akārantehi pāyato;

Vantusaddo paro hoti, tadantā guṇavādayo.

From masculine and neuter gender stems ending in -a, for the most part, the suffix '-vantu' follows; those ending in it are `guṇavā` and so forth.

Saññāvā rasmivā ceva, massuvā ca yasassivā;

Iccādidassanāpeso, ākārivaṇṇukārato;

Itthiliṅgādīsu hoti, katthacīti pakāsaye.

Saññāvā, rasmivā, massuvā, and yasassivā: with regard to the observation of these and other examples, one should declare that from stems ending in -ā, -i, and -u, it occurs in feminine and other genders in some cases.

Satimā gatimā attha-dassimā dhitimā tathā;

Mutimā matimā ceva, jutimā hirimāpi ca.

Mindful, having movement, seeing the meaning, and steadfast; having intuition, intelligent, radiant, and also modest.

Thutimā ratimā ceva, yatimā balimā tathā;

Kasimā sucimā dhīmā, rucimā cakkhumāpi ca.

Having praise and having delight, having restraint and likewise having strength; having cultivation, pure, wise, having liking, and also having eyes.

Bandhumā hetumā’yasmā, ketumā rāhumā tathā;

Khāṇumā bhāṇumā gomā, vijjumā vasumādayo.

Having relatives, having a cause, venerable, having a banner, and likewise having Rāhu; having a stump, radiant, having cattle, having lightning, Vasumā and others.

Pāpimā puttimā ceva, candimiccādayopi ca;

Ataṃsadisasaddāti, viññātabbā vibhāvinā.

Evil and having offspring, and Candimā and others too; these are to be known by the discerning as words similar to those.

Ivaṇṇukārokārehi, mantusaddo paro bhave;

Ākārantā cikārantā, imantūti vibhāvaye.

From stems ending in the letters -i, -u, and -o, the suffix '-mantu' should follow. One should discern that from stems ending in -ā and -i, the suffix is '-imantu'.

Guṇavā, guṇavā, guṇavanto. Guṇavantaṃ, guṇavante. Guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavatā, guṇavantā, guṇavantasmā, guṇavantamhā, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavati, guṇavante, guṇavantasmiṃ, guṇavantamhi, guṇavantesu. Bho guṇavā, bhavanto guṇavā, bhonto guṇavanto.

Nominative: Guṇavā, guṇavā, guṇavanto. Accusative: Guṇavantaṃ, guṇavante. Instrumental: Guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Genitive: Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Ablative: Guṇavatā, guṇavantā, guṇavantasmā, guṇavantamhā, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Dative: Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Locative: Guṇavati, guṇavante, guṇavantasmiṃ, guṇavantamhi, guṇavantesu. Vocative: Bho guṇavā, bhavanto guṇavā, bhonto guṇavanto.

Ettha [M 0.0193] pana “etha tumhe āvuso sīlavāhothā”ti ca,

Here, however, 'Come, friends, be virtuous,' and

“Balavanto dubbalā honti, thāmavantopi hāyare;

Cakkhumā andhikā honti, mātugāmavasaṃ gatā”ti ca

'The strong become weak, the powerful also decline; those with eyes become blind, having come under the sway of women.'

Pāḷiyaṃ “sīlavā, cakkhumā”ti paṭhamābahuvacanassa dassanato “guṇavā”ti paccattālapanaṭṭhāne bahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. “Guṇavā satimā”tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Cūḷaniruttiyampi hi “guṇavā”ti paccattālapanabahuvacanāni āgatāni, niruttipiṭake paccattekavacanabhāveneva āgataṃ, cūḷaniruttiyaṃ pana niruttipiṭake ca “bho guṇava”iti rassavasena ālapanekavacanaṃ āgataṃ. Mayaṃ pana “taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā. Kathaṃ nu bhagavā tuyhaṃ sāvako sāsane rato”tievamādīsu anekasatesu pāṭhesu “bhagavā”iti ālapanekavacanassa dīghabhāvadassanato vantupaccayaṭṭhāne “bho guṇavā”iccādi dīghavasena vacanaṃ yuttataraṃ viya maññāma, mantupaccayaṭṭhāne pana imantupaccayaṭṭhāne ca “sabbaverabhayātīta, pāde vandāmi cakkhuma. Evaṃ jānāhi pāpima”iccādīsu pāḷipadesesu “cakkhuma”iccādiālapanekavacanassa rassabhāvadassanato “bho satima, bho gatima”iccādi rassavasena vacanaṃ yuttataraṃ viya maññāma, atha vā mahāparinibbānasuttaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “āyasmā tissa” itidīghavasena vuttālapanekavacanassa dassanato “bhagavā, āyasmā” itidīghavasena vuttapadamattaṃ ṭhapetvā vantupaccayaṭṭhānepi mantupaccayanayo netabbo, mantupaccayaṭṭhānepi vantupaccayanayo netabbo. Tathā hi kaccāyanādīsu “bho guṇavaṃ, bho guṇava, bho guṇavā”iti niggahītarassadīghavasena tīṇi ālapanekavacanāni vuttāni, iminā “bho satimaṃ, bho satima, bho satimā”ti evamādinayopi dassito[M 0.0194]. Paṭhamābahuvacanaṭṭhāne pana “guṇavanto, guṇavantā, guṇavantī”ti tīṇi padāni vuttāni, imināpi “satimanto, satimantā, satimantī”ti evamādinayopi dassito. Tesu “bho guṇavaṃ bho satimaṃ, guṇavantā, guṇavantī”ti imāni padāni evaṃgatikāni ca aññāni padāni pāḷiyaṃ appasiddhāni yathā “āyasmantā”ti padaṃ pasiddhaṃ, tasmā yaṃ cūḷaniruttiyaṃ vuttaṃ, yañca niruttipiṭake, yañca kaccāyanādīsu, taṃ sabbaṃ pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāhi ca saddhiṃ yathā na virujjhati, gaṅgodakena yamunodakaṃ viya aññadatthu saṃsandati sameti, tathā gahetabbaṃ.

In the Pāli, for the purpose of showing the nominative plural forms 'sīlavā' and 'cakkhumā', the form 'guṇavā' is stated as a plural in the context of the individual vocative. The same method applies in instances such as 'guṇavā satimā'. Indeed, in the Cūḷanirutti, plural individual vocative forms of 'guṇavā' are found; in the Niruttipiṭaka, it is found only as a singular; but in both the Cūḷanirutti and the Niruttipiṭaka, the singular vocative 'bho guṇava' is found with a short vowel. We, however, observing in hundreds of texts such as 'taggha bhagavā bojjhaṅgā. Kathaṃ nu bhagavā tuyhaṃ sāvako sāsane rato' that the singular vocative 'bhagavā' is long, consider it more appropriate that 'bho guṇavā', etc., be spoken with a long vowel in the case of the -vantu suffix. In the case of the -mantu suffix and the -imantu suffix, however, observing in Pāli passages such as 'sabbaverabhayātīta, pāde vandāmi cakkhuma. Evaṃ jānāhi pāpima' that the singular vocative 'cakkhuma', etc., is short, we consider it more appropriate that 'bho satima, bho gatima', etc., be spoken with a short vowel. Alternatively, based on the singular vocative 'āyasmā tissa' stated with a long vowel in the Mahāparinibbānasutta Commentary, setting aside only the words stated with a long vowel, 'bhagavā' and 'āyasmā', the method for the -mantu suffix should be applied in the case of the -vantu suffix, and the method for the -vantu suffix should be applied in the case of the -mantu suffix. Thus, in Kaccāyana and other texts, three singular vocative forms are stated: 'bho guṇavaṃ', 'bho guṇava', and 'bho guṇavā', with a niggahīta, a short vowel, and a long vowel respectively; by this, the method for 'bho satimaṃ', 'bho satima', 'bho satimā', etc., is also shown. In the case of the nominative plural, however, three forms are stated: 'guṇavanto', 'guṇavantā', and 'guṇavantī'; by this, the method for 'satimanto', 'satimantā', and 'satimantī', etc., is also shown. Among these, the forms 'bho guṇavaṃ', 'bho satimaṃ', 'guṇavantā', 'guṇavantī', and other such forms are not established in the Pāli canon, whereas the form 'āyasmantā' is well-known. Therefore, what is stated in the Cūḷanirutti, what is in the Niruttipiṭaka, and what is in Kaccāyana and other texts, all that should be understood in such a way that it does not conflict with the Pāli canon and the commentaries, but rather blends and merges with them, just as the water of the Ganges with the water of the Yamunā.

Apicettha ayampi viseso gahetabbo. Taṃ yathā? “Tuyhaṃ dhītā mahāvīra, paññavanta jutindharā”ti pāḷiyaṃ “paññavanta”iti ālapanekavacanassa dassanato.

And here this distinction should also be understood. How so? From the observation in the Pāli of 'paññavanta' as a singular vocative in the verse: 'O great hero, O wise one, your daughter is a bearer of radiance.'

“Sabbā kirevaṃ pariniṭṭhitāni,

Yasassi naṃ paññavantaṃ visayha;

Yaso ca laddhā purimaṃ uḷāraṃ,

Nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇa”nti.

'Indeed, all these things are thus perfectly accomplished. O famous one, having overcome that wise one, and having gained former, great glory, you would not abandon your ancient complexion and strength.'

Imissā jātakapāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “paññavanta”iti ālapanekavacanassa dassanato ca “bho guṇavanta, bho guṇavantā, bho satimanta, bho satimantā”tiādīnipi ālapanekavacanāni avassamicchitabbāni. Tathā hi tissaṃ pāḷiyaṃ “yasassi paññavanta” iccālapanavacanaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyā icchanti. Nanti hi padapūraṇe nipātamattaṃ. Paññavantanti pana chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ anusārāgamaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Evaṃ pāvacane vantupaccayādisahitānaṃ saddānaṃ “bhagavā, āyasmā, paññavanta, cakkhuma, pāpima”itidassitanayena ālapanappavatti veditabbā. Ettha ca “gaṅgābhāgīrathī nāma, himavantā pabhāvitā”ti ca “kuto āgatattha bhanteti, himavantā mahārājā”ti ca dassanato [M 0.0195] “guṇavantā”ti pañcamiyā ekavacanaṃ kathitaṃ. Yathā guṇavantu saddassa nāmikapadamālā yojitā, evaṃ dhanavantubalavantādīnaṃ satimantu gatimantādīnañca nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

In the commentary on this Jātaka Pāli text, from the observation of 'paññavanta' as a singular vocative, singular vocative forms such as 'bho guṇavanta', 'bho guṇavantā', 'bho satimanta', 'bho satimantā', etc., must also necessarily be accepted. For in that Pāli text, the commentary masters accept 'yasassi paññavanta' as a vocative expression. For 'naṃ' is merely a particle for filling the meter. But 'paññavantaṃ' is stated with the addition of an anusvāra to preserve the meter. Thus, in the scriptures, the occurrence of the vocative for words with suffixes like -vantu, etc., should be known according to the method shown by 'bhagavā', 'āyasmā', 'paññavanta', 'cakkhuma', and 'pāpima'. And here, from the examples 'The river named Bhāgīrathī arises from the Himavant' and 'From where have you come, sir? From the Himavant, O great king', the form 'guṇavantā' is stated as a singular of the ablative case. Just as the nominal paradigm for the stem 'guṇavantu' has been set out, so too should the nominal paradigms for 'dhanavantu', 'balavantu', etc., and for 'satimantu', 'gatimantu', etc., be constructed.

Idāni vidvādipadānaṃ guṇavāpadena samānagatikattampi sotūnaṃ payogesu sammohāpagamatthaṃ ekadesato nibbacanādīhi saddhiṃ vidvantuiccādipakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate – ñāṇasaṅkhāto vedo assa atthīti vidvā, paṇḍito. Ettha ca vidvāsaddassa atthibhāve “iti vidvā samaṃ care”tiādi āhaccapāṭho nidassanaṃ. Atrāyaṃ padamālā – vidvā, vidvā, vidvanto. Vidvantaṃ, vidvante. Vidvatā, vidvantena. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. Vedanāvā, vedanāvā, vedanāvanto. Vedanāvantaṃ, vedanāvante. Vedanāvatā, vedanāvantena. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. Evaṃ “saññāvācetanāvā saddhāvā paññavā sabbāvā”iccādīsupi. Ettha ca “vedanāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ sabbāvantaṃ loka”ntiādīni nidassanapadāni. Tattha sabbāvantanti sabbasattavantaṃ, sabbasattayuttanti attho. Majjhedīghañhi idaṃ padaṃ. Yebhuyyena pana “paññavāpaññavanto”tiādīni majjherassānipi bhavanti. Yasassino parivārabhūtā janā assa atthīti yasassivā, atha vā yasassī ca yasassivā cāti yasassivā. Ekadesasarūpekasesoyaṃ. “Yasassivā”ti padassa pana atthibhāve –

Now, to dispel confusion among listeners regarding the uses of words like vidvā (wise), which have a similar declension to guṇavā (virtuous), a list of nominal forms based on the vidvantu stem, along with partial explanations, is being presented – this is called the nāmikapadamālā (list of nominal forms). Here, vidvā (wise) is defined as: 'one who has knowledge, which is called wisdom, is vidvā, a scholar.' And to illustrate the existence of the word vidvā, there is a direct passage such as 'iti vidvā samaṃ care' (thus, the wise should act impartially). Here is the paradigm: vidvā, vidvā, vidvanto. Vidvantaṃ, vidvante. Vidvatā, vidvantena. The rest should be understood accordingly. Similarly, for vedanāvā (one who has feeling): vedanāvā, vedanāvā, vedanāvanto. Vedanāvantaṃ, vedanāvante. Vedanāvatā, vedanāvantena. The rest should be understood accordingly. In the same way, for words like saññāvā (one who has perception), cetanāvā (one who has volition), saddhāvā (one who has faith), paññavā (one who has wisdom), sabbāvā (one who has all), and so on. Here, illustrative examples include: 'vedanāvantaṃ vā attānaṃ sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ' (either the self endowed with feelings or the world endowed with all). In this context, sabbāvantaṃ means 'possessed of all beings,' that is, 'connected with all beings.' Indeed, this word has a long vowel in the middle. But mostly, words like paññavā and paññavanto also have short vowels in the middle. Yasassivā (one who is famous) is derived as: 'one who has people as attendants because of his fame is called yasassivā,' or alternatively, 'yasassī ca yasassivā cāti yasassivā' (both yasassī and yasassivā [can mean the same]). This is a case of ekasesa due to partial similarity in form. Regarding the existence of the word yasassivā—

“Khattiyo jātisampanno, abhijāto yasassivā;

Dhammarājā videhānaṃ, putto uppajjate tavā”ti

'A khattiya endowed with noble birth, high-born and glorious; a righteous king of the Videhans, a son will be born to you.'

Idaṃ nidassanaṃ. “Yasassivā, yasassivā, yasassivanto. Yasassivantaṃ” iccādi netabbaṃ. Atthe dassanasīlaṃ atthadassi, kiṃ [M 0.0196] taṃ? Ñāṇaṃ. Atthadassi assa atthīti atthadassimā, ettha ca –

This is an illustration. 'Yasassivā, yasassivā, yasassivanto. Yasassivantaṃ,' etc., should be understood. The characteristic of seeing the meaning is atthadassi (seeing the meaning); what is that? Knowledge. One who has atthadassi is atthadassimā; and here—

“Taṃ tattha gatimā dhitimā, mutimā atthadassimā;

Saṅkhātā sabbadhammānaṃ, vidhuro etadabravī”ti

'Having gone there, resolute, intelligent, discerning the meaning, one who has comprehended all phenomena, Vidhura spoke thus.'

Idametassatthassa sādhakaṃ vacanaṃ. “Atthadassimā, atthadassimā, atthadassimanto. Atthadassimantaṃ” iccādi netabbaṃ. Pāpaṃ assa atthīti pāpimā, akusalarāsisamannāgato māro. Puttā assa atthīti puttimā, bahuputto. “Socati puttehi puttimā”ti ettha hi bahuputto “puttimā”ti vuccati. Cando assa atthīti candimā. Candoti cettha candavimānamadhippetaṃ, candavimānavāsī pana devaputto “candimā”ti. Tathā hi “cando uggato, pamāṇato cando āyāmavitthārato ubbedhato ca ekūnapaññāsayojano, parikkhepato tīhi yojanehi ūnadiyaḍḍhasatayojano”tiādīsu candavimānaṃ “cando”ti vuttaṃ. “Tathāgataṃ arahantaṃ, candimā saraṇaṃ gato”tiādīsu pana candadevaputto “candimā”ti. Aparo nayo – cando assa atthīti candimā. Candoti cettha candadevaputto adhippeto, tannivāsaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ pana candavimānaṃ “candimā”ti. Tathā hi “rāhu candaṃ pamuñcassu, cando maṇimayavimāne vasatī”tiādīsu candadevaputto “cando”ti vutto.

This is a confirmatory statement for this meaning. 'Atthadassimā, atthadassimā, atthadassimanto. Atthadassimantaṃ,' etc., should be understood. He has evil, therefore he is Pāpimā, Māra endowed with a mass of unwholesomeness. He has sons, therefore he is Puttimā, one with many sons. 'The one with sons grieves on account of his sons'—here indeed, one with many sons is called 'Puttimā.' He has the moon, therefore he is Candimā. Here, 'Cando' refers to the lunar mansion, but the deva-son dwelling in the lunar mansion is called 'Candimā.' For thus it is said: 'The moon has risen; the moon in size is forty-nine yojanas in length, width, and height, and in circumference is one hundred forty-seven yojanas'—here the lunar mansion is called 'Cando.' But in passages like 'The Tathāgata, the Arahant, Candimā has gone for refuge,' the moon-deva-son is called 'Candimā.' Another interpretation—he has the moon, therefore he is Candimā. Here, 'Cando' refers to the moon-deva-son, but the lunar mansion, which is his dwelling place, is called 'Candimā.' For thus it is said: 'Release the moon, O Rāhu, the moon dwells in a jeweled mansion'—here the moon-deva-son is called 'Cando.'

“Yo have daharo bhikkhu, yuñjati buddhasāsane;

Somaṃlokaṃpabhāseti, abbhā muttova candimā”ti

'Indeed, that young monk who strives in the Buddha's Dispensation illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.'

Ādīsu pana tannivāsaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ candavimānaṃ “candimā”ti vuttaṃ. Iti “cando”ti ca “candimā”ti ca candadevaputtassapi candavimānassapi [M 0.0197] nāmanti veditabbaṃ. Tatra “pāpimā puttimā candimā”ti imāni pāpasaddādito “tadassatthi” iccetasmiṃ atthe pavattassa imantupaccayassa vasena siddhimupāgatānīti gahetabbāni.

But in such passages, the lunar mansion, which is his dwelling place, is called 'Candimā.' Thus, it should be understood that both 'Cando' and 'Candimā' are names for the moon-deva-son as well as the lunar mansion. Here, 'pāpimā,' 'puttimā,' and 'candimā' should be understood as having attained their derivation by means of the affix '-imantu,' which occurs in the sense of 'having that' from the word 'pāpa' and so on.

Nanu ca bho mantupaccayavaseneva sādhetabbānīti? Na, katthacipi akārantato mantuno abhāvā. Nanu ca bho evaṃ santepi pāpa putta candato paṭhamaṃ ikārāgamaṃ katvā tato mantupaccayaṃ katvā sakkā sādhetunti? Sakkā rūpamattasijjhanato, nayo pana sobhano na hoti. Tathā hi pāpa puttādito akārantato ikārāgamaṃ katvā mantupaccaye vidhiyamāne aññehi guṇayasādīhi akārantehi ikārāgamaṃ katvā mantupaccayassa kātabbatāpasaṅgo siyā. Na hi anekesu pāḷisatasahassesu katthacipi akārantato guṇa yasādito ikārāgamena saddhiṃ mantupaccayo dissati, aṭṭhānattā pana pāpa puttādito akārantato ikārāgamaṃ akatvā imantupaccaye kateyeva “pāpimā puttimā”tiādīni sijjhantīti.

“But, sir, should they not be accomplished solely through the mantu suffix?” “No, because nowhere is a mantu suffix found attached to a stem ending in an ‘a’.” “But, sir, even so, could it not be accomplished by first adding the ‘i’ vowel to ‘pāpa,’ ‘putta,’ and ‘canda’ and then applying the mantu suffix?” “It can be accomplished merely for the sake of the form, but the method is not elegant. For if the ‘i’ vowel is added to words like ‘pāpa,’ ‘putta,’ etc., ending in ‘a’ and then the mantu suffix is applied, there would be the undesirable consequence that the same process would have to be done with other words ending in ‘a’ such as guṇa and yasa. Indeed, nowhere in the many hundreds of thousands of Pāli texts is the mantu suffix seen applied after adding the ‘i’ vowel to words ending in ‘a’ such as guṇa and yasa. Therefore, without adding the ‘i’ vowel to words like ‘pāpa,’ ‘putta,’ etc., ending in ‘a’, and simply applying the imantu suffix, forms like ‘pāpimā,’ ‘puttimā,’ etc., are correctly derived.”

Evaṃ santepi bho kasmā kaccāyanappakaraṇe mantupaccayova vutto, na imantupaccayoti? Dvayampi vuttameva. Kathaṃ ñāyatīti ce? Yasmā tattha “tapādito sī, daṇḍādito ika ī, madhvādito ro, guṇādito vantū”ti imāni cattāri suttāni sannihitatodantasaddabhāvena vatvā majjhe “satyādīhi mantū”ti aññathā suttaṃ vatvā tato sannihitatodantavasena “saddhādito ṇā”ti suttaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā tattha “satyādīhimantū”ti visadisaṃ katvā vuttassa suttassa vasena imantu paccayo ca vuttoti viññāyati. Pakati hesācariyānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena attano adhippāyaviññāpanaṃ. Ettha ca dutiyo attho sarasandhivasena gahetabbo. Tathā hissa “satyādīhi mantū”ti [M 0.0198] paṭhamo attho, “satyādīhi imantū”ti dutiyo attho. Iti “seto dhāvatī”ti payoge viya “satyādīhi mantū”ti sutte bhinnasattisamavetavasena atthadvayapaṭipatti bhavati, tasmā paramasukhumasugambhīratthavatā anena suttena katthaci sati gati setu goiccādito mantupaccayo icchito. Katthaci sati pāpa puttaiccādito imantupaccayo icchitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

“Even so, sir, why in the Kaccāyana treatise is the affix ‘mantu’ alone mentioned, and not ‘imantu’?” “Both are indeed stated. How is this to be known? Because there, after stating the four rules—‘from tapa comes sī, from daṇḍa comes ika or ī, from madhu comes ro, from guṇa comes vantū’—based on the nature of dental-ending sounds being proximate, and then in the middle stating the rule ‘from satya, etc., comes mantu’ differently, and thereafter, based on the proximity of dental-ending sounds, stating the rule ‘from saddhā comes ṇā,’ therefore, there, by stating ‘from satya, etc., comes mantu’ in a distinct manner, it is understood that the affix ‘imantu’ is also stated. This is the natural way of the teachers, to convey their intended meaning by any means. And here, the second meaning should be understood by means of vowel sandhi. For in this, the first meaning is ‘from satya, etc., comes mantu,’ and the second meaning is ‘from satya, etc., comes imantu.’ Thus, just as in the usage ‘seto dhāvatī’ (the white one runs), in the rule ‘from satya, etc., comes mantu,’ the comprehension of dual meanings arises through the combination of distinct grammatical powers. Therefore, due to the extremely subtle and profound meaning of this rule, it should be seen that in some cases, the affix ‘mantu’ is desired from sati, gati, setu, go, etc., and in some cases, the affix ‘imantu’ is desired from sati, pāpa, putta, etc.”

Yasmā pana satisaddo mantuvasena gatidhīsethugo iccādīhi, imantuvasena pāpaputtādīhi ca samānagatikattā tesaṃ pakārabhāvena gahito, tasmā evaṃ suttattho bhavati “satyādīhi mantu satippakārehi saddehi mantupaccayo hoti imantupaccayo ca yathārahaṃ ‘tadassatthi’ iccetasmiṃ atthe”ti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yathā “satimā”ti ettha satīti ikārantato mantupaccayo hoti, tathā “gatimā, dhīmā, setumā, gomā”tiādīsu ikāranta īkāranta ukārantaniccokārantato mantupaccayo hoti. Yathā ca “satimā”ti ettha “satī”ti ikārantato imantupaccayo hoti, tathā “gatimā, pāpimā, puttimā”tiādīsu ikāranta akārantato imantupaccayo hoti. Evaṃ satippakārehi saddehi yathāsambhavaṃ mantu imantupaccayā hontīti.

Since the word 'sati' is taken as an exemplar of those words—because, with respect to the suffix 'mantu', it has the same function as 'gati', 'dhī', 'setu', 'go', etc., and with respect to the suffix 'imantu', as 'pāpa', 'putta', etc.—the meaning of the sutta is thus: 'From sati and other words of the sati-type, the suffix mantu and the suffix imantu occur, as appropriate, in the sense of “that exists in him/it” (tadassatthi).’ Herein, this is the intention: just as in the word 'satimā', the suffix 'mantu' is from the i-final stem 'sati', so too in words like 'gatimā', 'dhīmā', 'setumā', and 'gomā', the suffix 'mantu' is from stems ending in i, ī, u, or the permanent o. And just as in 'satimā', the suffix 'imantu' is from the i-final stem 'sati', so too in words like 'gatimā', 'pāpimā', and 'puttimā', the suffix 'imantu' is from stems ending in i or a. Thus, from words of the sati-type, the suffixes mantu and imantu are formed as is possible.

Yajjevaṃ paccayadvayavidhāyakaṃ “daṇḍādito ika ī”ti suttaṃ viya “satyādito imantu mantū”ti vattabbaṃ, kasmā nāvocāti? Tathā avacane kāraṇamatthi. Yadi hi “daṇḍādito ika ī”ti suttaṃ viya “satyādito imantu mantū”ti suttaṃ vuttaṃ siyā, ekakkhaṇeyeva imantu mantūnaṃ vacanena daṇḍasaddato sambhūtaṃ “daṇḍiko daṇḍī”ti rūpadvayamiva satigatiāditopi visadisarūpadvayamicchitabbaṃ siyā, tañca natthi, tasmā [M 0.0199] “satyādito imantu mantū”ti na vuttaṃ. Apica tathā vutte bavhakkharatāya ganthagarutā siyā. Yasmā ca suttena nāma appakkharena asandiddhena sāravantena gūḷhaninnayena sabbatomukhena anavajjena bhavitabbaṃ. Kaccāyane ca yebhuyyena tādisāni gambhīratthāni suvisadañāṇavisayabhūtāni suttāni dissanti “upājhadhikissaravacane, sarā sare lopa”ntiādīni, idampi tesamaññataraṃ, tasmā “satyādito imantu mantū”ti na vuttaṃ. Evaṃ suttopadese akatepi imantunopi gahaṇatthaṃ bhinnasattisamavetavasena “satyādīhi mantū”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

If so, since this is a rule prescribing two suffixes, like the sutta 'from daṇḍa, etc., ika and ī', it should have been stated as 'from sati, etc., imantu and mantu'. Why was it not said so? There is a reason for not stating it so. For if a sutta had been stated as 'from sati, etc., imantu and mantu', like the sutta 'from daṇḍa, etc., ika and ī', then, by the statement of imantu and mantu at the same moment, two dissimilar forms would have to be desired from sati, gati, etc., just as the two forms 'daṇḍiko' and 'daṇḍī' arise from the word 'daṇḍa'—but this is not the case. Therefore, 'from sati, etc., imantu and mantu' was not stated. Moreover, if it were stated so, the text would become heavy due to many syllables. And a sutta should indeed be of few syllables, unambiguous, essential, profound in meaning, comprehensive, and faultless. In Kaccāyana's grammar, for the most part, such suttas are seen, which are profound in meaning and the domain of very clear knowledge, such as 'upājjhadhikissaravacane' and 'sarā sare lopaṃ'. This too is one of them. Therefore, 'from sati, etc., imantu and mantu' was not stated. Even though the sutta was not taught in this way, it should be understood that 'from sati, etc., mantu' is stated for the purpose of including imantu as well, by means of combining words having different powers.

Aparo nayo – “tapādito sī”tiādīsu todantasaddassa bahuvacanantatā na suṭṭhu pākaṭā topaccayassa ekatthabavhatthesu vattanato, “satyādīhi mantū”ti ettha pana hisaddassa bahuvacanatthatā atīva pākaṭā, tasmā bahuvacanaggahaṇena imantu paccayo hotītipi daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nanu ca bho vināpi imantupaccayena pāpamassatthīti pāpī, pāpī eva pāpimāti sakatthe māpaccaye kateyeva “pāpimā puttimā”tiādīni sijjhanti “chaṭṭhamo so parābhavo”ti ettha mapaccayena “chaṭṭhamo”ti padaṃ viyāti? Atinayaññū bhavaṃ, atinayaññū nāmāti bhavaṃ vattabbo, na pana bhavaṃ saddagatiṃ jānāti, saddagatiyo ca nāma bahuvidhā. Tathā hi chaṭṭhoyeva chaṭṭhamo, “suttameva suttanto”tiādīsu purisanayena yojetabbā saddagati, “devoyeva devatā”tiādīsu kaññānayena yojetabbā saddagati, “diṭṭhi eva diṭṭhigata”ntiādīsu cittanayena yojetabbā saddagati. Evaṃvidhāsu saddagatīsu “pāpī eva pāpimā”tiādikaṃ kataraṃ saddagatiṃ vadesi? “Satthā rājā brahmā sakhā attā sā pumā”tiādīsu [M 0.0200] ca kataraṃ saddagatiṃ vadesi? Katarasaddantogadhaṃ katarāya ca nāmikapadamālāyaṃ yojetabbaṃ maññasīti? So evaṃ puṭṭho addhā uttari kiñci adisvā tuṇhī bhavissati, tasmā tādiso nayo na gahetabbo. Tādisasmiñhi naye “pāpimatā pāpimato”tiādīni rūpāni na sijjhanti, imantupaccayanayena pana sijjhanti, tasmā ayameva nayo pasatthataro āyasmantehi sammā citte ṭhapetabbo. Atridaṃ nidassanaṃ –

Another method: In rules like 'from tapa, etc., sī', the fact that the word ending in to is plural is not very clear, because the suffix to is used in both singular and plural senses. However, in 'from sati, etc., mantu', the plural sense of the word ending in hi is very clear. Therefore, it should also be understood that the suffix imantu is indicated by the use of the plural. 'But, sir, even without the suffix imantu, forms like pāpimā, puttimā, etc., are accomplished. From pāpam assa atthi comes pāpī; pāpī itself becomes pāpimā when the suffix mā is added in its own sense, just as the word chaṭṭhamo is formed with the suffix ma in chaṭṭhamo so parābhavo.' You, sir, are an over-knower of methods! 'Over-knower of methods' is what you should be called. But you, sir, do not know the way of words, and the ways of words are of many kinds. For instance: chaṭṭho itself is chaṭṭhamo; this way of words should be connected with the masculine paradigm (purisanaya), as in suttam eva suttanto. Devo itself is devatā; this way of words should be connected with the feminine paradigm (kaññānaya). Diṭṭhi itself is diṭṭhigataṃ; this way of words should be connected with the neuter paradigm (cittanaya). Among such ways of words, which way of words do you say pāpī eva pāpimā is? And which way of words do you say is in satthā, rājā, brahmā, sakhā, attā, sā, pumā? Included in which word-ending, and connected with which nominal paradigm, do you think it should be? When questioned thus, surely, seeing no further reply, he will become silent. Therefore, such a method should not be accepted. For with such a method, forms like 'pāpimatā', 'pāpimato', etc., are not accomplished, but they are accomplished by the method of the imantu suffix. Therefore, this method alone is more excellent and should be well established in the mind by you, venerable ones. Here is an example:

“Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ,

Mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā,

Jayaṃ tadā devagaṇā mahesino”ti ca,

“This is indeed the victory of the glorious Buddha, and the defeat of the evil Māra. Then, at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, the delighted hosts of gods proclaimed the victory of the Great Sage.”

“Sākhāpattaphalūpeto, khandhimāvamahādumo”ti ca.

“Endowed with branches, leaves, and fruits, a great tree, possessed of a trunk.”

Pāpimā, pāpimā, pāpimanto. Pāpimantaṃ. Sesaṃ neyyaṃ, esa nayo “khandhimā, puttimā”tiādīsupi.

Pāpimā, pāpimā, pāpimanto. Pāpimantaṃ. The rest is to be inferred. This is the method also in 'khandhimā', 'puttimā', and so forth.

Idāni yathāpāvacanaṃ kiñcideva himavantu satimantādīnaṃ visesaṃ brūma. Himavantova pabbato. Satimaṃ bhikkhuṃ. Bandhumaṃ rājānaṃ. Candimaṃ devaputtaṃ. Satimassa bhikkhuno. Bandhumassa rañño. Iddhimassa ca parassa ca ekakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppajjati. Iccādi viseso veditabbo. Apicettha “āyasmantā”ti dvinnaṃ vattabbavacanaṃ, “āyasmanto”ti bahūnaṃ vattabbavacananti ayampi viseso veditabbo. Tathā hi “dvinnaṃ ārocentena ‘āyasmantā dhārentū’ti, tiṇṇaṃ ārocentena ‘āyasmanto dhārentū’ti vattabba”nti vuttaṃ. “Tiṇṇa”nti cettha kathāsīsamattaṃ, tena catunnampi pañcannampi atirekasatānampīti dassitaṃ [M 0.0201] hoti. Bahavohi upādāya “uddiṭṭhā kho āyasmanto cattāro pārājikā dhammā”tiādikā pāḷiyo ṭhapitā. Tattha “āyasmantā”tidaṃ vinayavohāravasena dveyeva sandhāya vuttattā na sabbasādhāraṇaṃ. Vinayavohārañhi vajjetvā aññasmiṃ vohāre na pavattati. “Āyasmanto”tidaṃ pana sabbattha pavattatīti dvinnaṃ viseso veditabbo.

Now, according to the texts, we shall explain some distinctions concerning terms like 'Himavantu', 'Satimantu', and so on. 'Himavantova pabbato' (Himavantu is a mountain). 'Satimaṃ bhikkhuṃ' (a mindful monk). 'Bandhumaṃ rājānaṃ' (King Bandhuma). 'Candimaṃ devaputtaṃ' (the celestial being Candima). 'Satimassa bhikkhuno' (of a mindful monk). 'Bandhumassa rañño' (of King Bandhuma). 'Iddhimassa ca parassa ca ekakkhaṇe cittaṃ uppajjati' (Of one with psychic power and of another, a thought arises in a single moment). Such distinctions should be understood. Moreover, herein, 'āyasmantā' is a word for addressing two, while 'āyasmanto' is a word for addressing many—this distinction too should be understood. For it is said: 'One announcing to two should say, “May the venerable ones (āyasmantā) bear this in mind”; one announcing to three should say, “May the venerable ones (āyasmanto) bear this in mind”.’ Herein, 'three' is merely the start of the discussion, by which it is shown that it applies to four, five, or even more than a hundred. For many Pāḷi passages have been established beginning with 'Venerable sirs (āyasmanto), the four pārājika rules have been recited'. Therein, 'āyasmantā', being stated with reference to only two by way of Vinaya usage, is not of general application. For, apart from Vinaya usage, it does not occur in other usage. 'Āyasmanto', however, occurs everywhere. Thus the distinction between the two should be understood.

Tatra “himavanto”ti idaṃ yebhuyyenekavacanaṃ bhavati, katthaci bahuvacanampi, tenāha niruttipiṭake thero “himavā tiṭṭhati, himavanto tiṭṭhantī”ti. “Himavantova pabbato”ti ayaṃ ekavacananayo yathārutapāḷivasena gahetabbo. Yathārutapāḷi ca nāma –

Therein, this word 'himavanto' is for the most part singular, but in some places it is also plural. Thus the Elder in the Niruttipiṭaka said: 'Himavā stands; himavanto stand.' The phrase 'Himavantova pabbato' is the singular usage, which should be understood according to the Pāḷi as it is recited. And the Pāḷi as it is recited is as follows:

“Dūre santo pakāsanti, himavantova pabbato;

Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṃ khittā yathā sarā.

“The good shine from afar, like the Himālaya mountain; the wicked here are not seen, like arrows shot in the night.”

Ahaṃ tena samayena, nāgarājā mahiddhiko;

Atulo nāma nāmena, puññavanto jutindharo.

“At that time, I was a nāga king of great psychic power, named Atula, meritorious and possessing radiance.”

Gatimanto satimanto, dhitimanto ca so isi;

Saddhammadhārako thero, ānando ratanākaro”

“That sage is possessed of good conduct, mindfulness, and fortitude; the Elder Ānanda, a bearer of the good Dhamma, a mine of gems.”

Iccādi. Ettha “puññavanto”tiādīni anekesu ṭhānesu bahuvacanabhāvena punappunaṃ vadantānipi katthaci ekavacanāni honti, ekavacanabhāvo ca nesaṃ gāthāvisaye dissati, tasmā tāni yathāpāvacanaṃ gahetabbāni.

And so on. Herein, words such as 'puññavanto', although repeatedly used in the plural form in many places, are sometimes singular. Their singular nature is seen in the context of verses; therefore, they should be understood according to the wording.

Evaṃ himavantusatimantusaddādīnaṃ visesaṃ ñatvā puna liṅgantavasena dviliṅgakapadānamattho ca pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā ca padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā ca vavatthapetabbā.

Having thus understood the special characteristics of words such as himavantu and satimantu, the meaning of words with two genders should be determined by way of their gender endings. The nominal paradigm of the base form and the similarity or dissimilarity of words must also be established.

Tatra [M 0.0202] hi “sirimā”ti padaṃ sutisāmaññavasena liṅgadvaye vattanato dvidhā bhijjati. “Sirimā puriso”ti hi atthe ākārantaṃ pulliṅgaṃ, “sirimā nāma devī”ti atthe ākārantaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ, ubhayampetaṃ ukārantatāpakatikā. Atha vā pana pacchimaṃ ākārantatāpakatikaṃ, sirī yassa atthi so sirimāti pulliṅgavasena nibbacanaṃ, sirī yassā atthi sā sirimāti itthiliṅgavasena nibbacanaṃ. Atrimāni kiñcāpi sutivasena nibbacanatthavasena ca aññamaññaṃ samānatthāni, tathāpi purisapadatthaitthipadatthavācakattā bhinnatthānīti veditabbāni. Esa nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo. Sirimā, sirimā, sirimanto. Sirimantaṃ, sirimante. Sirimatā, sirimantena. Guṇavantusaddasseva nāmikapadamālā. Sirimā, sirimā, sirimāyo. Sirimaṃ, sirimā, sirimāyo. Sirimāya. Vakkhamānakaññānayena ñeyyā. Evaṃ dvidhā bhinnānaṃ samānasutikasaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālāsu padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā vavatthapetabbā. Samānanibbacanatthassapi hi asamānasutikassa “sirimā”ti saddassa nāmikapadamālāyaṃ padānaṃ imehi padehi kācipi samānatā na labbhati. Atridaṃ vuccati –

For here, the word “sirimā” is divided in two because it occurs in two genders by way of similarity of sound.
