In the sense “Sirimā the man,” it is a masculine word ending in -ā; in the sense “the devī named Sirimā,” it is a feminine word ending in -ā. Both of these have bases ending in -u. Or else, the latter has a base ending in -ā. The derivation in the masculine is: “He who has glory (sirī) is Sirimā.” The derivation in the feminine is: “She who has glory is Sirimā.” Although these forms are mutually similar in meaning by way of sound and by way of the meaning to be expressed, they should be understood as having different meanings because they denote the meaning of the word “man” and the word “woman” respectively. This method should be applied in other such cases. Sirimā, sirimā, sirimanto. Sirimantaṃ, sirimante. Sirimatā, sirimantena. The nominal paradigm is just like that of the word guṇavantu. Sirimā, sirimā, sirimāyo. Sirimaṃ, sirimā, sirimāyo. Sirimāya. This should be understood by the method for kaññā that will be explained. Thus, in the nominal paradigms of words of similar sound that are divided in two, the similarity and dissimilarity of the forms should be established. For, in the nominal paradigm of a word like “sirimā” with a dissimilar sound, even if it has the same derived meaning, no similarity whatsoever is found between its forms and these forms. Here this is said:

“Sirimā”ti padaṃ dvedhā, pumitthīsu pavattito;

Bhijjatīti vibhāveyya, ettha pulliṅgamicchitaṃ.

“The word ‘sirimā’ is twofold, as it occurs in the masculine and feminine; one should understand that it is divided. Here, the masculine is intended.”

Iti abhibhavitā padena visadisāni guṇavāsatimādīni padāni dassitāni saddhiṃ nāmikapadamālāhi. Idāni aparānipi tabbisadisāni padāni dassessāma saddhiṃ nāmikapadamālāhi. Seyyathidaṃ?

Thus, dissimilar words such as guṇavā and satimā have been shown along with their nominal paradigms. Now we will show other words dissimilar to those, together with their nominal paradigms. They are as follows:

Rājā brahmā sakhā attā, ātumā sā pumā rahā;

Daḷhadhammā ca paccakkha-dhammā ca vivaṭacchadā.

King (rājā), brahmā, friend (sakhā), self (attā), self (ātumā), dog (sā), male (pumā), solitude (rahā); and one firm in the Dhamma (daḷhadhammā), one for whom the Dhamma is directly visible (paccakkhadhammā), and one with covering removed (vivaṭacchadā).

Vattahā [M 0.0203] ca tathā vutta-sirā ceva yuvāpi ca;

Maghava addha muddhādi, viññātabbā vibhāvinā.

And the speaker (vattahā), and one with a bound head (vuttasirā), and also a youth (yuvā); Maghavā, and words such as addhan (path) and muddhan (head)—these should be understood by the discerning one.

Ettha “sā”ti padameva ākārantatāpakatikamākārantaṃ, sesāni pana akārantatāpakatikāni ākārantāni.

Here, only the word “sā” is a word ending in -ā that has a base ending in -ā; the remaining words, however, are words ending in -ā that have bases ending in -a.

Rājā, rājā, rājāno. Rājānaṃ, rājaṃ, rājāno. Raññā, rājinā, rājūhi, rājūbhi. Rañño, rājino, raññaṃ, rājūnaṃ, rājānaṃ. Raññā, rājūhi, rājūbhi. Rañño, rājino, raññaṃ, rājūnaṃ, rājānaṃ. Raññe, rājini, rājūsu. Bho rāja, bhavanto rājāno, bhavanto rājā iti vā, ayamamhākaṃ ruci.

Rājā, rājā, rājāno. Rājānaṃ, rājaṃ, rājāno. Raññā, rājinā, rājūhi, rājūbhi. Rañño, rājino, raññaṃ, rājūnaṃ, rājānaṃ. Raññā, rājūhi, rājūbhi. Rañño, rājino, raññaṃ, rājūnaṃ, rājānaṃ. Raññe, rājini, rājūsu. Bho rāja, bhavanto rājāno, or bhavanto rājā—this is our preference.

Niruttipiṭakādīsu “rājā”ti bahuvacanaṃ na āgataṃ, cūḷaniruttiyaṃ pana āgataṃ. Kiñcāpi niruttipiṭakādīsu na āgataṃ, tathāpi “netādisā sakhā honti, labbhā me jīvato sakhā”ti pāḷiyaṃ bahuvacanekavacanavasena “sakhā”ti padassa dassanato “rājā”ti bahuvacanaṃ icchitabbameva. Tathā “brahmā, attā”iccādīnipi bahuvacanāni taggatikattā vinā kenaci rūpavisesena.

In the Niruttipiṭaka and other texts, the plural form “rājā” does not occur, but it does occur in the Cūḷanirutti. Although it does not occur in the Niruttipiṭaka and other texts, nevertheless, based on the Pāḷi passage “netādisā sakhā honti, labbhā me jīvato sakhā,” where the word “sakhā” is found used in both the plural and singular senses, the plural form “rājā” should indeed be accepted. Similarly, words such as “brahmā” and “attā” also have plural forms because they follow the same pattern, without any specific difference in form.

Ettha ca “gahapatiko nāma ṭhapetvā rājaṃ rājabhogaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ avaseso gahapatiko nāmā”ti dassanato rājanti vuttaṃ, idaṃ pana niruttipiṭake na āgataṃ. “Sabbadattena rājinā”ti dassanato “rājinā”ti vuttaṃ. “Ārādhayati rājānaṃ, pūjaṃ labhati bhattusū”ti dassanato catutthīchaṭṭhīvasena “rājāna”nti vuttaṃ. Kaccāyanarūpasiddhiganthesu pana “rājena, rājehi, rājebhi. Rājesū”ti padāni vuttāni. Cūḷaniruttiniruttipiṭakesu tāni nāgatāni, anāgatabhāvoyeva tesaṃ yuttataro pāḷiyaṃ adassanato, tasmā etthetāni [M 0.0204] amhehi na vuttāni. Pāḷinaye hi upaparikkhiyamāne īdisāni padāni samāseyeva passāma, na panāññatra, atrime payogā – “āvutthaṃ dhammarājenā”ti ca, “sivirājena pesito”ti ca, “pajāpatissa devarājassa dhajagga”nti ca, “nikkhamante mahārāje, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane”ti ca, evaṃ pāḷinaye upaparikkhiyamāne “rājenā”tiādīni samāseyeva passāma, na kevalaṃ pāḷinaye porāṇaṭṭhakathānayepi upaparikkhiyamāne samāseyeva passāma, na panāññatra, evaṃ santepi suṭṭhu upaparikkhitabbamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Ko hi nāma sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane sabbaso nayaṃ sallakkhetuṃ samattho aññatra pabhinnapaṭisambhidehi khīṇāsavehi.

And here, from the passage, “‘Householder’ means one who is other than a king, one who enjoys royal patronage, and a brahmin; the remainder are called householders,” the form rājaṃ is mentioned, but this is not found in the Niruttipiṭaka. From the passage, “by King Sabbadatta,” the form rājinā is mentioned. From the passage, “He pleases the king, he receives honor from his master,” the form rājānaṃ is mentioned in the dative and genitive sense. In the works of Kaccāyana and in the Rūpasiddhi, however, the forms rājena, rājehi, rājebhi, rājesu are mentioned. These are not found in the Cūḷanirutti and the Niruttipiṭaka. Their non-occurrence is more proper since they are not seen in the Pāḷi Canon; therefore, we have not mentioned them here. For when the Pāḷi usage is examined, we see such forms only in compounds, not elsewhere. These are the usages: “āvutthaṃ dhammarājenā,” “sivirājena pesito,” “pajāpatissa devarājassa dhajagga,” and “nikkhamante mahārāje, sivīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhane.” Thus, when examining the Pāḷi usage, we see forms like rājenā only in compounds. Not only when examining the Pāḷi usage, but also when examining the usage of the ancient commentaries, we see them only in compounds, not elsewhere. Even so, this point should be thoroughly investigated. For who indeed, other than Arahants with destroyed defilements who have attained the analytical knowledges, is capable of discerning every method in the word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries?

Ettha ca samāsantagatarāja-saddassa nāmikapadamālāyo dvidhā vuccante okārantākārantavasena. Tatrokārantā “mahārājo yuvarājo sivirājo dhammarājo”iccevamādayo bhavanti. Ākārantā pana “mahārājā yuvarājā sivirājā dhammarājā”iccevamādayo. Ettha kiñcāpi pāḷiyaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathāsu ca “mahārājo”tiādīni na santi, tathāpi “sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako”ti pāḷiyaṃ “sabbasakho”ti dassanato “mahārājo”tiādīnipi avassamicchitabbāni. Tathā hi samāsesu “dhammarājena, dhammarājassā”tiādīni dissanti. Etāni okārantarūpāni eva, nākārantarūpāni. Mahārājo, mahārājā. Mahārājaṃ, mahārāje. Mahārājena, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, mahārājānaṃ. Mahārājā, mahārājasmā, mahārājamhā, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, mahārājānaṃ. Mahārāje, mahārājasmiṃ, mahārājamhi, mahārājesu. Bho mahārāja, bhavanto mahārājā[M 0.0205]. Kaccāyanacūḷaniruttinayehi pana “bho mahārājā”iti ekavacanabahuvacanānipi daṭṭhabbāni. Yathā “mahārājo”ti okārantapadassa vasena, evaṃ “sivirājo dhammarājo devarājo”tiādīnampi okārantapadānaṃ vasena pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

Here the nominal paradigms of the word rāja at the end of a compound are said to be twofold: by way of ending in -o and by way of ending in -ā. Among these, the ones ending in -o are such as mahārājo, yuvarājo, sivirājo, and dhammarājo. The ones ending in -ā are such as mahārājā, yuvarājā, sivirājā, and dhammarājā. Here, although forms such as mahārājo are not found in the Pāḷi Canon and the ancient commentaries, still, based on the occurrence of sabbasakho in the Pāḷi passage “sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako,” forms such as mahārājo must necessarily be accepted. For in compounds, forms such as dhammarājena and dhammarājassa are seen. These are forms from an o-stem, not an ā-stem. Mahārājo, mahārājā. Mahārājaṃ, mahārāje. Mahārājena, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, mahārājānaṃ. Mahārājā, mahārājasmā, mahārājamhā, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi. Mahārājassa, mahārājānaṃ. Mahārāje, mahārājasmiṃ, mahārājamhi, mahārājesu. Bho mahārāja, bhavanto mahārājā. According to the methods of Kaccāyana and the Cūḷanirutti, “bho mahārājā” should be seen as both singular and plural. Just as in the case of the o-stem word mahārājo, so the nominal paradigm of the base form should be constructed for other o-stem words such as sivirājo, dhammarājo, and devarājo.

Ayaṃ panākārantavasena nāmikapadamālā –

This, however, is the nominal paradigm for the ā-stem:

Mahārājā, mahārājā, mahārājāno. Mahārājānaṃ, mahārājaṃ, mahārājāno. Mahāraññā, mahārājinā, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahāraññaṃ, mahārājūnaṃ. Mahāraññā, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahāraññaṃ, mahārājūnaṃ. Mahāraññe, mahārājini, mahārājūsu. Bho mahārāja, bhavanto mahārājāno.

Mahārājā, mahārājā, mahārājāno. Mahārājānaṃ, mahārājaṃ, mahārājāno. Mahāraññā, mahārājinā, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahāraññaṃ, mahārājūnaṃ. Mahāraññā, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahāraññaṃ, mahārājūnaṃ. Mahāraññe, mahārājini, mahārājūsu. Bho mahārāja, bhavanto mahārājāno.

Idhāpi pakaraṇadvayanayena “bho mahārājā” iti ekavacanabahuvacanānipi daṭṭhabbāni. Yathā ca “mahārājā”ti ākārantapadassa vasena, evaṃ “sivirājā, dhammarājā, devarājā”tiādīnampi ākārantapadānaṃ vasena pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

Here too, according to the method of the two treatises, “bho mahārājā” should be seen as both singular and plural. And just as in the case of the ā-stem word `mahārājā`, so the nominal paradigm of the base form should be constructed for other ā-stem words such as `sivirājā`, `dhammarājā`, and `devarājā`.

Idha aparāpi atthassa pākaṭīkaraṇatthaṃ kriyāpadehi saddhiṃ yojetvā ākārantokārantānaṃ missakavasena nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Here, for the purpose of clarifying the meaning by combining them with verbs, another nominal paradigm is stated, as a mixture of words ending in -ā and -o:

Mahārājā, mahārājo tiṭṭhati, mahārājāno, mahārājā tiṭṭhanti. Mahārājānaṃ, mahārājaṃ passati, mahārājāno, mahārāje passati. Mahāraññā, mahārājinā, mahārājena kataṃ, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi, mahārājehi, mahārājebhi kataṃ. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahārājassa dīyate, mahāraññā, mahārājā, mahārājasmā, mahārājamhā nissaṭaṃ, mahārājūhi, mahārājūbhi, mahārājehi[M 0.0206], mahārājebhi nissaṭaṃ. Mahārañño, mahārājino, mahārājassa pariggaho, mahāraññaṃ, mahārājūnaṃ, mahārājānaṃ pariggaho. Mahāraññe, mahārājini, mahārāje, mahārājasmiṃ, mahārājamhi patiṭṭhitaṃ, mahārājūsu, mahārājesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Bho mahārāja tvaṃ tiṭṭha, bhonto mahārājāno, mahārājā tumhe tiṭṭhathāti. Evaṃ “yuvarājā, yuvarājo”tiādīsupi.

The great king, the great king stands; the great kings, the great kings stand. He sees the great king, the great king; he sees the great kings, the great kings. Done by the great king, by the great king, by the great king; done by the great kings, by the great kings, by the great kings, by the great kings. It is given to the great king, to the great king, to the great king; released from the great king, from the great king, from the great king, from the great king; released from the great kings, from the great kings, from the great kings, from the great kings. The possession of the great king, of the great king, of the great king; the possession of the great kings, of the great kings, of the great kings. Established in the great king, in the great king, in the great king, in the great king, in the great king; established among the great kings, among the great kings. O great king, you stand; O venerable great kings, O great kings, you stand. Thus also in cases like 'the crown prince,' 'the crown prince,' and so on.

Kecettha vadeyyuṃ “kasmā pakaraṇakattunā imasmiṃ ṭhāne mahanto vāyāmo ca mahanto ca parakkamo kato, nanvetesupi padesu kānici buddhavacane vijjanti, kānici na vijjantīti? Viññūhi te evaṃ vattabbā “pakaraṇakattārenettha so ca mahanto vāyāmo so ca mahanto parakkamo sāṭṭhakathe navaṅge satthusāsane saddesu ca atthesu ca sotārānaṃ suṭṭhu kosalluppādanena sāsanassopakāratthaṃ kato, yāni cetāni tena padāni dassitāni, etesu kānici buddhavacane vijjanti, kānici na vijjanti. Ettha yāni buddhavacane vijjanti, tāni vijjamānavasena gahitāni. Yāni na vijjanti, tāni porāṇaṭṭhakathādīsu vijjamānavasena pāḷinayavasena ca gahitānī”ti. Atrāyaṃ saṅkhepato adhippāyavibhāvanā –

Some might say here, "Why has the author made such a great effort and exertion in this instance? Are not some of these words found in the Buddha's words while some are not?" The wise should say thus: "The author has made this great effort and exertion here to benefit the Teaching by skillfully generating expertise in sounds and meanings for the listeners, in the ninefold Teaching of the Teacher, along with its commentary. Some of the terms shown by him are found in the Buddha's words, and some are not. Those found in the Buddha's words are taken as existing. Those not found are taken as existing in the ancient commentaries and so on, and according to the method of the Pāli." Here is a brief explanation of the intention:

“Idaṃ vatvā mahārājā, kaṃso bārāṇasiggaho;

Dhanuṃ tūṇiñca nikkhippa, saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamī”ti

"Having said this, King Kaṃsa, who held Bārāṇasī, laid down his bow and quiver and undertook restraint."

Idaṃ ākārantassa mahārājasaddassa nidassanaṃ. Yasmā “sabbasakho”ti pāḷi vijjati, tasmā tena nayena “mahārājo”tipi okāranto diṭṭho nāma hoti purisanayena yojetabbo ca. Teneva ca “tamabravi mahārājā. Nikkhamante mahārāje”tiādīni dissanti.

This is an illustration of the word `mahārāja` ending in -ā. Since the Pāli word `sabbasakho` exists, by that method `mahārājo` ending in -o is also considered as seen, and it should be construed according to the `purisa` paradigm. For that very reason, such examples as 'the great king said to him' and 'as the great king was departing' are seen.

Evaṃ [M 0.0207] mahārājasaddassa okārantatte siddhe “mahārājā, mahārājasmā, mahārājamhā”ti pañcamiyā ekavacanañca “mahārāje, mahārājasmiṃ, mahārājamhī”ti sattamiyā ekavacanañca siddhāni eva honti pāḷiyaṃ avijjamānānampi nayavasena gahetabbattā. “Rājena, rājassā”tiādīni pana nayavasena gahetabbāni na honti. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā “rājā brahmā sakhā attā”iccevamādīni “puriso urago”tiādīni viya aññamaññaṃ sabbathā sadisāni na honti. Tathā hi nesaṃ “raññā brahmunā sakhinā attanā attena sānā pumunā”tiādīni visadisānipi rūpāni bhavanti, tasmā tāni na sakkā nayavasena jānituṃ. Evaṃ dujjānattā pana pāḷiyaṃ porāṇaṭṭhakathāsu ca yathārutapadāneva gahetabbāni. Mahārājasaddādīnaṃ pana okārantabhāve siddheyeva “purisanayogadhā ime saddā”ti nayaggahaṇaṃ dissati, tasmā amhehi nayavasena “mahārājā, mahārājasmā”tiādīni vuttāni. Yathā hi –

Thus, when the treatment of the word `mahārāja` as an o-stem word is established, the ablative singular forms `mahārājā`, `mahārājasmā`, `mahārājamhā` and the locative singular forms `mahārāje`, `mahārājasmiṃ`, `mahārājamhī` are also established, even though they are not found in the Pāli, because they should be accepted by analogy. However, forms like `rājena`, `rājassa`, and so on should not be accepted by analogy. Why is that? Because terms like `rājā`, `brahmā`, `sakhā`, `attā` are not entirely similar to each other, unlike terms such as `puriso`, `urago`. Indeed, their forms like `raññā`, `brahmunā`, `sakhinā`, `attanā`, `attena`, `sānā`, `pumunā` are also dissimilar, so they cannot be known by analogy. Due to this difficulty in knowing them, only the words as they are found in the Pāli and ancient commentaries should be accepted. However, once the o-stem nature of words like `mahārāja` is established, the acceptance of the principle that "these words follow the `purisa` paradigm" is seen, and therefore we have stated forms like `mahārājā`, `mahārājasmā`, and so on by analogy. For example—

“Etañhi te durājānaṃ, yaṃ sesi matasāyikaṃ;

Yassa te kaḍḍhamānassa, hatthā daṇḍona muccatī”ti

"This is indeed hard for you to understand, that you lie as if dead; while you are being dragged along, the staff is not released from your hand."

Ettha “hatthā”ti, “attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jāta”nti ettha pana “daṇḍā”ti ca okārantassa pañcamiyekavacanassa dassanato “uragā, paṭaṅgā, vihagā”tiādīnipi okārantāni pañcamiyekavacanāni gahetabbāni honti. Yathā ca “dāṭhini mātimaññavho, siṅgālo mama pāṇado”ti ettha “maññavho”ti, “suddhā suddhehi saṃvāsaṃ, kappayavho patissatā”ti ettha pana “kappayavho”ti ca kriyāpadassa dassanato “gacchavho, bhuñjavho, sayavho”tiādīnipi gahetabbāni honti. Gaṇhanti ca tādisāni padarūpāni sāsane sukusalā kusalā, tasmā amhehipi nayaggāhavasena “mahārājā[M 0.0208], mahārājasmā”tiādīni vuttāni. Nayaggāhavasena pana gahaṇe asati kathaṃ nāmikapadamālā paripuṇṇā bhavissanti, satiyeva tasmiṃ paripuṇṇā bhavanti.

Here, `hatthā` (from the hand), and `daṇḍā` (from the rod) in 'fear arises from taking up the rod' (`attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātaṃ`), are examples of the ablative singular of o-stem nouns. Therefore, other forms ending in -ā, such as `uragā` (from the serpent), `paṭaṅgā` (from the insect), and `vihagā` (from the bird), should also be taken as ablative singular forms of o-stem nouns. Similarly, in the phrase 'O fanged one, do not despise me; the jackal is my life-giver' (`dāṭhini mātimaññavho, siṅgālo mama pāṇado`), `maññavho` is an example of a verb form. Likewise, in 'The pure should associate with the pure; O mindful one, you should arrange it' (`suddhā suddhehi saṃvāsaṃ, kappayavho patissatā`), `kappayavho` is also an example of a verb form. Thus, forms like `gacchavho` (you all go), `bhuñjavho` (you all eat), `sayavho` (you all sleep), and others should also be accepted. Those skilled and proficient in the Teaching accept such word forms. Therefore, we too, by adopting the principle of analogy, have stated forms like `mahārājā` (from the great king) and `mahārājasmā` (from the great king). For without adopting the principle of analogy, how could the nominal paradigms be complete? Only with it do they become complete.

Tathā hi buddhavacane anekasatasahassāni nāmikapadāni kriyāpadāni ca pāṭiekkaṃ pāṭiekkaṃ ekavacanabahuvacanakāhi sattahi aṭṭhahi vā nāmavibhattīhi channavutiyā ca ākhyātikavacanehi yojitāni na santi, nayavasena pana santiyeva, iti nayavasena “mahārājā, mahārājasmā”tiādīni amhehi ṭhapitāni. “Mahārājā tiṭṭhanti, mahārājā tumhe tiṭṭhathā”ti imāni pana “atha kho cattāro mahārājā mahatiyā ca yakkhasenāya mahatiyā ca kumbhaṇḍasenāyā”ti dassanato,

For in the Buddha's words, there are not hundreds of thousands of nouns and verbs each individually combined with the singular and plural forms of the seven or eight nominal cases and the ninety-six verbal endings. Yet, they exist by way of analogy. Therefore, by way of analogy, we have established terms like `mahārājā` (ablative singular) and `mahārājasmā` (ablative singular). The forms `mahārājā tiṭṭhanti` (the great kings stand) and `mahārājā tumhe tiṭṭhathā` (O great kings, you stand)—these, however, are stated based on seeing such passages as 'Then the four great kings with a great host of yakkhas and a great host of kumbhaṇḍas',

“Cattāro te mahārājā, samantā caturo disā;

Daddaḷhamānā aṭṭhaṃsu, vane kāpilavatthave”ti

"Those four great kings, all around in the four directions, resplendent, stood in the forest of Kapilavatthu."

Dassanato ca vuttāni. “Mahārāja”ntiādīnipi pāḷiñca pāḷinayañca disvā eva vuttāni. Asamāse “rājaṃ, rājenā”tiādīni na passāma, tasmā suṭṭhu vicāretabbamidaṃ ṭhānaṃ. Idañhi duddasaṃ vīrajātinā jānitabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Sace panāyasmanto buddhavacane vā porāṇikāsu vā aṭṭhakathāsu asamāse “rājaṃ, rājenā”tiādīni passeyyātha, tadā sādhukaṃ manasi karotha. Ko hi nāma sabbappakārena buddhavacane vohārappabhedaṃ jānituṃ samattho aññatra pabhinnapaṭisambhidehi mahākhīṇāsavehi.

and were stated based on these examples. Forms like `mahārāja`, etc., were also stated only after seeing both the Pāli text and the Pāli method. In non-compounds, we do not see forms like `rājaṃ` or `rājena`, therefore this point should be carefully examined. For this is a difficult point, to be known by those of heroic birth. But if you, venerable ones, should see in the Buddha's words or in the ancient commentaries non-compound forms like `rājaṃ` or `rājena`, then pay close attention to it. For who indeed is capable of fully discerning the variations of usage in the Buddha's words other than the great Arahants with discriminating analytical knowledge?

Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Vītataṇho anādāno, niruttipadakovido;

Akkharānaṃ sannipātaṃ, jaññā pubbāparāni cā”ti.

"Free from craving, without grasping, skilled in the exposition of terms, one should know the combinations of letters, and what comes before and after."

Brahmā[M 0.0209], brahmā, brahmāno. Brahmānaṃ, brahmaṃ, brahmāno. Brahmunā, brahmehi, brahmebhi, brahmūhi, brahmūbhi. Brahmassa, brahmuno, brahmānaṃ, brahmūnaṃ. Brahmunā, brahmehi, brahmebhi, brahmūhi, brahmūbhi. Brahmassa, brahmuno, brahmānaṃ, brahmūnaṃ. Brahmani, brahmesu, bho brahma, bho brahme, bhavanto brahmāno.

Brahma, Brahmas, Brahmas. To a Brahma, to a Brahma, to Brahmas. By a Brahma, by Brahmas, by Brahmas, by Brahmas, by Brahmas. Of/for a Brahma, of/for a Brahma, of/for Brahmas, of/for Brahmas. From a Brahma, from Brahmas, from Brahmas, from Brahmas, from Brahmas. Of/for a Brahma, of/for a Brahma, of/for Brahmas, of/for Brahmas. In a Brahma, in Brahmas. O Brahma, O Brahma, O venerable Brahmas.

Yamakamahātheraruciyā “bho brahmā”iti bahuvacanaṃ vā. Ettha pana “paṇḍitapurisehi devehi brahmūhī”ti ṭīkāvacanassa dassanato, “brahmūnaṃ vacīghoso hotī”ti ca “brahmūnaṃ vimānādīsu chandarāgo kāmāsavo na hotī”ti ca aṭṭhakathāvacanassa dassanato, “vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ, dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme”ti āhaccabhāsitassa ca dassanato “brahmūhi, brahmūbhi, brahmūnaṃ, brahme”ti padāni vuttāni, etāni cūḷaniruttiniruttipiṭakakaccāyanesu na āgatāni.

According to the preference of the Yamaka Mahāthera, 'bho brahmā' is alternatively a plural form. Here, however, in accordance with the statement of the sub-commentary, 'by wise men, gods, and Brahmas' (paṇḍitapurisehi devehi brahmūhī); and in accordance with the statements of the commentary, 'there is the sound of the voice of the Brahmas' (brahmūnaṃ vacīghoso hotī) and 'in the mansions, etc., of the Brahmas, there is no sensual desire, the canker of sensual pleasure' (brahmūnaṃ vimānādīsu chandarāgo kāmāsavo na hotī); and in accordance with the occasional utterance, 'Perceiving harm, I did not speak fluently the sublime Dhamma among men, O Brahma' (vihiṃsasaññī paguṇaṃ na bhāsiṃ, dhammaṃ paṇītaṃ manujesu brahme); the words 'brahmūhi' (by the Brahmas), 'brahmūbhi' (by the Brahmas), 'brahmūnaṃ' (of the Brahmas), and 'brahme' (O Brahma) are stated. These words, however, do not appear in the Cūḷanirutti, the Niruttipiṭaka, or the Kaccāyana.

Sakhā, sakhā, sakhino, sakhāno, sakhāyo. Sakhaṃ, sakhāraṃ, sakhānaṃ, sakhino, sakhāno, sakhāyo. Sakhinā, sakhārehi, sakhārebhi, sakhehi, sakhebhi. Sakhissa, sakhino, sakhīnaṃ, sakhārānaṃ, sakhānaṃ. Sakhārasmā, sakhinā, sakhārehi, sakhārebhi, sakhehi, sakhebhi. Sakhissa, sakhino, sakhīnaṃ, sakhārānaṃ, sakhānaṃ. Sakhe, sakhesu, sakhāresu. Bho sakha, bho sakhā, bho sakhi, bho sakhī, bho sakhe, bhavanto sakhino, sakhāno, sakhāyo.

Friend, friend, friends, friends, friends. A friend, a friend, a friend, friends, friends, friends. By a friend, by friends, by friends, by friends, by friends. Of/for a friend, of/for a friend, of/for friends, of/for friends, of/for friends. From a friend, from a friend, from friends, from friends, from friends, from friends. Of/for a friend, of/for a friend, of/for friends, of/for friends, of/for friends. In a friend, in friends, in friends. O friend, O friend, O friend, O friend, O friend, O venerable friends, friends, friends.

Yamakamahātheramatena “bho sakhā”iti bahuvacanaṃ vā. Pāḷiyaṃ pana suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātake “hare sakhā kissa nu maṃ jahāsī”ti dīghavasena vutto sakhāsaddo ālapanekavacanaṃ, tasmā yamakamahātheranayo na yujjatīti ce[M 0.0210]? No na yujjati. Yasmā “netādisā sakhā honti, labbhā me jīvato sakhā”ti manojajātake sakhāsaddo ekavacanampi hoti bahuvacanampi. Tathā hi tattha paṭhamapāde bahuvacanaṃ, dutiyapāde panekavacanaṃ, tasmā yamakamahātherena paccattālapanabahuvacanaṭṭhāne sakhāsaddo vutto. Ettha ca “sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako”ti pāṭhānulomena samāse labbhamānassa sakhasaddassa nāmikapadamālā bhavati “sabbasakho, sabbasakhā, sabbasakhaṃ, sabbasakhe”tiādinā purisanayena. Tatrāyaṃ samāsaviggaho – sabbesaṃ janānaṃ sakhā, sabbe vā janā sakhino etassāti sabbasakho, yathā sabbaverīti.

According to the opinion of the Yamaka Mahāthera, 'bho sakhā' is alternatively a plural form. However, in the Pāli of the Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka, the word 'sakhā' is spoken with a long vowel in the vocative singular as 'hare sakhā kissa nu maṃ jahāsī' ('Alas, friend, why do you abandon me?'). Therefore, if it is said that the method of the Yamaka Mahāthera is not suitable, it is not so. It is not unsuitable. Because in the Manoja Jātaka, the word 'sakhā' is both singular and plural, as in 'netādisā sakhā honti, labbhā me jīvato sakhā' ('Friends are not like this; a friend is to be obtained by me while I live'). Indeed, there the first part of the verse is plural, but the second part is singular. Therefore, the word 'sakhā' was spoken by the Yamaka Mahāthera in the place of the vocative plural. And here, in accordance with the reading 'sabbamitto sabbasakho, sabbabhūtānukampako' ('a friend to all, a companion to all, compassionate to all beings'), the declension of the noun 'sakha' when it is part of a compound is according to the masculine paradigm, beginning with 'sabbasakho, sabbasakhā, sabbasakhaṃ, sabbasakhe'. Therein, this is the analysis of the compound: 'sabbesaṃ janānaṃ sakhā' (a friend of all people), or 'sabbe vā janā sakhino etassāti sabbasakho' (all people are friends to him, thus 'sabbasakho'), just like 'sabbaverī'.

Attā, attā, attāno. Attānaṃ, attaṃ, attāno. Attanā, attena, attanehi, attanebhi. Attano, attānaṃ. Attanā, attanehi, attanebhi. Attano, attānaṃ. Attani, attanesu. Bho atta, bhavanto attā, bhonto attāno.

Self, selves, selves. The self, the self, the selves. By the self, by the self, by the selves, by the selves. Of/for the self, of/for the selves. From the self, from the selves, from the selves. Of/for the self, of/for the selves. In the self, in the selves. O self, O venerable selves, O venerable selves.

Ettha pana attaṃ niraṅkatvāna piyāni sevati.

Here, having disregarded the self, one cultivates what is dear.

“Sace gacchasi pañcālaṃ, khippa’mattaṃ jahissasi;

Migaṃ panthānupannaṃva, mahantaṃ bhayamessatī”ti

If you go to Pañcāla, you will quickly lose yourself; like a deer that has come upon a path, great fear will come to you.

Pāḷīsu “atta”nti dassanato “atta”nti idha vuttaṃ, “attena vā attaniyena vā”ti pāḷidassanato pana “attenā”ti. Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ pana “attassā”ti catutthīchaṭṭhīnamekavacanaṃ āgataṃ, etaṃ kaccāyane niruttipiṭake ca na dissati. Katthaci pana “attesū”ti āgataṃ. Sabbānetāni sāṭṭhakathaṃ jinatantiṃ oloketvā gahetabbāni.

In the Pāli texts, the form is 'atta', and here too 'atta' is stated. However, from the appearance in the Pāli of 'attena vā attaniyena vā' ('by oneself or by what belongs to oneself'), the form 'attenā' is also seen. In the Cūḷanirutti, however, 'attassā' appears as the dative and genitive singular, but this is not seen in the Kaccāyana or the Niruttipiṭaka. In some places, 'attesū' also appears. All these forms should be accepted after consulting the canon of the Victor together with its commentaries.

“Ātumā[M 0.0211], ātumā, ātumāno. Ātumānaṃ, ātumaṃ, ātumāno. Ātumena, ātumehi, ātumebhī”tiādinā purisanayena vatvā “bho ātuma, bhavanto ātumā, ātumāno”ti vattabbaṃ.

Having stated the declension beginning with 'Ātumā, ātumā, ātumāno; Ātumānaṃ, ātumaṃ, ātumāno; Ātumena, ātumehi, ātumebhī', and so on, according to the masculine paradigm, one should state the vocative as 'bho ātuma, bhavanto ātumā, ātumāno'.

Tatra attasaddassa samāse “bhāvitatto, bhāvitattā. Bhāvitattaṃ, bhāvitatte. Bhāvitattena, bhāvitattehi, bhāvitattebhī”ti purisanayeneva nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

Therein, in a compound with the word 'atta', the nominal declension 'bhāvitatto, bhāvitattā; bhāvitattaṃ, bhāvitatte; bhāvitattena, bhāvitattehi, bhāvitattebhī' should be applied according to the masculine paradigm.

Sā, sā, sāno. Sānaṃ, sāne. Sānā, sānehi, sānebhi. Sāssa, sānaṃ. Sānā, sānehi, sānebhi. Sāssa, sānaṃ. Sāne, sānesu. Bho sā, bhavanto sāno. Sā vuccati sunakho.

Dog, dogs, dogs. A dog, dogs. By a dog, by dogs, by dogs. Of/for a dog, of/for dogs. From a dog, from dogs, from dogs. Of/for a dog, of/for dogs. In a dog, in dogs. O dog, O venerable dogs. 'Sā' means dog.

Ettha ca “na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti. Sāva vārenti sūkara”nti nidassanapadāni. Keci pana sāsaddassa dutiyātatiyādīsu “saṃ, se. Senā”tiādīni rūpāni vadanti, taṃ na yuttaṃ. Na hi tāni “saṃ, se. Senā”tiādīni rūpāni buddhavacane ceva aṭṭhakathādīsu ca niruttipiṭake ca dissanti. Evaṃ pana niruttipiṭake vuttaṃ “sā tiṭṭhati, sāno tiṭṭhanti. Sānaṃ passati, sāne passati. Sānā kataṃ, sānehi kataṃ, sānebhi kataṃ. Sāssa dīyate, sānaṃ dīyate. Sānā nissaṭaṃ, sānehi nissaṭaṃ, sānebhi nissaṭaṃ. Sāssa pariggaho, sānaṃ pariggaho. Sāne patiṭṭhitaṃ, sānesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Bho sā, bhavanto sāno”ti, tasmā niruttipiṭake vuttanayeneva nāmikapadamālā gahetabbā.

And here, the illustrative sentences are: 'Not where a dog is present. The dogs themselves ward off the pigs.' Some, however, state that in the accusative, instrumental, and other cases of the word 'sā', the forms are 'saṃ, se, senā', etc., but that is not correct. For such forms as 'saṃ, se, senā', etc., are not seen in the word of the Buddha, nor in the commentaries and other texts, nor in the Niruttipiṭaka. However, in the Niruttipiṭaka it is stated thus: 'A dog stands, dogs stand. One sees a dog, one sees dogs. Done by a dog, done by dogs, done by dogs. It is given to a dog, it is given to dogs. Released from a dog, released from dogs, released from dogs. The possession of a dog, the possession of dogs. Established in a dog, established in dogs. O dog, O venerable dogs.' Therefore, the declension of the noun should be taken only according to the method stated in the Niruttipiṭaka.

Atridaṃ [M 0.0212] vattabbaṃ – yathā “sehi dārehi asantuṭṭho”tiādīsu pulliṅge vattamānassa “sako”iti atthavācakassa sasaddassa “attano ayanti so”ti etasmiṃ atthe “so, sā. Saṃ, se. Sena, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Sā, sasmā, samhā, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Se, sasmiṃ, samhi, sesū”ti purisanayena rūpāni bhavanti, na tathā sunakhavācakassa sāsaddassa rūpāni bhavanti. Yathā vā “hiṃsanti attasambhūtā, tacasāraṃva saṃ phalaṃ. Sāni kammāni tappenti, kosalaṃ sena’santuṭṭhaṃ, jīvaggāhaṃ agāhayī”tiādīsu napuṃsakaliṅge vattamānassa sakamiccatthavācakassa sasaddassa “saṃ, sāni, sā. Saṃ, sāni, se. Sena, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Sā, sasmā, samhā, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Se, sasmiṃ, samhi, sesū”ti cittanayena rūpāni bhavanti, na tathā sunakhavācakassa sāsaddassa rūpāni bhavanti. Evaṃ sante kasmā tehi ācariyehi dutiyātatiyāṭhāne “saṃ, se. Senā”ti vuttaṃ, kasmā ca pañcamīṭhāne “sā, sasmā, samhā”ti vuttaṃ, sattamīṭhāne ca “se, sasmiṃ, samhī”ti ca vuttaṃ? Sabbametaṃ akāraṇaṃ, takkagāhamattena gahitaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Sunakhavācako hi sāsaddo ākārantatāpakatiko, na purisa cittasaddādayo viya akārantatāpakatiko. Yāya imassa īdisāni rūpāni siyuṃ, sā ca pakati natthi. Na ceso “rājā, brahmā, sakhā, attā” iccevamādayo viya paṭhamaṃ akārantabhāve ṭhatvā pacchā paṭiladdhaākārantatā, atha kho niccamokārantatāpakatiko gosaddo viya niccamākārantatāpakatiko. Niccamākārantatāpakatikassa ca evarūpāni rūpāni na bhavanti, tasmā niruttipiṭake pabhinnapaṭisambhidena āyasmatā mahākaccāyanena na vuttāni. Sacepi maññeyyuṃ “attaṃ, attenā’ti [M 0.0213] ca dassanato ‘saṃ, senā’ti imāni pana gahetabbānī”ti. Na gahetabbāni “rājā, brahmā, sakhā, attā, sā, pumā”iccevamādīnaṃ aññamaññaṃ padamālāvasena visadisattā nayavasena gahetabbākārassa asambhavato. Īdise hi ṭhāne nayaggāhavasena gahaṇaṃ nāma sadosaṃyeva siyā, tasmā nayaggāhavasenapi na gahetabbāni.

Herein, this should be said: just as in examples like 'sehi dārehi asantuṭṭho' (not content with his own wives), for the word 'sa', which expresses the meaning 'saka' (one's own) and occurs in the masculine gender, in the sense of 'attano ayaṃ, ti so' (this is one's own, thus 'so'), the forms 'so, sā. Saṃ, se. Sena, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Sā, sasmā, samhā, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Se, sasmiṃ, samhi, sesū' arise according to the paradigm of 'purisa', yet the forms for the word 'sā' which denotes a dog do not arise in that way. Or, just as in examples like 'hiṃsanti attasambhūtā, tacasāraṃva saṃ phalaṃ. Sāni kammāni tappenti, kosalaṃ sena’santuṭṭhaṃ, jīvaggāhaṃ agāhayī' (Born of oneself, they harm, like its own fruit the bamboo. One's own deeds torment, the Kosalan, not content with his own, seized him alive), for the word 'sa', which expresses the meaning 'saka' (one's own) and occurs in the neuter gender, the forms 'saṃ, sāni, sā. Saṃ, sāni, se. Sena, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Sā, sasmā, samhā, sehi, sebhi. Sassa, sānaṃ. Se, sasmiṃ, samhi, sesū' arise according to the paradigm of 'citta', yet the forms for the word 'sā' which denotes a dog do not arise in that way. This being so, why was it said by those teachers 'saṃ, se' in the second case and 'senā' in the third, and why was 'sā, sasmā, samhā' said in the fifth case, and 'se, sasmiṃ, samhi' in the seventh case? All this is without reason; it is a baseless assumption grasped merely through speculation. For the word 'sā' which denotes a dog is by nature an ā-stem, not like the words 'purisa', 'citta', and so on, which are by nature a-stems. And that nature by which such forms of this word might arise does not exist. Nor is this word like 'rājā, brahmā, sakhā, attā', and so on, which first exist as a-stems and afterwards acquire an -ā ending; rather, it is by nature always an ā-stem, just as the word 'go' is by nature always an o-stem. And for a word that is by nature always an ā-stem, such forms do not arise. Therefore, they were not stated in the Niruttipiṭaka by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, who had attained the analytical knowledges. And if they should think, 'From seeing 'attaṃ' and 'attenā', these forms 'saṃ' and 'senā' should be accepted,' they should not be accepted, because of the mutual dissimilarity of the paradigms of words such as 'rājā, brahmā, sakhā, attā, sā, pumā', and the impossibility of the manner of accepting them by way of analogy. For in such a case, acceptance by way of analogy would indeed be faulty. Therefore, they should not be accepted even by way of analogy.

Aparampi atra vattabbaṃ – yathā hi “sāhi nārīhi te yantī”ti vutte “attano nārī”ti, “sā nārī”ti evaṃ atthavato itthiliṅgassa kaññāsaddena sadisassa sāsaddassa “sā, sā, sāyo. Saṃ, sā, sāyo. Sāya, sāhi, sābhi. Sāya, sānaṃ. Sāya, sāhi, sābhi. Sāya, sānaṃ. Sāya, sāyaṃ, sāsū”ti kaññānayena rūpāni bhavanti, na tathā imassa sunakhavācakassa sāsaddassa rūpāni bhavanti. Evaṃ sante kasmā te ācariyā tatiyābahuvacanaṭṭhāne ca “sāhi, sābhī”ti rūpāni icchanti, kasmā ca sattamībahuvacanaṭṭhāne “sāsū”ti? Idampi akāraṇaṃ ākārantapulliṅgattā. Kasmā ca pana catutthīchaṭṭhekavacanaṭṭhāne pubbakkharassa rassavasena “sassa”iti rūpaṃ icchanti? Idampi akāraṇaṃ sunakhavācakassa sāsaddassa ākārantatāpakatikattā. Ākārantatāpakatikassa ca sāsaddassa yathā akārantatāpakatikassa purisasaddassa “purisassā”ti catutthīchaṭṭhekavacanarūpaṃ bhavati evarūpassa rūpassa abhāvato. Teneva āyasmā kaccāno niruttipiṭake sunakhavācakassa sāsaddassa rūpaṃ dassento catutthīchaṭṭhekavacanaṭṭhāne pubbakkharassa dīghavasena “sāssa”iti rūpamāha. Kasmā ca pana te ācariyā catutthekavacanaṭṭhāne “sāya”iti rūpaṃ icchanti? Idampi akāraṇaṃ, ṭhapetvā hi ākārantitthiliṅge ghasaññato ākārato paresaṃ nādīnaṃ āyādesañca akārantato punnapuṃsakaliṅgato [M 0.0214] parassa catutthekavacanassa āyādesañca ākārantapulliṅge aghato ākārantato parassa catutthekavacanassa katthacipi āyādeso na dissati. Niruttipiṭake ca tādisaṃ rūpaṃ na vuttaṃ, avacanaṃyeva yuttataraṃ buddhavacane aṭṭhakathādīsu ca anāgamanato. Yā panamhehi niruttipiṭakaṃ nissāya buddhavacanañca sunakhavācakassa sāsaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuttā, sāyeva sārato paccetabbā. Etthāpi nānāatthesu vattamānānaṃ liṅgattayapariyāpannānaṃ sā so saṃiccetesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ padānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāsu padānaṃ sadisāsadisatā daṭṭhabbā.

Furthermore, it should be said here: just as when it is said, “sāhi nārīhi te yantī,” it means “one’s own women” or “those women,” so for the feminine gender word 'sā', which has this meaning and is similar to the word 'kaññā', the forms arise according to the paradigm of 'kaññā' as follows: “sā, sā, sāyo. Saṃ, sā, sāyo. Sāya, sāhi, sābhi. Sāya, sānaṃ. Sāya, sāhi, sābhi. Sāya, sānaṃ. Sāya, sāyaṃ, sāsū.” But the forms for this word 'sā' meaning “dog” do not arise in this way. This being so, why do those teachers desire the forms 'sāhi' and 'sābhi' in the instrumental plural, and why 'sāsū' in the locative plural? This too is baseless, because it is a masculine ā-stem. And why do they desire the form 'sassa' with the shortening of the preceding vowel in the dative and genitive singular? This too is baseless, because the word 'sā' meaning “dog” is by nature an ā-stem. For the word 'sā', which is by nature an ā-stem, there is no such form, unlike the word 'purisa', which is by nature an a-stem and has the dative and genitive singular form 'purisassa'. For this reason, the Venerable Kaccāyana, in the Niruttipiṭaka, when showing the forms of the word 'sā' (dog), stated the form 'sāssa' with a long preceding vowel in the dative and genitive singular. And why do those teachers desire the form 'sāya' in the dative singular? This too is baseless, for apart from the substitution of 'āya' for endings such as 'nā' following the final -ā of feminine stems designated 'gha', and the substitution of 'āya' for the dative singular ending following masculine and neuter a-stems, the substitution of 'āya' for the dative singular ending is nowhere seen following a masculine ā-stem that is not designated 'gha'. In the Niruttipiṭaka such a form is not mentioned, and its non-mention is more fitting, as it does not occur in the word of the Buddha or in the commentaries and so on. The nominal paradigm for the word 'sā' (dog), which we have stated based on the Niruttipiṭaka and the word of the Buddha, should be accepted as essential. Here too, for the three words 'sā', 'so', and 'saṃ', which occur with various meanings and belong to the three genders, the similarities and dissimilarities of the words in the nominal paradigms of their base forms should be noted.

Ettha siyā – yo tumhehi sāsaddo “taṃsaddatthe ca sunakhe ca sakamiccatthe ca vattatī”ti icchito, kathaṃ taṃ “sā”ti vutteyeva “imassa atthassa vācako”ti jānantīti? Na jānanti, payogavasena pana jānanti lokiyajanā ceva paṇḍitā ca. Payogavasena hi “sā maddī nāgamāruhi, nātibaddhaṃva kuñjara”ntiādīsu sāsaddassa taṃsaddatthatā viññāyati, evaṃ sāsaddo taṃsaddatthe ca vattati. “Na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti. Bhagavato sājātimpi sutvā sattā amatarasabhāgino bhavantī”tiādīsu sāsaddassa sunakhavācakatā viññāyati.

Here it might be said: The word 'sā' is held by you to mean ‘that,’ ‘dog,’ and ‘one’s own.’ How, then, when just the word 'sā' is spoken, do people know which of these meanings it designates? They do not know inherently, but they understand through usage—both ordinary people and the wise. For through usage, in examples such as “That Maddī mounted the elephant, like an elephant not tightly bound,” the meaning of the word 'sā' as ‘that’ is understood. Thus the word 'sā' is used in the sense of ‘that.’ In examples such as “Where that dog is not present,” and “Having heard even the birth-story of the Lord's dog, beings become partakers of the deathless nectar,” the meaning of the word 'sā' as denoting a dog is understood.

“Annaṃ tavedaṃ pakataṃ yasassi,

Taṃ khajjare bhuñjare piyyare ca;

Jānāsi maṃ tvaṃ paradattūpajīviṃ,

Uttiṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ labhataṃ sapāko”ti

“This food is prepared for you, O glorious one; let it be eaten, enjoyed, and drunk. You know me as one who lives on what is given by others; let the dog-cooker receive the leftover alms.”

Ettha pana sāsaddassa rassabhāvakaraṇena “sapāko”ti pāḷi ṭhitāti atthaṃ aggahetvā “sānaṃ sunakhānaṃ idaṃ maṃsanti sa”miti atthaṃ gahetvā “saṃ pacatīti sapāko”ti vuttanti [M 0.0215] daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sapākoti sapākacaṇḍālo” icceva vuttaṃ. Tampi etadevatthaṃ dīpeti. Evaṃ sāsaddo sunakhe ca vattati. “Sā dārā jantūnaṃ piyā”ti vutte pana “sakā dārā sattānaṃ piyā”ti atthadīpanavasena sāsaddassa sakavācakatā paññāyati. Evaṃ sāsaddo sakamiccatthe ca vattati. Iti sāsaddaṃ payogavasena īdisatthassa vācakoti jānanti. Atridaṃ vuccati –

Here, however, it should be understood that, without taking the meaning that the Pāḷi word 'sapāko' is formed by shortening the word 'sā', it is said 'sapāko is one who cooks saṃ', taking 'saṃ' to mean 'the flesh of dogs' ('sānaṃ sunakhānaṃ idaṃ maṃsaṃ'). But in the Commentary, it is simply said: ‘Sapāko means a sapāka-caṇḍāla.’ That too illuminates this same meaning. Thus the word 'sā' is used for ‘dog.’ However, when it is said, “sā dārā jantūnaṃ piyā,” the meaning of 'sā' as ‘one’s own’ is made known by the explanation of the meaning as “sakā dārā sattānaṃ piyā” (one’s own wives are dear to beings). Thus the word 'sā' is also used in the sense of ‘one’s own.’ In this way, people know through usage that the word 'sā' is a designator of such meanings. Herein, it is said:

Taṃsaddatthe ca sunakhe,

Sakasmimpi ca vattati;

Sāsaddo so ca kho ñeyyo,

Payogānaṃ vasena ve.

In the sense of the pronoun ‘that,’ and for ‘dog,’ and also for ‘one’s own’ it is used; that word 'sā' should be known, indeed, by means of its usages.

Ettha ca pāḷiyaṃ “na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hotī”ti ekavacanappayogadassanato ca,

And here, from seeing the singular usage in the Pāḷi, “na yattha sā upaṭṭhito hoti,”

“Asantā kira maṃ jammā, tāta tātāti bhāsare;

Rakkhasā puttarūpena, sāva vārenti sūkara”nti

“Indeed, these vile wretches call me ‘dear father, dear father’; they are demons in the form of sons; like dogs, they keep the boar away.”

Bahuvacanappayogadassanato ca, niruttipiṭake “sāno”iccādidassanato ca “sā, sā, sāno. Sānaṃ, sāne. Sānā”tiādinā sunakhavācakassa sāsaddassa nāmikapadamālā kathitā.

And from the evidence of plural usage, and from seeing such forms as ‘sāno’ in the Niruttipiṭaka, the nominal paradigm of the word ‘sā’, meaning ‘dog’, is stated as follows: “sā, sā, sāno. Sānaṃ, sāne. Sānā,” and so on.

Idāni pumasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal paradigm of the word ‘puma’ is stated:

Pumā, pumā, pumāno. Pumānaṃ, pumāne. Pumānā, pumunā, pumena, pumānehi, pumānebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumānā, pumunā, pumānehi, pumānebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumāne, pumānesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumā, pumāno. “Bho pumā”iti bahuvacane nayopi ñeyyo.

Pumā, pumā, pumāno. Pumānaṃ, pumāne. Pumānā, pumunā, pumena, pumānehi, pumānebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumānā, pumunā, pumānehi, pumānebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumāne, pumānesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumā, pumāno. The form ‘Bho pumā’ in the vocative plural should also be understood.

Ettha [M 0.0216] pana –

Here, however:

“Thiyo tassa pajāyanti, na pumā jāyare kule;

Yo jānaṃ pucchito pañhaṃ, aññathā naṃ viyākare”ti

“To him are daughters born, no sons are born into his clan; he who, when asked a question, knowingly answers it falsely.”

Ayaṃ pāḷi pumasaddassa bahuvacanabhāvasādhikā, kaccāyane “he pumaṃ”iti sānusāraṃ ālapanekavacanaṃ dissati. Tadanekesu pāḷippadesesu ca aṭṭhakathāsu ca sānusārānaṃ ālapanavacanānaṃ adassanato idha na vadāmi. Upaparikkhitvā yuttaṃ ce, gahetabbaṃ. “Yasassi naṃ paññavantaṃ visayhā”ti ettha pana chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ āgamavasenevānusāro hoti, na sabhāvatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayamākārantavasena nāmikapadamālā.

This Pāli passage is proof of the plural form of the word ‘puma’. In Kaccāyana, the vocative singular with anusvāra, ‘he pumaṃ’, is seen. However, since vocative forms with anusvāra are not seen in many passages of the Pāli and the commentaries, I do not state them here. If, after investigation, it seems fitting, it should be accepted. But in the phrase “Yasassi naṃ paññavantaṃ visayhā”, it should be understood that the anusvāra is present by way of an augment for the sake of preserving the meter, not naturally. This is the nominal paradigm for the ā-stem.

“Soḷasitthisahassānaṃ,

Na vijjati pumo tadā;

Ahorattānamaccayena,

Nibbatto ahamekako”ti ca,

“Among sixteen thousand women, no male was then to be found; with the passing of days and nights, I alone was born.”

“Yathā balākayonimhi, na vijjati pumo sadā;

Meghesu gajjamānesu, gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti tā tadā”ti ca

“Just as in the crane species, a male is never found; when the clouds thunder, they then conceive.”

Pāḷidassanato pana okārantavasenapi nāmikapadamālā veditabbā.

However, from what is seen in the Pāli, the nominal paradigm should also be known by way of the o-ending.

Pumo, pumā. Pumaṃ, pume. Pumena, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumānaṃ. Pumā, pumasmā, pumamhā, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumānaṃ. Pume, pumasmiṃ, pumamhi, pumesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumā. “Bho pumā”iti vā, evaṃ pumasaddassa dvidhā nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

Pumo, pumā. Pumaṃ, pume. Pumena, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumānaṃ. Pumā, pumasmā, pumamhā, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumānaṃ. Pume, pumasmiṃ, pumamhi, pumesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumā. Or ‘Bho pumā’. Thus the nominal paradigm of the word ‘puma’ is twofold.

Idāni missakanayo vuccate –

Now the mixed paradigm is stated:

Pumā[M 0.0217], pumo, pumā, pumāno. Pumānaṃ, pumaṃ, pumāne, pume. Pumānā, pumunā, pumena, pumānehi, pumānebhi, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumānā, pumunā, pumā, pumasmā, pumamhā, pumānehi, pumānebhi, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumāne, pume, pumasmiṃ, pumamhi, pumānesu, pumesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumāno, bhavanto pumā. “Bho pumāno, bho pumā”iti vā.

Pumā, pumo, pumā, pumāno. Pumānaṃ, pumaṃ, pumāne, pume. Pumānā, pumunā, pumena, pumānehi, pumānebhi, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumānā, pumunā, pumā, pumasmā, pumamhā, pumānehi, pumānebhi, pumehi, pumebhi. Pumassa, pumuno, pumānaṃ. Pumāne, pume, pumasmiṃ, pumamhi, pumānesu, pumesu. Bho puma, bhavanto pumāno, bhavanto pumā. Or ‘Bho pumāno, bho pumā’.

Idāni rahasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal paradigm of the word ‘raha’ is stated:

Rahā vuccati pāpadhammo. Rahā, rahā, rahino. Rahānaṃ, rahāne. Rahinā, rahinehi, rahinebhi. Rahassa, rahānaṃ. Rahā, rahānehi, rahānebhi. Rahassa, rahānaṃ. Rahāne, rahānesu. Bho raha, bhavanto rahino, bhavanto rahā.

An evil quality is called ‘rahā’. Rahā, rahā, rahino. Rahānaṃ, rahāne. Rahinā, rahinehi, rahinebhi. Rahassa, rahānaṃ. Rahā, rahānehi, rahānebhi. Rahassa, rahānaṃ. Rahāne, rahānesu. Bho raha, bhavanto rahino, bhavanto rahā.

Idāni daḷhadhammasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal paradigm of the word ‘daḷhadhamma’ is stated:

Daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammāno. Daḷhadhammānaṃ, daḷhadhammāne. Daḷhadhamminā, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷhadhamminā, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷhadhamme daḷhadhammesu. Bho daḷhadhamma, bhavanto daḷhadhammāno, bhavanto daḷhadhammā. “Bho daḷhadhammāno, bho daḷhadhammā”iti puthuvacanampi ñeyyaṃ, evaṃ paccakkhadhammasaddassa nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

Daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammāno. Daḷhadhammānaṃ, daḷhadhammāne. Daḷhadhamminā, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷhadhamminā, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷhadhamme, daḷhadhammesu. Bho daḷhadhamma, bhavanto daḷhadhammāno, bhavanto daḷhadhammā. The alternative vocative forms ‘Bho daḷhadhammāno, bho daḷhadhammā’ should also be known. In the same way, the nominal paradigm of the word ‘paccakkhadhamma’ should be constructed.

Ettha ca “seyyathāpi bhikkhave cattāro dhanuggahā daḷhadhammā”ti idaṃ nidassanaṃ. Imissaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ “daḷhadhammā” iti bahuvacanavasena āgatattā daḷhadhammasaddo ākārantotipi okārantotipi appasiddho tadantānaṃ bahuvacanabhāve tulyarūpattā. Tathāpi amhehi padamālā ākārantavaseneva yojitā. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu daḷhadhammasaddo ākārantotipi okārantotipi vattuṃ yujjateva [M 0.0218] aparibyattarūpattā. Aññasmiṃ pana pāḷippadese atīva paribyatto hutvā okāranta daḷhadhammasaddo dvidhā dissati guṇasaddapaṇṇattivācakasaddavasena. Tattha “issatte casmi kusalo, daḷhadhammoti vissuto”ti ettha daḷhadhammasaddo okāranto guṇasaddo. “Bārāṇasiyaṃ daḷhadhammo nāma rājā rajjaṃ kāresī”ti ettha pana paṇṇattivācakasaddo. Evaṃ okāranto daḷhadhammasaddo dvidhā diṭṭho. Tassa pana “daḷhadhammo, daḷhadhammā. Daḷhadhammaṃ, daḷhadhamme”ti purisanayena nāmikapadamālā ñeyyā, ākārantokārantānaṃ vasena missakapadamālā ca. Kathaṃ?

Here, this is the illustration: “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were four archers of firm nature.” In this Pāli passage, since ‘daḷhadhammā’ occurs in the plural, the word ‘daḷhadhamma’ is not clearly established as ending in either -ā or -o, because the plural forms of stems with those endings are identical. Nevertheless, we have applied the declensional paradigm as if it ended in -ā. In such cases, it is indeed appropriate to say that the word ‘daḷhadhamma’ can end in either -ā or -o, as its form is not clearly distinguished. In another place in the Pāli, however, the word ‘daḷhadhamma’ ending in -o is very clearly distinguished and appears in two ways: as a qualitative word and as a word denoting a designation. There, in the phrase “I am skilled in archery, renowned as Daḷhadhamma,” the word ‘daḷhadhamma’ is an o-ending qualitative word. But in “In Bārāṇasī, a king named Daḷhadhammo ruled,” it is a word denoting a designation. Thus, the word ‘daḷhadhamma’ ending in -o is seen in two ways. Its nominal paradigm should be understood according to the masculine pattern: ‘daḷhadhammo, daḷhadhammā; daḷhadhammaṃ, daḷhadhamme,’ and also as a mixed paradigm based on the -ā and -o endings. How so?

Daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammo, daḷhadhammāno, daḷhadhammā. Daḷhadhammānaṃ, daḷhadhammaṃ, daḷhadhammāne, daḷhadhamme. Daḷhadhamminā, daḷhadhammena, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷadhamminā, daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammasmā, daḷhadhammamhā, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷhadhamme, daḷhadhammasmiṃ, daḷhadhammamhi, daḷhadhammesu. Bho daḷhadhamma, bhavanto daḷhadhammāno, bhavanto daḷhadhammāti. Evaṃ paccakkhadhammā, paccakkhadhammoti missakapadamālā ca yojetabbā.

Daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammo, daḷhadhammāno, daḷhadhammā. Daḷhadhammānaṃ, daḷhadhammaṃ, daḷhadhammāne, daḷhadhamme. Daḷhadhamminā, daḷhadhammena, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷhadhamminā, daḷhadhammā, daḷhadhammasmā, daḷhadhammamhā, daḷhadhammehi, daḷhadhammebhi. Daḷhadhammassa, daḷhadhammānaṃ. Daḷhadhamme, daḷhadhammasmiṃ, daḷhadhammamhi, daḷhadhammesu. Bho daḷhadhamma, bhavanto daḷhadhammāno, bhavanto daḷhadhammā. In this way, the mixed declensional paradigm for ‘paccakkhadhammā’ and ‘paccakkhadhammo’ should also be applied.

Idāni vivaṭacchadasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal paradigm of the word ‘vivaṭacchada’ is stated:

Vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadāno. Vivaṭacchadānaṃ, vivaṭacchadāne. Vivaṭacchadena, vivaṭacchadehi, vivaṭacchadebhi. Vivaṭacchadassa, vivaṭacchadānaṃ. Vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadehi, vivaṭacchadebhi. Vivaṭacchadassa, vivaṭacchadānaṃ. Vivaṭacchade, vivaṭacchadesu. Bho vivaṭacchada, bhavanto vivaṭacchadā, bhavanto vivaṭacchadāno.

Vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadāno. Vivaṭacchadānaṃ, vivaṭacchadāne. Vivaṭacchadena, vivaṭacchadehi, vivaṭacchadebhi. Vivaṭacchadassa, vivaṭacchadānaṃ. Vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadehi, vivaṭacchadebhi. Vivaṭacchadassa, vivaṭacchadānaṃ. Vivaṭacchade, vivaṭacchadesu. Bho vivaṭacchada, bhavanto vivaṭacchadā, bhavanto vivaṭacchadāno.

Ayaṃ nāmikapadamālā “sace pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭacchadā”ti [M 0.0219] pāḷidassanato ākārantavasena kathitā. “Loke vivaṭacchado”tipi pāḷidassanato pana okārantavasenapi kathetabbā “vivaṭacchado, vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadaṃ, vivaṭacchade”ti. Missakavasenapi kathetabbā “vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchado, vivaṭacchadāno, vivaṭacchadā. Vivaṭacchadānaṃ, vivaṭacchadaṃ, vivaṭacchadāne, vivaṭacchade”iti.

This nominal paradigm has been stated with an -ā ending based on the evidence from the Pāli: “sace pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭacchadā.” But based on the evidence from the Pāli “loke vivaṭacchado,” it should also be stated with an -o ending: “vivaṭacchado, vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchadaṃ, vivaṭacchade.” It should also be stated with a mixed paradigm: “vivaṭacchadā, vivaṭacchado, vivaṭacchadāno, vivaṭacchadā. Vivaṭacchadānaṃ, vivaṭacchadaṃ, vivaṭacchadāne, vivaṭacchade.”

Idāni vattahasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate – vattahāti sakko.

Now the nominal paradigm of the word 'vattaha' is stated—'vattahā' is Sakka.

Vattahā, vattahāno. Vattahānaṃ, vattahāne. Vattahānā, vattahānehi, vattahānebhi. Vattahino, vattahānaṃ. Vattahānā, vattahānehi, vattahānebhi. Vattahino, vattahānaṃ. Vattahāne, vattahānesu. Bho vattaha, bhavanto vattahāno. Atha vā “bho vattahā, bho vattahāno”iccapi.

Vattahā, vattahāno. Vattahānaṃ, vattahāne. Vattahānā, vattahānehi, vattahānebhi. Vattahino, vattahānaṃ. Vattahānā, vattahānehi, vattahānebhi. Vattahino, vattahānaṃ. Vattahāne, vattahānesu. Bho vattaha, bhavanto vattahāno. Or also: 'bho vattahā, bho vattahāno.'

Idāni vuttasirasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal paradigm of the word 'vuttasira' is stated:

Vuttasirā, vuttasirā, vuttasirāno. Vuttasirānaṃ, vuttasirāne. Vuttasirānā, vuttasirānehi, vuttasirānebhi. Vuttasirassa, vuttasirānaṃ, vuttasirā, vuttasirehi, vuttasirebhi. Vuttasirassa, vuttasirānaṃ. Vuttasire, vuttasiresu. Bho vuttasira, bhānto vuttasirānoti. “Vuttasiro”ti okārantapāṭhopi dissati.

Vuttasirā, vuttasirā, vuttasirāno. Vuttasirānaṃ, vuttasirāne. Vuttasirānā, vuttasirānehi, vuttasirānebhi. Vuttasirassa, vuttasirānaṃ. Vuttasirā, vuttasirehi, vuttasirebhi. Vuttasirassa, vuttasirānaṃ. Vuttasire, vuttasiresu. Bho vuttasira, bhavanto vuttasirāno. The reading 'vuttasiro' with an -o ending is also seen.

Idāni yuvasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal paradigm of the word 'yuva' is stated:

Yuvā, yuvā, yuvāno, yuvānā. Yuvānaṃ, yuvaṃ, yuvāne, yuve. Yuvānā, yuvena, yuvānena, yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi. Yuvānassa, yuvassa, yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ. Yuvānā[M 0.0220], yuvānasmā, yuvānamhā, yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi. Yuvānassa, yuvassa, yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ. Yuvāne, yuvānasmiṃ, yuvānamhi, yuve, yuvasmiṃ, yuvamhi, yuvānesu, yuvāsu, yuvesu. Bho yuva, yuvāna, bhavanto yuvānā.

Yuvā, yuvā, yuvāno, yuvānā. Yuvānaṃ, yuvaṃ, yuvāne, yuve. Yuvānā, yuvena, yuvānena, yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi. Yuvānassa, yuvassa, yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ. Yuvānā, yuvānasmā, yuvānamhā, yuvānehi, yuvānebhi, yuvehi, yuvebhi. Yuvānassa, yuvassa, yuvānānaṃ, yuvānaṃ. Yuvāne, yuvānasmiṃ, yuvānamhi, yuve, yuvasmiṃ, yuvamhi, yuvānesu, yuvāsu, yuvesu. Bho yuva, yuvāna, bhavanto yuvānā.

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne ekadesena ākārantanayo ca sabbathā okārantanayo ca ekadesena ca okārantanayoti tayo nayā dissanti.

In this case, three patterns are seen: the pattern of an -ā ending in part, the pattern of an -o ending in every respect, and the pattern of an -o ending in part.

Maghavasaddassapi “maghavā, maghavā, maghavāno, maghavānā”tiādinā yuvasaddasseva nāmikapadamālāyojanaṃ kubbanti garū. Niruttipiṭake pana “maghavā tiṭṭhati, maghavanto tiṭṭhanti. Maghavantaṃ passati, maghavante passati. Maghavatā kataṃ, maghavantehi kataṃ, maghavantebhi kataṃ. Maghavato dīyate, maghavantānaṃ dīyate. Maghavatā nissaṭaṃ, maghavantehi nissaṭaṃ, maghavantebhi nissaṭaṃ. Maghavato pariggaho, maghavantānaṃ pariggaho. Maghavati patiṭṭhitaṃ, maghavantesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Bho maghavā, bhavanto maghavanto”ti guṇavāpadanayena vuttaṃ, tathā cūḷaniruttiyampi. Taṃ pāḷiyā saṃsandati sameti. Pāḷiyañhi “sakko mahāli devānamindo pubbe manussabhūto samāno magho nāma māṇavo ahosi, tasmā maghavāti vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Etena “maghoti nāmaṃ assa atthīti maghavā”ti atthi atthavācakavantupaccayavasena padasiddhi dassitā hoti, tasmāssa guṇavantusaddassa viya ca nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

For the word 'maghava' too, the teachers form the nominal paradigm just like that of the word 'yuva,' with forms such as 'maghavā, maghavā, maghavāno, maghavānā,' and so on. In the Niruttipiṭaka, however, it is stated according to the pattern of words like 'guṇavā': 'maghavā tiṭṭhati, maghavanto tiṭṭhanti. Maghavantaṃ passati, maghavante passati. Maghavatā kataṃ, maghavantehi kataṃ, maghavantebhi kataṃ. Maghavato dīyate, maghavantānaṃ dīyate. Maghavatā nissaṭaṃ, maghavantehi nissaṭaṃ, maghavantebhi nissaṭaṃ. Maghavato pariggaho, maghavantānaṃ pariggaho. Maghavati patiṭṭhitaṃ, maghavantesu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Bho maghavā, bhavanto maghavanto.' The Cūḷanirutti also states similarly. This compares with and agrees with the Pāli canon. For in the Pāli it is said: 'Sakka, lord of the devas, Mahāli, when he was formerly a human being, was a young man named Magha; therefore he is called Maghavā.' By this, the derivation of the word is shown to be by means of the suffix '-vantu' in the sense of 'possessing'—that is, 'he has the name Magha, therefore he is Maghavā.' Therefore, its nominal paradigm should be applied just like that of the word 'guṇavantu'.

Idāni addhasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate – addhasaddassa hi yaṃ kāle magge ca vattamānassa “atīto addhā. Dīgho addhā suduggamo”tiādīsu “addhā”ti paṭhamantaṃ rūpaṃ dissati, taṃ “addhā idaṃ mantapadaṃ sududdasa”ntiādīsu ekaṃsatthe [M 0.0221] vattamānena “addhā”ti nipātapadena samānaṃ. Nipātānaṃ pana padamālā na rūhati, nāmikānaṃyeva rūhati.

Now the nominal paradigm of the word 'addha' is stated. For the word 'addha,' when it occurs in the sense of time and path, as in 'atīto addhā' (the past time) and 'dīgho addhā suduggamo' (the long road is hard to travel), the nominative form 'addhā' is seen. This is identical to the particle 'addhā' which occurs in the sense of certainty, as in 'addhā idaṃ mantapadaṃ sududdasaṃ' (truly, this sacred text is very hard to see). However, a declensional paradigm does not apply to particles; it applies only to nominals.

Addhā, addhā, addhāno. Addhānaṃ, addhāne. Addhunā, addhānehi, addhānebhi. Addhuno, addhānaṃ. Addhunā, addhānehi, addhānebhi. Addhuno, addhānaṃ. Addhani, addhāne, addhānesu. Bho addha, bhavanto addhā, addhāno.

Addhā, addhā, addhāno. Addhānaṃ, addhāne. Addhunā, addhānehi, addhānebhi. Addhuno, addhānaṃ. Addhunā, addhānehi, addhānebhi. Addhuno, addhānaṃ. Addhani, addhāne, addhānesu. Bho addha, bhavanto addhā, addhāno.

Ettha kiñci payogaṃ dassessāma – tayo addhā. Addhānaṃ vītivatto. Iminā dīghena addhunā. Dīghassa addhuno accayena. Pathaddhuno pannaraseva cando. Ahū atītamaddhāne, samaṇo khantidīpano. Addhāne gacchante paññāyissati. Iccādayo ñeyyā. Ayampi panettha nīti veditabbā “addhānanti dutiyekavacanantavasena catutthīchaṭṭhībahuvacanavasena ca vuttaṃ rūpaṃ. “Addhānamaggapaṭippanno hotī”tiādīsu dīghamaggavācakena “addhāna”nti napuṃsakena sadisaṃ sutisāmaññavasenāti.

Here we will show some usages: 'tayo addhā' (the three times); 'addhānaṃ vītivatto' (having transcended time); 'iminā dīghena addhunā' (by this long road); 'dīghassa addhuno accayena' (with the passing of a long time); 'pathaddhuno pannaraseva cando' (like the moon on the fifteenth day of the half-month's journey); 'ahū atītamaddhāne, samaṇo khantidīpano' (in a past time there was an ascetic, an illuminator of patience); 'addhāne gacchante paññāyissati' (as the journey proceeds, it will be known). These and others should be understood. This rule here should also be known: the form stated as 'addhānaṃ' is an accusative singular and also a dative-genitive plural. In phrases such as 'addhānamaggapaṭippanno hoti,' it is similar to the neuter word 'addhāna,' a designator of a long road, on account of the similarity in sound.

Idāni muddhasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal paradigm of the word 'muddha' is stated:

Muddhā, muddhā, muddhāno. Muddhaṃ, muddhe, muddhāne. Muddhānā, muddhehi, muddhebhi. Muddhassa, muddhānaṃ. Muddhānā, muddhehi, muddhebhi. Muddhassa, muddhānaṃ. Muddhani, muddhanesu. Bho muddha, bhavanto muddhā, muddhāno.

Muddhā, muddhā, muddhāno. Muddhaṃ, muddhe, muddhāne. Muddhānā, muddhehi, muddhebhi. Muddhassa, muddhānaṃ. Muddhānā, muddhehi, muddhebhi. Muddhassa, muddhānaṃ. Muddhani, muddhanesu. Bho muddha, bhavanto muddhā, muddhāno.

Evaṃ abhibhavitāpadena visadisapadāni bhavanti. Iti nānānayehi abhibhavitāpadena sadisāni vattādīni visadisāni guṇavādīni rājasāiccādīni ca ākārantapadāni dassitāni saddhiṃ nāmikapadamālāhi.

In this way, there are words dissimilar to the word 'abhibhavitar.' Thus, by various methods, words ending in -ā similar to 'abhibhavitar'—such as 'vattar' and so on—and dissimilar words—such as 'guṇavā,' 'rājasakha,' and so on—have been shown, together with their nominal paradigms.

Ettha [M 0.0222] yogaṃ sace poso, kare paṇḍitajātiko;

Tassa vohārabhedesu, vijambhe ñāṇamuttamaṃ.

If a person of wise birth applies himself to this, his supreme knowledge unfolds amidst the varieties of usage.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the nine-limbed teaching with its commentaries, in the Tipiṭaka, and in the paths of analysis...

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

In the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the sake of proficiency.

Savinicchayo ākārantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa

The determination concerning the natural form of masculine nouns ending in -ā.

Nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo nāma

The Section named the Division of Nominal Paradigms.

Chaṭṭho paricchedo.

The Sixth Chapter.

Ukāranta avaṇṇantatāpakatikaṃ

Concerning the natural form of stems ending in -u and consonants.

Ākārantapulliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

Here ends the section on masculine nouns ending in -ā.

7. Niggahītantapulliṅganāmikapadamālā

7. The Paradigms of Masculine Nouns Ending in Niggahīta (ṃ).

Atha pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā niggahītantapulliṅgānaṃ bhavanta karontaiccādikassa pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma –

Now, having given precedence to the view of the former teachers, we will explain the nominal paradigms of the natural form of masculine nouns ending in niggahīta, such as 'bhavant,' 'karont,' and so on:

Gacchaṃ mahaṃ caraṃ tiṭṭhaṃ, dadaṃ bhuñjaṃ suṇaṃ pacaṃ;

Jayaṃ jaraṃ cavaṃ mīyaṃ, saraṃ kubbaṃ japaṃ vajaṃ.

Going, honoring, walking, standing; giving, eating, hearing, cooking; conquering, aging, ceasing, dying; remembering, doing, muttering, going.

Gacchaṃ, gacchanto, gacchantā. Gacchantaṃ, gacchante. Gacchatā, gacchantehi, gacchanteti. Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchatā, gacchantehi, gacchantebhi. Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchati, gacchantesu. Bho gacchaṃ, bho gacchā, bhavanto gacchanto.

Gacchaṃ, gacchanto, gacchantā. Gacchantaṃ, gacchante. Gacchatā, gacchantehi, gacchanteti. Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchatā, gacchantehi, gacchantebhi. Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchati, gacchantesu. Bho gacchaṃ, bho gacchā, bhavanto gacchanto.

Gacchādīni aññāni ca taṃsadisānaṃ evaṃ ñeyyānīti yamakamahātheramataṃ. Kiñcāpettha tatiyekavacanaṭṭhānādīsu “gacchantena, gacchantā, gacchantasmā, gacchantamhā, gacchantasmiṃ, gacchantamhī”ti imāni padāni nāgatāni, tathāpi tattha tattha payogadassanato gahetabbāni.

It is the view of the Great Elder Yamaka that other similar words beginning with 'gacchant' should be understood in the same way. And although here, in the instrumental singular and other cases, such forms as 'gacchantena,' 'gacchantā,' 'gacchantasmā,' 'gacchantamhā,' 'gacchantasmiṃ,' and 'gacchantamhī' have not been given, they should nevertheless be adopted based on their observed usage in various places.

Tatra yamakamahātherena ālapanavacanaṭṭhāneyeva “gacchanto, mahanto, caranto”tiādīnaṃ bahuvacanattaṃ kathitaṃ, paccattavacanaṭṭhāne [M 0.0223] ekavacanattaṃ. Kehici pana paccattavacanaṭṭhāne ekavacanabahuvacanattaṃ, ālapanavacanaṭṭhāne bahuvacanattaṃyeva kathitaṃ. “Gacchaṃ, mahaṃ, cara”ntiādīnaṃ pana ālapanaṭṭhāne ekavacanattaṃ. Mayaṃ pana buddhavacane anekāsu cāṭṭhakathāsu “gacchanto, mahanto”tiādīnaṃ bahuvacanappayogānaṃ “gacchaṃ, mahaṃ”iccādīnañca sānusārālapanekavacanappayogānaṃ adassanato “gacchanto bhāradvājo. Sa gacchaṃ na nivattati. Mahanto lokasannivāso”tiādīnaṃ pana paccattekavacanappayogānaññeva dassanato tādisāni rūpāni anijjhānakkhamāni viya maññāma. Niruttipiṭake paccattālapanaṭṭhāne “mahanto, bhavanto, caranto”tiādīnaṃ bahuvacanattameva kathitaṃ, na ekavacanattaṃ. Tathā hi tattha “mahaṃ bhavaṃ caraṃ tiṭṭha”nti gāthaṃ vatvā “mahaṃ tiṭṭhati, mahanto tiṭṭhantī”ti ca, “bho mahā, bhavanto mahanto”ti ca, “bhavaṃ tiṭṭhati, bhavanto tiṭṭhantī”ti ca ādi vuttaṃ.

Therein, the Great Elder Yamaka has stated that in the vocative case, forms such as 'gacchanto,' 'mahanto,' and 'caranto' are plural, while in the nominative case they are singular. Some, however, say that in the nominative case they are both singular and plural, whereas in the vocative case they are only plural. Forms such as 'gacchaṃ,' 'mahaṃ,' and 'caraṃ,' however, are singular in the vocative. We, on the other hand, because in the word of the Buddha and in many commentaries we do not see plural usages of forms like 'gacchanto' and 'mahanto,' nor vocative singular usages with anusāra of forms like 'gacchaṃ' and 'mahaṃ,' and because we only see nominative singular usages such as 'gacchanto bhāradvājo' (Bhāradvāja, while going), 'Sa gacchaṃ na nivattati' (He, going, does not turn back), and 'Mahanto lokasannivāso' (Great is the worldly abode), we consider such forms to be, as it were, unworthy of consideration. In the Niruttipiṭaka, in the nominative and vocative cases, forms such as 'mahanto,' 'bhavanto,' and 'caranto' are described only as plural, not singular. For so it is said there, after quoting the verse 'mahaṃ bhavaṃ caraṃ tiṭṭhaṃ': 'mahaṃ tiṭṭhati, mahanto tiṭṭhanti' (the great one stands, the great ones stand); and 'bho mahā, bhavanto mahanto' (O great one, O venerable great ones); and 'bhavaṃ tiṭṭhati, bhavanto tiṭṭhanti' (the venerable one stands, the venerable ones stand), and so on.

Ettha pana “bhavaṃ, bhavanto”ti padāni yattha “honto hontā”ti kriyatthaṃ na vadanti, tattha “bhavaṃ kaccāno. Mā bhavanto evaṃ avacutthā”tiādīsu viya aññasmiṃ atthe patanato ekavacanabahuvacanāni bhavanti, tasmā “santo sappurisā loke”ti ettha “santo”ti padassa viya “arahanto sammāsambuddhā”ti ettha “arahanto”ti padassa viya ca “bhavanto”ti padassa bahuvacanattaṃ nijjhānakkhamaṃ. “Mahanto, caranto, tiṭṭhanto”tiādīnaṃ pana bahuvacanattaṃ na nijjhānakkhamaṃ viya amhe paṭibhāti. Na hi katthacipi “santo, arahanto, bhavanto”ti padavajjitānaṃ “gacchanto, mahanto, caranto”tiādīnaṃ anekapadasatānaṃ bahuvacanantatāpayoge passāma. Tathā hi –

Here, however, the words 'bhavaṃ' and 'bhavanto,' where they do not convey the verbal meaning of 'being' (honto, hontā), take singular and plural forms by pertaining to another meaning, as in 'bhavaṃ Kaccāno' (the venerable Kaccāna) and 'Mā bhavanto evaṃ avacutthā' (May the venerable ones not speak thus). Therefore, just as with the word 'santo' in 'santo sappurisā loke' (good people in the world) and the word 'arahanto' in 'arahanto sammāsambuddhā' (the Arahants, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones), the plurality of the word 'bhavanto' is worthy of consideration. But the plurality of words such as 'mahanto,' 'caranto,' and 'tiṭṭanto' appears to us as not worthy of consideration. For nowhere do we see, among hundreds of words, the plural usage of forms like 'gacchanto,' 'mahanto,' 'caranto,' etc., apart from the words 'santo,' 'arahanto,' and 'bhavanto.' Thus:

Bavhatte [M 0.0224] katthaci ṭhāne, “jāna”miccādayo yathā;

Dissanti nevaṃ bavhatte, “gacchanto” itiādayo.

Just as in some instances forms such as 'jānaṃ' are seen in the plural, so forms such as 'gacchanto' are not seen in the plural.

Bavhatte katthaci ṭhāne, “santo” iccādayopi ca;

Dissanti nevaṃ bavhatte, “gacchanto” itiādayo.

And in some instances in the plural, forms such as 'santo' are also seen; but forms such as 'gacchanto' are not so seen in the plural.

“Arahanto”ti bavhatte, ekanteneva dissati;

Nevaṃ dissanti bavhatte, “gacchanto” itiādayo.

'Arahanto' is definitely seen in the plural; but forms such as 'gacchanto' are not so seen in the plural.

Anekasatapāṭhesu, “viharanto”tiādīsu;

Ekassapi bahukatte, pavatti na tu dissati.

In many hundreds of texts, concerning 'viharanto' and so on, not even a single occurrence in the plural is seen.

Bahuvacananayena, “gacchanto”ti padassa hi;

Gahaṇe sati bahavo, dosā dissanti saccato.

For if the word 'gacchanto' is taken as plural, many faults are truly seen.

Yathekamhi ghare daḍḍhe, daḍḍhā sāmīpikā gharā;

Tathā bavhattavācitte, “gacchanto”ti padassa tu.

Just as when one house is burnt, the neighboring houses are also burnt; so it is with ascribing a plural meaning to the word 'gacchanto'.

“Viharanto”tiādīnaṃ, bavhattavācitā siyā;

Rūpanayo aniṭṭho ca, gahetabbo anekadhā.

Then 'viharanto' and so on would have a plural meaning, and an undesirable principle of form would have to be accepted in many ways.

Evaṃ santepi yasmā “niruttipiṭakaṃ nāma pabhinnapaṭisambhidena mahākhīṇāsavena mahākaccāyanena kata”nti loke pasiddhaṃ, tasmā idaṃ ṭhānaṃ punappunaṃ upaparikkhitabbaṃ. Kiñcāpettha there gāravena evaṃ vuttaṃ, tathāpi pāḷinayaṃ garuṃ katvā diṭṭhenekavacananayena adiṭṭho bahuvacananayo chaḍḍetabbo. Evaṃ sati niggahītantesu nayo sobhano bhavati. Ayaṃ pana amhākaṃ ruci –

Even so, since it is well-known in the world that 'the Niruttipiṭaka was composed by the great Arahant Mahākaccāyana, one who has attained the analytical knowledges,' this point should be examined again and again. And although this was said with respect for the Elder, still, giving weight to the canonical method, the unseen plural method should be abandoned in favor of the seen singular method. When this is done, the rule concerning words ending in niggahīta becomes elegant. This, however, is our own preference:

“Bhavaṃ karaṃ arahaṃ saṃ, mahaṃ” iti padāni tu;

Visadisāni sambhonti, aññamaññanti lakkhaye.

The words 'bhavaṃ,' 'karaṃ,' 'arahaṃ,' 'saṃ,' and 'mahaṃ,' however, become dissimilar; one should mark them as distinct from one another.

“Gacchaṃ caraṃ dadaṃ tiṭṭhaṃ, cintayaṃ bhāvayaṃ vadaṃ;

Jānaṃ passa”ntiādīni, sadisāni bhavanti hi.

'Gacchaṃ,' 'caraṃ,' 'dadaṃ,' 'tiṭṭhaṃ,' 'cintayaṃ,' 'bhāvayaṃ,' 'vadaṃ,' 'jānaṃ,' 'passaṃ,' and so on—these, indeed, are similar.

Tatra “jāna”ntiādīni, katthaci parivattare;

Vibhattiliṅgavacana-vasenāti vibhāvaye.

Therein, 'jānaṃ' and so on are sometimes transformed; one should understand this is according to case, gender, and number.

Tatra [M 0.0225] tāva bhavantasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccati – bhavaṃsaddo hi “vaḍḍhanto, honto”ti atthepi vadati. Tesaṃ vasena ayaṃ nāmikapadamālā.

First, the nominal paradigm of the word 'bhavant' is stated. For the word 'bhavant' is also used in the sense of 'growing' and 'being.' This nominal paradigm is according to those meanings.

Bhavaṃ, bhavanto, bhavantā. Bhavantaṃ, bhavante. Bhavantena, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ. Bhavantā, bhavantasmā, bhavantamhā, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ. Bhavante, bhavantasmiṃ, bhavantamhi, bhavantesu. He bhavanta, he bhavantā.

The growing one, the growing ones. The growing one, the growing ones. By the growing one, by the growing ones. To the growing one, to the growing ones. From the growing one, from the growing ones. Of the growing one, of the growing ones. In the growing one, in the growing ones. O growing one, O growing ones.

Tattha “bhavaṃ, bhavanto”tiādīnaṃ “vaḍḍhantohonto”tiādinā attho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “suvijāno bhavaṃ hoti. Dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hoti. Rājā bhavanto nānāsampattīhi modati. Kuḷīradaho gaṅgāya ekābaddho, gaṅgāya pūraṇakāle gaṅgodakena pūrati, udake mandī bhavante dahato udakaṃ gaṅgāya otaratī”ti payogā bhavanti, tasmā ayaṃ nāmikapadamālā sārato paccetabbā. Ettha bhavaṃsaddamattaṃ vajjetvā gacchamānacaramānasaddādīsu viya bhavantasadde “bhavanto, bhavantā”ti purisanayopi labbhati, napuṃsakaliṅge vattabbe “bhavantaṃ, bhavantānī”ti cittanayopi labbhati. Evaṃ vaḍḍhanabhavanatthavācakassa bhavantasaddassa nāmikapadamālā veditabbā.

Therein, the meaning of 'bhavaṃ,' 'bhavanto,' and so on should be understood as 'growing,' 'being,' and the like. For there are such usages as: 'One who knows well is prosperous.' 'One who loves the Dhamma is prosperous.' 'The king, being prosperous, rejoices in various fortunes.' 'A crab-lake is connected to the Ganges; when the Ganges floods, it is filled with Ganges water; when the water is becoming low, the water from the lake flows down into the Ganges.' Therefore, this nominal paradigm should be accepted as essential. Here, with the exception of the word 'bhavaṃ,' the masculine declension ('bhavanto, bhavantā') is also found for the word 'bhavant,' just as for words like 'gacchamāna' and 'caramāna'; and when the neuter gender is to be expressed, the declension like 'citta' ('bhavantaṃ, bhavantāni') is also found. In this way, the nominal paradigm of the word 'bhavant,' which expresses the meaning of growing and being, should be understood.

Ayañca viseso “bhavanto”ti padaṃ vaḍḍhanabhavanatthato aññatthe vattamānaṃ bahuvacanameva hoti, yathā “bhavanto āgacchantī”ti. Vaḍḍhanabhavanatthesu vattamānaṃ ekavacanameva. Atrime payogā “anupubbena bhavanto viññutaṃ pāpuṇāti. Samaṇena nāma īdisesu kammesu abyāvaṭena bhavitabbaṃ, evaṃ bhavanto hi samaṇo susamaṇo assā”ti. “Bhavaṃ” iti padaṃ pana ubhayatthāpi ekavacanameva, tasmā [M 0.0226] idāni “bhavaṃ ānando. Bhavanto āgacchanti, appasaddā bhavanto hontu, mā bhonto saddamakatthā”ti evamādipayogadassanavasena vohāravisese pavattaṃ aññaṃ atthaṃ paṭicca aparāpi nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

And this is the distinction: the word 'bhavanto,' when used in a sense other than growing and being, is only plural, as in 'bhavanto āgacchanti' (the venerable ones are coming). When used in the sense of growing and being, it is only singular. Here are the usages: 'Gradually, being prosperous, one attains distinction.' 'A recluse should be unengaged in such deeds; for being thus, a recluse would be a true recluse.' The word 'bhavaṃ,' however, is singular in both meanings. Therefore, now, based on observing usages such as 'bhavaṃ ānando' (the venerable Ānanda), 'Bhavanto āgacchanti' (The venerable ones are coming), 'appasaddā bhavanto hontu' (Let the venerable ones be quiet), and 'mā bhonto saddam akattha' (Venerable sirs, do not make a noise), another nominal paradigm is stated, which pertains to a different meaning that occurs in conventional usage:

Bhavaṃ, bhavanto, bhonto. Bhavantaṃ, bhavante. Bhavatā, bhotā, bhavantena, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ. Bhavatā, bhotā, bhavantehi, bhavantebhi. Bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa, bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ. Bhavati, bhavante, bhavantasmiṃ, bhavantamhi, bhavantesu. Bho, bhavanto, bhonto iti.

The venerable one (bhavaṃ), the venerable ones (bhavanto, bhonto). The venerable one (bhavantaṃ), the venerable ones (bhavante). By the venerable one (bhavatā, bhotā, bhavantena), by the venerable ones (bhavantehi, bhavantebhi). To/of the venerable one (bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa), to/of the venerable ones (bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ). From the venerable one (bhavatā, bhotā), from the venerable ones (bhavantehi, bhavantebhi). Of the venerable one (bhavato, bhoto, bhavantassa), of the venerable ones (bhavantānaṃ, bhavataṃ). In the venerable one (bhavati, bhavante, bhavantasmiṃ, bhavantamhi), in the venerable ones (bhavantesu). O sir (bho), O sirs (bhavanto, bhonto).

Ettha pana “bho”iccādīni tīṇi padāni yasmā vohāravisesapavattāni ālapanapadāni honti, tasmā “āvuso, bhante”ti padāni viya bhosaddādiupapadavantāni na bhavanti, “bho purisa, bhavanto brāhmaṇā, bhonto samaṇā, bho rāja”iccādīsu hi purisasaddādayoyeva bhosaddādi upapadavanto bhavanti. Idha ca “bhavaṃ ānando”ti ettha bhavaṃsaddena samānatthāni “bho, bhavanto, bhonto”ti padāni vuttāni, na pana “dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hotī”ti ettha bhavaṃsaddena samānatthāni. Paṭhamasmiñhi naye vaḍḍhanatthavasena “bho bhavanta, bhavanto bhavantā, bhonto bhavantā”ti bhosaddādayo ālapanapadānaṃ upapadāni bhavanti, na dutiyasmiṃ naye. Āmeḍitavasena pana “bho bho, bhavanto bhavanto, bhonto bhonto”ti padāni bhavanti yathā “bhante bhante”ti.

Here, the three words 'bho,' etc., since they are terms of address employed in specific conventional contexts, are not, like the words 'āvuso' and 'bhante,' preceded by words such as 'bho.' For in phrases like 'bho purisa' (good man), 'bhavanto brāhmaṇā' (sirs brahmins), 'bhonto samaṇā' (sirs recluses), and 'bho rāja' (O king), it is only words such as 'purisa' that are preceded by words such as 'bho.' And here, the words 'bho,' 'bhavanto,' and 'bhonto' are said to be synonymous with the word 'bhavaṃ' in 'bhavaṃ ānando' (the venerable Ānanda), but not with the word 'bhavaṃ' in 'dhammakāmo bhavaṃ hotī' (one who loves the Dhamma is prosperous). For in the first case, in the sense of honoring, words like 'bho' become preceding words to other terms of address, as in 'bho bhavanta,' 'bhavanto bhavantā,' and 'bhonto bhavantā,' but not in the second case. However, by way of repetition, the words 'bho bho,' 'bhavanto bhavanto,' and 'bhonto bhonto' occur, just as 'bhante bhante' does.

Atridaṃ bhūdhātuvasena saṅkhepato pāḷinidassanaṃ – kasmā bhavaṃ vijjanamaraññanissito. Kathaṃ panāhaṃ bho taṃ bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ jānissāmi. Evaṃ bhoti kho ambaṭṭho māṇavo [M 0.0227] brāhmaṇassa pokkharasātissa paṭissutvā. Mā bhavanto evaṃ avacuttha. Imaṃ bhonto nisāmetha. Evaṃ bho purisa jānāhi, pāpadhammā asaññatā iccevamādi. Ettha “bhavaṃ”iccādīni bhūdhātumayāni nāmapadānīti veditabbāni.

Here is a brief demonstration from the Pāḷi based on the root bhū: 'Why, sir (bhavaṃ), do you resort to a forest devoid of people?' 'How then, good sir (bho), shall I know that venerable (bhavantaṃ) Gotama?' 'So be it, sir (bhoti),' said the young man Ambaṭṭha, having assented to the brahmin Pokkharasāti. 'Sirs (bhavanto), do not speak thus.' 'Sirs (bhonto), listen to this.' 'Thus, good man (bho purisa), know this: of evil nature, unrestrained,' and so on. Here, it should be understood that 'bhavaṃ,' etc., are nouns derived from the root bhū.

Apica tesu “bho, bhavanto, bhonto”ti imāni nipātapadānipi hontīti vavatthapetabbaṃ. “Bho purisā”tiādīsu tesaṃ nipātānipātabhāve vivādo na karaṇīyo. Kaccāyanasmiñhi “bho ge tū”ti vuttaṃ. Aññattha pana “āmantanatthe nipāto”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tathā hi niruttimañjūsāyaṃ vuttaṃ “bhotidaṃ āmantanatthe nipāto.
