So na kevalaṃ ekavacanameva hoti, atha kho bahuvacanampi hotīti ‘bho purisā’ti bahuvacanappayogopi gahito. ‘Bhavanto’ti padaṃ pana bahuvacanameva hotīti ‘purisā’ti puna vutta”nti. Pāḷiyañhi aṭṭhakathāsu ca nipātabhūto bhosaddo ekavacanabahuvacanavasena dvidhā dissati, itare pana bahuvacanavaseneva dissanti. Tesaṃ tu nipātapadatte rūpanipphādanakiccaṃ natthi. Tesu bhosaddassa nipātapadattā āhaccabhāsite nijjīvālapane itthiliṅgavisayo “ummujja bho puthusile, pariplava bho puthusile”ti payogopi dissati. Atrimā bhosaddassa pavattiparidīpanī gāthāyo –

Moreover, it should be established that among these, the words 'bho,' 'bhavanto,' and 'bhonto' are also particles. In phrases like 'bho purisā' (O men), there should be no dispute about whether they are particles or not. For in the Kaccāyana grammar it is said: 'bho ge tū.' And elsewhere it is said: 'It is a particle in the sense of address,' and so on. Thus, in the Niruttimañjūsā it is stated: 'This "bho" is a particle in the sense of address. It is not only singular but also plural; thus the plural usage "bho purisā" is given. The word "bhavanto," however, is only plural, hence "purisā" is stated again.' In the Pāḷi Canon and the commentaries, the word 'bho' as a particle is seen in two forms, singular and plural, while the others are seen only as plural. But when they are particles, there is no task of morphological derivation. Among them, because the word 'bho' is a particle, in emphatic speech and in addressing the inanimate, a usage in the feminine gender is also seen, as in: 'Emerge, O broad stone! Float, O broad stone!' (ummujja bho puthusile, pariplava bho puthusile). These are the verses of Atri that illuminate the usage of the word 'bho':

“Ito bho sugatiṃ gaccha, manussānaṃ sahabyataṃ”;

Evamādīsu bhosaddo, ekavacanako mato.

'Go from here, sir, to a good destination, to companionship with human beings'; in such examples, the word 'bho' is considered to be singular.

“Passatha bho imaṃ kula-putta”miccevamādisu;

Bahuvacanako eso, bhosaddoti vibhāvaye.

'See, sirs, this son of good family'; in such cases and others like them, one should understand that this word 'bho' is plural.

Puggalālapane [M 0.0228] ceva, dhammassālapanepi ca;

Nijjīvālapane cāti, bhosaddo tīsu dissati.

In addressing a person, and in addressing the Dhamma, and also in addressing the inanimate—in these three the word 'bho' is seen.

Tatra dhammālapanamhi, ekavacova labbhati;

Itaresu siyā deka-vaco bahuvacopi ca.

Therein, in addressing the Dhamma, only the singular is found; in the other cases, it may be singular and also plural.

Nicchitabbaṃ guṇīpadaṃ, dhammassālapane dhuvaṃ;

“Acchariyaṃ vata bho”ti, idamettha nidassanaṃ.

In addressing the Dhamma, a word expressing a quality is definitely required; 'Wonderful indeed, sir!' (Acchariyaṃ vata bho) is the example here.

Icchitabbaṃ guṇīpadaṃ, puggalālapane pana;

“Evaṃ bho purisa jānāhi”, idamettha nidassanaṃ.

But in addressing a person, a word expressing a quality is optional; 'Thus, good man, you should know' (Evaṃ bho purisa jānāhi), this is the example here.

Guṇīpadaṃ asantampi, puggalālapanamhi tu;

Ajjhāharitvā pāvade, atthaṃ “bho ehi”ādisu.

Even when a word expressing a quality is not present in addressing a person, one should supply it to state the meaning in cases like 'Sir, come here!' (bho ehi).

Ghaṭādīnaṃ ālapanaṃ, nijjīvālapanaṃ bhave;

Jīvaṃva lokiyā loke, ālapanti kadāci tu.

Addressing things like pots is addressing the inanimate; but worldly people in the world sometimes address them as if they were alive.

Nijjīvālapanaṃ appaṃ, atthaviññāpane siyā;

“Ummujja bho puthusile”, iti pāḷi nidassanaṃ.

Addressing the inanimate is rare; it may occur to convey a meaning. 'Emerge, O broad stone!' (Ummujja bho puthusile) is the Pāḷi example.

Ettha liṅgavipallāsaṃ, keci icchanti paṇḍitā;

Tesaṃ matena bhotīti, liṅgaṃ vipariṇāmaye.

Here some pundits desire a change of gender; according to their opinion, one should alter the gender by using 'bhoti'.

Atha vā pana bhosaddo, nipāto sopadaṃ viya;

Tasmā virodhatā nāssa, tiliṅge vacanadvaye.

Alternatively, the word 'bho' is a particle; therefore, there is no conflict for it in the three genders or the two numbers.

Evaṃ santepi bhosaddo, dviliṅgeyeva pāyato;

Yasmā diṭṭho tato viññū, dviliṅgeyeva taṃ vade.

Even so, since the word 'bho' is mostly seen in only two genders, a wise person should therefore say it is of two genders.

Itthiliṅgamhi sampatte, “bho”ti iti payojaye;

Evaṃvidhaṃ payogañhi, suppayogaṃ budhābravuṃ.

When it comes to the feminine gender, one should use 'bho'; for the wise have declared such a usage to be a good usage.

Yajjevaṃ [M 0.0229] duppayogaṃva, siyā tumhehi dassitaṃ;

“Ummujja bho puthusile”, iccāhaccapadanti ce.

If you should point to this as an improper usage, saying: 'The phrase "Emerge, O broad stone!" is an emphatic utterance...'

Duppayogaṃ na taṃ yasmā, vohārakusalena ve;

Jinena bhāsite dhamme, duppayogā na vijjare.

That is not an improper usage, because for one skilled in conventional speech, indeed, in the Dhamma spoken by the Victor, no improper usages are found.

Itthiliṅgassa visaye, bhotisaddappayojanaṃ;

Kavīnaṃ pemanīyanti, mayā evamudīritaṃ.

In the domain of the feminine gender, the use of the word 'bhoti' is pleasing to poets—thus it has been declared by me.

Evaṃ bhavantasaddassa nāmikapadamālā pāḷinayānurūpaṃ dvidhā vibhattā vaḍḍhanabhavanatthatadaññatthavasena.

Thus the nominal declension of the word 'bhavanta,' in accordance with the Pāḷi method, is divided in two: based on the meaning of honoring, the meaning of being, and other such meanings.

Karontasaddassa pana –

Now, for the word 'karonta' (doing):

Karaṃ, karonto, karontā. Karontaṃ, karonte. Karotā, karontena, karontehi, karontebhi. Karoto, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karotā, karontā, karontasmā, karontamhā, karontehi, karontebhi. Karoto, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karonte, karontasmiṃ, karontamhi, karontesu. Bho karonta, bhavanto karontāti rūpāni bhavanti.

The forms are as follows: (Nom. sg./pl.) karaṃ, karonto, karontā. (Acc. sg./pl.) karontaṃ, karonte. (Ins. sg./pl.) karotā, karontena; karontehi, karontebhi. (Gen./Dat. sg./pl.) karoto, karontassa; karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. (Abl. sg./pl.) karotā, karontā, karontasmā, karontamhā; karontehi, karontebhi. (Loc. sg./pl.) karonte, karontasmiṃ, karontamhi; karontesu. (Voc. sg./pl.) bho karonta; bhavanto karontā.

“Karoto na kariyati pāpa”nti idamettha karotosaddassa atthitānidassanaṃ. Itthiliṅge vattabbe “karontī, karontiyo”tiādinā yojetabbāni, napuṃsakaliṅge vattabbe “karontaṃ, karontānī”tiādinā yojetabbāni.

'Evil is not done by the doer' (Karoto na kariyati pāpaṃ): this is a demonstration of the existence of the word 'karoto.' When the feminine gender is to be expressed, one should use the forms beginning with 'karontī, karontiyo.' When the neuter gender is to be expressed, one should use the forms beginning with 'karontaṃ, karontāni.'

Arahantasaddassa –

Of the word 'arahanta':

Arahaṃ, arahanto. Arahantaṃ, arahante. Arahatā, arahantena, arahantehi, arahantebhi. Arahato, arahantassa, arahantānaṃ, arahataṃ. Arahatā, arahantā, arahantasmā, arahantamhā, arahantehi, arahantebhi. Arahato, arahantassa, arahantānaṃ, arahataṃ. Arahante, arahantasmiṃ[M 0.0230], arahantamhi, arahantesu. Bho arahanta, bhavanto arahanto iti rūpāni bhavanti.

The forms are as follows: (Nom. sg./pl.) arahaṃ, arahanto. (Acc. sg./pl.) arahantaṃ, arahante. (Ins. sg./pl.) arahatā, arahantena; arahantehi, arahantebhi. (Gen./Dat. sg./pl.) arahato, arahantassa; arahantānaṃ, arahataṃ. (Abl. sg./pl.) arahatā, arahantā, arahantasmā, arahantamhā; arahantehi, arahantebhi. (Loc. sg./pl.) arahante, arahantasmiṃ, arahantamhi; arahantesu. (Voc. sg./pl.) bho arahanta; bhavanto arahanto.

Ayaṃ guṇavācakassa arahantasaddassa nāmikapadamālā. “Arahā, arahanto, arahantā”iti ca. Etañhi rūpaṃ samantapāsādikāyaṃ manussaviggahaṭṭhāne dissati. Uttarimanussadhammapāḷiyaṃ pana “mayañcamhā anarahanto”ti padaṃ dissati. Arahantaṃ, arahante. Arahatā, sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Ayaṃ paṇṇattivācakassa arahantasaddassa nāmikapadamālā.

This is the nominal declension of the word 'arahanta' when it denotes a quality. And also 'arahā, arahanto, arahantā.' Indeed, this form is seen in the Samantapāsādikā in the section on the human form. However, in the Pāḷi text on superhuman states, the phrase 'mayañcamhā anarahanto' (we are not Arahants) is seen. (The declension is:) Arahantaṃ, arahante. Arahatā... the rest should be elaborated. This is the nominal declension of the word 'arahanta' when it denotes a designation.

Tathā hi “arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Arahaṃ sugato loke. Arahanto sammāsambuddhā”tiādīsu arahaṃsaddādayo guṇavācakā. “Arahā ahosi. Ahañhi arahā loke. Eko arahā, ekasaṭṭhi arahanto loke ahesuṃ.

Thus, in phrases such as 'the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,' 'the Arahant, the Well-Farer in the world,' and 'the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones,' the words beginning with 'arahaṃ' denote a quality. In phrases such as 'He was an Arahant,' 'I am indeed an Arahant in the world,' and 'There was one Arahant, there were sixty-one Arahants in the world...'

Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Yattha arahanto viharanti, taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ.

Whether in a village or in the wilderness, whether in a valley or on high ground, wherever Arahants dwell, that spot of earth is delightful.

Mayañcamhā anarahanto”tiādīsu arahāsaddādayo paṇṇattivācakāti daṭṭhabbā. Idha itthinapuṃsakaliṅgavasena visuṃ vattabbanayo appasiddho. Yadi evaṃ āsavakkhayaṃ pattā itthī kathaṃ vattabbā, āsavakkhayaṃ pattaṃ cittaṃ kathaṃ vattabbanti? Itthī tāva “yaṃ itthī arahaṃ assa sammāsambuddho”ti vacanato “araha”nti vattabbā guṇavasena, paṇṇattivasena pana “itthī arahā ahosī”ti vattabbā. Cittaṃ pana guṇavaseneva “arahaṃ citta”nti vattabbanti.

In phrases such as 'we are not Arahants,' the words beginning with 'arahā' should be seen as designatory. Here a method of speaking separately according to feminine and neuter gender is not established. If so, how is a woman who has reached the destruction of the taints to be spoken of, and how is a mind that has reached the destruction of the taints to be spoken of? As to the woman, based on the phrase 'that a woman might be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One,' she should be called 'arahaṃ' by virtue of quality; but by way of designation, it should be said, 'the woman was an arahā.' As to the mind, it should be called 'arahaṃ cittaṃ' (an Arahant mind) solely by virtue of quality.

Santasaddassa [M 0.0231] –

Of the word 'santa':

Saṃ, santo, santo, santā. Saṃ, santaṃ, sante. Satā, santena, santehi, santebhi, sabbhi. Sato, santassa, santānaṃ, sataṃ, satānaṃ. Satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā, santehi, santebhi, sabbhi. Sato, santassa, santānaṃ, sataṃ, satānaṃ. Sati, sante, santasmiṃ, santamhi, santesu. Bho santa, bhavanto santoti rūpāni bhavanti.

The forms are as follows: (Nom. sg./pl.) saṃ, santo; santo, santā. (Acc. sg./pl.) saṃ, santaṃ; sante. (Ins. sg./pl.) satā, santena; santehi, santebhi, sabbhi. (Gen./Dat. sg./pl.) sato, santassa; santānaṃ, sataṃ, satānaṃ. (Abl. sg./pl.) satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā; santehi, santebhi, sabbhi. (Loc. sg./pl.) sati, sante, santasmiṃ, santamhi; santesu. (Voc. sg./pl.) bho santa; bhavanto santo.

Ettha pana “addhā hi tāta satanesa dhammo”ti jayaddisajātakapāḷidassanato “satāna”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha hi satanesāti satānaṃ esāti chedo, rassattaniggahītasaralopavasena ca rūpaniṭṭhānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tathā hi tadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “addhā ekaṃsena esa tāta satānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ dhammo sabhāvo”ti attho vutto. Ayaṃ ye loke “sappurisā”ti ca “ariyā”ti ca “paṇḍitā”ti ca vuccanti, tesaṃ vācakassa santasaddassa nāmikapadamālā. Tappaṭisedhassa pana asaṃ, asanto, katthaci asantā iccapi. Tathā hi “asantā kira maṃ jammā, tāta tātāti bhāsare”ti pāḷi dissati. “Asaṃ, asantaṃ, asante. Asatā”tiādinā yojetabbā. Imasmiṃ atthe “santo, asanto”timāni bahuvacanakāniyeva bhavanti, na katthacipi ekavacanakāni. Kasmā? Paṇṇattivācakattā. Aññatra pana “santo, danto”tiādīsu ekavacanāniyeva ṭhapetvā vijjamānatthavācakasantosaddaṃ, kasmā? Apaṇṇattivācakattāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Here, however, the word 'satānaṃ' is stated, as seen in the Pāli of the Jayaddisa Jātaka: 'addhā hi tāta satanesa dhammo.' There, 'satanesa' is parsed as 'satānaṃ esa,' and the form should be understood as established by means of shortening and the elision of the niggahīta and the vowel. Thus, in its commentary, the meaning is stated: 'Certainly, definitely, this, dear one, is the nature, the intrinsic quality, of the good, the wise.' This is the nominal paradigm for the word `santa`, which refers to those who in the world are called 'good people,' 'noble ones,' and 'wise ones.' For its negation, however, there are forms such as 'asaṃ,' 'asanto,' and sometimes 'asantā' as well. Thus, the Pāli text is seen: 'The base ones, it seems, dear one, call me “father, father.”' It should be construed with 'asaṃ, asantaṃ, asante, asatā,' and so on. In this sense, 'santo' and 'asanto' are always plurals; they are never singulars anywhere. Why? Because they are designatory terms. Elsewhere, however, it should be understood that, apart from the word `santo` which denotes an existing thing, in cases such as `santo, danto` (being, tamed), they are only singulars. Why? Because they are not designatory terms.

Idāni paṇṇattivācakānaṃ tesaṃ kānici payogāni kathayāma –

Now we shall state some applications of those designatory terms.

Sameti [M 0.0232] asatā asaṃ. Yaṃ yañhi rāja bhajati, santaṃ vā yadi vā asaṃ. Na sā sabhā yattha na santi santo. Asanto nirayaṃ yanti, santo saggaparāyaṇā. Asante nopaseveyya, sante seveyya paṇḍito. Sabbhireva samāsetha. Sataṃ dhammo iccevamādīni bhavanti.

The bad person associates with the bad. Whatever a king resorts to, whether a good person or a bad one. That is no assembly where there are no good people. The bad go to hell, the good are bound for heaven. One should not associate with the bad; a wise person should associate with the good. One should associate only with the good. 'The nature of the good,' and so forth, are examples.

Yo panamhehi padamālāyaṃ “sabbhī”ti ayaṃ saddo tatiyāpañcamībahuvacanavasena yojito, so ca kho santaiti akārantapakativasena, aññattha pana “sabbhī”ti ikārantapakativasena yojetabbo. Tathā hi sabbhīti sappuriso nibbānañca, sundarādhivacanaṃ vā etaṃ sabbhīti. Sabbo cāyamattho sāṭṭhakathāya “bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātavedā”ti imāya pāḷiyā “santo have sabbhi pavedayantī”ti imāya ca dīpetabbo.

Now, the word 'sabbhi', which was used by us in the paradigm in the sense of the third and fifth case plural, is indeed from the word `santa`, by way of its nature as an a-stem. Elsewhere, however, the word 'sabbhi' should be construed by way of its nature as an i-stem. For thus 'sabbhi' means a good person and Nibbāna, or 'sabbhi' is a synonym for 'beautiful.' And all this meaning should be illuminated by the Pāli with its commentary: 'bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātavedā' and 'santo have sabbhi pavedayantī'.

Ālapane ca paccatte, tatiyāpañcamīsu ca;

Samāsamhi ca yojeyya, sabbhisaddaṃ sumedhaso.

In the vocative and in the nominative, and in the third and fifth cases, and also in a compound, a wise person should use the word `sabbhi`.

Atrāyaṃ yojanā – bho sabbhi tiṭṭha, sabbhi tiṭṭhati, sabbhi saha gacchati, sabbhi apehi, asabbhirūpo puriso. Yasmā panāyaṃ sāsanānukūlā, tasmā imissā tadanukūlattaṃ dassetuṃ idha sāsanato payoge dassessāma atakkāvacare vicitte sugatapāḷinaye sotūnaṃ visāradamatipaṭilābhatthaṃ. Taṃ yathā? Bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātaveda, yaṃ taṃ vāladhinā’bhipūjayāma. Sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ. Yaṃ sālavanasmiṃ senako, pāpakammamakari asabbhirūpaṃ. Ābādhoyaṃ asabbhirūpo. Asammodako thaddho asabbhirūpo”ti[M 0.0233]. Tattha ālapanavacane diṭṭheyeva paccattavacanaṃ pāḷiyaṃ sarūpato anāgatampi diṭṭhameva hoti. Tathā karaṇavacane diṭṭheyeva nissakkavacanampi diṭṭhameva hoti. Samāse saddarūpe diṭṭheyeva byāse saddarūpaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti ṭhapetvā “hetusatthāradassana”ntiādīni. Tattha ca nibbānavācako ce, sabbhisaddo itthiliṅgo santivisuddhi nibbutisaddā viya, so ca yamakamahātheramate rattinayena yojetabbo. Sabbesamikārantitthiliṅgānaṃ sādhāraṇo hi so nayo. Sundaratthavācako ce, aggi ratti aṭṭhinayehi yojetabbo vāccaliṅgattā. “Sabbhidhammabhūtaṃ nibbāna”nti ettha hi sundaradhammabhūtaṃ nibbānanti attho. Evaṃ pāḷinayavasena ālapanādīsu pañcasu ṭhānesu sabbhisaddassa pavattiṃ ñatvā puna aṭṭhakathānayavasenapi tappavatti veditabbā. Kathaṃ? Yasmā sagāthāvaggassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “santo ‘sabbhīhi saddhiṃ sataṃ dhammo na jaraṃ upetī’ti pavedayantī”ti imasmiṃ padese “sabbhīhī”ti hivacanavasena saddaracanāviseso aṭṭhakathācariyehi dassito, tasmā sabbhisaddo sabbesupi vibhattivacanesu yojetabbo. Atridaṃ vadāma –

Here is the application: 'O good one, stand!'; 'A good person stands'; 'He goes together with a good person'; 'Depart from the good person'; 'A man of an un-good nature.' Since this is in accordance with the teaching, in order to show its conformity with it, we will now demonstrate its usage from the teaching, from the subtle and variegated Pāli method of the Sugata which is beyond the sphere of logic, for the sake of the listeners' attainment of confident and superior wisdom. That is: 'Much indeed, O Jātaveda, is this for the un-good one, that we honor you with a tail.' 'One should make acquaintance with the good.' 'That evil deed which Senaka, of an un-good nature, committed in the Sāla grove.' 'This affliction is of an un-good nature.' 'Uncongenial, stubborn, of an un-good nature.' Therein, when the vocative case is seen, the nominative case, though not present in its own form in the Pāli, is also considered as seen. Similarly, when the instrumental case is seen, the ablative case is also considered as seen. When the word-form is seen in a compound, the word-form in the uncompounded phrase is also considered as seen as may be possible, except for cases like 'hetusatthāradassana.' And there, if the word `sabbhi` denotes Nibbāna, it is feminine, like the words `santi`, `visuddhi`, and `nibbuti`, and it should be construed according to the method for `ratti` (night) in the opinion of the great elder Yamaka. For that method is common to all feminine i-stems. If it denotes the meaning 'beautiful,' it should be construed according to the methods for `aggi`, `ratti`, and `aṭṭhi`, because its gender is determined by the noun it qualifies. For here, in 'sabbhidhammabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ,' the meaning is 'Nibbāna which has the nature of the beautiful Dhamma.' Thus, having known the occurrence of the word `sabbhi` in the five places—the vocative and so on—according to the method of the Pāli, its occurrence should be understood again according to the method of the commentary. How? Because in the commentary on the Sagāthāvagga, in this passage 'the good declare: “The nature of the good, together with the good, does not go to decay,”' the commentary masters have shown a special word-formation by means of the instrumental plural ending `-hi` in 'sabbhīhi'; therefore, the word `sabbhi` should be used in all cases and numbers. Here we say this:

Garū “sabbhīhi saddhi”nti, atthaṃ bhāsiṃsu pāḷiyā;

Yato tato sabbhisaddaṃ, dhīro sabbattha yojaye.

Since the teachers have stated the meaning in the Pāli as 'sabbhīhi saddhiṃ' (together with the good), a wise person should therefore use the word `sabbhi` everywhere.

“Asabbhirūpo”itipi, samāsavisaye sutaṃ;

Yasmā tasmā sabbhisaddaṃ, viññū sabbadhi yojaye.

Since 'asabbhirūpo' (of an un-good nature) is also heard in the context of compounds, a discerning person should therefore use the word `sabbhi` everywhere.

“Ovadeyyānusāseyya[M 0.0234], asabbhā ca nivāraye”ti ettha pana “asabbhā”tipadaṃ vicitravuttīsu taddhitapaccayesu ṇyapaccayavasena nipphattimupāgatanti veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Yebhuyyena asabbhīsu bhavaṃ asabbhaṃ. Kiṃ taṃ? Akusalaṃ, tato asabbhā akusaladhammā nivāraye ca, kusaladhamme patiṭṭhapeyyāti attho. “Amhe asabbhāhi vācāhi vikkosamānā tibbāhi sattīhi hanissantī”ti ettha tu asabbhīnaṃ etāti asabbhā, na vā sabbhīnaṃ etātipi asabbhāti nibbacanaṃ, ṇyapaccayavasena ca padasiddhi veditabbā. Yā ca panettha amhehi santasaddassa “saṃ, santo. Saṃ, santaṃ, sante”tiādinā padamālā dassitā, tattha “sameti asatā asa”nti pāḷiyaṃ “asa”nti pade diṭṭheyeva “sa”nti padaṃ pāḷiyaṃ anāgatampi diṭṭhameva hoti yugaḷabhāvena vijjamānatārahattā. Evaṃ diṭṭhena adiṭṭhassa gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Atha vā “asa”nti ettha na saṃ asanti samāsaviggahavasenādhigantabbattā “sa”miti padaṃ diṭṭhameva hoti. Evamaññatrāpi nayo. Tatra santi sappuriso. Asanti asappuriso. Itthiliṅgevattabbe “asatī, asā”ti rūpāni bhavanti. “Asatī, asatī, asatiyo, asā. Asatiṃ, asatī, asatiyo. Asāya, asatiyā, asatīhi, asatībhi. Asatiyā, asatīna”nti vakkhamāna itthinayena nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

'One should advise, one should instruct, and one should restrain from the unseemly.' Here, the word 'asabbhā' should be understood as having been formed by means of the `ṇya` suffix among the various `taddhita` suffixes. How so? 'Asabbhaṃ' is what occurs mostly among the unvirtuous. What is that? The unwholesome. Therefore, the meaning is: one should restrain from unwholesome states and establish wholesome states. But in 'They will strike us with sharp spears, reviling us with unseemly words,' here 'asabbhā' is derived as 'belonging to the unseemly,' or alternatively 'not belonging to the seemly,' and the word-formation should be understood as being by means of the `ṇya` suffix. And with regard to the paradigm for the word `santa` shown by us as 'saṃ, santo; saṃ, santaṃ, sante,' etc., there, in the Pāli 'sameti asatā asaṃ', when the word 'asaṃ' is seen, the word 'saṃ', though not present in the Pāli, is also considered as seen, because of its existence as one of a pair. Thus the unseen should be understood through the seen. Or, in 'asaṃ', the word 'saṃ' is considered as seen because it is to be understood by means of the compound analysis 'na saṃ = asaṃ'. The method is the same elsewhere too. Therein, `santi` means a good person; `asanti` means a bad person. When the feminine is to be expressed, the forms are 'asatī' and 'asā'. The nominal paradigm 'asatī, asatī, asatiyo, asā; asatiṃ, asatī, asatiyo; asāya, asatiyā, asatīhi, asatībhi; asatiyā, asatīnaṃ' should be construed according to the feminine declension that will be explained.

Ettha pana “asā lokitthiyo nāma, velā tāsaṃ na vijjati. Mā ca vasaṃ asatīnaṃ nigacche”tiādīni dassetabbāni. Asāti cettha asatīti ca samānatthā, asantajātikāti hi tesaṃ attho. Yasmā pana jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “asāti asatiyo lāmikā, atha vā sātaṃ vuccati sukhaṃ, taṃ tāsu natthi, attani paṭibaddhacittānaṃ asātameva dentītipi asā[M 0.0235], dukkhā, dukkhavatthubhūtāti attho”ti atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇesuṃ, tasmā sātaṃ natthi etissanti asāti atthe “asā”ti padassa yathā ritto assādo etthāti rittassantipadassa luttuttarakkharassa “rittassaṃ, rittassāni. Rittassa”nti cittanayena nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā, tathā “asā, asā, asāyo. Asaṃ, asā, asāyo. Asāyā”ti kaññānayena yojetabbā.

Here, however, passages such as the following should be shown: 'Women in the world are indeed unvirtuous; no limit is found for them. Do not fall under the sway of unvirtuous women.' Here, 'asā' and 'asatī' have the same meaning, for their meaning is 'of an unvirtuous class.' However, since in the Jātaka commentary they explained the meaning thus: '`asā` means immoral, base women; or, `sāta` is called happiness, and that they lack; because they give only displeasure (`asāta`) to those whose minds are attached to them, they are called `asā`—the meaning is miserable, a basis for suffering,' therefore, in the sense of 'asā' meaning 'pleasure does not exist in them,' the nominal paradigm for the word 'asā' should be construed according to the method for `kaññā` (maiden) as 'asā, asā, asāyo; asaṃ, asā, asāyo; asāyā,' just as the nominal paradigm for the word `rittassa`—where the final letter of `rittassādo` has been elided, from 'ritto assādo etthā' (empty flavor is in this)—is construed according to the method for `citta` as 'rittassaṃ, rittassāni, rittassa'.

Ettha ca yo amhehi “santo”iti saddo dassito. So katthaci ekavacanabahuvacanabhāvena saṃvijjamānasaddassatthampi vadati, tassa vasena ayaṃ nāmikapadamālā –

And here, the word 'santo' has been shown by us. It also expresses the meaning of the word 'saṃvijjamāna' (existing), being found in both singular and plural forms. By its means, this is the nominal paradigm:

Santo, santo, santā. Santaṃ, sante. Satā, santena, santehi, santebhi. Sato, santassa, sataṃ, santānaṃ. Satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā, santehi, santebhi. Sato, santassa, sataṃ, santānaṃ. Sati, sante, santasmiṃ, santamhi, santesu. Bho santa, bhavanto santo, bhavanto santā.

Santo, santo, santā. Santaṃ, sante. Satā, santena, santehi, santebhi. Sato, santassa, sataṃ, santānaṃ. Satā, santā, santasmā, santamhā, santehi, santebhi. Sato, santassa, sataṃ, santānaṃ. Sati, sante, santasmiṃ, santamhi, santesu. Bho santa, bhavanto santo, bhavanto santā.

Ettha pana “ayaṃ kho bhikkhave aṭṭhamo bhaddo assājānīyo santo saṃvijjamāno lokasmiṃ. Cattārome bhikkhave puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Asatā tucchā musā abhūtena abbhācikkhanti. Bhave kho sati jāti hoti”iccevamādīni payogāni bhavanti. “Saṅkhāresu kho sati viññāṇaṃ hotī”tiādīsu pana satisaddo vacanavipallāsavasena ṭhitoti gahetabbo.

Here there are such usages as: 'Indeed, bhikkhus, this is the eighth fine thoroughbred horse, being, existing in the world.' 'Bhikkhus, these four persons are, existing in the world.' 'They accuse with what is untrue, empty, false, and not real.' 'When being exists, there is birth.' But in such cases as 'When formations exist, consciousness comes to be,' the word 'sati' should be understood as standing by way of an exchange of grammatical number.

Tatra ekavacanabahuvacanavasena dvidhā ṭhitesu santosaddesu bahuvacanasantosaddaṃ ṭhapetvā sesā samānasaddassatthampi vadanti, tasmā “santoti samāno, santāti samānā”tiādinā [M 0.0236] attho kathetabbo. Samānoti imassa ca “honto”ti attho “pahu samāno vipulatthacintī, kiṃ kāraṇā me na karosi dukkha”ntiādīsu viya. Payogāni pana –

Therein, among the words for 'santa', which occur in two forms, singular and plural, setting aside the plural word 'santā', the remaining ones also convey the meaning of the word 'samāna' (similar). Therefore, the meaning should be stated thus: 'santo means samāno; santā means samānā,' and so on. And of this 'samāno', the meaning is also 'being,' as in such instances as: 'Being able, thinking of great benefit, why do you not end my suffering?' The usages, however, are:

“Yo mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ;

Pahu santo na bharati, taṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ.

One who, though capable, does not support his mother or father, aged and past their youth—that is a cause of his downfall.

Idheva tiṭṭhamānassa, devabhūtassa me sato;

Punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisā”ti

While I was standing right here, being one who had become a deva, life was again obtained by me. Thus know, O worthy one.

Evamādīni bhavanti.

And so on.

Apica santosaddo yasmā “kilanto”ti ca “upasanto”ti ca “niruddho”ti ca atthaṃ vadati, tasmā tesaṃ vasena santasaddassa “santo, santā. Santaṃ, sante. Santenā”ti purisanayena nāmikapadamālā veditabbā. Ettha ca “santo tasito. Dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ. Santo danto niyato brahmacārī. Santo niruddho atthaṅgato abbhatthaṅgato”tiādīni payogāni. Napuṃsakaliṅge vattabbe “santaṃ, santānī”ti cittanayena nāmikapadamālā. Sā ca “saṃvijjamānaṃ samānaṃ kilantaṃ upasantaṃ niruddha”miti atthadīpakāpadavatīti veditabbā. Atha vā “upādāne kho sati bhavo hotī”tiādīsu napuṃsakappayogadassanato santasaddassa saṃvijjamānasaddatthavācakatte tatiyāpañcamīcatutthīchaṭṭhīsattamīṭhāne “satā, sato, sataṃ, satī”ti padāni adhikāni vattabbāni, sesāni cittanayena ñeyyāni. Itthiliṅge pana vattabbe “santā, santā, santāyo. Santaṃ, santā, santāyo. Santāyā”ti kaññānayena ca, santī, santī, santiyo[M 0.0237]. Santiṃ, santī, santiyo. Santiyā”ti itthinayena ca nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Etāsu paṭhamā “saṃvijjamānā kilantā upasantā niruddhā”ti atthadīpakāpadavatī, ettha payogā suviññeyyāva. Dutiyā pana “saṃvijjamānā samānā”ti atthadīpakāpadavatī. Tathā hi “santī āpatti āvikātabbā”ti ettha saṃvijjamānā “santī”ti vuccati.

Moreover, since the word 'santa' conveys meanings such as 'weary,' 'calmed,' and 'ceased,' therefore, on the basis of these, the nominal declension of the word 'santa' should be understood according to the masculine paradigm as 'santo, santā. Santaṃ, sante. Santenā.' Here, usages are found such as: 'santo tasito' (the weary one is thirsty); 'dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ' (long is the journey for the weary one); 'santo danto niyato brahmacārī' (the calm one is tamed, restrained, and celibate); and 'santo niruddho atthaṅgato abbhatthaṅgato' (the ceased one is stopped, set, vanished). When it is to be expressed in the neuter gender, the nominal declension is 'santaṃ, santāni,' according to the 'citta' paradigm. And this should be understood as having words that illuminate the meanings 'existing, similar, weary, calmed, ceased.' Alternatively, because neuter usages are seen in such phrases as 'upādāne kho sati bhavo hotī' (when there is clinging, there is becoming), when the word 'santa' expresses the meaning of 'existing,' the additional forms 'satā, sato, sataṃ, satī' should be stated for the third, fifth, fourth, sixth, and seventh cases. The rest should be known according to the 'citta' paradigm. But when it is to be expressed in the feminine gender, the nominal declension should be formed according to the 'kaññā' (maiden) paradigm as 'santā, santā, santāyo; santaṃ, santā, santāyo; santāyā,' and according to the 'itthi' (woman) paradigm as 'santī, santī, santiyo; santiṃ, santī, santiyo; santiyā.' Among these, the first has words illustrating the meanings 'existing, weary, calmed, ceased,' and here the usages are very easy to understand. The second, however, has words illustrating the meanings 'existing, similar.' For indeed, in 'santī āpatti āvikātabbā' (an existing offense should be confessed), 'santī' is said to mean 'existing'.

“Yāya mātu bhato poso,

Imaṃ lokaṃ avekkhati;

Tampi pāṇadadiṃ santiṃ,

Hanti kuddho puthujjano”ti

The mother by whom a man, being supported, beholds this world—even her, the life-giver, the good one, an angry worldling kills.

Ettha pana samānā “santī”ti vuccati. Aparāpi itthiliṅge vattabbe padamālā veditabbā. Santīsaddassa hi saṃvijjamānasaddatthavācakatte “jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hotī”tiādinā itthiliṅgappayogadassanato sattamīṭhāne “sati, satiyā, satiyaṃ, santiyā, santiyaṃ, santīsū”ti rūpāni vattabbāni. Sesāni itthinayena ñeyyāni. Ayaṃ tatiyā, ettha ca “asantiyā āpattiyā tuṇhī bhavitabba”nti pāḷi “santiyā”iccādīnaṃ atthibhāve nidassanaṃ. Aparo nayo – satīsaddassa “samānā”ti imasmiṃ atthe “yā tvaṃ vasasi jiṇṇassa, evaṃ dahariyā satī”ti ca “ye taṃ jiṇṇassa pādaṃsu, evaṃ dahariyaṃ sati”nti ca pāḷidassanato “satī, satī, satiyo. Satiṃ, satī, satiyo. Satiyā”tiādīnipi rūpāni yojetabbāni, saṃyoge nakāralopavasena vā.

Here, however, 'santī' is said to mean 'samānā' (similar/equal). Another declension to be expressed in the feminine gender should also be known. For, since the word 'santī' expresses the meaning of 'existing,' because feminine usages are seen in such phrases as 'jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti' (when there is birth, there is aging and death), the forms 'sati, satiyā, satiyaṃ, santiyā, santiyaṃ, santīsu' should be stated for the locative case. The rest should be known according to the 'itthi' paradigm. This is the instrumental, and here the Pāli 'asantiyā āpattiyā tuṇhī bhavitabbaṃ' (one should be silent about a non-existent offense) is an example for the existence of 'santiyā' and so on. Another method: for the word 'satī' in this sense of 'samānā' (equal), because of seeing the Pāli 'yā tvaṃ vasasi jiṇṇassa, evaṃ dahariyā satī' (you who live with an old man, being so young) and 'ye taṃ jiṇṇassa pādaṃsu, evaṃ dahariyaṃ sati' (those who served the feet of that old man, she being so young), the forms 'satī, satī, satiyo; satiṃ, satī, satiyo; satiyā,' and so on, should also be formed, or by way of elision of the 'n' in conjunction.

Idāni “santo, santā”ti padadvayassa payoganicchayaṃ kathayāma payogesu sotūnaṃ asammūḷhabhāvāya. Tathā hi “sappurisā”ti vā “paṇḍitā”ti vā bahuvacanavasena atthaṃ [M 0.0238] vattukāmena “santo danto”ti evaṃ vuttaekavacanasadisaṃ “santo”ti bahuvacanaṃ vattabbaṃ. “Saṃvijjamāno”ti ekavacanavasena atthaṃ vattukāmena “santo”ti ekavacanaṃ vattabbaṃ. “Saṃvijjamānā”ti bahuvacanavasena atthaṃ vattukāmena “santo sappurisā”ti, “santo saṃvijjamānā”ti ca evaṃ vuttabahuvacanasadisaṃ “santo”ti vā “santā”ti vā bahuvacanaṃ vattabbaṃ, “kilanto”ti vā “samāno”ti vā “upasanto”ti vā “niruddho”ti vā ekavacanavasena atthaṃ vattukāmena “santo sappurisā”ti evaṃ vuttabahuvacanasadisaṃ “santo”ti ekavacanaṃ vattabbaṃ. Teyevatthe bahuvacanavasena vattukāmena pana “santā sūnehi pādehi, ko ne hatthe gahessatī”ti ettha viya “santā”ti bahuvacanaṃ vattabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nīti sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā. Idañhi mandabuddhīnaṃ sammohaṭṭhānaṃ. Ayampi panettha saṅgaho veditabbo –

Now, for the non-confusion of listeners regarding the usages, we shall state the determination of the usage of the two words 'santo' and 'santā'. For instance, when wishing to express the meaning in the plural, such as 'good people' or 'wise people,' one should say the plural 'santo,' which is similar to the singular form 'santo' in the phrase 'santo danto.' When wishing to express the meaning 'existing' in the singular, one should say the singular 'santo.' When wishing to express the meaning 'existing' in the plural, one should say the plural 'santo' or 'santā,' which is similar to the plural form in phrases like 'santo sappurisā' or 'santo saṃvijjamānā.' When wishing to express in the singular the meaning 'weary,' 'similar,' 'calmed,' or 'ceased,' one should say the singular 'santo,' which is similar to the plural form mentioned in a phrase like 'santo sappurisā.' But when wishing to express these same meanings in the plural, one should say the plural 'santā,' as here: 'santā sūnehi pādehi, ko ne hatthe gahessatī' (Being weary, with swollen feet, who will take them by the hand?). This rule should be well kept in mind, for this is a cause of confusion for the dull-witted. And this summary here should be understood:

“Tiliṅgatthe ca ekatthe, bavhatthepi ca dissati;

Sattamyanto satisaddo, vipallāse bahumhi so”ti.

It is seen in the sense of the three genders, in the singular sense, and also in the plural sense; that word 'sati', ending in the seventh case, is frequent in inversion.

Idāni mahantasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now the nominal declension of the word 'mahant' is stated:

Mahaṃ, mahā, mahanto, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahante. Mahatā, mahantena, mahantehi, mahantebhi. Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahatā, mahantā, mahantasmā, mahantamhā, mahantehi, mahantebhi. Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahati, mahante, mahantasmiṃ, mahantamhi, mahantesu. Bho maha, bho mahā, bhavanto mahantoti ayamamhākaṃ ruci.

Mahaṃ, mahā, mahanto, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahante. Mahatā, mahantena, mahantehi, mahantebhi. Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahatā, mahantā, mahantasmā, mahantamhā, mahantehi, mahantebhi. Mahato, mahantassa, mahantānaṃ, mahataṃ. Mahati, mahante, mahantasmiṃ, mahantamhi, mahantesu. Bho maha, bho mahā, bhavanto mahanto—this is our preference.

Ettha “mahanto, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahante. Mahantenā”ti purisanayopi labbhati, tasmā “bho mahanta, bhavanto mahantā”ti ālapanapadāni yojetabbāni. Napuṃsakaliṅge vattabbe [M 0.0239] “mahantaṃ, mahantānī”ti cittanayopi labbhati. Itthiliṅge vattabbe “mahatī, mahatī, mahatiyo. Mahatiṃ, mahatī, mahatiyo. Mahatiyā, mahatīhi mahatībhī”ti itthinayopi labbhati. “Mahatiyā ca yakkhasenāyā”tiādīnettha nidassanapadāni. Aparopi “mahantā, mahantā, mahantāyo. Mahanta”nti kaññānayopi labbhati, “mahantā nidhikumbhiyo”tiādīnettha nidassanapadāni. Kaccāyane pana “mahantī”iti padaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. Taṃ “guṇavantī, kulavantī”iccādīni viya pāḷiyaṃ appasiddhattā vīmaṃsitabbaṃ.

Here, the masculine paradigm ('purisa-naya') is also found, thus: 'mahanto, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahante. Mahantenā.' Therefore, the vocative words 'bho mahanta, bhavanto mahantā' should be formed. When it is to be expressed in the neuter gender, the 'citta' paradigm is also found, thus: 'mahantaṃ, mahantāni.' When it is to be expressed in the feminine gender, the 'itthi' paradigm is also found, thus: 'mahatī, mahatī, mahatiyo. Mahatiṃ, mahatī, mahatiyo. Mahatiyā, mahatīhi mahatībhī.' Here, 'mahatiyā ca yakkhasenāyā' (and with a great army of yakkhas) and so on are examples. Another paradigm, that of 'kaññā' (maiden), is also found, thus: 'mahantā, mahantā, mahantāyo. Mahantaṃ.' Here, 'mahantā nidhikumbhiyo' (great treasure pots) and so on are examples. In Kaccāyana's grammar, however, the word 'mahantī' is seen. Like 'guṇavantī' and 'kulavantī', it should be investigated, since it is not established in the Pāli canon.

Nanu bho yasmā sāsanepi “gacchantī, carantī”tiādīni ca “iddhimantī”ti ca padaṃ dissati, tasmā “mahantī, guṇavantī”tiādīnipi bhavitabbanti? Na bhavitabbaṃ tathārūpassa nayassa vasena aggahetabbattā, “mahatī, guṇavatī”iccādinayasseva dassanato ca. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu ca “seyyathāpi nāma mahatī naṅgalasīsā, itthī siyā rūpavatī, sā ca sīlavatī siyā. Satimatī cakkhumatī. Iddhimatī pattimatī”ti ca “mahatiṃ senaṃ disvā mahosadhasenā mandā, ayaṃ ativiya mahatī senā dissatī”ti ca ādīni payogāni dissanti, na “mahantī, rūpavantī”iccādīni.

But, sirs, since in the Teaching words like 'gacchantī' (going), 'carantī' (walking), and the word 'iddhimantī' (possessing psychic power) are seen, shouldn't words like 'mahantī' and 'guṇavantī' also exist? They should not exist. This is because a method of that kind is not to be accepted, and because the method of 'mahatī', 'guṇavatī', and so on is what is seen. For indeed, in the Pāli and the commentaries, usages are seen such as: 'just as a great plowshare'; 'a woman might be beautiful (rūpavatī), and she might be virtuous (sīlavatī)'; 'mindful (satimatī), possessing vision (cakkhumatī)'; 'possessing psychic power (iddhimatī), having attained (pattimatī)'; and 'having seen the great (mahatiṃ) army, Mahosadha's army is small; this army is seen to be exceedingly great (mahatī)'; but not 'mahantī', 'rūpavantī', and so on.

Keci pana “mahāiti saddo byāse na labbhati, samāseyeva labbhati ‘mahāpuriso’ti ettha viyā”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. “Mahā te upāsaka pariccāgo. Mahā vatāyaṃ bhante bhūmicālo. Ghoso ca vipulo mahā. Bārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma mahā. Senā sādissate mahā”ti payogadassanato. Evaṃ byāsepi labbhatīti [M 0.0240] veditabbaṃ, tasmā “mahaṃ, mahā, mahanto, mahantā. Bho mahanta, bhavanto mahantā”ti pulliṅge, “mahantaṃ, mahā, mahantāni. Bho mahanta, bhavanto mahantānī”ti napuṃsakaliṅge, “mahantā, mahā, mahantā, mahantāyo. Bhoti mahante, bhotiyo mahantā, mahantāyo”ti itthiliṅge sabbaṃ sampuṇṇaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Samāse pana “mahāsatto mahāupāsako mahāupāsikā mahabbalo mahāvanaṃ mahaggataṃ mahapphalaṃ mahabbhaya”ntiādīni rūpāni bhavanti, taddhite “mahattano mahattaṃ mahantattaṃ mahantatā”ti rūpāni bhavanti. Gacchantasaddassa pana “gacchanto gacchantā”ti rūpāni vatvā sesāni mahantasadde vuttanayena vitthāretvā nāmikapadamālā veditabbā. Tathā “gacchanto, gacchantā”ti purisanayo ca “gacchantaṃ, gacchantānī”ti cittanayo ca “gacchantī, gacchantī, gacchantiyo”ti itthinayo ca gahetabbo. Evaṃ liṅgattayavasena “caraṃ caranto carantaṃ carantī, dadaṃ dadanto dadantaṃ dadantī”tiādīnaṃ anekapadasahassānaṃ nāmikapadamālā vitthāretabbā.

However, some say: "The word 'mahā' is not found uncompounded, but only in compounds, for example, in 'mahāpuriso' (great man)." This should not be accepted. From its usage, for example, we find: "Great, O lay disciple, is your sacrifice. Truly great, venerable sir, is this earthquake. The sound is vast and great. The kingdom of Bārāṇasī is called great. The army appears great." Thus, it should be understood that it is also found uncompounded. Therefore, the complete paradigm should be applied: in the masculine gender, "mahaṃ, mahā, mahanto, mahantā. O great one (bho mahanta), you great ones (bhavanto mahantā)"; in the neuter gender, "mahantaṃ, mahā, mahantāni. O great one (bho mahanta), you great ones (bhavanto mahantāni)"; in the feminine gender, "mahantā, mahā, mahantā, mahantāyo. O great lady (bhoti mahante), you great ladies (bhotiyo mahantā, mahantāyo)." In compounds, however, forms such as "mahāsatto (great being), mahāupāsako (great male lay follower), mahāupāsikā (great female lay follower), mahabbalo (of great strength), mahāvanaṃ (great forest), mahaggataṃ (exalted), mahapphalaṃ (great fruit), mahabbhayaṃ (great fear)" and so on arise. In derivatives, forms such as "mahattano (of a great one), mahattaṃ (greatness), mahantattaṃ (greatness), mahantatā (greatness)" arise. Regarding the word 'gacchanta' (going), after stating the forms "gacchanto, gacchantā," the rest should be elaborated in the manner explained for the word 'mahanta'; the paradigm of nominal stems should be understood. Thus, the masculine paradigm "gacchanto, gacchantā," the neuter paradigm "gacchantaṃ, gacchantāni," and the feminine paradigm "gacchantī, gacchantī, gacchantiyo" should be taken. In this way, for the three genders, the paradigm of nominal stems for many thousands of words such as "caraṃ (moving), caranto, carantaṃ, carantī; dadaṃ (giving), dadanto, dadantaṃ, dadantī" and so on should be elaborated.

Ye panācariyā “gacchanto”tiādīnaṃ paccattālapanabahuvacanattañca “gacchaṃ”iccādīnaṃ ālapanekavacanattañca icchanti, te samamhehi payogo sāsane na diṭṭho nayavasenāgahetabbattā. Tasmā tāni ettha na vadāma. Ayaṃ pana viseso diṭṭho. Seyyathidaṃ?

As for those teachers who hold that 'gacchanto' and so on are plural vocatives, and that 'gacchaṃ' and so on are singular vocatives, such usage has not been seen by us in the Dispensation, as it should not be accepted according to the proper method. Therefore, we do not state those forms here. This distinction, however, is seen. As follows:

“Gacchaṃ vidhama”miccādi-padāni munisāsane;

Katthacākhyātikā honti, katthaci pana nāmikā.

Words such as 'gacchaṃ,' 'vidhamaṃ,' in the Sage's Dispensation, are sometimes verbal, and at other times nominal.

“Tassāhaṃ santike gacchaṃ,

So me satthā bhavissati;

Vidhamaṃ deva te raṭṭhaṃ,

Putto vessantaro tava.

I shall go to his presence, he will be my teacher; your son Vessantara, O king, is destroying your kingdom.

Adhammaṃ [M 0.0241] sārathi kayirā, mañce tvaṃ nikkhanaṃ vane”;

Iccevamādayo ñeyyā, payogā ettha dhīmatā.

The charioteer might do wrong, you are digging on a couch in the forest.” These and similar usages should be understood here by the wise.

“Gacchissāmi vidhamī”ti-ādinā jinasāsane;

Nānākālapurisānaṃ, vasenatthaṃ vade vidū.

By means of forms such as ‘Gacchissāmi’ (I will go) and ‘vidhamī’ (I destroy) in the Conqueror's Dispensation, the wise should state the meaning according to the various tenses and persons.

Nāmatte pana “gacchanto, vidhamanto”tiādinā;

“Gaccha”miccevamādīna-matthamatthavidū vade.

But in the case of a nominal form, the wise should state the meaning of ‘gacchaṃ’ and so on by means of ‘gacchanto,’ ‘vidhamanto,’ and so on.

Idāni samagatikattepi “jānaṃ, passa”ntiādīnaṃ liṅgavibhattivacanantaravasena yo viseso dissati, taṃ vadāma. Tathā hi “sā jānaṃyeva āha na jānāmīti, passaṃyeva āha na passāmī”ti evamādīsu jānaṃ passaṃ saddānaṃ “jānantī passantī”ti liṅgantaravasena parivattanaṃ bhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iminā “gacchaṃ”iti saddassapi yathāpayogaṃ “gacchantī”ti itthiyā kathanattho labbhati tehi samānagatikattā, na “gacchanto”ti saddassa “gacchantī”ti itthiyā kathanattho labbhati tehi asamānagatikattāti kāraṇaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. “Api nu tumhe āyasmanto ekantasukhaṃ lokaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ viharathā”ti ettha “jānantā passantā”ti vacanantaravasena parivattanaṃ bhavatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iminā pana “gacchaṃ”iti saddassapi yathāpayogaṃ “gacchantā”ti bahuvacanattho labbhati tehi samānagatikattā, na “gacchante”ti saddassa “gacchantā”ti bahuvacanattho labbhati tehi asamānagatikattāti kāraṇaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Esa nayo uttaratrāpi. “Bharanti mātāpitaro, pubbe katamanussara”nti ettha anussaraṃsaddassa “anussarantā”ti vacanantaravasena parivattanaṃ bhavati. “Saddhammo garukātabbo, saraṃ buddhāna sāsana”nti ettha saraṃsaddassa sarantenāti vibhattantaravasena parivattanaṃ bhavati. “Phusaṃ bhūtāni saṇṭhānaṃ, manasā gaṇhato [M 0.0242] yathā”ti ettha phusaṃsaddassapi “phusantassā”ti vibhattantaravasena parivattanaṃ bhavati. Tathā “yācaṃ adadamappiyo”ti etthāpi yācaṃsaddassa “yācantassā”ti vibhattantaravasena parivattanaṃ bhavati. Yācanti vā yācitabbaṃ dhanaṃ, iminā nayena nānappakārato parivattanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Iti “bhavaṃkara”ntiādīnaṃ visadisapadamālā ca “gacchaṃ, cara”ntiādīnaṃ sadisapadamālā ca “jānaṃ, passa”ntiādīnaṃ liṅgavibhattivacanantaravasena katthaci parivattananti ayaṃ tividhopi ākāro ākhyātikapadatthavibhāvanāya saddhiṃ kathito pāvacanavare sotūnaṃ saddesvatthesu ca visāradabuddhipaṭilābhatthaṃ. Sabbametañhi sandhāya imā gāthā vuttā –

Now, even when they have the same paradigm, we will explain the distinction that is seen among words such as ‘jānaṃ’ and ‘passaṃ’ by way of a different gender, case, or number. For example, in such phrases as “she, while knowing, said ‘I do not know’; while seeing, said ‘I do not see’,” it should be understood that the words ‘jānaṃ’ and ‘passaṃ’ undergo a transformation into ‘jānantī’ and ‘passantī’ by way of a different gender. By this it is shown that for the word ‘gacchaṃ’ too, the meaning of expressing the feminine form ‘gacchantī’ is obtained where appropriate, because they have the same paradigm; but for the word ‘gacchanto,’ the meaning of expressing the feminine ‘gacchantī’ is not obtained, because they have a different paradigm. This is the reason. In the phrase “Venerable ones, do you dwell knowing and seeing a world of exclusive pleasure?” it should be understood that a transformation into ‘jānantā’ and ‘passantā’ occurs by way of a different number. By this it is shown that for the word ‘gacchaṃ’ too, the plural meaning ‘gacchantā’ is obtained where appropriate, because they have the same paradigm; but for the word ‘gacchante,’ the plural meaning ‘gacchantā’ is not obtained, because they have a different paradigm. This is the reason. This is the method in what follows as well. In “Parents support, remembering what was done before,” the word ‘anussaraṃ’ undergoes a transformation into ‘anussarantā’ by way of a different number. In “The good Dhamma should be respected, remembering the Buddhas' Dispensation,” the word ‘saraṃ’ undergoes a transformation into ‘sarantena’ by way of a different case. In “Just as for one who grasps with the mind the constitution of beings while touching them,” the word ‘phusaṃ’ undergoes a transformation into ‘phusantassa’ by way of a different case. Similarly, in “unloved for not giving when begged,” the word ‘yācaṃ’ undergoes a transformation into ‘yācantassa’ by way of a different case. Or, ‘they beg for wealth that is to be begged for’; in this way the transformation should be understood in various ways. Thus, the dissimilar paradigm of ‘bhavaṃkara,’ etc., the similar paradigm of ‘gacchaṃ,’ ‘cara,’ etc., and the transformation of ‘jānaṃ,’ ‘passaṃ,’ etc., in some cases by way of a different gender, case, or number—this threefold manner has been explained along with the analysis of the meanings of verbal forms, in this excellent teaching, for the purpose of listeners gaining expert understanding in words and their meanings. It is with reference to all this that these verses are stated:

“Bhavaṃ karaṃ arahaṃ saṃ, mahaṃ”iti padāni tu;

Visadisāni sambhonti, aññamaññanti lakkhaye.

The words ‘bhavaṃ,’ ‘karaṃ,’ ‘arahaṃ,’ ‘saṃ,’ and ‘mahaṃ,’ however, arise as dissimilar; one should recognize that they are dissimilar from one another.

“Gacchaṃ caraṃ dadaṃ tiṭṭhaṃ, cintayaṃ bhāvayaṃ vadaṃ;

Jānaṃ passa”ntiādīni, samānāni bhavanti hi.

‘Gacchaṃ,’ ‘caraṃ,’ ‘dadaṃ,’ ‘tiṭṭhaṃ,’ ‘cintayaṃ,’ ‘bhāvayaṃ,’ ‘vadaṃ,’ ‘jānaṃ,’ ‘passaṃ,’ and so on, are indeed similar.

Tatra “jāna”ntiādīnaṃ, katthaci parivattanaṃ;

Liṅgavibhattivacana-ntarato pana dissatīti.

Among them, for ‘jānaṃ’ and so on, a transformation is sometimes seen on account of another gender, case, or number.

Apica ayaṃ sabbesampi niggahītantapulliṅgānaṃ pakati, yadidaṃ dvīsu liṅgesu chasu vibhattīsu terasasu vacanesu aññataraliṅgavibhattivacanavasena parivattanaṃ. Ayampi panettha nīti veditabbā.

Furthermore, this is the nature of all masculine nouns with a stem ending in niggahīta: namely, the transformation by way of another gender, case, or number among the two genders, six cases, and thirteen number-forms. This rule, too, should be understood here.

“Gacchaṃ cara”ntiādīni, vippakatavaco siyuṃ;

“Gacchamāno caramāno”, iccādīni padāni ca.

Words like ‘gacchaṃ,’ ‘caraṃ’ would be of incomplete action; and words like ‘gacchamāno,’ ‘caramāno’...

“Mahaṃ bhava”nti etāni, vippakatavacopi ca;

Avippakatavaco ca, siyuṃ atthānurūpato.

These words, ‘mahaṃ’ and ‘bhavaṃ,’ can be words of incomplete action and also words of complete action, according to the meaning.

“Arahaṃ [M 0.0243] sa”nti etāni, vinimuttāni sabbathā;

Ākāraṃ tividhampetaṃ, kare citte sumedhasoti.

These words, ‘arahaṃ’ and ‘saṃ,’ are completely free in every way. The wise person should bear this threefold manner in mind.

Savinicchayoyaṃ niggahītantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed analysis of the division of the paradigm of nominal stems for the natural form of masculine nouns with a stem ending in niggahīta.

Ākārantatāpakatikaṃ niggahītantapulliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on masculine nouns with a stem ending in niggahīta of the natural form is concluded.

Idāni dhanabhūtiiccetassa pakatirūpassa aññesañca taṃsadisānaṃ nāmikapadamālāvibhāgaṃ vakkhāmi pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā.

Now I will explain the division of the paradigm of nominal stems for the natural form of ‘Dhanabhūti’ and for others similar to it, having taken the view of the ancient teachers as my guide.

Aggi, aggī, aggayo. Aggiṃ, aggī, aggayo. Agginā, aggīhi, aggībhi. Aggissa, aggino, aggīnaṃ. Agginā, aggīhi, aggībhi. Aggissa, aggino, aggīnaṃ. Aggismiṃ, aggimhi, aggīsu. Bho aggi, bho aggī, bhavanto aggayo. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

Aggi, aggī, aggayo. Aggiṃ, aggī, aggayo. Agginā, aggīhi, aggībhi. Aggissa, aggino, aggīnaṃ. Agginā, aggīhi, aggībhi. Aggissa, aggino, aggīnaṃ. Aggismiṃ, aggimhi, aggīsu. Bho aggi, bho aggī, bhavanto aggayo. This is the view of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Ettha kiñcāpi nissakkavacanaṭṭhāne “aggismā, aggimhā”ti imāni nāgatāni, tathāpi tattha tattha taṃsadisappayogadassanato gahetabbāni. “Agginā, aggismā, aggimhā”ti kamo ca veditabbo.

Here, although the forms ‘aggismā’ and ‘aggimhā’ have not been given in the ablative case, they should nevertheless be accepted, as similar usages are seen in various places. And the sequence should be understood as ‘agginā, aggismā, aggimhā’.

Dhanabhūti, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtiṃ, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino, dhanabhūtīnaṃ. Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtismā, dhanabhūtimhā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino, dhanabhūtīnaṃ. Dhanabhūtismiṃ, dhanabhūtimhi, dhanabhūtīsu. Bho dhanabhūti, bho dhanabhūtī, bhavanto dhanabhūtayo.

Dhanabhūti, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtiṃ, dhanabhūtī, dhanabhūtayo. Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino, dhanabhūtīnaṃ. Dhanabhūtinā, dhanabhūtismā, dhanabhūtimhā, dhanabhūtīhi, dhanabhūtībhi. Dhanabhūtissa, dhanabhūtino, dhanabhūtīnaṃ. Dhanabhūtismiṃ, dhanabhūtimhi, dhanabhūtīsu. Bho dhanabhūti, bho dhanabhūtī, bhavanto dhanabhūtayo.

Siribhūti sotthibhūti, suvatthibhūti aggini;

Gini joti dadhi pāṇi, isi sandhi muni maṇi.

Siribhūti, Sotthibhūti, Suvatthibhūti, Agginī, Ginī, Joti, Dadhi, Pāṇi, Isi, Sandhi, Muni, Maṇi.

Byādhi [M 0.0244] gaṇṭhi ravi muṭṭhi, kavi giri kapi nidhi;

Kucchi vatthi vidhi sāli, vīhi rāsi ahi masi.

Byādhi (disease), gaṇṭhi (knot), ravi (sun), muṭṭhi (fist); kavi (poet), giri (mountain), kapi (monkey), nidhi (treasure); kucchi (belly), vatthi (bladder), vidhi (rule), sāli (fine rice); vīhi (paddy-rice), rāsi (heap), ahi (snake), masi (ink).

Sāti kesi kimi bondi, bodhi dīpi pati hari;

Ari dhani timi kali, sārathyudadhi añjali,

Sāti, Kesi, Kimi, Bondi, Bodhi, Dīpi, Pati, Hari; Ari, Dhani, Timi, Kali, Sārathi, Udadhi, Añjali,

Adhipati narapati, asi ñāti nirūpadhi;

Samādhi jaladhiccādī, dhanabhūtisamā matā.

Adhipati, narapati, asi, ñāti, nirūpadhi, samādhi, jaladhi, and so on, are considered to be like ‘Dhanabhūti’.

Atha vā etesu adhipatisaddassa “adhipatiyā sattā”ti pāḷidassanato “adhipatiyā”ti sattamīrūpampi icchitabbaṃ. Apica “asāre sāramatino”ti pāḷiyaṃ ikārantasamāsapadato yovacanassa noādesadassanato kvaci adhipatiiccādīnaṃ ikārantasamāsapadānaṃ “adhipatino”tiādināpi paccattopayogarūpāni icchitabbāni īkārantānaṃ daṇḍīsaddādīnaṃ “daṇḍino”tiādīni paccattopayogasampadānasāmivacanarūpāni viya. Gahapatijānipatisaddādīnaṃ pana samāsapadānampi evarūpāni paccattopayogarūpāni na icchitabbāni “gahapatayo jānipatayo”tiādinā nayena yathāpāvacanaṃ gahetabbarūpattā. Isi munisaddānaṃ panālapanaṭṭhāne “ise, muse”ti rūpantarampi gahetabbaṃ “putto uppajjataṃ ise. Paṭiggaṇha mahāmune”ti dassanato.

Alternatively, in these cases, because the word 'adhipati' is seen in the Pāli as 'adhipatiyā sattā,' the locative form 'adhipatiyā' should also be accepted. Moreover, in the Pāli text 'asāre sāramatino,' because one sees the substitution of 'no' for the plural ending 'yo' after a compound word ending in 'i', sometimes for compound words ending in 'i' like 'adhipati,' singular forms in the objective cases such as 'adhipatino' should also be accepted, just as for words ending in 'ī' like 'daṇḍī,' singular forms in the accusative, dative, and genitive cases such as 'daṇḍino' are found. However, such singular objective forms are not to be accepted for compound words like 'gahapati' and 'jānipati'; rather, their plural forms like 'gahapatayo' and 'jānipatayo' should be taken as found in the texts. Furthermore, for the words 'isi' and 'muni,' in the vocative case, alternative forms like 'ise' and 'muse' should also be accepted, as seen from 'putto uppajjataṃ ise' and 'paṭiggaṇha mahāmune.'

Ye panettha amhehi aggini ginisaddā vuttā, tatreke evaṃ vadanti “agginisaddo paccattekavacanabhāveyeva labbhati, na paccattabahuvacanabhāve upayogabhāvādīsu vā”ti. Keci pana “pāḷiyaṃ agginisaddo nāma natthi, ginisaddoyeva atthī”ti vadanti. Keci “ginisaddo nāma natthi, agginisaddoyevatthī”ti [M 0.0245] vadanti. Sabbametaṃ na yujjati aggini ginisaddānamupalabbhanato, sabbāsupi vibhattīsu dvīsu vacanesu yojetabbatādassanato ca. Tathā hi suttanipāte kokālikasutte –

Now, regarding the words 'aggini' and 'gini' that we have mentioned here, some say: 'The word 'aggini' is found only in the singular nominative, not in the plural, nor in the accusative and other cases.' Others say: 'In the Pāli texts, the word 'aggini' does not exist; only 'gini' does.' Still others say: 'The word 'gini' does not exist; only 'aggini' does.' All this is incorrect, since both 'aggini' and 'gini' are found, and because it is seen that they can be conjugated in all cases and in both numbers. For example, in the Kokālika Sutta of the Suttanipāta:

“Na hi vaggu vadanti vadantā,

Nābhijavanti na tāṇamupenti;

Aṅgāre santhate senti,

Agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ pavisantī”ti

For speakers do not speak what is lovely,

They do not conquer, nor do they find protection;

They lie on a spread of embers,

And enter a blazing fire.

Imasmiṃ padese “aggini”nti upayogavacanaṃ dissati. Tenāha aṭṭhakathācariyo “agginiṃ sampajjalitanti samantatojālaṃ sabbadisāsu ca sampajjalitamaggi”nti. Tatreva ca suttanipāte kokālikasutte –

In this passage, 'agginiṃ' is seen as an accusative form. Therefore the commentator said: "'Agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ' means a fire with flames all around and blazing in all directions." And in that same Kokālika Sutta of the Suttanipāta:

“Atha lohamayaṃ pana kumbhiṃ,

Agginisañjalitaṃ pavisanti;

Paccanti hi tāsu cirarattaṃ,

Agginisamāsu samuplavāte”ti

Then they enter an iron pot,

Blazing with fire;

For they are cooked in them for a long time,

Boiling up in those that are like fire.

Imasmiṃ padese samāsavisayattā agginisañjalitanti agginīhi sañjalitanti attho labbhati, tathā agginisamāsūti agginīhi sadisāsūti atthopi. Evaṃ samāsavidhānamukhena “agginīhī”ti karaṇavacanampi dissati.

In this passage, because it is a compound, the meaning of 'agginisañjalitaṃ' is 'blazing with fires' (agginīhi sañjalitaṃ), and similarly the meaning of 'agginisamāsu' is 'like fires' (agginīhi sadisāsu). Thus, by means of compound formation, the instrumental form 'agginīhi' is also seen.

Ginisaddopi ca pāḷiyaṃ dissati. Tathā hi “tameva kaṭṭhaṃ dahati, yasmā so jāyate ginī”ti cūḷabodhicariyāyaṃ ginisaddo diṭṭho. Keci panettha sandhivasena akāralopaṃ saññogādissa ca gakārassa lopaṃ vadanti, tampi na yujjati tassā pāḷiyā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “yasmāti [M 0.0246] yato kaṭṭhā. Ginīti aggī”ti evaṃ ginisaddassa ulliṅgetvā vacanato. Tathā “channā kuṭi āhito ginī”ti imassa dhaniyasuttassa aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “āhitoti ābhato jālito vā. Ginīti aggī”ti vacanato, tatheva ca “mahāgini pajjalito, anāhāropasammatī”ti imissā theragāthāya saṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “ginīti aggī”ti vacanato. Yadi hi ginisaddo visuṃ na siyā, aṭṭhakathācariyā “jāyate ginī”tiādīni “jāyate agginī”tiādinā padacchedavasena atthaṃ vadeyyuṃ. Yasmā evaṃ na vadiṃsu, “ginīti aggī”ti pana vadiṃsu, tena ñāyati “ginisaddopi visuṃ atthī”ti. Ye “ginisaddo natthī”ti vadanti, tesaṃ vacanaṃ na gahetabbameva sāsane ginisaddassupalabbhanato. Suttanipātaṭṭhakathāyañhi “channā kuṭi āhito ginī”ti pāṭhassa saṃvaṇṇanāyameva “tesu ṭhānesu aggini ‘ginī’ti vohariyatī”ti tassa abhidhānantaraṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā mayamettha gāthāracanaṃ karissāma –

And the word 'gini' is also seen in the Pāli. For instance, in the Cūḷabodhi Cariyā, the word 'gini' is seen: 'It burns that very wood from which that fire (ginī) is born.' Some here say that due to sandhi there is an elision of the vowel 'a' and an elision of the consonant 'g' at the beginning of the cluster. But this too is not correct, because in the commentary on that Pāli passage, it is explained by pointing out the word 'gini' thus: '“Yasmā” means from which wood. “Ginī” means fire (aggi).' Similarly, in the commentary on this verse from the Dhaniya Sutta, 'channā kuṭi āhito ginī' (My hut is roofed, the fire is kindled), it is said: '“Āhito” means brought or lit. “Ginī” means fire (aggi).' And likewise in the explanation of this Theragāthā verse, 'mahāgini pajjalito, anāhāropasammatī' (A great fire blazes, but without fuel it is quenched), it is said: '“Ginī” means fire (aggi).' If the word 'gini' did not exist separately, the commentators would have explained phrases like 'jāyate ginī' by splitting the words, as 'jāyate agginī.' Since they did not speak thus, but instead said, '“Ginī” means fire (aggi),' it is understood that the word 'gini' also exists separately. The statement of those who say, 'The word “gini” does not exist,' should not be accepted at all, since the word 'gini' is found in the Dispensation. For in the Suttanipāta commentary, in the explanation of the reading 'channā kuṭi āhito ginī,' another term for it is given: 'In those places, fire (aggini) is called “ginī.”' Therefore, we shall compose a verse on this.

Videharaṭṭhamajjhamhi, yaṃ taṃ nāmena vissutaṃ;

Raṭṭhaṃ pabbataraṭṭhanti, dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ.

In the middle of the Videha country,

Is that which is famous by name:

The country called the Mountain Country,

Lovely to see and delightful.

Dhammakoṇḍavhayaṃ tattha, nagaraṃ atthi sobhanaṃ;

Tamhi ṭhāne manussānaṃ, bhāsā eva giniccayaṃ.

There is a beautiful city there, named Dhammakoṇḍa;

In that place, the language of the people is indeed 'gini'.

“Gini ginī ginayo”ti-ādinā pavade vidū;

Padamālaṃ yathā aggi-saddasseva sumedhaso.

The wise, O intelligent one, should recite the paradigm

Beginning with 'gini, ginī, ginayo,' etc.,

Just like that of the word 'aggi'.

Iti alābu lābusaddā viya aggini ginisaddāpi bhagavato pācane dissantīti veditabbā. Yathā pana agginisaddassa sabbāsu vibhattīsu dvīsu vacanesu yojetabbatā siddhā, tathā ginisaddassapi siddhāva hoti. Tasmātra –

Thus, it should be understood that just as there are the words 'alābu' and 'lābu,' so too the words 'aggini' and 'gini' are seen in the Blessed One's teaching. And just as it is established that the word 'aggini' can be conjugated in all cases and in both numbers, so too is it established for the word 'gini.' Therefore:

Aggini[M 0.0247], agginī, agginayo. Agginiṃ, agginī, agginayo. Aggininā, agginīhi, agginībhi. Agginissa, agginīnaṃ. Aggininā, agginismā, agginimhā, agginīhi, agginībhi. Agginissa, agginīnaṃ. Agginismiṃ, agginimhi, agginīsu. Bho aggini, bhavanto agginī, bhavanto agginayo.

Nom: aggini, agginī, agginayo. Acc: agginiṃ, agginī, agginayo. Instr: aggininā, agginīhi, agginībhi. Dat: agginissa, agginīnaṃ. Abl: aggininā, agginismā, agginimhā, agginīhi, agginībhi. Gen: agginissa, agginīnaṃ. Loc: agginismiṃ, agginimhi, agginīsu. Voc: bho aggini, bhavanto agginī, bhavanto agginayo.

“Gini, ginī, ginayo. Giniṃ, ginī, ginayo, gininā”ti sabbaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Iti pāḷinayānusārena aggini ginisaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālā yojitā. Atha vā yathā sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ satva paddhasvāminīti saññogavasena vuttānaṃ saddānaṃ māgadhabhāsaṃ patvā sattavapadumasuvāminīti nissaññogavasena uccāritā pāḷi dissati “tvañca uttamasattavo”tiādinā, tathā sakkaṭabhāsāyaṃ agnīti saññogavasena vuttassa māgadhabhāsaṃ patvā “agginī”ti saññoganakāravasena uccāritā pāḷi dissati “agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ pavisantī”tiādikā. Yathā ca veyyākaraṇehi sakkaṭabhāsābhūto agnisaddo sabbāsu vibhattīsu tīsu vacanesu yojiyati, tathā māgadhabhāsābhūto agginisaddopi sabbāsu vibhattīsu dvīsu vacanesu yojetabbova hoti, tasmā so idhamhehi yojiyati, ginisaddopi agginisaddena samānatthattā, īsakañca sarūpattā tatheva yojiyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Gini, ginī, ginayo. Giniṃ, ginī, ginayo, gininā,' etc.—the entire paradigm should be formed. Thus, according to the Pāli method, the nominal paradigms for the words 'aggini' and 'gini' have been constructed. Alternatively, just as in the Sanskrit language, words spoken with consonant clusters like sattva, padma, and svāmin are seen in Pāli pronounced without clusters as sattava, paduma, and suvāmin when they enter the Māgadhan language, as in 'tvañca uttamasattavo,' etc.; similarly, what is spoken in Sanskrit with a cluster as agni is seen in Pāli pronounced as 'aggini' when it enters the Māgadhan language, as in 'agginiṃ sampajjalitaṃ pavisantī,' etc. And just as the word agni, which belongs to the Sanskrit language, is conjugated by grammarians in all cases and three numbers, so too the word 'aggini,' which belongs to the Māgadhan language, must be conjugated in all cases and two numbers. Therefore, it is conjugated here by us. It should be understood that the word 'gini,' being synonymous with 'aggini' and also slightly similar in form, is conjugated in the same way.

Ettha siyā – yadi agginisaddo sabbesu vibhattivacanesu yojetabbo, atha kasmā kaccāyane “aggissinī”ti lakkhaṇena simhi pare aggisaddantassa iniādeso dassitoti? Saccaṃ, yathā navakkhattuṃ ṭhapetvā katekasesassa dasasaddassa yovacanamhi navādesaṃ katvā yovacanassa utiādesaṃ kasmā “navutī”ti rūpe nipphanne puna “navutī”ti pakatiṃ ṭhapetvā tato naṃvacanaṃ katvā “navutīna”nti rūpaṃ nipphāditaṃ[M 0.0248]. Itthiliṅge pana nādiekavacanāni katvā tesaṃ yāādesaṃ katvā “navutiyā”ti rūpaṃ nipphāditaṃ. Tathā hi “channavutīnaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃ dhammānaṃ pavaraṃ yadidaṃ sugatavinayaṃ navutiyā haṃsasahassehi parivuto”tiādīni payogāni dissanti. Tathā simhi aggisaddantassa iniādesakaraṇavasena “agginī”ti rūpe nipphannepi puna “agginī”ti pakatiṃ ṭhapetvā tato yoaṃnādayo vibhattiyo katvā “aggini, agginī, agginayo. Agginiṃ, agginī, agginayo. Aggininā”tiādīni kathaṃ na nipphajjissantīti sanniṭṭhānaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Here it might be asked: if the word 'aggini' is to be applied in all cases and numbers, then why in Kaccāyana's grammar, by the rule 'aggissa inī,' is the substitution 'inī' shown for the end of the word 'aggi' when 'si' follows? True; just as after the form 'navuti' is derived, then taking 'navuti' again as the base stem, the form 'navutīnaṃ' is produced by applying the 'naṃ' ending, and in the feminine the form 'navutiyā' is produced by the substitution of 'yā' for the case ending—for indeed usages are seen such as 'channavutīnaṃ pāsaṇḍānaṃ... pavaraṃ' (the best of the ninety-six doctrines of the sectarians) and 'navutiyā haṃsasahassehi parivuto' (surrounded by ninety thousand swans)—so too, even though the form 'agginī' is produced by substituting 'inī' for the end of the word 'aggi' when 'si' follows, it should be concluded: why should the forms 'aggini, agginī, agginayo; agginiṃ, agginī, agginayo; aggininā,' etc., not be produced by taking 'agginī' again as the base stem and applying the case endings 'yo,' 'aṃ,' 'nā,' and so on?

Savinicchayoyaṃ ikārantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed analysis and division of the nominal paradigm for the regular form of masculine nouns ending in 'i'.

Ikārantatāpakatikaṃ ikārantapulliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on masculine nouns ending in 'i' of the regular 'i'-stem type is concluded.

Idāni bhāvī iccetassa pakatirūpassa aññesañca taṃsadisānaṃ nāmikapadamālāvibhāgaṃ vakkhāma pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā.

Now, following the opinion of former teachers, we will explain the division of the nominal paradigms for the regular form 'bhāvī' and for other similar words.

Daṇḍī, daṇḍī, daṇḍino. Daṇḍiṃ, daṇḍī, daṇḍino. Daṇḍinā, daṇḍīhi, daṇḍībhi. Daṇḍissa, daṇḍino, daṇḍīnaṃ. Daṇḍinā, daṇḍīhi, daṇḍībhi. Daṇḍissa, daṇḍino, daṇḍīnaṃ. Daṇḍismiṃ, daṇḍimhi, daṇḍīsu. Bho daṇḍi, bho daṇḍī, bhavanto daṇḍino. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

Nominative: daṇḍī, daṇḍī, daṇḍino. Accusative: daṇḍiṃ, daṇḍī, daṇḍino. Instrumental: daṇḍinā, daṇḍīhi, daṇḍībhi. Dative: daṇḍissa, daṇḍino, daṇḍīnaṃ. Ablative: daṇḍinā, daṇḍīhi, daṇḍībhi. Genitive: daṇḍissa, daṇḍino, daṇḍīnaṃ. Locative: daṇḍismiṃ, daṇḍimhi, daṇḍīsu. Vocative: bho daṇḍi, bho daṇḍī, bhavanto daṇḍino. This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Ettha kiñcāpi “daṇḍina”nti upayogekavacanañca “daṇḍismā, daṇḍimhā”ti nissakkavacanañca “daṇḍinī”ti bhummekavacanañca nāgataṃ, tathāpi tattha tattha taṃsadisassa payogassa dassanato gahetabbameva.

Here, although the singular instrumental form 'daṇḍina,' the singular ablative forms 'daṇḍismā, daṇḍimhā,' and the singular locative form 'daṇḍinī' are not given, nevertheless, wherever a similar usage is seen, it should be understood by that example.

“Bhaṇa [M 0.0249] samma anuññāto, atthaṃ dhammañca kevalaṃ;

Santi hi daharā pakkhī, paññavanto jutindharā”ti

"Speak, friend, with permission, solely of the meaning and the Dhamma; for there are young birds, wise and radiant."

Pāḷiyaṃ “pakkhī”iti paccattabahuvacanassa dassanato pana “daṇḍī”iti paccattopayogabahuvacanāni vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

However, it should be understood that in the Pāli text, from the example of the nominative plural 'pakkhī,' the form 'daṇḍī' is stated for the nominative and accusative plural.

Bhāvī, bhāvī, bhāvino. Bhāviṃ, bhāvinaṃ, bhāvī, bhāvino. Bhāvinā, bhāvīhi, bhāvībhi. Bhāvissa, bhāvino, bhāvīnaṃ. Bhāvinā, bhāvismā, bhāvimhā, bhāvīhi, bhāvībhi. Bhāvissa, bhāvino, bhāvīnaṃ. (Bhāvini) bhāvismiṃ, bhāvimhi, bhāvīsu. Bho bhāvi, bho bhāvī, bhavanto bhāvino.

Bhāvī, bhāvī, bhāvino. Bhāviṃ, bhāvinaṃ, bhāvī, bhāvino. Bhāvinā, bhāvīhi, bhāvībhi. Bhāvissa, bhāvino, bhāvīnaṃ. Bhāvinā, bhāvismā, bhāvimhā, bhāvīhi, bhāvībhi. Bhāvissa, bhāvino, bhāvīnaṃ. (Bhāvini) bhāvismiṃ, bhāvimhi, bhāvīsu. Bho bhāvi, bho bhāvī, bhavanto bhāvino.

Evaṃ vibhāvī sambhāvī, paribhāvī dhajī gaṇī;

Sukhī rogī sasī kuṭṭhī, makuṭī kusalī balī.

Similarly: the discerning one, the esteemed one, the contemptuous one, the banner-bearer, the group-leader; the happy one, the sick one, the hare-marked one (the moon), the leper, the crowned one, the skillful one, the strong one.

Jaṭī yogī karī yānī, tomarī musalī phalī;

Dantī mantī sudhī medhī, bhāgī bhogī nakhī sikhī.

The matted-haired one, the yogi, the doer, the one with a vehicle; the javelin-bearer, the pestle-bearer, the fruitful one; the tusked one, the one with mantras, the wise one, the intelligent one; the fortunate one, the enjoyer, the clawed one, the crested one.

Dhammī saṅghī ñāṇī atthī, hatthī cakkhī pakkhī dāṭhī;

Raṭṭhī chattī mālī cammī, cārī cāgī kāmī sāmī.

The one of Dhamma, the one of the Saṅgha, the knowing one, the one with wealth; the one with a trunk (elephant), the one with eyes, the winged one, the tusked one; the ruler, the one with an umbrella, the one with a garland, the one with a leather shield; the one who fares, the generous one, the one with desires, the lord.

Mallakārī pāpakārī, sattughātī dīghajīvī;

Dhammavādī sīhanādī, bhūmisāyī sīghayāyī.

The garland-maker, the evil-doer, the killer of beings, the long-lived one; the speaker of Dhamma, the one who roars like a lion, the one who lies on the ground, the swift-goer.

Vajjadassī ca pāṇī ca, yasassiccādayopi ca;

Etesaṃ koci bhedo tu, ekadesena vuccate.

The fault-seer, the living being, the famous one, and others like them; of these, a certain distinction is stated in part.

Īkārantapulliṅgapadesu hi “vajjadassī, pāṇī”iccevamādīnaṃ upayogabhummavacanaṭṭhāne “vajjadassinaṃ, pāṇine”tiādīnipi rūpāni bhavanti. Ettha ca –

For, in the case of masculine nouns ending in -ī, such as 'vajjadassī' (fault-seer) and 'pāṇī' (living being), in the accusative and locative cases, forms such as 'vajjadassinaṃ' and 'pāṇine' also occur. And here:

“Nidhīnaṃva pavattāraṃ, yaṃ passe vajjadassinaṃ;

Evaṃ jarā ca maccu ca, adhivattanti pāṇine.

"Like one who points out a treasure, one should regard the seer of faults; thus do aging and death overcome a living being."

Samupagacchati [M 0.0250] sasini gaganatalaṃ.

The moon approaches the surface of the sky.

Upahacca manaṃ majjho, mātaṅgasmiṃ yasassine;

Ucchinno saha raṭṭhena, majjhāraññaṃ tadā ahu.

King Madda, having become hostile in mind towards the glorious Mātaṅga, was uprooted along with his kingdom; then it became a central forest.

Susukhaṃ vata jīvāma, verinesu averino”ti

"So very happily we live, free from hate among those who hate."

Evamādayo payogā veditabbā, ayaṃ nayo daṇḍīpadādīsupi labbhateva samānagatikattā daṇḍīpadādīnaṃ vajjadassīpadādīhi. Tasmā upayogaṭṭhāne “daṇḍiṃ, daṇḍinaṃ, daṇḍino, daṇḍine”ti yojetabbaṃ. Bhummaṭṭhāne “daṇḍismiṃ, daṇḍimhi, daṇḍini, daṇḍine, daṇḍīsu, daṇḍinesū”ti yojetabbaṃ. Esa nayo gāmaṇī senānīiccādīni vajjetvā yathārahaṃ īkārantapulliṅgesu netabbo.

Usages such as these should be understood. This method also applies to words like 'daṇḍī' and so on, because words like 'daṇḍī' have the same declension as words like 'vajjadassī.' Therefore, in the accusative case, the forms 'daṇḍiṃ, daṇḍinaṃ, daṇḍino, daṇḍine' should be applied. In the locative case, the forms 'daṇḍismiṃ, daṇḍimhi, daṇḍini, daṇḍine, daṇḍīsu, daṇḍinesū' should be applied. This method should be applied as appropriate to masculine nouns ending in -ī, excluding words such as 'gāmaṇī' (village chief) and 'senānī' (general).

Savinicchayoyaṃ īkārantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed analysis and division of the nominal paradigm for the regular form of masculine nouns ending in -ī.

Īkārantatāpakatikaṃ īkārantapulliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on regular masculine nouns ending in -ī is concluded.

Idāni bhūdhātumayānaṃ ukārantapulliṅgānaṃ appasiddhattā aññesaṃ ukārantapulliṅgānaṃ vasena pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālaṃ pūressāma. Katamāni tāni? “Bhikkhu hetu setu ketu rāhu bhāṇu khāṇu saṅku ucchu veḷu maccu jantu sindhu bandhu ruru neru sattu babbu paṭu bindu garu”iccādīni.

Now, due to the scarcity of masculine nouns ending in -u derived from the root 'bhū,' we will complete the nominal paradigm of the regular form by means of other masculine nouns ending in -u. Which are they? They are 'bhikkhu' (monk), 'hetu' (cause), 'setu' (bridge), 'ketu' (banner), 'rāhu' (Rāhu), 'bhāṇu' (sun), 'khāṇu' (stump), 'saṅku' (stake), 'ucchu' (sugarcane), 'veḷu' (bamboo), 'maccu' (death), 'jantu' (creature), 'sindhu' (river), 'bandhu' (relative), 'ruru' (a kind of deer), 'neru' (Mount Meru), 'sattu' (enemy), 'babbu' (cat), 'paṭu' (clever), 'bindu' (drop), 'garu' (teacher), and so on.

Bhikkhu, bhikkhū, bhikkhavo. Bhikkhuṃ, bhikkhū, bhikkhavo. Bhikkhunā, bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūbhi. Bhikkhussa, bhikkhuno, bhikkhūnaṃ. Bhikkhunā, bhikkhusmā, bhikkhumhā, bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūbhi. Bhikkhussa, bhikkhuno, bhikkhūnaṃ. Bhikkhusmiṃ, bhikkhumhi, bhikkhūsu. Bho bhikkhu, bhavanto bhikkhū, bhikkhave, bhikkhavo. Bhikkhuādīni aññāni ca taṃsadisāni evaṃ ñeyyāni.

Bhikkhu, bhikkhū, bhikkhavo. Bhikkhuṃ, bhikkhū, bhikkhavo. Bhikkhunā, bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūbhi. Bhikkhussa, bhikkhuno, bhikkhūnaṃ. Bhikkhunā, bhikkhusmā, bhikkhumhā, bhikkhūhi, bhikkhūbhi. Bhikkhussa, bhikkhuno, bhikkhūnaṃ. Bhikkhusmiṃ, bhikkhumhi, bhikkhūsu. Bho bhikkhu, bhavanto bhikkhū, bhikkhave, bhikkhavo. Other similar words beginning with 'bhikkhu' should be understood in the same way.

Ayampi [M 0.0251] panettha viseso ñeyyo – hetu, hetū, hetuyo, hetavo. Hetuṃ, hetū, hetuyo, hetavo. Bho hetu, bhavanto hetū, hetave, hetavo. Sesaṃ bhikkhusamaṃ.

Here, too, this special feature should be known—for 'hetu' (cause): hetu, hetū, hetuyo, hetavo. Hetuṃ, hetū, hetuyo, hetavo. Bho hetu, bhavanto hetū, hetave, hetavo. The rest is the same as for 'bhikkhu.'

Atha vā “hetuyā”tiādīnaṃ dassanato “dhenuyā”ti itthiliṅgarūpena sadisaṃ “hetuyā”ti pulliṅgarūpampi sattamīṭhāne icchitabbaṃ. Kānici hi pulliṅgarūpāni kehici itthiliṅgarūpehi sadisāni bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? “Uṭṭhehi katte taramāno. Ehi bālekhamāpehi, kusarājaṃ mahabbalaṃ. Bhātarā mātarā adhipatiyā rattiyā hetuyo dhenuyo matyā petyā”ti evaṃ nayadassanena “hetuyā tīṇi. Adhipatiyā satta. Uṭṭhehi katte”tiādīsu liṅgavipallāsacintā na uppādetabbā.

Alternatively, from the usage of forms like 'hetuyā,' the masculine form 'hetuyā,' which is similar to the feminine form 'dhenuyā,' should also be accepted in the locative case. For some masculine forms are similar to certain feminine forms. For example: 'Uṭṭhehi katte taramāno. Ehi bālekhamāpehi, kusarājaṃ mahabbalaṃ. Bhātarā mātarā adhipatiyā rattiyā hetuyo dhenuyo matyā petyā.' By seeing this method, in cases like 'hetuyā tīṇi,' 'adhipatiyā satta,' and 'uṭṭhehi katte,' one should not raise concerns about gender confusion.

Jantu, jantū, jantuyo, jantuno, jantavo. Jantuṃ, jantū, jantuyo, jantuno, jantavo. Bho jantu, bhavanto jantū, jantave jantavo. Sesaṃ bhikkhusamaṃ.

Jantu, jantū, jantuyo, jantuno, jantavo. Jantuṃ, jantū, jantuyo, jantuno, jantavo. Bho jantu, bhavanto jantū, jantave, jantavo. The rest is the same as for 'bhikkhu.'

Garu, garū, garavo, garuno. Garuṃ, garū, garavo, garuno. Bho garu, bhavanto garū, garavo, garuno. Sesaṃ bhikkhusamaṃ. Ettha pana “bhattu ca garuno sabbe, paṭipūjeti paṇḍitā”tipāḷinidassanaṃ. Tatra “bhikkhave”ti āmantanapadaṃ cuṇṇiyapadesveva dissati, na gāthāsu. “Bhikkhavo”ti paccattapadaṃ gāthāsuyeva dissati, na cuṇṇiyapadesu, apica “bhikkhave”ti āmantanapadaṃ sāvakassa bhikkhūnaṃ āmantanapāḷiyaṃ sandhivisayeyeva dissati, na asandhivisaye, buddhassa pana bhikkhūnaṃ āmantanapāḷiyaṃ sandhivisayepi asandhivisayepi dissati. “Bhikkhavo”ti āmantanapadaṃ buddhassa bhikkhūnaṃ āmantanapāḷiyaṃ gāthāsu ca dissati[M 0.0252], cuṇṇiyapadesu ca sandhivisayeyeva dissati. Sāvakassa pana bhikkhūnaṃ āmantanapāḷiyaṃ na dissatīti ayaṃ dvinnaṃ viseso daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “evañca pana bhikkhave imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyāthā”tiādīsu “bhikkhave”ti padaṃ cuṇṇiyapadesveva diṭṭhaṃ. “Bhikkhavo tisatā ime, yācanti pañjalīkatā”tiādīsu “bhikkhavo”ti paccattapadaṃ gāthāsuyeva diṭṭhaṃ. “Āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi āvuso bhikkhave”ti evamādīsu sāvakassa bhikkhūnaṃ āmantanapāḷīsu sandhivisayeyeva “bhikkhave”ti padaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. “Bhikkhū āmantesi sotukāmattha bhikkhave”ti “idha bhikkhave bhikkhū”tiādīsu pana buddhassa bhikkhūnaṃ āmantanapāḷīsu sandhivisayāvisayesu “bhikkhave”ti padaṃ diṭṭhaṃ. “Araññe rukkhamūle vā, suññāgāreva bhikkhavo”ti “tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi bhikkhavo”ti evamādīsu buddhassa bhikkhūnaṃ āmantanapāḷīsu “bhikkhavo”ti āmantanapadaṃ gāthāsu ca diṭṭhaṃ, cuṇṇiyapadesu ca sandhivisayeyeva diṭṭhaṃ. Iccevaṃ –

Garu, garū, garavo, garuno. Garuṃ, garū, garavo, garuno. Bho garu, bhavanto garū, garavo, garuno. The rest is the same as for 'bhikkhu.' Here, however, is an example from the Pāli canon: 'bhattu ca garuno sabbe, paṭipūjeti paṇḍitā.' Therein, the vocative 'bhikkhave' is seen only in prose passages, not in verses. The nominative 'bhikkhavo' is seen only in verses, not in prose passages. Moreover, the vocative 'bhikkhave' in a disciple's address to the bhikkhus appears only in a context of sandhi, not where there is no sandhi; whereas in the Buddha's address to the bhikkhus, it appears both in contexts with and without sandhi. The vocative 'bhikkhavo' in the Buddha's address to the bhikkhus appears in verses and also in prose passages, but only in a context of sandhi. In a disciple's address to the bhikkhus, however, it does not appear. This distinction between the two should be noted. For example, in passages like 'evañca pana bhikkhave imaṃ sikkhāpadaṃ uddiseyyāthā,' the word 'bhikkhave' is seen only in prose passages. In verses like 'bhikkhavo tisatā ime, yācanti pañjalīkatā,' the nominative 'bhikkhavo' is seen only in verses. In passages like 'Āyasmā Sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi āvuso bhikkhave,' the word 'bhikkhave' in a disciple's address to the bhikkhus is seen only in a context of sandhi. But in passages like 'bhikkhū āmantesi sotukāmattha bhikkhave' or 'idha bhikkhave bhikkhū,' the word 'bhikkhave' in the Buddha's address to the bhikkhus is seen in contexts both with and without sandhi. In verses like 'araññe rukkhamūle vā, suññāgāreva bhikkhavo' or in prose passages like 'tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi bhikkhavo,' the vocative 'bhikkhavo' in the Buddha's address to the bhikkhus is seen in verses and also in prose passages, but only in a context of sandhi. Thus—

Cuṇṇiyeva pade diṭṭhaṃ, “bhikkhave”ti padaṃ dvidhā;

Yato pavattate sandhi-visayāvisayesu taṃ.

The word 'bhikkhave' is seen only in prose passages; it occurs in two ways, that is, in contexts with and without sandhi.

“Bhikkhavo”ti padaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, gāthāyañceva cuṇṇiye;

Padasmimpi ca sandhissa, visayevāti niddiseti.

The word 'bhikkhavo' is seen both in verse and in prose; and in prose passages, it is pointed out to occur only in a context of sandhi.

Savinicchayoyaṃ ukārantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed analysis of the nominal paradigm for regular masculine nouns ending in -u.

Ukārantatāpakatikaṃ ukārantapulliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on regular masculine nouns ending in -u is concluded.

Idāni pana sayambhūiccetassa pakatirūpassa taṃsadisānañca nāmikapadamālaṃ kathayāma –

Now, however, we will explain the nominal paradigm of the regular form 'sayambhū' and of similar words:

Sayambhū[M 0.0253], sayambhū, sayambhuvo. Sayambhuṃ, sayambhū, sayambhuvo. Sayambhunā, sayambhūhi, sayambhūbhi. Sayambhussa, sayambhuno, sayambhūnaṃ. Sayambhunā, sayambhusmā, sayambhumhā, sayambhūhi, sayambhūbhi. Sayambhussa, sayambhuno, sayambhūnaṃ. Sayambhusmiṃ, sayambhumhi, sayambhūsu. Bho sayambhu, bho sayambhū, bhavanto sayambhū, sayambhuvo. Evaṃ pabhū abhibhūvibhū iccādīnipi.

Sayambhū, sayambhū, sayambhuvo. Sayambhuṃ, sayambhū, sayambhuvo. Sayambhunā, sayambhūhi, sayambhūbhi. Sayambhussa, sayambhuno, sayambhūnaṃ.
