Sayambhunā, sayambhusmā, sayambhumhā, sayambhūhi, sayambhūbhi. Sayambhussa, sayambhuno, sayambhūnaṃ. Sayambhusmiṃ, sayambhumhi, sayambhūsu. Bho sayambhu, bho sayambhū, bhavanto sayambhū, sayambhuvo. Likewise for 'pabhū' (lord), 'abhibhū' (conqueror), 'vibhū' (sovereign), and so on.

Sabbaññū, sabbaññū, sabbaññuno. Sabbaññuṃ, sabbaññū, sabbaññuno. Bho sabbaññu, bhavanto sabbaññū, sabbaññuno, sesāsu vibhattīsu padāni bhikkhusadisāni bhavanti, evaṃ vidū viññū kataññū maggaññū dhammaññū atthaññū kālaññū rattaññū mattaññū vadaññū avadaññū iccādīni.

Sabbaññū, sabbaññū, sabbaññuno. Sabbaññuṃ, sabbaññū, sabbaññuno. Bho sabbaññu, bhavanto sabbaññū, sabbaññuno. In the remaining cases, the forms are similar to those for 'bhikkhu.' Likewise for 'vidū' (the wise), 'viññū' (the discerning), 'kataññū' (the grateful), 'maggaññū' (the knower of the path), 'dhammaññū' (the knower of the Dhamma), 'atthaññū' (the knower of the meaning), 'kālaññū' (the knower of time), 'rattaññū' (one of long standing), 'mattaññū' (the knower of measure), 'vadaññū' (the liberal), 'avadaññū' (the illiberal), and so on.

Tatra “ye ca laddhā manussattaṃ, vadaññū vītamaccharā”ti ettha “vadaññū”ti paccattabahuvacanassa dassanato sayambhū sabbaññū iccādīnampi paccattopayogabahuvacanattaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Apica “vidū, viññū”tiādīsu “paracittavidunī”ti itthiliṅgadassanato itthiliṅge vattabbe “vidunī, vidunī, viduniyo. Viduniṃ, vidunī, viduniyo. Viduniyā”ti itthinayena padamālā kātabbā. Tathā “viññū paṭibalā subhāsitadubbhāsitaṃ duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullaṃ ājānitu”nti ettha “viññū”ti itthiliṅgadassanato “kodhanā akataññū ca, pisuṇā mittabhedikā”ti ettha ca “akataññū”ti itthiliṅgadassanatopi “viññū, viññū, viññuyo. Viññuṃ, viññū, viññuyo. Viññuyā”ti ca “kataññū, kataññū, kataññuyo. Kataññuṃ, kataññū, kataññuyo, kataññuyāti ca jambūnayena padamālā kātabbā. Evaṃ “maggaññū, dhammaññū”iccādīsupi. “Sayambhū”ti pade pana [M 0.0254] “sayambhu ñāṇaṃ gotrabhu citta”nti dassanato napuṃsakaliṅgatte vattabbe “sayambhu, sayambhū, sayambhūni. Sayambhuṃ, sayambhū, sayambhūnī”ti napuṃsake āyunayopi gahetabbo. Esa nayo sesesupi yathārahaṃ gahetabbo.

Here, in the phrase 'ye ca laddhā manussattaṃ, vadaññū vītamaccharā' (those who have obtained human birth, are generous and free from stinginess), since 'vadaññū' is seen as a nominative plural, even terms like 'sayambhū' (self-existent) and 'sabbaññū' (all-knowing) should be understood as having nominative and vocative plural forms. Furthermore, in words like 'vidū' and 'viññū' (wise, discerning), since the feminine form 'paracittavidunī' (knower of others’ minds) is seen, when it is to be spoken in the feminine gender, the word paradigm should be formed as 'vidunī, vidunī, viduniyo. Viduniṃ, vidunī, viduniyo. Viduniyā' following the feminine pattern. Similarly, in the phrase 'viññū paṭibalā subhāsitadubbhāsitaṃ duṭṭhullāduṭṭhullaṃ ājānituṃ' (the discerning one is capable of understanding what is well-spoken and ill-spoken, coarse and refined), since 'viññū' is seen in the feminine gender, and in 'kodhanā akataññū ca, pisuṇā mittabhedikā' (angry and ungrateful, slanderous and a breaker of friendships), since 'akataññū' is also seen in the feminine gender, the word paradigms should be formed as: 'viññū, viññū, viññuyo. Viññuṃ, viññū, viññuyo. Viññuyā' and 'kataññū, kataññū, kataññuyo. Kataññuṃ, kataññū, kataññuyo, kataññuyā' following the Jambū pattern. The same applies to terms like 'maggaññū' (knower of the path) and 'dhammaññū' (knower of the Dhamma). In the case of the word 'sayambhū', however, since 'sayambhu ñāṇaṃ gotrabhu cittaṃ' (self-existent knowledge, lineage-consciousness) is seen, when it is to be spoken in the neuter gender, it should be declined as 'sayambhu, sayambhū, sayambhūni. Sayambhuṃ, sayambhū, sayambhūnī' according to the āyu pattern for neuter nouns. This method should be applied to the remaining terms as appropriate.

Savinicchayoyaṃ ūkārantapulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed analysis of the nominal paradigm for regular masculine nouns ending in -ū.

Ūkārantatāpakatikaṃ ūkārantapulliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on regular masculine nouns ending in -ū is concluded.

Iti sabbathāpi pulliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa

Thus, in every way, of the regular form of masculine nouns,

Nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo samatto.

the analysis of the nominal paradigm is complete.

Yasmā panāyaṃ samattopi pāvacanādīsu yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ sotūnaṃ sammuyhanaṭṭhānaṃ dissati, tattha tattha sotūnamanuggahāya codanāsodhanāvasena saṃsayaṃ samugghāṭetvā puna vattabbo hoti, tasmā kiñci padesamettha kathayāma.

Moreover, since even in this complete teaching, in the discourses and so forth, wherever a point is seen that is a place of confusion for the listeners, there, for the sake of assisting the listeners, having dispelled doubt through inquiry and clarification, it should be spoken of again. Therefore, let us explain a certain passage here.

Yaṃ kira bho pāḷiyaṃ “saññate brahmacārayo, apace brahmacārayo”ti ca rūpaṃ ikārantassa aggisaddassa “aggayo”ti rūpamiva vuttaṃ, taṃ tathā avatvā īkārantassa daṇḍīsaddassa “daṇḍino”ti rūpamiva “brahmacārino”icceva vattabbanti? Saccaṃ, tattha “brahmaṃ caratīti brahmacāri yathā munātīti munī”ti evaṃ ikārantavasena icchitattā. “Munayo aggayo”ti rūpāni viya “brahmacārayo”ti rūpaṃ bhavati. Aññattha pana “brahmaṃ caraṇasīloti brahmacārī, yathā dukkaṭaṃ kammaṃ karaṇasīloti dukkaṭakammakārī”ti evaṃ tassīlatthaṃ gahetvā īkārantavasena gahaṇe “dukkaṭakammakārino”ti rūpamiva “daṇḍo assa atthīti daṇḍī”ti īkārantassa saddassa “daṇḍino”ti rūpamiva ca “brahmacārino”ti rūpaṃ bhavati. Tathā hi “ime hi nāma dhammacārino samacārino brahmacārino saccavādino [M 0.0255] sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā paṭijānissantī”ti pāḷi dissati. Evaṃ ikārantavasena “brahmacārayo”ti paccattopayogālapanabahuvacanarūpaṃ yujjati, puna īkārantavasena “brahmacārino”ti paccattopayogālapanabahuvacanarūpampi yujjati, tasmā “brahmacāri, brahmacārī, brahmacārayo”ti agginayena, “brahmacārī, brahmacārī, brahmacārino”ti daṇḍīnayena ca padamālā gahetabbā.

Indeed, sir, in the Pāli, the form in 'saññate brahmacārayo, apace brahmacārayo' is spoken of like the form 'aggayo' of the word 'aggi' ending in 'i'. Instead of saying it thus, should it be said as 'brahmacārino', like the form 'daṇḍino' of the word 'daṇḍī' ending in 'ī'? True. There, because it is intended as ending in 'i' thus: 'one who fares in the Brahma-faring is a brahmacārī, just as one who knows is a munī', the form 'brahmacārayo' occurs, like the forms 'munayo' and 'aggayo'. Elsewhere, however, when taking the meaning of 'one who has the habit of...' thus: 'one who has the habit of faring in the Brahma-faring is a brahmacārī, just as one who has the habit of doing a wrong deed is a dukkaṭakammakārī', and when taking it as ending in 'ī', the form 'brahmacārino' occurs, like the form 'dukkaṭakammakārino' and like the form 'daṇḍino' of the word 'daṇḍī' (one who has a staff) ending in 'ī'. For thus the Pāli is seen: 'ime hi nāma dhammacārino samacārino brahmacārino saccavādino sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā paṭijānissantī'. Thus, as an i-kāranta, the form 'brahmacārayo' is suitable as the nominative, accusative, and vocative plural. Again, as an ī-kāranta, the form 'brahmacārino' is also suitable as the nominative, accusative, and vocative plural. Therefore, the paradigm should be taken according to the 'aggi' pattern as 'brahmacāri, brahmacārī, brahmacārayo', and according to the 'daṇḍī' pattern as 'brahmacārī, brahmacārī, brahmacārino'.

Yaṃ pana āyasmā buddhaghoso “yathā sobhanti yatino, sīlabhūsanabhūsitā”ti ettha yatisaddassa ikārantassa aggisaddassa “aggayo”ti rūpaṃ viya “yatayo”ti rūpaṃ avatvā kasmā īkārantassa daṇḍīsaddassa “daṇḍino”ti rūpaṃ viya “yatino”ti rūpaṃ dasseti. Nanvesā pamādalekhā viya dissati. Yathā hi “kukkuṭā maṇayo daṇḍā sivayo deva te kuddhā”ti pāḷigatiyā upaparikkhiyamānāya “yatayo”ti rūpeneva bhavitabbaṃ ikārantattāti? Nāyaṃ pamādalekhā. “Vadanasīlo vādī”ti ettha viya tassīlatthaṃ gahetvā īkārantavasena yojane niddosattā, tasmā “yatanasīlo yatī”ti evaṃ tassīlatthaṃ cetasi sannidhāya īkārantavasena “yatino”ti sampadānasāmīnamekavacanasadisaṃ paccattabahuvacanarūpaṃ bhadantena buddhaghosena dassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Upayogālapanabahuvacanarūpampi tādisameva.

But why does the Venerable Buddhaghosa, in the phrase 'yathā sobhanti yatino, sīlabhūsanabhūsitā' (as ascetics adorned with the adornment of virtue shine), present the form 'yatino', like the form 'daṇḍino' from the word 'daṇḍī' which ends in 'ī', instead of using the form 'yatayo' like the form 'aggayo' from the word 'aggi' which ends in 'i'? Does this not appear like a careless writing? For, when examining according to the course of Pāli, as in the phrase 'kukkuṭā maṇayo daṇḍā sivayo deva te kuddhā', should it not be the form 'yatayo' since it ends in 'i'? This is not a careless writing. Just as in the phrase 'vadanasīlo vādī' (one who is in the habit of speaking is a speaker), where the meaning of 'having that habit' is taken and the ending 'ī' is used without fault, so too here, having kept the meaning of 'yatanasīlo yatī' (one who is in the habit of striving is an ascetic) in mind, the Venerable Buddhaghosa presents the form 'yatino' with the 'ī' ending as a nominative plural form resembling the dative and genitive singular. The accusative and vocative plural form is also similar.

Yattha pana tassīlatthaṃ aggahetvā “yo munāti ubho loke, muni tena pavuccatī”ti ettha viya “yatati vīriyaṃ karotīti yatī”ti kattukārakavasena ikārantabhāvo gayhati. Tattha “munayo maṇayo sivayo”ti yokārantarūpāni viya “yatayo”ti yokārantaṃ paccattabahuvacanarūpañca [M 0.0256] upayogālapanabahuvacanarūpañca bhavati, evaṃ īkārantapulliṅgānaṃ tīsu ṭhānesu yokārantāneva rūpāni bhavantīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Where, however, without taking the meaning of 'having that habit', as in the phrase 'yo munāti ubho loke, muni tena pavuccatī' (he who understands both worlds is called a muni), the i-ending state is taken in the sense of the agent, as in 'yatati vīriyaṃ karotīti yatī' (one who strives and exerts is called an ascetic). There, just as forms ending in 'yo' like 'munayo, maṇayo, sivayo' occur, so too the nominative plural form and the accusative and vocative plural form 'yatayo' occur. Thus, it should be understood that for masculine nouns ending in 'ī', in these three instances, only forms ending in 'yo' appear.

Yadi evaṃ ikārantapulliṅgānaṃ sāramati suddhadiṭṭhisammādiṭṭhimicchādiṭṭhivajirabuddhi saddādī kathanti? Etesaṃ pana ikārantavasena niddiṭṭhānampi samāsapadattā agginaye aṭṭhatvā yathāsambhavaṃ daṇḍīnaye tiṭṭhanato nokārantāneva rūpāni. Tathā hi “asāre sāramatino”ti nokārantapaccattabahuvacanapāḷi dissati, upayogālapanabahuvacanarūpampi tādisameva daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nanu ca bho kaccāyanappakaraṇe “atthe visāradamatayo”ti ettha samāsapadassa ikārantapulliṅgassa yokārantassa paccattabahuvacanapāṭhassa dassanato sāramatisaddādīnampi “visāradamatayo”ti rūpena viya yokārantehi rūpehi bhavitabbanti? Napi bhavitabbaṃ buddhavacane samāsapadānaṃ ikārantapulliṅgānaṃ “visāradamatayo”ti rūpasadisassa rūpassa adassanatoti.

If so, how are words like sāramati, suddhadiṭṭhi, sammādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhi, vajirabuddhi, and so on, which are masculine nouns ending in 'i', explained? However, even though these are specified as ending in 'i', because they are compound words, they do not follow the 'aggi' pattern, but follow the 'daṇḍī' pattern as appropriate, so their forms only end in 'no'. For instance, the Pāli passage 'asāre sāramatino' shows a nominative plural form ending in 'no'. The accusative and vocative plural form should also be understood as similar. Now, is it not the case that in the Kaccāyana treatise, the phrase 'atthe visāradamatayo' is found? Here, since a compound word, a masculine noun ending in 'i', is seen with a nominative plural reading ending in 'yo', should not words like sāramati also have forms ending in 'yo', just like 'visāradamatayo'? But this should not be, because in the word of the Buddha, no form similar to 'visāradamatayo' is seen for compound masculine nouns ending in 'i'.

Nanu ca bho buddhavacane “pañcime gahapatayo ānisaṃsā. Te honti jānipatayo, aññamaññaṃ piyaṃvadā”ti samāsapadānaṃ ikārantapulliṅgānaṃ “visāradamatayo”ti rūpasadisāni yokārantāni rūpāni dissanti. Evaṃ sante kasmā “buddhavacane samāsapadānaṃ ikārantapulliṅgānaṃ “visāradamatayo”ti rūpasadisassa yokārantassa rūpassa adassanato”ti vuttanti? Ettha vuccate – visadisattaṃ paṭicca. Gahapatisaddādīsu hi yasmā patisaddo sabhāveneva pulliṅgo, na tu samāsato pubbe itthiliṅgapakatiko hutvā pacchā pulliṅgabhāvaṃ patto, tasmā īdisesu ṭhānesu “gahapatayo, jānipatayo”ti yokārantāni, “senāpatayo, senāpatino”ti yo nokārantāni [M 0.0257] ca paccattopayogālapanabahuvacanarūpāni bhavanti. Tathā hi “tattakā senāpatino”ti aṭṭhakathāpāṭho dissati. Yasmā pana sāramati suddhadiṭṭhisammādiṭṭhi micchādiṭṭhi vajirabuddhi saddādīsu matidiṭṭhisaddādayo samāsato pubbe itthiliṅgapakatikā hutvā pacchā bahubbīhisamāsavasena pulliṅgabhāvappattā, tasmā īdisesu ṭhānesu “sāramatino suddhadiṭṭhino sammādiṭṭhino micchādiṭṭhino vajirabuddhino”tiādīni’nokārantāniyeva paccattopayogālapanabahuvacanarūpāni bhavanti, sampadānasāmīnamekavacanehi sadisānīti niṭṭhametthāvagantabbaṃ.

But indeed, sir, in the word of the Buddha, are not forms similar to 'visāradamatayo', ending in 'yo', seen for compound masculine nouns ending in 'i', as in 'pañcime gahapatayo ānisaṃsā. Te honti jānipatayo, aññamaññaṃ piyaṃvadā' (These five are the benefits for householders. They become masters of their wives, speaking affectionately to one another)? If this is so, why was it said, 'because in the word of the Buddha, no form similar to 'visāradamatayo' ending in 'yo' is seen for compound masculine nouns ending in 'i''? Here it is said: on account of dissimilarity. For in words like 'gahapati', the word 'pati' is masculine by its very nature, not having been of a feminine nature before compounding and later having attained a masculine state. Therefore, in such cases, 'yo'-ending forms like 'gahapatayo, jānipatayo', and both 'yo'- and 'no'-ending forms like 'senāpatayo, senāpatino', occur as nominative, accusative, and vocative plural forms. Indeed, the commentary passage 'tattakā senāpatino' is seen. But because in words like 'sāramati', 'suddhadiṭṭhi', 'sammādiṭṭhi', 'micchādiṭṭhi', 'vajirabuddhi', and so on, the words 'mati', 'diṭṭhi', etc., were originally feminine before compounding and later became masculine by means of a bahubbīhi compound, in such cases, only 'no'-ending forms like 'sāramatino, suddhadiṭṭhino, sammādiṭṭhino, micchādiṭṭhino, vajirabuddhino', and so on, occur as nominative, accusative, and vocative plural forms, similar to the dative and genitive singular forms. This conclusion should be understood here.

Seṭṭhi sārathicakkavattisāmiiccetesu kathanti? Ettha pana ayaṃ viseso veditabbo – katthaci pāṭhe “seṭṭhī sārathī cakkavattī sāmī”ti antakkharassa dīghattaṃ dissati, katthaci pana “seṭṭhi sārathi cakkavatti sāmi”iti antakkharassa rassattaṃ dissati. Kiñcāpi rassattametesaṃ dissati, tathāpi tattha tattha paccattavacanādibhāvena “seṭṭhino sārathino”tiādipayogadassanato rassaṃ katvā etāni uccāriyantīti ñāyati, tasmā evaṃ nibbacanattho gahetabbo – seṭṭhaṃ dhanasāraṃ, ṭhānantaraṃ vā assa atthīti seṭṭhī. Assadammādayo sāraṇasīloti sārathī. Cakkaṃ pavattanasīloti cakkavattī. Saṃ etassa atthīti sāmīti. Assatthikatassīlatthasaddā hi nokārantarūpavasena samānagatikā bhavanti yathā “daṇḍino bhūmisāyino”ti. Aparopi nibbacanattho īkārantavasena assadammādayo sāretīti sārathī. Tathā hi “purisadamme sāretīti purisadammasārathī”ti vuttaṃ. Cakkaṃ vattetīti cakkavattī. Evaṃ kattukārakavasena īkārantattaṃ gahetvā katthaci labbhamānampi ikārantattaṃ anapekkhitvā buddhavacanānurūpena “sārathino [M 0.0258] cakkavattino”tiādīni nokārantarūpāni gahetvā daṇḍīnayena yojetabbāni “daṇḍinī”tiādikaṃ vajjitabbaṃ vajjetvā. Evaṃ “seṭṭhino sārathino cakkavattino sāmino”tiādīni nokārantāniyeva rūpāni ñeyyāni.

Regarding the words 'seṭṭhi,' 'sārathi,' 'cakkavatti,' and 'sāmi,' what is the explanation? Herein, this distinction is to be understood: in some readings, the final syllable is seen as long, as in 'seṭṭhī,' 'sārathī,' 'cakkavattī,' 'sāmī'; but in some, the final syllable is seen as short, as in 'seṭṭhi,' 'sārathi,' 'cakkavatti,' 'sāmi.' Although their short form is seen, nevertheless, since in various places usages like 'seṭṭhino,' 'sārathino,' etc., are seen by way of the genitive singular and other case endings, it is known that these are pronounced with a short vowel. Therefore, the etymological meaning is to be taken thus: One has excellent wealth or an eminent position, and is therefore a 'seṭṭhī.' He is accustomed to training horses to be tamed, etc., and is therefore a 'sārathī.' He is accustomed to turning the wheel, and is therefore a 'cakkavattī.' He has ownership, and is therefore a 'sāmī.' For words in the sense of 'possessing that' or 'having that as a habit' have the same declension by way of the -no ending, as in 'daṇḍino,' 'bhūmisāyino.' Another etymological meaning by way of the -ī ending is: he trains horses to be tamed, etc., and is therefore a 'sārathī.' For it is said: 'He trains men to be tamed, and is therefore a trainer of men to be tamed.' He turns the wheel, and is therefore a 'cakkavattī.' Thus, having taken the -ī ending in the agent sense, and disregarding the -i ending which is sometimes found, in accordance with the word of the Buddha, forms such as 'sārathino,' 'cakkavattino,' etc., which have the -no ending, should be construed in the manner of 'daṇḍī,' avoiding what should be avoided, such as 'daṇḍinī.' Thus, forms such as 'seṭṭhino,' 'sārathino,' 'cakkavattino,' 'sāmino' should be known as forms with the -no ending only.

Atra kiñci payogaṃ nidassanamattaṃ kathayāma. “Tāta tayo seṭṭhino amhākaṃ bahūpakārā”ti ca “te katabhattakiccā ‘mahāseṭṭhino mayaṃ gamissāmā’ti vadiṃsū”ti ca “sārathino āhaṃsū”ti ca “dve cakkavattino”ti ca evamādīni. Tattha kiñcāpi katthaci “seṭṭhi sārathi”iccādi rassattapāṭho dissati, tathāpi so sabhāvena rassattabhāvo pāṭho na hoti, dīghassa rassattakaraṇapāṭhoti veditabbo. Padamālā cassa vuttanayena veditabbā.

Here, we will state some usages for the sake of illustration: 'Dear father, these three merchants are of great help to us'; and 'Having finished their meal, they said, "We great merchants will go"'; and 'The charioteers said'; and 'Two wheel-turning monarchs,' and so on. Therein, although in some places a reading with short vowels such as 'seṭṭhi,' 'sārathi' is seen, that reading is not naturally short; it should be understood as a reading that makes a long vowel short. And its paradigm should be known according to the method stated.

Mahesīti ettha kathanti? “Mahesī”ti ettha kiñcāpi mahesīsaddo īkārantavasena niddisiyati, tathāpi isisaddena samānagatikattā isisaddassa aggisaddena samānapadamālattā agginayena padamālā kātabbā. Nanu ca bho ettha tassīlattho dissati “mahante sīlakkhandhādayo dhamme esanasīloti mahesī”ti, tasmā “bhūmisāyī”ti padassa viya daṇḍīnayeneva padamālā kātabbāti? Na kātabbā tassīlatthassa asambhavato. Imassa hi “mahante sīlakkhandhādayo dhamme esi gavesi esitvā ṭhitoti mahesī”ti atassīlattho eva yujjati. Katakaraṇīyesu buddhādīsu ariyesu pavattanāmattā. Isisaddena cāyaṃ saddo īsakaṃ samāno kevalaṃ samāsapariyosāne dīghavasena uccāriyati, rassavasena pana “mahā isi mahesī”ti sandhiviggaho[M 0.0259]. Yasmā rassattaṃ gahetvā tassa padamālākaraṇaṃ yujjati, tasmā “saṅgāyiṃsu mahesayo”ti ikārantarūpaṃ dissati. Na hi sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane katthacipi catutthīchaṭṭhekavacanarūpaṃ viya “mahesino”ti paccattopayogālapanabahuvacanarūpaṃ dissati. Tasmā īkārantavasena uccāritassapi sato rassavasena uccāritassa viya “mahesi, mahesī, mahesayo. Mahesiṃ, mahesī, mahesayo. Mahesinā”ti padamālā kātabbā. Apica mahesīsaddo yattha rājaggubbarivācako, tattha itthiliṅgo hoti, tabbasena pana “mahesī, mahesī, mahesiyo. Mahesiṃ, mahesī, mahesiyo. Mahesiyā”ti ca vakkhamānaitthīnayena padamālā kātabbā. Hatthīsadde kathanti? Hatthīsaddassa pana hattho assa atthīti evaṃ īkārantavasena gahaṇe “hatthino”ti rūpaṃ bhavati. Tathā hi “vane hatthino”ti payogo dissati. Tasseva tasmiṃyevatthe rassaṃ katvā gahaṇe “hatthayo”ti rūpaṃ bhavati. Tathā hi –

Regarding 'mahesī,' what is the explanation? Here, although the word 'mahesī' is stated as ending in -ī, still, because it has the same declension as the word 'isi,' and because the word 'isi' has the same paradigm as the word 'aggi,' its paradigm should be formed in the manner of 'aggi.' But, sir, is not the sense of 'having that as a habit' seen here, as in 'he is accustomed to seeking the great qualities, such as the aggregates of virtue; therefore he is a 'mahesī''? Therefore, should not the paradigm be formed in the manner of 'daṇḍī,' like the word 'bhūmisāyī'? It should not be formed so, because the sense of 'having that as a habit' is impossible. For this word, the meaning 'he sought, searched for, and stood firm after seeking the great qualities, such as the aggregates of virtue; therefore he is a 'mahesī'' is suitable, which is not the sense of 'having that as a habit.' This is because it is merely a name applied to noble ones such as the Buddha, who have done what was to be done. And this word is slightly similar to 'isi,' being pronounced with a long vowel only at the end of a compound. With a short vowel, however, the analysis of the compound is 'mahā isi,' a great seer. Since it is suitable to form its paradigm by taking the short form, the -i ending form 'mahesayo' is seen in 'saṅgāyiṃsu mahesayo.' Indeed, nowhere in the Tipiṭaka with its commentary, the word of the Buddha, is a form like 'mahesino'—like the dative or genitive singular, or the nominative, vocative, or accusative plural—found. Therefore, although it is pronounced with an -ī ending, its paradigm should be formed as if it were pronounced with a short vowel, thus: 'mahesi, mahesī, mahesayo. Mahesiṃ, mahesī, mahesayo. Mahesinā,' etc. Moreover, when the word 'mahesī' denotes a queen, it is feminine. In that case, its paradigm should be formed in the manner of the feminine nouns to be discussed later, thus: 'mahesī, mahesī, mahesiyo. Mahesiṃ, mahesī, mahesiyo. Mahesiyā,' etc. What is the explanation for the word 'hatthī'? When the word 'hatthī' is taken as ending in -ī in the sense of 'it has a trunk,' the form 'hatthino' occurs. For the usage 'hatthino in the forest' is seen. When the same word in the same sense is taken having been made short, the form 'hatthayo' occurs. For example:

“Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā ca, hatthayo pasadā migā;

Sabbe sīhassa bhāyanti, natthi kāyasmi tulyatā.

Swans, herons, and peacocks, elephants and spotted deer; all are afraid of the lion; there is no equality in physical stature.

Evameva manussesu, daharo cepi paññavā;

Sopi tattha mahā hoti, neva bālo sarīravā”ti

Just so among human beings, even if one is young, if he is wise, he is great among them; but not the fool, though he has a large body.

Imasmiṃ keḷisīlajātake “hatthayo”ti āhaccapadaṃ dissati. Evamassa daṇḍīnayena ca agginayena ca dvidhā padamālā, veditabbā. Iminā nayena avuttesupi ṭhānesu pāḷinayānurūpena [M 0.0260] porāṇaṭṭhakathānurūpena ca padamālā yojetabbā.

In this Keḷisīlajātaka, the word 'hatthayo' is seen as an exceptional usage. Thus, its paradigm should be known in two ways: in the manner of 'daṇḍī' and in the manner of 'aggi.' By this method, even in cases not mentioned, the paradigm should be construed in accordance with the method of the Pāli texts and in accordance with the ancient commentaries.

Ettāvatā bhūdhātumayānaṃ pulliṅgānaṃ nāmikapadamālā saddhiṃ liṅgantarehi saddantarehi atthantarehi ca nānappakārato dassitā.

Thus far, the nominal paradigm of masculine substantive nouns has been shown in various ways, together with other genders, other word-endings, and other meanings.

Imaṃ saddanītiṃ sunītiṃ vicittaṃ,

Sapaññehi sammā parīpālanīyaṃ;

Sadā suṭṭhu cinteti vāceti yo so,

Naro ñāṇavitthinnataṃ yāti seṭṭhaṃ.

This Saddanīti, well-ordered and variegated, should be rightly guarded by the wise; whatever person constantly reflects on it and recites it well, he attains the supreme vastness of knowledge.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the ways of expression concerning the nine-limbed scriptures with their commentaries and the Tipiṭaka,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the treatise Saddanīti, made for the purpose of their skill,

Savinicchayo niggahītantādipulliṅgānaṃ

The Analysis of Masculine Nouns ending in a Nasal, -ant, etc.

Pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo

The Division of the Nominal Paradigm of the Natural Form.

Sattamo paricchedo.

The Seventh Chapter.

Sabbathāpi pulliṅgaṃ samattaṃ.

The masculine gender is in every way completed.

8. Itthiliṅganāmikapadamālā

8. The Nominal Paradigm of Feminine Nouns

Atha itthiliṅgesu ākārantassa bhūdhātumayassa pakatirūpabhūtassa bhāvikāsaddassa nāmikapadamālāyaṃ vattabbāyampi pasiddhassa tāva kaññāsaddassa nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma –

Now, among feminine nouns, although the declension of the noun 'bhāvikā'—an ā-stem, a substantive noun, and a natural form—is to be explained, we will first explain the declension of the well-known noun 'kaññā'.

Kaññā, kaññā, kaññāyo. Kaññaṃ, kaññā, kaññāyo. Kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi. Kaññāya, kaññānaṃ. Kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi. Kaññāya, kaññānaṃ. Kaññāya, kaññāyaṃ, kaññāsu. Bhoti kaññe, bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo. Ayamamhākaṃ ruci.

Kaññā, kaññā, kaññāyo. Kaññaṃ, kaññā, kaññāyo. Kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi. Kaññāya, kaññānaṃ. Kaññāya, kaññāhi, kaññābhi. Kaññāya, kaññānaṃ. Kaññāya, kaññāyaṃ, kaññāsu. Bhoti kaññe, bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo. This is our preference.

Ettha [M 0.0261] “kaññā”ti ekavacanabahuvacanavasena vuttaṃ, niruttipiṭake bahuvacanavasena vutto nayo natthi. Tathā hi tattha “saddhā tiṭṭhati, saddhāyo tiṭṭhanti. Saddhaṃ passati, saddhāyo passatī”ti ettakameva vuttaṃ, “saddhā”ti bahuvacanaṃ na āgataṃ. Kiñcāpi nāgataṃ, tathāpi “bāhā paggayha pakkanduṃ, sivikaññā samāgatā. Ahetu appaccayā purisassa saññā uppajjantipi nirujjhantipī”tiādipāḷidassanato bāhākaññā saññāsaddādīnaṃ bahuvacanatā gahetabbā. Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ “bhoti kaññe, bhoti kaññā”ti dve ekavacanāni vatvā “bhotiyo kaññāyo”ti ekaṃ bahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Niruttipiṭake pana “bhoti saddhā”ti ekavacanaṃ vatvā “bhotiyo saddhāyo”ti ekaṃ bahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Mayaṃ panettha “ehi bāle khamāpehi, kusarājaṃ mahabbalaṃ. Phussatī varavaṇṇābhe. Ehi godhe nivattassū”tiādipāḷidassanato “bhoti kaññe, bhotiyo kaññā, kaññāyo”ti evaṃpakārāniyeva ālapanekavacanabahuvacanāni icchāma. Ettha “bhoti kaññe”ti ayaṃ nayo ammādīsu mātādīsu ca na labbhati.

Here, the form 'kaññā' is stated for both singular and plural, but in the Niruttipiṭaka, the rule for the plural form 'kaññā' is not given. For there, only this much is stated: 'Saddhā tiṭṭhati' (Faith stands), 'saddhāyo tiṭṭhanti' (Faiths stand); 'Saddhaṃ passati' (He sees faith), 'saddhāyo passati' (He sees faiths). The plural form 'saddhā' does not appear. Although it does not appear, nevertheless, from seeing Pāli passages such as: 'Having raised their arms (bāhā), they cried out'; 'The young women (kaññā) of the palanquin gathered'; and 'Without cause or condition, a man's perceptions (saññā) arise and cease,' the plurality of nouns such as bāhā, kaññā, and saññā should be accepted. In the Cūḷanirutti, having stated two singulars, 'bhoti kaññe' and 'bhoti kaññā,' one plural 'bhotiyo kaññāyo' is stated. But in the Niruttipiṭaka, having stated the singular 'bhoti saddhā,' one plural 'bhotiyo saddhāyo' is stated. Here, from seeing Pāli passages such as: 'Come, foolish one (bāle), ask forgiveness from the mighty king Kusa'; 'O Phussatī of excellent complexion (varavaṇṇābhe)!'; 'Come, iguana (godhe), turn back!,' we prefer just such vocative singular and plural forms as 'bhoti kaññe,' 'bhotiyo kaññā,' and 'kaññāyo.' Here, this rule for 'bhoti kaññe' is not found for nouns like 'ammā,' 'mātā,' etc.

Bhāvikā, bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo. Bhāvikaṃ, bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāhi, bhāvikābhi. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikānaṃ. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāhi, bhāvikābhi. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikānaṃ. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāyaṃ, bhāvikāsu. Bhoti bhāvike, bhotiyo bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo.

Bhāvikā, bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo. Bhāvikaṃ, bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāhi, bhāvikābhi. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikānaṃ. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāhi, bhāvikābhi. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikānaṃ. Bhāvikāya, bhāvikāyaṃ, bhāvikāsu. Bhoti bhāvike, bhotiyo bhāvikā, bhāvikāyo.

Evaṃ heṭṭhuddiṭṭhānaṃ sabbesaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ “bhāvanā vibhāvanā”iccevamādīnaṃākārantapadānaṃ aññesañcākārantapadānaṃ nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Etthaññāni ākārantapadāni nāma saddhādīni.

Thus, the declension of nouns should be applied for all the below-mentioned nouns ending in -ā that are derived from the root 'bhū', such as 'bhāvanā', 'vibhāvanā', etc., and for other nouns ending in -ā. Here, the other nouns ending in -ā are 'saddhā' and so on.

Saddhā [M 0.0262] medhā paññā vijjā, cintā mantā taṇhā’bhijjhā;

Icchā pucchā jāyā māyā, mettā mattā sikkhā saṅkhā.

Faith, intelligence, wisdom, knowledge, thought, counsel, craving, covetousness; wish, question, wife, illusion, loving-kindness, measure, training, enumeration.

Jaṅghā bāhā gīvā jivhā, vācā chāyā gaṅgā nāvā;

Niddā kantā sālā mālā, velā vīṇā bhikkhā lākhā.

Shin, arm, neck, tongue, speech, shadow, the Ganges, boat; sleep, beloved woman, hall, garland, time, lute, alms-food, lac.

Gāthā senā lekhā’pekkhā, āsā pūjā esā kaṅkhā;

Aññā muddā khiḍḍā bhassā, bhāsā kīḷā sattā cetā.

Verse, army, letter, expectation, hope, homage, seeking, doubt; other woman, seal, amusement, chatter, language, sport, attachment, volition.

Pipāsā vedanā saññā, cetanā tasiṇā pajā;

Devatā vaṭṭakā godhā, balākā vasudhā sabhā.

Thirst, feeling, perception, volition, craving, offspring; deity, quail, iguana, crane, the earth, assembly.

Ukkā sephālikā sikkā, salākā vālikā sikhā;

Kāraṇā visikhā sākhā, vacā vañjhā jaṭā ghaṭā.

Torch, jasmine, carrying-net, ticket, sand, crest; cause, street, branch, sweet flag, barren woman, matted hair, throng.

Pīḷā soṇḍā vitaṇḍā ca, karuṇā vanitā latā;

Kathā nindā sudhā rādhā, vāsanā siṃsapā papā.

Oppression, elephant's trunk, sophistry, and compassion, woman, creeper; talk, blame, nectar, success, latent impression, rosewood tree, water-stall.

Pabhā sīmā khamā ejā,

Khattiyā sakkharā surā;

Dolā tulā silā līlā,

Lāle’ḷā mekhalā kalā.

Lustre, boundary, patience, craving; noblewoman, gravel, liquor; swing, scales, stone, grace; saliva, cardamom, girdle, art.

Vaḷavā suṇisā mūsā, mañjūsā sulasā disā;

Nāsā juṇhā guhā īhā, lasikā parisā nisā;

Mātikiccādayo ceva, bhāvikāpadasādisā.

Mare, daughter-in-law, crucible, casket, Sulasā, direction; nose, moonlight, cave, striving, synovial fluid, assembly, night; 'Mātikā' and so on are also similar to the noun 'bhāvikā'.

Ammannambā ca tātā ca, kiñcideva samā siyuṃ;

Mātā dhītā panattādī, puthageva ito siyuṃ.

The words 'ammā,' 'ambā,' and 'tātā' would be somewhat similar; but 'mātā,' 'dhītā,' 'panattā,' and so on would be different from this.

Parisāsaddassa pana sattamīṭhāne “parisāya, parisāyaṃ, parisati, parisāsū”ti yojetabbaṃ “ekamidaṃ bho gotama samayaṃ todeyyassa brāhmaṇassa parisati parūpārambhaṃ vattentī”ti pāḷidassanato. Ammādīnaṃ pana “ammā, ammā, ammāyo”tiādinā [M 0.0263] kaññānayena vatvā avasāne “bhoti amma, bhoti ammā, bhotiyo ammā, ammāyo”tiādinā yojetabbaṃ.

For the noun 'parisā,' in the locative case, it should be formed as 'parisāya, parisāyaṃ, parisati, parisāsu,' as seen from the Pāli passage: 'Once, Master Gotama, in the assembly (parisati) of the brahmin Todeyya, a discussion involving verbal attacks on others was taking place.' For nouns like 'ammā,' etc., having declined them according to the 'kaññā' model as 'ammā, ammā, ammāyo,' etc., at the end the vocative forms 'bhoti amma, bhoti ammā, bhotiyo ammā, ammāyo,' etc., should be applied.

Mātā, mātā, mātaro. Mātaraṃ, mātaro. Mātarā, mātuyā, matyā, mātūhi, mātūbhi. Mātu, mātuyā, matyā, mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ. Mātarā, mātuyā, matyā, mātūhi, mātūbhi. Mātu, mātuyā, matyā, mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ. Mātari, mātuyā, matyā, mātuyaṃ, matyaṃ, mātūsu. Bhoti mātā, bhotiyo mātā, mātaro.

Mātā, mātā, mātaro. Mātaraṃ, mātaro. Mātarā, mātuyā, matyā, mātūhi, mātūbhi. Mātu, mātuyā, matyā, mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ. Mātarā, mātuyā, matyā, mātūhi, mātūbhi. Mātu, mātuyā, matyā, mātarānaṃ, mātānaṃ, mātūnaṃ. Mātari, mātuyā, matyā, mātuyaṃ, matyaṃ, mātūsu. Bhoti mātā, bhotiyo mātā, mātaro.

Ettha pana yasmā pāḷiyaṃ itthiliṅgānaṃ sakārantāni rūpāni ehi ebhi esukārantādīni ca enantādīni ca na dissanti, tasmā kehici vuttānipi “mātussa mātarehī”tiādīni na vuttāni, esa nayo itaresupi. “Yaṃkiñcitthikataṃ puññaṃ, mayhañca mātuyā ca te. Anuññāto ahaṃ matyā”ti pāḷidassanato pana karaṇasampadānanissakkasāmibhummavacanaṭṭhāne “mātuyā, matyā”ti ca vuttaṃ itthiliṅgaṭṭhāne samānagatikattā tesaṃ vacanānaṃ. Tathā hi ummādantijātake “matyā”ti padaṃ pañcamītatiyekavacanavasena āgataṃ, yathā pana “khattiyā”ti padaṃ majjhasaralopavasena “khatyā”ti bhavati, tathā “mātuyā mātuya”nti ca padaṃ “matyā, matya”nti bhavati, ayaṃ nayo dhītusaddādīsu na labbhati.

Here, however, since in Pāli feminine nouns, forms with the genitive singular ending -sa, and forms with endings such as -ehi, -ebhi, -esu, and -ena are not seen, we have not stated forms like 'mātussa,' 'mātarehi,' etc., although they are stated by some. This principle applies to other nouns as well. However, from the Pāli passage, 'Whatever merit has been made by a woman, by me and by your mother (mātuyā)'; and 'I have been permitted by my mother (matyā),' it is seen that the forms 'mātuyā' and 'matyā' are stated for the instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive, and locative cases, because of the similar formation of these cases for feminine nouns. Thus, in the Ummādantī Jātaka, the word 'matyā' appears as the ablative and instrumental singular. Just as the word 'khattiyā' becomes 'khatyā' by eliding the middle vowel, so too the words 'mātuyā' and 'mātuya' become 'matyā' and 'matya.' This rule is not found for nouns like 'dhītu,' etc.

Dhītā, dhītā, dhītaro. Dhītaṃ, dhītaraṃ, dhītaro. Dhītuyā, dhītūhi, dhītūbhi. Dhītu, dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītarā, dhītuyā, dhītūhi, dhītūbhi. Dhītu, dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītari, dhītuyā, dhītuyaṃ, dhītūsu. Bhoti dhītu, bhoti dhītā, bhotiyo dhītā, dhītaro. Ettha pana.

Dhītā, dhītā, dhītaro. Dhītaṃ, dhītaraṃ, dhītaro. Dhītuyā, dhītūhi, dhītūbhi. Dhītu, dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītarā, dhītuyā, dhītūhi, dhītūbhi. Dhītu, dhītuyā, dhītarānaṃ, dhītānaṃ, dhītūnaṃ. Dhītari, dhītuyā, dhītuyaṃ, dhītūsu. Bhoti dhītu, bhoti dhītā, bhotiyo dhītā, dhītaro. Here, however:

“Jāliṃ [M 0.0264] kaṇhājinaṃ dhītaṃ, maddideviṃ patibbataṃ;

Cajamāno na cintesiṃ, bodhiyāyeva kāraṇā”ti

'Giving away Jāli, my daughter Kaṇhājinā, and my devoted wife Queen Maddī, I did not hesitate, for the sake of enlightenment alone.'

Pāḷiyaṃ “dhīta”nti dassanato upayogavacanaṭṭhāne “dhīta”nti vuttaṃ, tasmā idaṃ sārato gahetabbaṃ, tathā pāḷiyaṃ “assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā”ti samāsapadassa dassanato tatiyekavacanantapadasadisaṃ “seṭṭhidhītarā”tiādikaṃ paṭhamekavacanantampi samāsapadaṃ gahetabbameva, niruttipiṭake pana “mātā dhītā”ti padadvayaṃ saddhānaye pakkhitta, tamamhehi “saddhāyā”ti padassa viya “mātāyā”tiādīnaṃ pāḷiādīsu byāse adassanato visuṃ gahitaṃ samāseyeva hi īdisiṃ saddagatiṃ passāma “rājamātāya rājadhītāya seṭṭhidhītāyā”ti. Evaṃ kaññānayopi ekadesena labbhati, tathā “acchariyaṃ nandamāte, abbhutaṃ nandamāte”ti pāḷiyaṃ “nandamāte”ti dassanato “bhoti rājamāte, bhoti rājadhīte”ti evamādinayopi labbhati, tatra nandamāteti nandassa mātā nandamātā, bhoti nandamāte, evaṃ samāseyeva īdisī saddagati hoti, tasmā samāsapadatte “mātu dhītu duhitu”iccetesaṃ pakatirūpānaṃ dve koṭṭhāsā gahetabbā paṭhamaṃ dassitarūpakoṭṭhāso ca kaññānayo rūpakoṭṭhāso cāti. Nattādīni padāni na kevalaṃ pulliṅgāniyeva honti, atha kho itthiliṅgānipi. Tathā hi “visākhāya nattā kālaṅkatā hoti. Catasso mūsikā gādhaṃ kattā, no vasitā”tiādīni payogāni sāsane dissanti.

In the Pāli, the form 'dhītaṃ' is stated in the accusative case; therefore, this should be taken as the essential point. Similarly, from seeing the compound word in the Pāli 'assamaṇī hoti asakyadhītarā' (she is not a nun, not a daughter of the Sakyans), a nominative singular compound like 'seṭṭhidhītarā,' which is similar to a word ending in the instrumental singular, should also be accepted. In the Niruttipiṭaka, however, the two nouns 'mātā' and 'dhītā' are included in the 'saddhā' paradigm. We have treated them separately because an uncompounded form like 'mātāya,' similar to the word 'saddhāya,' is not seen in Pāli and other texts. Indeed, we see such word-formations only in compounds, such as 'rājamātāya,' 'rājadhītāya,' 'seṭṭhidhītāya.' Thus, the 'kaññā' paradigm is also partially found. Likewise, in the Pāli passage 'acchariyaṃ nandamāte, abbhutaṃ nandamāte' (wonderful, mother of Nanda; marvelous, mother of Nanda), from the use of 'nandamāte,' rules for forms such as 'bhoti rājamāte,' 'bhoti rājadhīte' are also found. Here, 'nandamātā' means 'Nanda's mother,' and its vocative is 'bhoti nandamāte.' Such a word-formation occurs only in compounds. Therefore, when they are compound words, two sets of paradigms should be accepted for the base forms 'mātu,' 'dhītu,' 'duhitu': the set of forms shown first, and the set of forms following the 'kaññā' paradigm. Nouns like 'nattā' are not only masculine but also feminine. For in the scriptures, usages like 'Visākhā's granddaughter (nattā) has died' and 'Four female mice were the makers (kattā) of the hole, not the dwellers (vasitā)' are seen.

Nattā, nattā, nattāro. Nattaṃ, nattāraṃ, nattāro. Nattārā, nattuyā, nattūhi, nattūbhi. Nattu, nattuyā, nattārānaṃ [M 0.0265] nattānaṃ, nattūnaṃ. Nattārā, nattuyā, nattūhi, nattūbhi. Nattu, nattuyā, nattārānaṃ, nattānaṃ, nattūnaṃ. Nattari, nattuyā, nattuyaṃ, nattūsu. Bhoti natta, bhoti nattā, bhotiyo nattā, nattāro.

Nattā, nattā, nattāro. Nattaṃ, nattāraṃ, nattāro. Nattārā, nattuyā, nattūhi, nattūbhi. Nattu, nattuyā, nattārānaṃ, nattānaṃ, nattūnaṃ. Nattārā, nattuyā, nattūhi, nattūbhi. Nattu, nattuyā, nattārānaṃ, nattānaṃ, nattūnaṃ. Nattari, nattuyā, nattuyaṃ, nattūsu. Bhoti natta, bhoti nattā, bhotiyo nattā, nattāro.

Evaṃ “kattā vasitā bhāsitā” iccādīsupi samāsapadatte pana “rājamātāya nandamāte”tiādīni viya “rājanattāya, rājanatte”tiādīni rūpāni bhavanti.

Thus, also for nouns like 'kattā,' 'vasitā,' 'bhāsitā,' etc., when they are part of a compound, forms like 'rājanattāya,' 'rājanatte,' etc., occur, similar to forms like 'rājamātāya,' 'nandamāte,' etc.

Savinicchayoyaṃ ākārantukārantitthiliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the determination of the classification of the nominal word paradigm for ā-ending and u-ending feminine nouns in their natural form.

Ākārantukārantatāpakatikaṃ

The section on natural ā-ending and u-ending nouns.

Ākārantitthiliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The feminine nouns ending in ā are completed.

Idāni bhūmipadādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā –

Now we will explain the nominal paradigm for words beginning with 'bhūmi,' having made the opinion of the ancient teachers our guide—

Ratti, rattī, rattiyo. Rattiṃ, rattī, rattiyo. Rattiyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, rattiyaṃ, rattīsu. Bhoti ratti, bhotiyo rattiyo. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

Ratti, rattī, rattiyo. Rattiṃ, rattī, rattiyo. Rattiyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, rattiyaṃ, rattīsu. Bhoti ratti, bhotiyo rattiyo. The opinion of the great elder Yamaka.

“Bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo. Bhūmiṃ, bhūmī, bhūmiyo”ti sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. Evaṃ “bhūti satti patti vutti mutti kitti khanti titti siddhi iddhi vuddhi suddhi buddhi bodhi pīti nandi mati asani vasani sati gati vuḍḍhi yuvati aṅguli bondi diṭṭhi tuṭṭhi nābhi” iccādīnampi nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Apica “ratyo amoghā gacchanti. Divā ca ratto ca haranti ye baliṃ. Na bhūmyā caturaṅgulo. Seti bhūmyā anutthunaṃ. Bhūmyā so patitaṃ pāsaṃ. Gīvāya paṭimuñcati. Imā ca nabhyo satarājicittitā. Sateratā vijjurivappabhāsare”ti evamādīnaṃ [M 0.0266] payogānaṃ dassanato ratti bhūmi nābhisaddādīnaṃ ayampi nāmikapadamālāviseso veditabbo. Kathaṃ?

"'Bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo. Bhūmiṃ, bhūmī, bhūmiyo'—all should be understood thus. Similarly, the nominal declension series for words like 'bhūti' (existence), 'satti' (power), 'patti' (attainment), 'vutti' (conduct), 'mutti' (release), 'kitti' (fame), 'khanti' (patience), 'titti' (satisfaction), 'siddhi' (success), 'iddhi' (psychic power), 'vuddhi' (growth), 'suddhi' (purity), 'buddhi' (wisdom), 'bodhi' (enlightenment), 'pīti' (joy), 'nandi' (delight), 'mati' (thought), 'asani' (thunderbolt), 'vasani' (dwelling), 'sati' (mindfulness), 'gati' (destination), 'vuḍḍhi' (increase), 'yuvati' (young woman), 'aṅguli' (finger), 'bondi' (body), 'diṭṭhi' (view), 'tuṭṭhi' (contentment), 'nābhi' (navel), and so on, should be applied. Moreover, from observing such usages as 'Nights pass not in vain,' 'By day and by night, they carry away those who offer oblations,' 'Not even four fingers on the ground,' 'He lies on the ground without lamenting,' 'He releases from his neck the snare that has fallen to the ground,' and 'And these navels, adorned with a hundred lines, resplendent like flashing lightning,' this special nominal declension series for words like 'night,' 'earth,' 'navel,' etc., should also be understood. How?

Ratti, rattī, rattiyo, ratyo. Rattiṃ, rattī, rattiyo, ratyo. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattiyaṃ ratyaṃ, ratto, rattīsu. Bhoti ratti, bhotiyo rattī, rattiyo, ratyo.

Ratti, rattī, rattiyo, ratyo. Rattiṃ, rattī, rattiyo, ratyo. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīhi, rattībhi. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattīnaṃ. Rattiyā, ratyā, rattiyaṃ, ratyaṃ, ratto, rattīsu. Bhoti ratti, bhotiyo rattī, rattiyo, ratyo.

Ettha “ratto”ti rūpanayaṃ vajjetvā “bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo, bhūmyo”ti sabbaṃ neyyaṃ.

Here, excluding the form 'ratto,' all should be understood as 'bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo, bhūmyo.'

Nābhi, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. Nābhiṃ, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhiyaṃ, nabhyaṃ, nābhīsu. Bhoti nābhi, bhotiyo nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo.

Nābhi, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. Nābhiṃ, nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīhi, nābhībhi. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhīnaṃ. Nābhiyā, nabhyā, nābhiyaṃ, nabhyaṃ, nābhīsu. Bhoti nābhi, bhotiyo nābhī, nābhiyo, nabhyo.

Bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho. Bodhiṃ, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi, bodhībhi. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi, bodhībhi. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhīsu. Bhoti bodhi, bhotiyo bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho.

Bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho. Bodhiṃ, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi, bodhībhi. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīhi, bodhībhi. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhīnaṃ. Bodhiyā, bojjhā, bodhiyaṃ, bojjhaṃ, bodhīsu. Bhoti bodhi, bhotiyo bodhī, bodhiyo, bojjho.

Ettha pana “bujjhassu jina bodhiyaṃ. Aññatra bojjhā tapasā”ti vicitrapāḷinayadassanato vicitranayā nāmikapadamālā vuttā. Sabbopi cāyaṃ nayo aññatthāpi yathārahaṃ yojetabbo.

Here, however, from observing the varied methods in the Pāli texts, such as 'Awaken, O Conqueror, to enlightenment!' and 'Apart from enlightenment, by austerity,' a varied nominal declension series has been stated. And all these methods should be applied elsewhere as appropriate.

Savinicchayoyaṃ ikārantitthiliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed classification of the nominal declension series for the natural forms of i-ending feminine nouns.

Ikārantatāpakatikaṃ ikārantitthiliṅgaṃ

I-ending feminine nouns with regular declension.

Niṭṭhitaṃ.

Finished.

Idāni [M 0.0267] bhūrīsaddādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā –

Now, having made the opinion of the ancient teachers our guide, we will explain the nominal declension series for words like 'bhūrī' and so on—

Itthī, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiṃ, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībhi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ. Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībhi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ. Itthiyā, itthiyaṃ, itthīsu. Bhoti itthi, bhotiyo itthiyo. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

Itthī, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiṃ, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībhi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ. Itthiyā, itthīhi, itthībhi. Itthiyā, itthīnaṃ. Itthiyā, itthiyaṃ, itthīsu. Bhoti itthi, bhotiyo itthiyo. The opinion of the great elder Yamaka.

“Bhūrī, bhūrī, bhūriyo. Bhūriṃ, bhūrī, bhūri yo”ti itthiyā samaṃ. Evaṃ bhūtī bhotī vibhāvinī iccādīnaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ aññesañca īkārantasaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Etthaññe īkārantasaddā nāma –

'Bhūrī, bhūrī, bhūriyo. Bhūriṃ, bhūrī, bhūriyo'—thus it is similar to 'woman'. In this way, the nominal declension series should be applied to words like 'bhūtī,' 'bhotī,' 'vibhāvinī,' etc., which are formed from the root 'bhū,' and to other ī-ending words. Here, other ī-ending words are—

“Mātulānī ca bhaginī, bhikkhunī sāmugī ajī;

Vāpī pokkharaṇī devī, nāgī yakkhinī rājinī.

'Aunt and sister, nun, Sāmugī, she-goat; Pond, lotus pond, goddess, female serpent, female spirit, queen.'

Dāsī ca brāhmaṇī muṭṭha-ssatinī sīghayāyinī;

Sākiyānī”ti cādīni, payogāni bhavanti hi.

'Slave woman and brahmin woman, forgetful and swift-moving; And words like 'Sākiyānī' and so on are indeed usages.'

Tatra “pokkharaṇī dāsī, brāhmaṇi”ccādinaṃ gati;

Aññathāpi siyā gāthā-cuṇṇiyesu yathārahaṃ.

In this regard, the usage of words like 'pokkharaṇī,' 'dāsī,' 'brāhmaṇī,' and so on, is to be understood. Alternatively, it may occur in verses and prose passages as appropriate.

“Kusāvatī”tiādīnaṃ, gāthāsveva visesato;

Rūpāni aññathā honti, ekavacanato vade.

For words like 'Kusāvatī' and so on, especially in verses, the forms are different when one speaks in the singular.

“Kāsī avantī”iccādī, bahuvacanato vade;

“Candavatī”tiādīni, payogassānurūpato.

Words like 'Kāsī,' 'Avantī,' and so on, should be spoken in the plural; words like 'Candavatī' and so on, according to the suitability of usage.

Tathā hi “pokkharañño sumāpitā. Tā ca sattasatā bhariyā, dāsyo sattasatāni ca. Dārake ca ahaṃ nessaṃ[M 0.0268], brāhmaṇyā paricārake. Najjo sandanti. Najjā nerañjarāya tīre. Lakkhyā bhava nivesanaṃ.

For indeed: 'The lotus ponds were well made.' 'And those seven hundred wives, and seven hundred female slaves.' 'And I will lead the boys, attendants of the brahmin woman.' 'Rivers flow.' 'On the bank of the Nerañjarā River.' 'Let the dwelling be marked by a sign.'

Bārāṇasyaṃ mahārāja, kākarājā nivāsako;

Asītiyā sahassehi, supatto parivārito.

In Bārāṇasī, O great king, the crow king, the well-winged one, had his dwelling, surrounded by eighty thousand.

Rājā yathā vessavaṇo naḷiñña”nti

The king is like Vessavaṇa at Naḷinī.

Evamādīnaṃ pāḷīnaṃ dassanato pokkharaṇī iccādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālāyo savisesā yojetabbā. Kathaṃ? ‘Pokkharaṇī, pokkharaṇī, pokkharaṇiyo, pokkharañño. Pokkharaṇi”ntiādinā vatvā karaṇasampadānanissakkasāmivacanaṭṭhāne “pokkharaṇiyā, pokkharaññā”ti ekavacanāni vattabbāni. Bhummavacanaṭṭhāne pana “pokkharaṇiyā, pokkharaññā, pokkharaṇiyaṃ, pokkharañña”nti ca ekavacanāni vattabbāni. Sabbattha ca padāni paripuṇṇāni kātabbāni. Tathā “dāsī, dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyo. Dāsiṃ, dāsiyaṃ, dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyo”ti vatvā karaṇavacanaṭṭhānādīsu “dāsiyā, dāsyā”ti ekavacanāni vattabbāni. Bhummavacanaṭṭhāne pana “dāsiyā, dāsyā, dāsiyaṃ, dāsya”nti ca ekavacanāni vattabbāni. Sabbattha padāni paripuṇṇāni kātabbāni. Ettha pana “yaṭṭhiyā paṭikoṭeti, ghare jātaṃva dāsiyaṃ. Phusissāmi vimuttiya”nti payogānaṃ dassanato aṃvacanassa yamādesavasena “dāsiya”nti vuttaṃ. Tesu ca “ghare jātaṃva dāsiya”nti ettha aṃvacanassa yamādesato aññopi saddanayo labbhati. Kathaṃ? Yathā daharī eva “dahariyā”ti vuccati, evaṃ dāsī eva “dāsiyā”ti.

From observing such Pāli passages, the nominal declension series for words like 'pokkharaṇī' and so on should be applied with their distinctions. How? By stating 'pokkharaṇī, pokkharaṇī, pokkharaṇiyo, pokkharañño. Pokkharaṇi,' and so on, the singular forms 'pokkharaṇiyā, pokkharaññā' should be stated in the instrumental, dative, ablative, and genitive cases. But in the locative case, the singular forms 'pokkharaṇiyā, pokkharaññā, pokkharaṇiyaṃ, pokkharañña' should be stated. And in all instances, the words should be made complete. Similarly, by stating 'dāsī, dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyo. Dāsiṃ, dāsiyaṃ, dāsī, dāsiyo, dāsyo,' the singular forms 'dāsiyā, dāsyā' should be stated in the instrumental case and so on. But in the locative case, the singular forms 'dāsiyā, dāsyā, dāsiyaṃ, dāsya' should be stated. And in all instances, the words should be made complete. Here, from observing usages such as 'he strikes with a stick,' 'like a slave woman born in the house,' 'I will touch liberation,' the form 'dāsiyaṃ' is stated by way of the 'ya' substitution for the 'aṃ' ending. And in these cases, such as 'like a slave woman born in the house,' another grammatical rule can also be obtained, apart from the 'ya' substitution for the 'aṃ' ending. How? Just as 'daharī' is also called 'dahariyā,' so too 'dāsī' is 'dāsiyā.'

Ettha pana “passāmi vohaṃ dahariṃ, kumāriṃ cārudassana”nti ca “ye taṃ jiṇṇassa pādaṃsu, evaṃ dahariyaṃ sati”nti ca pāḷi nidassanaṃ[M 0.0269], upayogavacanicchāya “dāsiya”nti vuttaṃ, imasmiṃ panādhippāye “dāsiyā, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo. Dāsiyaṃ, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo. Dāsiyāyā”ti kaññānayeneva nāmikapadamālā bhavati “kumāriyā”ti saddasseva. Tathā hi “kumāriye upaseniye”ti pāḷi dissati. Tathā “pupphavatiyā, pupphavatiyaṃ, pupphavatiyāya, pupphavatiyāyaṃ, bhoti pupphavatiye”ti kaññānayanissitena ekavacananayena nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

Here, indeed, the Pāli passages "I see you, a young woman, a charming maiden" and "those who gave that to the old man, while there was a young woman" are cited as examples. And with the intention of illustrating usage, the term 'dāsiya' is mentioned. But with this intention, the nominal declension series 'dāsiyā, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo. Dāsiyaṃ, dāsiyā, dāsiyāyo. Dāsiyāyā' follows the pattern of 'kaññā,' just like the word 'kumāriyā.' Thus, the Pāli passage "O maiden Upasenī" is seen. Similarly, the nominal declension series 'pupphavatiyā, pupphavatiyaṃ, pupphavatiyāya, pupphavatiyāyaṃ, O Pupphavatī' occurs according to the singular pattern based on the 'kaññā' model.

Ettha pana “atīte ayaṃ bārāṇasī pupphavatiyā nāma ahosi. Rājāsi luddakammo, ekarājā pupphavatiyāyaṃ. Uyyassu pubbena pupphavatiyāyā”ti pāḷi ca aṭṭhakathāpāṭho ca nidassanaṃ. Aparo nayo – “dāsiyā dahariyā kumāriyā”tiādīsu kakārassa yakārādesopi daṭṭhabbo. Brāhmaṇīsaddassa tu “brāhmaṇī, brāhmaṇī, brāhmaṇiyo, brāhmaṇyo. Brāhmaṇi”ntiādīni vatvā karaṇavacanaṭṭhānādīsu “brāhmaṇiyā, brāhmaṇyā”ti ekavacanāni vattabbāni, sabbattha ca padāni paripuṇṇāni kātabbāni. Nadīsaddassa “nadī, nadī, nadiyo, najjo. Nadi”ntiādinā vatvā “nadiyā, najjā”ti ca “nadiyaṃ, najja”nti ca vattabbaṃ, sabbattha ca padāni paripuṇṇāni kātabbāni. Itthiliṅgesu hi paccattabahuvacane diṭṭheyeva upayogabahuvacanaṃ anāgatampi diṭṭhameva hoti, tathā upayogabahuvacane diṭṭheyeva paccattabahuvacanaṃ anāgatampi diṭṭhameva hoti, karaṇasampadānanissakkasāmibhummavacanānampi aññatarasmiṃ diṭṭheyeva aññataraṃ diṭṭhameva hoti. Tathā hi “dāsā ca dāsyo anujīvino cā”ti ettha “dāsyo”ti paccattabahuvacane diṭṭheyeva aparampi “dāsyo”ti upayogabahuvacanaṃ taṃsadisattā diṭṭhameva hoti.

Here, the Pāli passage and the commentary text are examples: "In the past, this Bārāṇasī was named Pupphavatī. The king was of cruel deeds, the sole ruler in Pupphavatī. Go forth to the east of Pupphavatī." Another method—in instances such as 'dāsiyā, dahariyā, kumāriyā,' the substitution of the letter 'k' with 'y' should also be noted. As for the word 'brāhmaṇī,' after stating forms such as 'brāhmaṇī, brāhmaṇī, brāhmaṇiyo, brāhmaṇyo. Brāhmaṇi,' the singular forms 'brāhmaṇiyā, brāhmaṇyā' should be stated in the instrumental case and so on. And in all instances, the words should be made complete. As for the word 'nadī,' after stating forms such as 'nadī, nadī, nadiyo, najjo. Nadi,' 'nadiyā, najjā' and 'nadiyaṃ, najjaṃ' should also be stated. And in all instances, the words should be made complete. Indeed, in feminine genders, when the nominative plural is seen, the accusative plural, even if not yet encountered, is understood as seen; likewise, when the accusative plural is seen, the nominative plural, even if not yet encountered, is understood as seen. Similarly, for the instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive, and locative cases, if one of them is seen, another is understood as seen. For example, in "male slaves and female slaves and dependents," when 'dāsyo,' the nominative plural, is seen, the other 'dāsyo,' the accusative plural, is also understood as seen because of its similarity.

“Sakko [M 0.0270] ca me varaṃ dajjā, so ca labbhetha me varo;

Ekarattaṃ dvirattaṃ vā, bhaveyyaṃ abhipārako;

Ummādantyā ramitvāna, sivirājā tato siya”nti

If Sakka would grant me a boon, and if that boon could be obtained by me, for one night or two I would be Abhipāraka; having delighted with Ummādantī, then I would be king of Sivi.

Ettha “ummādantyā”ti karaṇavacane diṭṭheyeva taṃsadisāni sampadānanissakkasāmibhummavacanānipi diṭṭhāniyeva honti. “Brāhmaṇyā paricārake”ti ettha “brāhmaṇyā”ti sāmivacane diṭṭheyeva taṃsadisāni karaṇasampadānanissakkabhummavacanānipi diṭṭhāniyeva honti. “Seti bhūmyā anutthuna”nti ettha “pathabyā cārupubbaṅgī”ti ettha ca “bhūmyā, pathabyā”ti sattamiyā ekavacane diṭṭheyeva taṃsadisāni karaṇasampadānanissakkasāmivacanānipi diṭṭhāniyeva honti. “Bārāṇasyaṃ mahārājā”ti ettha “bārāṇasya”nti bhummavacane diṭṭheyeva taṃsadisāni aññānipi “brāhmaṇyaṃ ekādasyaṃ pañcamya”ntiādīni bhummavacanāni diṭṭhāniyeva honti.

Here, in 'ummādantyā,' when the instrumental case is seen, similar forms for the dative, ablative, genitive, and locative cases are also understood as seen. In 'brāhmaṇyā paricārake,' when 'brāhmaṇyā' in the genitive case is seen, similar forms for the instrumental, dative, ablative, and locative cases are also understood as seen. In 'seti bhūmyā anutthunaṃ' and in 'pathabyā cārupubbaṅgī,' when 'bhūmyā' and 'pathabyā' in the locative singular are seen, similar forms for the instrumental, dative, ablative, and genitive cases are also understood as seen. In 'bārāṇasyaṃ mahārāja,' when 'bārāṇasyaṃ' in the locative case is seen, other similar locative forms like 'brāhmaṇyaṃ, ekādasyaṃ, pañcamyaṃ,' and so on, are also understood as seen.

Gaṇhanti ca tādisāni rūpāni pubbācariyāsabhāpi gāthābhisaṅkharaṇavasena. Sāsanepi pana etādisāni rūpāni yebhuyyena gāthāsu sandissanti.

Such forms are also adopted by the foremost ancient teachers through the composition of verses. Moreover, in the Dispensation, such forms are generally found in verses.

Kusāvatī. Kusāvatiṃ. Kusāvatiyā, kusāvatyā. Kusāvatiyaṃ, kusāvatyaṃ. Bhoti kusāvati.

Kusāvatī. Kusāvatiṃ. By Kusāvatī, for Kusāvatī, from Kusāvatī, of Kusāvatī. In Kusāvatī. O Kusāvati.

Bārāṇasī. Bārāṇasiṃ. Bārāṇasiyā, bārāṇasyā. Bārāṇasiyaṃ, bārāṇasyaṃ, bārāṇassaṃ iccapi, bhoti bārāṇasi.

Benares. Benares (acc.). By Benares, for Benares, from Benares, of Benares. In Benares, and so on. O Benares.

Naḷinī. Naḷiniṃ. Naḷiniyā, naḷiññā. Naḷiniyaṃ, naḷiññaṃ. Bhoti naḷini. Aññānipi yojetabbāni.

The lotus pond. The lotus pond (acc.). By the lotus pond, for the lotus pond, from the lotus pond, of the lotus pond. In the lotus pond. O lotus pond. Others should also be applied.

Gāthāvisayaṃ pana patvā “kusāvatimhi, bārāṇasimhi, naḷinimhī”tiādinā saddarūpānipiyojetabbāni. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ “kusāvatimhi”ādīni mhiyantāni itthiliṅgarūpāni gāthāsuyeva [M 0.0271] paññāyanti, na cuṇṇiyapadaracanāyaṃ. Akkharasamaye pana tādisāni rūpāni anivāritāni “nadimhā cā”tiādidassanato. Yaṃ pana aṭṭhakathāsu cuṇṇiyapadaracanāyaṃ “sammādiṭṭhimhī”tiādikaṃ itthiliṅgarūpaṃ dissati, taṃ akkharavipallāsavasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ cuṇṇiyapadaṭṭhāne “sammādiṭṭhiyaṃ paṭisandhiyaṃ sugatiyaṃ duggatiya”ntiādidassanato. Ayaṃ panettha niyamo sugatasāsane gāthāyaṃ cuṇṇiyapadaṭṭhāne ca “kaññā ratti itthī yāgu vadhū”ti evaṃ pañcantehi itthiliṅgehi saddhiṃ nā sa smā smiṃ mhā mhiiccete saddā sarūpato parattaṃ na yanti. Mhisaddo pana gāthāyaṃ ivaṇṇantehi itthiliṅgehi saddhiṃ parattaṃ yāti. Tatridaṃ vuccati –

However, having come to the domain of verses, word-forms such as 'kusāvatimhi, bārāṇasimhi, naḷinimhi' should also be applied. Indeed, in the Pāli, feminine forms ending in -mhi, such as 'kusāvatimhi,' are found only in verses, not in prose compositions. In the science of letters, however, such forms are not prohibited, as seen from the example 'nadimhā.' Moreover, the feminine form 'sammādiṭṭhimhi' and so on that appears in the commentaries in prose compositions should be understood as stated due to a textual corruption, because in prose sections, forms like 'sammādiṭṭhiyaṃ, paṭisandhiyaṃ, sugatiyaṃ, duggatiyaṃ' are seen. Herein is the rule in the Sugata's dispensation: in verse and in prose, these sounds—nā, sa, smā, smiṃ, mhā, mhi—are not affixed in their own form after feminine nouns ending in these five vowels: ā, i, ī, u, ū (as exemplified by kaññā, ratti, itthī, yāgu, vadhū). The sound mhi, however, is affixed in verse after feminine nouns ending in i. Regarding this, it is said:

“Gāthāyaṃ cuṇṇiye cāpi, nā sasmādī sarūpato;

Nākārantaivaṇṇanta-itthīti parataṃ gatā.

In verse and also in prose, nā, sa, smā, and so on, in their own form, are not affixed after feminine nouns ending in ā and i.

Mhisaddo pana gāthāyaṃ, ivaṇṇantitthibhī saha;

Ya’to parattametassa, payogāni bhavanti hi.

However, the word `mhi` in a verse, together with feminine nouns ending in the letter `i`; for this reason, its usages indeed become different.

Yathā balākayonimhi, na vijjati pumo sadā;

Kusāvabhimhi nagare, rājā āsi mahīpatī”ti.

As in a heron's womb, a male is never found; in the city of Kusāvatī, a king was lord of the land.

Evaṃ kusāvatī iccādīni aññathā bhavanti, nagaranāmattā panekavacanānipi, na janapadanāmāni viya bahuvacanāni. “Kāsī, kāsiyo. Kāsīhi, kāsībhi. Kāsīnaṃ. Kāsīsu. Bhotiyo kāsiyo. Evaṃ avantī avantiyo”tiādināpi nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Aññānipi padāni gahetabbāni. Evaṃ kāsīiccādīni janapadanāmattā rūḷhīvasena bahuvacanāneva bhavanti atthassa ekattepi.

Thus, `Kusāvatī` and so forth are formed differently; but being city names, they are singular, not plural like country names. 'Kāsī, Kāsiyo. Kāsīhi, Kāsībhi. Kāsīnaṃ. Kāsīsu. Bhotiyo Kāsiyo.' Similarly, with `Avantī, Avantiyo`, and so forth, the nominal paradigm should be applied. Other words should also be taken. Thus, `Kāsī` and so forth, being country names, are by convention always plural, even when the meaning is singular.

Candavatī, candavatiṃ, candavatiyā, candavatiyaṃ, bhoti candavati, evaṃ ekavacanavasena vā, candavatiyo, candavatiyo, candavatīhi, candavatībhi, candavatīnaṃ, candavatīsu, bhotiyo [M 0.0272] candavatiyo, evaṃ bahuvacanavasena vā nāmikapadamālā veditabbā, aññānipi padāni yojetabbāni. “Candavatī”iccādīni hi ekissā bahūnañcitthīnaṃ paṇṇattibhāvato payogānurūpena ekavacanavasena vā bahuvacanavasena vā yojetabbāni bhavanti. Esa nayo aññatrāpi.

`Candavatī, candavatiṃ, candavatiyā, candavatiyaṃ, bhoti candavati`, thus in the singular; or `candavatiyo, candavatiyo, candavatīhi, candavatībhi, candavatīnaṃ, candavatīsu, bhotiyo candavatiyo`, thus in the plural, the nominal paradigm should be understood. Other words should also be applied. For `Candavatī` and so forth, since they are designations for one or for many women, they should be applied in the singular or in the plural according to usage. This is the method elsewhere too.

Savinicchayoyaṃ īkārantitthiliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed classification of the nominal paradigm for the natural form of feminine nouns ending in `ī`.

Īkārantatāpakatikaṃ īkārantitthiliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the natural form of feminine nouns ending in `ī` is concluded.

Idāni bhūdhātumayānaṃ ukārantitthiliṅgānaṃ appasiddhattā aññena ukārantitthiliṅgena nāmikapadamālaṃ pūressāma –

Now, due to the infrequency of usage of feminine nouns ending in `u` derived from the root `bhū`, we will complete the nominal paradigm with another feminine noun ending in `u`.

Yāgu, yāgū, yāguyo. Yāguṃ, yāgū, yāguyo. Yāguyā, yāgūhi, yāgūbhi. Yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ. Yāguyā, yāgūhi, yāgūbhi. Yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ. Yāguyā, yāguyaṃ, yāgūsu. Bhoti yāgu, bhotiyo yāgū, yāguyo.

Yāgu, yāgū, yāguyo. Yāguṃ, yāgū, yāguyo. Yāguyā, yāgūhi, yāgūbhi. Yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ. Yāguyā, yāgūhi, yāgūbhi. Yāguyā, yāgūnaṃ. Yāguyā, yāguyaṃ, yāgūsu. Bhoti yāgu, bhotiyo yāgū, yāguyo.

Evaṃ “dhātu dhenu kāsu daddu kaṇḍu kacchu rajju”iccādīni. Tatra dhātusaddo rasarudhiramaṃsamedanhāruaṭṭhiaṭṭhimiñjasukkasaṅkhātadhātuvācako pulliṅgo, sabhāvavācako pana sugatādīnaṃ sārīrikavācako lokadhātuvācako ca cakkhādivācako ca itthiliṅgo, bhū hū karapacādisaddavācako itthiliṅgoceva pulliṅgo ca. Atra panitthiliṅgo adhippeto.

Similarly, `dhātu, dhenu, kāsu, daddu, kaṇḍu, kacchu, rajju`, and so forth. Therein, the word `dhātu` is masculine when it denotes the elements enumerated as rasa, blood, flesh, fat, sinew, bone, bone-marrow, and semen. However, when it denotes nature, the bodily relics of the Sugata and others, the world-element, and the eye-faculty and so forth, it is feminine. When it denotes verbal roots such as `bhū`, `hū`, `kara`, `paca`, etc., it is both feminine and masculine. Here, however, the feminine gender is intended.

Savinicchayoyaṃukārantitthiliṅgānaṃ nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed classification of the nominal paradigm of feminine nouns ending in `u`.

Ukārantatāpakatikaṃ ukārantitthiliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the natural form of feminine nouns ending in `u` is concluded.

Idāni bhūsaddādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā –

Now we will explain the nominal paradigm of the word `bhū` and others, having taken the opinion of the ancient teachers as our guide.

Jambū, jambū, jambuyo. Jambuṃ, jambū, jambuyo. Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi. Jambuyā, jambūnaṃ. Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi. Jambuyā[M 0.0273], jambūnaṃ. Jambuyā, jambuyaṃ, jambūsu. Bhoti jambu, bhotiyo jambū, jambuyo. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

`Jambū, jambū, jambuyo. Jambuṃ, jambū, jambuyo. Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi. Jambuyā, jambūnaṃ. Jambuyā, jambūhi, jambūbhi. Jambuyā, jambūnaṃ. Jambuyā, jambuyaṃ, jambūsu. Bhoti jambu, bhotiyo jambū, jambuyo.` This is the opinion of the Great Elder Yamaka.

Ettha jambūsaddassa itthiliṅgattaṃ “ambā sālā ca jambuyo”tiādinā pasiddhaṃ. “Ime te jambukā rukkhā”ti ettha pana rukkhasaddaṃ apekkhitvā “jambukā”ti pulliṅganiddeso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi jambūti kathetabbāti jambukā. Ke re ge saddeti dhātu. Atha vā itthiliṅgavasena jambū eva jambukā, jambukā ca tā rukkhā cāti jambukārukkhā, yathā laṅkādīpo, pulliṅgapakkhe vā samāsavasena “jambukarukkhā”ti vattabbe gāthāvisayattā chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ dīghaṃ katvā “jambukārukkhā”ti vuttaṃ “saraṇāgamane kañcī”ti ettha viya.

Here, the feminine gender of the word `jambū` is established by such as 'ambā sālā ca jambuyo.' However, in the phrase 'ime te jambukā rukkhā,' it should be understood that the masculine designation `jambukā` is used with reference to the word `rukkha`. For `jambukā` is that which is to be called `jambū`. The root is `ke re ge` in the sense of 'to sound'. Alternatively, from the feminine perspective, `jambū` itself is `jambukā`, and `jambukā ca tā rukkhā ca` becomes `jambukārukkhā`, like `laṅkādīpo`. Or, on the masculine side, by way of a compound, when `jambukarukkhā` should be said, the long vowel is made to protect the meter as it is a matter of verse, and `jambukārukkhā` is said, just as in `saraṇāgamane kañcī`.

Bhū, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuṃ, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhuyaṃ, bhūsu. Bhoti bhu, bhotiyo bhū, bhuyo.

Bhū, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuṃ, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhuyaṃ, bhūsu. Bhoti bhu, bhotiyo bhū, bhuyo.

Evaṃ “abhū, abhū, abhuyo. Abhuṃ, abhū, abhuyo. Abhuyā”tiādinā yojetabbā. Atra “abhuṃ me kathaṃ nu bhaṇasi, pāpakaṃ vata bhāsasī”ti nidassanapadaṃ.

Similarly, it should be applied with `abhū, abhū, abhuyo; abhuṃ, abhū, abhuyo; abhuyā`, and so forth. Here, 'Abhuṃ me kathaṃ nu bhaṇasi, pāpakaṃ vata bhāsasī' is an example phrase.

“Vadhū ca sarabhū ceva, sarabū sutanū camū;

Vāmūrū nāganāsūrū”, iccādī jambuyā samā.

`Vadhū ca sarabhū ceva, sarabū sutanū camū; Vāmūrū nāganāsūrū`, and so forth, are similar to `jambuyā`.

Idaṃ pana sukhumaṃ ṭhānaṃ suṭṭhu manasi kātabbaṃ. “Vadaññū, vadaññū, vadaññuyo. Vadaññuṃ, vadaññū, vadaññuyo. Vadaññuyā”ti jambūsamaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Evaṃ “maggaññū dhammaññū kataññū”iccādīsupi.

However, this subtle point should be well kept in mind. `Vadaññū, vadaññū, vadaññuyo. Vadaññuṃ, vadaññū, vadaññuyo. Vadaññuyā` should be declined like `jambū`. It is similar also with `maggaññū, dhammaññū, kataññū`, and so forth.

Nanu ca bho –

Well now, sir—

“Sohaṃ nūna ito gantvā, yoniṃ laddhāna mānusiṃ;

Vadaññū sīlasampanno, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahu”nti

'Surely I, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, being generous and endowed with virtue, will perform much that is wholesome.'

Evamādippayogadassanato vadaññūsaddādīnaṃ pulliṅgabhāvo pasiddho, evaṃ sante kasmā idha itthiliṅganayo dassitoti? Vadaññūiccādīnaṃ ekantapulliṅgabhāvābhāvato dviliṅgāni tesaṃ vāccaliṅgattā. Tathā hi –

From seeing such usages, the masculine nature of words like `vadaññū` is well-known. This being so, why is the rule for the feminine gender shown here? Because `vadaññū` and so forth do not have an exclusively masculine nature; they are of two genders, as their gender depends on the subject. For example—

“Sāhaṃ gantvā manussattaṃ, vadaññū vītamaccharā;

Saṅghe dānāni dassāmi, appamattā punappuna”nti ca,

'I (she), having attained a human state, being generous and free from avarice, will give gifts to the Saṅgha, diligently, again and again.'

“Kodhanā akataññū cā”ti ca itthiliṅgapayogikā bahū pāḷiyo dissanti, tasmā evaṃ nīti amhehi ṭhapitā.

And in 'Kodhanā akataññū cā,' and so forth, many Pāli passages with feminine usage are seen. Therefore, this rule has been thus established by us.

Savinicchayoyaṃ ūkārantitthiliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the detailed classification of the nominal paradigm for the natural form of feminine nouns ending in `ū`.

Ūkārantatāpakatikaṃ ūkārantitthiliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the natural form of feminine nouns ending in `ū` is concluded.

Okārantapadaṃ bhūdhātumayaṃ itthiliṅgamappasiddhaṃ, aññaṃ panokārantaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ pasiddhaṃ.

A feminine word ending in -o derived from the root `bhū` is uncommon, but other feminine words ending in -o are common.

Okārantaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ, gosaddoti vibhāvaye;

Gosaddasseva pulliṅge, rūpamassāhu kecana;

A feminine noun ending in `o`, one should understand as the word `go`. Some say its form is the same as that of the word `go` in the masculine gender.

Tathā hi keci “go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvu”ntiādinā nayena vuttāni pulliṅgassa gosaddassa rūpāni viya itthiliṅgassa gosaddassa rūpāni icchanti, tesaṃ mate majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇānaṃ vaṇṇavisesābhāvo viya rūpavisesābhāvato gosaddassa itthiliṅgabhāvapaṭipādanaṃ anijjhānakkhamaṃ. Kasmāti ce? Yasmā mātugāmasaddassa “mātugāmo, mātugāmā. Mātugāma”ntiādinā nayena dve padamālā katvā ekā pulliṅgassa padamālā, ekā itthiliṅgapadamālāti vuttavacanaṃ viya idaṃ vacanaṃ amhe paṭibhāti, tasmā anijjhānakkhamaṃ.

For some desire the forms of the feminine word `go` to be like the forms of the masculine word `go`, which are given in the manner of `go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvu`, and so forth. In their opinion, just as there is no distinction in color among broken pieces of gold, so too, due to the absence of distinct forms, the establishment of the feminine gender of the word `go` is unworthy of consideration. If you ask why, it is because this statement appears to us like the statement concerning the word `mātugāma`, where, having made two paradigms in the manner of `mātugāmo, mātugāmā. Mātugāma`, and so forth, it is said that one is the paradigm for the masculine and one is the paradigm for the feminine. Therefore, it is unworthy of consideration.

Apica itthiliṅgassa gosaddassa rūpesu pulliṅgassa gosaddassa rūpehi samesu santesu kathaṃ gosaddassa itthiliṅgabhāvo [M 0.0275] siyā? Rūpamālāvisesābhāvato. Yathā hi ratti aggi aṭṭhisaddānaṃ ikārantabhāvena samattepi itthiliṅgapumanapuṃsakaliṅgalakkhaṇabhūto rūpamālāviseso dissati. Yathā pana dvinnaṃ dhātusaddānaṃ pumitthiliṅgapariyāpannānaṃ rūpamālāviseso dissati, na tathā tehācariyehi abhimatassa itthiliṅgassa gosaddassa rūpamālāviseso dissati. Yathā pana dvinnaṃ dhātusaddānaṃ pumitthiliṅgapariyāpannānaṃ rūpamālāviseso bhavati, yathā dvinnaṃ gosaddānaṃ pumitthiliṅgapariyāpannānaṃ rūpamālāvisesena bhavitabbaṃ, yathā ca dvinnaṃ āyusaddānaṃ punnapuṃsakaliṅgapariyāpannānaṃ rūpamālāviseso dissati, tathā dvinnaṃ gosaddānaṃ pumitthiliṅgapariyāpannānaṃ rūpamālāvisesena bhavitabbaṃ. Avisesatte sati kathaṃ tesaṃ pumitthiliṅgavavatthānaṃ siyā, kathañca visadāvisadākāravohāratā siyā. Idaṃ ṭhānaṃ atīva saṇhasukhumaṃ paramagambhīraṃ mahāgahanaṃ na sakkā sabbasattānaṃ mūlabhāsābhūtāya sabbaññujineritāya māgadhikāya sabhāvaniruttiyā nayaṃ sammā ajānantena akatañāṇasambhārena kenaci ajjhogāhetuṃ vā vijaṭetuṃ vā, amhākaṃ pana mate dvinnaṃ gosaddānaṃ rūpamālāviseso ceva dissati, pumitthiliṅgavavatthānañca dissati, visadāvisadākāravohāratā ca dissati, napuṃsakaliṅgassa tadubhayamuttākāravohāratā ca dissatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Moreover, if the forms of the feminine word 'go' are the same as the forms of the masculine word 'go,' how can the word 'go' be feminine? Because there is no distinct difference in the declensional paradigm. For just as, although the words 'ratti' (night), 'aggi' (fire), and 'aṭṭhi' (bone) are the same in that they end in -i, a distinctive characteristic of their declensional paradigms is seen, which is the mark of their being feminine, masculine, and neuter respectively. And just as a distinctive characteristic of the declensional paradigm is seen in the two 'dhātu' words that are included in the masculine and feminine genders, such a distinctive characteristic of the declensional paradigm of the feminine 'go' as accepted by those teachers is not seen. Just as a distinctive characteristic of the declensional paradigm occurs with the two 'dhātu' words included in the masculine and feminine genders, so it should occur with the two 'go' words included in the masculine and feminine genders; and just as a distinctive characteristic of the declensional paradigm is seen with the two 'āyu' words included in the masculine and neuter genders, so it should occur with the two 'go' words included in the masculine and feminine genders. If there is no distinction, how can their classification as masculine and feminine be established, and how can there be clear and unclear modes of expression? This point is exceedingly subtle and delicate, extremely profound and deeply intricate. It is not possible for anyone who does not rightly understand the method of Māgadhī—the original language of all beings, spoken by the All-Knowing Conqueror, with its natural mode of expression—and who lacks the accumulation of knowledge, to penetrate or unravel it. However, in our opinion, a distinctive characteristic of the declensional paradigm is indeed seen in the two 'go' words, the classification of masculine and feminine is seen, clear and unclear modes of expression are seen, and it should be understood that the neuter gender has a mode of expression free from both of these.

Idāni imassatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne imaṃ nītiṃ ṭhapessāma. Evañhi sati pariyattisāsane paṭipannakā nikkaṅkhabhāvena na kilamissanti. Ettha tāva atthaggahaṇe viññūnaṃ kosalluppādanatthaṃ tisso nāmikapadamālāyo kathessāma – seyyathidaṃ?

Now, to make this matter clear, we will establish this principle in this place. For when this is so, those who are engaged in the study of the Teaching will not become weary, being free from doubt. Here, first, to develop the skill of the wise in grasping the meaning, we will state three nominal declensional paradigms—namely:

Gāvī, gāvī, gāviyo. Gāviṃ, gāvī, gāviyo. Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi. Gāviyā, gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi. Gāviyā[M 0.0276], gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyā, gāviyaṃ, gāvīsu. Bhoti gāvi, bhotiyo gāvī, gāviyo.

Gāvī, gāvī, gāviyo. Gāviṃ, gāvī, gāviyo. Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi. Gāviyā, gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi. Gāviyā, gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyā, gāviyaṃ, gāvīsu. Bhoti gāvi, bhotiyo gāvī, gāviyo.

Ayaṃ gosaddato vihitassa īpaccayassa vasena nipphannassa itthivācakassa īkārantitthiliṅgassa gāvīsaddassa nāmikapadamālā.

This is the nominal declensional paradigm of the word 'gāvī', a feminine noun ending in -ī, which denotes the feminine, formed from the word 'go' by means of the suffix -ī.

Go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvo, gavo. Gāvena, gavena, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāvā, gāvasmā, gāvamhā, gavā, gavasmā, gavamhā, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāve, gāvasmiṃ, gāvamhi, gave, gavasmiṃ, gavamhi, gāvesu, gavesu, gosu. Bho go, bhavanto gāvo, gavo.

Go, gāvo, gavo. Gāvuṃ, gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvo, gavo. Gāvena, gavena, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāvā, gāvasmā, gāvamhā, gavā, gavasmā, gavamhā, gohi, gobhi. Gāvassa, gavassa, gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gāve, gāvasmiṃ, gāvamhi, gave, gavasmiṃ, gavamhi, gāvesu, gavesu, gosu. Bho go, bhavanto gāvo, gavo.

Ayaṃ pumavācakassa okārantapulliṅgassa gosaddassa nāmikapadamālā.

This is the nominal declensional paradigm of the masculine word 'go,' which ends in -o and denotes the masculine.

Go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo. Gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāviṃ, gāvo, gāvī gavo. Gohi, gobhi. Gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gohi, gobhi. Gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gosu. Bhoti go, bhotiyo gāvo, gāvī, gavo. Ayaṃ pumitthivācakassa okārantassitthipulliṅgassa gosaddanāmikapadamālā.

Go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo. Gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāviṃ, gāvo, gāvī gavo. Gohi, gobhi. Gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gohi, gobhi. Gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ. Gosu. Bhoti go, bhotiyo gāvo, gāvī, gavo. This is the nominal declensional paradigm of the word 'go,' which ends in -o and is of both feminine and masculine gender, denoting both masculine and feminine.

Ettha pana “gāvu”nti padaṃ ekantapumavācakattā na vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, ekantapumavācakattañcassa āhaccapāḷiyā ñāyati “idha pana bhikkhave vassūpagataṃ bhikkhuṃ itthī nimantesi ‘ehi bhante, hiraññaṃ vā te demi, suvaṇṇaṃ vā te demi, khettaṃ vā te demi, vatthuṃ vā te demi, gāvuṃ vā te demi, gāviṃ vā te demi. Dāsaṃ vā te demi, dāsiṃ vā te demi, dhītaraṃ vā te demi bhariyatthāya, ahaṃ vā te bhariyā homi, aññaṃ vā te bhariyaṃ ānemī’ti” evaṃ āhaccapāḷiyā ñāyati.

Here, however, it should be understood that the word 'gāvuṃ' is not mentioned because it exclusively denotes the masculine, and its exclusive denotation of the masculine is known from a Pāḷi citation: 'Here, monks, a woman invites a monk who has entered the rains residence, saying, “Come, venerable sir, I will give you silver, or I will give you gold, or I will give you a field, or I will give you a site, or I will give you a bull (gāvuṃ), or I will give you a cow (gāviṃ). I will give you a male slave, or I will give you a female slave, or I will give you my daughter to be your wife, or I myself will be your wife, or I will bring another wife for you.”' Thus it is known from a Pāḷi citation.

Ettha [M 0.0277] hi “gāvu”nti vacanena pumā vutto, “gāvi”nti vacanena itthī, yaṃ pana imissaṃ okārantitthiliṅgapadamālāyaṃ “gāvī”ti padaṃ catukkhattuṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ “kaññā”ti padaṃ viya itthiliṅgassa avisadākāravohāratāviññāpane samatthaṃ hoti. Na hi itaresu liṅgesu samānasutikabhāvena catukkhattuṃ āgatapadaṃ ekampi atthi, “gāvī gāvi”nti ca imesaṃ saddānaṃ katthaci ṭhāne itthipumesu sāmaññavasena pavattiṃ upari kathayissāma. Yā panamhehi okārantitthiliṅgassa “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo. Gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvi”ntiādinā nayena padamālā katā, tattha gosaddato siyonaṃ īkārādeso aṃvacanassa ca iṃkārādeso bhavati, tena okārantitthiliṅgassa “gāvī gāvī gāvi”nti rūpāni dassitāni. Tathā hi mukhamattadīpaniyaṃ saddasatthavidunā vajirabuddhācariyena niruttinaye kosallavasena gosaddato yonamīkārādeso vutto. Yathā pana gosaddato yonamīkārādeso bhavati, tathā sissīkārādeso aṃvacanassa ca iṃkārādeso bhavati. Atrimā nayaggāhaparidīpaniyo gāthā –

Here, indeed, by the word 'gāvuṃ' the masculine is stated, and by the word 'gāviṃ' the feminine. However, the word 'gāvī,' which is mentioned four times in this declensional paradigm of feminine words ending in -o, is capable of making known the indistinct mode of expression of the feminine gender, just like the word 'kaññā.' For in other genders, there is not even a single word that appears four times with the same sound. And regarding the words 'gāvī' and 'gāvi,' we will discuss their general usage for both feminine and masculine in a later place. Moreover, in the declensional paradigm we have made for the feminine gender ending in -o according to the method beginning 'go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo. Gāvaṃ, gavaṃ, gāvi,' and so forth, there is the substitution of -ī for the endings `si` and `yo` from the word 'go,' and the substitution of -iṃ for the ending `aṃ`. Thus, the forms 'gāvī, gāvī, gāvi' are shown for the feminine gender ending in -o. Indeed, in the Mukhamattadīpanī, the grammarian Vajirabuddhācariya, skilled in the method of grammar, has stated the substitution of -ī for the `yo` ending from the word 'go'. Just as there is the substitution of -ī for the `yo` ending from the word 'go', so too there is the substitution of -ī for the `si` ending, and the substitution of -iṃ for the `aṃ` ending. These are the verses from the Nayaggāhaparidīpanī by Atri:

Īpaccayā siddhesvapi, “gāvī gāvī”tiādisu;

Paṭhamekavacanādi-antesu jinasāsane.

In the Dispensation of the Conqueror, even for forms such as 'gāvī, gāvī', etc., which are formed by the suffix -ī, there are the nominative singular and other case endings.

Vadatā yonamīkāraṃ, gosaddassitthiyaṃ pana;

Avisadattamakkhātuṃ, nayo dinnoti no ruci.

But the method given, which states the substitution of -ī for the `yo` ending of the word 'go' in the feminine in order to explain its indistinctness, is not to our liking.

Kiñca bhiyyo aṭṭhakathāsu ca –

And furthermore, in the commentaries:

“Gāvo”ti vatvā “gāvi”nti-vacanena panitthiyaṃ;

Avisadattamakkhātuṃ, nayo dinnoti no ruci.

Having said 'gāvo,' then by the word 'gāvi' in the feminine, a method is given to explain its indistinctness; this is not to our liking.

Tathā hi samantapāsādikādīsu aṭṭhakathāsu “cheko hi gopālako sakkharāyo ucchaṅgena gahetvā rajjudaṇḍahattho pātova vajaṃ gantvā gāvo piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā palighathambhamatthake [M 0.0278] nisinno dvāraṃ pattaṃ pattaṃ gāviṃ ‘eko dve’ti sakkharaṃ khipitvā gaṇetī”ti imasmiṃ padese “gāvo”ti vatvā “gāvi”nti vacanena itthipumavācakassa okārantitthiliṅgassa gosaddassa avisadākāravohāratā vihitā. “Gāvo”ti hi iminā sāmaññato itthipumabhūtā goṇā gahitā, tathā “gāvi”nti imināpi itthibhūto pumabhūto ca goṇo. Evaṃ “gāvo”ti ca “gāvi”nti ca ime saddā saddasatthavidūhi aṭṭhakathācariyehi niruttinayakusalatāya samānaliṅgavasena ekasmiṃyeva pakaraṇe ekasmiṃyeva vākye piṇḍīkatā.
