Yadi hi itthiliṅge vattamānassa itthipumavācakassa okārantitthiliṅgassa gosaddassa padamālāyaṃ “gāvī gāvi”miccetāni rūpāni na labbheyyuṃ, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “gāvo”ti vatvā “gāva”nticceva vattabbaṃ siyā, “gāvi”nti pana na vattabbaṃ. Yathā ca pana aṭṭhakathācariyehi “gāvo”ti itthipumavasena sabbesaṃ gunnaṃ saṅgāhakavacanaṃ vatvā teyeva gāvo sandhāya puna “dvāraṃ pattaṃ pattaṃ gāvi”nti saddaracanaṃ kubbiṃsu, tasmā “gāvi”nti idampi sabbasaṅgāhakavacanamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asabbasaṅgāhakavacanaṃ idaṃ gāvīsaddena itthiyāyeva gahetabbattāti ce? Na, pakaraṇavasena atthantarassa viditattā. Na hi sabbavajesu “itthiyoyeva vasanti, na pumāno”ti ca, “pumānoyeva vasanti, na itthiyo”ti ca sakkā vattuṃ. Apica “gāvimpi disvā palāyanti ‘bhikkhū’ti maññamānā”ti pāḷi dissati, etthāpi “gāvi”nti vacanena itthibhūto pumabhūto ca sabbo go gahitoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Itarathā “itthibhūtoyeva go bhikkhūti maññitabbo”ti āpajjati. Iti pāḷinayena itthiliṅge vattamānamhā itthipumavācakasmā gosaddato aṃvacanassa iṃkārādeso hotīti viññāyati.

For in the commentaries such as the Samantapāsādikā, it is stated: 'Indeed, a clever cowherd, taking pebbles in the fold of his garment and holding a rope and stick in hand, goes to the cattle pen early in the morning. Having struck the cattle on their backs, he sits atop the gate-post and counts each cow that reaches the gate, throwing a pebble, saying, “one, two.”' In this passage, after saying 'gāvo' (cattle), by the word 'gāviṃ,' an unclear usage of form is established for the word 'go,' which is feminine in gender, ends in 'o', and can denote both feminine and masculine. For by 'gāvo,' both female and male cattle are generally taken, and similarly by 'gāviṃ,' both a female and a male bovine are taken. Thus, the words 'gāvo' and 'gāviṃ' are combined by the commentators, who are skilled in the method of etymology, as having the same gender in the very same context and in the very same sentence. If, for the word 'go,' which is used in the feminine gender and can denote both feminine and masculine, the forms 'gāvī' and 'gāvi' were not obtainable in the declension table, then in the commentary, having said 'gāvo,' it should have been said just 'gāvaṃ,' but 'gāviṃ' should not have been said. But since the commentators, having said 'gāvo' as a term inclusive of all cattle, both feminine and masculine, and referring to those same cattle, then constructed the phrase 'each cow (gāviṃ) that reaches the gate,' therefore it should be understood that 'gāvi' is also an all-inclusive term. If it is said that this is not an all-inclusive term, but that by the word 'gāvī' only the feminine should be taken, this is not so, because another meaning is known from the context. For it cannot be said of all cattle pens that 'only females live there, not males,' or 'only males live there, not females.' Moreover, the Pāli text is seen: 'Seeing even a cow (gāviṃ), they flee, thinking, “They are bhikkhus!”' Here too, it should be understood that by the word 'gāviṃ,' every bovine, whether female or male, is taken. Otherwise, it would follow that 'only a female bovine is to be mistaken for a bhikkhu.' Thus, according to the Pāli method, it is understood that for the word 'go,' which is used in the feminine gender and can denote both feminine and masculine, there is a substitution of 'iṃ' for the accusative ending 'aṃ'.

Vajirabuddhācariyenapi [M 0.0279] gosaddato īpaccaye kātabbepi akatvā yonamīkārādeso kato. Tassādhippāyo evaṃ siyā gosaddato īpaccaye kate sati īpaccayavasena “gāvī”ti nipphannasaddo yattha katthaci visaye “migī morī kukkuṭī”iccādayo viya itthivācakoyeva siyā, na katthacipi itthipumavācako, tasmā sāsanānukūlappayogavasena yonamīkārādeso kātabboti. Iti vajirabuddhācariyamate gosaddato yonaṃ īkārādeso hotīti ñāyati.

Also by the teacher Vajirabuddhi, although the suffix 'ī' should have been applied to the word 'go,' this was not done; instead, the substitution of 'ī' for the plural ending 'yo' was made. His intention might have been this: if the suffix 'ī' were applied to 'go,' the resulting word 'gāvī,' formed by means of the suffix 'ī,' would in any context be only a designator of the feminine—like 'migī' (doe), 'morī' (peahen), 'kukkuṭī' (hen), etc.—and would nowhere designate both feminine and masculine. Therefore, for the sake of a usage suitable to the Teaching, the substitution of 'ī' for 'yo' should be made. Thus, in the opinion of the teacher Vajirabuddhi, it is known that from the word 'go,' there is a substitution of 'ī' for the plural ending 'yo'.

Kiñca bhiyyo – yasmā aṭṭhakathācariyehi “gāvo piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā”tiādinā nayena racitāya “dvāraṃ pattaṃ pattaṃ gāviṃ ‘eko dve’ti sakkharaṃ khipitvā gaṇetī”ti vacanapariyosānāya saddaracanāyaṃ “eko gāvī, dve gāvī”ti atthayojanānayo vattabbo hoti, “gāvi”nti upayogavacanañca dissati. Iti aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ mate gosaddato siyonamīkārādeso aṃvacanassa iṃkārādeso hotīti ñāyati. Tasmāyevamhehi yā sā okārantatāpakatikassa itthiliṅgassa gosaddassa “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo, gāvaṃ, gāvi”ntiādinā nayena padamālā ṭhapitā, sā pāḷinayānukūlā aṭṭhakathānayānukūlā kaccāyanācariyamataṃ gahetvā padanipphattijanakassa garuno ca matānukūlā, “gāvī”ti padassa catukkhattuṃ āgatattā pana okārantitthiliṅgassa gosaddassa avisadākāravohārattañca sādheti. Iccesā pāḷinayādīsu ñāṇena sammā upaparikkhiyamānesu atīva yujjati, natthettha appamattakopi doso. Ettha pana paccattopayogālapanānaṃ bahuvacanaṭṭhāne “gāviyo”ti padañca karaṇasampadānanissakkasāmīnamekavacanaṭṭhāne “gāviyā”ti padañca karaṇanissakkānaṃ bahuvacanaṭṭhāne “gāvīhi gāvībhī”ti padāni ca sampadānasāmīnaṃ [M 0.0280] bahuvacanaṭṭhāne “gāvīna”nti padañca bhummavacanaṭṭhāne “gāviyā, gāviyaṃ, gāvīsū”ti padāni cāti imāni vitthārato soḷasa padāni ekantena īpaccayavasena siddhattā ekantitthivācakattā ca na vuttānīti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore, because for the phrasing composed by the commentators in the manner of 'having struck the cattle on the back,' etc., and concluding with the words 'he counts each cow that reaches the gate, throwing a pebble, saying, “one, two,”' the method of applying the meaning as 'one cow (gāvī), two cows (gāvī)' is acknowledged, and the accusative form 'gāviṃ' is also seen. Thus, in the opinion of the commentators, it is known that from the word 'go,' there is a substitution of 'ī' for the nominative singular 'si' and the plural 'yo,' and a substitution of 'iṃ' for the accusative singular 'aṃ.' Therefore, the declension table established by us for the word 'go,' which is feminine and whose nature is to end in 'o'—in the manner of 'go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo, gāvaṃ, gāvi,' etc.—is in accordance with the Pāli method, the commentarial method, and taking the opinion of the teacher Kaccāyana, it is also in accordance with the opinion of the venerable one who is the originator of the derivation of words. Moreover, since the word 'gāvī' appears four times, it also establishes the unclear nature of the usage of the form of the word 'go,' which is feminine and ends in 'o.' Thus, when this is properly examined with knowledge in the Pāli method and so on, it is very fitting; there is not the slightest fault here. It should be understood, however, that here the word 'gāviyo' in the place of the plural accusative and vocative; the word 'gāviyā' in the place of the singular instrumental, dative, ablative, and genitive; the words 'gāvīhi' and 'gāvībhī' in the place of the plural instrumental and ablative; the word 'gāvīnaṃ' in the place of the plural dative and genitive; and the words 'gāviyā,' 'gāviyaṃ,' and 'gāvīsū' in the place of the locative—these sixteen words in total are not mentioned because they are formed exclusively by means of the suffix 'ī' and are exclusively designators of the feminine.

Ayaṃ panettha nicchayo vuccate sotūnaṃ nikkaṅkhabhāvāya – itthiliṅgapadesu hi “gāvī gāvi”nti imāni īpaccayavasena vā īkāriṃkārādesavasena vā sijjhanti. Etesu pacchimanayo idhādhippeto, pubbanayo aññattha. Tathā “gāvī gāvi”nti imāni īpaccayavasenapi siddhattā yebhuyyena itthivācakāni bhavanti īkāriṃkārādesavasenapi siddhattā. Katthaci ekakkhaṇeyeva sabbasaṅgāhakavasena itthipumavācakāni bhavanti. Etesupi pacchimoyeva nayo idhādhippeto, pubbanayo aññattha. “Gāviyo. Gāviyā, gāvīhi, gāvībhi. Gāvīnaṃ. Gāviyaṃ, gāvīsū”ti etāni pana īpaccayavaseneva siddhattā sabbathāpi itthīnaṃyeva vācakāni bhavanti. Itthibhūtesveva godabbesu lokasaṅketavasena visesato pavattattā ekantato itthidabbesu pavattāni “migī morī kukkuṭī”iccādīni padāni viya. Kiñcāpi pana “nadī mahī”iccādīnipi itthiliṅgāni īpaccayavaseneva siddhāni, tathāpi tāni aviññāṇakattā tadatthānaṃ itthidabbesu vattantīti vattuṃ na yujjati. Itthipumanapuṃsakabhāvarahitā hi tadatthā. Yasmā pana itthiliṅge gosadde enayogo esukāro ca na labbhati, tasmā “gāvena gavena gāvesu gavesū”ti padāni na vuttāni. Yasmā ca itthiliṅgena gosaddena saddhiṃ sasmāsmiṃvacanāni sarūpato parattaṃ na yanti, tasmā “gāvassa gavassa gāvasmā gavasmā gāvasmiṃ gavasmi”nti padāni na vuttāni. Yasmā ca tattha smāvacanassa ādesabhūto ākāro ca mhākāro ca na labbhati, tasmā “gāvā gavā gāvamhā gavamhā”ti padāni na vuttāni. Yasmā ca smiṃvacanassa ādesabhūto ekāro [M 0.0281] ca mhikāro ca na labbhati, tasmā “gāve gave gāvamhi gavamhī”ti padāni na vuttāni. Apica “yāya tāyā”tiādīhi samānādhikaraṇapadehi yojetuṃ ayuttattāpi “gāvena gavenā”tiādīni itthiliṅgaṭṭhāne na vuttāni. Tathā hi “yāya tāya”iccādīhi saddhiṃ “gāvena gavenā”tiādīni na yojetabbāni ekantapulliṅgarūpattā.

Here this conclusion is stated for the sake of the listeners' freedom from doubt. In the case of feminine-gender terms, the forms 'gāvī' and 'gāvi' are derived either by means of the suffix 'ī' or by means of the substitution of the letters 'ī' and 'iṃ.' Among these, the latter method is intended here, while the former applies elsewhere. Similarly, these forms 'gāvī' and 'gāvi,' because they are also formed by means of the suffix 'ī,' are for the most part designators of the feminine; and because they are also formed by means of the substitution of 'ī' and 'iṃ,' they are sometimes, in a single instance, designators of both feminine and masculine in an all-inclusive sense. Here too, the latter method is intended, while the former applies elsewhere. However, the forms 'gāviyo,' 'gāviyā,' 'gāvīhi,' 'gāvībhi,' 'gāvīnaṃ,' 'gāviyaṃ,' and 'gāvīsū' are formed solely by means of the suffix 'ī' and thus in every way are designators only of females. This is because by worldly convention they are specially used for female bovine beings, just like words such as 'migī' (doe), 'morī' (peahen), and 'kukkuṭī' (hen), which apply exclusively to female beings. And although feminine-gender words such as 'nadī' (river) and 'mahī' (earth) are also formed by means of the suffix 'ī,' it is not right to say that they apply to female beings, because their referents are non-sentient. For their referents are devoid of feminine, masculine, or neuter state. Furthermore, since the suffix 'ena' and the substitution 'esu' are not found with the feminine-gender word 'go,' the forms 'gāvena,' 'gavena,' 'gāvesu,' and 'gavesu' are not stated. And since, with the feminine-gender word 'go,' the endings 'smā' and 'smiṃ' do not undergo a change of form, the forms 'gāvassa,' 'gavassa,' 'gāvasmā,' 'gavasmā,' 'gāvasmiṃ,' and 'gavasmiṃ' are not stated. And since the substitutions 'ā' and 'mhā' for the ending 'smā' are not found there, the forms 'gāvā,' 'gavā,' 'gāvamhā,' and 'gavamhā' are not stated. And since the substitutions 'e' and 'mhi' for the ending 'smiṃ' are not found there, the forms 'gāve,' 'gave,' 'gāvamhi,' and 'gavamhī' are not stated. Moreover, because it is also improper to combine them with co-referential words such as 'yāya,' 'tāyā,' etc., forms such as 'gāvena,' 'gavenā,' etc., are not stated in the place of the feminine gender. For indeed, forms such as 'gāvena,' 'gavenā,' etc., should not be combined with words such as 'yāya,' 'tāyā,' etc., because they are exclusively masculine in form.

Keci panettha vadeyyuṃ – yā tumhehi okārantatāpakatikassa itthiliṅgassa gosaddassa “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo”tiādinā nayena padamālā ṭhapitā, sā “mātugāmo itthī mātugāmā itthiyo”ti vuttasadisā ca hotīti? Tanna. Mātugāmaitthīsaddā hi nānāliṅgā pumitthiliṅgabhāvena, nānādhātukā ca gamu isudhātuvasena, imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne go gāvīsaddā ekaliṅgā itthi liṅgabhāvena, ekadhātukā ca gamudhātuvasenāti. Yajjevaṃ goṇasaddassa gosaddassādesavasena kaccāyanena vuttattā tadādesattaṃ ekadhātukattañcāgamma tenāpi saddhiṃ missetvā padamālā vattabbāti? Na, goṇasaddassa accantapulliṅgattā akārantatāpakatikattā ca. Tathā hi so visuṃ pulliṅgaṭṭhāne uddiṭṭho. Ayaṃ pana “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo”tiādikā padamālā okārīkārantapadāni missetvā katāti na sallakkhetabbā, atha kho vikappena gosaddato paresaṃ si yo aṃvacanānaṃ īkāriṃkārādesavasena vuttapadavantattā okārantitthiliṅgapadamālā icceva sārato paccetabbā.

Some here might say: 'The paradigm that you have established by the method beginning “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo” for the feminine word ‘go,’ which naturally ends in ‘o,’ is similar to what is stated as “mātugāmo itthī, mātugāmā itthiyo” (a woman, women). Is that so?' That is not so. For the words ‘mātugāma’ and ‘itthī’ are of different genders, being masculine and feminine respectively, and from different roots, namely ‘gam’ and ‘isu.’ In this case, however, the words ‘go’ and ‘gāvī’ are of a single gender, the feminine, and from a single root, ‘gam.’ 'If so, since it has been stated by Kaccāyana that ‘goṇa’ (bull) is a substitute for the word ‘go,’ and on account of it being a substitute and from a single root, should a paradigm be stated by mixing it with that too?' No, because ‘goṇa’ is exclusively masculine and naturally ends in ‘a.’ For it is pointed out separately in the section on the masculine. This paradigm beginning “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo,” however, should not be regarded as being formed by mixing words ending in ‘o’ and ‘ī.’ Rather, because it possesses words stated by way of substituting ‘ī’ and ‘iṃ’ optionally for the case endings ‘si,’ ‘yo,’ and ‘aṃ’ after the word ‘go,’ it should be essentially understood as just a paradigm for the feminine o-stem.

Idāni gosaddassa itthiliṅgabhāvasādhakāni suttapadāni lokikappayogāni ca kathayāma – “seyyathāpi bhikkhave vassānaṃ pacchime māse saradasamaye kiṭṭhasambādhe gopālako [M 0.0282] gāvo rakkheyya, tā gāvo tato tato daṇḍena ākoṭeyya.

Now we will state the Sutta passages and worldly usages that establish the feminine gender of the word ‘go’: “Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of the rainy season, in the autumn, when the crops are dense, a cowherd would guard his cattle; he would tap those cattle here and there with a stick.”

Annadā baladā cetā, vaṇṇadā sukhadā ca tā;

Etamatthaṃ vasaṃ ñatvā, nāssu gāvo haniṃsu te.

They are givers of food, givers of strength, givers of beauty, and givers of happiness. Having understood this benefit, those brahmins of old did not kill cattle.

Sabbā gāvo samāharati. Gamissanti bhante gāvo vacchagiddhiniyo”ti imāni suttapadāni. “Gosu duyhamānāsu gato”tiādīni pana lokikappayogāni. Iti gosaddassa itthiliṅgabhāvopi pulliṅgabhāvo viya sārato paccetabbo.

“He gathers all the cattle. Venerable sir, the cows, yearning for their calves, will go”—these are Sutta passages. But such phrases as “He went while the cows were being milked” are worldly usages. Thus, the feminine gender of the word ‘go’ should be essentially understood just like its masculine gender.

Tatra “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo”tiādīni kiñcāpi itthiliṅgabhāvena vuttāni, tathāpi yathāpayogaṃ “pajā devatā”tipadāni viya itthipurisavācakāneva bhavanti, tasmā itthiliṅgavasena “sā go”ti vā “tā gāvo”ti vā vutte itthipumabhūtā sabbepi goṇā gahitāti veditabbā. Na hi īdise ṭhāne ekantato liṅgaṃ padhānaṃ, atthoyeva padhāno. “Vajegāvo duhantī”ti vutte kiñcāpi “gāvo”ti ayaṃ saddo pumepi vattati, tathāpi duhanakriyāya pume asambhavato atthavasena itthiyo ñāyante. “Gāvī duhantī”ti vutte pana liṅgavasena atthavasena ca vacanato ko saṃsayamāpajjissati viññū. “Tā gāvo carantī”ti vutte itthiliṅgavasena vacanato kadāci kassaci saṃsayo siyā “nanu itthiyo”ti, pulliṅgavasena pana “te gāvo carantī”ti vutte saṃsayo natthi, itthiyo ca pumāno ca ñāyante pulliṅgabahuvacanena katthaci itthipumassa gahitattā. “Athettha sīhā byagghā cā”tiādīsu viya “gāvī caratī”ti ca “gāviṃ passatī”ti ca vutte itthī viññāyate gāvīsaddena itthiyā gahetabbattā[M 0.0283]. Lokikappayogesu hi sāsanikappayogesu ca gāvīsaddena itthī gayhati. Ekaccaṃ pana sāsanikappayogaṃ sandhāya “gāvī”ti, “gāvi”nti ca “itthipurisasādhāraṇavacanamavocumha. Tathā hi “seyyathāpi bhikkhave dakkho goghātako vā goghātakantevāsī vā gāviṃ vadhitvā catumahāpathe bilaso vibhajitvā nisinno assā”ti pāḷi dissati. Aṭṭhakathāsu ca “gāvo”ti itthipumasādhāraṇaṃ saddaracanaṃ katvā puna tadeva itthipumaṃ sandhāya “dvāraṃ pattaṃ pattaṃ gāvi”nti racitā saddaracanā dissati.

Here, although such words as “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo” are stated in the feminine gender, still, according to usage, like the words “pajā” and “devatā,” they become designators of both female and male. Therefore, when it is said “sā go” or “tā gāvo” using the feminine gender, it should be known that all cattle, whether female or male, are included. For in such a case, gender is not exclusively primary; meaning alone is primary. When it is said “vajegāvo duhantī” (they milk the cattle in the pen), although this word “gāvo” also applies to males, females are understood by way of the meaning, since the act of milking is impossible for males. But when it is said “gāvī duhantī” (they milk the cow), what wise person would have any doubt, on account of both the gender and the meaning? When it is said “tā gāvo carantī” (those [fem.] cattle are grazing), on account of the feminine gender, someone might sometimes have the doubt, “Surely these are females?” But when it is said “te gāvo carantī” (those [masc.] cattle are grazing) using the masculine gender, there is no doubt; both females and males are understood, because the masculine plural sometimes includes both female and male, as in such phrases as “Here there are lions and tigers.” And when it is said “gāvī caratī” (a cow is grazing) or “gāviṃ passatī” (he sees a cow), a female is understood, because a female is to be taken by the word “gāvī.” For in both worldly and scriptural usages, a female is understood by the word “gāvī.” However, with reference to a certain scriptural usage, we have said that “gāvī” and “gāvi” are words common to female and male. For the Pāḷi is seen: “Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled butcher or his apprentice, having slaughtered a cow (gāviṃ), might sit at a crossroads displaying it piece by piece.” And in the commentaries, having formed the word-construction “gāvo” as common to female and male, again with reference to that same female-and-male group, a word-construction is seen to be composed as “dvāraṃ pattaṃ pattaṃ gāvi” (a cow at every door).

Ettha hi gojātiyaṃ ṭhitā itthīpi pumāpi “gāvī”ti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Visesato pana “gāvī”ti idaṃ itthiyā adhivacanaṃ. Tathā hi tattha tattha pāḷippadesādīsu “acirapakkantassa bhagavato bāhiyaṃ dārucīriyaṃ gāvī taruṇavacchā adhipatitvā jīvitā voropesī”ti, “gāvuṃ vā te demi, gāviṃ vā te demī”ti ca “tiṇasīho kapotavaṇṇagāvīsadiso”ti ca payogadassanato itthī kathiyatīti vattabbaṃ. Gosaddena pana “goduhanaṃ. Gadduhanaṃ. Gokhīraṃ godhano gorūpāni cā”ti dassanato itthīpi pumāpi kathiyatīti vattabbaṃ.

Here, indeed, both a female and a male belonging to the bovine species are reckoned as ‘gāvī.’ But ‘gāvī’ is especially a designation for the female. For, since usages are seen in various Pāḷi passages such as: “Not long after the Blessed One had departed, a cow with a young calf attacked Bāhiya Dārucīriya and deprived him of life”; and “I will give you a gāvuṃ or I will give you a gāviṃ”; and “a grass-lion, similar to a dove-colored cow,” it should be said that a female is spoken of. But with the word ‘go,’ since such examples are seen as “cow-milking,” “milking-pail,” “cow’s milk,” “cattle-wealth,” and “forms of cattle,” it should be said that both female and male are spoken of.

Idāni okārantassa itthiliṅgassa gosaddassa padamālāyaṃ pāḷinayādinissito atthayuttinayo vuccate viññūnaṃ kosallajananatthaṃ –

Now, for the paradigm of the feminine o-stem word ‘go,’ the method of reasoning about the meaning, which is based on the Pāḷi method, is stated for the purpose of generating skill in the wise:

Sā go gacchati, sā gāvī gacchati, tā gāvo, gāvī, gavo gacchanti. Taṃ gāvaṃ, gāviṃ, gavaṃ passati, tā gāvo, gāvī, gavo passati. Tāhi gohi, gobhi kataṃ. Tāsaṃ gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ deti. Tāhi gohi, gobhi apeti. Tāsaṃ gavaṃ[M 0.0284], gunnaṃ, gonaṃ siṅgāni. Tāsu gosu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Bhoti go tvaṃ tiṭṭha, bhotiyo gāvo gāvī, gavā tumhe tiṭṭhatha.

That cow (go) goes; that cow (gāvī) goes; those cows (gāvo, gāvī, gavo) go. One sees that cow (gāvaṃ, gāviṃ, gavaṃ); one sees those cows (gāvo, gāvī, gavo). Done by those cows (gohi, gobhi). One gives to those cows (gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ). One goes away from those cows (gohi, gobhi). The horns of those cows (gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ). Established in those cows (gosu). Good cow (bhoti go), you stand! Good cows (bhotiyo gāvo, gāvī, gavā), you stand!

Aparopi vuccate –

Another method is also stated:

Sā go nadiṃ tarantī gacchati, sā gāvī nadiṃ tarantī gacchati, tā gāvo, gāvī, gavo nadiṃ tarantīyo gacchanti. Taṃ gāvaṃ, gāviṃ, gavaṃ nadiṃ tarantiṃ passati, tā gāvo, gāvī, gavo nadiṃ tarantiyo passati. Tāhi gohi, gobhi nadiṃ tarantīhi kataṃ. Tāsaṃ gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ nadiṃ tarantīnaṃ deti. Tāhi gohi, gobhi nadiṃ tarantīhi apeti. Tāsaṃ gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ nadiṃ tarantīnaṃ santakaṃ. Tāsu gosu nadiṃ tarantīsu patiṭṭhitanti.

That cow (go), crossing the river, goes; that cow (gāvī), crossing the river, goes; those cows (gāvo, gāvī, gavo), crossing the river, go. One sees that cow (gāvaṃ, gāviṃ, gavaṃ) crossing the river; one sees those cows (gāvo, gāvī, gavo) crossing the river. Done by those cows (gohi, gobhi) crossing the river. One gives to those cows (gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ) crossing the river. One goes away from those cows (gohi, gobhi) crossing the river. The property of those cows (gavaṃ, gunnaṃ, gonaṃ) crossing the river. Established in those cows (gosu) crossing the river.

Tatra yā sā “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo”tiādinā okārantassitthiliṅgassa gosaddassa padamālā ṭhapitā, sā “go, gāvo gavo”tiādinā vuttassa okārantapulliṅgassa gosaddassa padamālāto savisesā paccattopayogālapanaṭṭhāne catunnaṃ kaññāsaddānaṃ viya gāvīsaddānaṃ vuttattā. Yasmā panāyaṃ viseso, tasmā imassa okārantitthiliṅgassa gosaddassa aññesamitthiliṅgānaṃ viya avisadākāravohāratā sallakkhetabbā, na pulliṅgānaṃ viya visadākāravohāratā, nāpi napuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ viya ubhayamuttākāravohāratā sallakkhetabbā. Ettha nicchayakaraṇī gāthā vuccati –

Here, the paradigm established for the feminine o-stem word ‘go,’ beginning “go, gāvī, gāvo, gāvī, gavo,” is distinct from the paradigm of the masculine o-stem word ‘go,’ stated as beginning “go, gāvo, gavo,” because of the statement of the ‘gāvī’ words in the nominative, accusative, and vocative cases, like the four ‘kaññā’ words. And since this distinction exists, the indistinct mode of usage of this feminine o-stem word ‘go’ should be noted, like other feminine words; the clearly distinguishable mode of usage, like masculine words, should not be noted, nor the mode of usage free from both, like neuter words. Here a verse that makes a decision is stated:

Duvinnaṃ dhātusaddānaṃ, yathā dissati nānatā;

Gosaddānaṃ tathā dvinnaṃ, icchitabbāva nānatā.

Just as a difference is seen between the two words ‘dhātu,’ so too a difference should be accepted between the two words ‘go.’

Tathā hi pumitthiliṅgavasena dvinnaṃ dhātusaddānaṃ viseso dissati. Taṃ yathā?

For a distinction is seen between the two words ‘dhātu’ based on masculine and feminine gender. How so?

Dhātu[M 0.0285], dhātū, dhātavo. Dhātuṃ, dhātū, dhātavo. Dhātunā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātussa, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātusmā, dhātumhā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātussa, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātusmiṃ, dhātumhi, dhātūsu. Ayaṃ pulliṅgaviseso.

Dhātu, dhātū, dhātavo. Dhātuṃ, dhātū, dhātavo. Dhātunā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātussa, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātusmā, dhātumhā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātussa, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātusmiṃ, dhātumhi, dhātūsu. This is the masculine paradigm.

Dhātu, dhātū, dhātuyo. Dhātuṃ, dhātū, dhātuyo. Dhātuyā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātuyā, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātuyā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātuyā, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātuyā, dhātuyaṃ, dhātūsu. Ayaṃ itthiliṅgassa viseso.

Dhātu, dhātū, dhātuyo. Dhātuṃ, dhātū, dhātuyo. Dhātuyā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātuyā, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātuyā, dhātūhi, dhātūbhi. Dhātuyā, dhātūnaṃ. Dhātuyā, dhātuyaṃ, dhātūsu. This is the feminine paradigm.

Yathā ca dvinnaṃ dhātusaddānaṃ viseso paññāyati, tathā dvinnampi gosaddānaṃ viseso paññāyateva. Yathā ca punnapuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ dvinnaṃ āyusaddānaṃ “āyu, āyū, āyavo”tiādinā, “āyu, āyū, āyūnī”tiādinā ca viseso paññāyati, yathā dvinnampi gosaddānaṃ viseso paññāyateva. Tathā hi visadākāravohāro pulliṅgaṃ, avisadākāravohāro itthiliṅgaṃ, ubhayamuttākāravohāro napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

And just as a distinction is discerned between the two words ‘dhātu,’ so too a distinction is indeed discerned between the two words ‘go.’ And just as a distinction is discerned between the two words ‘āyu’ of masculine and neuter gender by way of the paradigms beginning “āyu, āyū, āyavo” and “āyu, āyū, āyūnī” respectively, so too a distinction is indeed discerned between the two words ‘go.’ For a clearly distinguishable mode of usage is masculine gender, an indistinct mode of usage is feminine gender, and a mode of usage free from both is neuter gender.

Idāni imamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ katvā saṅkhepato kathayāma – purisoti visadākāravohāro, kaññāti avisadākāravohāro, rūpanti ubhayamuttākāravohāro. Puriso tiṭṭhati, kaññā tiṭṭhati, kaññā tiṭṭhanti, kaññā passati, bhotiyo kaññā tiṭṭhatha, etthekapadamasamaṃ, cattāri samāni. Purisā tiṭṭhanti, purisā nissaṭaṃ, bhavanto purisā gacchatha. Kaññāyo tiṭṭhanti, kaññāyo passati, bhotiyo kaññāyo gacchatha, tīṇi tīṇi samāni. Purisaṃ passati, kaññaṃ passati, dve asamāni. Purise passati, purise patiṭṭhitaṃ, dve samāni. Tena purisena kataṃ, tāya kaññāya kataṃ, tāya kaññāya deti, tāya kaññāya [M 0.0286] apeti, tāya kaññāya santakaṃ, tāya kaññāya patiṭṭhitaṃ, ekamasamaṃ, pañca samāni. Evaṃ pulliṅgassa visadākāravohāratā dissati, itthiliṅgassa avisadākāravohāratā dissati. Napuṃsakaliṅgassa pana “rūpaṃ, rūpāni, rūpā. Rūpaṃ, rūpāni, rūpe. Bho rūpa, bhavanto rūpāni, rūpā”ti evaṃ tīsu paccattopayogālapanaṭṭhānesu sanikārāya visesāya rūpamālāya vasena ubhayamuttākāravohāratā dissati, pumitthiliṅgānaṃ tīsu ṭhānesu sanikārāni rūpāni sabbadā na santi, iti visadākāravohāro pulliṅgaṃ, avisadākāravohāro itthiliṅgaṃ, ubhayamuttākāravohāro napuṃsakaliṅganti veditabbaṃ.

Now, making this matter clearer, we shall briefly explain: 'puriso' (a man) is a clearly distinguishable expression, 'kaññā' (a maiden) is an indistinct expression, and 'rūpaṃ' (form) is an expression free from both. 'Puriso tiṭṭhati' (a man stands), 'kaññā tiṭṭhati' (a maiden stands), 'kaññā tiṭṭhanti' (maidens stand), 'kaññā passati' (one sees maidens), 'bhotiyo kaññā tiṭṭhatha' (honored maidens, stand)—here one word is dissimilar, four are similar. 'Purisā tiṭṭhanti' (men stand), 'purisā nissaṭaṃ' (men have departed), 'bhavanto purisā gacchatha' (honored men, go). 'Kaññāyo tiṭṭhanti' (maidens stand), 'kaññāyo passati' (one sees maidens), 'bhotiyo kaññāyo gacchatha' (honored maidens, go)—three are similar, three are similar. 'Purisaṃ passati' (one sees a man), 'kaññaṃ passati' (one sees a maiden)—two are dissimilar. 'Purise passati' (one sees men), 'purise patiṭṭhitaṃ' (established among men)—two are similar. 'Tena purisena kataṃ' (done by that man), 'tāya kaññāya kataṃ' (done by that maiden), 'tāya kaññāya deti' (one gives to that maiden), 'tāya kaññāya apeti' (one departs from that maiden), 'tāya kaññāya santakaṃ' (belonging to that maiden), 'tāya kaññāya patiṭṭhitaṃ' (established by that maiden)—one is dissimilar, five are similar. Thus, the clearly distinguishable nature of the masculine gender is seen, and the indistinct nature of the feminine gender is seen. As for the neuter gender, with 'rūpaṃ, rūpāni, rūpā. Rūpaṃ, rūpāni, rūpe. Bho rūpa, bhavanto rūpāni, rūpā'—in these three cases of nominative, accusative, and vocative, due to the special paradigm with its variety of forms, a nature free from both is seen. For masculine and feminine genders, in these three cases, forms with such variation are not always present. Thus, it should be understood: a clearly distinguishable expression is the masculine gender, an indistinct expression is the feminine gender, and an expression free from both is the neuter gender.

Ayaṃ nayo “saddhā sati hirī, yā itthī saddhā pasannā, te manussā saddhā pasannā, pahūtaṃ saddhaṃ paṭiyattaṃ, saddhaṃ kula”ntiādīsu samānasutikasaddesupi padamālāvasena labbhateva. Yā ca pana itthiliṅgassa avisadākāravohāratā vuttā, sā ekaccesupi saṅkhyāsaddesu labbhati. Tathā hi vīsatiādayo navutipariyantā saddā ekavacanantā itthiliṅgāti vuttā, ettha “vīsatiyā”ti pañcakkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ, tathā “tiṃsāyā”tiādīnaṃ “navutiyā”ti padapariyantānaṃ, evaṃ vīsatiādīnaṃ kaññāsaddasseva avisadākāravohāratā labbhatīti avagantabbaṃ. Yadi evaṃ ticatusaddesu kathanti? Ticatusaddā pana yasmā “tayo tisso tīṇi, cattāro caturo catasso cattārī”ti attano attano rūpāni abhidheyyaliṅgānugabhattā yathāsakaliṅgavasena “purisā kaññāyo cittānī”tiādīhi visadāvisadobhayarahitākāravohārasaṅkhātehi saddehi yogaṃ gacchanti, tasmā paccekaliṅgavasena visadāvisadobhayarahitākāravohārāti vattumarahanti.

This method is obtained, by way of word-series, even in words of similar sound, as in 'faith, mindfulness, moral shame,' 'that woman is faithful and devoted,' 'those people are faithful and devoted,' 'abundant faith is prepared,' 'a faithful family,' and so on. And the indistinct mode of usage mentioned for the feminine gender is also found in some numerical terms. For example, words from 'vīsati' (twenty) up to 'navuti' (ninety) are said to be singular and of feminine gender. Here, 'vīsatiyā' should be said five times, and similarly for 'tiṃsāyā' and so on, up to the word 'navutiyā.' Thus, it should be understood that the indistinct mode of usage of words like 'vīsati' is similar to that of 'kaññā' (maiden). If so, what about the words 'three' and 'four'? Since the words 'three' and 'four'—'tayo, tisso, tīṇi' and 'cattāro, caturo, catasso, cattārī'—have their own forms which, conforming to the gender of what they denote, combine with words like 'purisā,' 'kaññāyo,' 'cittānī,' etc., which are characterized by modes of usage that are distinct, indistinct, or neither, therefore they are fit to be described as having modes of usage that are distinct, indistinct, or neither, according to their individual genders.

Sabbanāmesupi [M 0.0287] ayaṃ tividho ākāro labbhati rūpavisesayogato. Kathaṃ? Punnapuṃsakavisaye “tassa kassa” iccādīni sabbāni sabbanāmikarūpāni catutthīchaṭṭhiyantāni bhavanti, itthiliṅgavisaye “tassā kassā” iccādīni sabbanāmikarūpāni tatiyācatutthīpañcamīchaṭṭhīsattamiyantāni bhavanti, tasmā sabbanāmattepi itthiliṅgassa avisadākāravohāratā ekantato sampaṭicchitabbā. Ettha pana sulabhāni catutthīchaṭṭhīrūpāni anāharitvā sudullabhabhāvena tatiyāpañcamīsattamīrūpāni sāsanato āharitvā dassessāma bhagavato pāvacane nikkaṅkhabhāvena sotūnaṃ paramasaṇhasukhumañāṇādhigamatthaṃ. Taṃ yathā? “Āyasmā udāyī yena sā kumārikā tenupasaṅkami, upasaṅkamitvā tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ eko ekāya raho paṭicchanne āsane alaṃkammanīye nisajjaṃ kappesī”ti. Ettha “tassā”ti tatiyāya rūpaṃ, “tassā”ti tatiyāya rūpe diṭṭheyeva “sabbassā katarissā”tiādīni tatiyārūpāni pāḷiyaṃ anāgatānipidiṭṭhāniyeva nāma tesaṃ aññamaññasamānagatikattā, diṭṭhena ca adiṭṭhassapi yuttassa gahetabbattā. “Kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmī”ti ettha “kassā”ti pañcamiyā rūpaṃ, “kassā”ti pañcamiyā rūpe diṭṭheyeva “sabbassā katarissā”tiādīni pañcamiyā rūpāni pāḷiyaṃ anāgatānipi diṭṭhāniyeva nāma. “Aññataro bhikkhu vesāliyaṃ mahāvane makkaṭiṃ āmisena upalāpetvā tassā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevati. Aññataro bhikkhu aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto hotī”ti ca ettha “tassā aññatarissā”ti ca sattamiyā rūpaṃ, tasmiṃ diṭṭheyeva “sabbassā katarissā”tiādīni sattamiyā rūpāni pāḷiyaṃ anāgatānipi diṭṭhāniyeva nāmāti.

In all pronouns, this threefold mode is found due to connection with specific forms. How so? In the masculine and neuter genders, all pronominal forms such as 'tassa kassa' end in the fourth or sixth case. In the feminine gender, forms such as 'tassā kassā' end in the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh case. Therefore, even in pronouns, the indistinct mode of usage for the feminine gender must be entirely accepted. Here, however, not presenting the easily found fourth and sixth case forms, we will, due to their extreme rarity, instead present the third, fifth, and seventh case forms, having brought them from the teaching to demonstrate them for the sake of listeners who are free from doubt in the Blessed One’s teaching, for the attainment of the highest, subtle, and refined knowledge. For example: 'The Venerable Udāyī approached that maiden, and having approached, he arranged to sit down alone with that maiden on a secluded, suitable seat.' Here, 'tassā' is a form of the third case. When the third case form 'tassā' is seen, other third case forms such as 'sabbassā katarissā', even though they have not appeared in the Pāḷi, are indeed to be considered as seen due to their shared grammatical nature, and because what is suitable, though unseen, is to be inferred from what is seen. In 'From whom am I separated? By what am I diminished?', 'kassā' is a form of the fifth case. When the fifth case form 'kassā' is seen, other fifth case forms such as 'sabbassā katarissā', even though they have not appeared in the Pāḷi, are likewise to be considered as seen. In 'A certain monk in Vesālī, in the Great Wood, having enticed a female monkey with bait, engaged in sexual intercourse with her,' and 'A certain monk is emotionally attached to a certain woman,' here 'tassā' and 'aññatarissā' are forms of the seventh case. When these are seen, other seventh case forms such as 'sabbassā katarissā', even though they have not appeared in the Pāḷi, are similarly to be considered as seen.

Nanu [M 0.0288] ca bho “tassā kumārikāya saddhi”nti ettha “tassā”ti idaṃ vibhattivipallāsena vuttaṃ, “tāyā”ti hissa attho, tathā “kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmī”ti idampi vibhattivipallāsena vuttaṃ. “Kāyā”ti hissa attho. “Aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto”ti etthāpi “aññatarissā”ti idaṃ vibhattivipallāsena vuttaṃ. “Aññatarissa”nti hissa atthoti? Tanna, īdisesu cuṇṇiyapadavisayesu vibhattivipallāsassa anicchitabbattā. Nanu ca bho cuṇṇiyapadavisayepi “saṅghe gotami dehī”tiādīsu “saṅghassā”ti vibhattivipallāsatthaṃ vadanti garūti? Saccaṃ, tathāpi tādisesu ṭhānesu dve adhippāyā bhavanti ādhārapaṭiggāhakabhāvena bhummasampadānānamicchitabbattā. Tathā hi “saṅghassa dethā”ti vattukāmassa sato “saṅghe dethā”ti vacanaṃ na virujjhati, yujjatiyeva. Tathā “saṅghe dethā”ti vattukāmassapi sato “saṅghassa dethā”ti vacanampi na virujjhati, yujjatiyeva, yathā pana alābu lābusaddesu visuṃ visuṃ vijjamānesupi “lābūni sīdanti silā plavantī”ti ettha chandānurakkhaṇatthaṃ akāralopo hotīti akkharalopo buddhiyā kariyati. Tathā “saṅghe gotami dehī”tiādīsupi buddhiyā vibhattivipallāsassa parikappanaṃ katvā “saṅghassā”ti vipallāsatthamicchanti ācariyā. Tasmā “saṅghe gotami dehi. Vessantare varaṃ datvā”tiādīsu vibhattivipallāso yutto “tassā kumārikāyā”tiādīsu pana na yutto, vibhattivipallāso ca nāma yebhuyyena “neva dānaṃ viramissa”ntiādīsu gāthāsu icchitabbo.

But, sir, is it not so that in 'with that maiden' ('tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ'), 'tassā' is said through case-interchange, its meaning being 'with her' ('tāyā'); similarly, in 'From whom am I separated? By what am I diminished?' ('kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmī'), is this also said through case-interchange, its meaning being 'from whom' ('kāyā'); and again here, in 'his mind was attached to a certain woman' ('aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto'), is 'aññatarissā' also said through case-interchange, its meaning being 'to a certain one' ('aññatarassa')? That is not so, because case-interchange should not be accepted in such contexts of prose passages. But, sir, even in contexts of prose passages, do not the teachers say that in cases such as 'Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha' ('saṅghe gotami dehī'), the meaning is that of 'saṅghassa' through case-interchange? It is true, yet in such places, two intentions are possible, through the state of being a location or a recipient, since the locative and dative cases are to be accepted. For instance, for one intending to say 'give to the Saṅgha' ('saṅghassa dethā'), the statement 'give in the Saṅgha' ('saṅghe dethā') is not contradictory—it is indeed acceptable. Similarly, for one intending to say 'give in the Saṅgha' ('saṅghe dethā'), the statement 'give to the Saṅgha' ('saṅghassa dethā') is also not contradictory—it is indeed acceptable. Just as, although 'alābu' and 'lābu' exist as distinct words, in 'gourds sink, stones float' ('lābūni sīdanti silā plavantī'), the elision of the letter 'a' occurs for the sake of maintaining the meter, and this elision of the letter is done mentally. Likewise, in cases such as 'Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha' ('saṅghe gotami dehī'), the teachers, having mentally conceived of a case-interchange, accept the meaning of 'saṅghassa' through interchange. Therefore, in expressions like 'Gotamī, give to the Saṅgha' and 'having given the boon to Vessantara,' case-interchange is appropriate, but in phrases like 'with that maiden,' it is not appropriate. And case-interchange is mostly to be accepted in verses, as in 'nor would he refrain from giving' ('neva dānaṃ viramissa').

Tathāpi vadeyya yā sā tumhehi “tassā methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevatī”ti pāḷi ābhatā, na sā sattamīpayogā. “Tassā”ti [M 0.0289] hi idaṃ chaṭṭhiyantapadaṃ “tassāmakkaṭiyāaṅgajāte methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevatī”ti atthasambhavatoti? Tanna, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tassāti bhummavacana”nti vuttattā. Kiñca bhiyyo – aṭṭhakathāyaṃyeva “tassā ca sikkhāya sikkhaṃ paripūrento sikkhati, tasmiñca sikkhāpade avītikkamanto sikkhatī”ti imasmiṃ padese “tassā”ti bhummavacanaṃ niddeso katoti. Nanu ca bho tatthāpi “tassā”ti idaṃ vibhattivipallāsavasena bhummatthe sāmivacananti? “Ativiya tvaṃ vibhattivipallāsanaye kusalosi, vibhattivipallāsiko nāmā”ti bhavaṃ vattabbo. Yo tvaṃ dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi vuttapāḷimpi ullaṅghasi, aṭṭhakathāvacanampi ullaṅghasi, aparampi te niddesapāḷiṃ āharissāma. Sace tvaṃ paṇḍitajātiko, saññattiṃ gamissasi. Sace apaṇḍitajātiko, attano gāhaṃ amuñcantoyeva saññattiṃ na gamissati, sāsane cittiṃ katvā suṇohīti. “Tasmā hi sikkhetha idheva jantū”ti imissā pāḷiyā atthaṃ niddisantena pabhinnapaṭisambhidena satthukappena aggasāvakena dhammasenāpatinā āyasmatā sāriputtena “idhāti imissā diṭṭhiyā imissā khantiyā imissā ruciyā imasmiṃ ādāye imasmiṃ dhamme”ti evaṃ “imissā”ti padaṃ bhummavacanavasena vuttaṃ. Tañhi “idhā”ti padassa atthavācakattā sattamiyā rūpanti viññāyati. Iti “imissā”ti sattamiyā rūpe diṭṭheyeva “sabbassā katarissā”tiādīni sattamiyā rūpāni pāḷiyaṃ anāgatānipi diṭṭhāniyeva nāma.

Still, one might say: ‘The Pāḷi passage brought forward by you, “he engages in sexual intercourse with her,” is not a locative usage. For is not this word “tassā” a word ending in the genitive case, as the meaning is possible: “he engages in sexual intercourse in the sexual organ of that female monkey”?’ That is not so, for in the commentary it is said: ‘“tassā” is a locative expression.’ Furthermore, in the commentary itself, in this passage, ‘He trains by fulfilling the training in that training, and he trains by not transgressing that training rule,’ the word ‘tassā’ is explained as a locative expression. But, sir, even there, is not this word ‘tassā’ a genitive expression in the locative sense by way of case-interchange? One should say to him: ‘You are very skilled in the method of case-interchange; you are indeed an expert in case-interchange!’ You who transgress the Pāḷi stated by the Elder Compilers of the Dhamma and also transgress the word of the commentary, we will bring you another explanatory Pāḷi passage. If you are of a wise nature, you will be convinced. If you are of an unwise nature, not abandoning your own grasp, you will not be convinced. Listen, having paid respect to the Teaching. When indicating the meaning of this Pāḷi passage, ‘Therefore a person should train right here,’ the Venerable Sāriputta—the General of the Dhamma, the chief disciple, equal to the Teacher, who had attained the analytical knowledges—stated the word ‘imissā’ in the locative sense thus: ‘“Here” means in this view, in this forbearance, in this inclination, in this acceptance, in this Dhamma.’ For since it is a word expressing the meaning of the word ‘idha,’ it is known to be a form of the locative. Thus, when the locative form ‘imissā’ is seen, locative forms such as ‘sabbassā,’ ‘katarissā,’ etc., even though they have not appeared in the Pāḷi, are indeed to be considered as seen.

Aparampi te sabbalokānukampakena sabbaññunā āhaccabhāsitaṃ pāḷiṃ āharissāma, cittiṃ katvā suṇohi, “aṭṭhānametaṃ bhikkhave anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā [M 0.0290] apubbaṃ acarimaṃ dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā uppajjeyyu”nti ettha “ekissā”ti idaṃ sattamiyā rūpaṃ. Evaṃ “ekissā”ti sattamiyā rūpe diṭṭheyeva “sabbassā katarissā”tiādīni sattamiyā rūpāni pāḷiyaṃ anāgatānipi diṭṭhāniyeva nāma. Na hi sabbathāpi vohārā sarūpato pāḷiādīsu dissanti, ekacce dissanti, ekacce na dissantiyeva. Atridaṃ vuccati –

Furthermore, we will bring you a Pāḷi passage spoken deliberately by the Omniscient One, who has compassion for the whole world. Listen, having paid respect: ‘Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is not possible that in one world-system two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise neither before nor after one another.’ Here, ‘ekissā’ is a form of the locative. Thus, when the locative form ‘ekissā’ is seen, locative forms such as ‘sabbassā,’ ‘katarissā,’ etc., even though they have not appeared in the Pāḷi, are indeed to be considered as seen. For usages are not in every way seen in their own form in the Pāḷi and so on; some are seen, some are not seen at all. Herein this is said:

“Tassā”iccādayo saddā, “tāya”iccādayo viya;

Ñeyyā pañcasu ṭhānesu, tatiyādīsu dhīmatā.

Words such as ‘tassā,’ like those such as ‘tāya,’ should be known by the wise in five cases, from the instrumental onwards.

Tiṇṇannaṃ pana nādīnaṃ, hoti sabyapadesato;

“Tassā kassā”tiādīni, bhavanti tatiyādisu.

But for the three pronouns, by way of a special designation, forms such as ‘tassā,’ ‘kassā,’ etc., occur in the instrumental and subsequent cases.

Atra panāyaṃ pāḷinayavibhāvanā aṭṭhakathānayavibhāvanā ca – tassā kaññāya saddhiṃ gacchati, tassā kaññāya kataṃ, tassā kaññāya deti, tassā kaññāya apeti, tassā kaññāya ayaṃ kaññā hīnā, tassā kaññāya ayaṃ kaññā adhikā, tassā kaññāya santakaṃ, tassā kaññāya patiṭṭhitanti. Dullabhāyaṃ nīti sādhukaṃ cittiṃ katvā pariyāpuṇitabbā sāsanassa ciraṭṭhitatthaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi pāḷiaṭṭhakathānayānusārena itthiliṅgassa avisadākāravohāratā ñātabbā.

Herein, this is the explanation of the method of the Pāḷi and the explanation of the method of the commentary: he goes with that girl, it is done by that girl, he gives to that girl, he departs from that girl, this girl is inferior to that girl, this girl is superior to that girl, it belongs to that girl, it is established in that girl. This principle is hard to find; having paid careful respect, it should be thoroughly learned for the long endurance of the Teaching. Thus, in every way, the indistinct mode of usage of the feminine gender should be known in accordance with the method of the Pāḷi and the commentaries.

Evaṃ pana ñatvā viññujātinā “dvinnaṃ gosaddānaṃ rūpamālāvisesena liṅganānattaṃ hotī”ti niṭṭhametthāvagantabbaṃ. Gosaddo hi “puriso mātugāmo orodho āpo satthā”tiādayo viya na niyogā visadākāravohāro, nāpi “kaññā ratti itthī”tiādayo viya niyogā avisadākāravohāro. Tathā hi ayaṃ pulliṅgabhāve dhātusaddo viya visadākāravohāro, itthiliṅgabhāve avisadākāravohāro[M 0.0291]. Iti imassa atthassa sotūnaṃ ñāpanena paramasaṇhasukhumañāṇappaṭilābhattaṃ “go, gāvī gāvo. Gāviṃ, gavo”tiādinā okārantassa itthiliṅgassa gosaddassa āveṇikā nāmikapadamālā vuttā. Ettha pana “gāvi”nti ekakkhattumāgataṃ, “go gohī”tiādīni dvikkhattuṃ, “gāvo gāvī gāva”nti tikkhattuṃ, “gāviyā”ti pañcakkhattuṃ, evamettha pañcakkhattuṃ āgatapadānaṃ vasena avisadākāro dissatīti idaṃ itthiliṅganti gahetabbaṃ. Imañhi nayaṃ muñcitvā natthi añño nayo yena gosaddo itthiliṅgo siyā. Tasmā idameva amhākaṃ mataṃ sārato paccetabbaṃ. Pumitthiliṅgasaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnaṃ gosaddānaṃ rūpamālāya nibbisesataṃ vadantānaṃ pana ācariyānaṃ mataṃ pulliṅge vattamānena gosaddeni’tthiliṅge vattamānassa gosaddassa rūpamālāya sadisatte sati mātugāmasaddassa nāmikapadamālāyo samaṃ yojetvā pumitthiliṅgabhāvaparikappanaṃ viya hotīti na sārato paccetabbaṃ.

Having thus understood, a wise person should arrive at the conclusion: ‘The two words “go” have a difference of gender because of the difference in their paradigm of forms.’ For the word ‘go’ is not necessarily a usage with a distinct form like ‘puriso,’ ‘mātugāmo,’ ‘orodho,’ ‘āpo,’ ‘satthā,’ etc., nor is it necessarily a usage with an indistinct form like ‘kaññā,’ ‘ratti,’ ‘itthī,’ etc. For this word, when it is masculine, is a usage with a distinct form like the word ‘dhātu,’ but when it is feminine, it is a usage with an indistinct form. Thus, by way of making this meaning known to the listeners and for the attainment of the most subtle and refined knowledge, the specific nominal paradigm of the feminine word ‘go’ ending in ‘o’ has been stated as: ‘go, gāvī, gāvo. Gāviṃ, gavo,’ etc. Herein, ‘gāvi’ has come once; ‘go,’ ‘gohī,’ etc., twice; ‘gāvo,’ ‘gāvī,’ ‘gāva,’ thrice; ‘gāviyā,’ five times. Thus, herein, by way of the words that have come five times, an indistinct form is seen. This should be taken as feminine. For apart from this method, there is no other method by which the word ‘go’ could be feminine. Therefore, this very view of ours should be accepted as essential. But the view of those teachers who say that the paradigm of forms of the two words ‘go,’ designated as masculine and feminine, is without difference—since, when the paradigm of forms of the word ‘go’ in the feminine is similar to the word ‘go’ in the masculine, it is like the positing of masculine and feminine states by combining equally the nominal paradigms of the word ‘mātugāma’—should not be accepted as essential.

Ettha pana kiñci liṅgasaṃsandanaṃ kathayāma – heṭṭhā niddiṭṭhassa okārantapulliṅgassa gosaddassa nāmikapadamālāyaṃ “gāvuṃ gāvaṃ gāvenā”tiādīni ekakkhattumāgatāni, “go gohī”tiādīni dvikkhattuṃ, “gāvo gavo gava”nti imāni pana “satthā rājā”tiādīni viya tikkhattuṃ, catukkhattuṃ vā panettha pañcakkhattuṃ vā āgatapadāni na santi. Tadabhāvato visadākāro dissati. Purisasaddassa nāmikapadamālāyampi “puriso purisa”ntiādīni ekakkhattumāgatāni, “purise”tiādīni dvikkhattuṃ, “purisā”ti tikkhattuṃ. Evaṃ visadākāro dissati. Ākārantitthiliṅgassa pana “kañña”ntiādīni ekakkhattumāgatāni, “kaññāhī”tiādīni dvikkhattuṃ, “kaññāyo”tiādīni tikkhattuṃ, “kaññā”ti idaṃ catukkhattuṃ, “kaññāyā”ti idaṃ pana pañcakkhattuṃ. Evaṃ avisadākāro dissati. Ākārantapulliṅgassatu “sattharī”tiādīni ekakkhattumāgatāni, “satthū”tiādīni [M 0.0292] dvikkhattuṃ, “satthā”tiādīni tikkhattuṃ, evaṃ visadākāro dissati. Iminā nayena sabbāsupi pumitthiliṅgapadamālāsu visadākāro ca avisadākāro ca veditabbo. Napuṃsakaliṅgassa pana nāmikapadamālāyaṃ “cittenā”tiādīni ekakkhattumāgatāni, “citta”ntiādīni dvikkhattuṃ, “cittānī”ti idaṃ tikkhattuṃ āgataṃ. Aṭṭhi āyusaddādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettha ubhayamuttākāro dissati. Kiñcāpettha catukkhattuṃ pañcakkhattuṃ vā āgatapadānaṃ abhāvato visadākāro upalabbhamāno viya dissati, tathāpi yasmā “cittaṃ aṭṭhi āyū”tiādīni napuṃsakāni “gacchaṃ aggi bhikkhū”tiādīnaṃ pulliṅgānaṃ nayena appavattanato visadākārañca, “ratti yāgū”tiādīnaṃ itthiliṅgānaṃ nayena appavattanato avisadākārañca ubhayamanupagamma visesato “cittaṃ, cittāni, cittā. Cittaṃ, cittāni, citte”tiādinā sanikārāya rūpamālāya rūpavantāni bhavanti, tasmā tesamākāro ubhayamuttoti daṭṭhabbo.

Herein we shall speak of some comparison of genders: In the nominal paradigm of the masculine word ‘go’ ending in ‘o’ indicated below, forms such as ‘gāvuṃ,’ ‘gāvaṃ,’ ‘gāvena,’ etc., have come once; forms such as ‘go,’ ‘gohī,’ etc., twice; but these forms ‘gāvo,’ ‘gavo,’ ‘gava,’ like ‘satthā,’ ‘rājā,’ etc., thrice. Herein there are no words that have come four or five times. Because of their absence, a distinct form is seen. Also in the nominal paradigm of the masculine word ‘purisa,’ forms such as ‘puriso,’ ‘purisa,’ etc., have come once; ‘purise,’ etc., twice; ‘purisā,’ thrice. Thus a distinct form is seen. But for the feminine ending in -ā, forms such as ‘kañña,’ etc., have come once; ‘kaññāhī,’ etc., twice; ‘kaññāyo,’ etc., thrice; this ‘kaññā’ four times; but this ‘kaññāyā’ five times. Thus an indistinct form is seen. But for the masculine ending in -ā, forms such as ‘sattharī,’ etc., have come once; ‘satthū,’ etc., twice; ‘satthā,’ etc., thrice. Thus a distinct form is seen. By this method, in all masculine and feminine paradigms, the distinct form and the indistinct form should be understood. But in the nominal paradigm of a neuter gender word, forms such as ‘cittenā,’ etc., have come once; ‘citta,’ etc., twice; this ‘cittāni’ has come thrice. This is the same method for the words ‘aṭṭhi,’ ‘āyu,’ etc. Herein a form free from both is seen. And although herein, because of the absence of words that have come four or five times, a distinct form seems to be found, nevertheless, because neuter words such as ‘cittaṃ,’ ‘aṭṭhi,’ ‘āyu,’ etc., not following the method of masculine words such as ‘gacchaṃ,’ ‘aggi,’ ‘bhikkhū,’ etc., and not following the method of feminine words such as ‘ratti,’ ‘yāgu,’ etc., do not fall into either the distinct form or the indistinct form, but are specifically formed with a paradigm of forms with ‘-ni,’ such as ‘cittaṃ, cittāni, cittā. Cittaṃ, cittāni, citte,’ etc., therefore their form should be seen as free from both.

Tividhopāyaṃ ākāro sakkaṭabhāsāsu na labbhati. Tenesa sabbesupi byākaraṇasatthesu na vutto. Sabbasattānaṃ pana mūlabhāsābhūtāya jineritāya māgadhikāya sabhāvaniruttiyā labbhati. Tathā hi ayaṃ niruttimañjūsāyaṃ vutto –

This threefold form is not found in the Sanskrit languages. Therefore it is not stated in any of the grammatical treatises. But it is found in the natural language of Māgadhī, spoken by the Jina, which is the root language of all beings. For thus it is stated in the Niruttimañjūsā:

Kiṃ panetaṃ liṅgaṃ nāma? Keci tāva vadanti –

But what is this thing called gender? Some say:

“Thanakesavatī itthī, massuvā puriso siyā. Ubhinnamantaraṃ etaṃ, itaro’bhayamuttako’ti

A woman has breasts and hair, a man would have a beard. This is the difference between the two; the other is free from both.

Vuttattā visiṭṭhā thanakesādayo liṅga”nti, etaṃ na sabbattha, gaṅgāsālārukkhādīnaṃ thanādinā sambandhābhāvato.

Because it is said, ‘Specific things like breasts, hair, etc., are gender.’ This is not so everywhere, because of the absence of a connection with breasts and so on for things like the Ganges, a hall, a tree, etc.

Apare [M 0.0293] vadanti – “na liṅgaṃ nāma paramatthato kiñci atthi, lokasaṅketarūḷho pana vohāro liṅgaṃ nāmā”ti. Idamettha sanniṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbaliṅgikopi saddo hoti taṭaṃ taṭī taṭoti. Yadi ca paramatthato liṅgaṃ nāma siyā, kathaṃ aññamaññaviruddhānaṃ tesaṃ ekattha samāveso bhavati, tasmā yassa kassaci atthassa avisadākāravohāro itthiliṅgaṃ, visadākāravohāro pulliṅgaṃ, ubhayamuttākāravohāro napuṃsakaliṅganti veditabbanti.

Others say: 'In an ultimate sense, there is nothing at all called gender; rather, “gender” is a conventional usage established by worldly convention.' This is the conclusion here. A word can also be of all genders, such as taṭaṃ, taṭī, and taṭo. If gender existed in an ultimate sense, how could there be a convergence of those mutually contradictory forms in one place? Therefore, it should be known that for any given meaning, the usage with an indistinct form is the feminine gender, the usage with a distinct form is the masculine gender, and the usage with a form devoid of both is the neuter gender.

Ettha pana nāmikapadamālāsaṅkhātapabandhavaseneva avisadākāravohārāditā gahetabbā, na ekekapadavasena. Tathā hi “kaññā puriso citta”nti ca, “kaññāyo purisā cittānī”ti ca evamādikassa ekekapadassa avisadākāravohārāditā na dissati. Yasmā pana pabandhavasena visadākāravohārādibhāve siddheyeva samudāyāvayavattā ekekapadassapi avisadākāravohārāditā sijjhateva.

Here, however, indistinctness of form in usage and so on should be understood by way of the composition known as the series of nominal words, not by way of individual words. For in expressions such as 'a maiden, a man, a mind' and 'maidens, men, minds,' the indistinctness of form in usage and so on is not seen in each individual word. But since the state of having a distinct form in usage and so on is established by way of the composition, the indistinctness of form in usage and so on of each individual word is also established, because it is a part of the whole.

Keci pana nāmikapadamālāsaṅkhātaṃ pabandhaṃ aparāmasitvā ekekapadavaseneva avisadākāravohārādikaṃ icchanti, te vattabbā “yadi ekekapadasseva avisadākāravohārāditā siyā, evaṃ sante ‘kaññā purisā satthā guṇavā rājā’tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ ākārasutivasena, ‘puriso satthāro kaññāyo’tiādīnaṃ pana okārasutivasena, ‘cittaṃ purisaṃ kañña’ntiādīnaṃ anusārasutivasena aññamaññaṃ samānasutisambhavā kathaṃ avisadākāravohārāditā siyā”ti? Kiñcāpi te evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “siyā eva, nānattaṃ pana tesaṃ duppaṭivedha”nti. Te vattabbā “mā tumhe evamavacuttha, dujjānatarampi nibbānaṃ kathanasamatthaṃ puggalaṃ nissāya jānanti, tasmā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā vadethā”ti. Evañca pana vatvā [M 0.0294] tato uttari te pañhaṃ pucchitabbā “bodhisaddo āyusaddo ca kataraliṅgo”ti. Te jānantā evaṃ vakkhanti “bodhisaddo itthiliṅgo ceva pulliṅgo ca, āyusaddo ca pana napuṃsakaliṅgo ca pulliṅgo cāti dviliṅgā ete saddā”ti. Te vattabbā “yadi bodhisaddo ca āyusaddo ca dviliṅgā ete saddā, evaṃ sante dvinnaṃ bodhisaddānaṃ ekapadabhāvena vavatthitānaṃ accantasamānasutikānaṃ kathaṃ avisadākāravohāratā ca visadākāravohāratā ca siyā, kathañca pana dvinnaṃ āyusaddānaṃ ekapadabhāvena vavatthitānaṃ accantasamānasutikānaṃ ubhayamuttākāravohāratā ca visadākāravohāratā ca siyā”ti? Evaṃ vuttā te addhā kiñci uttari apassantā niruttarā bhavissanti. Saddasatthavidū pana saddasatthato nayaṃ gahetvā vadanti –

Some, however, without considering the composition known as the series of nominal words, desire indistinct usage and so on based on individual words alone. They should be told: 'If each individual word were to have its own indistinct usage and so on, then, in that case, for words like ‘kaññā, purisā, satthā, guṇavā, rājā’ due to the sound of ‘ā,’ for words like ‘puriso, satthāro, kaññāyo’ due to the sound of ‘o,’ and for words like ‘cittaṃ, purisaṃ, kaññaṃ’ due to the sound of the nasalization, since there is the possibility of them having mutually similar sounds, how could there be indistinct usage and so on?' Even if they were to say, 'It could be so, but their distinctions are difficult to penetrate,' they should be told: 'Do not speak thus. Even Nibbāna, which is more difficult to know, is known by relying on a person capable of explaining it. Therefore, you should speak only after thorough investigation.' Having said this, they should then be asked a further question: 'Of which gender are the words ‘bodhi’ and ‘āyu’?' Those who know will answer: 'The word ‘bodhi’ is both feminine and masculine, and the word ‘āyu’ is both neuter and masculine—thus, these words are of dual gender.' They should then be told: 'If the words ‘bodhi’ and ‘āyu’ are of dual gender, then how could two instances of ‘bodhi,’ established as a single word-form and having exactly the same sound, have both indistinct usage and distinct usage? And how could two instances of ‘āyu,’ established as a single word-form and having exactly the same sound, have both usage devoid of both forms and distinct usage?' When addressed thus, they will surely find nothing further to say and will become silent. But those skilled in the science of words, taking the method from the science of words, say—

“Ese’sā eta’miti ca,

Pasiddhi atthesu yesu lokassa;

‘Thīpumanapuṃsakānī’ti,

Vuccante tāni nāmānī”ti.

In whatsoever meanings the world’s convention

Is established as ‘this (he),’ ‘this (she),’ and ‘this (it),’

Those nouns are called

‘Feminine, masculine, and neuter.’

Tesaṃ kira ayamadhippāyo – “eso puriso, eso mātugāmo, eso rājā, esā itthī, esā latā, etaṃ napuṃsakaṃ, etaṃ citta”nti evaṃ purisādīsu yesu atthesu lokassa “eso esā eta”nti ca pasiddhi hoti, tesu atthesu tāni nāmāni “pumitthinapuṃsakaliṅgānī”ti vuccanti, taṃdvārena aññānipīti. Evaṃ vadantehi tehi “iminā nāma ākārena ‘eso esā eta’nti nāmāni aññāni ca pulliṅgādināmaṃ labhantī”ti ayaṃ viseso na dassito, saddhammanayaññūhi pana neruttikehi dassito “yassa kassaci atthassa avisadākāravohāro itthiliṅga”ntiādinā.

It seems their intention is this: In whatever meanings pertaining to persons and so on—such as 'this (masc.) is a man,' 'this (masc.) is a woman,' 'this (masc.) is a king,' 'this (she) is a woman,' 'this (she) is a creeper,' 'this (it) is a neuter thing,' 'this (it) is a mind'—the world’s convention is established as 'this (he),' 'this (she),' and 'this (it),' in respect to those meanings those nouns are called 'masculine, feminine, and neuter genders,' and by this means other nouns as well. By saying this, they have not shown this specific point: 'It is in this way that the nouns ‘eso, esā, etaṃ’ and others acquire the names masculine and so on.' But it has been shown by the etymologists who know the method of the true teaching, with the statement beginning: 'For any given meaning, the usage with an indistinct form is the feminine gender.'

Keci [M 0.0295] pana “avisadākārānaṃ atthānaṃ vācako vohāro itthiliṅga”ntiādīni vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Yadi hi avisadākārānaṃ atthānaṃ vācako vohāro itthiliṅgaṃ, evaṃ sante mātugāmakalattakantakaṇṭakagumbādayopi vohārā itthiliṅgāni siyuṃ avisadākārattā tadatthānaṃ. Yadi pana visadākārānaṃ atthānaṃ vācako vohāro pulliṅgaṃ, evaṃ sante “devatā saddhā ñāṇa”miccādayopi vohārā pulliṅgāni siyuṃ visadākārattā tadatthānaṃ. Atha vā yadi avisadākārānaṃ atthānaṃ vācako vohāro itthiliṅgaṃ, visadākārānaṃ panatthānaṃ vācako vohāro pulliṅgaṃ, evaṃ sante ekassevatthassa ekakkhaṇe dvīhi liṅgehi na vattabbatā siyā –

Some, however, say such things as: 'The usage that expresses things of an indistinct form is the feminine gender.' That should not be accepted. For if the usage that expresses things of an indistinct form were the feminine gender, then in that case usages such as 'mātugāma' (woman), 'kalatta' (wife), 'kaṇṭaka' (thorn), and 'gumba' (thicket) would be feminine, because the things they refer to have an indistinct form. And if the usage that expresses things of a distinct form were the masculine gender, then in that case usages such as 'devatā' (deity), 'saddhā' (faith), and 'ñāṇa' (knowledge) would be masculine, because the things they refer to have a distinct form. Alternatively, if the usage that expresses things of an indistinct form is the feminine gender, and the usage that expresses things of a distinct form is the masculine gender, then it would not be possible for a single thing to be expressed by two genders at a single moment—

“Atthakāmosi me yakkha, hitakāmāsi devate;

Karomi te taṃ vacanaṃ, tvaṃsi ācariyo mamā”ti.

'You are my well-wisher, O yakkha; you desire my welfare, O deity. I will do that word of yours; you are my teacher.'

Yadi ca ubhayamuttākārānaṃ atthānaṃ vācako vohāro napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ, evaṃ sante ubhayamuttākārānaṃ atthānaṃ tiṇarukkhādīsu “idaṃ nāmā”ti niyamābhāvato liṅgavacanaṃ viruddhaṃ siyā. Apica “paññāratanaṃ. Sāriputtamoggallānaṃ sāvakayuga”nti ca ādinā napuṃsakaliṅgavacanena tadatthānampi ubhayamuttākāratā vuttā siyā. Apica ekampi tīraṃ “taṭaṃ taṭī taṭo”ti tīhi liṅgehi na vattabbaṃ siyā. Ekampi ca ñāṇaṃ “paññāṇaṃ paññā pajānanā amoho”tiādinā tīhi liṅgehi na vattabbaṃ siyā, tasmā taṃ nayaṃ aggahetvā yathāvuttoyeva nayo gahetabbo.

And if the usage that expresses meanings devoid of both forms were the neuter gender, then in that case, for things devoid of both forms like grass, trees, and so on, because there is no fixed rule such as 'this is the name,' the statement about gender would be contradicted. Moreover, by neuter expressions such as 'the jewel of wisdom' and 'the pair of disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna,' it would be said that their meanings too are devoid of both forms. Furthermore, a single shore could not be expressed by three genders as 'taṭaṃ, taṭī, taṭo.' And a single knowledge could not be expressed by three genders with words such as 'paññāṇaṃ, paññā, pajānanā, amoho.' Therefore, not accepting that method, the method already stated should be accepted.

Lokasmiñhi itthīnaṃ heṭṭhimakāyo visado hoti, uparimakāyo avisado, uramaṃsaṃ avisadaṃ, gamanādīnipi avisadāni[M 0.0296]. Itthiyo hi gacchamānā avisadaṃ gacchanti, tiṭṭhamānā nipajjamānā nisīdamānā khādamānā bhuñjamānā avisadaṃ bhuñjanti. Purisampi hi avisadaṃ disvā “mātugāmo viya gacchati tiṭṭhati nipajjati nisīdati khādati bhuñjatī”ti vadanti. Iti yathā itthiyo yebhuyyena avisadākārā, tathā yassa kassaci saviññāṇakassa vā aviññāṇakassa vā atthassa ye vohārā yebhuyyena avisadākārā, teyeva itthiliṅgāni nāma bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? “Kaññā devatā dhītalikā dubbā saddhā ratti itthī yāgu vadhū” iccevamādīni. Purisānaṃ pana heṭṭhimakāyo avisado hoti, uparimakāyo visado, uramaṃsaṃ visadaṃ, gamanādīnipi visadāni honti. Purisā hi gacchamānā visadaṃ gacchanti, tiṭṭhamānā nipajjamānā nisīdamānā khādamānā bhuñjamānā visadaṃ bhuñjanti. Itthimpi hi gamanādīni visadāni kurumānaṃ disvā “puriso viya gacchatī”tiādīni vadanti. Iti yathā purisā yebhuyyena visadākārā, tathā yassa kassaci saviññāṇakassa vā aviññāṇakassa vā atthassa ye vohārā yebhuyyena visadākārā, teyeva pulliṅgāni nāma bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? “Puriso mātugāmo orodho āpo rukkho moho satthā” iccevamādīni. Yathā ca pana napuṃsakā ubhayamuttākārā, tathā yassa kassaci saviññāṇakassa vā aviññāṇakassa vā atthassa ye vohārā ubhayamuttākārā, teyeva napuṃsakaliṅgāni nāma bhavanti. Taṃ yathā? “Cittaṃ rūpaṃ itthāgāraṃ kalattaṃ nāṭakaṃ ratanaṃ ñāṇaṃ aṭṭhi āyu”iccevamādīni. Iccevaṃ nāmikānaṃ sabbesampi vohārānaṃ –

In the world, for women, the lower part of the body is distinct, while the upper part is indistinct; the flesh of the chest is indistinct, and their movements and so on are also indistinct. For women walk indistinctly, stand indistinctly, lie down indistinctly, sit indistinctly, and eat indistinctly. Indeed, on seeing a man acting indistinctly, people say, 'He moves, stands, lies down, sits, and eats like a woman.' Thus, just as women are for the most part characterized by indistinctness, so too whatever usages—whether for a sentient or an insentient thing—are for the most part indistinct in form, they are called feminine gender nouns. For example: ‘kaññā’ (maiden), ‘devatā’ (deity), ‘dhītalikā’ (doll), ‘dubbā’ (grass), ‘saddhā’ (faith), ‘ratti’ (night), ‘itthī’ (woman), ‘yāgu’ (rice-gruel), ‘vadhū’ (bride), and so on. For men, on the other hand, the lower part of the body is indistinct, while the upper part is distinct; the flesh of the chest is distinct, and their movements and so on are also distinct. For men walk distinctly, stand distinctly, lie down distinctly, sit distinctly, and eat distinctly. Indeed, on seeing a woman performing movements distinctly, people say, 'She moves like a man,' and so on. Thus, just as men are for the most part characterized by distinctness, so too whatever usages—whether for a sentient or an insentient thing—are for the most part distinct in form, they are called masculine gender nouns. For example: ‘puriso’ (man), ‘mātugāmo’ (woman), ‘orodho’ (harem), ‘āpo’ (water), ‘rukkho’ (tree), ‘moho’ (delusion), ‘satthā’ (teacher), and so on. And just as eunuchs are characterized by being devoid of both forms, so too whatever usages—whether for a sentient or an insentient thing—are devoid of both forms, they are called neuter gender nouns. For example: ‘cittaṃ’ (mind), ‘rūpaṃ’ (form), ‘itthāgāraṃ’ (women’s quarters), ‘kalattaṃ’ (wife), ‘nāṭakaṃ’ (drama), ‘ratanaṃ’ (jewel), ‘ñāṇaṃ’ (knowledge), ‘aṭṭhi’ (bone), ‘āyu’ (life-span), and so on. Thus, for all nominal usages—

Visadāvisadākārā, ākāro’bhayamuttako;

Liṅgassa lakkhaṇaṃ etaṃ, ñeyyaṃ syādippabandhato.

The distinct and indistinct forms,

And the form that is devoid of both:

This is the characteristic of gender,

To be known from the pronominal composition.

Idaṃ [M 0.0297] ṭhānaṃ dubbinivijjhaṃ mahāvanagahanaṃ niggumbaṃ nijjaṭaṃ katvā dassitaṃ sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ. Iti sabbesaṃ nāmikapadānaṃ pabandhanissitena avisadākāravohārādibhāvena itthiliṅgādibhāvassa sambhavato dvinnampi gosaddānaṃ pabandhanissitena avisadākāravohārādibhāvena yathāsakaṃ itthiliṅgādibhāvo veditabbo.

This topic, difficult to penetrate, a great forest thicket, has been shown having been made free of undergrowth and disentangled; it should be carefully borne in mind. Thus, since for all nominal words the state of being feminine gender, etc., is possible through the indistinct usage, etc., which is dependent on the composition, the respective state of being feminine gender, etc., of both words for 'cow' should be understood as being through the indistinct usage, etc., which is dependent on the composition.

Savinicchayoyaṃ okārantitthiliṅgassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the classification, with its analysis, of the paradigms of nominal words for the feminine gender ending in -o.

Okārantatāpakatikaṃ okārantitthiliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the feminine gender ending in -o is completed.

Evaṃ sabbathāpi ākāranta ivaṇṇanta uvaṇṇantokārantavasena chabbidhāni itthiliṅgāni niravasesato gahitāni bhavanti. Etesu pana kesañci ākārantānaṃ īkārantānañca katthaci paccattekavacanassa ekārādesavasena yo pabhedo dissati, so idāni vuccati. Tathā hi –

Thus, in all ways, the six types of feminine nouns—those ending in -ā, -i, -ī, -u, -ū, and -o—are completely covered. However, among these, a variation is sometimes seen in the nominative singular of some nouns ending in -ā and -ī, due to the substitution of -e. This will now be stated. For example:

“Na tvaṃ rādha vijānāsi, aḍḍharatte anāgate;

Abyayataṃ vilapasi, viratte kosiyāyane”ti

"You do not understand, Rādha, before midnight has come; you lament for one who is not gone, for Kosiyāyanī who has become disaffected."

Imasmiṃ rādhajātake “virattā”ti ākārantavasena vattabbe paccattavacanassa ekārādesavasena “viratte”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā “kosiyāyanī”ti īkārantavasena vattabbe paccattavacanassa ekārādesavasena “kosiyāyane”ti vuttaṃ. Tena aṭṭhakathācariyo “viratte kosiyāyaneti mātā no kosiyāyanī brāhmaṇī virattā amhākaṃ pitari nippemā jātā”ti atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇesi. Nanu ca bho pāḷiyaṃ “viratte”ti, “kosiyāyane”ti ca paccattavacanassa dassanato “ekārantampi itthiliṅgaṃ atthī”ti vattabbanti? Na vattabbaṃ ākārīkārantogadharūpavisesattā tesaṃ rūpānaṃ. Ādesavasena [M 0.0298] hi siddhattā visuṃ ekārantaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā itthiliṅgānaṃ yathāvuttā chabbidhatāyeva gahetabbā.

In this Rādhajātaka, when 'virattā' should have been said as an -ā-stem, it is stated as 'viratte' due to the substitution of -e for the nominative singular. Similarly, when 'kosiyāyanī' should have been said as an -ī-stem, it is stated as 'kosiyāyane' due to the substitution of -e for the nominative singular. Therefore, the commentator explained the meaning thus: “'viratte kosiyāyane' means ‘our mother, the brahmin woman Kosiyāyanī, has become disaffected, without affection for our father.’” But, good sirs, since the Pāḷi shows 'viratte' and 'kosiyāyane' as nominative singulars, should it not be said that “there is also a feminine noun ending in -e”? It should not be said, because those forms are specific variations of forms that are fundamentally -ā and -ī stems. Indeed, since they are established through substitution, there is no separate feminine noun ending in -e as such; therefore, the sixfold nature of feminine nouns should be understood only as has been stated.

Iccevaṃ itthiliṅgānaṃ, pakiṇṇanayasālinī;

Padamālā vibhattā me, sāsanatthaṃ sayambhuno.

Thus, concerning feminine nouns, this paradigm possessing varied methods has been analyzed by me for the benefit of the Dispensation of the Self-Existent One.

Saddanītisūriyoyaṃ,

Anekasuvinicchayarasmikalāpo;

Saṃsayandhakāranudo,

Kassa matipadumaṃ na vikāse.

This sun of the Saddanīti, whose collection of rays are many fine resolutions, a dispeller of the darkness of doubt—whose lotus of the mind would it not cause to bloom?

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the ninefold teaching with its commentary, the Tipiṭaka, and the paths of exposition,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the purpose of acquiring skill,

Itthiliṅgānaṃ nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo

The Division of the Paradigms of Nominal Words of Feminine Nouns,

Aṭṭhamo paricchedo.

The Eighth Chapter.

9. Napuṃsakaliṅganāmikapadamālā

9. The Paradigms of Nominal Words of the Neuter Gender

Atha pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā niggahītantanapuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ “bhūtaṃ”iccādikassa pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma –

Now, having first followed the opinion of the earlier teachers, we will state the paradigm of nominal words of the natural form 'bhūtaṃ' and so on, for neuter nouns ending in niggahīta:

Cittaṃ, cittāni. Cittaṃ, cittāni. Cittena, cittehi, cittebhi. Cittassa, cittānaṃ. Cittā, cittasmā, cittamhā, cittehi, cittebhi. Cittassa, cittānaṃ. Citte, cittasmiṃ, cittamhi, cittesu. Bho citta, bho cittā, bhavanto cittāni. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

Cittaṃ, cittāni (Nom.). Cittaṃ, cittāni (Acc.). Cittena; cittehi, cittebhi (Ins.). Cittassa; cittānaṃ (Dat./Gen.). Cittā, cittasmā, cittamhā; cittehi, cittebhi (Abl.). Cittassa; cittānaṃ (Gen.). Citte, cittasmiṃ, cittamhi; cittesu (Loc.). Bho citta; bho cittā, bhavanto cittāni (Voc.). This is the opinion of the Elder Yamaka.

Ettha kiñcāpi “cittā”ti paccattabahuvacanaṃ “citte”ti upayogabahuvacanañca anāgataṃ, tathāpi tattha tattha aññesampi tādisānaṃ niggahītantanapuṃsakarūpānaṃ dassanato vibhaṅgapāḷiyañca “cha cittā abyākatā”tiādidassanato gahetabbameva[M 0.0299], tasmā “cittaṃ, cittāni, cittā. Cittaṃ, cittāni, citte”ti kamo veditabbo. Niggahītantānañhi napuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ katthaci okārantapulliṅgānaṃ viya paccattopayogabahuvacanāni bhavanti. Tāni ca pulliṅgena vā saliṅgena vā aliṅgena vā saddhiṃ samānādhikaraṇāni hutvā kevalāni vā pāvacane sañcaranti. Atra “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Cattāro sammappadhānā. Sabbe mālā upentimaṃ. Yassa ete dhanā atthi. Cattāro mahābhūtā. Tīṇindriyā. Dve indriyā. Dasindriyā. Dve mahābhūte nissāya dve mahābhūtā, pañca viññāṇā, caturo aṅge adhiṭṭhāya, semi vammikamatthake, rūpā saddā rasā gandhā. Rūpe ca sadde ca atho rase ca. Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”nti evamādayo anekasatā pāḷippadesā daṭṭhabbā.

Here, although the nominative plural 'cittā' and the accusative plural 'citte' are not given in the preceding paradigm, they should still be accepted, since other such neuter forms ending in niggahīta are seen in various places, and since in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi one sees such phrases as 'six unclassified cittas.' Therefore, the sequence should be understood as: 'cittaṃ, cittāni, cittā' (Nom.); 'cittaṃ, cittāni, citte' (Acc.). For neuter nouns ending in niggahīta, the nominative and accusative plurals are sometimes like those of masculine nouns ending in -o. And these, being in apposition with masculine, its own gender (neuter), or another gender, or standing alone, are found in the scriptures. Here, hundreds of Pāḷi passages such as the following should be noted: 'Four foundations of mindfulness. Four right efforts. All garlands approach this one. One who has these riches. Four great elements. Three faculties. Two faculties. Ten faculties. Two great elements depending on two great elements, five consciousnesses, establishing the four limbs, I lie on top of the anthill, forms, sounds, tastes, smells. In forms and sounds and also in tastes. Eye-consciousness arises dependent on the eye and on forms.' And so on, hundreds of such Pāḷi passages are to be seen.

Ettha pana “satipaṭṭhānā”tiādīni padāni liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttānīti na gahetabbāni satipaṭṭhānasaddādīnaṃ paṭhamekavacanaṭṭhāne okārantapulliṅgabhāvena ṭhitabhāvassa adassanato. “Cattāro”tiādīniyeva pana padāni liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttānīti gahetabbāni niyogā niggahītantehi napuṃsakaliṅgehi satipaṭṭhānasaddādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvassa dassanatoti.

Here, however, words such as 'satipaṭṭhānā' should not be taken as spoken with a change of gender, because there is no instance of words like 'satipaṭṭhāna' standing as masculine -o stems in the nominative singular. But words such as 'cattāro' should indeed be taken as spoken with a change of gender, because they are necessarily seen to be in apposition with neuter nouns ending in niggahīta, such as 'satipaṭṭhāna'.

Kecettha vadeyyuṃ – nanu “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā”tiādippayogadassanato satipaṭṭhānasaddādīnaṃ [M 0.0300] okārantapulliṅgabhāvo labbhati. Evaṃ sante kasmā tumhehi “satipaṭṭhānasaddādīnaṃ paṭhamekavacanaṭṭhāne okārantapulliṅgabhāvena ṭhitabhāvassa adassanato”ti vuttaṃ, kasmā ca ekantato satipaṭṭhānasaddādīnaṃ niggahītantanapuṃsakaliṅgatā anumatā, nanu “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā”tiādidassanato “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādīsupi “satipaṭṭhānasaddādayo liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttā”ti vattabbāti? Na vattabbā, kasmāti ce? “Satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā”tiādīsupi satipaṭṭhānacittasaddādīnaṃ liṅgavipallāsavasena anicchitabbato. Tattha hi pulliṅgena dhammasaddena yojetuṃ dhammissaro bhagavā dhammāpekkhaṃ katvā “satipaṭṭhāno, citto, cittā”ti ca abhāsi. Kevalā hi satipaṭṭhāna cittasaddādayo okārantapulliṅgabhāvena katthacipi yojitā na santi, niggahītantanapuṃsakabhāvena pana yojitā santi.

Some might say here: 'Is it not so that from seeing usages such as “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā,” the status of being masculine -o stems is obtained for words like satipaṭṭhāna? This being so, why did you state that “there is no instance of words like satipaṭṭhāna standing as masculine -o stems in the nominative singular,” and why is their status as neuter nouns ending in niggahīta exclusively approved? Is it not so that, from seeing usages such as 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo...', it should be said that in cases like 'cattāro satipaṭṭhānā' too, words like 'satipaṭṭhāna' are stated with a change of gender?' It should not be said. If asked why: because even in such phrases as “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā,” a change of gender for words like satipaṭṭhāna and citta is not to be accepted. For there the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma, spoke “satipaṭṭhāno,” “citto,” and “cittā” out of consideration for the word “dhamma,” in order to connect them with the masculine word “dhamma.” For the words satipaṭṭhāna, citta, and so on, are nowhere used by themselves as masculine -o stems, but they are used as neuter nouns ending in niggahīta.

Tathā hi “citto gahapatī”ti etthāpi pulliṅgagahapatisaddaṃ apekkhitvā viññāṇe pavattaṃ cittanāmaṃ paṇṇattivasena puggale āropetvā puggalavācakaṃ katvā “citto”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi pana viññāṇasaṅkhātaṃ cittamadhippetaṃ siyā, “citta”micceva vucceyya. Tasmā “citto gahapati, cittā itthī”tiādīsu liṅgavipallāso na icchitabbo sāpekkhattā cittasaddādīnaṃ. Yathā ca ettha, evaṃ “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā”tiādīsupi liṅgavipallāso na icchitabbo. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādīsu pana satipaṭṭhānasaddādīnaṃ apekkhitabbāni padāni na santi, yehi te pulliṅgāni siyuṃ, tasmā “cattāro”tiādīniyeva padāni parivattetvā “cattāri, sabbāni, etānī”ti napuṃsakaliṅgavasena gahetvā “satipaṭṭhānā[M 0.0301], sammappadhānā”tiādīhi padehi yojetabbāni. Īdisesu ṭhānesu keci aṭṭhakathācariyā nikāralopaṃ icchanti “yā pubbe bodhisattānaṃ, pallaṅkavaramābhuje, nimittāni padissantī”ti ettha viya. Adassanañhi lopo, tasmā “cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni, cattāri sammappadhānāni, sabbāni mālānī’tiādikā yojanā kātabbā.

For example, in the phrase 'Citto the householder,' with reference to the masculine word 'householder,' the name 'Citta,' which pertains to consciousness, is superimposed on a person by way of designation, making it a personal name; hence, 'Citto' is said. But if what was intended was the mind itself, designated as consciousness, it would have been said as 'cittaṃ.' Therefore, in expressions like 'Citto the householder, Cittā the woman,' a change of gender should not be accepted, due to the dependent nature of words like 'citta.' And just as here, so too in phrases like 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo' (the foundation of mindfulness is a dhamma), 'citto dhammo' (the mind is a dhamma), and 'cittā dhammā' (minds are dhammas), a change of gender should not be accepted. But in expressions like 'the four foundations of mindfulness,' there are no words to be referred to by 'satipaṭṭhāna' and so on, by which they would become masculine. Therefore, it is the words like 'cattāro' that should be changed and taken in the neuter gender as 'cattāri,' 'sabbāni,' 'etāni,' and then connected with words like 'satipaṭṭhānā,' 'sammappadhānā.' In such cases, some commentators accept the elision of the '-ni' suffix, as in the case of: 'Formerly, for the bodhisattas, seated on the excellent cross-legged seat, the signs will appear.' For elision is non-appearance. Therefore, the construction should be made as 'cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni,' 'cattāri sammappadhānāni,' 'sabbāni mālānī,' and so on.

Keci pana “sabbe mālā upenti ma”nti ettha mālāsaddaṃ itthiliṅganti maññitvā pulliṅgabhūtaṃ sabbesaddaṃ itthiliṅgavasena parivattetvā “sabbā mālā”ti atthaṃ kathenti. Taṃ kiñcāpi yuttataraṃ viya dissati, tathāpi na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi so bhagavā liṅgaṃ naññāsi, na ca “sabbā mālā upenti ma”nti dve padāni itthiliṅgāni katvā vattuṃ na sakkhi. Yo evaṃ visadisaliṅgāni padāni uccāresi. Jānantoyeva pana bhagavā vattuṃ sakkontoyeva ca “sabbe mālā upenti ma”nti visadisaliṅgāni padāni uccāresi, tasmā pulliṅgabhūtaṃ sabbesaddaṃ “sabbānī”ti napuṃsakaliṅgavasena parivattetvā vibhaṅgapāḷiyaṃ “tīṇindriyā”ti padaṃ viya luttanikārena napuṃsakaliṅgena mālāsaddena yojetvā “sabbāni mālānī”ti attho gahetabbo katthaci “yassa ete dhanā atthī”ti ettha viya. Ettha hi yassa etāni dhanānīti attho. Idampettha sallakkhitabbaṃ. Mālāsaddo dviliṅgo itthinapuṃsakavasena. Tiṭṭhatu tassitthiliṅgattaṃ suviññeyyattā, napuṃsakatte pana tīṇi mālāni. “Mālehi ca gandhehi ca bhagavato sarīraṃ pūjentī”tiādayo napuṃsakappayogānipi bahū sandissantīti.

Some, however, thinking that the word 'mālā' here is feminine, change the masculine word 'sabbe' into the feminine form and explain the meaning as 'sabbā mālā.' Although this may seem more appropriate, it should not be accepted. For the Blessed One was not ignorant of gender, nor was he incapable of saying 'sabbā mālā upenti ma' with two words in the feminine gender. The Blessed One, who uttered words with differing genders thus, uttered 'sabbe mālā upenti ma' with differing genders knowingly and while being fully capable. Therefore, changing the masculine word 'sabbe' into the neuter form 'sabbāni,' and connecting it with the word 'mālā' in the neuter gender with the elision of the ending—like the word 'tīṇindriyā' in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi—the meaning should be taken as 'sabbāni mālāni,' just as in some places like 'yassa ete dhanā atthī,' where the meaning is 'yassa etāni dhanāni.'
