This should be carefully noted here. The word 'mālā' has two genders, feminine and neuter. Let its feminine gender stand, as it is easily understood; but in the neuter, there are examples such as 'tīṇi mālāni.' Many instances of neuter usage are also seen, such as 'Mālehi ca gandhehi ca bhagavato sarīraṃ pūjentī,' and so on.

Yadi pana bho mālasaddo itthinapuṃsakavasena dviliṅgo, “sabbe mālā upenti ma”nti ettha mālāsaddassa itthiliṅgabhāvaparikappane ko doso atthīti? Attheva itthiliṅgasaddassa [M 0.0302] pulliṅgabhūtena sabbanāmikapadena saddhiṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvassābhāvato, napuṃsakaliṅgassa pana pulliṅgabhūtena sabbanāmikapadena saddhiṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvassa upalabbhanato. Teneva ca “ete dhanā”tiādayo payogā pāvacane bahudhā diṭṭhā. Etthāpi pana vadeyyuṃ “dhanātiādīni vipallāsavasena pulliṅgāniyeva “ete”tiādīhi samānādhikaraṇapadehi yojitattā”ti. Na, napuṃsakāniyevetāni. Yadi hi “dhanā”tiādīni pulliṅgāni siyuṃ, katthaci paccattekavacanaṭṭhāne “eso”tiādīhi okārantasamānādhikaraṇapadehi yojitā okārantadhanasaddādayo siyuṃ. Tathārūpānaṃ abhāvato pana “dhanā indriyā viññāṇā”tiādayo saddā napuṃsakaliṅgāniyeva honti. Ayaṃ nayo paccattabahuvacanaṭṭhāneyeva labbhati. Napuṃsakaliṅgāni hi visadākārāni pulliṅgarūpāni viya hutvā pulliṅgehipi saddhiṃ caranti, napuṃsakā viya purisavesadhārino purisehīti niṭṭhametthāvagantabbaṃ.

But if, sir, the word 'mālā' has two genders, feminine and neuter, what is the fault in assuming a feminine gender for the word 'mālā' in the phrase 'sabbe mālā upenti ma'? There is indeed a fault, because of the absence of a coreferential relationship between a feminine word and a masculine pronoun. A coreferential relationship, however, is found between a neuter word and a masculine pronoun. For this very reason, usages like 'ete dhanā' are frequently seen in the scriptures. Here, some might argue that words like 'dhanā' are masculine due to gender inversion and are thus connected with coreferential words like 'ete.' No, they are indeed neuter. For if words like 'dhanā' were masculine, then in some singular instances, they would be connected with coreferential words ending in '-o,' such as 'eso,' and there would be words like 'dhana' ending in '-o.' Since such forms do not exist, words like 'dhanā,' 'indriyā,' and 'viññāṇā' are indeed neuter. This principle is found only in the plural. For neuter words, having forms similar to masculine forms, associate with masculine words, just as eunuchs wearing men's clothes move among men. This is the conclusion to be understood here.

Athāpi te pubbe vuttavacanaṃ puna parivattetvā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “citto gahapati, cittā itthī”tiādīsu cittaṃ etassa atthīti citto, cittaṃ etissā atthīti cittā yathā “saddho, saddhā”ti evaṃ assatthīti atthavasena gahetabbato liṅgavipallāso nicchitabbo, “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā”tiādīni pana evarūpassa atthassa aggahetabbato “satipaṭṭhānaṃ dhammo, cittaṃ dhammo, cittāni dhammā”ti vattabbe liṅgavipallāsena “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā”tiādi vuttanti liṅgavipallāso icchitabbo”ti? Tanna, “citto gahapatī”tiādīsu pana “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo”tiādīsu ca cittasatipaṭṭhānasaddādīnaṃ gahapati dhammādīnaṃ apekkhanavasena niccaṃ pulliṅgabhāvassa icchitattā.

Furthermore, revising their previous statement, they might say this: 'In cases like “Citto the householder” and “Cittā the woman,” the gender inversion should be determined based on the possessive meaning, as in “he has a mind (cittaṃ), thus Citto” and “she has a mind, thus Cittā,” just like “saddho” (a faithful man) and “saddhā” (a faithful woman). But in phrases like “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo” (the foundation of mindfulness is a dhamma), “citto dhammo” (the mind is a dhamma), and “cittā dhammā” (minds are dhammas), since such a possessive meaning cannot be taken, it should be accepted that this is a case of gender inversion, where “satipaṭṭhānaṃ dhammo,” “cittaṃ dhammo,” and “cittāni dhammā” are stated as “satipaṭṭhāno dhammo,” etc.' This is not so, because in cases like 'Citto the householder' and 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo,' the masculine gender of words like 'citta' and 'satipaṭṭhāna' is always required due to their dependence on words like 'gahapati' and 'dhamma.'

Tathā [M 0.0303] hi ekantanapuṃsakaliṅgopi puññasaddo abhisaṅkhārāpekkhanavasena “puñño abhisaṅkhāro”ti pulliṅgo jāto, tathā ekantanapuṃsakaliṅgāpi paduma maṅgalasaddādayo aññassatthassāpekkhanavasena “padumo bhagavā, padumā devī, maṅgalo bhagavā, maṅgalā itthī”ti ca pumitthiliṅgā jātā. Ekantapulliṅgāpi hatthivisesavācakā kālāvaka gaṅgeyyasaddādayo kulāpekkhanavasena “kālāvakañca gaṅgeyya”ntiādinā napuṃsakaliṅgā jātā. Tadapekkhanavasena hi aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “kālāvako ca gaṅgeyyo”tiādi pulliṅganiddeso dissati. Evaṃ taṃtadatthānamapekkhanavasena taṃtaṃpakatiliṅgaṃ nāsetvā aparaṃ liṅgaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā niddeso dissati, na ca tāni sabbānipi liṅgāni taddhitavasena aññaliṅgāni jātāni, atha kho gahapatidhammādīnaṃ apekkhanavaseneva aññaliṅgāni jātāni, tasmā “petāni bhoti puttāni, khādamānā tuvaṃ pure. Siviputtāni cavhaya. Evaṃ dhammāni sutvāna, vippasīdanti paṇḍitā”tiādīsuyeva liṅgavipallāso icchitabbo anaññāpekkhakattā vuttadhammasaddādīnaṃ, na pana “citto gahapati, cittā itthī, satipaṭṭhāno dhammo, citto dhammo, cittā dhammā”tiādīsu cittasaddādīnaṃ vipallāso icchitabbo gahapati dhammādīnaṃ apekkhakattā tesanti niṭṭhametthāvagantabbaṃ, idañca ekaccānaṃ sammohaṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā saddhammaṭṭhitiyā ayaṃ nīti saddhāsampannehi kulaputtehi sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā.

Thus, the word 'puñña,' though exclusively neuter, becomes masculine as 'puñño abhisaṅkhāro' due to its dependence on 'abhisaṅkhāra.' Similarly, words like 'paduma' and 'maṅgala,' though exclusively neuter, become masculine and feminine as in 'padumo bhagavā,' 'padumā devī,' 'maṅgalo bhagavā,' and 'maṅgalā itthī,' due to their dependence on another meaning. And words like 'kālāvaka' and 'gaṅgeyya,' which denote specific types of elephants and are exclusively masculine, become neuter as in 'kālāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ' due to their dependence on 'kula' (lineage). Indeed, in dependence on that, the masculine designation 'kālāvako ca gaṅgeyyo' is seen in the commentary. Thus, a designation is seen where the natural gender is eliminated and another gender is established in dependence on this or that meaning. Not all of these become a different gender by way of taddhita derivation; rather, they become a different gender simply by dependence on words like 'gahapati' and 'dhamma.' Therefore, gender inversion should be accepted only in cases like 'petāni bhoti puttāni...' and 'Evaṃ dhammāni sutvāna...,' because the words 'dhamma,' etc., that are mentioned do not depend on anything else. But in cases like 'citto gahapati,' 'cittā itthī,' 'satipaṭṭhāno dhammo,' 'citto dhammo,' and 'cittā dhammā,' an inversion for words like 'citta' should not be accepted, because they are dependent on 'gahapati,' 'dhamma,' etc. This is the conclusion to be understood here. This is a point of confusion for some. Therefore, for the stability of the good Dhamma, this principle should be well kept in mind by faithful clansmen.

Badaratitthavihāravāsī ācariyadhammapālo pana “aparimāṇā padā aparimāṇā akkharā aparimāṇā byañjanāti pāḷippadese [M 0.0304] ‘padā akkharā byañjanā’ti liṅgavipallāso katoti daṭṭhabba”nti āha. Etthāpi mayaṃ “padā”ti idaṃ “indriyā rūpā”tiādīni viya napuṃsakaliṅgamevāti vadāma okārantavasena paṭhamekavacanantabhāvābhāvato, itaradvayaṃ pana napuṃsakaliṅgantipi pulliṅgantipi gahetabbaṃ niggahītantokārantavasena paṭhamekavacanantabhāvassūpalabbhanato. Tathā hi “puttāni latāni pabbatāni dhammānī”tiādīnaṃyeva liṅgavipallāsāni icchitabbāni niggahītantavasena paṭhamekavacanantatāya anupaladdhito, tesañcokārantākārantavasena paṭhamekavacanantatādassanato. “Jarādhammaṃ mā jīrī”ti idaṃ pana aññapadatthavasena napuṃsakaṃ jātanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

But the teacher Dhammapāla, resident of the Badaratittha Vihāra, said: 'In the Pāḷi passage “aparimāṇā padā aparimāṇā akkharā aparimāṇā byañjanā,” it should be seen that a gender inversion has been made in “padā, akkharā, byañjanā.”' Here, we say that 'padā' is indeed neuter, like 'indriyā,' 'rūpā,' etc., because it does not have a nominative singular form ending in '-o.' The other two, however, can be taken as either neuter or masculine, because a nominative singular form is found ending in either a niggahīta (e.g., akkharaṃ) or in '-o' (e.g., akkharo). Thus, gender inversions should be accepted only for words like 'puttāni,' 'latāni,' 'pabbatāni,' and 'dhammānī,' because their nominative singular is not found with a niggahīta ending, and their nominative singular is seen with an '-o' or '-ā' ending. The phrase 'jarādhammaṃ mā jīrī,' however, should be understood as having become neuter by being a compound referring to something else.

Bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūtā. Bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūte. Bhūtena, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūtā, bhūtasmā, bhūtamhā, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūte, bhūtasmiṃ, bhūtamhi, bhūtesu. Bho bhūta, bhavanto bhūtāni, bhavanto bhūtā. Evaṃ cittanayena nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

Bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūtā. Bhūtaṃ, bhūtāni, bhūte. Bhūtena, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūtā, bhūtasmā, bhūtamhā, bhūtehi, bhūtebhi. Bhūtassa, bhūtānaṃ. Bhūte, bhūtasmiṃ, bhūtamhi, bhūtesu. Bho bhūta, bhavanto bhūtāni, bhavanto bhūtā. Thus is the paradigm of the noun, following the pattern of 'citta'.

Iminā nayena “mahābhūtaṃ bhavittaṃ bhūnaṃ bhavana”miccādīnaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ niggahītantapadānaṃ aññesañca “vatta”miccādīnaṃ niggahītantapadānaṃ nāmikapadamālā veditabbā.

In this way, the nominal paradigm should be understood for words ending in a niggahīta that are formed from the root 'bhū,' such as 'mahābhūtaṃ,' 'bhavittaṃ,' 'bhūnaṃ,' 'bhavanaṃ,' etc., and for other words ending in a niggahīta, such as 'vattaṃ,' etc.

Vattaṃ rūpaṃ sotaṃ ghānaṃ, dukkhaṃ pupphaṃ jhānaṃ ñāṇaṃ;

Dānaṃ sīlaṃ puññaṃ pāpaṃ, vajjaṃ saccaṃ yānaṃ chattaṃ.

Duty, form, ear, nose; suffering, flower, jhāna, knowledge; giving, virtue, merit, evil; fault, truth, vehicle, umbrella.

Sakaṭaṃ kanakaṃ tagaraṃ nagaraṃ, taraṇaṃ caraṇaṃ dharaṇaṃ maraṇaṃ;

Nayanaṃ vadanaṃ karaṇaṃ lavanaṃ, vasanaṃ pavanaṃ bhavanaṃ gaganaṃ.

Cart, gold, tagara, city; crossing, walking, holding, death; eye, face, making, reaping; dwelling, wind, existence, sky.

Amataṃ puḷinaṃ mālaṃ, āsanaṃ savanaṃ mukhaṃ;

Padumaṃ uppalaṃ vassaṃ, locanaṃ sādhanaṃ sukhaṃ.

The deathless, sandbank, garland; seat, hearing, face; pink lotus, blue water lily, rain; eye, means, happiness.

Tāṇaṃ [M 0.0305] mūlaṃ dhanaṃ kūlaṃ, maṅgalaṃ naḷinaṃ phalaṃ;

Hiraññaṃ ambujaṃ dhaññaṃ, jālaṃ liṅgaṃ padaṃ jalaṃ.

Protection, root, wealth, bank; blessing, lotus, fruit; gold, lotus, grain; net, gender, foot, water.

Aṅgaṃ paṇṇaṃ susānaṃ saṃ, āvudhaṃ hadayaṃ vanaṃ;

Sopānaṃ cīvaraṃ pāṇaṃ, alātaṃ indriyaṃ kulaṃ.

Limb, leaf, charnel ground; weapon, heart, forest; stairway, robe, life-breath; firebrand, faculty, clan.

Lohaṃ kaṇaṃ balaṃ pīṭhaṃ, aṇḍaṃ ārammaṇaṃ puraṃ;

Araññaṃ tīramassattha-miccādīni samuddhare.

Metal, speck, strength, stool; egg, object, city; forest, shore, the Assattha tree—and so on, one should cite.

Imāni cittasaddena sabbathāpi sadisāni, imāni pana visadisāni. Seyyathidaṃ –

These are in every way similar to the word 'citta,' but the following are dissimilar. As follows:

“Cammaṃ vesma”ntiādīni, ekadhāyeva bhijjare;

“Kammaṃ thāmaṃ guṇava”nti-ādīni tu anekadhā.

Words such as 'cammaṃ' and 'vesma' are inflected in only one way; but words such as 'kammaṃ,' 'thāmaṃ,' and 'guṇavaṃ' are inflected in many ways.

Kathaṃ?

How so?

Camme, cammasmiṃ, cammamhi, cammani, vesme, vesmasmiṃ, vesmamhi, vesmani, ghamme, ghammasmiṃ, ghammamhi, ghammani. Evaṃ aññānipi yojetabbāni.

In the skin, in the skin, in the skin, in the skin; in the house, in the house, in the house, in the house; in the heat, in the heat, in the heat, in the heat. Similarly, others should be applied.

Kammaṃ, kammāni, kammā. Kammaṃ, kammāni, kamme. Kammena, kammunā, kammanā, kammehi, kammebhi. Kammassa, kammuno, kammānaṃ. Kammasmā, kammamhā, kammunā, kammehi, kammebhi. Kammassa, kammuno, kammānaṃ. Kamme, kammasmiṃ, kammamhi, kammani, kammesu. Bho kamma, bhavanto kammāni, bhavanto kammā.

Action, actions, actions. Action, actions, actions. By action, by action, by action; by actions, by actions. Of action, of action; of actions. From action, from action, from action; from actions, from actions. Of action, of action; of actions. In action, in action, in action, in action; in actions. O action, O actions, O actions.

Thāmasaddassa pana tatiyekavacanaṭṭhānādīsu “thāmena, thāmunā, thāmassa, thāmuno”ti ca, “thāmā, thāmasmā, thāmamhā, thāmunā”ti ca yojetabbaṃ.

For the word 'thāma,' in the instrumental singular and other cases, 'thāmena, thāmunā, thāmassa, thāmuno,' and 'thāmā, thāmasmā, thāmamhā, thāmunā' should be construed.

Vantu mantu imantupaccayavataṃ pana niggahītantasaddānaṃ “guṇavaṃ cittaṃ, rucimaṃ pupphaṃ, pāpimaṃ kulaṃ” iccādipayogavasena –

For words ending in niggahīta (ṃ) and having the suffixes -vantu, -mantu, and -imantu, as in the usages 'guṇavaṃ cittaṃ' (virtuous mind), 'rucimaṃ pupphaṃ' (pleasing flower), 'pāpimaṃ kulaṃ' (evil family), and so on, the following applies:

Guṇavaṃ[M 0.0306], guṇavantāni, guṇavantā, guṇavanti. Guṇavantaṃ, guṇavantāni, guṇavante guṇavanti. Guṇavatā, guṇavantena, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavatā, guṇavantā, guṇavantasmā, guṇavantamhā, guṇavantehi, guṇavantebhi. Guṇavato, guṇavantassa, guṇavataṃ, guṇavantānaṃ. Guṇavati, guṇavante, guṇavantasmiṃ, guṇavantamhi, guṇavantesu. Bho guṇava, bhavanto guṇavantāni, guṇavanti.

Virtuous, virtuous ones, virtuous ones, virtuous ones. Virtuous one, virtuous ones, virtuous ones, virtuous ones. By the virtuous one, by the virtuous one; by the virtuous ones, by the virtuous ones. Of the virtuous one, of the virtuous one; of the virtuous ones, of the virtuous ones. From the virtuous one, from the virtuous one, from the virtuous one, from the virtuous one; from the virtuous ones, from the virtuous ones. Of the virtuous one, of the virtuous one; of the virtuous ones, of the virtuous ones. In the virtuous one, in the virtuous one, in the virtuous one, in the virtuous one; in the virtuous ones. O virtuous one, O virtuous ones, O virtuous ones.

Evaṃ “rucimaṃ, rucimantāni, rucima”ntiiccādinā, “pāpimaṃ, pāpimantāni, pāpima”nti iccādinā ca yojetabbaṃ. Apicettha “guṇavaṃ balavaṃ yasavaṃ satimaṃ gatimaṃ”iccādinā payogā vitthāretabbā.

Thus, it should be construed with 'rucimaṃ, rucimantāni, rucimaṃ' and so on, and with 'pāpimaṃ, pāpimantāni, pāpimaṃ' and so on. Moreover, here the usages should be expanded with 'guṇavaṃ' (virtuous), 'balavaṃ' (strong), 'yasavaṃ' (famous), 'satimaṃ' (mindful), 'gatimaṃ' (intelligent), and so on.

Karontasaddassa “karontaṃ cittaṃ, karontaṃ kula”nti payogavasena –

For the word 'karonta' (doing), by way of its usage as in 'karontaṃ cittaṃ' (a mind that is doing) and 'karontaṃ kulaṃ' (a family that is doing) –

Karontaṃ, karontāni, karontā, karonti. Karontaṃ, karontāni, karonte, karonti. Karotā, karontena, karontehi, karontebhi. Karoto, karato, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karotā, karontā, karontasmā, karontamhā, karontehi, karontebhi. Karoto, karato, karontassa, karontānaṃ, karotaṃ. Karoti, karonte, karontasmiṃ, karontamhi, karontesu. Bho karonta, bhavanto, karontāni, karontā, karontīti yojetabbaṃ.

One doing, those doing, those doing, those doing. One doing, those doing, those doing, those doing. By one doing, by one doing; by those doing, by those doing. Of one doing, of one doing, of one doing; of those doing, of those doing. From one doing, from one doing, from one doing, from one doing; from those doing, from those doing. Of one doing, of one doing, of one doing; of those doing, of those doing. In one doing, in one doing, in one doing, in one doing; in those doing. O one doing, O venerable ones, O those doing, O those doing, O those doing. Thus should it be applied.

Gacchantasaddassa tu “gacchantaṃ cittaṃ, gacchantaṃ kula”nti payogavasena –

For the word 'gacchanta' (going), by way of its usage as in 'gacchantaṃ cittaṃ' (a mind that is going) and 'gacchantaṃ kulaṃ' (a family that is going) –

Gacchantaṃ, gacchantāni, gacchantā. Gacchantaṃ, gacchantāni, gacchante. Gacchatā, gacchantena, gacchantehi, gacchantebhi. Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchatā, gacchantā, gacchantasmā, gacchantamhā, gacchantehi[M 0.0307], gacchantebhi. Gacchato, gacchantassa, gacchantānaṃ, gacchataṃ. Gacchati, gacchante, gacchantasmiṃ, gacchantamhi, gacchantesu. Bho gacchaṃ, bho gacchantā, bhavanto gacchantāni, gacchantāti yojetabbaṃ.

One going, those going, those going. One going, those going, those going. By one going, by one going; by those going, by those going. Of one going, of one going; of those going, of those going. From one going, from one going, from one going, from one going; from those going, from those going. Of one going, of one going; of those going, of those going. In one going, in one going, in one going, in one going; in those going. O one going, O those going, O venerable ones, O those going, O those going. Thus should it be applied.

Evaṃ “carantaṃ dadantaṃ tiṭṭhantaṃ cintayanta”ntiādīsupi nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

Similarly, the nominal paradigms should be applied also to instances such as 'wandering,' 'giving,' 'standing,' 'thinking,' and so forth.

Mahantasaddassa pana koci bhedo, tathā hi “bārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma mahā”ti evaṃ “mahā”iti napuṃsakapayogadassanato “mahantaṃ, mahā, mahantāni, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahantāni, mahante. Mahatā”ti kamo veditabbo. Sabbānetāni cittasaddena visadisāni.

For the word 'mahanta' (great), however, there is some distinction. For instance, from seeing the neuter usage 'mahā' in the phrase 'the kingdom of Bārāṇasī is called great' (bārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma mahā), the sequence 'mahantaṃ, mahā, mahantāni, mahantā. Mahantaṃ, mahantāni, mahante. Mahatā' should be understood. All these are dissimilar to the word 'citta' (mind).

Savinicchayoyaṃ niggahītantanapuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the classification, established by analysis, of the nominal paradigm for the natural form of neuter nouns ending in 'ṃ'.

Avaṇṇukārantatāpakatikaṃ niggahītantaṃ

The natural form of a-stems ending in 'ṃ'.

Napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The neuter gender [section] is concluded.

Idāni tassīlatthassa katarassassa atthavibhāvi iccetassa saddassa nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā –

Now, we shall explain the nominal paradigm of the word 'atthavibhāvi' (meaning-illuminating), which has a habitual meaning and is of the 'katara' class, having made the opinion of the ancient teachers foremost –

Aṭṭhi, aṭṭhī, aṭṭhīni. Aṭṭhiṃ, aṭṭhī, aṭṭhīni. Aṭṭhinā, aṭṭhīhi, aṭṭhībhi. Aṭṭhissa, aṭṭhino, aṭṭhīnaṃ. Aṭṭhinā, aṭṭhīhi, aṭṭhībhi. Aṭṭhissa, aṭṭhino, aṭṭhīnaṃ. Aṭṭhismiṃ, aṭṭhimhi, aṭṭhīsu. Bho aṭṭhi, bhavanto aṭṭhī, bhavanto aṭṭhīni. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

Bone, bones, bones. Bone, bones, bones. By a bone; by bones, by bones. Of a bone, of a bone; of bones. From a bone; from bones, from bones. Of a bone, of a bone; of bones. In a bone, in a bone; in bones. O bone, O venerable bones, O venerable bones. This is the opinion of the great elder Yamaka.

Kiñcāpettha nissakkavacanaṭṭhāne “aṭṭhismā, aṭṭhimhā”ti padāni anāgatāni, tathāpi tattha tattha taṃsadisappayogadassanā gahetabbāni. Yathā pana aṭṭhisaddassa, evaṃ “satthi dadhi vāri akkhi acchi”iccādīnampi rūpāni bhavanti.

Although the forms 'aṭṭhismā' and 'aṭṭhimhā' are not given here in the ablative case, they should nevertheless be understood from seeing similar usages in various places. Just as with the word 'aṭṭhi', so too are the forms of words such as 'satthi' (thigh), 'dadhi' (curd), 'vāri' (water), 'akkhi' (eye), 'acchi' (eye), and so forth.

Atthavibhāvi[M 0.0308], atthavibhāvī, atthavibhāvīni. Atthavibhāviṃ, atthavibhāvī, atthavibhāvīni. Atthavibhāvinā, atthavibhāvīhi, atthavibhāvībhi. Atthavibhāvissa, atthavibhāvino, atthavibhāvīnaṃ. Atthavibhāvinā, atthavibhāvismā atthavibhāvimhā, atthavibhāvīhi, atthavibhāvībhi. Atthavibhāvissa, atthavibhāvino, atthavibhāvīnaṃ. Atthavibhāvismiṃ, atthavibhāvimhi, atthavibhāvīsu. Bho atthavibhāvi, bhavanto atthavibhāvī, bhavanto atthavibhāvīni.

Meaning-illuminating, meaning-illuminating, meaning-illuminating. Meaning-illuminating, meaning-illuminating, meaning-illuminating. By a meaning-illuminating one; by meaning-illuminating ones, by meaning-illuminating ones. Of a meaning-illuminating one, of a meaning-illuminating one; of meaning-illuminating ones. From a meaning-illuminating one, from a meaning-illuminating one, from a meaning-illuminating one; from meaning-illuminating ones, from meaning-illuminating ones. Of a meaning-illuminating one, of a meaning-illuminating one; of meaning-illuminating ones. In a meaning-illuminating one, in a meaning-illuminating one; in meaning-illuminating ones. O meaning-illuminating one, O venerable meaning-illuminating ones, O venerable meaning-illuminating ones.

Evaṃ “dhammavibhāvi, cittānuparivatti, sukhakāri”iccādīnipi. Tattha aṭṭhi satthiādīni padhānaliṅgāni anaññāpekkhakattā, atthavibhāvi dhammavibhāviādīni appadhānaliṅgāni aññāpekkhakattā.

Thus also for 'dhammavibhāvi' (Dhamma-illuminating), 'cittānuparivatti' (following the mind), 'sukhakāri' (producing happiness), and so forth. Therein, 'aṭṭhi' (bone), 'satthi' (thigh), and so forth are primary nouns, because they are not dependent on another; 'atthavibhāvi' (meaning-illuminating), 'dhammavibhāvi' (Dhamma-illuminating), and so forth are secondary nouns, because they are dependent on another.

Savinicchayoyaṃ ikārantanapuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the classification, established by analysis, of the nominal paradigm for the natural form of neuter nouns ending in 'i'.

Ivaṇṇantatāpakatikaṃ ikārantanapuṃsakaliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on the natural form of neuter i-stems is concluded.

Idāni katarassassa gotrabhu iccetassa saddassa nāmikapadamālaṃ vakkhāma pubbācariyamataṃ purecaraṃ katvā –

Now, we shall explain the nominal paradigm of the word 'gotrabhu', which is of the 'katara' class, having made the opinion of the ancient teachers foremost –

Āyu, āyū, āyūni. Āyuṃ, āyū, āyūni. Āyunā, āyūhi, āyūbhi. Āyussa, āyuno, āyūnaṃ. Āyunā, āyūhi, āyūbhi. Āyussa, āyuno, āyūnaṃ. Āyusmiṃ, āyumhi, āyūsu. Bho āyu, bhavanto āyū, bhavanto āyūni. Yamakamahātheramataṃ.

Life, lives, lives. Life, lives, lives. By life; by lives, by lives. Of life, of life; of lives. From life; from lives, from lives. Of life, of life; of lives. In life, in life; in lives. O life, O venerable lives, O venerable lives. This is the opinion of the great elder Yamaka.

Kiñcāpettha nissakkavacanaṭṭhāne “āyusmā, āyumhā”ti padāni anāgatāni, tathāpi tattha tattha taṃsadisappayogadassanato gahetabbāni. Ettha ca āyusaddo puṃnapuṃsakaliṅgo daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu ca tassa dviliṅgatā [M 0.0309] dissati. “Punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisa. Āyu cassā parikkhīṇo ahosī”tiādīsu hi āyusaddo pulliṅgo, tabbasena “āyu, āyū, āyavo”tiādinā bhikkhunayena yathāsambhavaṃ nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. “Aggaṃ āyu ca vaṇṇo ca. Kittakaṃ panassa āyū”tiādīsu pana napuṃsakaliṅgo, tabbasena “āyu, āyū, āyūnī”ti yojitā.

Although the forms 'āyusmā' and 'āyumhā' are not given here in the ablative case, they should nevertheless be understood from seeing similar usages in various places. And here, the word 'āyu' should be seen as being of both masculine and neuter gender. Indeed, its dual-gender nature is seen in the Pāli texts and the commentaries. For in phrases such as 'Punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisa' (And life has been obtained again by me, know this, good sir) and 'Āyu cassā parikkhīṇo ahosi' (And her life was exhausted), the word 'āyu' is masculine. Accordingly, the nominal paradigm beginning with 'āyu, āyū, āyavo', and so forth, should be applied as is possible, according to the method for 'bhikkhu'. In phrases such as 'Aggaṃ āyu ca vaṇṇo ca' (Foremost is life and beauty) and 'Kittakaṃ panassa āyū' (How long, then, is his life-span?), on the other hand, it is neuter. Accordingly, the forms 'āyu, āyū, āyūnī' are applied.

Gotrabhu, gotrabhū, gotrabhūni. Gotrabhuṃ, gotrabhū, gotrabhūni. Gotrabhunā, gotrabhūhi, gotrabhūbhi. Gotrabhussa, gotrabhuno, gotrabhūnaṃ. Gotrabhunā, gotrabhusmā, gotrabhumhā, gotrabhūhi, gotrabhūbhi. Gotrabhussa, gotrabhuno, gotrabhūnaṃ. Gotrabhusmiṃ, gotrabhumhi, gotrabhūsu. Bho gotrabhu, bhavanto gotrabhū, bhavanto gotrabhūni. Bho gotrabhū, bho gotrabhūni, evaṃ bahuvacanaṃ vā. Ayamamhākaṃ mataṃ, evaṃ “cittasahabhu”iccādīnaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ ukārantasaddānaṃ aññesampi taṃsadisānaṃ nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Puggalavācako pana ūkāranto gotrabhūsaddo pulliṅgapariyāpannattā sabbaññūnaye paviṭṭho. Tatraññe saddā nāma “cakkhu vasu dhanu dāru tipu madhu siṅgu hiṅgu cittagu”iccādayo.

The gotrabhu, the gotrabhūs, the gotrabhūs. The gotrabhu, the gotrabhūs, the gotrabhūs. By the gotrabhu; by the gotrabhūs, by the gotrabhūs. Of the gotrabhu, of the gotrabhu; of the gotrabhūs. From the gotrabhu, from the gotrabhu, from the gotrabhu; from the gotrabhūs, from the gotrabhūs. Of the gotrabhu, of the gotrabhu; of the gotrabhūs. In the gotrabhu, in the gotrabhu; in the gotrabhūs. O gotrabhu, O venerable gotrabhūs, O venerable gotrabhūs. Or thus in the plural: O gotrabhūs, O gotrabhūs. This is our opinion. Thus, the nominal paradigm should be applied to other similar u-stem words formed from the root 'bhū', such as 'cittasahabhu' (arisen together with the mind), and so forth. However, the word 'gotrabhū', which denotes a person and ends in 'ū', is included in the masculine gender and thus follows the declension of 'sabbaññū'. Other such words are, namely: 'cakkhu' (eye), 'vasu' (wealth), 'dhanu' (bow), 'dāru' (wood), 'tipu' (tin), 'madhu' (honey), 'siṅgu' (horn), 'hiṅgu' (asafoetida), 'cittagu' (variegated cow), and so forth.

Savinicchayoyaṃ ukārantanapuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo.

This is the classification, established by analysis, of the nominal paradigm for the natural form of neuter nouns ending in 'u'.

Uvaṇṇokārantatāpakatikaṃ

The natural form of u-stems.

Ukārantanapuṃsakaliṅgaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The section on neuter nouns ending in 'u' is concluded.

Evaṃ niggahītanta ikāranta ukārantavasena tividhāni napuṃsakaliṅgāni niravasesato gahitāneva honti. Tesu kesañci [M 0.0310] niggahītantānaṃ kvaci paccattekavacanassa bahuvacanassa ekārādesavasena bhedo dissati. Seyyathidaṃ? “Sukhe dukkhe. Ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasate ekūnapaññāsa paribbājakasate”iccevamādi. Nanu bho evaṃvidhānaṃ rūpānaṃ pāḷiyaṃ dassanato “ekārantampi napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ atthī”ti vattabbanti? Na vattabbaṃ niggahītantogadharūpavisesattā tesaṃ rūpānaṃ. Ādesavasena hi siddhattā visuṃ ekārantaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ nāma natthi. Tasmā napuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ yathāvuttā tividhatāyeva gahetabbāti.

Thus, neuter genders are completely included in three types: those ending in 'ṃ' (niggahītanta), those ending in 'i' (ikāranta), and those ending in 'u' (ukāranta). Among these, for some of those ending in 'ṃ', a distinction is sometimes seen in the singular and plural due to the substitution of 'e'. For example: 'sukhe dukkhe,' 'ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasate ekūnapaññāsa paribbājakasate,' and so forth. Now, seeing such forms in the Pāli, should it not be said, 'there is also a neuter gender ending in 'e''? It should not be said, because those forms are a specific type included within those ending in 'ṃ'. Since they are formed by way of substitution, there is no separate neuter gender ending in 'e'. Therefore, the neuter genders should be understood as only the aforementioned three types.

Napuṃsakānamiccevaṃ, liṅgānaṃ nayasālinī;

Padamālā vibhattā me, sāsanatthaṃ mahesino.

Thus for the neuter genders, this methodical garland of words, a guide to the genders, has been classified by me for the benefit of the Great Sage's Dispensation.

Yassesā paguṇā sadda-nītiresā subhāvitā;

Sāsane kulaputtānaṃ, saraṇaṃ so parāyaṇaṃ.

For whom this Saddanīti is mastered and well-cultivated, he is a refuge and final resort for the sons of good family in the Dispensation.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for those wise in the ninefold scripture with its commentaries and the three Piṭakas, skilled in the paths of expression,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise composed for the purpose of proficiency,

Napuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ pakatirūpassa nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo

The Classification of the Garland of Nominal Words for the Natural Form of Neuter Genders.

Navamo paricchedo.

The Ninth Chapter.

10. Liṅgattayamissakanāmikapadamālā

10. The Garland of Nominal Words Mixed with the Three Genders

Adhikūnakato ceka-kkharato ca ito paraṃ;

Tīṇi liṅgāni missetvā, padamālamanākulaṃ.

Henceforth, from the excessive and the deficient, and from single syllables, having mixed the three genders, a clear garland of words,

Nānāsukhumasaṅketa-gatesvatthesu viññunaṃ;

Gambhīrabuddhicāratthaṃ, pavakkhāmi yathābalaṃ.

for the wise, for the sake of the exercise of their profound intelligence in meanings reached by various subtle indications, I will explain according to my ability.

Itthī thī ca pabhā bhā ca, girā rā pavanaṃ vanaṃ;

Udakañca dakaṃ kañca, vitakko iti cādayo.

'Itthī' and 'thī', 'pabhā' and 'bhā', 'girā', 'rā', 'pavanaṃ', 'vanaṃ', 'udakaṃ' and 'dakaṃ' and 'kaṃ', 'vitakko', and so forth.

Bhū [M 0.0311] bhūmi ceva araññaṃ, araññānīti cādayo;

Paññā paññāṇaṃ ñāṇañca, iccādī ca tidhā siyuṃ.

'Bhū' and 'bhūmi', and 'araññaṃ' and 'araññānī', and so forth; 'paññā', 'paññāṇaṃ', and 'ñāṇaṃ', and others like them, may be of three kinds.

Ko vi sā ceva bhā rā ca, thī dhī ku bhū tatheva kaṃ;

Khaṃ go mo mā ca saṃ yaṃ taṃ, kimiccādī ca ekikāti.

'Ko', 'vi', 'sā', and 'bhā', and 'rā', 'thī', 'dhī', 'ku', 'bhū', and likewise 'kaṃ', 'khaṃ', 'go', 'mo', and 'mā', 'saṃ', 'yaṃ', 'taṃ', 'kiṃ', and so forth, are single-syllable words.

Ayaṃ liṅgattayamissako nāmikapadamālāuddeso. Tatra itthī, itthī, itthiyo. Itthiṃ…pe… bhotiyo itthiyo.

This is the exposition of the garland of nominal words mixed with the three genders. Therein: 'itthī' (woman), 'itthī', 'itthiyo'. 'Itthiṃ'...[etc.]...'bhotiyo itthiyo' (O women).

Thī thī, thiyo. Thiṃ, thī, thiyo. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thiyaṃ, thīsu. Bhoti thi, bhotiyo thī, bhotiyo thiyo. Ettha –

Thī, thī, thiyo. Thiṃ, thī, thiyo. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thīhi, thībhi. Thiyā, thīnaṃ. Thiyā, thiyaṃ, thīsu. Bhoti thi, bhotiyo thī, bhotiyo thiyo. Herein—

“Kukkuṭā maṇayo daṇḍā, thiyo ca puññalakkhaṇā;

Uppajjanti apāpassa, katapuññassa jantuno;

Thiyā guyhaṃ na saṃseyya; Thīnaṃ bhāvo durājāno”ti

“Cocks, jewels, staves, and women marked by merit arise for a being without evil, who has done meritorious deeds. One should not reveal a woman's secret; the nature of women is hard to know.”

Ādīni nidassanapadāni.

These are illustrative examples.

Pabhā, pabhā, pabhāyo. Pabhaṃ…pe… bhotiyo pabhāyo.

Pabhā, pabhā, pabhāyo. Pabhaṃ…[etc.]… bhotiyo pabhāyo.

Bhā, bhā, bhāyo. Bhaṃ, bhā, bhāyo. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ. Bhāya, bhāyaṃ, bhāsu. Bhoti bhe, bhotiyo bhā, bhotiyo bhāyo. Ettha ca “bhākaro bhānu”iccādīni nidassanapadāni.

Bhā, bhā, bhāyo. Bhaṃ, bhā, bhāyo. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ. Bhāya, bhāhi, bhābhi. Bhāya, bhānaṃ. Bhāya, bhāyaṃ, bhāsu. Bhoti bhe, bhotiyo bhā, bhotiyo bhāyo. And here, 'bhākaro' (light-maker), 'bhānu' (sun), and so forth, are illustrative examples.

Girā[M 0.0312], girā, girāyo. Giraṃ…pe… bhotiyo girāyo. “Vācā girā byappatho. Ye vohaṃ kittayissāmi, girāhi anupubbaso”ti imāni girāsaddassa itthiliṅgabhāve nidassanapadāni.

Girā, girā, girāyo. Giraṃ…[etc.]… bhotiyo girāyo. “Vācā girā byappatho (Speech, 'girā', is the path of expression). Ye vohaṃ kittayissāmi, girāhi anupubbaso (Whom I shall praise, with speeches, in succession)”—these are illustrative examples of the word 'girā' being in the feminine gender.

Suvaṇṇavācako rāsaddo pulliṅgo, idha pana saddavācako rāsaddo itthiliṅgo.

The word 'rā' denoting gold is masculine, but here the word 'rā' denoting sound is feminine.

Rā, rā, rāyo. Raṃ, rā, rāyo. Rāya, rāhi, rābhi. Rāya, rānaṃ. Rāya, rāhi, rābhi. Rāya, rānaṃ. Rāya, rāyaṃ, rāsu. Bhoti re, bhotiyo rā, bhotiyo rāyo.

Rā, rā, rāyo. Raṃ, rā, rāyo. Rāya, rāhi, rābhi. Rāya, rānaṃ. Rāya, rāhi, rābhi. Rāya, rānaṃ. Rāya, rāyaṃ, rāsu. Bhoti re, bhotiyo rā, bhotiyo rāyo.

Rā vuccati saddo. Aggaññasuttaṭīkāyañhi “rā saddo tiyati chijjati etthāti ratti, sattānaṃ saddassa vūpasamakālo”ti vuttaṃ. Tasmā rāsaddassa saddavācakatte “rattī”ti padaṃ nidassanaṃ.

'Rā' is called sound. For in the commentary to the Aggañña Sutta it is said: '`rā` (sound) ceases, is cut off, herein, hence `ratti` (night); it is the time of the cessation of sound for beings.' Therefore, for the word 'rā' having the meaning of sound, the word 'ratti' is an illustration.

Pavanaṃ, pavanāni, pavanā. Pavanaṃ, pavanāni, pavane.

Pavanaṃ, pavanāni, pavanā. Pavanaṃ, pavanāni, pavane.

Vanaṃ, vanāni, vanā. Vanaṃ, vanāni, vane. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ neyyaṃ.

Vanaṃ, vanāni, vanā. Vanaṃ, vanāni, vane. All the rest is to be understood.

Pavana vanasaddā kadāci samānatthā kadāci bhinnatthā. Te hi araññavācakatte samānatthā “te dhamme paripūrento, pavanaṃ pāvisiṃ tadā. Saputto pāvisiṃ vana”ntiādīsu. Yathākkamaṃ pana te vāyutaṇhāvanavācakatte bhinnatthā “paramaduggandhapavanavicarite. Chetvā vanañca vanathaṃ, nibbanā hotha bhikkhavo”tiādīsu.

The words 'pavana' and 'vana' sometimes have the same meaning, sometimes different meanings. For when denoting a forest, they have the same meaning, as in: 'Having fulfilled those qualities, I then entered the forest (`pavanaṃ`). With my son, I entered the forest (`vanaṃ`),' and so forth. But respectively, when they denote wind and craving-forest, they have different meanings, as in: 'Roaming in a wind (`pavana`) of extreme foulness. Having cut down the forest (`vana`) and the undergrowth (`vanathaṃ`), be without craving (`nibbanā`), O monks,' and so forth.

Udakaṃ, udakāni, udakā. Udakaṃ, udakāni, udake.

Udakaṃ, udakāni, udakā. Udakaṃ, udakāni, udake.

Dakaṃ, dakāni, dakā. Dakaṃ, dakāni, dake. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ neyyaṃ.

Dakaṃ, dakāni, dakā. Dakaṃ, dakāni, dake. All the rest is to be understood.

“Ambapakkaṃ [M 0.0313] dakaṃ sītaṃ. Thalajā dakajā pupphā”tiādīnettha nidassanapadāni. “Nīlodaṃ vanamajjhato. Mahodadhi. Udabindunipātena, udakumbhopi pūratī”ti pāḷippadesesu pana samāsantagatanāmattā udasaddeneva udakattho vutto “rittassāda”nti vattabbaṭṭhāne “rittassa”nti saddena rittassādattho viya. Pāḷiyañhi kevalo udasaddo na diṭṭhapubbo. Atthi ce, suṭṭhu manasi kātabbo.

Here, illustrative examples are 'Ambapakkaṃ dakaṃ sītaṃ' (a ripe mango, cool water), 'Thalajā dakajā pupphā' (flowers born on land, born in water), and so forth. However, in Pāli passages such as 'Nīlodaṃ vanamajjhato' (blue water from the midst of the forest), 'Mahodadhi' (great ocean), 'Udabindunipātena, udakumbhopi pūratī' (even a water pot is filled by the falling of drops of water), the meaning of water is expressed by the word 'uda' alone, due to its being a noun at the end of a compound, just as the meaning of 'devoid of taste' is expressed by the word 'rittassa' in the place where 'rittassāda' should be said. Indeed, in the Pāli, the word 'uda' alone has not been seen before. If it exists, it should be well borne in mind.

Kaṃ, kāni, kā. Kaṃ, kāni, ke. Kena, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Kā, kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Ke, kasmiṃ, kamhi, kesu. Bho ka, bhavanto kā, bhavanto kāni. Bhosaddena vā bahuvacanaṃ yojetabbaṃ “bho kāni, bho kā”ti.

Kaṃ, kāni, kā. Kaṃ, kāni, ke. Kena, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Kā, kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Ke, kasmiṃ, kamhi, kesu. Bho ka, bhavanto kā, bhavanto kāni. Or, the plural should be combined with the word 'bho', as in: 'bho kāni, bho kā'.

Ettha kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ sīsaṃ sukhañca. Atra “kantāro kandaro kevaṭṭā kesā karuṇā nāko”tiādīni payogāni veditabbāni. Tatra kantāroti kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena taritabbo atikkamitabboti kantāro, nirudakappadeso. Corakantārantiādīsu pana rūḷhiyā duggamanaṭṭhānepi kantārasaddo pavattatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kandaroti etthāpi kaṃ vuccati udakaṃ, tena dārito bhinnoti kandaro. Kevaṭṭātiādīsu pana ke udake vattanato gahaṇatthaṃ pavattanato kevaṭṭā. Ke sīse senti uppajjantīti kesā. Kaṃ sukhaṃ rundhatīti karuṇā. Nākoti saggo. Kanti hi sukhaṃ, na kaṃ akaṃ, dukkhaṃ, taṃ natthi etthāti nākoti attho gahetabbo[M 0.0314]. Yathettha itthīsaddādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālā yojitā, evaṃ “vitakko vicāro ābhā padīpo”tiādīnampi yojetabbā.

Here, 'kaṃ' is said to be water, the head, and happiness. Here, usages such as 'kantāro' (desert), 'kandaro' (ravine), 'kevaṭṭā' (fishermen), 'kesā' (hair), 'karuṇā' (compassion), 'nāko' (heaven), and so forth, should be understood. In that context, 'kantāro' is so called because 'kaṃ' is said to be water, and it is a place to be crossed or passed over by that; it is a waterless region. However, in terms like 'corakantāro' (thieves' desert), it should be noted that the word 'kantāra' is conventionally used to mean a difficult place to traverse. In 'kandaro' also, 'kaṃ' is said to be water; because it is split or broken by that, it is a 'kandaro' (ravine). In terms like 'kevaṭṭā', because they operate in water (ke) for the purpose of catching, they are 'kevaṭṭā' (fishermen). Because they lie or arise on the head (ke), they are 'kesā' (hair). Because it obstructs happiness (kaṃ), it is 'karuṇā' (compassion). 'Nāko' is heaven. For 'kaṃ' is happiness; 'na kaṃ' is 'akaṃ', which is suffering; because that does not exist there, it is 'nāko'—this meaning should be taken. Just as the nominal paradigm for words like 'itthī' has been applied here, so too should it be applied for those like 'vitakko' (thought), 'vicāro' (investigation), 'ābhā' (splendor), 'padīpo' (lamp), and so forth.

Bhū, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuṃ, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhuyaṃ, bhūsu. Bhoti bhu, bhotiyo bhū, bhotiyo bhuyo. Ettha ca “bhūruho bhūpālo bhūbhujo bhūtala”nti nidassanapadāni.

Bhū (earth), bhū, bhuyo. Bhuṃ, bhū, bhuyo. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhūhi, bhūbhi. Bhuyā, bhūnaṃ. Bhuyā, bhuyaṃ, bhūsu. Bhoti bhu (O earth), bhotiyo bhū, bhotiyo bhuyo. And here, 'bhūruho' (earth-born), 'bhūpālo' (earth-protector), 'bhūbhujo' (earth-enjoyer), 'bhūtala' (earth's surface) are illustrative terms.

Bhūmi, bhūmī, bhūmiyo; Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ;

Araññaṃ, araññāni, araññā; Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Bhūmi (earth), bhūmī, bhūmiyo; The rest is to be elaborated. Araññaṃ (forest), araññāni, araññā; The rest is to be elaborated.

Araññānī vuccati mahāaraññaṃ, “gahapatānī”ti padamiva inīpaccayavasena sādhetabbaṃ padaṃ itthiliṅgañca. “Araññānī”ti hi aṭṭhakathāpāṭhopi dissati.

'Araññānī' is said to be a great forest; it is a feminine word to be formed like the word 'gahapatānī' by means of the suffix 'inī'. For the reading 'araññānī' is also seen in the commentaries.

Araññānī, araññānī, araññāniyo. Araññāniṃ, araññānī, araññāniyo. Araññāniyā, araññānīhi, araññānībhi. Araññāniyā, araññānīnaṃ. Araññāniyā, araññānīhi, araññānībhi. Araññāniyā, araññānīnaṃ. Araññāniyā, araññāniyaṃ, araññānīsu. Bhoti araññāni, bhotiyo araññānī, bhotiyo araññāniyo.

Araññānī (great forest), araññānī, araññāniyo. Araññāniṃ, araññānī, araññāniyo. Araññāniyā, araññānīhi, araññānībhi. Araññāniyā, araññānīnaṃ. Araññāniyā, araññānīhi, araññānībhi. Araññāniyā, araññānīnaṃ. Araññāniyā, araññāniyaṃ, araññānīsu. Bhoti araññāni (O great forest), bhotiyo araññānī, bhotiyo araññāniyo.

Yathettha uttarādhikavasena yojitā, evaṃ “sabhā, sabhāya”ntiādīsupi yojetabbā. Sabhāyanti sabhā eva[M 0.0315], liṅgabyattayavasena pana evaṃ vuttaṃ. “Sabhāye vā dvāramūle vā vatthabba”nti pāḷi ettha nidassanaṃ.

Just as it has been applied here by way of further extension, so too should it be applied in cases like 'sabhā, sabhāya', and so forth. 'Sabhāya' means 'sabhā' itself, but it is stated thus due to the variation in gender. The Pāli passage 'Sabhāye vā dvāramūle vā vatthabba' (One should dwell either in the assembly hall or at the door) is an illustration here.

Paññā, paññā, paññāyo. Paññaṃ, paññā, paññāyo. Paññāya.

Paññā (wisdom), paññā, paññāyo. Paññaṃ, paññā, paññāyo. Paññāya.

Paññāṇaṃ, paññāṇāni, paññāṇā. Paññāṇaṃ, paññāṇāni, paññāṇe. Paññāṇena.

Paññāṇaṃ (cognition), paññāṇāni, paññāṇā. Paññāṇaṃ, paññāṇāni, paññāṇe. Paññāṇena.

“Tathā hi bhante bhagavato sīlapaññāṇaṃ. Sādhu paññāṇavā naro”tiādīnettha nidassanapadāni.

'Indeed, venerable sir, such is the Blessed One's virtue and cognition.' 'Good is the person with cognition,' and so forth, are illustrative terms here.

Ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇāni, ñāṇā. Ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇāni, ñāṇe. Ñāṇena. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ neyyaṃ. “Aggi aggini gini”iccādīsupi uttarādhikavasena nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

Ñāṇaṃ (knowledge), ñāṇāni, ñāṇā. Ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇāni, ñāṇe. Ñāṇena. All the rest is to be inferred. Even in cases like 'aggi' (fire), 'aggini', 'gini', and so forth, the nominal paradigm should be applied by way of further extension.

Ko vī sādīsupi ekakkharesu ko vuccati brahmā vāto ca sarīrañca, tassa tabbācakatte ime payogā. Seyyathidaṃ?

Even among single-syllable words like 'ko', 'vī', and 'sā', 'ko' is said to be Brahmā, wind, and body. When it denotes those, these are the usages. As follows:

“Jinena yena ānītaṃ, lokassa amitaṃ hitaṃ;

Tassa pādambujaṃ vande, kamoḷialisevitaṃ.

By which Conqueror immeasurable welfare was brought to the world, I venerate his lotus feet, served by the bees that are the head-ornaments of Brahmā.

Kakudharukkho. Karajakāyo” iccevamādayo. Tattha kamoḷialisevitanti vandantānaṃ anekasatānaṃ brahmānaṃ moḷibhamarasevitanti kavayo icchanti. Kakudharukkhoti ettha pana ko vuccati vāto, tassa yo kujjhati, vātarogāpanayanavasena taṃ nivāreti, tasmā so rukkho kakudhoti vuccatībhi ācariyā. Karajakāyoti ettha tu ko vuccati sarīraṃ, tattha pavatto rajo karajo. Kiṃ taṃ[M 0.0316]? Sukkasoṇitaṃ. Tañhi “rāgo rajo, na ca pana reṇu vuccatī”ti evaṃ vuttarāgarajaphalattā sarīravācakena kasaddena visesetvā phalavohārena “karajo”ti vuccati. Tena sukkasoṇitasaṅkhātena karajena sambhūto kāyo karajakāyoti ācariyā. Tathā hi “kāyo mātāpettikasambhavo”ti vutto, mahāassapūrasuttaṭīkāyaṃ pana “kariyati gabbhāsaye khipiyatīti karo, sambhavo. Karato jātoti karajo, mātāpettikasambhavoti attho. Mātuādīnaṃ saṇṭhāpanavasena karato jātoti apare, ubhayathāpi karajakāyanti catusantatirūpamāhā”ti vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ panattho idha nādhippeto, purimoyevattho adhippeto kasaddādhikārattā.

'The Kakudha tree. The body born of impurities,' and so forth. Here, 'kamoḷialisevitaṃ' is interpreted by poets as 'served by the bees that are the topknots of many hundreds of Brahmās paying homage.' Regarding 'kakudharukkho', here 'ka' is said to be the wind; because it counteracts the wind when it is agitated, preventing it by way of removing wind-diseases, therefore the teachers say that tree is called 'kakudha'. Regarding 'karajakāyo', here 'ka' is said to be the body; the impurity (rajo) that arises therein is 'karaja'. What is that? Semen and blood. For, since it is said, 'Passion is impurity, but it is not called dust,' it is called 'karaja' by way of a result-based designation, being the result of the passion-impurity so stated, and being specified by the word 'ka' which denotes the body. Thus, the teachers say that the body produced from the 'karaja' designated as semen and blood is called 'karajakāya'. Indeed, it is said, 'the body has its origin in mother and father.' However, in the subcommentary to the Mahāassapūra Sutta, it is said: 'Because it is made or cast into the womb, it is 'kara', the origin. 'Karaja' means born from 'kara'; the meaning is 'of maternal and paternal origin'. Others say it is born from 'kara' by way of establishing the mother, etc.; in both ways, 'karajakāya' refers to the form of the four continuities.' But this meaning is not intended here; the former meaning is intended because this is the section on the word 'ka'.

Ko, kā. Kaṃ, ke. Kena, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Kā, kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Ke, kasmiṃ, kamhi, kesu. Bho ka, bhavanto kā.

Ko, kā. Kaṃ, ke. Kena, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Kā, kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kānaṃ. Ke, kasmiṃ, kamhi, kesu. Bho ka, bhavanto kā.

Tatra vi vuccati pakkhī. Tathā hi pakkhīnaṃ issaro supaṇṇarājā vindoti kathiyati. Etamatthañhi sandhāya pubbācariyenapi ayaṃ gāthā bhāsitā –

There, 'vi' is said to be a bird. For the lord of birds, the Supaṇṇa-king, is called Vinda. With this meaning in mind, this verse was also spoken by the ancient teachers:

“Saddhānate muddhani saṇṭhapemi, muninda nindāpagataṃ tavaggaṃ;

Devindanāgindanarindavinda-na taṃ vibhinnaṃ caraṇāravinda”nti.

O Lord of Sages, on my head bowed in faith I place your supreme, blameless lotus feet, bowed to by the lord of devas, the lord of nāgas, the lord of men, and the lord of birds (Vinda).

Tattha vīnaṃ indoti vindo, pakkhijātiyā jātānaṃ supaṇṇānaṃ rājāti attho.

Here, 'vinda' means the lord of birds ('vīnaṃ indo'), that is, the king of the Supaṇṇas born of the bird species.

Viṃ, vī, vayo. Viṃ, vī, vayo. Vinā, vīhi, vībhi. Vissa, vino, vīnaṃ. Vinā, vismā, vimhā, vīhi, vībhi. Vissa, vino, vīnaṃ. Vismiṃ, vimhi, vīsu. Bho vi, bhavanto vayo.

Viṃ, vī, vayo. Viṃ, vī, vayo. Vinā, vīhi, vībhi. Vissa, vino, vīnaṃ. Vinā, vismā, vimhā, vīhi, vībhi. Vissa, vino, vīnaṃ. Vismiṃ, vimhi, vīsu. Bho vi, bhavanto vayo.

Sā [M 0.0317] vuccati sunakho, “mātā me atthi, sā mayā posetabbā”tiādīsu pana sāsaddo sabbanāmikapariyāpanno parammukhavacano tasaddena sambhūto daṭṭhabbo. Sāsaddassa bhā rā thī bhū kasaddānañca nāmikapadamālā heṭṭhā pakāsitā.

'Sā' is said to be a dog. However, in phrases like 'I have a mother, she must be supported by me,' the word 'sā' should be understood as being included in the category of pronouns, referring to one who is not present, and originating from the word 'ta'. The nominal paradigms of the words 'sā,' 'bhā,' 'rā,' 'thī,' 'bhū,' and 'ka' have been explained below.

Dhī vuccati paññā. Ettha ca “amacce tāta jānāhi, dhīre atthassa kovide”ti. “Dhīmā, dhīmati, sudhī, sudhinī, dhīyutta”nti ca ādīni nidassanapadāni.

'Dhī' is said to be wisdom. Here, 'Know, dear child, the ministers who are wise, skilled in the goal,' and 'Dhīmā, dhīmati, sudhī, sudhinī, dhīyutta,' etc., are illustrative examples.

Dhī, dhī, dhiyo. Dhiṃ, dhī, dhiyo. Dhiyā, dhīhi, dhībhi. Dhiyā, dhīnaṃ. Dhiyā, dhīhi, dhībhi. Dhiyā, dhīnaṃ. Dhiyā, dhiyaṃ, dhīsu. Bhoti dhi, bhotiyo dhī, bhotiyo dhiyo.

Dhī, dhī, dhiyo. Dhiṃ, dhī, dhiyo. Dhiyā, dhīhi, dhībhi. Dhiyā, dhīnaṃ. Dhiyā, dhīhi, dhībhi. Dhiyā, dhīnaṃ. Dhiyā, dhiyaṃ, dhīsu. Bhoti dhi, bhotiyo dhī, bhotiyo dhiyo.

Ku vuccati pathavī. Ettha ca “kudālo. Kumudaṃ. Kuñjaro”ti imāni nidassanapadāni. Tatra kuṃ pathaviṃ dālayati padāleti bhindati etenāti kudālo. Kuyaṃ pathaviyaṃ modatīti kumudaṃ. Kuṃ jaratīti kuñjaro. Tathā hi vimānavatthuaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “kuṃ pathaviṃ tadabhighātena jarayatīti kuñjaro”ti.

'Ku' is said to be the earth. Here, 'kudālo' (spade), 'kumudaṃ' (lotus), and 'kuñjaro' (elephant) are illustrative examples. There, 'kudālo' is so called because by it one splits, breaks, or shatters 'ku' (the earth). 'Kumudaṃ' is so called because it delights in 'ku' (the earth). 'Kuñjaro' is so called because it wears down 'ku' (the earth). As indeed stated in the Vimānavatthu commentary: 'Because it wears down the earth ('ku') by its impact, it is called 'kuñjaro'.'

Ku, kū, kuyo. Kuṃ, kū, kuyo. Kuyā, kūhi, kūbhi. Kuyā, kūnaṃ. Kuyā, kūhi, kūbhi. Kuyā, kūnaṃ. Kuyā, kuyaṃ, kūsu. Bhoti ku, bhotiyo kū, bhotiyo kuyo.

Ku, kū, kuyo. Kuṃ, kū, kuyo. Kuyā, kūhi, kūbhi. Kuyā, kūnaṃ. Kuyā, kūhi, kūbhi. Kuyā, kūnaṃ. Kuyā, kuyaṃ, kūsu. Bhoti ku, bhotiyo kū, bhotiyo kuyo.

Kha’mindriyaṃ pakathitaṃ, kha’mākāsamudīritaṃ;

Saggaṭṭhānampi khaṃ vuttaṃ, suññattampi ca khaṃ mataṃ.

'Kha' is explained as a sense faculty; 'kha' is declared as space; the celestial realm is also said to be 'kha,' and emptiness, too, is considered 'kha.'

Tatrindriyaṃ [M 0.0318] cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ gatinivāsabhāvato “kha”nti vuccati, ākāsaṃ vivittaṭṭhena. Saggo katasucaritehi ekantena gantabbatāya “kha”nti saṅkhaṃ gacchati. “Khago yathā hi rukkhagge, nilīyantova sākhino. Sākhaṃ ghaṭṭetī”ti ca, “khe nimmito acari aṭṭhasataṃ sayambhū”ti ca ādi ettha nidassanaṃ.

Here, the sense faculty is called 'kha' because it is the sphere and abode of eye-consciousness and so on; as is space, on account of its void nature. Heaven is designated as 'kha' because it is to be reached exclusively by those who have performed good deeds. Illustrations of this are: 'Just as a bird at the treetop, as if hiding among the branches, strikes a branch,' and 'The self-existent one, fashioned in the sky, wandered for eight hundred [years],' and so forth.

Khaṃ, khāni, khā. Khaṃ, khāni, khe. Khena, khehi, khebhi. Khassa, khānaṃ. Khā, khasmā, khamhā, khehi, khebhi. Khassa, khānaṃ. Khe, khasmiṃ, khamhi, khesu. Bho kha, bhavanto khāni, bhavanto khā.

Khaṃ (sg.), khāni, khā (pl.). Khaṃ (sg.), khāni, khe (pl.). By khena (sg.); by khehi, khebhi (pl.). Of khassa (sg.); of khānaṃ (pl.). From khā, khasmā, khamhā (sg.); from khehi, khebhi (pl.). Of khassa (sg.); of khānaṃ (pl.). In khe, khasmiṃ, khamhi (sg.); in khesu (pl.). O kha (sg.); O you khāni, O you khā (pl.).

Gosaddassa atthuddhāro vuccate –

The explanation of the meaning of the word 'go' is stated.

Go goṇe cindriye bhūmyaṃ, vacane ceva buddhiyaṃ;

Ādicce rasmiyañceva, pānīyepi ca vattate;

Tesu atthesu goṇe thi-pumā ca itare pumā.

The word 'go' refers to cattle, the senses, the earth, speech, and wisdom; also to the sun, its rays, and to water. Among these meanings, in the sense of cattle, it is feminine and masculine, while in the others it is masculine.

Tathā hi “gosu duyhamānāsu gato. Gopañcamo”tiādīsu gosaddo goṇe vattati. Gocaroti etthindriyepi vattati gāvo cakkhādīnindriyāni caranti etthāti gocaro. Tathā hi porāṇā kathayiṃsu “gāvo caranti etthāti gocaro, gocaro viya gocaro, abhiṇhaṃ caritabbaṭṭhānaṃ. Gāvovācakkhādīnindriyāni, tehi caritabbaṭṭhānaṃ gocaro”ti. “Gomatiṃ gotamaṃ name”ti porāṇakaviracanāyaṃ pana pathaviyaṃ vattati. “Bhūripaññaṃ gotamaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃvandāmī”ti hi attho. Tathā suttanipātaṭṭhakathāyavāseṭṭhasuttasaṃvaṇṇanappadese “gorakkhanti khettarakkhaṃ, kasirakkhanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pathavī hi “go”ti vuccati, tappabhedo ca khetta”nti vuttaṃ.

For in such phrases as 'when the cows are being milked, he went,' and 'with a cow as the fifth,' the word 'go' applies to cattle. In 'gocara' it is also used in the sense of the faculties, meaning 'the cows, which are the faculties of the eye, etc., roam here—thus, it is gocara.' Indeed, the ancients explained: 'The cows roam here—thus, it is gocara. Like a pasture, it is a gocara—a place to be frequently wandered. The cows are the faculties of the eye, etc., and the place they wander is the gocara.' In the ancient poet’s composition, 'I bow to Gotama, the possessor of earth,' the term refers to the earth. The meaning is: 'I venerate the greatly wise Gotama, the perfectly self-enlightened one.' Similarly, in the commentary on the Sutta Nipāta, in the section explaining the Vāseṭṭha Sutta, it is said: ''Gorakkha' means protecting the field; it is said to mean 'kasirakkha'. For the earth is called 'go,' and the field is a division of it.'

“Gottavasena [M 0.0319] gotamo”ti ettha tu vacane buddhiyañca vattati. Tenāhu porāṇā “gaṃ tāyatīti gottaṃ. Gotamoti hi pavattamānaṃ gaṃ vacanaṃ buddhiñca tāyati ekaṃsikavisayatāya rakkhatīti gottaṃ. Yathā hi buddhi ārammaṇabhūtena atthena vinā na vattati, evaṃ abhidhānaṃ abhidheyyabhūtena, tasmā so gottasaṅkhāto attho tāni tāyati rakkhatīti vuccati. Ko pana soti? Aññakulaparamparāsādhāraṇaṃ tassa kulassa ādipurisasamudāgataṃ taṃkulapariyāpannasādhāraṇaṃ sāmaññarūpanti daṭṭhabba”nti. Tathā hi taṃgottajātā suddhodanamahārājādayopi gotamotveva vuccanti. Bhena bhagavā attano pitaraṃ suddhodanamahārājānaṃ “atikkantavarā kho gotama tathāgatā”ti avoca. Vessavaṇopi mahārājā bhagavantaṃ “vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotama”nti avoca, āyasmāpi vaṅgīso āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ “sādhu nibbāpanaṃ brūhi, anukampāya gotamā”ti avoca. Evaṃ idaṃ sāmaññarūpaṃ gaṃ tāyatīti gottanti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana gotamagottakassapagottādivasena bahuvidhaṃ.

In 'Gotama by lineage,' it applies to both speech and wisdom. Therefore, the ancients said: 'It is called 'gotta' because it protects (tāyati) speech (gaṃ).' For 'Gotama' signifies that which protects and safeguards ongoing speech and wisdom by means of having a singular object. Just as wisdom cannot function without an object, so too a name cannot function without that which is named. Hence, that meaning designated as 'gotta' is said to protect and preserve them. But what is it? It should be understood as the common characteristic of that clan, originating from its founding ancestor, shared among all members of that lineage. For example, those born into the Gotama lineage, such as King Suddhodana and others, are also called 'Gotama.' Indeed, the Blessed One himself addressed his father, King Suddhodana, saying, 'O Gotama, the Tathāgatas have gone beyond.' Likewise, the great king Vessavaṇa addressed the Blessed One, saying, 'We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama, accomplished in knowledge and conduct.' The venerable Vaṅgīsa also said to the venerable Ānanda, 'O Gotama, out of compassion, speak for the sake of quenching.' Thus, this general characteristic is expressed as 'gotta'—that which protects speech. Now, this 'gotta' is of many kinds, such as the Gotama lineage, the Kassapa lineage, and so forth.

Tathā gosaddo ādicce vattati. “Gogottaṃ gotamaṃ name”ti porāṇakaviracanā ettha nidassanaṃ, ādiccabandhuṃ gotamaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ vandāmīti attho. Ādiccopi hi gotamagotte jāto bhagavāpi, evaṃ tena samānagottatāya tattha tattha “ādiccabandhū”tiādinā bhagavato thomanā dissati “pucchāmi taṃ ādiccabandhu, vivekaṃ santipadañca mahesī”ti ca, “vande jetavanaṃ niccaṃ, vihāraṃ ravibandhuno”ti ca, “lokekabandhu’maravindasahāyabandhu”nti ca. “Uṇhagū”ti ettha pana gosaddo rasmiyaṃ [M 0.0320] vattati. Uṇhā gāvo rasmiyo etassāti uṇhagū, sūriyo. Pubbācariyāpi hi chandovicitisatthe imamevatthaṃ byākariṃsu.

Likewise, the word 'go' applies to the sun. 'Gogottaṃ Gotamaṃ name' – this is an illustration from an ancient poetic composition, meaning: 'I pay homage to Gotama of the sun-lineage, the perfectly self-enlightened Buddha.' For the sun was born in the Gotama lineage, and so was the Blessed One. Thus, due to their shared lineage, the Blessed One is praised in various places with terms like 'kinsman of the sun,' as seen in: 'I ask you, kinsman of the sun, about seclusion and the peaceful state, O great sage.' And: 'I constantly venerate Jetavana, the dwelling of the kinsman of the sun.' And: 'The one kinsman of the world, kinsman of the friend of the lotus.' But in 'uṇhagū,' the word 'go' applies to a ray. 'Uṇhagū' means 'he whose rays are hot,' that is, the sun. Indeed, the ancient teachers also explained this very meaning in the Chandoviciti treatise.

“Gosītacandana”nti ettha pānīye vattati. Gosaddena hi jalaṃ vuccati. Go viya sītaṃ candanaṃ, tasmiṃ pana uddhanato uddharitapakkuthitatelamhi pakkhitte taṅkhaṇaññeva taṃ telaṃ susītalaṃ hoti.

In 'gosītacandana,' it applies to water. For by the word 'go,' water is meant. Sandalwood is cool like water; when boiled oil, taken from the hearth, is poured into it, that oil instantly becomes very cool.

Ettheke vadanti “kasmā bho ‘gopadatthe vattamāno gosaddo itthiliṅgo ceva pulliṅgo cā’ti vadatha, kasmā ca pana ‘indriyapathavīvacanabuddhisūriyarasmipānīyesu vattamāno pulliṅgo’ti vadatha, etesu sūriyatthe vattamāno pulliṅgo hotu, nanu indriyavacanapānīyesu vattamānena pana gosaddena napuṃsakaliṅgena bhavitabbaṃ, pathavībuddhirasmīsu vattamānena itthiliṅgena bhavitabbaṃ indriyādipathavādipadatthesu vattamānānaṃ indriyasaddādipathavīsaddādīnaṃ napuṃsakitthiliṅgavasena niddesassa dassanato”ti? Tanna, niyamābhāvato. Itthipadatthe vattamānassāpi hi sato kassaci saddassa pulliṅgavasena niddeso dissati yathā “orodho”ti. Purisapadatthe vattamānassāpi ca sato kassaci itthiliṅgavasena niddeso dissati, yathā “atthakāmosi me yakkha, hitakāmāsi devate”ti. Itthipurisapadatthesu pana avattamānānampi sataṃ kesañci saddānaṃ ekasmiṃyeva ñāṇādiatthe vattamānānaṃ itthipumanapuṃsakaliṅgavasena niddeso dissati yathā “paññā amoho ñāṇa”nti, “taṭaṃtaṭītaṭo”ti ca. Tathā hi anitthibhūtopi samāno “mātulā”ti itthiliṅgavasena rukkhopi [M 0.0321] nāmaṃ labhati, tabbasena nagarampi. Tenāha cakkavattisuttaṭīkāyaṃ “mātulāti itthiliṅgavasena laddhanāmo eko rukkho, tāya āsannappadese māpitattā nagarampi ‘mātulā’tveva paññāyittha. Tena vuttaṃ mātulāyanti evaṃnāmake nagare”ti.

Here some say: "Why, sir, do you say that the word 'go' is both feminine and masculine when it has the meaning of cattle? And why do you say it is masculine when it has the meaning of sense faculty, earth, speech, wisdom, sun, ray, or water? Let it be masculine when it has the meaning of sun, but should not the word 'go', when it refers to sense faculty, speech, or water, be neuter? And when it refers to earth, wisdom, or rays, should it not be feminine? For we see that the words 'indriya', 'pathavī', etc., which refer to the meanings of sense faculty, earth, etc., are designated with neuter and feminine genders respectively." That is not so, due to the absence of a fixed rule. For even when a word refers to a feminine meaning, it is sometimes designated with a masculine gender, as in the case of 'orodho'. And even when a word refers to a masculine meaning, it is sometimes designated with a feminine gender, as in, 'You are my well-wisher, O yakkha; you are my benefactor, O devatā.' Moreover, even when words do not refer to specifically feminine or masculine meanings, some words referring to a single meaning like 'knowledge' are designated with feminine, masculine, and neuter genders, as in 'paññā, amoho, ñāṇa,' and 'taṭaṃ, taṭī, taṭo.' For example, though not actually feminine, a tree receives the name 'mātulā' in the feminine gender, and based on that, a city does as well. Therefore, it is said in the subcommentary to the Cakkavatti Sutta: "'Mātulā' is the name of a certain tree, received in the feminine gender. Because a city was founded in its vicinity, it also became known as 'Mātulā'. Hence it is said: 'in the city named Mātulā'."

Gosaddassa nāmikapadamālā heṭṭhā pakāsitā.

The nominal paradigm of the word 'go' is set forth below.

Mo vuccati cando, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “mā vuccati cando”ti ākārantapāṭho dissati, okārantapāṭhena tena bhavitabbaṃ sakkaṭabhāsāya ekakkharakosato nayaṃ gahetvā “mo sivo candimā cevā”ti okārantavasena vattabbattā. Ettha ca okārantavasena vuttassa masaddassa candavācakatte “puṇṇamī, puṇṇamā”ti ca nidassanapadāni. Tattha puṇṇo mo etthāti puṇṇamī, evaṃ puṇṇamā, rattāpekkhaṃ itthiliṅgavacanaṃ. Ettha pana “visākhapuṇṇamāya rattiyā paṭhamayāmepubbenivāsaṃ anussarī”ti idaṃ nidassanaṃ. Ettha siyā – yadi “puṇṇamā”ti ayaṃsaddo rattāpekkho itthiliṅgo.

The moon is called 'mo'. In the commentary, however, the reading 'the moon is called mā', with an ā-ending, is seen. It should be the reading with an o-ending, taking the principle from a single-syllable dictionary in the Sanskrit language, because it is to be stated with an o-ending, as in 'mo sivo candimā ceva'. And here, when the word 'ma' spoken with an o-ending signifies the moon, the example words are 'puṇṇamī' and 'puṇṇamā'. Therein, 'puṇṇamī' means 'the moon (mo) is full (puṇṇo) in this [night]', and similarly 'puṇṇamā', a feminine word with reference to the night. An example here is: 'On the night of the Visākha full moon, in the first watch, he recollected his past lives.' Here it might be asked: If this word 'puṇṇamā' is feminine with reference to the night...

“Puṇṇamāye yathā cando, parisuddho virocati;

Tatheva tvaṃ puṇṇamano, viroca dasasahassiyaṃ.

Just as the moon on the full-moon night, perfectly pure, shines brightly; so too, you, with a full mind, shine forth over the ten-thousand-fold world.

Anvaddhamāse pannarase, puṇṇamāye uposathe;

Paccayaṃ nāgamāruyha, dānaṃ dātumupāgami”nti

Every half-month, on the fifteenth, on the full-moon Uposatha day, having mounted the elephant named Paccaya, he came to give a gift.

Ādīsu kathaṃ “puṇṇamāye”ti padasiddhīti? Yakārassa yekārādesavasena. Dhammissarena hi bhagavatā “puṇṇamāyā”ti vattabbe “puṇṇamāye”ti vadatā yakārassa ṭhāne yekāro paṭhito itthiliṅgavisaye ttākārassa ṭhāne ttekāro [M 0.0322] viya, nīkārassa ṭhāne nekāro viya ca. Tathā hi yathā “abyayataṃ vilapasi viratte kosiyāyane”ti imasmiṃ rādhajātake “virattā”ti vattabbe “viratte”ti vadantena ttākārassa ṭhāne ttekāro paṭhito, “kosiyāyanī”ti ca vattabbe “kosiyāyane”ti vadantena nīkārassa ṭhāne nekāro paṭhito. Evaṃ “puṇṇamāyā”ti vattabbe “puṇṇamāye”ti vadatā yakārassa ṭhāne yekāro paṭhito. Yathā ca “dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅgha”nti imasmiṃ mahāsamayasuttappadese “dakkhitāyā”ti vattabbe “dakkhitāye”ti vadatā yakārassa ṭhāne yekāro paṭhito, evamidhāpi. Yathā pana “sabhāye vā dvāramūle vā”ti ettha “sabhāya”nti liṅgabyattayavasena sabhā vuttā, na tathā idha “puṇṇamāya”nti liṅgabyattayena puṇṇamā vuttā, atha kho “puṇṇamā”ti ākārantitthiliṅgavasena vuttā. Tathā hi “puṇṇamāyo”ti padaṃ yakāraṭṭhāne yekāruccāraṇavasena sambhūtaṃ bhummavacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

How is the word 'puṇṇamāye' formed in the aforementioned instances? By the substitution of the letter 'ya' with 'ye'. Indeed, when the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma, said 'puṇṇamāye' where 'puṇṇamāyā' should have been said, 'ye' was recited in place of 'ya' in the feminine gender, just as 'tte' is used in place of 'ttā', and 'ne' in place of 'nī'. Thus, for example, in the Rādhajātaka, in the verse 'abyayataṃ vilapasi viratte kosiyāyane', when 'virattā' should have been said, by saying 'viratte', 'tte' was recited in place of 'ttā'; and when 'kosiyāyanī' should have been said, by saying 'kosiyāyane', 'ne' was recited in place of 'nī'. Similarly, when 'puṇṇamāyā' should have been said, by saying 'puṇṇamāye', 'ye' was recited in place of 'ya'. And just as in the passage from the Mahāsamayasutta, 'dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅgha', when 'dakkhitāyā' should have been said, by saying 'dakkhitāye', 'ye' was recited in place of 'ya', so it is here also. However, just as in the phrase 'sabhāye vā dvāramūle vā', the word 'sabhā' is expressed as 'sabhāya' by way of gender variation, it is not so here that 'puṇṇamā' is expressed as 'puṇṇamāya' by gender variation; rather, it is expressed as 'puṇṇamā' by way of being a feminine noun ending in 'ā'. Thus, the word 'puṇṇamāye' should be understood as a locative singular form that has arisen from the pronunciation of 'ye' in place of 'ya'.

Mā vuccati sirī. Tathā hi vidvamukhamaṇḍanaṭīkāyaṃ “mālinī”ti padassatthaṃ vadatā “mā vuccati lakkhī, alinī bhamarī”ti vuttaṃ. Lakkhīsaddo ca sirīsaddena samānattho, tena “mā vuccati sirī”ti attho amhehi anumato, tathā porāṇehipi “maṃ siriṃ dhāreti vidadhāti cāti mandhātā”ti attho pakāsito, tasmā “mālinī mandhātā”ti ca imānettha nidassanapadāni. Tatra pulliṅgassa tāva masaddassa ayaṃ nāmikapadamālā –

Mā is called sirī (splendor, fortune). For in the Vidvamukhamaṇḍanaṭīkā, when explaining the meaning of the word 'mālinī', it is said: 'mā is called lakkhī (fortune), and alinī is a bee.' The word lakkhī is synonymous with the word sirī; therefore, the meaning 'mā is called sirī' is approved by us. Likewise, by the ancients the meaning has been declared: 'he holds and provides splendor (maṃ) and fortune (siriṃ), therefore he is Mandhātā.' Therefore, 'mālinī' and 'Mandhātā' are example words here. Therein, first is the nominal paradigm of the masculine word ma:

Mo, mā. Maṃ, me. Mena, mehi, mebhi. Massa, mānaṃ. Mā, masmā, mamhā, mehi, mebhi. Massa, mānaṃ. Me, masmiṃ, mamhi, mesu. Bho ma, bhavanto mā.

Mo, mā. Maṃ, me. Mena, mehi, mebhi. Massa, mānaṃ. Mā, masmā, mamhā, mehi, mebhi. Massa, mānaṃ. Me, masmiṃ, mamhi, mesu. Bho ma, bhavanto mā.

Ayaṃ [M 0.0323] pana itthiliṅgassa māsaddassa nāmikapadamālā –

This, however, is the nominal paradigm of the feminine word mā:

Mā, mā, māyo. Maṃ, mā, māyo. Māya, māhi, mābhi. Māya, mānaṃ. Māya, māhi, mābhi. Māya, mānaṃ. Māya, māyaṃ, māsu. Bhoti me, bhotiyo māyo.

Mā, mā, māyo. Maṃ, mā, māyo. Māya, māhi, mābhi. Māya, mānaṃ. Māya, māhi, mābhi. Māya, mānaṃ. Māya, māyaṃ, māsu. Bhoti me, bhotiyo māyo.

Ettha pana sirīvācako māsaddo ca saddavācako rāsaddo cāti ime samānagatikā ekakkharattā niccamākārantapakatikattā itthiliṅgattā ca.

Here, the word mā denoting sirī, and the word rā denoting sound—these are similar in their declension, due to being single-syllable, always naturally ending in ā, and being feminine in gender.

Tatra saṃ vuccati santacitto puriso. Yaṃ loke “sappuriso”ti ca, “ariyo”ti ca, “paṇḍito”ti ca vadanti, tassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ yadidaṃ “sa”nti. Evaṃ sappurisāriyapaṇḍitavācakassa saṃsaddassa paccattavacanavasena atthibhāve “sameti asatā asa”nti idaṃ payoganidassanaṃ. Ettha hi “na saṃ asa”nti samāsacintāya sappurisāsappurisapadatthā saṃ asaṃsaddehi vuttāti ñāyanti, tasmā “sappurisapadattho paccattavacanena saṃsaddena vutto natthī”ti vacanaṃ na vattabbaṃ. Ye “natthī”ti vadanti, tesaṃ vacanaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Nāmikapadamālā panassa “saṃ, santaṃ, sante”tiādinā heṭṭhā pakāsitā. Napuṃsakaliṅgatte saṃ vuccati dhanaṃ, “manussassaṃ. Parassaṃ. Sabbassaṃ. Sabbassaharaṇaṃ. Parassaharaṇa”ntiādīnettha nidassanapadāni. Tattha manussassa saṃ manussassaṃ. Evaṃ parassa saṃ parassaṃ. Sabbassa saṃ sabbassaṃ. Tassa haraṇaṃ parassaharaṇaṃ sabbassaharaṇanti samāso. Tathā saṃ vuccati sukhaṃ santi ca. Vuttañhi tabbācakattaṃ porāṇakaviracanāyaṃ –

Therein, saṃ is said to be a person with a peaceful mind. That which in the world is called 'a good person' (sappuriso), 'a noble one' (ariyo), or 'a wise one' (paṇḍito), this is a designation for that, namely, saṃ. Thus, regarding the existence of the word saṃ denoting a good person, a noble one, or a wise one, as an individual word, this is an example of its usage: 'sameti asatā asaṃ'. Here, if considering the compound as 'na saṃ asaṃ', it is understood that the meanings of 'good person' (sappurisa) and 'not a good person' (asappurisa) are expressed by the words saṃ and asaṃ. Therefore, the statement, 'the meaning of "good person" is not expressed by the individual term saṃ,' should not be made. The statement of those who say 'it does not exist' should not be accepted. Its nominal paradigm is explained below as 'saṃ, santaṃ, sante', etc. In the neuter gender, saṃ is said to be wealth; 'manussassaṃ' (a person's wealth), 'parassaṃ' (another's wealth), 'sabbassaṃ' (all wealth), 'sabbassaharaṇaṃ' (the taking of all wealth), 'parassaharaṇaṃ' (the taking of another's wealth) are examples here. Therein, 'manussassa saṃ' is 'manussassaṃ'. Likewise, 'parassa saṃ' is 'parassaṃ', and 'sabbassa saṃ' is 'sabbassaṃ'. The compound 'parassaharaṇaṃ' or 'sabbassaharaṇaṃ' means 'the taking of that'. Likewise, saṃ is called happiness and peace. Indeed, its function as a term for that is stated in an ancient poetic composition:

“Devadevo [M 0.0324] saṃdehī no, hīno devātidehato;

Hatopapātasaṃsāro, sāro saṃ detu dehina”nti.

O God of gods, grant us happiness, which is devoid of a body superior to the gods. May he, who has destroyed the saṃsāra of rebirth and falling away, the excellent one, grant happiness to embodied beings.

Tasmā ayamettha gāthā, “sakalalokasaṅkaro dīpaṅkaro”ti ettha “saṅkaro”ti padañcanidassanaṃ. “Saṃ, sāni, sā. Saṃ, sāni, se. Sena”iccādi pubbe pakāsitanayena ñeyyaṃ. Ettha ca sotūnaṃ sugatamatavare kosallajananatthaṃ samāsantagatassa saṃsaddassa nāmikapadamālaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ katvā kathayāma –

Therefore, this is the verse here. And in the phrase 'sakalalokasaṅkaro dīpaṅkaro', the word 'saṅkaro' is also an example. 'Saṃ, sāni, sā. Saṃ, sāni, se. Sena', and so on, should be understood according to the method previously explained. And here, for the sake of generating skill in the excellent doctrine of the Sugata for the listeners, we shall state the complete nominal paradigm for the word saṃ when it occurs at the end of a compound:

Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussassā. Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussasse. Manussassena, manussassehi, manussassebhi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ. Manussassā, manussassasmā, manussassamhā, manussassehi, manussassebhi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ. Manussasse, manussassasmiṃ, manussassamhi, manussassesu. Bho manussassa, bhonto manussassāni, manussassā. Esa nayo “parassaṃ sabbassa”ntiādīsupi, sabbānetāni padāni abhidheyyaliṅgānīti gahetabbāni.

Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussassā. Manussassaṃ, manussassāni, manussasse. Manussassena, manussassehi, manussassebhi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ. Manussassā, manussassasmā, manussassamhā, manussassehi, manussassebhi. Manussassassa, manussassānaṃ. Manussasse, manussassasmiṃ, manussassamhi, manussassesu. Bho manussassa, bhonto manussassāni, manussassā. This is the method also in 'parassaṃ', 'sabbassaṃ', etc.; all these words should be understood as having the gender of that which they denote.

Yaṃ taṃ kimitisaddānaṃ, nāmamālaṃ panattari;

Sabbanāmaparicchede, pakāsissaṃ tiliṅgato.

However, the nominal paradigm of the words yaṃ, taṃ, and kiṃ, I will explain in the chapter on pronouns, according to the three genders.

Iccevaṃ heṭṭhā uddiṭṭhānaṃ ko vi sādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālā saddhiṃ atthantaranidassanapadehi vibhattā. Tatridaṃ liṅgavavatthānaṃ –

Thus, the nominal paradigm of the words ko, vi, sa, etc., mentioned previously, has been analyzed along with illustrative examples of their different meanings. Here is the determination of genders:

Ko vi sā honti pulliṅge, bhā rā thī dhī ku bhū thiyaṃ;

Kaṃ khaṃ napuṃsake go tu, pume cevitthiliṅgake.

Ko, vi, and sā are in the masculine; bhā, rā, thī, dhī, ku, and bhū are in the feminine. Kaṃ and khaṃ are in the neuter. Go and tu are in the masculine and also in the feminine.

Mo pume itthiliṅge mā, saṃ pume ca napuṃsake;

Yaṃ taṃ kimiti sabbatra, liṅgesveva pavattare.

Mo is in the masculine, mā in the feminine. Saṃ is in the masculine and also in the neuter. Yaṃ, taṃ, and kiṃ occur everywhere in all genders.

Ito aññānipi ekakkharāni upaparikkhitvā gahetabbāni.

Other single-syllable words besides these should also be examined and understood.

Evaṃ [M 0.0325] viññūnaṃ nayaññūnaṃ saddaracanāvisaye paramavisuddhavipulabuddhipaṭilābhatthaṃ paramasaṇhasukhumatthesu payogesu asammohatthaṃ suvaṇṇatale sīhavijambhanena kesarīsīhassa vijambhanamiva tepiṭake buddhavacane ñāṇavijambhanena vijambhanatthañca adhikūnekakkharavasena liṅgattayaṃ missetvā nāmikapadamālā vibhattā.

Thus, for the discerning who understand the method, in the domain of word formation, for the sake of obtaining utmost pure and vast wisdom, and for the purpose of avoiding confusion in the application of extremely subtle and profound meanings—just as the stretching of a maned lion on a golden surface is a display of might, so too for the sake of the unfolding of knowledge in the Buddha’s words of the Tipiṭaka—the nominal paradigms have been divided, mixing the three genders, according to the inclusion of more or fewer single-syllable words.

Sadde bhavanti kusalā na tu keci atthe,

Atthe bhavanti kusalā na tu keci sadde.

Some are skilled in words, but not in meaning; some are skilled in meaning, but not in words.

Kosallameva paramaṃ dubhayattha tasmā,

Yogaṃ kareyya satataṃ matimā varanti.

Therefore, skill in both is supreme; a wise person should constantly make the effort, the excellent ones declare.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu

Thus, concerning the modes of expression in the nine-limbed dispensation, with its commentaries, and in the three baskets,

Viññūnaṃ kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the treatise on the principles of grammar, composed for the proficiency of the discerning,

Liṅgattayamissako nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo

The Division of Nominal Paradigms Intermixed with the Three Genders.

Dasamo paricchedo.

The Tenth Chapter.

11. Vāccābhidheyyaliṅgādiparidīpananāmikapadamālā

11. Nominal Paradigms Elucidating Expressed and Denoted Genders, and so forth.

Vāccābhidheyyaliṅgādi-vasenapi ito paraṃ;

Bhāsissaṃ padamālāyo, bhāsitassānurūpato.

Hereafter, in accordance with what has been said, I shall speak of the nominal paradigms, also by way of the expressed and denoted genders, and so forth.

Tattha vāccaliṅgānīti appadhānaliṅgāni, guṇanāmasaṅkhātāni vā liṅgāni. Abhidheyyaliṅgānīti padhānaliṅgāni, guṇīpadasaṅkhātāni vā liṅgāni. Yasmā pana tesu vāccaliṅgāni nāma abhidheyyaliṅgānuvattakāni bhavanti, tasmā sabbāni bhūdhātumayāni ca vāccaliṅgāni abhidheyyaliṅgānurūpato yojetabbāni. Tesaṃ bhūdhātumayāni vāccaliṅgāni sarūpato nāmikapadamālāya ayojitānipi tattha tattha nayato yojitāni[M 0.0326], tasmā na dāni dassessāma. Abhūdhātumayānipi kiñcāpi nayato yojitāni, tathāpi sotārānaṃ payogesu kosallajananatthaṃ kathayāma, nāmikapadamālañca nesaṃ dassessāma kiñci payogaṃ vadantā.

Herein, 'expressed genders' are secondary genders, or genders designated as quality-names. 'Denoted genders' are primary genders, or genders designated as substance-terms. However, since among these, the expressed genders follow the denoted genders, therefore all expressed genders derived from the root 'bhū' should be construed in accordance with the denoted genders. Even though the expressed genders derived from the root 'bhū' are not construed according to their own form in the nominal paradigms, they are construed according to the method here and there; therefore, we will not demonstrate them now. Even though those not derived from the root 'bhū' are also construed according to the method, nevertheless, for the sake of generating skill in the applications for the listeners, we will explain them, and we will also show their nominal paradigms while speaking of some usage.

Dīgho rasso nīlo pīto,

Sukko kaṇho seṭṭho pāpo;

Saddho suddho ucco nīco,

Katotīto iccādīni.

Long, short, blue, yellow, white, black, superior, evil, faithful, pure, high, low, made, past, and so on.

Dīghā jāgarato ratti, dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ;

Dīgho bālāna saṃsāro, saddhammaṃ avijānataṃ.

Long is the night for one who is awake; long is a league for one who is weary; long is saṃsāra for fools who do not know the true Dhamma.

Dīgho, dīghā. Dīghaṃ, dīghe. Dīghena, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghā, dīghasmā, dīghamhā, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghe, dīghasmiṃ, dīghamhi, dīghesu. Bho dīgha, bhavanto dīghā. “Dīghāti maṃ pakkoseyyāthā”ti idamettha nidassanaṃ.

Dīgho, dīghā. Dīghaṃ, dīghe. Dīghena, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghā, dīghasmā, dīghamhā, dīghehi, dīghebhi. Dīghassa, dīghānaṃ. Dīghe, dīghasmiṃ, dīghamhi, dīghesu. Bho dīgha, bhavanto dīghā. ‘You may call me “Dīgha”’—this is the illustration here.

Dīghā, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghaṃ, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghāya. Sesaṃ kaññānayena ñeyyaṃ.

Dīghā, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghaṃ, dīghā, dīghāyo. Dīghāya. The rest should be understood according to the 'kaññā' paradigm.

Dīghaṃ, dīghāni, dīghā. Dīghaṃ, dīghāni, dīghe. Dīghena. Sesaṃ cittanayena ñeyyaṃ. Rassādīni ca evameva vitthāretabbāni. Ayaṃ vāccaliṅgānaṃ nāmikapadamālā, “guṇanāmānaṃ nāmikapadamālā”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Dīghaṃ, dīghāni, dīghā. Dīghaṃ, dīghāni, dīghe. Dīghena. The rest should be understood according to the 'citta' paradigm. And 'rassa', etc., should be expanded in the same way. This is the nominal paradigm of expressed genders; it is also proper to call it 'the nominal paradigm of quality-names.'

Abhidheyyakaliṅgesu, savisesāni yāni hi;

Tesaṃ dāni yathāpāḷiṃ, padamālaṃ kathessahaṃ.

Among the denoted genders, for those that are indeed distinctive, I shall now relate their nominal paradigms according to the Pāli text.

Katamāni tāni padāni, yāni savisesāni?

What are those words that are distinctive?

Bhavābhavādikaṃ laṅkā-dīpo iccādikāni ca;

Bodhi sandhīti cādīni, savisesāni honti tu.

Those beginning with 'bhavābhava,' and those beginning with 'laṅkādīpa,' and those beginning with 'bodhi' and 'sandhi'—these are indeed distinctive.

Etesu [M 0.0327] hi –

Among these, indeed—

Bhavābhavapadaṃ deka-vaco bahuvaco kvaci;

Samāse asamāsepi, sambhavo tassa icchito.

The term 'bhavābhava' is sometimes singular and sometimes plural. Its occurrence is intended whether in a compound or not in a compound.

Viggahañca padatthañca, vatvā padassimassa me;

Vuccamānamavikkhittā, padamālaṃ nibodhatha.

Having stated the analysis and the meaning of this word, listen undistracted to the nominal paradigm being spoken by me.

Bhavo ca abhavo ca bhavābhavaṃ. Atha vā bhavo ca abhavo ca bhavābhavāni, ayaṃ viggaho. Tatra bhavoti khuddako bhavo. Abhavoti mahanto bhavo. Vuddhatthavācako hettha akāro. Ettha ca sugatiduggativasena hīnapaṇītavasena ca khuddakamahantatā veditabbā. Atha vā bhavoti vuddhi. Abhavoti avuddhi. Ayaṃ padattho. Ayaṃ pana nāmikapadamālā –

'Bhavo ca abhavo ca' is 'bhavābhavaṃ'. Or, 'bhavo ca abhavo ca' is 'bhavābhavāni'—this is the analysis. Therein, 'bhava' means small existence. 'Abhava' means great existence. Here, the prefix 'a-' denotes the meaning of increase. And here, the smallness and greatness should be understood by way of fortunate and unfortunate destinations, and by way of inferior and superior states. Or, 'bhava' means growth, and 'abhava' means non-growth. This is the meaning of the word. Now, this is the nominal paradigm—

Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavena, bhavābhavassa, bhavābhavā, bhavābhavasmā, bhavābhavamhā, bhavābhavassa, bhavābhave, bhavābhavasmiṃ, bhavābhavamhi, bho bhavābhava. Iti bhavābhavapadaṃ ekavacanakaṃ bhavati. Dissati ca tassekavacanatā pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāyañca –

Bhavābhavaṃ (Nom. sg.), bhavābhavaṃ (Acc. sg.), bhavābhavena (Inst. sg.), bhavābhavassa (Dat. sg.), bhavābhavā (Abl. sg.), bhavābhavasmā (Abl. sg.), bhavābhavamhā (Abl. sg.), bhavābhavassa (Gen. sg.), bhavābhave (Loc. sg.), bhavābhavasmiṃ (Loc. sg.), bhavābhavamhi (Loc. sg.), bho bhavābhava (Voc. sg.). Thus, the word 'bhavābhava' occurs in the singular. And its singular form is seen in the Pāli texts and commentaries—

“Atītakappe caritaṃ, ṭhapayitvā bhavābhave;

Imasmiṃ kappe caritaṃ, pavakkhissaṃ suṇohi me”

‘Having set aside the conduct in past aeons, I shall declare the conduct in this aeon within existence and non-existence; listen to me.’

Iti vā,

Or thus,

“Evaṃ bahuvidhaṃ dukkhaṃ, sampattiñca bahūvidhaṃ;

Bhavābhave anubhavitvā, patto sambodhimuttamaṃ”

‘Thus having experienced manifold suffering and manifold good fortune in existence and non-existence, he attained the supreme enlightenment.’

Iti vā evaṃ pāḷiyaṃ bhavābhava padassa ekavacanatā diṭṭhā.

Or thus, in this way, the singular form of the word 'bhavābhava' is seen in the Pāli text.

Aṭṭhakathāyampi [M 0.0328] –

In the commentaries also—

“Asambudhaṃ buddhanisevitaṃ yaṃ,

Bhavābhavaṃ gacchati jīvaloko;

Namo avijjādikilesajāla-

Viddhaṃsino dhammavarassa tassā”ti

‘The world of living beings, unenlightened, goes to existence and non-existence, though it is frequented by Buddhas. Homage to that excellent Dhamma, destroyer of the net of defilements beginning with ignorance.’

Evaṃ tassekavacanatā diṭṭhā.

Thus its singular form is seen.

Bhavābhavāni, bhavābhavā, bhavābhavāni, bhavābhave, bhavābhavehi, bhavābhavebhi, bhavābhavānaṃ, bhavābhavehi, bhavābhavebhi, bhavābhavānaṃ, bhavābhavesu, bhavanto bhavābhavāni. Iti bhavābhavapadaṃ bahuvacanakampi bhavati. Dissati ca tassa bahuvacanakatā pāḷiyaṃ “dhonassa hi natthi kuhiñci loke. Pakappikā diṭṭhi bhavābhavesū”ti. Ubhayampi nayaṃ vomissetvā nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Kathaṃ? “Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavāni. Bhavābhavaṃ, bhavābhavāni. Bhavābhavena, bhavābhavehi, bhavābhavebhi”iccevamādinā cittanayena yojetabbā.
