Bhavābhavāni (Nom. pl.), bhavābhavā (Nom. pl.), bhavābhavāni (Acc. pl.), bhavābhave (Acc. pl.), bhavābhavehi (Inst. pl.), bhavābhavebhi (Inst. pl.), bhavābhavānaṃ (Dat. pl.), bhavābhavehi (Abl. pl.), bhavābhavebhi (Abl. pl.), bhavābhavānaṃ (Gen. pl.), bhavābhavesu (Loc. pl.), bhavanto bhavābhavāni (Voc. pl.). Thus, the word 'bhavābhava' also occurs in the plural. And its plural form is seen in the Pāli text: ‘For the purified one, there is indeed nothing anywhere in the world. Fabricated views are in existences and non-existences.’ Both methods should be combined, and the nominal paradigm should be applied. How? It should be applied according to the 'citta' paradigm, beginning with ‘bhavābhavaṃ (sg.), bhavābhavāni (pl.); bhavābhavaṃ (sg.), bhavābhavāni (pl.); bhavābhavena (sg.), bhavābhavehi (pl.), bhavābhavebhi (pl.)’ and so on.

Napuṃsakekavacana-bahuvacanakā imā;

Padamālā samāsatte, katāti paridīpaye.

These nominal paradigms are for the neuter singular and plural; when in a compound, they are thus explained.

Samāsakapadañceva, asamāsakameva ca;

Bhavābhavapadaṃ dvedhā, iti vidvā vibhāvaye.

Both the compound word and the non-compound word—the word 'bhavābhava' is twofold; thus the discerning one should understand.

Napuṃsakaṃ samāsatte, pulliṅgamitarattane;

Napuṃsakaṃ tu pāyena, ekavacanakaṃ vade.

It is neuter when in a compound, and masculine in the other case. But the neuter is generally spoken of in the singular.

“Bhavo ca abhavo cā”ti, samāsatthaṃ vade budho;

“Bhavato bhava”miccatthaṃ, asamāsassa bhāsaye.

‘Bhava and abhava’—the wise should state this as the meaning of the compound. ‘Bhava from bhava’—this meaning should be spoken for the non-compound.

Pulliṅgattamhi so ñeyyo, nissakkaupayogato;

Evaṃ visesato jaññā, bhavābhavapadaṃ vidū.

It should be understood as masculine due to its usage in the ablative case. Thus, the discerning one should know the word 'bhavābhava' distinctly.

Yathā [M 0.0329] cettha bhavābhavapadassa nāmikapadamālā yojitā, evaṃ “kammākammaṃ phalāphala”ntiādīnampi nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Atthopi nesaṃ yathārahaṃ vattabbo. Yebhuyyenetāni ekavacanakāni bhavanti. Evaṃ tāva bhavābhavapadādīnaṃ visesavantatā daṭṭhabbā.

Just as the nominal paradigm of the word 'bhavābhava' is applied here, so too should the nominal paradigms of 'kammākamma' (action and non-action), 'phalāphala' (fruit and non-fruit), etc., be applied. Their meanings should also be stated appropriately. For the most part, these are singular. Thus, the distinctiveness of words like 'bhavābhava' should be understood.

Laṅkādīpo, laṅkādīpaṃ, laṅkādīpena, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpā, laṅkādīpasmā, laṅkādīpamhā, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpe, laṅkādīpasmiṃ, laṅkādīpamhi, bho laṅkādīpa. Ayaṃ samāsatte nāmikapadamālā. Asamāsattepi pana yojetabbā.

Laṅkādīpo, laṅkādīpaṃ, laṅkādīpena, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpā, laṅkādīpasmā, laṅkādīpamhā, laṅkādīpassa, laṅkādīpe, laṅkādīpasmiṃ, laṅkādīpamhi, bho laṅkādīpa. This is the nominal paradigm when in a compound. However, it should also be applied when not in a compound.

Laṅkā dīpo, laṅkaṃ dīpaṃ, laṅkāya dīpena, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpā, laṅkāya dīpasmā, laṅkāya dīpamhā, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpe, laṅkāya dīpasmiṃ, laṅkāya dīpamhi, bhoti laṅke dīpa. Ayaṃ byāse nāmikapadamālā. Ayaṃ nayo “jambudīpo”ti ettha na labbhati kevalena jambūsaddena jambudīpassa akathanato, yathā kevalena laṅkāsaddena laṅkādīpo kathiyati. Ayaṃ pana byāse padamālānayo visesato kabbaracanāyaṃ kavīnaṃ upakārāya saṃvattati sāsanassāpi. Tathā hi byāsavasena porāṇakaviracanā dissati –

Laṅkā dīpo, laṅkaṃ dīpaṃ, laṅkāya dīpena, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpā, laṅkāya dīpasmā, laṅkāya dīpamhā, laṅkāya dīpassa, laṅkāya dīpe, laṅkāya dīpasmiṃ, laṅkāya dīpamhi, O island of Laṅkā. This is the nominal declension in the non-compound form. This method is not applicable in the case of “Jambudīpa” because Jambudīpa is not expressed by the mere word “Jambu,” unlike how Laṅkādīpa is expressed by the mere word “Laṅkā.” However, this method of non-compound declension is especially beneficial for poets in composing poetry and also for the Dispensation. Indeed, ancient poetic compositions are seen in the non-compound form—

“Vandāmi selamhi samantakūṭe,

Laṅkāya dīpassa sikhāyamāne;

Āvāsabhūte sumanāmarassa,

Buddhassa taṃ pādavaḷañjamagga”nti.

“I venerate that path marked by the Buddha’s footprint on Samantakūṭa peak, the crest of the island of Laṅkā, the dwelling place of the one named Sumana.”

Sāsanepi byāsavasena “dibbo ratho pāturahu, vedehassa yasassino”tiādikā pāḷi dissati.

In the Dispensation too, passages such as “A divine chariot appeared for the glorious Videha” and similar Pāli passages are found in the non-compound form.

Yathā [M 0.0330] pana “jambudīpo”ti ettha ayaṃ nayo na labbhati, tathā “nāgadīpo”tiādīsupi kevalena jambūsaddena jambudīpassa akathanamiva kevalena nāgasaddādinā nāgadīpādīnaṃ akathanatoti. Nanu ca bho “buddhassa jambunadaraṃsino taṃ, dāṭhaṃ mayaṃ jambunarā namāmā”ti porāṇakaviracanāyaṃ jambūsaddena jambudīpo vutto “jambudīpanarā”ti atthasambhavatoti? Saccaṃ “jambudīpanarā”ti attho sambhavati, kevalena pana jambūsaddena jambudīpatthaṃ na vadati, kintu “jambudīpanarā”ti vattabbe gāthāvisayattā adhikakkharadosaṃ parivajjantena dīpasaddalopaṃ katvā “jambunarā”ti vuttaṃ, evaṃ uttarapadalopavasena vutto jambusaddo narasaddaṃ paṭicca samāsabalena “jambudīpanarā”ti atthappakāsane samattho hoti, na kevalo byāsakāle, tathā hi “jambū”ti vutte jambudīpo na ñāyati, atha kho jamburukkhoyeva ñāyati.

Just as this method is not applicable in the case of “Jambudīpa,” so too in “Nāgadīpa” and others, Nāgadīpa and so forth are not expressed by the mere word “nāga” and so on, just as Jambudīpa is not expressed by the mere word “jambū.” But, sir, in the ancient poetic composition, “We bow to that tooth of the Buddha, whose rays are like the Jambu river; we, the people of Jambu, bow,” is not Jambudīpa referred to by the word “jambū,” with the meaning “people of Jambudīpa” being possible? It is true that the meaning “people of Jambudīpa” is possible, but the word “jambū” alone does not convey the meaning of Jambudīpa. Rather, when “people of Jambudīpa” should be said, to avoid the fault of excessive syllables due to the nature of verse, the word “dīpa” is omitted, and “jambunarā” is said. Thus, the word “jambu,” stated by way of elision of the latter part of the compound, relying on the force of the compound with the word “nara,” is capable of expressing the meaning “people of Jambudīpa,” but not by itself in the non-compound state. For when “jambū” is said, Jambudīpa is not understood; rather, only the Jambu tree is understood.

Kiṃ pana bho “kāko dāso, kākaṃ dāsaṃ, kākena dāsenā”ti ayaṃ nayo labbhati, na labbhatīti? Labbhati, kākasaddena kākanāmakassa dāsassa kathanaṃ hoti. Yadi evaṃ “jambudīpo”ti etthāpi “jambunāmako dīpo”ti atthaṃ gahetvā “jambū dīpo, jambuṃ dīpaṃ, jambuyā dīpenā”ti ayaṃ nayo labbhatīti? Na labbhati jambūsaddassa paṇṇattivasena dīpe appavattanato. Jambūsaddo hi rukkheyeva paṇṇattivasena pavattati, na dīpe. Yathā pana cittavohāro cittanāmake gahapatimhipi manepi pavattati “citto gahapati. Cittaṃ mano mānasa”ntiādīsu. Yathā ca kusavohāro kusanāmake raññepi kusatiṇepi pavattati –

“But, sir, is this method, ‘kāko dāso, kākaṃ dāsaṃ, kākena dāsena,’ applicable or not?” It is applicable, for by the word ‘kāka’ a slave named Kāka is expressed. “If that is so, then in the case of ‘Jambudīpa’ too, taking the meaning as ‘an island named Jambu,’ is this method, ‘jambū dīpo, jambuṃ dīpaṃ, jambuyā dīpena,’ applicable?” It is not applicable, because the word ‘jambu’ does not function as a designation for an island. The word ‘jambu’ functions as a designation only for a tree, not for an island. Just as the term ‘citta’ functions as a designation for both a householder named Citta and for the mind—as in ‘Citta the householder,’ ‘Citta, the mind, the intellect,’ and so on. And just as the term ‘kusa’ functions as a designation for both a king named Kusa and for kusa grass—

“Pabhāvatiñca [M 0.0331] ādāya, maṇiṃ verocanaṃ kuso;

Kusāvatiṃ kusarājā, agamāsi mahabbalo;

Kuso yathā duggahito, hatthamevānukantatī”ti

“Taking Pabhāvatī and the radiant jewel, Kusa, the mighty King Kusa, went to Kusāvatī; just as kusa grass, when wrongly grasped, cuts the very hand.”

Ādīsu, tathā kākasaddopi vāyase, evaṃnāmake dāsepi pavattati “kāko ravati, kāko nāma dāso saṭṭhiyojanāni gacchatī”tiādīsu. Jambūsaddo pana gahapatimanādīsu citta kusa kākasaddā viya paṇṇattivasena dīpasmiṃ na pavattati, tasmā yathāvuttoyeva nayo manasikaraṇīyo.

and so on. Similarly, the word ‘kāka’ applies to a crow and also to a slave so named, as in “The crow caws,” “A slave named Kāka travels sixty leagues,” and so on. However, the word ‘jambu,’ unlike the words ‘citta,’ ‘kusa,’ and ‘kāka’ in relation to householders, minds, and so forth, does not function as a designation for an island. Therefore, the method should be considered just as explained.

Yathā panettha “laṅkādīpo”ti saddassa nāmikapadamālā samāsavasena byāsavasena ca yojitā, evaṃ “pubbavidehadīpo, aparagoyānadīpo, uttarakurudīpo, assayujanakkhattaṃ, citramāso, vessantararājā, setavatthaṃ, dibbaratho”tiādīnampi nāmikapadamālā samāsavasena byāsavasena ca yojetabbā. Pubbavidehādisaddehi pubbavidehadīpādīnaṃ kathanañca veditabbaṃ. “Dibbaratho”tiādīnaṃ samāsagatapadānaṃ payojane sati byāsavasena visuṃ kattabbatā ca veditabbā. Tathā hi byāsavasena “dibbo ratho”tiādinā dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ padānaṃ samānādhikaraṇavasena paccekavibhattiyuttabhāve sati gāthāsu vuttipālanasukhuccāraṇaguṇo bhavati. So ca sāsanānukūlo hi ayaṃ nayo ṭhapito. Tathā hi pāvacane “dibbo ratho pāturahu, vedehassa yasassino”tiādikā pāḷiyo bahū dissanti, evaṃ laṅkādīpādisaddānaṃ visesavantatā bhavati.

Just as here the nominal declension of the word “Laṅkādīpo” is applied in both compound and non-compound forms, so too should the nominal declensions of words like “Pubbavidehadīpo, Aparagoyānadīpo, Uttarakurudīpo, Assayujanakkhattaṃ, Citramāso, Vessantararājā, Setavatthaṃ, Dibbaratho” and so forth be applied in both compound and non-compound forms. And it should be understood that by words like Pubbavideha and so forth, the islands such as Pubbavidehadīpa and so forth are expressed. And it should be understood that when there is occasion to use compounded words like “Dibbaratho” and so forth, they should be separated into their non-compound forms. For when, in the non-compound form, two words like “dibbo ratho” have the same case ending and refer to the same thing, there is the quality of preserving the meter and ease of pronunciation in verses. And this method is indeed established in accordance with the Dispensation. Thus, in the canonical texts, many passages like “A divine chariot appeared for the glorious Videha” are seen, and in this way, words like Laṅkādīpa and so forth gain distinctiveness.

Idāni bodhisandhiādīnaṃ visesavantatā vuccati –

Now, the distinctiveness of words such as ‘bodhi,’ ‘sandhi,’ and so forth is stated—

Bodhi sandhi vibhattā’yu, dhātuyeva pajāpati;

Dāmā dāmaṃ tathā saddhā, saddhaṃ taṭaṃ taṭī taṭo.

Bodhi, sandhi, vibhatti, āyu, dhātu, pajāpati; Dāmā, dāmaṃ, likewise saddhā, saddhaṃ, taṭaṃ, taṭī, taṭo.

Byañjanaṃ [M 0.0332] byañjano attho, atthamakkharamakkharo;

Ajjavaṃ ajjavo ceva, tathā maddavagāravā.

Byañjanaṃ, byañjano, attho, atthaṃ, akkharaṃ, akkharo; Ajjavaṃ, ajjavo, and also maddava and gārava.

Vaco vacīti cādīni, samarūpā sarūpato;

Dvittiliṅgāni sambhonti, yathāsambhavamuddise.

Words such as ‘vaco,’ ‘vacī,’ and so forth, being similar in form and appearance, occur in two or three genders, and should be indicated as is possible.

Etesu hi bodhisaddassa tāva “bodhi rājakumāro”ti ca, “ariyasāvako ‘bodhī’ti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgoti bojjhaṅgo”ti ca evaṃ puggalavacanassa “bodhi, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhinā”ti pulliṅge agginayena nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

Among these, first, regarding the word ‘bodhi’: it is used for a person as in ‘Bodhi the prince,’ and also as in ‘a noble disciple is called “bodhī,” and a factor of that bodhi is “bojjhaṅga.”’ Thus, for the word referring to a person, the nominal declension in the masculine gender follows the pattern of ‘aggi’: ‘bodhi, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhinā,’ and so on.

Rukkhamagganibbānasabbaññutaññāṇavacanassa pana “bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiyā”ti itthiliṅge rattinayena nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

However, for the word referring to the tree, the path, Nibbāna, and omniscient knowledge, the nominal declension in the feminine gender follows the pattern of ‘ratti’: ‘bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiyā,’ and so on.

Keci pana “rukkhavacano bodhisaddo pulliṅgo”ti vadanti, taṃ āgamena viruddhaṃ viya dissanato vicāretabbaṃ. Na hi āgame rukkhavacanassa bodhisaddassa pulliṅgabhāvo dissati, puggalavacanassa pana dissati. Yadi ca “sālo dhavo khadīro”tiādīnaṃ viya rukkhavacanassa bodhisaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ siyā, jambū simbalī pāṭalīsaddādīnaṃ rukkhavācakattā pulliṅgattaṃ siyā, na tesaṃ imassa ca rukkhavācakattepi pulliṅgabhāvo upalabbhati. Yadi hi rukkhavacano bodhisaddo pulliṅgo, evaṃ sante nibbānavacano sabbaññutaññāṇavacano ca bodhisaddo napuṃsakaliṅgo siyā “nibbāna”ntiādinā napuṃsakaliṅgavasena niddiṭṭhassa nibbānādino atthassa kathanato.

Some, however, say that the word ‘bodhi’ referring to a tree is masculine. That should be examined as it appears to contradict the canonical texts. For in the canonical texts, the masculine gender of the word ‘bodhi’ referring to a tree is not seen, but that of the word referring to a person is seen. And if the word ‘bodhi’ referring to a tree were masculine, like ‘sāla,’ ‘dhava,’ ‘khadīra,’ and so forth, then words like ‘jambū,’ ‘simbalī,’ ‘pāṭalī,’ and so forth, being tree-names, should also be masculine—yet their being masculine is not found, even though they are tree-names. If indeed the word ‘bodhi’ referring to a tree were masculine, then in that case, the word ‘bodhi’ referring to Nibbāna and omniscient knowledge would be neuter, because it expresses the meaning of Nibbāna and the like, which are designated in the neuter gender, as in “nibbāna,” and so forth.

Ye evaṃ vadanti “rukkhavacano bodhisaddo pulliṅgo”ti, te “bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ, taṃ ettha bhagavā pattoti [M 0.0333] rukkhopi bodhicceva vuccatī”ti vuttamatthaṃ cetasi sannidhāya “bujjhati etthāti bodhī”ti nibbacanavasena “kiṃ rukkhavacano bodhisaddo pulliṅgo na bhavissatī”ti maññamānā vadanti maññe. Nevaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, evañca pana daṭṭhabbaṃ, “bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ, taṃ ettha bhagavā pattoti rukkhopi bodhicceva vuccatī”ti vadantehi garūhi ñāṇavacanaṃ itthi liṅgabhūtaṃ bodhīti ñāṇassa nāmaṃ paṇṇattiantaraparikappanenatthaṃ parikappentena bujjhanaṭṭhānabhūte rukkhe āropetvā rukkho “bodhī”ti vutto, tasmā īdisesu ṭhānesu nibbacane ādaro na kātabbo. Na hi “bujjhati etthāti bodhī”ti nibbacanakaraṇaṃ rukkhavacanassa bodhisaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti saṅketasiddhattā vohārassa, tasmā rukkhaṃ sayaṃ abodhimpi samānaṃ bodhiyā paṭilābhaṭṭhānattā saṅketasiddhena “bodhī”ti itthiliṅgavohārena voharanti sāsanikā, bodhiyā vā kāraṇattā phalavohārena. Etamatthaṃyeva hi sandhāya “bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ, taṃ ettha bhagavā pattoti rukkhopi bodhicceva vuccatī”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, evaṃ “bodhī”ti itthiliṅgavasena rukkhanāmaṃ pavattatīti. Tenāha āyasmā sāriputto dhammasenāpati anudhammacakkavattī vohārakusalo itthiliṅgavohārena “buddhānaṃ bhagavantānaṃ bodhiyā mūle saha sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭilābhā sacchikā paññatti yadidaṃ buddho”ti. Apica tattha tattha “bodhiyā sākhā”ti ca, “kenaṭṭhena mahābodhi, kassa sambandhinī ca sā”ti ca,

Those who say, "The word 'bodhi' referring to a tree is masculine," consider the meaning stated as follows: "'Bodhi' means the knowledge in the four paths; since the Blessed One attained it there, even the tree is called 'bodhi.'" Reflecting on this, and thinking, "Since 'bodhi' is derived with the meaning 'one awakens here,' how can the word 'bodhi' referring to a tree not be masculine?", they speak thus, I think. This should not be understood in such a way. Instead, it should be understood thus: When the venerable teachers say, "'Bodhi' means the knowledge in the four paths; since the Blessed One attained it there, even the tree is called 'bodhi,'" they, by conceiving the meaning through an imagined secondary designation, superimpose the name of the knowledge—which is feminine, namely, 'bodhi'—onto the tree, the place of awakening, and say the tree is 'bodhi'. Therefore, in such contexts, one should not be concerned with etymological derivations. For the etymological derivation "one awakens here, hence 'bodhi'" cannot make the word 'bodhi' masculine when it refers to a tree, since its conventional usage is established. Thus, the adherents of the Dispensation refer to the tree—even though it is itself without awakening—as 'bodhi' in the feminine gender by a conventionally established usage, since it is the place where awakening was attained, or because it is the cause of awakening, by way of a designation of the result. This is precisely the meaning intended when it is said, "'Bodhi' means the knowledge in the four paths; since the Blessed One attained it there, even the tree is called 'bodhi.'" Thus, the name of the tree prevails as 'bodhi' in the feminine gender. Hence, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, the secondary Turner of the Wheel of Dhamma, skilled in conventional usage, declared with feminine gender usage: "At the root of the Bodhi tree of the Blessed Buddhas, along with the attainment of omniscient knowledge, is the realized designation, that is, 'Buddha'." Moreover, in various places, expressions like "the branch of the Bodhi tree" and "For what reason is it the Great Bodhi, and to whom does it belong?" are found.

“Hatthato muttamattā sā, asītiratanaṃ nabhaṃ;

Uggantvāna tadā muñci, chabbaṇṇā rasmiyo subhā”ti ca

As soon as it was released from the hand, it rose eighty cubits into the sky. Having risen, it then released beautiful six-colored rays.

Evamādayo [M 0.0334] rukkhavācakassa bodhisaddassa itthiliṅgabhāve payogā dissanti.

These and similar usages are seen for the word 'bodhi' referring to a tree when it is in the feminine gender.

Atha vā rukkhavācako bodhisaddo dviliṅgo pumitthiliṅgavasena. Tathā hi samantapāsādikāyaṃ vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ mahāveyyākaraṇassa pāḷinayaviduno buddhaghosācariyassa evaṃ saddaracanā dissati “sakkhissasi tvaṃ tāta pāṭaliputtaṃ gantvā mahābodhinā saddhiṃ ayyaṃ saṅghamittattheriṃ ānetu”nti ca, “sāpi kho mahābodhisamārūḷhā nāvā passato mahārājassa mahāsamuddatalaṃ pakkhandā”ti ca tassa rukkhavācakassa bodhisaddassa “bujjhati etthāti bodhī”ti nibbacanavasena “bodhi, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhinā”tiādinā padamālā veditabbā. Rukkhavācakasseva pana tassa ñāṇe pavattitthiliṅgavohārena saṅketasiddhena rūḷhatthadīpakena “bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiyā”tiādinā padamālā veditabbā. Iccevaṃ –

Alternatively, the word 'bodhi,' which refers to a tree, is of dual gender, being both masculine and feminine. Indeed, in the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya, the great grammarian skilled in the Pāli method, the venerable teacher Buddhaghosa, uses such word formations: "Will you be able, dear one, to go to Pāṭaliputta and bring back the noble elder nun Saṅghamittā along with the Great Bodhi tree?" and also, "That ship, with the Great Bodhi tree embarked upon it, plunged into the surface of the great ocean as the great king watched." For this word 'bodhi,' which denotes a tree, based on the etymological derivation, "one awakens here, therefore it is 'bodhi'," the declension should be understood as follows: "bodhi, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhayo. Bodhinā," and so on. However, for this same word which denotes a tree, by its feminine usage established by convention in reference to knowledge, which indicates its conventional meaning, the declension should be understood as: "bodhi, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiṃ, bodhī, bodhiyo. Bodhiyā," and so on. Thus—

Puggalavācako bodhi-saddo pulliṅgiko bhave;

Ñāṇādivācako itthi-liṅgoyeva siyā sadā.

The word 'bodhi' denoting a person is masculine. When denoting knowledge and the like, it should always be feminine.

Bodhipādapavacano, pumitthiliṅgiko bhave;

Evaṃ santepi etassa, itthiliṅgattameva tu;

Icchitabbataraṃ yasmā, dhammasenāpatīritaṃ.

The word referring to the Bodhi tree can be masculine and feminine. Even so, its feminine gender is indeed more desirable, because it was declared by the General of the Dhamma.

Sandhisaddādīnampi nayānusārena nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Sandhisaddo hi sarasandhiādivācako pulliṅgo, paṭisandhiyādivācako itthiliṅgo “sandhino. Sandhiyā”tiādidassanato. Vibhattisaddo vibhajanavācako itthiliṅgo[M 0.0335], syādivācako pulliṅgo ceva itthiliṅgo ca “vibhattissa. Vibhattiyā”tiādidassanato.

For the word 'sandhi' and others, the nominal declensions should also be applied according to this method. For the word 'sandhi' is masculine when denoting vowel combination and the like, but feminine when denoting rebirth-linking and the like, as seen in examples such as 'sandhino' and 'sandhiyā'. The word 'vibhatti' is feminine when denoting division, but both masculine and feminine when denoting case endings, as seen in examples such as 'vibhattissa' and 'vibhattiyā'.

Āyusaddo pana jīvitindriyavācakoyeva hutvā punnapuṃsakaliṅgo, “punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisā”ti “ettakaṃyeva te āyu, cavanakālo bhavissatī”ti ca dassanato.

The word 'āyu', however, denoting the life faculty, is masculine and neuter, as illustrated by: "Again, life has been obtained by me. Know thus, O friend," and "Just this much is your life; the time of your passing away will be."

Dhātusaddo sabhāvādivācako itthiliṅgo, karapacādivācako pumitthiliṅgo “cakkhudhātuyā. Karotissa dhātussa. Dhātuyo dhātuyā”ti dassanato.

The word 'dhātu' is feminine when denoting intrinsic nature and the like; it is masculine and feminine when denoting verbal roots such as 'kar', 'pac', and so on, as illustrated by 'cakkhudhātuyā', 'karotissa dhātussa', 'dhātuyo', and 'dhātuyā'.

Pajāpatisaddo devavisesavācako pulliṅgo, kalattajinamātucchāvācako itthiliṅgo “pajāpatissa devarājassa dhajaggaṃ ullokeyyātha”, “attano pajāpatiyā saddhiṃ mahāpajāpatiyā”ti ca dassanato.

The word 'pajāpati' is masculine when referring to a particular deity. It is feminine when it denotes a wife, the mother of a Jina, or a maternal aunt, as seen in phrases like: "You should look up at the banner of Pajāpati, the king of devas," and "with his wife, Mahāpajāpatī."

Dāmā dāmaṃ saddā mālatīdāmādibhedabhinnassa ekassa vatthussa yathākkamaṃ itthinapuṃsakaliṅgā. Tathā hi “mālatīdāmā lolāḷiṅgalīlā. Mālatīdāmaṃ. Siṅghitaṃ dāmaṃ bhamarehi. Ratanadāmā. Ratanadāma”nti ca dviliṅgabhāve lokikappayogā dissanti sāsanānukūlā.

The words 'dāmā' and 'dāmaṃ' refer to a single object with different varieties, such as a jasmine garland, and are feminine and neuter respectively. For example: 'mālatīdāmā lolāḷiṅgalīlā' (a jasmine garland with the playful grace of humming bees), 'mālatīdāmaṃ' (a jasmine garland), 'siṅghitaṃ dāmaṃ bhamarehi' (a garland hummed by bees), 'ratanadāmā' (a jeweled garland), and 'ratanadāmaṃ' (a jeweled garland). In worldly usage, these dual-gender forms are seen, and they are in accordance with the Dispensation.

Saddhaṃ saddhāsaddā pana bhinnavatthūnaṃ vācakā itthinapuṃsakaliṅgā, saddhāsaddo pasādalakkhaṇavācako itthiliṅgo, saddhaṃsaddo matakabhattavācako napuṃsakaliṅgo “saddhā saddahanā. Mayamassubho gotamabrāhmaṇā nāma dānāni dema saddhāni karomā”ti dassanato. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne “saddho puriso[M 0.0336], saddhā itthī, saddhaṃ kula”nti imāni vāccaliṅgattā saṅgahaṃ na gacchantīti daṭṭhabbāni.

The words 'saddhā' and 'saddhaṃ', however, denote different objects and are feminine and neuter. The word 'saddhā', denoting the characteristic of confidence, is feminine. The word 'saddhaṃ', denoting food for the dead, is neuter, as seen in the examples: "Faith is confidence," and "We, venerable Gotama, brahmins by name, give gifts and perform funeral rites." However, in this context, it should be understood that phrases like 'saddho puriso' (a faithful man), 'saddhā itthī' (a faithful woman), and 'saddhaṃ kulaṃ' (a faithful family) are not included in this category, because their gender is determined by the noun they qualify.

Taṭaṃ taṭī taṭotime saddā tīrasaṅkhāte ekasmiṃyevatthe thīpunnapuṃsakaliṅgā.

The words 'taṭaṃ', 'taṭī', and 'taṭo' all denote the same thing, namely 'shore', and are neuter, feminine, and masculine respectively.

Byañjanasaddo upasecanaliṅgavākyāveṇikasarīrāvayavavācako napuṃsakaliṅgo, akkharavācako punnapuṃsakaliṅgo. Tatrupasecane “sūpaṃ vā byañjanaṃ vā”ti napuṃsakaniddeso dissati. Tathā liṅge “itthibyañjanaṃ purisabyañjana”nti napuṃsakaniddeso. Vākye “padabyañjanāni sādhukaṃ uggahetvā”ti napuṃsakaliṅganiddeso. Āveṇike “asīti anubyañjanānī”ti napuṃsakaniddeso. Sarīrāvayave “kilesānaṃ anu anu byañjanato pākaṭabhāvakaraṇato anubyañjana”nti evaṃ napuṃsakaniddeso. Ettha hi anubyañjanaṃ nāma hatthapādasitahasitakathitavilokitādibhedo ākāro. So eva “sarīrāvayavo”ti vuccatīti. Akkhare “byañjano. Byañjana”nti ca punnapuṃsakaniddeso.

The word 'byañjana' is neuter when it denotes seasoning, a sexual characteristic, an expression, a minor characteristic, or a part of the body; it is masculine and neuter when it denotes a letter. Therein, regarding seasoning, the neuter designation is seen in "soup or seasoning." Likewise, regarding a sexual characteristic, the neuter designation is seen in "feminine characteristic" and "masculine characteristic." Regarding an expression, the neuter designation is seen in "having thoroughly learned the words and expressions." Regarding a minor characteristic, the neuter designation is seen in "eighty minor characteristics." Regarding a part of the body, the neuter designation is seen in the etymology: "It is an 'anubyañjana' (minor characteristic) because it makes the defilements manifest by revealing them little by little." For here, 'anubyañjana' refers to a gesture, of which there are various kinds, such as those of the hands and feet, smiling, laughing, speaking, and looking. That itself is called a 'part of the body'. Regarding a letter, both masculine and neuter designations are seen in 'byañjano' and 'byañjanaṃ'.

Atthasaddo nibbānavacano napuṃsakaliṅgo, abhidheyyadhanakāraṇapayojananivatyābhisandhānādivacano pana pulliṅgo. Tathā hi kathāvatthumhi “atthatthamhī”ti imissā pāḷiyā atthasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “atthaṃ vuccati nibbāna”nti napuṃsakaliṅganiddesena atthasaddo vutto. Iti atthasaddo dviliṅgo.

The word 'attha', when denoting Nibbāna, is of the neuter gender; however, when denoting meaning, wealth, cause, purpose, cessation, intention, and so forth, it is masculine. For example, in the Kathāvatthu, in the explanation of the meaning of the Pāli phrase 'atthatthamhī,' the word 'attha' is stated to be Nibbāna with a neuter gender designation, as in 'atthaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ.' Thus, the word 'attha' has two genders.

Akkharasaddo ca “yo pubbo akkharo akkharānī”ti ca dassanato. Apica akkharasaddo nibbānavacano nāmapaṇṇattivacano ca sabbadānapuṃsakaliṅgo bhavati “padamaccutamakkharaṃ, mahājanasammatoti [M 0.0337] kho vāseṭṭha ‘mahāsammato’tveva paṭhamaṃ akkharaṃ nibbatta”nti evamādīsu. “Akkharāya deseti, akkharakkharāya āpatti pācittiyassā”ti ettha pana pulliṅgotipi napuṃsakaliṅgotipi vattabbo, itthiliṅgoti pana na vattabbo. Ayañhi “asakkatā casma dhanañcayāya. Viramathāyasmanto mamavacanāyā”tiādīsu “dhanañcayāya, vacanāyā”ti saddā viya vibhattivipallāsena vutto, na liṅgavipallāsavasenāti.

The word 'akkhara' is also seen to have two genders from such examples as 'yo pubbo akkharo akkharānī' (the former letter; letters). Moreover, the word 'akkhara', when denoting Nibbāna or a name-concept, is always of the neuter gender, as in 'padamaccutamakkharaṃ' (the imperishable, unaging state) and 'O Vāseṭṭha, because he was approved by the great multitude, the first name 'Mahāsammata' arose,' and similar passages. However, in the phrase 'Akkharāya deseti, akkharakkharāya āpatti pācittiyassā' (He teaches for the letter; for each letter there is a pācittiya offense), it can be said to be either masculine or neuter, but not feminine. For this is spoken with an alteration of case ending, like the words 'dhanañcayāya' and 'vacanāyā' in examples such as 'asakkatā casma dhanañcayāya' and 'Viramathāyasmanto mamavacanāyā,' not by way of an alteration of gender.

Ajjava maddava gāravasaddā pana punnapuṃsakaliṅgā. “Ajjavo ca maddavo ca. Ajjavamaddavaṃ. Gāravo ca nivāto ca. Saha āvajjite thūpe, gāravaṃ hoti me tadā”ti ca ādidassanato.

The words 'ajjava,' 'maddava,' and 'gārava' are of masculine and neuter gender. For example: 'Ajjavo ca maddavo ca' (honesty and gentleness, masculine); 'Ajjavamaddavaṃ' (honesty and gentleness, neuter); 'Gāravo ca nivāto ca' (respect and humility, masculine); and 'Saha āvajjite thūpe, gāravaṃ hoti me tadā' (When I reflected on the stupa, respect arose in me then). This is seen from these and other examples.

Vacovacīsaddā pana ghaṭoghaṭīsaddā viya pumitthiliṅgā, tattha vacīsaddassa “vacī, vacī, vaciyo. Vaciṃ, vacī, vaciyo. Vaciyā”ti nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Keci “duccaritapayogaviññattisaddādīsu paresu vacasaddassanto īkāro hoti, tena “vacīduccarita”ntiādīni rūpāni dissantī”ti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ vacasaddato visuṃ vacīsaddassa dassanato. Atrimāni pāḷito ca aṭṭhakathāto ca nidassanapadāni. “Vacī vacīsaṅkhāro, vacīsaṅkhāro vacī, vaciñca vacīsaṅkhāre ca ṭhapetvā avasesā na ceva vacī, na ca vacīsaṅkhāro. Gadito vacībhi satimābhinande”ti imāni pāḷito nidassanapadāni. “Copanasaṅkhātā vacī eva viññatti vacīviññatti, vaciyā bhedo vacībhedo”ti imāni aṭṭhakathāto nidassanapadāni. Iminā nayena aññesampi sarūpāsarūpapadānaṃ [M 0.0338] yathārahaṃ dvitiliṅgatā vavatthapetabbā. Evaṃ abhidheyyakaliṅgesu savisesāni abhidheyyaliṅgāni veditabbāni.

The words 'vaca' and 'vacī', like the words 'ghaṭa' and 'ghaṭī', are of masculine and feminine gender respectively. For the word 'vacī', the nominal paradigm should be applied thus: 'vacī, vacī, vaciyo. Vaciṃ, vacī, vaciyo. Vaciyā.' Some say, 'When followed by words such as duccarita, payoga, and viññatti, the word vaca takes a final ī, and thus forms like vacīduccarita are seen.' This should not be accepted, as the word 'vacī' is seen to be distinct from the word 'vaca'. Here are illustrative examples from the Pāli and the commentaries. From the Pāli: 'Speech is verbal formation; verbal formation is speech. Setting aside speech and verbal formation, the remainder is neither speech nor verbal formation. The mindful one rejoices in words.' From the commentaries: 'Verbal intimation, which is called prompting, is speech itself, hence vacīviññatti; a division of speech is vacībhedo.' In this way, the two-gendered nature of other words, both similar and dissimilar in form, should be determined as is appropriate. Thus, among the genders based on meaning, the specific genders based on meaning should be understood.

Idāni katthaci vāccaliṅgabhūtānaṃ abhidheyyaliṅgānañca taddhibhantaliṅgānañca dhammādivasena nāmikapadamālā vuccate. Tathā hi –

Now, in some instances, a nominal paradigm is stated according to 'dhamma,' etc., for words with gender based on form, gender based on meaning, and gender derived from taddhita suffixes. Indeed—

Dhammabho puggalā ceva, dhammapuggalatopi ca;

Ekantadhammato ceva, tathevekantapuggalā.

[Paradigms are formed] from the standpoint of Dhamma and of person, and also from the standpoint of Dhamma-and-person; and from the standpoint of Dhamma exclusively, and likewise from the standpoint of person exclusively.

Padamālā siyuṃ tāsu, paccattādivasena tu;

Padaṃ samaṃ visamañca, jaññā sabbasamampi ca.

Among these there may be nominal paradigms, but by way of individual usage and so forth, one should know a word to be similar, dissimilar, and also entirely similar.

Kathaṃ? “Micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsaṅkappo, micchāvācā, micchāvāco, micchādiṭṭhiko, micchāsaṅkappī” iccetesaṃ nāmikapadamālā evaṃ veditabbā.

How? The nominal paradigm for these terms—'wrong view,' 'wrong intention,' 'wrong speech' (feminine), 'wrong speech' (masculine), 'one of wrong view,' 'one of wrong intention'—should be understood thus.

“Micchādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhiyo. Micchādiṭṭhiṃ, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhiyo. Micchādiṭṭhiyā”ti evaṃ dhammato, “micchādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhino. Micchādiṭṭhiṃ, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhino. Micchādiṭṭhinā”ti evaṃ puggalato, “micchāsaṅkappo, micchāsaṅkappā. Micchāsaṅkappa”nti evaṃ dhammapuggalato, “micchāvācā, micchāvācā, micchāvācāyo. Micchāvācaṃ, micchāvācā micchāvācāyo. Micchāvācāya” evaṃ ekantadhammato, “micchāvāco, micchāvācā. Micchāvācaṃ, micchāvāce. Micchāvācena” evaṃ ekantapuggalato, “micchādiṭṭhiko. Micchādiṭṭhikā. Micchādiṭṭhika”nti evampi ekantapuggalato, “micchāsaṅkappī, micchāsaṅkappino. Micchāsaṅkappi”nti evampi ekantapuggalato nāmikapadamālā bhavati. Paccattopayogavacanādivasena pana padaṃ sadisaṃ visadisaṃ sabbathā sadisampi ca bhavati. Esa nayo sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappādīsupi.

'Micchādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhiyo...' (declension of 'wrong view')—thus from the standpoint of the Dhamma. 'Micchādiṭṭhi, micchādiṭṭhī, micchādiṭṭhino...' (declension of 'one with wrong view')—thus from the standpoint of the person. 'Micchāsaṅkappo, micchāsaṅkappā...' (declension of 'wrong intention')—thus from the standpoint of both Dhamma and person. 'Micchāvācā, micchāvācā, micchāvācāyo...' (declension of 'wrong speech')—thus entirely from the standpoint of the Dhamma. 'Micchāvāco, micchāvācā...' (declension of 'one with wrong speech')—thus entirely from the standpoint of the person. 'Micchādiṭṭhiko, micchādiṭṭhikā...' (declension of 'one with wrong view')—thus also entirely from the standpoint of the person. 'Micchāsaṅkappī, micchāsaṅkappino...' (declension of 'one with wrong intention')—thus also entirely from the standpoint of the person, a nominal paradigm is formed. However, by way of individual usage, application, expression, and so forth, a word may be similar, dissimilar, or also entirely similar. This same method applies to right view, right intention, and so on.

Atrime [M 0.0339] āhaccabhāsitā payogā – avijjāgatassa bhikkhave aviddasuno micchādiṭṭhi pahoti. Micchādiṭṭhissa micchāsaṅkappo pahoti. Micchāsaṅkappassa micchāvācā pahoti. Micchāvācassa micchākammanto pahoti. Micchākammantassa micchāājīvo pahoti. Micchāājīvassa micchāvāyāmo pahoti. Micchāvāyāmassa micchāsati pahoti. Micchāsatissa micchāsamādhi pahotīti. Vijjāgatassa bhikkhave viddasuno sammādiṭṭhi pahoti. Sammādiṭṭhissa sammāsaṅkappo pahotīti vitthāro, evaṃ katthaci vāccaliṅgabhūtānaṃ abhidheyyaliṅgānañca taddhitantaliṅgānañca nāmikapadamālā sappayogā kathitā.

Here are the applications spoken in this connection: 'Bhikkhus, for one who has come to ignorance, who is without knowledge, wrong view arises. For one of wrong view, wrong intention arises. For one of wrong intention, wrong speech arises. For one of wrong speech, wrong action arises. For one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises. For one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises. For one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises. For one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.' And, 'Bhikkhus, for one who has come to knowledge, who has knowledge, right view arises. For one of right view, right intention arises'—and so on in detail. Thus, in some instances, the nominal paradigm for words with gender based on form, gender based on meaning, and gender of taddhita-derivatives has been stated along with its application.

Idāni nevābhidheyyaliṅgassa bhavitabbasaddassa ca abhidheyyaliṅgānaṃ sotthi suvatthi saddānañca vāccaliṅgābhidheyyaliṅgassa abbhutasaddassa ca vāccaliṅgassa abhūtasaddassacāti imesaṃ kiñci visesaṃ kathayāma, nāmikapadamālañca yathārahaṃ yojessāma. Etesu hi bhavitabbasaddo ekantabhāvavācako napuṃsakaliṅgo ekavacanantoyeva hoti. Tatiyantapadehi evaṃsadda nasaddādīhi ca yojetabbo ca hoti. Nāssa nāmikapadamālā labbhati, atrime ca payogā “saddhammagarukena bhavitabbaṃ, no āmisagarukena, iminā corena bhavitabbaṃ, imehi corehi bhavitabbaṃ, imāya coriyā bhavitabbaṃ, imāhi corīhi bhavitabbaṃ, anena cittena bhavitabbaṃ, imehi cittehi bhavitabbaṃ, evaṃ bhavitabbaṃ, aññathā bhavitabba”nti. Atridaṃ vuccati –

Now, we shall explain some distinctions regarding the word 'bhavitabba,' which is not of gender by meaning; the words 'sotthi' and 'suvatthi,' which are of gender by meaning; the word 'abbhuta,' which is of gender by form and meaning; and the word 'abhūta,' which is of gender by form. We shall also apply the nominal paradigms as appropriate. Among these, the word 'bhavitabba' is exclusively expressive of being, is neuter in gender, and is only used in the singular. It is to be used with words in the instrumental case and with words such as 'evaṃ' and 'na.' No nominal paradigm is found for it. Here are examples of its usage: 'One should be respectful of the good Dhamma, not of material things'; 'It should be by this thief'; 'It should be by these thieves'; 'It should be by this female thief'; 'It should be by these female thieves'; 'It should be by this mind'; 'It should be by these minds'; 'Thus it should be'; 'Otherwise it should be.' Herein, this is said:

Bhavitabbapadaṃ niccaṃ, sabbaññuvarasāsane;

Paṭhamekavaco bhāva-vācakañca napuṃsakaṃ.

In the teaching of the Supreme Omniscient One, the word 'bhavitabba' is always in the first case, singular, neuter, and expressive of being.

Tatiyantapadehevaṃ-saddādīhi [M 0.0340] ca dhīmatā;

Yojetabbaṃva sambhoti, iti vidvā vibhāvaye.

The wise one should combine it with words ending in the instrumental case and with 'evaṃ' and other such words. The learned one should understand that it is used in this way.

Ayaṃ “bhavitabba”nti padassa viseso.

This is the special characteristic of the word 'bhavitabba.'

Sotthi bhaddante hotu rañño, sotthiṃ gacchati nhāpito. Sotthināmhi samuṭṭhito. Suvatthi, suvatthiṃ, suvatthinā, ayaṃ dhasātthisaddādīnaṃ viseso.

'May there be well-being for the king, venerable sirs.' 'The barber goes to well-being.' 'I have arisen from well-being.' 'Suvatthi, suvatthiṃ, suvatthinā.' This is the special characteristic of the words 'sotthi,' 'suvatthi,' and so on.

Ayaṃ pana “abbhutaṃ abhūta”nti dvinnaṃ viseso. Bhūsaddassa bbhū, saṃyogapare paṭisedhatthavati aitinipāte upapade sati ekantena rassattamupayāti. Kvatthe? “Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūta”ntiādīsvatthesu. Tathāvidhe asaññogapare rassattaṃ na upayāti. Kvatthe? “Asacca”ntiādīsvatthesu. Tathā hi “abbhuta”nti padassa “abhūtapubbaṃ bhūta”ntipi attho bhavati, “abbhutakaraṇa”ntipi attho bhavati. “Abhūta”nti padassa pana “asacca”ntipi attho bhavati, “ajāta”ntipi attho bhavati. Tatra “acchariyaṃ vata bho abbhutaṃ vata bho. Accheraṃ vata lokasmiṃ, abbhutaṃ lomahaṃsanaṃ” iccevamādayo “abhūtapubbaṃ bhūta”nti atthe payogā.

This, however, is the distinction between 'abbhutaṃ' and 'abhūtaṃ'. The vowel of the root 'bhū' is invariably shortened when the negative particle 'a' is prefixed and a conjunct consonant follows. In what sense? In senses such as 'what has come to be that never existed before'. In such a case, when a conjunct consonant does not follow, shortening does not occur. In what sense? In senses such as 'untrue'. Thus, the word 'abbhutaṃ' has the meaning 'what has come to be that never existed before', and also the meaning 'causing wonder'. On the other hand, the word 'abhūtaṃ' has the meaning 'untrue', and also the meaning 'unborn'. In this regard, usages such as, 'How amazing indeed, friends, how wonderful indeed! How astonishing in the world, how hair-raising!' are in the sense of 'what has come to be that never existed before'.

“Tvaṃ maṃ nāgena ālampa,

Ahaṃ maṇḍūkachāpiyā;

Hotu no abbhutaṃ tattha,

Āsahassehi pañcahī”ti

"You wager an elephant against me,

I, a young frog;

Let there be a contest between us there,

For five thousand."

Iccevamādayo abbhutakaraṇatthe payogā. Evaṃ rassavasena, dīghavasena pana nissaṃyoge “abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ. Atathaṃ”iccevamādayo [M 0.0341] asaccatthe payogā, “abhūtaṃ ajātaṃ asañjāta”nti iccevamādayo ajātatthe payogā. Bhavanti catra –

These and so on are usages in the sense of 'causing wonder'. Thus it is by way of the short vowel; but by way of the long vowel, without a conjunct consonant, usages such as 'untrue, false, unreal' are in the sense of 'untruth'; and usages such as 'unborn, unarisen, unproduced' are in the sense of 'unborn'. And here there are these verses:

“Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūta”nti, atthasmiṃ abbhutantidaṃ;

Padaṃ viññūhi viññeyyaṃ, rassabhāvena saṇṭhitaṃ.

In the sense 'what has come to be that was not before,' this word 'abbhutaṃ', established by way of shortness, is to be understood by the wise.

Abbhutakaraṇatthepi, abbhutanti padaṃ tathā;

Saṇṭhitaṃ rassabhāvena, iti vidvā vibhāvaye.

Also in the sense of 'causing wonder', the word 'abbhutaṃ' is likewise established by way of shortness; thus a wise person should discern.

Abhūtamiti dīghatta-vasena kathitaṃ pana;

Padaṃ samadhigantabba-masaccājātavācakaṃ.

But the word 'abhūta' is spoken of by way of length; the word should be understood as signifying the untrue and the unborn.

Abbhutaṃ, abbhutāni. Cittanayena, abbhuto, abbhutā. Abbhutaṃ, purisanayena, abbhutā, abbhutā, abbhutāyo. Abbhutaṃ. Kaññānayena ñeyyaṃ. Evaṃ bhūtasaddassapi nāmikapadamālā tidhā gahetabbā. Atra “abbhuta”miti padaṃ vāccaliṅgampi bhavati abhidheyyaliṅgampi. “Abhūta”miti padaṃ pana vāccaliṅgaṃ abhidheyyaliṅgampi vā saccasaddo viya katthaci. Itissa yathārahaṃ ayampi sappayogā nāmikapadamālā kathitā.

Neuter: `abbhutaṃ, abbhutāni`. According to the masculine paradigm: `abbhuto, abbhutā`. According to the feminine paradigm: `abbhutā, abbhutāyo`. Thus, the nominal paradigm of the word 'bhūta' should also be taken in three ways. Here, the word 'abbhuta' can have the gender of the word it qualifies (adjectival) or the gender of the thing it denotes (substantival). The word 'abhūta', however, is sometimes like the word 'sacca', having the gender of the word it qualifies or the gender of the thing it denotes. Thus, this nominal paradigm with its applications has been stated as is appropriate.

Idāni āgamikānaṃ kosallajananatthaṃ padasamodhānavasena nāmikapadamālā vuccate – buddho bhagavā, buddhā bhagavanto. Buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ, buddhe bhagavante. Buddhena bhagavatā, sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Ayaṃ padamālā ekavacanabahuvacanavasena ñeyyā.

Now, for the purpose of generating skill in students, a nominal paradigm is stated by way of combining words—the Buddha, the Blessed One; the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. The Buddha, the Blessed One; the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. By the Buddha, by the Blessed One; the rest should be elaborated. This paradigm should be understood in its singular and plural forms.

Devā tāvatiṃsā. Deve tāvatiṃse. Devehi tāvatiṃsehi. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Bahuvacanavasena ñeyyā padamālā.

The Tāvatiṃsa gods. The Tāvatiṃsa gods. By the Tāvatiṃsa gods. The rest should be elaborated. The paradigm should be understood in the plural form.

So [M 0.0342] bhagavā jānaṃ passaṃ arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, taṃ bhagavantaṃ jānantaṃ passantaṃ arahantaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena, tassa bhagavato jānato passato arahato sammāsambuddhassa. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Ekavacanavasena ñeyyā padamālā.

That Blessed One, knowing and seeing, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; that Blessed One, knowing and seeing, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; by that Blessed One, knowing and seeing, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One; of that Blessed One, knowing and seeing, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The rest should be elaborated. The paradigm is to be understood in the singular.

Rājā suddhodano, rājānaṃ suddhodanaṃ, raññā suddhodanena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

King Suddhodana (nominative), King Suddhodana (accusative), by King Suddhodana (instrumental). The rest should be elaborated.

Rājā passenadī kosalo, rājānaṃ passenadiṃ kosalaṃ, raññā passenadinā kosalena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

King Pasenadi of Kosala (nominative), King Pasenadi of Kosala (accusative), by King Pasenadi of Kosala (instrumental). The rest should be elaborated.

Rājā māgadho seniyo bimbisāro, rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ seniyaṃ bimbisāraṃ, raññā māgadhena seniyena bimbisārena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

King Bimbisāra of Magadha, the Seniya (nominative); King Bimbisāra of Magadha, the Seniya (accusative); by King Bimbisāra of Magadha, the Seniya (instrumental). The rest should be elaborated.

Rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto, rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ, raññā māgadhena ajātasattunā vedehiputtena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Videha queen (nominative); King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Videha queen (accusative); by King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Videha queen (instrumental). The rest should be elaborated.

Mahāpajāpatī gotamī, mahāpajāpatiṃ gotamiṃ, mahāpajāpatiyā gotamiyāti pañcakkhattuṃ vattabbaṃ. Mahāpajāpatiyaṃ gotamiyaṃ, bhoti mahāpajāpati gotami.

Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī (nominative), Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī (accusative); the form `mahāpajāpatiyā gotamiyā` (instrumental, etc.) is to be stated five times. In Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī (locative), O Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī (vocative).

Makkhali gosālo. Makkhaliṃ gosālaṃ. Makkhalinā gosālena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Makkhali Gosāla (nominative). Makkhali Gosāla (accusative). By Makkhali Gosāla (instrumental). The rest should be elaborated.

Sāriputtamoggallānaṃ sāvakayugaṃ. Sāriputtamoggallānaṃ sāvakayugaṃ, sāriputtamoggallānena sāvakayugena, sāriputtamoggallānassa [M 0.0343] sāvakayugassa. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Sabbāpetā padamālā ekavacanavasena ñeyyā. Sāriputtamoggallānā aggasāvakā, sāriputtamoggallāne aggasāvake, sāriputtamoggallānehi aggasāvakehi. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Bahuvacanavasena ñeyyā. Ito aññesupi eseva nayo.

Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the pair of disciples (nominative/accusative singular); by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the pair of disciples (instrumental singular); of Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the pair of disciples (genitive singular). The rest should be elaborated. This entire paradigm should be understood in the singular. Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the chief disciples (nominative plural); Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the chief disciples (accusative plural); by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the chief disciples (instrumental plural). The rest should be elaborated. This should be understood in the plural. This same method applies in other cases as well.

So dāro, sā dārā. Saṃ dāraṃ, se dāre. Sena dārena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Sā nārī, sā nāriyo. Saṃ nāriṃ, sā nāriyo. Sāya nāriyā. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Saṃ kammaṃ, sāni kammāni. Sena kammena. Saṃ phalaṃ, sāni phalāni. Sena phalena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

That wife, those wives. That wife, those wives. By that wife. The rest should be elaborated. That woman, those women. That woman, those women. By that woman. The rest should be elaborated. That deed, those deeds. By that deed. That fruit, those fruits. By that fruit. The rest should be elaborated.

Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ, paṭhamena jhānena, paṭhamassa jhānassa. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

The first jhāna (nominative/accusative), by the first jhāna (instrumental), of the first jhāna (genitive). The rest should be elaborated.

Catutthī disā, catutthiṃ disaṃ, catutthiyā disāya.

The fourth direction (nominative), the fourth direction (accusative), by/of the fourth direction (instrumental/genitive).

Dhammī kathā, dhammiṃ kathaṃ, dhammiyā kathāya, dhammiyaṃ kathāyaṃ. Evaṃ anupubbī kathā, evarūpī kathā. Iminā nayena aññesupi ṭhānesu padasamodhānavasena liṅgato ca antato ca vacanato ca apekkhitabbaṃ. Padato ca nānappakārā nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā.

A Dhamma talk (nominative), a Dhamma talk (accusative), by a Dhamma talk (instrumental), in a Dhamma talk (locative). Likewise, a gradual talk, a talk of such a kind. By this method, in other instances as well, word combinations should be considered according to gender, ending, and number. And various kinds of nominal paradigms should be constructed from the words.

Idāni ekappakārānaṃ saddānaṃ liṅgaantavasena nānattaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kathaṃ? Yādiso, yādisī, yādisaṃ. Tādiso, tādisī, tādisaṃ. Etādiso, etādisī, etādisaṃ. Kīdiso, kīdisī, kīdisaṃ. Īdiso, īdisī, īdisaṃ. Ediso[M 0.0344], edisī, edisaṃ. Sadiso, sadisī, sadisaṃ. Kadāci pana “yādisā tādisā”ti evamādīni itthiliṅgarūpānipi bhavanti. Nāmikapadamālā nesaṃ purisa itthī cittanayena yojetabbā.

Now, the diversity of words of one type should be understood in terms of gender and ending. How? `Yādiso` (of which kind, masc.), `yādisī` (fem.), `yādisaṃ` (neut.). `Tādiso` (of that kind, masc.), `tādisī` (fem.), `tādisaṃ` (neut.). `Etādiso` (of this kind, masc.), `etādisī` (fem.), `etādisaṃ` (neut.). `Kīdiso` (of what kind, masc.), `kīdisī` (fem.), `kīdisaṃ` (neut.). `Īdiso` (of this kind, masc.), `īdisī` (fem.), `īdisaṃ` (neut.). `Ediso` (of this kind, masc.), `edisī` (fem.), `edisaṃ` (neut.). `Sadiso` (similar, masc.), `sadisī` (fem.), `sadisaṃ` (neut.). Occasionally, however, feminine forms like “yādisā tādisā” also occur. Their nominal paradigms should be constructed according to the masculine, feminine, and neuter methods.

Idāni samāsataddhitapadabhūtānaṃ amamasaddādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālā vuccate – amamo, amamā, amamaṃ, amame. Amamena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Now, the nominal paradigm of words such as 'amama', which are formed as compounds and derivatives, is stated: `amamo, amamā` (nom. sg/pl); `amamaṃ, amame` (acc. sg/pl). `Amamena` (inst. sg). The rest should be elaborated.

Mayhako, mayhakā. Mayhakaṃ, mayhake. Mayhakena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

`Mayhako, mayhakā` (nom. sg/pl). `Mayhakaṃ, mayhake` (acc. sg/pl). `Mayhakena` (inst. sg). The rest should be elaborated.

Āmā, āmā, āmāyo. Āmaṃ, āmā, āmāyo. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

`Āmā` (nom. sg); `āmā, āmāyo` (nom. pl). `Āmaṃ` (acc. sg); `āmā, āmāyo` (acc. pl). The rest should be elaborated.

Tatra amamoti natthi taṇhāmamattaṃ diṭṭhimamattañca etassāti amamo, ko so, arahāyevāti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Apica yesataṇhāpi sadiṭṭhīpi “mama ida”nti mamattaṃ na karonti, tepi amamāyeva. Ettha ca “manussā tattha jāyanti, amamā apariggahā”ti idaṃ sāsanato nidassanaṃ. “Amamo nirahaṅkāro”ti idaṃ pana lokato nidassanaṃ. Itthiliṅge vattabbe “amamā, amamā, amamāyo”ti padamālā. Napuṃsake vattabbe “amamaṃ, amamānī”ti padamālā. Tatra mayhakoti “idampi mayhaṃ idampi mayha”nti vippalapatīti mayhako, eko pakkhiviseso. Vuttañhetaṃ jātake –

Therein, 'without mine' (`amamo`) means that for him there is no 'mine-ness' of craving and 'mine-ness' of views. Who is that? It is fitting to say, an Arahant. Moreover, those who do not engage in making things 'mine' through craving or through views, thinking 'this is mine,' they too are without 'mine-ness.' And here, 'People are born there, without 'mine-ness,' without possessions' is an example from the Dispensation. But 'Without 'mine-ness,' without ego' is an example from the world. When speaking in the feminine gender, the word-series is 'amamā, amamā, amamāyo.' When speaking in the neuter gender, the word-series is 'amamaṃ, amamāni.' Therein, as for 'mayhako': one who chatters 'this is mine, this is mine' is a `mayhako`, a certain kind of bird. For this is said in the Jātaka—

“Sakuṇo mayhako nāma, girisānudarīcaro;

Pakkaṃ pipphalimāruyha, ‘mayhaṃ mayha’nti kandatī”ti.

“A bird named Mayhaka, who roams on mountain slopes and in caves; having climbed a ripe fig tree, it cries, ‘Mine! Mine!’”

Itthiliṅge vattabbe “mayhakī, mayhakī, mayhakiyo”ti padamālā. Tatra āmāti “āma ahaṃ tumhākaṃ dāsī”ti evaṃ dāsibhāvaṃ paṭijānātīti āmā. Gehadāsī. Vuttañhetaṃ jātakesu [M 0.0345] “yattha dāso āmajāto, ṭhito thullāni gacchatī”ti ca, “āmāya dāsāpi bhavanti loke”ti ca, tasmā imānevettha nidassanapadāni.

When speaking in the feminine gender, the word-series is 'mayhakī, mayhakī, mayhakiyo.' Here, as for `āmā`: because she acknowledges her slave status by saying, 'Yes (`āma`), I am your slave,' she is called an `āmā`; a household slave. For this is said in the Jātakas: 'Where a home-born slave (`āmajāto`), standing, undertakes coarse tasks,' and also, 'Through a female slave (`āmā`), there are also slaves in the world.' Therefore, these are the illustrative examples here.

Idāni kati katipaya katimīsaddānaṃ viseso vuccate yathārahaṃ nāmikapadamālā ca. Tatra katimīsaddassa nāmikapadamālā na labbhati “ajja bhante katimī”ti evaṃ pucchāvasena āgatamattato. Kati katipayasaddānaṃ pana labbhateva, sā ca bahuvacanikā. Visuddhimaggaṭīkāyaṃ pana katipayasaddo ekavacaniko vutto. Kati purisā tiṭṭhanti, kati purise passati. Kati itthiyo, kati kulāni. Kati lokasmiṃ chiddāni yattha cittaṃ na tiṭṭhati. Kati kusalā. Kati dhātuyo. Kati āyatanāni. Katihi khandhehi katihāyatanehi katihi dhātūhi saṅgahitaṃ. Katibhi rajamāneti, katibhi parisujjhati. Katipayā purisā, katipayā itthiyo, katipayāni cittāni. Imā pana nāmikapadamālā.

Now, the distinction between the words “kati,” “katipaya,” and “katimī,” and their respective nominal word-series, are explained as appropriate. Of these, a nominal word-series for the word “katimī” is not found, as it occurs only in questions like, “Venerable sir, which day of the month is it today?” But a nominal word-series for the words “kati” and “katipaya” is indeed found, and it is plural. However, in the sub-commentary to the Visuddhimagga, the word “katipaya” is stated to be singular. How many men stand? How many men does one see? How many women? How many families? How many openings are there in the world where the mind does not abide? How many wholesome qualities? How many elements? How many sense bases? By how many aggregates, by how many sense bases, by how many elements is it comprised? By how many is it soiled? By how many is it purified? Several men, several women, several minds. These, indeed, are the nominal word-series.

Kati. Katihi, katibhi. Katinaṃ. Katisu.

How many (Nom./Acc.). By/From how many (Inst./Abl.). Of/For how many (Gen./Dat.). In/Among how many (Loc.).

Katipayā. Katipayehi, katipayebhi. Katipayānaṃ. Katipayesu. Katipayāyo. Katipayāhi, katipayābhi. Katipayānaṃ. Katipayāsu. Katipayāni. Katipaye. Katipayehi, katipayebhi. Katipayānaṃ. Katipayesūti. Sabbāpetā sattannaṃ vibhattīnaṃ vasena ñeyyā, samāsavidhimhipi kati [M 0.0346] katipayasaddā bahuvacanavaseneva yojetabbā. “Katisaṅgātigo bhikkhu, oghatiṇṇoti vuccati. Katipayajanakata”ntiādīsu hi “kati kittakā saṅgā katisaṅgā”tiādinā sabbadā bahuvacanasamāso daṭṭhabbo.

Some (Masc.). By/From some. Of/For some. In/Among some. Some (Fem.). By/From some. Of/For some. In/Among some. Some (Neut.). Some. By/From some. Of/For some. In/Among some. All these should be understood according to the seven cases. In compound formations as well, the words “kati” and “katipaya” should always be construed in the plural. For in phrases like “A monk who has transcended how many attachments is called one who has crossed the flood,” or “done by several people,” and so on, the plural compound should always be seen, as in the explanation: “how many, what number of, attachments are meant by ‘how many attachments,’” and so on.

Idāni rūḷhīsaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālā vuccate – idha rūḷhīsaddā nāma yevāpanakasaddādayo. Yevāpanako, yevāpanakā. Yevāpanakaṃ. Yevāpano, yevāpanā. Yevāpanaṃ. Yaṃvāpanakaṃ, yaṃvāpanakāni. Sesaṃ sabbattha vitthāretabbaṃ. Tatra yevāpanakoti “phasso hoti vedanā hotī”tiādinā vuttā phassādayo viya sarūpato avatvā “ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye aññepi atthi paṭiccasamuppannā arūpino dhammā”ti evaṃ “yevāpanā”ti padena vutto yevāpanako, evaṃ “yevāpano”ti etthāpi. Tathā “yaṃ vā panaññampi atthi rūpa”nti evaṃ “yaṃvāpanā”ti padena vuttaṃ yaṃvāpanakaṃ. Esa nayo yathārahaṃ yassakaṃ yatthakantiādīsupi netabbo.

Now, the nominal word-series of conventional words is stated. Here, conventional words are such words as `yevāpanaka` and so on. Yevāpanako, yevāpanakā. Yevāpanakaṃ. Yevāpano, yevāpanā. Yevāpanaṃ. Yaṃvāpanakaṃ, yaṃvāpanakāni. The rest should be expanded in all cases. Here, as for `yevāpanako`: it refers to that which is spoken of by the phrase beginning `ye vā pana`, as in, 'or whatever (`ye vā pana`) other conditionally arisen immaterial phenomena exist at that time.' This is in contrast to stating them by their own form, such as contact and feeling, which are spoken of as 'contact arises, feeling arises,' and so on. The same applies to `yevāpano`. Likewise, `yaṃvāpanakaṃ` refers to that which is spoken of by the phrase beginning `yaṃ vā pana`, as in, 'or whatever (`yaṃ vā pana`) other material form exists.' This method should be applied as appropriate to terms like `yassakaṃ`, `yatthakaṃ`, and so on.

Ettha siyā – nanu ca bho panasaddo nipāto, nipātānañca abyayabhāvo siddho tīsu liṅgesu sabbavibhattivacanesu ca vayābhāvato, so kasmā “yevāpano”ti okāranto jātoti? Saccaṃ panasaddo nipāto, so ca kho “ye vā pana tasmiṃ samaye”ti vā, “yaṃ vā panaññampī”ti vā, “brāhmaṇā panā”ti vā evamādīsu nipāto, “yevāpanako”ti vā, “yevāpano”ti vā evamādīsu nipāto nāma na hoti. Anukaraṇamattañhetaṃ, tasmā īdisesu panasaddasahitā payogā rūḷhīsaddāti gahetabbā. Yajjevaṃ kasmā nibbacanamudāhaṭanti? Atthassa pākaṭīkaraṇatthaṃ.

Here, it might be asked: “But venerable sir, is not the word ‘pana’ a particle? And is not the indeclinable nature of particles established, due to their being without change in all three genders and in all cases and numbers? So why has ‘yevāpano’ come to end with an ‘o’?” It is true that ‘pana’ is a particle, and it is a particle in such phrases as “or whatever (`ye vā pana`) at that time,” or “or whatever (`yaṃ vā pana`) else,” or “but the brahmins (`brāhmaṇā pana`),” and so on. However, in formations like “yevāpanako” or “yevāpano,” it is not a particle. This is merely an imitation. Therefore, such usages containing the word ‘pana’ should be understood as conventional words. If so, why are those source phrases cited here? For the sake of clarifying the meaning.

Tayodhammajātakaṃ[M 0.0347]. Tayodhammajātakaṃ. Tayodhammajātakena. Tayodhammajātakassa. Tayodhammajātakā, tayodhammajātakasmā. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Tayodhammajātakaṃ (Nom.). Tayodhammajātakaṃ (Acc.). Tayodhammajātakena (Inst.). Tayodhammajātakassa (Gen./Dat.). Tayodhammajātakā, tayodhammajātakasmā (Abl.). The rest should be expanded.

Tayosaṅkhārā. Tayosaṅkhāre. Tayosaṅkhārehi, tayosaṅkhārebhi. Tayosaṅkhārānaṃ. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

Tayosaṅkhārā (Nom.). Tayosaṅkhāre (Acc.). Tayosaṅkhārehi, tayosaṅkhārebhi (Inst./Abl.). Tayosaṅkhārānaṃ (Gen./Dat.). The rest should be expanded.

Cattāripurisayugo saṅgho. Cattāripurisayugaṃ saṅghaṃ. Cattāripurisayugena saṅghena. Cattāripurisayugassa saṅghassa. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

The Sangha of four pairs of persons (Nom.). The Sangha of four pairs of persons (Acc.). By the Sangha of four pairs of persons (Inst.). Of the Sangha of four pairs of persons (Gen./Dat.). The rest should be expanded.

Satokārī, satokārī, satokārino. Satokāriṃ, satokārī, satokārino. Satokārinā, satokārīhi, satokārībhi. Satokārissa. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Ettha satokārīti saratīti sato, sato eva hutvā karaṇasīloti satokārī.

The mindful one, the mindful one, the mindful ones. The mindful one, the mindful one, the mindful ones. By the mindful one, by the mindful ones, by the mindful ones. Of the mindful one. The rest should be expanded. Here, as for `satokārī`: because one remembers (`sarati`), one is mindful (`sato`); being mindful and having the nature to act (`karaṇasīlo`), one is a `satokārī`.

Aparesampi rūḷhīsaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālā vuccate saddhimatthavibhāvanāya. Aṅgā. Aṅge. Aṅgehi, aṅgebhi. Aṅgānaṃ. Aṅgehi, aṅgebhi. Aṅgānaṃ. Aṅgesu. Bhonto aṅgā.

Further, the nominal word-series of other conventional words is stated, together with an explanation of the meaning. The Aṅgas (Nom.). The Aṅgas (Acc.). By the Aṅgas (Inst.). Of the Aṅgas (Gen./Dat.). From the Aṅgas (Abl.). Of the Aṅgas (Gen.). In the Aṅgas (Loc.). O Aṅgas (Voc.).

Aṅgā janapado. Aṅge janapadaṃ. Aṅgehi, aṅgebhi janapadena. Aṅgānaṃ janapadassa. Aṅgehi, aṅgebhi janapadasmā. Aṅgānaṃ janapadassa. Aṅgesu janapade. Bhonto aṅgā janapada. Evaṃ magadhakosalādīnampi yojetabbā.

The Aṅgas, the country (Nom.). The Aṅgas, the country (Acc.). By the Aṅgas, by the country (Inst.). Of the Aṅgas, of the country (Gen./Dat.). From the Aṅgas, from the country (Abl.). Of the Aṅgas, of the country (Gen.). In the Aṅgas, in the country (Loc.). O Aṅgas, O country (Voc.). In this way, it should also be applied to Magadha, Kosala, and so on.

Itthiliṅge kāsī, kāsiyo, kāsī, kāsiyo. Kāsīhi, kāsībhi. Kāsīnaṃ. Kāsīhi, kāsībhi. Kāsīnaṃ. Kāsīsu. Bhotiyo kāsiyo. Atrāyamatthavibhāvanā – kāsī, kāsiyo janapado. Kāsī, kāsiyo janapadaṃ[M 0.0348]. Kāsīhi, kāsībhi janapadena. Kāsīnaṃ janapadassa. Kāsīhi, kāsībhi janapadasmā. Kāsīnaṃ janapadassa. Kāsīsu janapade. Bhotiyo kāsiyo janapada. Evaṃ avantīcetī vajjī iccetesampi padānaṃ yojetabbā. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā “kurūsu janapade”ti. Evaṃ aṅgādīni atthassa ekattepi janapadanāmattā rūḷhīvasena bahuvacanāneva bhavanti. Tathā hi tattha tattha “aṅgesu viharati. Magadhesu cārikaṃ caramāno”tiādinā, “aṅgānaṃ magadhānaṃ kāsīnaṃ kosalāna”ntiādinā ca bahuvacanapāḷiyo dissanti. Evaṃ rūḷhīsaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālā bhavanti.

In the feminine gender: Kāsī, Kāsiyo (Nom.). Kāsī, Kāsiyo (Acc.). By the Kāsīs (Inst.). Of the Kāsīs (Gen./Dat.). From the Kāsīs (Abl.). Of the Kāsīs (Gen.). In the Kāsīs (Loc.). O Kāsiyo (Voc.). Here is the explanation of the meaning: The Kāsīs, the country (Nom.). The Kāsīs, the country (Acc.). By the Kāsīs, by the country (Inst.). Of the Kāsīs, of the country (Gen./Dat.). From the Kāsīs, from the country (Abl.). Of the Kāsīs, of the country (Gen.). In the Kāsīs, in the country (Loc.). O Kāsiyo, O country (Voc.). In this way, it should also be applied to these words: Avanti, Ceti, and Vajjī. Therefore the commentary masters have said, 'in the Kurus, in the country' (`kurūsu janapade`). Thus Aṅga and other such names of countries, though singular in meaning, are by convention always plural. For indeed, plural Pāli passages are seen in various places, such as 'he dwells in Aṅga' (`aṅgesu`), 'wandering on tour in Magadha' (`magadhesu`), and 'of the Aṅgas, of the Magadhas, of the Kāsīs, of the Kosalas.' Thus are the nominal word-series of conventional words.

Idāni aparāpi ito savisesatarā saddabhede sammohaviddhaṃsanakārikā paramasukhumañāṇāvahā nāmikapadamālāyo kathayāma sotūnaṃ atthabyañjanaggahaṇe paramakosallasampādanatthaṃ. Tā ca kho “sambuddho paṭijānāsi. Kassako paṭijānāsi. Upāsako paṭijānāsi. Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato ime dhammā anabhisambuddhā”tiādayo pāḷinaye nissāyeva. Tattha sambuddhopaṭijānāsīti “tvaṃ ‘ahaṃ sammāsambuddho’ti paṭijānāsī”ti itisaddalopavasena attho gahetabbo. Esa nayo “kassako paṭijānāsī”tiādīsupi. “Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato”ti ettha pana “ahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti paṭijānantassa tavāti evaṃ itisaddalopayojanāvasena añño saddasanniveso teneva añño atthapaṭivedho ca bhavati. “Khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānatoti”ādīsupi eseva nayo. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānatoti “ahaṃ sammāsambuddho, sabbe dhammā mayā abhisambuddhā”ti [M 0.0349] evaṃ paṭijānato tavāti yo attho vutto, sopi yathādassito atthoyeva. Evaṃpakāraṃ ñatvā paṇḍitajātiyena kulaputtena amhehi vuccamānā “ahaṃ sammāsambuddho’ti tvaṃ paṭijānāsī”ti etasmiṃ atthe sakriyāpadā ayaṃ padamālā vavatthapetabbā –

Now, we shall also explain other nominal paradigms, even more specific than these, which dispel confusion regarding distinctions of words and lead to extremely subtle knowledge, for the sake of enabling listeners to attain the highest skill in grasping meaning and expression. And these are based on the canonical method, such as: 'You claim to be a Buddha. You claim to be a farmer. You claim to be a lay follower. For you, who claim to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, these things are not fully understood.' Here, 'sambuddho paṭijānāsi' should be understood as 'you claim, “I am a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,”' by way of elision of the word 'iti.' The same method applies to 'kassako paṭijānāsi' and so on. However, in 'sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato,' by applying the elision of the word 'iti' as 'for you who claim, “I am a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,”' a different word arrangement and thus a different understanding of the meaning arises. The same method applies to 'khīṇāsavassa te paṭijānato' and so on. In the commentary, the meaning stated for 'sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato' as 'for you who claim, “I am a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, all things have been fully understood by me,”' is indeed the meaning as shown. Having understood this manner, a wise son of good family should establish this paradigm with finite verbs, which is taught by us in the sense of 'you claim, “I am a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.”'

Sammāsambuddho tvaṃ paṭijānaṃ tiṭṭhasi. Sammāsambuddhaṃ taṃ paṭijānantaṃ passati. Sammāsambuddhena te paṭijānatā dhammo desito. Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato dīyate. Sammāsambuddhasmā tayā paṭijānatā apeti. Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānato dhammo. Sammāsambuddhasmiṃ tayi paṭijānante patiṭṭhitanti. Tathā “khīṇāsavo tvaṃ paṭijānāsī”tiādināpi vitthāretabbaṃ.

You stand claiming to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. One sees you claiming to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The Dhamma has been taught by you, claiming to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. It is given to you, claiming to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. It departs from you, claiming to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. The Dhamma belongs to you, claiming to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. It is established in you, claiming to be a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Similarly, it should be elaborated with 'You claim to be one whose taints are destroyed,' and so on.

Iddhimā bhikkhu ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti. Iddhimanto bhikkhū ekopi hutvā bahudhā honti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hontīti imasmiṃ panatthe ayampi sakriyāpadā padamālā vavatthapetabbā –

A monk endowed with psychic power, being one, becomes many; being many, becomes one. Monks endowed with psychic power, being one, become many; being many, become one. In this sense, this paradigm with finite verbs should also be established:

Ekopi hutvā bahudhā honto bahudhāpi hutvā eko honto bhikkhu tiṭṭhati, ekopi hutvā bahudhā hontā bahudhāpi hutvā eko hontā bhikkhū tiṭṭhanti. Ekopi hutvā bahudhā hontaṃ bahudhāpi hutvā eko hontaṃ bhikkhuṃ passati, ekopi hutvā bahudhā honte bahudhāpi hutvā eko honte bhikkhū passati. Ekopi hutvā bahudhā hontena bahudhāpi hutvā eko hontena bhikkhunā dhammo desito, ekopi hutvā bahudhā hontehi bahudhāpi hutvā eko hontehi bhikkhūhi dhammo desito. Ekopi hutvā bahudhā hontassa bahudhāpi hutvā eko hontassa bhikkhuno dīyate. Sesaṃ [M 0.0350] vitthāretabbaṃ. Bho ekopi hutvā bahudhā honta bahudhāpi hutvā eko honta bhikkhu tvaṃ dhammaṃ desehi, bhonto ekopi hutvā bahudhā hontā bahudhāpi hutvā eko hontā tumhe dhammaṃ desethāti. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne kevaṭṭasuttaṃ sādhakaṃ. “Idha kevaṭṭa bhikkhu anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti. Ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti, āvibhāvaṃ…pe… tamenaṃ aññataro saddho pasanno passati taṃ bhikkhuṃ anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhontaṃ ekopi hutvā bahudhā hontaṃ bahudhāpi hutvā eko honta”nti idaṃ kevaṭṭasuttaṃ.

A monk, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one, stands; monks, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one, stand. One sees a monk, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one; one sees monks, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one. The Dhamma is taught by a monk, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one; the Dhamma is taught by monks, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one. It is given to a monk, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one. The rest should be expanded. 'O monk, you who are being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one, teach the Dhamma.' 'O monks, you who are being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one, teach the Dhamma.' In this context, the Kevaṭṭa Sutta is the supporting text. 'Here, Kevaṭṭa, a monk experiences various kinds of psychic power. Being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one. He appears… and so on. Then a certain faithful, devoted person sees that monk experiencing various kinds of psychic power, being one and becoming many, and being many and becoming one.' This is the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.

Ekoekāya mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho nisajjaṃ kappento bhikkhu evaṃ vadati, ekoekāya mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho nisajjaṃ kappentā bhikkhū evaṃ vadanti. Ekoekāya mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho nisajjaṃ kappentaṃ bhikkhuṃ passati, ekoekāya mātugāmena saddhiṃ raho nisajjaṃ kappente bhikkhū passati. Sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Ettha pana “na tveva ekoekāya, mātugāmena sallape”tiādikaṃ pāḷipadaṃ sādhakaṃ. Ettha hi ekoekāyāti idaṃ abyayapadasadisaṃ rūḷhīpadanti gahetabbaṃ, aññamaññanti saddassa viya ca ekapadattūpagamanañcassa veditabbaṃ. Bhikkhu vinā dutiyena sayaṃ eko hutvā ekāya itthiyā saddhinti imasmiṃ atthe “ekoekāyā”ti idaṃ padaṃ na rūḷhīpadanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ santepi na “eko”ti saddo “bhikkhū”ti padena samānādhikaraṇo. Yadi samānādhikaraṇo siyā, “nisajjaṃ kappenta”ntiādi na vattabbaṃ siyā. “Ekāyā”ti saddopi na ajjhāharitabbena “itthiyā”ti padena samānādhikaraṇo. Yadi samānādhikaraṇo siyā, “mātugāmenā”ti [M 0.0351] na vattabbaṃ siyā visesābhāvato dviruttabhāvāpajjanato ca. Kiñca bhiyyo “mātugāmenā”ti vuttattā “ekenā”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, ekantato pana “ekoekāyā”ti idaṃ padaṃ pumitthisaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ apekkhati, na samānādhikaraṇapadaṃ, tasmā “dve jānipatayo aññamaññaṃ sallapentī”tiādīsu “aññamañña”nti padassa viya ca “ekoekāyā”ti imassa ekapadattañca nisajjaṃ kappentassa bhikkhuno visesanattañca veditabbaṃ. Atha vā yassaṃ nisajjakriyāyaṃ bhikkhupi ekova hoti, itthīpi ekāva. Sā kriyā rūḷhīvasena “ekoekāyā”ti vuccati, tādisāya ekoekāya nisajjakriyāya bhikkhu mātugāmena saddhintipi attho gahetabbo. Iminā nayena aññesampi rūḷhīsaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālā yathāpayogaṃ ekavacanabahuvacanavasena yojetabbā. Iccevaṃ vāccābhidheyyaliṅgādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālā nānappakārato pakāsitā.

A monk, arranging to sit alone with a woman in private, speaks thus; monks, arranging to sit alone with a woman in private, speak thus. One sees a monk arranging to sit alone with a woman in private; one sees monks arranging to sit alone with a woman in private. All should be elaborated. Here, however, the Pāli phrase 'one should not converse with a woman one on one,' and so on, is the supporting text. Here, indeed, 'ekoekāya' should be understood as a conventional term similar to an indeclinable word, and its becoming a single word, like the word 'aññamañña' (each other), should be known. In the sense that 'a monk, being alone without a second person, with a single woman,' the word 'ekoekāya' should not be seen as a conventional term. Even so, the word 'eko' is not in apposition with the word 'bhikkhu.' If it were in apposition, 'nisajjaṃ kappenta' and so on would not need to be stated. The word 'ekāya' also is not in apposition with the implied word 'itthiyā' (woman). If it were in apposition, 'mātugāmena' would not need to be stated, due to the absence of distinction and the risk of becoming a duplication. Furthermore, since 'mātugāmena' is stated, 'ekena' should have been said. But ultimately, the word 'ekoekāya' refers to a meaning encompassing masculine and feminine, not as an appositional word. Therefore, just as in phrases like 'dve jānipatayo aññamaññaṃ sallapentī' (a married couple conversing with each other), the word 'aññamañña' is used, so too 'ekoekāya' should be understood as a single word and as a qualifier of the monk engaged in sitting. Alternatively, in an act of sitting where the monk is alone and the woman is alone, that act is conventionally called 'ekoekāya.' Thus, the meaning should be understood as 'a monk with a woman in such an 'ekoekāya' sitting arrangement.' In this way, the nominal paradigms of other conventional terms should also be formed according to usage, in the singular and plural. Thus, the nominal paradigms related to expression, denotation, gender, and so on, have been explained in various ways.

Sumadhuratarasaddanitiṃ imaṃ,

Paṭutaramatitaṃ susikhe varaṃ;

Viduvimatitamopahariṃ raviṃ,

Matikumudapabodhinisāpatiṃ.

This Saddanīti, exceedingly sweet, more skillful, surpassing the best of the well-taught; like the sun that dispels the darkness of the doubt of the wise, like the lord of the night that awakens the water-lily of the mind.

Kataviññūjanassāsa-sāsanassābhivuddhiyā;

Dhiyā nītimimaṃ sādhu, sādhukaññeva lakkhaye.

For the growth of the teaching, which is the life of the discerning; with wisdom, one should well discern this treatise, indeed very well discern it.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the discerning in the ninefold division with its commentary and the three Piṭakas, skilled in the ways of exposition,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the purpose of proficiency.

Vāccābhidheyyaliṅgādiparidīpano nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo

The Division of Nominal Paradigms, Elucidating Expression, Denotation, Gender, and so forth.

Ekādasamo paricchedo.

The Eleventh Chapter.

Ettāvatā [M 0.0352] bhūdhātumayānaṃ pulliṅgānaṃ itthiliṅgānaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgānañca nāmikapadamālā yathārahaṃ liṅgantarehi saddantarehi atthantarehi ca saddhiṃ nānappakārato dassitā. Sabbanāmāni hi ṭhapetvā nayato aññāni kānici nāmāni aggahitāni nāma natthi.

Thus far, the nominal paradigms of masculine, feminine, and neuter genders, derived from substantives, have been shown in various ways, together with their appropriate other genders, other words, and other meanings. Indeed, apart from pronouns, there are scarcely any other nouns left unexamined by way of rule.

12. Sabbanāmataṃsadisanāmanāmikapadamālā

12. Nominal Paradigms of Pronouns and Words Resembling Them.

Ito paraṃ pavakkhāmi, sabbanāmañca tassamaṃ;

Nāmañca yojitaṃ nānā-nāmeheva visesato.

Henceforth, I shall explain pronouns and their equivalents, and nouns joined specifically with various other nouns.

Yāni honti tiliṅgāni, anukūlāni yāni ca;

Tiliṅgānaṃ visesena, padānetāni nāmato.

Those which are of three genders, and those which are suitable—these words are designated by name especially for the three genders.

“Sabbasādhāraṇakāni, nāmāni”cceva atthato;

Sabbanāmāni vuccanti, sattavīsati saṅkhato.

Words that are 'common to all' in meaning are indeed called pronouns, numbering twenty-seven.

Tesu kānici rūpehi, sesāññehi ca yujjare;

Kānici pana saheva, etesaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ idaṃ.

Among them, some are joined by their forms, and others by the remaining. Some, however, are joined together; this is their characteristic.

Etasmā lakkhaṇā muttaṃ, na padaṃ sabbanāmikaṃ;

Tasmātītādayo saddā, guṇanāmāni vuccare.

A word devoid of this characteristic is not pronominal. Therefore, words such as 'atīta' and so forth are called qualitative nouns.

Sabbanāmāni nāma – sabba katara katama ubhaya itaraañña aññatara aññatama pubba para apara dakkhiṇa uttara adharayata eta ima amukiṃ eka ubha dviti catu tumha amha iccetāni sattavīsa.

The pronouns are: sabba, katara, katama, ubhaya, itara, añña, aññatara, aññatama, pubba, para, apara, dakkhiṇa, uttara, adhara, ya, ta, eta, ima, amu, kiṃ, eka, ubha, dvi, ti, catu, tumha, amha—these are the twenty-seven.

Etesu sabbasaddo sakalattho, so ca sabbasabbādivasena ñeyyo. Katara katamasaddā pucchanatthā. Ubhayasaddo dviavayavasamudāyavacano. Itarasaddo vuttapaṭiyogīvacano. Aññasaddo adhigatāparavacano. Aññatara aññatamasaddā aniyamatthā. Pubbādayo uttarapariyantā disākālādivavatthāvacanā. Tathā hi pubba [M 0.0353] parā para dakkhiṇuttarasaddā pulliṅgatte yathārahaṃ kāladesādivacanā, itthiliṅgatte disādivacanā, napuṃsakaliṅgatte ṭhānādivacanā. Adharasaddopi heṭṭhimatthavācako vavatthāvacanoyeva, so ca tiliṅgo “adharo patto. Adharā araṇī, adharaṃ bhājana”miti, yaṃsaddo aniyamattho. Taṃsaddo parammukhāvacano. Etasaddo samīpavacano. Imasaddo accantasamīpavacano. Amusaddo dūravacano. Kiṃsaddo pucchanattho. Ekasaddo saṅkhādivacano. Vuttañhi –

Among these, the word 'sabba' denotes 'all'; it is to be understood through examples such as 'sabba', 'sabbādi'. The words 'katara' and 'katama' have an interrogative meaning. The word 'ubhaya' signifies a collection of two constituents. The word 'itara' denotes the counterpart of what has been stated. The word 'añña' denotes another than what has been understood. The words 'aññatara' and 'aññatama' have an indefinite meaning. The words from 'pubba' to 'uttara' express the determination of direction, time, and so forth. Thus, in the masculine gender, the words 'pubba', 'para', 'apara', 'dakkhiṇa', and 'uttara' appropriately express time, place, and so forth; in the feminine gender, they express direction, and so forth; and in the neuter gender, they express place, and so forth. The word 'adhara', expressing the meaning 'lower', is also a word of determination; it is of three genders, as in 'adharo patto', 'adharā araṇī', 'adharaṃ bhājanaṃ'. The word 'ya' has an indefinite meaning. The word 'ta' denotes that which is not present. The word 'eta' denotes proximity. The word 'ima' denotes extreme proximity. The word 'amu' denotes distance. The word 'kiṃ' has an interrogative meaning. The word 'eka' denotes number, and so forth. For it is said—

Ekasaddo aññatthaseṭṭhaasahāyasaṅkhādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti, ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu aññatthe dissati. “Cetaso ekodibhāva”ntiādīsu seṭṭhe. “Eko vūpakaṭṭho”tiādīsu asahāye. “Ekova kho bhikkhave khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu saṅkhāyanti.

The word 'eka' appears in the senses of 'other', 'excellent', 'alone', 'number', and so forth. Thus, in passages such as 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is vain—thus some (eke) declare', it appears in the sense of 'other'. In phrases such as 'one-pointedness of mind' (cetaso ekodibhāva), it is in the sense of 'excellent'. In phrases such as 'alone and secluded' (eko vūpakaṭṭho), it is in the sense of 'alone'. In passages such as 'Monks, there is just one (ekova) moment and one opportunity for living the holy life', it is in the sense of 'number'.

Yatthesa saṅkhāvacano, tatthekavacanantova. Ubhasaddo dvisaddapariyāyo. Dviticatusaddā saṅkhāvacanā, sabbakālaṃ bahuvacanantāva. Tumhasaddo yena katheti, tasmiṃ vattabbavacanaṃ. Amhasaddo attani vattabbavacanaṃ.

Where this ('eka') is a numeral, it is always in the singular number. The word 'ubha' is a synonym for the word 'dvi'. The words 'dvi', 'ti', and 'catu' are numerals, and are always in the plural number. The word 'tumha' is a word to be used in reference to the one spoken to. The word 'amha' is a word to be used in reference to oneself.

Idāni tesaṃ nāmikapadamālaṃ kathayāma –

Now, we shall declare the nominal paradigms of these.

Sabbo, sabbe. Sabbaṃ, sabbe. Sabbena, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmā, sabbamhā, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ, sabbamhi, sabbesu. Bho sabba, bhavanto sabbe.

Sabbo, sabbe. Sabbaṃ, sabbe. Sabbena, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmā, sabbamhā, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ, sabbamhi, sabbesu. Bho sabba, bhavanto sabbe. (Masculine paradigm).

Tatra [M 0.0354] “sabbo bhūto, sabbe bhūtā”tiādinā, “sabbo puriso, sabbe purisā”tiādinā ca nayena sabbāni pulliṅganāmehi saddhiṃ yojetabbāni. Yāni pana yamakamahātherena punnapuṃsakavisaye sabba katara katamādīnaṃ aññānipi rūpāni vuttāni. Taṃ yathā?
