Herein, by the method of 'sabbo bhūto, sabbe bhūtā' (every being, all beings), and 'sabbo puriso, sabbe purisā' (every man, all men), and so forth, they should be conjoined with all masculine nouns. However, other forms of 'sabba', 'katara', 'katama', and so forth, have been stated by the great elder Yamaka in the domain of the masculine and neuter. How so?

“Sabbā” iccādikaṃ rūpaṃ, nissakke bhummake pana;

“Sabbe” iccādikaṃ rūpaṃ, yamakena pakāsitaṃ.

The form 'sabbā' and so forth, in the feminine and neuter, and the form 'sabbe' and so forth, were declared by Yamaka.

Tañce upaparikkhitvā, yuttaṃ gaṇhantu yogino;

Sabbanāmikarūpañhi, vividhaṃ dubbudhaṃ yato.

Having examined this, let the diligent grasp what is suitable, for pronominal forms are indeed diverse and difficult to understand.

Sabbā, sabbā, sabbāyo. Sabbaṃ, sabbā, sabbāyo. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāhi, sabbābhi. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāsaṃ. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāhi, sabbābhi. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāsaṃ. Sabbāyaṃ, sabbassā, sabbassaṃ, sabbāsu. Bhoti sabbe, bhotiyo sabbā, sabbāyo. Itthiliṅgatte nāmikapadamālā.

Sabbā, sabbā, sabbāyo. Sabbaṃ, sabbā, sabbāyo. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāhi, sabbābhi. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāsaṃ. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāhi, sabbābhi. Sabbāya, sabbassā, sabbāsaṃ. Sabbāyaṃ, sabbassā, sabbassaṃ, sabbāsu. Bhoti sabbe, bhotiyo sabbā, sabbāyo. (The nominal paradigm in the feminine gender).

Ettha “sabbā bhāvikā, sabbā bhāvikāyo”ti, “sabbā kaññā, sabbā kaññāyo”ti ca ādinā itthiliṅgasabbanāmāni sabbehi itthiliṅgehi saddhiṃ yojetabbāni. Ettha ca “sabbassā”ti padaṃ tatiyācatutthīpañcamīchaṭṭhīsattamīvasena pañcadhā vibhattaṃ “tassā kumārikāya saddhi”nti karaṇappayogādidassanato. Sabbassā kaññāya kataṃ. Sabbassā kaññāya deti. Ayaṃ kaññā sabbassā kaññāya hīnā virūpā. Ayaṃ kaññā sabbassā kaññāya uttamā abhirūpā. Sabbassā kaññāya apeti, sabbassā kaññāya dhanaṃ. Sabbassā kaññāya patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Herein, by way of 'sabbā bhāvikā, sabbā bhāvikāyo' and 'sabbā kaññā, sabbā kaññāyo', and so forth, feminine pronouns should be conjoined with all feminine nouns. And here, the word 'sabbassā' is divided in five ways according to the instrumental, dative, ablative, genitive, and locative cases, as is seen from the instrumental usage and so forth in the example 'tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ'. 'Done by every girl.' 'Gives to every girl.' 'This girl is inferior and ugly compared to every other girl.' 'This girl is superior and beautiful compared to every other girl.' 'Departs from every girl.' 'The wealth of every girl.' 'Established in every girl.'

Sabbaṃ, sabbāni. Sabbaṃ, sabbāni. Sabbena, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmā, sabbamhā, sabbehi, sabbebhi[M 0.0355]. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ, sabbamhi, sabbesu. Bho sabba, bhavanto sabbāni. Napuṃsakaliṅgatte nāmikapadamālā.

Sabbaṃ, sabbāni. Sabbaṃ, sabbāni. Sabbena, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmā, sabbamhā, sabbehi, sabbebhi. Sabbassa, sabbesaṃ, sabbesānaṃ. Sabbasmiṃ, sabbamhi, sabbesu. Bho sabba, bhavanto sabbāni. (The nominal paradigm in the neuter gender).

Ettha “sabbaṃ bhūtaṃ, sabbāni bhūtāni. Sabbaṃ cittaṃ, sabbāni cittānī”ti ca ādinā napuṃsakaliṅgasabbanāmāni sabbehi napuṃsakaliṅgehi saddhiṃ yojetabbāni. Evaṃ sabbasaddassa liṅgattayavasena padamālā bhavati.

Herein, by way of 'sabbaṃ bhūtaṃ, sabbāni bhūtāni' (every being, all beings) and 'sabbaṃ cittaṃ, sabbāni cittāni' (every mind, all minds), and so forth, neuter pronouns should be conjoined with all neuter nouns. Thus, the paradigm of the word 'sabba' occurs according to the three genders.

Idānissa parapadena saddhiṃ samāso veditabbo “sabbasādhāraṇo sabbaverī”iti. Tattha sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇo sabbasādhāraṇo. Sabbesaṃ verī, sabbe vā verino yassa soyaṃ sabbaverīti samāsaviggaho. Yathā pana sabbasaddassa padamālā liṅgattayavasena yojitā, evaṃ katarasaddādīnampi adharasaddapariyantānaṃ yojetabbā.

Now, its compounding with a subsequent word is to be understood, as in 'sabbasādhāraṇo, sabbaverī'. Therein, 'sabbasādhāraṇo' is 'common to all (sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇo)'. 'Sabbaverī' is 'an enemy to all (sabbesaṃ verī)', or 'he of whom all are enemies (sabbe vā verino yassa)'; this is the analysis of the compound. Just as the paradigm of the word 'sabba' is formed according to the three genders, so too should the paradigms of the words from 'katara' up to 'adhara' be formed.

Tatrāyaṃ ubhayasaddavajjito pulliṅgapeyyālo –

Herein is the masculine series, excluding the word 'ubhaya'—

Kataro, katare. Kataraṃ…pe… bho katara, bhavanto katare. Katamo, katame. Itaro, itare. Añño, aññe. Aññataro, aññatare. Aññatamo, aññatame. Pubbo, pubbe. Paro, pare. Aparo, apare. Dakkhiṇo, dakkhiṇe. Uttaro, uttare. Adharo, adhare…pe… bho adhara, bhavanto adhareti.

Kataro, katare. Kataraṃ… (and so forth) …bho katara, bhavanto katare. Katamo, katame. Itaro, itare. Añño, aññe. Aññataro, aññatare. Aññatamo, aññatame. Pubbo, pubbe. Paro, pare. Aparo, apare. Dakkhiṇo, dakkhiṇe. Uttaro, uttare. Adharo, adhare… (and so forth) …bho adhara, bhavanto adhare.

Ayaṃ pana ubhayasaddasahito napuṃsakaliṅgapeyyālo –

This, however, is the neuter series, including the word 'ubhaya'—

Kataraṃ, katarāni. Kataraṃ…pe… bho katara, bhavanto katarāni. Katamaṃ. Ubhayaṃ. Itaraṃ. Aññaṃ. Aññataraṃ. Aññatamaṃ. Pubbaṃ. Paraṃ. Aparaṃ. Dakkhiṇaṃ. Uttaraṃ. Adharaṃ, adharāni. Adharaṃ…pe… bho adhara, bhavanto adharānīti.

Kataraṃ, katarāni. Kataraṃ… (and so forth) …bho katara, bhavanto katarāni. Katamaṃ. Ubhayaṃ. Itaraṃ. Aññaṃ. Aññataraṃ. Aññatamaṃ. Pubbaṃ. Paraṃ. Aparaṃ. Dakkhiṇaṃ. Uttaraṃ. Adharaṃ, adharāni. Adharaṃ… (and so forth) …bho adhara, bhavanto adharāni.

Idāni [M 0.0356] punnapuṃsakaliṅgānaṃ parasaddādīnaṃ rūpantaraniddeso vuccati. Kaccāyanasmiñhi “purisā”ti viya “parā”ti paṭhamābahuvacanaṃ dissati. Evarūpo nayo aparasabbakatarādīsu aññatamapariyosānesu navasu appasiddho, labbhamāno pubbadakkhiṇuttarādharesu catūsu labbheyya. Tathā “purise”ti viya pāḷiādīsu “pubbe”ti saccasaṅkhepe “itare”ti, kaccāyane ca “pare”ti sattamīekavacanaṃ dissati. Evarūpo nayo sabba aññasaddesu appasiddho, labbhamāno katarakatamādīsu sesesu adharapariyosānesu dvādasasu labbheyya. Tathā “purisā”ti viya sabbā katarā iccādi pañcamīekavacananayo pāḷiādīsu appasiddho. Evaṃ santepi ayaṃ nayo punappunaṃ upaparikkhitvā yutto ce, gahetabbo.

Now, the explanation of other forms for the masculine and neuter genders of words such as 'para' is stated. Indeed, in Kaccāyana, the nominative plural 'parā' is seen, like 'purisā'. Such a rule is not established for the nine words beginning with 'apara', 'sabba', 'katara', etc., and ending with 'aññatama'; but if found, it could apply to the four words: 'pubba', 'dakkhiṇa', 'uttara', and 'adhara'. Similarly, like 'purise', the locative singular 'pubbe' is seen in the Saccasaṅkhepa, 'itare' in Pāli texts and so on, and 'pare' in Kaccāyana. Such a rule is not established for the words 'sabba' and 'añña'; but if found, it could apply to the remaining twelve words beginning with 'katara', 'katama', etc., and ending with 'adhara'. Likewise, the rule for the ablative singular like 'purisā', for words such as 'sabbā', 'katarā', etc., is not established in Pāli texts and so on. Even so, this rule should be repeatedly examined and, if suitable, adopted.

Ayaṃ pana ubhayasaddasahito itthiliṅgapeyyālo –

This, however, is the feminine-gender section, including the word 'ubhaya'—

Katarā, katarā, katarāyo. Kataraṃ…pe… bhoti katare, bhotiyo katarā, katarāyo. Katamā. Ubhayā. Itarā. Aññatarā. Aññatamā. Pubbā. Parā. Aparā. Dakkhiṇā. Uttarā. Adharā, adharā, adharāyo. Adharaṃ…pe… bhoti adhare, bhotiyo adharā, adharāyoti.

Katarā, katarā, katarāyo. Kataraṃ…pe… bhoti katare, bhotiyo katarā, katarāyo. Katamā. Ubhayā. Itarā. Aññatarā. Aññatamā. Pubbā. Parā. Aparā. Dakkhiṇā. Uttarā. Adharā, adharā, adharāyo. Adharaṃ…pe… bhoti adhare, bhotiyo adharā, adharāyo.

Yasmā panetesu itara añña aññatara aññatamānaṃ pāḷiyādīsu “itarissā”tiādidassanato koci bhedo vattabbo[M 0.0357], tasmā catutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ ekavacanaṭṭhāne “itarissā, itarāya, aññissā, aññāya. Aññatarissā, aññatarāya, aññatamissā, aññatamāyā”ti yojetabbaṃ. Tathā tatiyāpañcamīnamekavacanaṭṭhāne “tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ. Kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmī”ti karaṇanissakkappayogadassanato sattamiyā panekavacanaṭṭhāne “itarissā, itarissaṃ, itarāya, itarāyaṃ, aññissā, aññissaṃ, aññāya, aññāyaṃ, aññatarissā, aññatarissaṃ, aññatarāya, aññatarāyaṃ, aññatamissā, aññatamissaṃ, aññatamāya, aññatamāya”nti yojetabbaṃ “aññataro bhikkhu aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto hotī”ti pāḷidassanato.

Since in these words—'itara,' 'añña,' 'aññatara,' and 'aññatama'—a certain distinction is known in Pāli and other texts, as seen in forms like 'itarissā,' etc., therefore, in the singular of the fourth and sixth cases, they should be construed as 'itarissā, itarāya, aññissā, aññāya, aññatarissā, aññatarāya, aññatamissā, aññatamāyā.' Similarly, in the singular of the third and fifth cases, as seen in expressions like 'tassā kumārikāya saddhiṃ' and 'kassāhaṃ kena hāyāmī,' which illustrate instrumental and ablative usage, and in the singular of the seventh case, they should be construed as 'itarissā, itarissaṃ, itarāya, itarāyaṃ, aññissā, aññissaṃ, aññāya, aññāyaṃ, aññatarissā, aññatarissaṃ, aññatarāya, aññatarāyaṃ, aññatamissā, aññatamissaṃ, aññatamāya, aññatamāyaṃ,' as seen in the Pāli phrase 'aññataro bhikkhu aññatarissā itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto hoti.'

Tatra sabbasaddo sabbasabbaṃ, padesasabbaṃ, āyatanasabbaṃ, sakkāyasabbanti catūsu visayesu diṭṭhappayogo. Tathā hesa “sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthamāgacchantī”tiādīsu sabbasabbasmiṃ āgato. “Sabbesaṃ vo sāriputtā subhāsitaṃ pariyāyenā”tiādīsu padesasabbasmiṃ. “Sabbaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmi, taṃ suṇātha sādhukaṃ manasi karotha, bhāsissāmi…pe… katamañca bhikkhave sabbaṃ cakkhuñceva rūpā ca…pe… mano ceva dhammā cā”ti ettha āyatanasabbasmiṃ. “Sabbaṃ sabbato sañjānātī”tiādīsu sakkāyasabbasmiṃ. Tattha sabbasabbasmiṃ āgato nippadeso, itaresu tīsu sappadesoti veditabbo. Iccevaṃ –

Here, the word 'sabba' is used in four contexts: all in every way, all in part, all of the sense-bases, and all of personality. Thus, it occurs as 'all in every way' in statements like, 'all phenomena in every way come within the range of the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One.' It occurs as 'all in part' in statements like, 'Of all of you, Sāriputta, it is well-spoken in turn.' In passages such as, 'Monks, I will teach you the all. Listen, attend carefully, I will speak... And what, monks, is the all? The eye and forms... the mind and mental objects,' it occurs as 'all of the sense-bases.' It occurs as 'all of personality' in statements like, 'one perceives the all from the all.' Herein, that which occurs as 'all in every way' is without qualification; the other three are to be understood as qualified. Thus—

Sabbasabbapadesesu[M 0.0358], atho āyatanepi ca;

Sakkāye cāti catūsu, sabbasaddo pavattati.

In 'all in every way' and 'all in part', and also in the sense-bases; And in personality—in these four, the word 'sabba' occurs.

Katara katamasaddesu katarasaddo appesu ekaṃ vā dve vā tīṇi vā bhiyyo vā appamupādāya vattati. Katamasaddo bahūsu ekaṃ vā dve vā tīṇi vā bahuṃ vā upādāya vattati. Katarasaddo hi appavisayo, katamasaddo bahuvisayo. Tatrime payogā “katarena maggena gantabbaṃ. Samuddo kataro ayaṃ. Katamo tasmiṃ samaye phasso hoti. Katame dhammā kusalā. Disā catasso vidisā catasso, uddhaṃ adho dasa disatā, imāyo, katamaṃ disaṃ tiṭṭhati nāgarājā”. Iccevamādayo bhavanti. Ubhayo. Ubhayaṃ. Ubhayo. Ubhayena. Sesaṃ pulliṅge sabbasaddasamaṃ. Ubhayo janā tiṭṭhanti. Ubhayo jane passati. Yathā ubho puttā. Ubho putteti. “Ubhayo”ti hi padaṃ “ubho”ti padamiva bahuvacanantabhāvena pasiddhaṃ, na tvekavacanantabhāvena. Ettha hi –

Regarding the words 'katara' and 'katama': the word 'katara' is used with reference to a few, whether one, two, three, or more, but still a small number. The word 'katama' is used with reference to many, whether one, two, three, or a large number. For the word 'katara' has a limited scope, while the word 'katama' has a broad scope. Here are some examples: 'By which path should one go? Which is this ocean? Which contact is present at that time? Which phenomena are wholesome? The four directions, the four intermediate directions, above, below—these ten directions—in which direction does the Nāga king stand?' and so on. Ubhayo. Ubhayaṃ. Ubhayo. Ubhayena. The rest is the same as the word 'sabba' in the masculine gender. 'Both people stand.' 'One sees both people.' As in 'both sons,' 'both sons.' Indeed, the word 'ubhayo' is known to function as a plural, like the word 'ubho', and not as a singular. Here—

“Ekarattena ubhayo, tuvañca dhanusekha ca;

Annamevābhinandanti, ubhayo devamānusā”

'In a single night, both you and Dhanusekha; Both gods and humans rejoice in food.'

“Ubhayo te pitābhātaro”ti tadatthasādhakāni nidassanapadāni veditabbāni. Yadā panāyasmanto “ubhayo”ti ekavacanantaṃ passeyyātha, tadā sādhukaṃ manasi karotha. Ko hi samattho anantanayapaṭimaṇḍite sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake jinasāsane niravasesato nayaṃ daṭṭhuṃ [M 0.0359] dassetuñca aññatra āgamādhigamasampannena pabhinnapaṭisambhidena. Idañcetthupalakkhitabbaṃ –

'Both of them are your father and brother'—the illustrative examples that convey this meaning should be understood. But when you, venerable sirs, see the word 'ubhayo' as a singular form, then consider it carefully. For who is capable of fully seeing and demonstrating the method without omission in the three baskets of the Buddha’s dispensation, adorned with endless approaches and its commentaries, except one accomplished in scripture and realization, endowed with the analytical knowledges? And this should be noted here—

Aññasaddo pubbasaddo, dakkhiṇo cuttaro paro;

Sabbanāmesu gayhanti, asabbanāmikesupi.

The word 'añña', the word 'pubba', 'dakkhiṇa', 'uttara', and 'para'; These are included among pronouns, and also among non-pronouns.

Etesañhi sabbanāmesu saṅgaho vibhāvitova.

For their inclusion among pronouns has indeed been demonstrated.

Idāni asabbanāmesu saṅgaho vuccate – tattha aññasaddo tāva yadā bālavācako, tadā sabbanāmaṃ nāma na hoti. Asabbanāmattā ca sabbathāpi purisa kaññā cittanayeneva yojetabbo. Tathā hi na jānātīti añño, bālo puriso. Na jānātīti aññā, bālā itthī. Na jānātīti aññaṃ, bālaṃ kulanti vacanattho. Evaṃ viditvā pulliṅgaṭṭhāne “añño, aññā. Aññaṃ, aññe”tiādinā purisanayeneva nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Itthiliṅgaṭṭhāne “aññā, aññā, aññāyo”tiādinā kaññānayeneva, napuṃsakaliṅgaṭṭhāne “aññaṃ, aññānī”tiādinā cittanayeneva yojetabbā.

Now, their inclusion among non-pronouns is stated—first, when the word 'añña' signifies a fool, then it is not a pronoun. And since it is not a pronoun, in every way, it must be construed according to the rule of 'purisa', 'kaññā', or 'citta'. For example: 'He does not know' means 'añño,' a foolish man. 'She does not know' means 'aññā,' a foolish woman. 'It does not know' means 'aññaṃ,' a foolish family—this is the meaning of the expression. Having understood thus, in masculine instances, the series of nominal forms such as 'añño, aññā. Aññaṃ, aññe,' etc., should be construed according to the rule of 'purisa'. In feminine instances, forms such as 'aññā, aññā, aññāyo,' etc., should follow the rule of 'kaññā'. In neuter instances, forms such as 'aññaṃ, aññānī,' etc., should be construed according to the rule of 'citta'.

Imasmiñhi atthavisese bālajane vattukāmena “aññā janā”ti avatvā “aññe janā”ti vutte tassa taṃ vacanaṃ adhippetatthaṃ na sādheti aññathā atthassa gahetabbattā. Tathā “aññānaṃ janāna”nti avatvā “aññesaṃ janānaṃ, aññesānaṃ janāna”nti vā vutte tassa taṃ vacanaṃ adhippetatthaṃ na sādheti. Tathā “aññānaṃ itthīna”nti avatvā “aññāsaṃ itthīna”nti vuttepi, “aññānaṃ kulāna”nti avatvā “aññesaṃ kulānaṃ, aññesānaṃ kulāna”nti vā vuttepi. Sabbanāmikavasena pana adhigatāparavacanicchāyaṃ “aññe janā”tiādinā vattabbaṃ, na “aññā janā”tiādinā. Tathā hi “aññā janā”tiādinā vuttavacanaṃ adhippetatthaṃ na sādheti aññathā atthassa [M 0.0360] gahetabbattā. Iti yattha “aññā janā”tiādivacanaṃ upapajjati, “aññe janā”tiādivacanaṃ nupapajjati, yattha pana “aññe janā”tiādivacanaṃ upapajjati, “aññā janā”tiādivacanaṃ nupapajjati. Yā etasmiṃ atthavisese sallakkhaṇā paññā, ayaṃ nītiyā maggo yuttāyuttivicāraṇe hetuttā, lokasmiñhi yuttāyuttivicāraṇā nītīti vuttā. Sā ca vinā paññāya na sijjhati. Evaṃ aññasaddo asabbanāmikopi bhavati.

In this particular matter, when one wishes to speak about foolish people, saying 'aññā janā' instead of 'aññe janā' does not achieve the intended meaning, because the sense would be understood differently. Similarly, saying 'aññānaṃ janānaṃ' instead of 'aññesaṃ janānaṃ' or 'aññesānaṃ janānaṃ' does not achieve the intended meaning of that statement. Likewise, saying 'aññānaṃ itthīnaṃ' instead of 'aññāsaṃ itthīnaṃ', or saying 'aññānaṃ kulānaṃ' instead of 'aññesaṃ kulānaṃ' or 'aññesānaṃ kulānaṃ', also does not achieve the intended meaning. However, when desiring to convey another meaning by way of a pronoun, one should say 'aññe janā' and so on, not 'aññā janā' and so on. For this reason, the statement made by saying 'aññā janā' and so on does not achieve the intended meaning, because the sense would be understood differently. Thus, where the expression 'aññā janā' and so on is appropriate, the expression 'aññe janā' and so on is not appropriate; and where the expression 'aññe janā' and so on is appropriate, the expression 'aññā janā' and so on is not appropriate. That wisdom which carefully observes this particular distinction is the path of logic, being a cause for deliberation on what is fit and unfit; for in the world, deliberation on what is fit and unfit is called logic. And that is not accomplished without wisdom. Thus, the word 'añña' can also be non-pronominal.

Pubba dakkhiṇuttara parasaddesu pubbasaddo yattha padhānavācako, yattha ca “semhaṃ pubbo”tiādīsu lohitakopajavācako, tattha asabbanāmiko. Paṭhamatthe tiliṅgo, dutiyatthe ekaliṅgo. Uttamatthavācako pana uttarasaddo ca parasaddo ca asabbanāmiko tiliṅgoyeva. Tathā “dakkhiṇassā vahantima”nti ettha viya susikkhitatthacaturatthavācako dakkhiṇasaddo. “Petānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dajjā”tiādīsu pana deyyadhammavācako dakkhiṇāsaddo niyogā itthiliṅgo asabbanāmikoyeva. Evaṃ añña pubba dakkhiṇuttara parasaddā asabbanāmikāpi santīti tesaṃ sabbanāmesupi asabbanāmesupi saṅgaho veditabbo.

Among the words 'pubba,' 'dakkhiṇa,' 'uttara,' and 'para,' the word 'pubba' is non-pronominal where it denotes the primary sense, and where it denotes pus, as in 'semhaṃ pubbo.' In the first sense, it has three genders; in the second, it has one gender. The words 'uttara' and 'para,' when denoting the highest sense, are also non-pronominal and have three genders. Similarly, the word 'dakkhiṇa' is non-pronominal when, as in 'dakkhiṇassā vahantima,' it denotes the sense of 'well-trained' or 'clever.' However, in phrases like 'Petānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ dajjā,' the word 'dakkhiṇā,' denoting a gift, is necessarily feminine and non-pronominal. Thus, since the words 'añña,' 'pubba,' 'dakkhiṇa,' 'uttara,' and 'para' can also be non-pronominal, their inclusion should be understood both among pronouns and among non-pronouns.

Idāni katarasaddādīnaṃ parapadena saddhiṃ samāso nīyate “kataragāmavāsī katamagāmavāsī. Ubhayagāmavāsino, itaragāmavāsī aññataragāmavāsī, pubbadisā, parajano, dakkhiṇadisā, uttaradisā, adharapatto”ti. Tatra “kataro gāmo kataragāmo, katamo gāmo katamagāmo, ubhayo gāmā ubhayagāmā”tiādinā yathārahaṃ samāsaviggaho, katarasaddassa pana katamasaddena saddhiṃ samāsaṃ icchanti dvidhā ca rūpāni garū “kataro ca katamo ca katarakatame katarakatamā vā”ti[M 0.0361]. Tasmā sabbanāmikanayena suddhanāmikesu purisanayena ca katara katamasaddassa nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā, tenassa sampadānasāmivacanaṭṭhānesu “katarakatamesaṃ, katarakatamesānaṃ, katarakatamāna”nti tīṇi rūpāni siyuṃ “katarā ca katamā ca katarakatamā”ti evaṃ itthiliṅgavasena katasamāse pana sabbanāmikanayena, suddhanāmikesu kaññānayena ca yojetabbā. “Katarañca katamañca katarakatamānī”ti evaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgavasena katasamāse sabbanāmikanayena, suddhanāmikesu cittanayena ca yojetabbā.

Now, the compounding of words such as 'katara' with a subsequent word is presented: 'kataragāmavāsī, katamagāmavāsī, ubhayagāmavāsino, itaragāmavāsī, aññataragāmavāsī, pubbadisā, parajano, dakkhiṇadisā, uttaradisā, adharapatto.' Here, the compound analysis is 'kataro gāmo = kataragāmo; katamo gāmo = katamagāmo; ubhayo gāmā = ubhayagāmā,' and so on, as appropriate. However, teachers desire to compound 'katara' with 'katama,' and there are two forms: 'kataro ca katamo ca = katarakatame or katarakatamā.' Therefore, for the word 'katarakatama', the nominal paradigm should be formed according to the pronominal method and, for pure nouns, according to the 'purisa' paradigm. By this, in the dative and genitive plural, there would be three forms: 'katarakatamesaṃ, katarakatamesānaṃ, katarakatamānaṃ.' When the compound is formed in the feminine gender as 'katarā ca katamā ca = katarakatamā,' the paradigm should be formed according to the pronominal method and, for pure nouns, according to the 'kaññā' paradigm. When the compound is formed in the neuter gender as 'katarañca katamañca = katarakatamāni,' the paradigm should be formed according to the pronominal method and, for pure nouns, according to the 'citta' paradigm.

Ayaṃ panettha visesopi veditabbo – pubbāparādisaddā dvandasamāsādividhiṃ patvā sehi rūpehi rūpavanto na honti, taṃ yathā? Pubbāparā, adharuttarā, māsapubbā purisā, diṭṭhapubbā purisā, tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbā sāvakā, idaṃ pulliṅgatte paṭhamābahuvacanarūpaṃ. Etthekāro ādesabhūto na dissati. Pubbāparānaṃ adharuttarānaṃ, māsapubbānaṃ purisānaṃ, idaṃ pulliṅgatte catutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ bahuvacanarūpaṃ. Ettha saṃ sānamiccete ādesabhūtā na dissanti. Tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbānaṃ sāvakānaṃ, tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbānaṃ sāvikānaṃ, kulānaṃ vā, idaṃ tiliṅgatte catutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ bahuvacanarūpaṃ. Etthāpi saṃ sānamiccete ādesabhūtā na dissanti. Māsapubbāyaṃ māsapubbāya, piyapubbāyaṃ piyapubbāya, idamitthiliṅgatte sattamīcatutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ ekavacanarūpaṃ. Etthādesabhūtā saṃ sā na dissanti. Māsapubbānaṃ itthīnaṃ, piyapubbānaṃ itthīnaṃ, idamitthiliṅgatte catutthīchaṭṭhībahuvacanarūpaṃ. Ettha panādesabhūto samicceso na dissati. Aññānipi yathāsambhavaṃ yojetabbāni, pubbāparādīnaṃ samāsaviggahaṃ samāsaparicchede pakāsessāma.

Here, this distinction should also be understood: words such as 'pubba' and 'apara', having entered into a dvanda compound or other such formation, are not formed with their own pronominal forms. How so? 'Pubbāparā, adharuttarā, māsapubbā purisā, diṭṭhapubbā purisā, tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbā sāvakā'—this is the nominative plural form in the masculine gender. Here, the substitute 'e' is not seen. 'Pubbāparānaṃ, adharuttarānaṃ, māsapubbānaṃ purisānaṃ'—this is the dative and genitive plural form in the masculine gender. Here, the substitutes 'saṃ' and 'sānaṃ' are not seen. 'Tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbānaṃ sāvakānaṃ, tathāgataṃ diṭṭhapubbānaṃ sāvikānaṃ, kulānaṃ vā'—this is the dative and genitive plural form in the three genders. Here too, the substitutes 'saṃ' and 'sānaṃ' are not seen. 'Māsapubbāyaṃ, māsapubbāya, piyapubbāyaṃ, piyapubbāya'—this is the locative, dative, and genitive singular form in the feminine gender. Here, the substitutes 'saṃ' and 'sā' are not seen. 'Māsapubbānaṃ itthīnaṃ, piyapubbānaṃ itthīnaṃ'—this is the dative and genitive plural form in the feminine gender. Here, however, the substitute 'saṃ' is not seen. Other examples should be applied as is possible. We will explain the analysis of compounds like 'pubbāparā' in the chapter on compounds.

Idāni [M 0.0362] yaṃsaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal paradigm of the word 'ya' is stated:

Yo, ye. Yaṃ, ye. Yena, yehi, yebhi. Yassa, yesaṃ, yesānaṃ. Yasmā, yamhā, yehi, yebhi. Yassa, yesaṃ, yesānaṃ. Yasmiṃ, yamhi, yesu. Idaṃ pulliṅgaṃ. Yaṃ, yāni. Yaṃ, yāni. Yena. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Atha vā yaṃ, yāni, yā. Yaṃ, yāni, ye. Yena. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Katthaci hi nikāralopo bhavati. Atha vā pana nikārassa ākārekārādesāpi gāthāvisaye.

Yo, ye. Yaṃ, ye. Yena, yehi, yebhi. Yassa, yesaṃ, yesānaṃ. Yasmā, yamhā, yehi, yebhi. Yassa, yesaṃ, yesānaṃ. Yasmiṃ, yamhi, yesu. This is the masculine. Yaṃ, yāni. Yaṃ, yāni. Yena. The rest is like the masculine. This is the neuter. Alternatively: Yaṃ, yāni, yā. Yaṃ, yāni, ye. Yena. The rest is like the masculine. For sometimes the elision of the syllable 'ni' occurs. Or, moreover, in verse, there are also the substitutes 'ā' and 'e' for the syllable 'ni'.

“Yā pubbe bodhisattānaṃ, pallaṅkavaramābhuje;

Nimittāni padissanti, tāni ajja padissare”ti ca,

“Whatever signs were to appear before on the excellent seat of the Bodhisattas, those same signs will be seen today.”

“Kiṃ māṇavassa ratanāni atthi, ye taṃ jinanto hare akkhadhutto”ti ca idamettha pāḷinidassanaṃ. Idaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

“What treasures does the young man possess that the winning gambler might seize?” This is the Pāli example given here. This is the neuter gender.

Yā, yā, yāyo. Yaṃ, yā, yāyo. Yāya, yāhi, yābhi. Yāya, yassā, yāsaṃ. Yāya, yāhi, yābhi. Yāya, yassā, yāsaṃ. Yassaṃ, yāyaṃ, yāsu. Itthiliṅgaṃ. Evaṃ yaṃsaddassa liṅgattayavasena padamālā bhavati. Etthālapanapadāni na labbhanti. Tathā taṃsaddādīnaṃ padamālādīsupi.

Yā, yā, yāyo. Yaṃ, yā, yāyo. Yāya, yāhi, yābhi. Yāya, yassā, yāsaṃ. Yāya, yāhi, yābhi. Yāya, yassā, yāsaṃ. Yassaṃ, yāyaṃ, yāsu. This is the feminine. Thus, the nominal paradigm of the word 'ya' is formed according to the three genders. Here, vocative forms are not found. Likewise for the word 'ta' and others in their paradigms.

Ettha pana yanti saddassa atthuddhāro vuccate – yanti saddo “yaṃ me bhante devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ sammukhā sutaṃ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ, ārocemi taṃ bhante bhagavato”tiādīsu paccattavacane dissati. “Yantaṃ apucchimha akittayī no, aññaṃ taṃ pucchāma tadiṅgha brūhī”tiādīsu upayogavacane. “Aṭṭhā nametaṃ bhikkhave anavakāso, yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā”tiādīsu karaṇavacane. “Yaṃ vipassī bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho [M 0.0363] loke udapādī”tiādīsu bhummavacane dissati. Etthedaṃ vuccati –

Here, however, the explanation of the meaning of the word 'yaṃ' is stated: the word 'yaṃ' is seen in the nominative case in phrases like, “That which I, venerable sir, heard face to face from the Tāvatiṃsa devas, received face to face, I report that to the Blessed One, venerable sir.” It is seen in the accusative case in phrases like, “That which we asked, you did not explain to us; we ask you another thing, so please speak of it.” It is seen in the instrumental case in phrases like, “There is no possibility, monks, that in one world-system…” It is seen in the locative case in phrases like, “When the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, arose in the world…” Here, this is said:

“Paccatte upayoge ca, bhumme ca karaṇepi ca;

Catūsvetesu ṭhānesu, yanti saddo pavattatī”ti.

“In the nominative, in the accusative, in the locative, and in the instrumental; in these four places, the word 'yaṃ' occurs.”

Parapadena saddhiṃ yaṃsaddassa samāsopi veditabbo “yaṃkhandhādi, yaṃguṇā, yagguṇā”ti. Tattha yo khandhādi yaṃkhandhādi, ye guṇā yaṃguṇāti samāsaviggaho. Tathā hi visuddhimagge “yaṃguṇanemittikañcetaṃ nāmaṃ, tesaṃ guṇānaṃ pakāsanatthaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ vadantī”ti etasmiṃ pade “ye guṇā yaṃguṇā, yaṃguṇā eva nimittaṃ yaṃguṇanimittaṃ, tato jātaṃ ‘bhagavā’ti idaṃ nāmanti yaṃguṇanemittika”nti nibbacanamicchitabbaṃ. Yagguṇāti ettha pana “yassa guṇā yagguṇā”ti nibbacanaṃ. Tathā hi –

The compounding of the word `yaṃ` with a subsequent word should also be understood, as in `yaṃkhandhādi`, `yaṃguṇā`, and `yagguṇā`. Therein, the analysis of the compound is: `yo khandhādi` is `yaṃkhandhādi`, and `ye guṇā` is `yaṃguṇā`. For so it is in the Visuddhimagga, in the passage, “And this name is `yaṃguṇanemittika`; for the purpose of revealing those qualities, they recite this verse,” it should be understood that: ‘`ye guṇā` is `yaṃguṇā`; `yaṃguṇā` itself is the cause (`nimittaṃ`), hence `yaṃguṇanimittaṃ`; from that is born this name ‘Bhagavā’, thus it is `yaṃguṇanemittika`.’ As for `yagguṇā`, however, the derivation is `yassa guṇā yagguṇā`. Indeed—

“Api sabbaññutā paññā, yagguṇantaṃ na jāniyā;

Atha kā tassa vijaññā, taṃ buddhaṃ bhūguṇaṃ name”ti

“Even the wisdom of omniscience would not know the end of his virtues; who then could understand them? To that Buddha, abounding in virtues, I bow.”

Porāṇakaviracanāyaṃ “yassa guṇā yagguṇā”ti nibbacanamicchitabbaṃ.

In this ancient poetic composition, it should be understood that `yassa guṇā` is `yagguṇā`.

Yasaddassa samāsamhi, saddhiṃ parapadehi ve;

Niggahītāgamo vātha, dvibhāvo vā siyā dvidhā.

In the compounding of the word `yaṃ` with subsequent words, there may be either an insertion of a niggahīta or a doubling; thus it occurs in two ways.

Evaṃ yasaddassa samāso sallakkhitabbo.

Thus, the compounding of the word `yaṃ` should be carefully noted.

Idāni tasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal paradigm of the word `ta` is stated:

So, te. Naṃ, taṃ, ne, te. Nena, tena, nehi, tehi, nebhi, tebhi. Assa, nassa, tassa, ‘nesaṃ, tesaṃ (āsaṃ). Asmā, nasmā, tasmā, namhā, tamhā, nehi, tehi, nebhi, tebhi. Assa, nassa, tassa, nesaṃ, tesaṃ (āsaṃ). Asmiṃ, nasmiṃ, tasmiṃ, amhi, namhi, tamhi, tyamhi, nesu, tesu. Idaṃ pulliṅgaṃ. Ettha [M 0.0364] ca āsaṃsaddassa atthibhāve “nevāsaṃ kesā dissanti, hatthapādā ca jālino”ti gāthā nidassanaṃ, so ca tiliṅgo daṭṭhabbo. Tyamhīti padassa atthibhāve –

So, te. Naṃ, taṃ, ne, te. Nena, tena, nehi, tehi, nebhi, tebhi. Assa, nassa, tassa, nesaṃ, tesaṃ (āsaṃ). Asmā, nasmā, tasmā, namhā, tamhā, nehi, tehi, nebhi, tebhi. Assa, nassa, tassa, nesaṃ, tesaṃ (āsaṃ). Asmiṃ, nasmiṃ, tasmiṃ, amhi, namhi, tamhi, tyamhi, nesu, tesu. This is the masculine gender. And here, regarding the existence of the word `āsaṃ`, the verse “Neither is their hair seen, nor are their hands and feet webbed” is an example, and this form should be understood as belonging to all three genders. Regarding the existence of the word `tyamhi`—

“Yadāssa sīlaṃ paññañca, soceyyañcādhigacchati;

Atha vissāsate tyamhi, guyhañcassa na rakkhatī”ti

“When one finds in him virtue, wisdom, and purity, then one trusts in him and does not keep a secret from him.”

Ayaṃ gāthā nidassanaṃ. Ayamettha rūpaviseso sallakkhitabbo – ariyavinayeti vā sappurisavinayeti vā. Ese se eke ekaṭṭheti pāḷippadese paccattekavacanakānameta tasaddānaṃ ekārantaniddesopi dissatīti.

This verse is an illustration. This special form here should be carefully noted in the Discipline of the Noble Ones or the Discipline of the Good Person. In Pāli passages such as `ese`, `se`, `eke`, `ekaṭṭhe`, the designation of these `ta`-words with a final `-e` in the nominative singular is also seen.

Ettha pana tesaddassa atthuddhāro vuccate – tesaddo “na te sukhaṃ pajānanti, ye na passanti nandana”ntiādīsu taṃsaddassa vasena paccattabahuvacane āgato, “te na passāmi dārake”tiādīsu upayogabahuvacane. “Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama. Namo te buddha vīratthū”ti ca ādīsu tumhasaddassa vasena sampadāne, tuyhanti atthoti vadanti. “Kinte diṭṭhaṃ kinti te diṭṭhaṃ, upadhī te samatikkantā, āsavā te padālitā”ti ca ādīsu karaṇe. “Kinte vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariya”ntiādīsu sāmiatthe, tavāti atthoti vadanti. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Here, however, the elucidation of the meaning of the word `te` is stated: the word `te` appears in contexts such as “They do not know happiness, who do not see Nandana,” where it occurs in the nominative plural, derived from the word `ta`. In phrases such as “I do not see those children,” it is in the accusative plural. In expressions such as “Homage to you, O noble man, homage to you, O supreme man. Homage to you, O Buddha, O hero,” it is in the dative case, derived from the word `tumha`, meaning `tuyha`, they say. In phrases such as “What has been seen by you? What is it that has been seen by you? Attachments have been transcended by you, the corruptions have been shattered by you,” it is in the instrumental case. In statements such as “What is your vow? What then is your holy life?” it is in the genitive case, meaning `tava`, they say. Regarding this, it is said:

“Paccatte upayoge ca, karaṇe sampadāniye;

Sāmimhi cāti tesaddo, pañcasvatthesu dissatī”ti.

“In the nominative, in the accusative, in the instrumental, in the dative, and in the sense of ownership; in these five senses, the word `te` is seen.”

Taṃ, tāni. Taṃ, tāni. Nena, tena iccādi. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Idaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

Taṃ, tāni. Taṃ, tāni. Nena, tena, etc. The rest is similar to the masculine gender. This is the neuter gender.

Sā[M 0.0365], tā, tāyo. Naṃ, taṃ, nā, tā, nāyo, tāyo. Nāya, tāya, nāhi, tāhi, nābhi, tābhi. Assā, nassā, (tissā,) tassā, nāya, tāya, nāsaṃ, tāsaṃ, sānaṃ, āsaṃ. Assā, nassā, tassā, nāya, tāya, nāhi, tāhi, nābhi, tābhi. Assā, nassā, (tissā,) tassā, nāya, tāya, nāsaṃ, tāsaṃ, sānaṃ, āsaṃ. Nāya, tāya, assaṃ, nassaṃ, tissaṃ, tassaṃ, nāyaṃ, tāyaṃ, nāsu, tāsu, tyāsu. Idaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ.

Sā, tā, tāyo. Naṃ, taṃ, nā, tā, nāyo, tāyo. Nāya, tāya, nāhi, tāhi, nābhi, tābhi. Assā, nassā, (tissā,) tassā, nāya, tāya, nāsaṃ, tāsaṃ, sānaṃ, āsaṃ. Assā, nassā, tassā, nāya, tāya, nāhi, tāhi, nābhi, tābhi. Assā, nassā, (tissā,) tassā, nāya, tāya, nāsaṃ, tāsaṃ, sānaṃ, āsaṃ. Nāya, tāya, assaṃ, nassaṃ, tissaṃ, tassaṃ, nāyaṃ, tāyaṃ, nāsu, tāsu, tyāsu. This is the feminine gender.

Ettha pana “abhikkamo sānaṃ paññāyati, nāsaṃ kujjhanti paṇḍitā. Khiḍḍā paṇihitā tyāsu, rati tyāsu patiṭṭhitā. Bījāni tyāsu ruhantī”ti payogadassanato “sānaṃ āsaṃ tyāsū”ti imāni vuttāni akkharacintakānaṃ ñāṇacakkhusammuyhanaṭṭhānabhūtāni. Evaṃ parammukhavacanassa taṃsaddassa nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

Here, indeed, from seeing the usage in phrases such as “Their progress is discerned,” “The wise do not get angry with them,” “Play is directed towards them,” “Delight is established in them,” and “Seeds grow in them,” these forms `sānaṃ`, `āsaṃ`, and `tyāsu` are stated, which are places of confusion for the wisdom-eye of grammarians. Thus occurs the nominal paradigm of the word `ta` when referring to one who is not present.

Ettha ca idaṃ vattabbaṃ –

And here, this should be stated:

“Taṃ tvaṃ gantvāna yācassu”, iccādīsu padissare;

Ādo taṃ tetiādīni, nantiādīni no tathā.

“In such phrases as ‘Go and ask for that,’ `taṃ`, `te`, and so on, appear at the beginning of a clause; but `naṃ`, `ne`, and so on, do not.”

Naṃ ne nenātiādīni, vo noiccādayo viya;

Padato parabhāvamhi, diṭṭhāni jinasāsane.

`Naṃ`, `ne`, `nena`, etc., like `vo`, `no`, etc., are seen in the Dispensation of the Conqueror in a position after a word.

“Atha naṃ atha ne āha, na ca naṃ paṭinandati”;

Iccādīni payogāni, dassetabbāni viññunā.

Usages such as “Then he said to him, then he said to them,” and “and he does not approve of him/it” should be shown by the wise.

Ko cettha vadeyya –

Should someone here say—

“Yathā nadī ca pantho ca, pānāgāraṃ sabhā papā;

Evaṃ lokitthiyo nāma, nāsaṃ kujjhanti paṇḍitā”ti

“Just as a river, a path, a tavern, an assembly hall, and a public watering place, so indeed are the women of the world; the wise do not get angry with them.”

Ettha [M 0.0366] –

Here—

Padato aparattepi, nāsaṃsaddassa dassanā;

Ādopi icchitabbāva, naṃ neiccādayo iti.

“Since the word `nāsaṃ` is seen even when not following another word, it should be accepted that `naṃ`, `ne`, and so on, can also appear at the beginning.”

So panevantu vattabbo, “tava vāde na labbhati;

Nāsaṃsaddo nasaddo ca, āsaṃsaddo ca labbhare.

But he should be told thus: “Your argument does not hold. The word `nāsaṃ` is not found as a single form; rather, the words `na` and `āsaṃ` are found.”

Tasmā ‘āsaṃ na kujjhanti, itthīnaṃ paṇḍitā’iti;

Atthova bhavate evaṃ, suṭṭhu dhārehi paṇḍitā”ti.

“Therefore, the meaning is thus: ‘The wise do not get angry with them (women)’ (`āsaṃ na kujjhanti`). O wise one, understand this well.”

Atha vā yasmā niruttipiṭake “naṃ purisaṃ passati, ne purise passatī”tiādinā padato aparattepi “naṃ, ne” iccādīni padāni vuttāni, tasmā tenāpi nayena padato aparānipi tāni kadāci siyuṃ. Mayaṃ pana pāḷinayānusārena tesaṃ pavattiṃ vadāma, idaṃ ṭhānaṃ suṭṭhu vicāretabbaṃ.

Alternatively, since in the Nirutti Piṭaka, in such examples as ‘He sees the man’ (`naṃ purisaṃ passati`) and ‘He sees the men’ (`ne purise passati`), the words `naṃ`, `ne`, and so on, are stated even when not following another word, therefore, according to that method also, they may sometimes not follow another word. We, however, state their occurrence according to the Pāli method; this point should be well investigated.

Ettha pana tasaddassa parapadehi saddhiṃ samāsopi veditabbo “taṃputto, taṃsadiso, tanninno, tappoṇo, tappabbhāro, tabbhūto, tagguṇo, tassadiso”ti.

Here, however, the compounding of the word `ta` with subsequent words should also be understood, as in `taṃputto` (his son), `taṃsadiso` (similar to him), `tanninno` (inclined to that), `tappoṇo` (devoted to that), `tappabbhāro` (sloping towards that), `tabbhūto` (become that), `tagguṇo` (his quality), and `tassadiso` (like him).

Tasaddassa samāsamhi, saddhiṃ parapadehi ve;

Niggahītāgamo pubba-pade dvittantu pacchime.

In the compounding of the word `ta` with subsequent words, there is an insertion of a niggahīta in the preceding member, and a doubling in the following member.

Evaṃ tasaddassa samāso sallakkhitabbo.

Thus, the compounding of the word `ta` should be carefully noted.

Idāni etasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal paradigm of the word `eta` is stated:

Eso, ete. Etaṃ, ete. Etena, etehi, etebhi. Etassa, etesaṃ, etesānaṃ. Etasmā, etamhā, etehi, etebhi. Etassa, etesaṃ, etesānaṃ. Etasmiṃ, etamhi, etesu. Idaṃ pulliṅgaṃ.

Eso, ete. Etaṃ, ete. Etena, etehi, etebhi. Etassa, etesaṃ, etesānaṃ. Etasmā, etamhā, etehi, etebhi. Etassa, etesaṃ, etesānaṃ. Etasmiṃ, etamhi, etesu. This is the masculine gender.

Etaṃ, etāni. Etaṃ, etāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ, idaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

Etaṃ (this), etāni (these). Etaṃ (this), etāni (these). The rest is similar to the masculine gender. This is the neuter gender.

Esā[M 0.0367], etā, etāyo. Etaṃ, etā, etāyo. Etāya, etāhi, etābhi. Etāya, etissā, etissāya, etāsaṃ. Etāya, etāhi, etābhi. Etāya, etissā, etissāya, etāsaṃ. Etāya, etissaṃ, etāsu. Idaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ. Evaṃ etasaddassa nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

Esā (this), etā (these), etāyo (these). Etaṃ (this), etā (these), etāyo (these). Etāya (by this), etāhi (by these), etābhi (by these). Etāya (to/for this, of this), etissā (to/for this, of this), etissāya (to/for this, of this), etāsaṃ (to/for these, of these). Etāya (from this), etāhi (from these), etābhi (from these). Etāya (to/for this, of this), etissā (to/for this, of this), etissāya (to/for this, of this), etāsaṃ (to/for these, of these). Etāya (in/on this), etissaṃ (in/on this), etāsu (in/on these). This is the feminine gender. Thus the nominal paradigm of the word 'eta' is formed.

Parapadenettha saddhiṃ samāsopissa veditabbo “etadatthāya lokasmiṃ, nidhi nāma nidhiyyati. Etapparamāyeva devatā sannipatitā ahesu”ntiādīsu.

Here, its compound with other words should also be understood, as in 'etadatthāya lokasmiṃ, nidhi nāma nidhiyyati' (for this purpose in the world, a treasure is called a treasure, that is stored) and 'etapparamāyeva devatā sannipatitā ahesuṃ' (only this many deities had assembled).

Samāse etasaddassa, saddhiṃ parapadehi ve;

Niggahītāgamo pubba-pade hoti na hoti ca.

In compounds of the word 'eta' together with other words, the niggahīta augment may or may not appear in the first word.

Idāni idaṃsaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal paradigm of the word 'idaṃ' is stated.

Ayaṃ, ime. Imaṃ, ime. Anena, iminā, ehi, ebhi, imehi, imebhi. Assa, imassa, esaṃ, esānaṃ, imesaṃ, imesānaṃ. Asmā, imasmā, imamhā, ehi, ebhi, imehi, imebhi. Assa, imassa, esaṃ, esānaṃ, imesaṃ, imesānaṃ. Asmiṃ, imasmiṃ, amhi, imamhi, esu, imesu. Idaṃ pulliṅgaṃ.

Ayaṃ (this), ime (these). Imaṃ (this), ime (these). Anena (by this), iminā (by this), ehi (by these), ebhi (by these), imehi (by these), imebhi (by these). Assa (to/for this, of this), imassa (to/for this, of this), esaṃ (to/for these, of these), esānaṃ (to/for these, of these), imesaṃ (to/for these, of these), imesānaṃ (to/for these, of these). Asmā (from this), imasmā (from this), imamhā (from this), ehi (from these), ebhi (from these), imehi (from these), imebhi (from these). Assa (to/for this, of this), imassa (to/for this, of this), esaṃ (to/for these, of these), esānaṃ (to/for these, of these), imesaṃ (to/for these, of these), imesānaṃ (to/for these, of these). Asmiṃ (in/on this), imasmiṃ (in/on this), amhi (in/on this), imamhi (in/on this), esu (in/on these), imesu (in/on these). This is the masculine gender.

Idaṃ, imāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Idaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

Idaṃ (this), imāni (these). The rest is similar to the masculine gender. This is the neuter gender.

Ayaṃ, imā, imāyo. Imaṃ, imā, imāyo. Imāya, imāhi, imābhi. Assā, assāya, imissā, imissāya, imāya, imāsaṃ. Assā, imissā, imāya, imāhi, imābhi. Assā, assāya, imissā, imissāya, imāya, imāsaṃ. Assaṃ, imissaṃ, imāya, imāyaṃ, imāsu. Idaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ. Evaṃ idaṃsaddassa nāmikapadamālā bhavati.

Ayaṃ (this), imā (these), imāyo (these). Imaṃ (this), imā (these), imāyo (these). Imāya (by this), imāhi (by these), imābhi (by these). Assā (to/for this, of this), assāya (to/for this, of this), imissā (to/for this, of this), imissāya (to/for this, of this), imāya (to/for this, of this), imāsaṃ (to/for these, of these). Assā (from this), imissā (from this), imāya (from this), imāhi (from these), imābhi (from these). Assā (to/for this, of this), assāya (to/for this, of this), imissā (to/for this, of this), imissāya (to/for this, of this), imāya (to/for this, of this), imāsaṃ (to/for these, of these). Assaṃ (in/on this), imissaṃ (in/on this), imāya (in/on this), imāyaṃ (in/on this), imāsu (in/on these). This is the feminine gender. Thus the nominal paradigm of the word 'idaṃ' is formed.

Kaccāyane tu “imassidamaṃsisu napuṃsake”ti imasaddoyeva pakatibhāvena vutto, idha pana idaṃsaddoyeva “idappaccayatā”ti ettha “ida”nti pakatiyā dassanato. Tathā [M 0.0368] hi “imesaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā, idappaccayānaṃ vā samūho idappaccayatā”ti vuttaṃ. Ettha ca idappaccayā eva idappaccayatāti tāsaddena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ na kiñci atthantaraṃ yathā devo eva devatāti. Idappaccayānaṃ samūho idappaccayatāti samūhatthaṃ tāsaddamāha yathā janānaṃ samūho janatāti. Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ niruttipiṭake ca idaṃsaddoyeva pakatibhāvena vutto.

But in Kaccāyana, in the rule 'imassidamaṃsisu napuṃsake,' the word 'ima' itself is stated in its natural form; here, however, the word 'idaṃ' itself is shown as the base in 'idappaccayatā,' in that 'ida' is displayed as the base. For it is said: 'imesaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā, idappaccayānaṃ vā samūho idappaccayatā.' And here, 'idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā' means the word is extended by the suffix '-tā,' with no other difference in meaning, just as 'devo eva devatā.' 'Idappaccayānaṃ samūho idappaccayatā' states the suffix '-tā' in the sense of a collection, just as 'janānaṃ samūho janatā.' In the Cūḷanirutti and the Nirutti Piṭaka, the word 'idaṃ' itself is stated in its natural form.

Samāse idaṃsaddassa, saddhiṃ parapadena ve;

Idappaccayatātveva, rūpaṃ dvittaṃ siyuttare.

In compounds of the word 'idaṃ' together with another word, when it is in the state of 'idappaccayatā,' a doubled form may occur in the latter part.

Idāni amusaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal paradigm of the word 'amu' is stated.

Asu, amu, amū. Amuṃ, amū. Amunā, amūhi, amūbhi. Amussa, dussa, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ. Amusmā, amumhā, amūhi, amūbhi. Amussa, dussa, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ. Amusmiṃ, amumhi, amūsu. Idaṃ pulliṅgaṃ.

Asu (that), amu (that), amū (those). Amuṃ (that), amū (those). Amunā (by that), amūhi (by those), amūbhi (by those). Amussa (to/for that, of that), dussa (to/for that, of that), amūsaṃ (to/for those, of those), amūsānaṃ (to/for those, of those). Amusmā (from that), amumhā (from that), amūhi (from those), amūbhi (from those). Amussa (to/for that, of that), dussa (to/for that, of that), amūsaṃ (to/for those, of those), amūsānaṃ (to/for those, of those). Amusmiṃ (in/on that), amumhi (in/on that), amūsu (in/on those). This is the masculine gender.

Aduṃ, amūni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Idaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

Aduṃ (that), amūni (those). The rest is similar to the masculine gender. This is the neuter gender.

Asu, amu, amū, amuyo. Amūṃ, amū, amuyo. Amuyā, amūhi, amūbhi. Amussā, amuyā, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ. Amuyā, amūhi, amūbhi. Amussā, amuyā, amūsaṃ, amūsānaṃ. Amuyā, amuyaṃ, amussaṃ, amūsu. Idaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ. Evaṃ amusaddassa nāmikapadamālā bhavati, samāso pana appasiddho.

Asu (that), amu (that), amū (those), amuyo (those). Amūṃ (that), amū (those), amuyo (those). Amuyā (by that), amūhi (by those), amūbhi (by those). Amussā (to/for that, of that), amuyā (to/for that, of that), amūsaṃ (to/for those, of those), amūsānaṃ (to/for those, of those). Amuyā (from that), amūhi (from those), amūbhi (from those). Amussā (to/for that, of that), amuyā (to/for that, of that), amūsaṃ (to/for those, of those), amūsānaṃ (to/for those, of those). Amuyā (in/on that), amuyaṃ (in/on that), amussaṃ (in/on that), amūsu (in/on those). This is the feminine gender. Thus the nominal paradigm of the word 'amu' is formed. However, its compounds are not well-established.

Tatra “dussa me khettapālassa, rattibhattaṃ apābhata”nti payogadassanato “dussā”ti padamamhehi ṭhapitaṃ. Kakārāgamavasena aññānipi asabbanāmikarūpāni bhavanti. Tesaṃ [M 0.0369] vasena ayaṃ liṅgattayassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Here, from the usage 'dussa me khettapālassa, rattibhattaṃ apābhata' (for that field-guard of mine, the night-meal was brought), the word 'dussā' is established by us. Due to the addition of the augment 'ka,' other non-pronominal forms also arise. Based on these, this nominal paradigm for the three genders is stated.

“Asuko, asukā. Asukaṃ, asuke”tiādinā, “amuko, amukā. Amukaṃ, amuke”tiādinā ca purisanayopi labbhati. “Asukā, asukāyo”tiādinā, “amukā, amukāyo”tiādinā ca kaññānayopi labbhati. “Asukaṃ, asukānī”tiādinā, “amukaṃ, amukānī”tiādinā ca cittanayopi labbhati. Imānettha padāni asabbanāmikānipi kakārāgamavasena nānattadassanatthaṃ vuttāni.

The masculine paradigm is also obtained, as in 'asuko, asukā. Asukaṃ, asuke' and so on, and 'amuko, amukā. Amukaṃ, amuke' and so on. The feminine paradigm is also obtained, as in 'asukā, asukāyo' and so on, and 'amukā, amukāyo' and so on. The neuter paradigm is also obtained, as in 'asukaṃ, asukānī' and so on, and 'amukaṃ, amukānī' and so on. Here, these words, although not pronominal, are stated to show various forms due to the addition of the 'ka' augment.

Idāni kiṃsaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal paradigm of the word 'kiṃ' is stated.

Ko, ke. Kaṃ, ke. Kena, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kissa, kesaṃ. Kasmā, kamhā, kehi, kebhi. Kassa, kissa, kesaṃ. Kasmiṃ, kismiṃ, kamhi, kimhi, kesu. Idaṃ pulliṅgaṃ.

Ko (who), ke (who). Kaṃ (whom), ke (whom). Kena (by whom), kehi (by whom), kebhi (by whom). Kassa (to/for whom, of whom), kissa (to/for whom, of whom), kesaṃ (to/for whom, of whom). Kasmā (from whom, why), kamhā (from whom, why), kehi (from whom), kebhi (from whom). Kassa (to/for whom, of whom), kissa (to/for whom, of whom), kesaṃ (to/for whom, of whom). Kasmiṃ (in/on whom, where), kismiṃ (in/on whom, where), kamhi (in/on whom, where), kimhi (in/on whom, where), kesu (in/on whom). This is the masculine gender.

Rūpavisesopettha veditabbo “ke gandhabbe ca rakkhase nāge, ke kimpurise ca mānuse, ke paṇḍite sabbakāmadade, dīghaṃ rattaṃ bhattā me bhavissati, ke ca chave pāthikaputte, kā ca tathāgatānaṃ arahantānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ āsādanā”ti pāḷidassanato. Yasmā pana ke gandhabbe ca rakkhase nāge itiādīsu pāḷīsu “ke”ti paccattavacanaṃ ekārantampi dissati, tasmā “ke”ti rūpabhedo cettha ñeyyo. Tathā “kissassa ekadhammassa, vadhaṃ rocesi gotama. Kismiṃ me sivayo kuddhā. Kamhi kāle tayā vīra, patthitā bodhimuttamā”tiādīni ca nidassanapadāni ñeyyāni. Apica –

Here, a distinction of form should be understood from Pāli passages such as: 'ke gandhabbe ca rakkhase nāge' (In which gandhabba, rakkhasa, and nāga?), 'ke kimpurise ca mānuse' (In which kimpurisa and human?), 'ke paṇḍite sabbakāmadade' (In which wise one, giver of all desires?), 'dīghaṃ rattaṃ bhattā me bhavissati' (Who will be my husband for a long time?), 'ke ca chave pāthikaputte' (And who are the contemptible Pāthikaputtas?), and 'kā ca tathāgatānaṃ arahantānaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ āsādanā' (And what is the offense against the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones?). Since in Pāli passages like 'ke gandhabbe ca rakkhase nāge' and so on, the word 'ke' is also seen as a nominative singular form ending in 'e', therefore the variant form 'ke' should be understood here. Similarly, example passages like 'kissassa ekadhammassa, vadhaṃ rocesi gotama' (Of what single thing, Gotama, do you approve the destruction?), 'kismiṃ me sivayo kuddhā' (At what are my relatives angry?), 'kamhi kāle tayā vīra, patthitā bodhimuttamā' (At what time, O hero, was supreme enlightenment aspired to by you?) should be understood. Furthermore—

“Ko te balaṃ mahārāja”, itiādīsu pāḷisu;

Kvasaddatthe vattatīti, ñeyyā ko iccayaṃ suti.

In Pāli passages like 'Ko te balaṃ mahārāja' (What is your strength, O great king?), and so on, it should be known that this word 'ko' functions in the sense of the word 'kva' (where).

Petaṃ [M 0.0370] taṃ sāmamaddakkhiṃ, ko nu tvaṃ sāma jīvasi;

Iti pāṭhe kathaṃsaddā-bhidheyye vattatīti ca.

And in the reading 'Petaṃ taṃ sāmamaddakkhiṃ, ko nu tvaṃ sāma jīvasi' (I myself saw that Sāma as dead; how indeed, Sāma, are you alive?), it functions in the sense of the word 'kathaṃ' (how).

Etesu dvīsu atthesu, diṭṭho ko iccayaṃ ravo;

Nipātoti gahetabbo, sutisāmaññato ruto.

In these two meanings, this sound 'ko' is seen; it should be taken as a particle, spoken from common usage.

Napuṃsakaliṅge kaṃ, kāni. Kaṃ, kāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Atha vā “kiṃ cittaṃ. Kiṃ rūpaṃ. Kiṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ. Kiṃ icchasī”tiādipayogadassanato pana “kiṃ, kāni. Kiṃ, kānī”ti vatvā sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ yojetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo yuttataro, idaṃ napuṃsakaliṅgaṃ.

In the neuter gender: Kaṃ (what), kāni (what). Kaṃ (what), kāni (what). The rest should be formed like the masculine. Alternatively, from seeing usages such as: 'kiṃ cittaṃ' (what is mind?), 'kiṃ rūpaṃ' (what is form?), 'kiṃ parābhavato mukhaṃ' (what is the cause of ruin?), 'kiṃ icchasi' (what do you desire?), one may say 'kiṃ, kāni. Kiṃ, kāni' and the rest should be formed like the masculine. This method is more appropriate. This is the neuter gender.

Kā, kā, kāyo. Kaṃ, kā, kāyo. Kāya, kāhi, kābhi. Kāya, kassā, kāsaṃ, kāsānaṃ. Kāya, kassā, kāhi, kābhi. Kāya, kassā, kāsaṃ kāsānaṃ. Kāya, kassā, kāyaṃ, kassaṃ, kāsu.

Kā (who), kā (who), kāyo (who). Kaṃ (whom), kā (whom), kāyo (whom). Kāya (by whom), kāhi (by whom), kābhi (by whom). Kāya (to/for whom, of whom), kassā (to/for whom, of whom), kāsaṃ (to/for whom, of whom), kāsānaṃ (to/for whom, of whom). Kāya (from whom), kassā (from whom), kāhi (from whom), kābhi (from whom). Kāya (to/for whom, of whom), kassā (to/for whom, of whom), kāsaṃ (to/for whom, of whom), kāsānaṃ (to/for whom, of whom). Kāya (in/on whom), kassā (in/on whom), kāyaṃ (in/on whom), kassaṃ (in/on whom), kāsu (in/on whom).

Ettha pana kāyoti padassa atthibhāve “kāyo amoghā gacchantī”ti nidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Idaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ. Evaṃ kiṃsaddassa nāmikapadamālā bhavati. Etthetassa atthuddhāro vuccate – kiṃ saddo “kiṃ rājā yo lokaṃ na rakkhati. Kiṃ nu kho nāma tumhe maṃ vattabbaṃ maññathā”tiādīsu garahane āgato. “Yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppanna”ntiādīsu aniyame. “Kinte vakkali iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena, yo kho vakkali dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”tiādīsu nippayojanatāyaṃ. “Kiṃ na kāhāmi te vaco”tiādīsu sampaṭicchane. “Kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha”ntiādīsu pucchāyaṃ, pucchā ca nāma kāraṇapucchādivasena [M 0.0371] anekavidhā, ato kāraṇapucchādivasenapi kiṃsaddassa pavatti vitthārato ñeyyā. Tathā hi ayaṃ “kiṃ nu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khaṇasi sārathi. Kiṃ nu jātiṃ na rocesi. Kena tetādiso vaṇṇo”tiādīsu kāraṇapucchāyaṃ vattati. “Kiṃ kāsuyā karissatī”tiādīsu kiccapucchāyaṃ. “Kiṃ sīlaṃ. Ko samādhī”tiādīsu sarūpapucchāyaṃ. “Kiṃ khādasi. Kiṃ pivasī”tiādīsu vatthupucchāyaṃ. “Khādasi kiṃ pivasi ki”ntiādīsu kriyāpucchāyaṃ vattati. Adiṭṭhajotanāpucchāti evamādikā pana pañcavidhā pucchā kiṃsaddassa atthuddhāre anāharitabbattā anāgatāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Here, for the word 'kāyo' in the sense of existence, the example 'kāyo amoghā gacchantī' (the body moves unfailingly) should be seen. This is feminine. Thus is the nominal declension of the word 'kiṃ'. Here, the extraction of its meaning is stated: The word 'kiṃ' is used in contexts of censure, as in 'kiṃ rājā yo lokaṃ na rakkhati' (What kind of king is he who does not protect the world?) or 'kiṃ nu kho nāma tumhe maṃ vattabbaṃ maññathā' (What indeed do you think you should say to me?). It is used in indefinite contexts, as in 'yaṃ kiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppanna' (whatever form, past, future, or present). It denotes uselessness, as in 'kinte vakkali iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena, yo kho vakkali dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passati' (What use, Vakkali, is seeing this foul body? He who sees the Dhamma sees me). It expresses acceptance, as in 'kiṃ na kāhāmi te vaco' (Why should I not do as you say?). It is used in questions, as in 'kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha' (What, here, is the best wealth for a man?). Questions, indeed, are of many kinds—such as questions about the cause, etc. Therefore, the application of 'kiṃ' should be understood extensively through questions about the cause and other types. For example, it functions in questions about the cause like: 'kiṃ nu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khaṇasi sārathi' (Why, charioteer, do you dig a pit while hastening?), 'kiṃ nu jātiṃ na rocesi' (Why do you not approve of birth?), 'kena tetādiso vaṇṇo' (Why is your complexion like that?). It is used in questions about purpose, as in 'kiṃ kāsuyā karissati' (What will he do with the pit?). It is used in questions about nature, as in 'kiṃ sīlaṃ, ko samādhī' (What is virtue? What is concentration?). It is used in questions about the substance, as in 'kiṃ khādasi, kiṃ pivasī' (What do you eat? What do you drink?). It functions in questions about the action, as in 'khādasi kiṃ pivasi ki' (Do you eat? Do you drink?). Questions about making known the unseen, and so on, are fivefold, but since they are not to be brought in for the extraction of the meaning of 'kiṃ,' they should be understood as not included here. Thus, this is said—

Garahāyaṃ aniyame, nippayojanatāya ca;

Sampaṭicchanapucchāsu, kiṃsaddo sampavattati.

In censure, in indefiniteness, and in uselessness; in acceptance and questions, the word 'kiṃ' occurs.

Parapadena saddhiṃ samāsopissa veditabbo “kiṃsamudayo, kiṃvedano, kiṃsaññojano”ti. Ettha “ko, ke. Kā, kā, kāyo. Kiṃ, kānī”ti evaṃ liṅgattayavasena vibhattāni kiṃsaddamayāni padāni samāsapadatte puna kimiti pakatibhāveneva tiṭṭhanti. Nāmasaddena pana samāse tesaṃ dvidhā gati dissati “kinnāmo, konāmo”ti. Sabbāni panetāni itthinapuṃsakaliṅgavasena bahuvacanavasena ca yojetabbāni.

Its compound with other words should be understood, as in 'kiṃsamudayo' (what-origin), 'kiṃvedano' (what-feeling), 'kiṃsaññojano' (what-fetter). Here, the words derived from 'kiṃ', which are declined according to the three genders as 'ko, ke'; 'kā, kā, kāyo'; 'kiṃ, kānī', remain in their natural form as 'kim' when part of a compound word. However, in a compound with the word 'nāma' (name), their form is seen in two ways: 'kinnāmo' and 'konāmo'. And all of these should be construed according to the feminine and neuter genders, and in the plural.

Kiṃsaddassa samāsamhi, saddhiṃ nāmaravena ve;

“Kinnāmo” iti “konāmo”, iti cevaṃ gati dvidhā.

In the compounding of the word 'kiṃ' together with the word 'nāma', the form is twofold: 'kinnāmo' and 'konāmo'.

“Konāmo [M 0.0372] te upajjhāyo”, iccādettha nidassanaṃ;

Sahaññena samāsamhi, “kiṃ kiṃ”icceva suyyate.

'What is the name of your preceptor?' This is an example here. In a compound with another word, only 'kiṃ' is heard.

Tathā hi “kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhu. Kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī”tiādīsu kiṃsaddo sarūpamavijahanto tiṭṭhati. Tattha hi kiṃcittaṃ yassa so kiṃcitto. “Kiṃ karomi sāmī”ti evaṃ kinti kāro karaṇaṃ saddanicchāraṇaṃ kiṃkāro, taṃ paṭissāvetīti kiṃkārapaṭissāvinītiādi nibbacanamicchitabbaṃ. “Kinnaro. Kiṃpakkamiva bhakkhita”ntiādīsu pana nibbacanamappasiddhaṃ, kiṃsaddoyeva padāvayavabhāvena suto. Tathā hi so katthaci padāvayavabhāvena katthaci nu su nukho kāraṇādisaddehi sahacāribhāvena ca suyyati. Atrime payogā – esā te itthī kiṃ hoti. Ete manussā tumhākaṃ kiṃ honti. Kimpurisānuciṇṇo. Kiṃ nu bhītova tiṭṭhasi. Kiṃsuchetvā sukhaṃ seti. Kiṃ nukho kāraṇaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā amma tuvaṃ pamajjasi, kiñhi nāma cajantassa, vācāya adadamappakanti evamādayo. Atridaṃ vuccati –

For in such cases as 'kiṃcitto tvaṃ bhikkhu' (Of what mind are you, monk?) and 'kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī' (she who responds to 'what'), the word 'kiṃ' remains without abandoning its own form. Here, 'he whose mind is what' is 'kiṃcitto'. The utterance of the sound 'kiṃ', as in 'kiṃ karomi sāmī' (What shall I do, master?), is 'kiṃkāro'; she who responds to that is 'kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī'—the word-analysis should be understood in this way. But in cases like 'kinnaro' (what-man) or 'kiṃpakkamiva bhakkhita' (as if eaten by a kiṃpakka fruit), the word-analysis is not established; the word 'kiṃ' is simply heard as a part of the word. Indeed, in some places it is heard as a part of a word, and in others, in conjunction with particles like 'nu', 'su', 'nukho', or words indicating cause. Here are some examples: 'esā te itthī kiṃ hoti' (What is this woman to you?). 'Ete manussā tumhākaṃ kiṃ honti' (What are these people to you?). 'Kimpurisānuciṇṇo' (Frequented by Kimpurisas). 'Kiṃ nu bhītova tiṭṭhasi' (Why do you stand as if afraid?). 'Kiṃsuchetvā sukhaṃ seti' (Having cut off what does one sleep happily?). 'Kiṃ nukho kāraṇaṃ' (What, then, is the reason?). 'Kiṃ kāraṇā amma tuvaṃ pamajjasi' (For what reason, mother, are you negligent?), 'kiñhi nāma cajantassa, vācāya adadamappakanti' (For what indeed, for one abandoning, not giving even a little by speech)—and so on. Herein it is said:

“Visuṃ padāvayavo vā, hutvā nvādīhi vā pana;

Yutto saddehi kiṃsaddo, diṭṭho sugatasāsane.

The word 'kiṃ' is seen in the Sugata's Teaching, either as a separate part of a word, or connected with particles like 'nu' and so on.

Pāḷinayānusārena, sesānaṃ sambhavopi ca;

Ñeyyo viññūhi saddhamma-nayaññūhi pabhedato”ti.

According to the method of the Pāli texts, the occurrence of the rest should also be known in detail by the wise who understand the method of the true Dhamma.

Idāni [M 0.0373] sabbanāmikabhāve ṭhitehi ko kaṃsaddehi samānasutikānaṃ aññesaṃ ko kaṃsaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālāviseso vattabbo siyā, so heṭṭhā liṅgattayamissakaparicchede vutto. Asabbanāmikattā pana purisa cittanayeneva vibhatto. Tathā hi yadā kosaddo brahmavātakāyatthavācako, kaṃsaddo pana sirojalasukhatthavācako, tadā tāni padāni asabbanāmikāni, kasmā? Akiṃsaddamayattā sabbanāmikarūpasaṅkhātehi asādhāraṇarūpehi virahitattā pucchatthato atthantaravācakattā ca. Ettha pana samānasutivasena atthantaraviññāpanatthaṃ kosaddo kaṃsaddoti ca vuttaṃ, ekantato pana sabbanāmikatte kiṃsaddoyeva, suddhanāmatte kasaddoyevāti gahetabbaṃ. Iccevaṃ –

Now, for the words 'ko' and 'kaṃ' that are established as pronouns, what special nominal declension should be stated for other 'ko' and 'kaṃ' words that have similar sounds? That has been stated below in the chapter on the combination of the three genders. But because of their non-pronominal nature, they are declined according to the paradigm of 'purisa' and 'citta'. Thus, when the word 'ko' signifies Brahma, wind, or body, and the word 'kaṃ' signifies head, water, or happiness, then those words are not pronouns. Why? Because they are not derived from the word 'kiṃ', because they lack the special forms reckoned as pronominal forms, and because they express a meaning different from the interrogative. Here, however, 'ko' and 'kaṃ' are mentioned to indicate a different meaning due to the similarity of sounds. But it should be understood that when strictly pronominal, it is only the word 'kiṃ', and when merely a noun, it is only the word 'ka'. Thus:

Kāye brahmani vāte ca, sīse jalasukhesu ca;

Kasaddo vattatī tīsu, pumā tīsu napuṃsako.

The word 'ka' applies to body, Brahma, and wind, where it is masculine; and to head, water, and happiness, where it is neuter.

Evaṃ sabbanāmabhūtānaṃ kiṃkasaddānaṃ pavatti veditabbā.

Thus, the application of the words 'kiṃ' and 'ka', which are pronouns, should be understood.

Idha vuttappakārānaṃ, atthānaṃ dāni saṅgaho;

Paññāvepullakaraṇo, ekadesena vuccate.

Here, a summary of the meanings explained is now presented in part, which serves to expand wisdom.

Kiṃ kiṃpakkena sadisaṃ, kāyo kiṃpabhavo vada;

Kiṃpakkasadiso kāmo, kāyo taṇhādisambhavo.

What is like the kiṃpakka fruit? Tell me, from what is the body born? Sense-desire is like the kiṃpakka fruit, and the body is born from craving and so on.

Uṇhakāle ka’micchanti, ka’micchanti pipāsitā;

Paccāmittā ka’micchanti, ka’micchanti dukhaṭṭitā.

In the hot season, they desire water (kaṃ); the thirsty desire water (kaṃ); enemies desire the head (kaṃ); those afflicted by suffering desire happiness (kaṃ).

Kāyassa kassa ko āyo,

Ko nātho kassa bhūtale;

Kassa kaṃ jhānajaṃ sātaṃ,

Kassaṅgesu ca kaṃ paranti.

Of whose body is what the source? Who is the protector of whom on earth? For whom is what pleasure born of meditation? And in whose limbs do they enjoy what?

Yā [M 0.0374] pana tā heṭṭhā amhehi liṅgattayavasena kiṃsaddassa sabbanāmikasaññitassa nāmikapadamālā vibhattā, etāsu pulliṅganapuṃsakaliṅgaṭṭhāne “kebhi, kissa, kasmā, kamhā, kamhī”ti imāni padāni pahāya itthiliṅgaṭṭhāne “kāyo, kābhi, kāsānaṃ, kāyaṃ, kassa”nti imāni ca padāni pahāya tato tato sesapadato yathāsambhavaṃ cisaddaṃ canasaddaṃ canaṃsaddañca nipātetvā evarūpāni rūpāni gahetabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ?

Now, regarding those nominal declensions of the word 'kiṃ', designated as a pronoun, which were analyzed by us below: from these, abandoning in the masculine and neuter genders the forms 'kebhi, kissa, kasmā, kamhā, kamhī', and abandoning in the feminine gender the forms 'kāyo, kābhi, kāsānaṃ, kāyaṃ, kassa', then from the remaining forms, by adding the particles 'ci', 'cana', and 'canaṃ' as appropriate, such forms should be taken. For example:

Koci, keci, kecana. Kiñci, kiñcanaṃ, keci, kecana. Kenaci, kehici. Kassaci, kesañci. Pañcamiyā ekavacanaṃ ūnaṃ pāḷiyaṃ anāgatattā. Kehici. Kassaci, kesañci. Kasmiñci, kismici, kesuci. Pulliṅganapuṃsakaliṅgavasena daṭṭhabbāni. Atra kismicīti anusāralopavasena vuttaṃ.

Koci, keci, kecana (someone, some, certain ones). Kiñci, kiñcanaṃ, keci, kecana (something, a little, some, certain ones). Kenaci, kehici (by someone, by some). Kassaci, kesañci (to/of someone, to/of some). The ablative singular is missing, as it is not found in the Pāli canon. Kehici (by/from some). Kassaci, kesañci (to/of someone, to/of some). Kasmiñci, kismici, kesuci (in someone, in something, in some). These should be understood according to the masculine and neuter genders. Here, 'kismici' is stated with the elision of the anusāra.

Itthiliṅgavasena pana kāci itthī, kāci itthiyo. Kāci, kāci. Kiñci, kāci. Kāyaci, kāhici. Kāyaci, kassāci, kāsañci. Kāyaci, kāhici. Kāyaci, kassāci, kāsañci. Kāyaci, kāsucīti rūpāni.

In the feminine gender, the forms are: kāci itthī, kāci itthiyo (some woman, some women). Kāci, kāci. Kiñci, kāci. Kāyaci, kāhici. Kāyaci, kassāci, kāsañci. Kāyaci, kāhici. Kāyaci, kassāci, kāsañci. Kāyaci, kāsucīti.

Ettha “iti bhāsanti kecana, na naṃ hiṃsāmi kiñcana”ntiādayo payogā veditabbā. Iti liṅgattayavasena vuttāni koci kāci kiñcītiādīni appamattakānaṃ saṅgāhakavacanānīti veditabbāni.

Here, usages such as 'iti bhāsanti kecana' (thus some speak) and 'na naṃ hiṃsāmi kiñcana' (I do not harm him at all) are to be understood. Thus, words such as 'koci', 'kāci', 'kiñci', etc., spoken in terms of the three genders, are to be understood as words denoting a small quantity.

Punetāniyeva yathārahaṃ yaṃsaddena yojetvā dassessāmi –

Again, I will show these same words appropriately connected with the word 'yaṃ' as follows:

Yo koci, ye keci. Yaṃ kiñci, ye keci. Yena kenaci, yehi kehici. Yassa kassaci, yesaṃ kesañci. Yasmā kasmāci, yehi kehici. Yassa kassaci, yesaṃ kesañci. Yasmiṃ kasmiñci, yesu kesuci.

Whoever, whoever (pl.). Whomever, whomever (pl.). By whomever, by whomever (pl.). To/of whomever, to/of whomever (pl.). From whomever, from whomever (pl.). Of whomever, of whomever (pl.). In whomever, in whomever (pl.).

Ettha [M 0.0375] “yo koci maṃ aṭṭhi katvā suṇeyya. Ye kecime atthi rasā pathabyā, saccaṃ tesaṃ sādhutaraṃ rasāna”ntiādayo payogā veditabbā. Pulliṅgarūpāni.

Here, usages such as “yo koci maṃ aṭṭhi katvā suṇeyya. Ye kecime atthi rasā pathabyā, saccaṃ tesaṃ sādhutaraṃ rasāna” are to be understood. These are masculine forms.

Yaṃ kiñci, yāni kānici. Yaṃ kiñci, yāni kānici. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Ettha “yaṃ kiñci ratanaṃ atthi, dhataraṭṭhanivesane. Yaṃ kiñci vittaṃ idha vā huraṃ vā. Yāni kānici rūpānī”tiādayo payogā veditabbā. Napuṃsakaliṅgarūpāni.

Whatever, whatever (pl.). Whatever, whatever (pl.). The rest is similar to the masculine. Here, usages such as “yaṃ kiñci ratanaṃ atthi, dhataraṭṭhanivesane. Yaṃ kiñci vittaṃ idha vā huraṃ vā. Yāni kānici rūpāni” should be understood. These are neuter forms.

Yā kāci itthī, yā kāci itthiyo. Yaṃ kiñci, yā kāci. Yāya kāyaci, yāhi kāhici. Yāya kāyaci, yāsaṃ kāsañci. Yāya kāyaci, yāhi kāhici. Yāya kāyaci, yāsaṃ kāsañci. Yāya kāyaci, yāsu kāsuci.

Whichever woman, whichever women. Whichever (woman), whichever (women). By whichever (woman), by whichever (women). To/of whichever (woman), to/of whichever (women). From whichever (woman), from whichever (women). Of whichever (woman), of whichever (women). In whichever (woman), in whichever (women).

Ettha “yā kāci vedanā atītānāgatapaccuppannā”tiādayo payogā veditabbā. Itthiliṅgarūpāni. Iti liṅgattayavasena vuttāni yo koci, yā kāci, yaṃ kiñcītiādīni anavasesapariyādānavacanānīti veditabbāni. Sabbāni cetāni na nipātapadāni, nipātapatirūpakā saddagatiyoti veditabbāni. Yadi nipātapadāni siyuṃ, tīsu liṅgesu sattasu vibhattīsu ekākārena tiṭṭheyyuṃ, na ca tiṭṭhanti, tasmā na nipātapadāni, nipātapatirūpakā saddagatiyoyeva.

Here, usages such as “whatever feeling, past, future, or present” should be understood. These are feminine forms. Thus, words like “yo koci” (whoever), “yā kāci” (whichever, fem.), and “yaṃ kiñci” (whatever, neut.) are to be understood as expressions of complete inclusion. All these are not indeclinable particles, but should be understood as word-forms resembling indeclinables. If they were indeclinable particles, they would remain in one form in all three genders and seven cases, but they do not. Therefore, they are not indeclinable particles, but merely word-forms resembling indeclinables.

Apica ya ta kiṃ etaiccetehi sabbanāmehi liṅgānurūpato ttakattikapaccaye katvā vatticchāyaṃ yāni padāni sijjhanti, tāni paricchedavacanāni asabbanāmikāniyeva bhavanti. Tesaṃ nāmikapadamālā purisa citta kaññānayena yojetabbā. Taṃ yathā?

Furthermore, from these pronouns—ya, ta, kiṃ, and eta—when the suffixes -ttaka and -ttika are added according to gender to express a certain meaning, the resulting words are delimiting but are indeed not pronouns. Their nominal declension should be constructed according to the model of purisa, citta, and kaññā. As for instance:

Yattako [M 0.0376] jano, yattakaṃ cittaṃ, yattikā itthī. Tattako, tattakaṃ, tattikā. Kittako, kittakaṃ, kittikā. Ettako, ettakaṃ, ettikāti. Imāni padāni asabbanāmikānipi paccayavasena sambhūtatthantaresu viññūnaṃ kosallatthaṃ vuttāni.

“Yattako jano” (however many people), “yattakaṃ cittaṃ” (however much mind), “yattikā itthī” (however many women). “Tattako,” “tattakaṃ,” “tattikā” (so many, so much, so many). “Kittako,” “kittakaṃ,” “kittikā” (how many, how much, how many?). “Ettako,” “ettakaṃ,” “ettikā” (this many, this much, this many). These words, though not pronouns, are stated for the skill of the wise regarding the different meanings that arise due to the suffixes.

Idāni saṅkhādivacanassa ekasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal declension for the word “eka,” which expresses number and other meanings, is stated:

Ekasaddo hi saṅkhāvacano ca hoti asadisavacano ca asahāyavacano ca ekaccavacano ca missībhūtavacano ca. Yadā saṅkhā’sadisā’sahāyavacano, tadā ekavacanako bhavati.

The word “eka” can function as a numeral, as expressing uniqueness, as expressing being without a companion, as expressing a certain one, and as expressing being mixed. When it functions as a numeral, as expressing uniqueness, or as expressing being without a companion, then it is in the singular number.

Eko, ekaṃ, ekena, ekassa, ekasmā, ekamhā, ekassa, ekasmiṃ, ekamhīti. Evaṃ saṅkhādivacano ekasaddo ekavacanako. Tathā hi “eko dve tayo”ti saṅkhāvisaye ekasaddo ekavacanakova. “Ekomhi sammāsambuddho. Eko rāja nipajjāmī”ti asadisāsahāyakathanepi ekavacanakova. Ayaṃ ekavacanikā sabbanāmikapadamālā.

Eko, ekaṃ, ekena, ekassa, ekasmā, ekamhā, ekassa, ekasmiṃ, ekamhī. Thus, the word “eka,” expressing number and other meanings, is singular. For example, in the context of counting—“eko, dve, tayo” (one, two, three)—the word “eka” is only singular. Similarly, in statements like “Ekomhi sammāsambuddho” (I am the one Perfectly Enlightened One), or “Eko rāja nipajjāmi” (I alone, a king, lie down), in the sense of uniqueness and being without a companion, it is only singular. This is the singular pronominal declension.

Yadā pana saṅkhatthā ca asahāyā ca bahū vattabbā siyuṃ, tadā ekasaddato kakārāgamaṃ katvā ekakā, ekake, ekakehi, ekakebhi. Purisanaye bahuvacanavasena nāmikapadamālā yojetabbā. Tathā hi saṅkhatthāpi bahū honti. “Cattāro ekakā siyu”nti hi vuttaṃ. Asahāyāpi bahū honti. Tathā hi “ayampi gahapati ekova āgato, ayampi ekova āgato”ti vattabbe “ime gahapatayo ekakā āgatā”ti vattabbatā dissati. Ayaṃ nayo sabbanāmikapakkhaṃ na bhajati asādhāraṇarūpābhāvato, atthantaraviññāpanatthaṃ pana vutto.

However, when many things that are enumerated or solitary are to be spoken of, then by adding the suffix -ka to the word “eka,” the forms are ekakā, ekake, ekakehi, ekakebhi. The nominal declension should be constructed in the plural according to the model of purisa. For instance, enumerated things can also be many. For it is said, “There might be four single ones.” Solitary things can also be many. For example, instead of saying, “This householder also came alone, this one also came alone,” it is seen that it is proper to say, “These householders came singly.” This method does not belong to the pronominal class, due to the absence of special forms, but is stated for the purpose of making known a different meaning.

Yadā [M 0.0377] ekaccavacano, tadā “eke, eke, ekehi, ekebhi ekesaṃ, ekehi, ekebhi, ekesaṃ, ekesū”ti vattabbaṃ. Ayampi bahuvacanikā sabbanāmikapadamālā. Ettha eketi ekacce. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yadā pana missībhūtavacano, tadā “ekā, eke, ekehi, ekebhi, ekāna”nti purisanaye bahuvacanavasena vattabbaṃ. “Pañcālo ca videho ca, ubho ekā bhavantu te”ti pāḷi dissati. Ayaṃ nayo sabbanāmikapakkhaṃ na bhajati asādhāraṇarūpābhāvato, atthantaraviññāpanatthaṃ pana vutto. Tattha ekā bhavantūti ekībhavantu missībhavantu, gaṅgodakena yamunodakaṃ viya aññadatthu saṃsandantu samentūti vacanattho.

When it expresses “a certain one,” then it should be stated as “eke, eke, ekehi, ekebhi, ekesaṃ, ekehi, ekebhi, ekesaṃ, ekesū.” This is also a plural pronominal declension. Here, “eke” means “some” (ekacce). This method applies to the rest as well. But when it expresses “being mixed,” then it should be stated in the plural according to the masculine pattern as “ekā, eke, ekehi, ekebhi, ekāna.” The Pāli passage is seen as “May Pañcāla and Videha, both of them, become one.” This method does not belong to the pronominal class because of the absence of a special form; however, it is stated for the purpose of making known a different meaning. There, “ekā bhavantu” means “let them become unified, let them become mixed, let them flow together and unite, like the water of the Ganges with the water of the Yamunā, let them combine into one thing”—this is the meaning of the statement.

Ācariyā pana evaṃ vibhāgaṃ adassetvā ekasaddassa sabbanāmattameva gahetvā sabbasaddassa viya nāmikapadamālaṃ yojenti. Kathaṃ?

However, some teachers, without showing this distinction, take only the pronominal nature of the word “eka” and apply a nominal declension to it as if it were the word “sabba” (all). How so?

Eko, eke. Ekaṃ, eke. Ekena, ekehi, ekebhi. Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmā, ekamhā, ekehi, ekebhi. Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmiṃ, ekamhi, ekesūti. Ayaṃ sabbanāmikapadamālāti veditabbā.

Eko, eke. Ekaṃ, eke. Ekena, ekehi, ekebhi. Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmā, ekamhā, ekehi, ekebhi. Ekassa, ekesaṃ, ekesānaṃ. Ekasmiṃ, ekamhi, ekesū. This should be known as the pronominal declension.

Keci “ekasaddo saṅkhyātulyāsahāyaññavacano. Yadā saṅkhyāvacano, tadā sabbatthekavacanantova, aññattha bahuvacanantopi, eko ekā ekaṃ iccādi sabbattha sabbasaddasamaṃ. Saṃsāsveva viseso”ti liṅgattaye yojanānayaṃ vadanti. Evaṃ vadantā ca te vibhāgaṃ adassetvā vadanti. Mayaṃ pana sotūnaṃ payogesu kosalluppādanatthaṃ vibhāgaṃ dassetvā vadāma.

Some say: “The word ‘eka’ has the meanings of number, similarity, being without a companion, and otherness. When it has the meaning of number, it is always in the singular, but in other meanings, it can also be in the plural; ‘eko,’ ‘ekā,’ ‘ekaṃ,’ and so on, are in all cases like the word ‘sabba’ (all). The difference is only in the forms with ‘sa’ and ‘sā’.” Thus, they state a method of applying it in all three genders. And those who speak thus, speak without showing the distinction. But we, in order to produce skill in the usages for listeners, speak showing the distinction.

Apicettha [M 0.0378] ayaṃ visesopi sallakkhitabbo “eke ekaṭṭhe same samabhāge’ti pāḷippadese paccattekavacanassa ekasaddassa ekārantaniddesopi dissatī”ti. Pulliṅgarūpāni.

Furthermore, this special point should also be noted: in the Pāli passage “eke ekaṭṭhe same samabhāge” (some in one place, equal, in an equal share), the specification of the word eka, in its distributive sense, as ending in -ā is also seen. These are masculine forms.

Ekaṃ, ekāni. Ekaṃ, ekāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Tattha ekānīti ekaccāni. Esa nayo sesabahuvacanesupi, napuṃsakaliṅgarūpāni.

Ekaṃ, ekāni. Ekaṃ, ekāni. The rest is similar to the masculine. There, “ekāni” means “some” (ekaccāni). This method applies to the remaining plural forms as well. These are neuter forms.

Ekā, ekā, ekāyo. Ekaṃ, ekā, ekāyo. Ekāya, ekāhi, ekābhi. Ekāya, ekissā, ekāsaṃ. Ekāya, ekāhi, ekābhi. Ekāya, ekissā, ekāsaṃ. Ekāya, ekāyaṃ, ekissaṃ, ekāsu. Ettha bahuvacanaṭṭhāne ekāti ekaccā, ekāhīti ekaccāhi, ekāsanti ekaccānaṃ ekāsūti ekaccāsu. Itthiliṅgarūpāni. Sabbānetāni sabbanāmāni ekavacanabahuvacanavasena vuttāni.

Ekā, ekā, ekāyo. Ekaṃ, ekā, ekāyo. Ekāya, ekāhi, ekābhi. Ekāya, ekissā, ekāsaṃ. Ekāya, ekāhi, ekābhi. Ekāya, ekissā, ekāsaṃ. Ekāya, ekāyaṃ, ekissaṃ, ekāsu. Here, in the plural, “ekā” means “some” (ekaccā); “ekāhi” means “by some” (ekaccāhi); “ekāsaṃ” means “of some” (ekaccānaṃ); and “ekāsu” means “in some” (ekaccāsu). These are feminine forms. All these pronouns are stated in terms of singular and plural.

Apica ekasadde vicchāvasena vattabbe liṅgattayarūpāni ekavacanāneva bhavanti. Kathaṃ?

Furthermore, when the word “eka” is to be expressed in a distributive sense, the forms of the three genders are only singular. How so?

Ekeko, ekekaṃ, ekekena, ekekassa, ekekasmā, ekekamhā, ekekassa, ekekasmiṃ, ekekamhīti pulliṅgarūpāni.

Ekeko, ekekaṃ, ekekena, ekekassa, ekekasmā, ekekamhā, ekekassa, ekekasmiṃ, ekekamhī. These are the masculine forms.

Ekekaṃ, ekekaṃ. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ, napuṃsakaliṅgarūpāni. Ekekā, ekekaṃ, ekekāya, ekekissā, ekekāya, ekekissā, ekekāyaṃ, ekekissaṃ. Itthiliṅgarūpāni.

Ekekaṃ, ekekaṃ. The rest is similar to the masculine. These are neuter forms. Ekekā, ekekaṃ, ekekāya, ekekissā, ekekāya, ekekissā, ekekāyaṃ, ekekissaṃ. These are feminine forms.

Sabbānetāni vicchāsabbanāmānīti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Bahuvacanāni panettha na santi payogābhāvato. Iti imesu vicchāvasena vuttesu liṅgattayarūpesu samāsacintā na uppādetabbā anibbacanīyattā vicchāsaddānaṃ. Tathā hi “pabbaṃ pabbaṃ [M 0.0379] sandhi sandhi odhi odhi hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilā viya taṭataṭāyantā saṅkhārā bhijjantī”tiādīsu pabbapabbasaddādīnaṃ samāsakaraṇavasena nibbacanaṃ pubbācariyehi na dassitaṃ. Yasmā ca vicchāyaṃ vattamānānaṃ dvirutti lokato eva siddhā, na lakkhaṇato, tasmā tattha samāsacintā na uppādetabbā.

All these can be called distributive pronouns. However, plural forms are not found here due to lack of usage. Thus, in these cases where the three genders have been expressed distributively, the thought of compounding should not be produced, as distributive words are indefinable. For example, in phrases like “piece by piece, joint by joint, layer by layer, like sesame seeds thrown into a heated pot, the conditioned phenomena crackle and break,” the ancient teachers did not show a definition through compounding for words like “pabbaṃ pabbaṃ,” etc. Since the reduplication of those existing in distribution is established only by convention, not by rule, therefore the thought of compounding should not be produced there.

Idāni ekacca ekatiya ekacciyasaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālāyo vuccante – pulliṅge tāva ekacco, ekacce. Ekaccaṃ, ekacce. Sesaṃ purisasaddasamaṃ. Ettha ekacceti paccattabahuvacanameva sabbanāmikarūpasamaṃ asādhāraṇarūpattā. “Idhekacco kulaputto. Idhekacce moghapurisā”ti nidassanapadāni.

Now, the nominal paradigms for the words “ekacca,” “ekatiya,” and “ekacciya” are stated—first, in the masculine: “ekacco,” “ekacce.” “Ekaccaṃ,” “ekacce.” The rest are similar to the word “purisa.” Here, “ekacce” is a nominative/accusative plural form, similar to a pronominal form due to its unique nature. Examples are: “Here, a certain clansman.” “Here, certain foolish men”—these are illustrative examples.

Ekatiyo, ekatiye. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiye. Sesaṃ purisasaddasamaṃ. Idhāpi ekatiyeti paccattabahuvacanameva sabbanāmikarūpasamaṃ asādhāraṇarūpattā. Ekatiye manussā.

Ekatiyo, ekatiye. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiye. The rest are similar to the word “purisa.” Here too, “ekatiye” is a nominative/accusative plural form, similar to a pronominal form due to its unique nature. An example is: “Certain people.”

“Na vissase ekatiyesu eva,

Agārisu pabbajitesu cāpi;

Sādhūpi hutvāna asādhu honti;

Asādhu hutvā puna sādhu hontī”ti

“One should not trust certain ones only, whether householders or renunciates; even good ones become bad; having been bad, they become good again.”

Nidassanapadāni. Ekacciyasaddassa atthitāyaṃ pana –

These are illustrative examples. But regarding the existence of the word “ekacciya”:

“Saccaṃ kirevamāhaṃsu, narā ekacciyā idha;

Kaṭṭhaṃ niplavitaṃ seyyo, na tvevekacciyo naro.

“Indeed, certain men here say thus: ‘A floating log is better, but not a certain man.’

Ekacciyaṃ āhāra”nti nidassanapadāni. Ekacciyo, ekacciyā. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciyeti sabbathāpi purisanayo. Pulliṅgarūpāni.

“A certain meal”—these are illustrative examples. Ekacciyo, ekacciyā. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciye—in all cases, it follows the pattern of purisa. These are masculine forms.
