Ekaccaṃ[M 0.0380], ekaccāni. Ekaccaṃ, ekaccāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiyāni. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiyāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciyāni. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciyāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Napuṃsakaliṅgarūpāni.

Ekaccaṃ, ekaccāni. Ekaccaṃ, ekaccāni. The rest are similar to the masculine forms. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiyāni. Ekatiyaṃ, ekatiyāni. The rest are similar to the masculine forms. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciyāni. Ekacciyaṃ, ekacciyāni. The rest are similar to the masculine forms. These are neuter forms.

“Ekaccā, ekaccā, ekaccāyo”ti kaññānayena, tathā “ekatiyā, ekatiyā, ekatiyāyo. Ekatiya”nti ca, “ekacciyā, ekacciyā, ekacciyāyo. Ekacciya”nti ca kaññānayena yojetabbaṃ. Itthiliṅgarūpāni.

“Ekaccā, ekaccā, ekaccāyo” according to the pattern of kaññā; likewise, “ekatiyā, ekatiyā, ekatiyāyo. Ekatiya” and “ekacciyā, ekacciyā, ekacciyāyo. Ekacciya” should be applied according to the pattern of kaññā. These are feminine forms.

Idāni ekākī ekākiyasaddavasena nāmikapadamālā vuccante –

Now, the nominal paradigms for the words “ekākī” and “ekākiya” are stated:

Ekākī, ekākī, ekākino. Ekākiṃ, ekākī, ekākino. Daṇḍīnayena ñeyyā. Ekākiyo, ekākiyā. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiye. Ekākiyena. Purisanayena ñeyyaṃ. Pulliṅgarūpāni.

Ekākī, ekākī, ekākino. Ekākiṃ, ekākī, ekākino. These should be understood according to the daṇḍin paradigm. Ekākiyo, ekākiyā. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiye. Ekākiyena. These should be understood according to the purisa paradigm. These are masculine forms.

Ekāki kulaṃ, ekākī, ekākīni. Ekākiṃ, ekākī, ekākīni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyāni. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyāni. Sesaṃ pulliṅgasadisaṃ. Napuṃsakaliṅgarūpāni.

Ekāki kulaṃ, ekākī, ekākīni. Ekākiṃ, ekākī, ekākīni. The rest is similar to the masculine. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyāni. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyāni. The rest is similar to the masculine. These are neuter forms.

Ekākinī, ekākinī, ekākiniyo. Ekākiniṃ, ekākinī, ekākiniyo. Ekākiniyāti itthīsadisaṃ. Ekākiyā, ekākiyā, ekākiyāyo. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyā, ekākiyāyo. Ekākiyāyāti kaññāsadisaṃ. Itthiliṅgarūpāni. Sabbāni panetāni asabbanāmikarūpāni atthantaraviññāpanatthaṃ vuttānīti daṭṭhabbāni.

Ekākinī, ekākinī, ekākiniyo. Ekākiniṃ, ekākinī, ekākiniyo. The declension of `ekākinī` is similar to that of `itthī`. Ekākiyā, ekākiyā, ekākiyāyo. Ekākiyaṃ, ekākiyā, ekākiyāyo. The declension of `ekākiyā` is similar to that of `kaññā`. These are feminine forms. But all these non-pronominal forms should be understood as having been stated for the purpose of indicating a difference in meaning.

Idāni dvisaddapariyāyassa sadā bahuvacanantassa sabbanāmikapadassa ubhasaddassa nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the nominal paradigm is stated for the word `ubha`, a pronominal word which is a synonym of the word `dvi` and always occurs in the plural.

“Ubho[M 0.0381], ubho, ubhohi, ubhobhi, ubhinnaṃ, ubhohi, ubhobhi, ubhinnaṃ, ubhosū”ti ayaṃ pāḷinayānurūpena vuttapadamālā. Atrime payogā – ubho kumārā nikkītā. Ubho itthiyo tiṭṭhanti, ubho cittāni tiṭṭhanti, ubho putte adāsi. Ubho kaññāyo passati. Ubho pādāni bhinditvā, saññamissāmi vo ahaṃ. Ubhohi hatthehi. Ubhohi bāhāhi, ubhohi cittehi, ubhinnaṃ janānaṃ, ubhinnaṃ itthīnaṃ, ubhinnaṃ cittānaṃ, ubhosu purisesu, ubhosu itthīsu, ubhosu passesūti, ayamasmākaṃ ruci. Ācariyā pana “ubhehi, ubhebhi, ubhesū”tipi icchanti. Kaccāyanepi hi “ubhe tappurisā”ti vuttaṃ. Sabbānipi etāni manasi kātabbāniyeva. Ubhasaddassa samāso appasiddho. Liṅgattayasādhāraṇarūpāni.

“Ubho, ubho, ubhohi, ubhobhi, ubhinnaṃ, ubhohi, ubhobhi, ubhinnaṃ, ubhosu”—this is the paradigm stated according to the Pāli tradition. Here are the usages: “Both boys are bought.” “Both women stand.” “Both minds stand.” “He gave both sons.” “He sees both maidens.” “Having broken both feet, I will restrain you.” “With both hands.” “With both arms.” “With both minds.” “Of both people.” “Of both women.” “Of both minds.” “Among both men.” “Among both women.” “Among both sides”—this is our preference. However, the teachers also accept “ubhehi, ubhebhi, ubhesu.” For in Kaccāyana it is also said, “ubhe tappurisā.” All these should indeed be kept in mind. The compounding of the word “ubha” is not established. These forms are common to all three genders.

Idāni saṅkhāvacanānaṃ dviti catusaddānaṃ sadā bahuvacanantānaṃ sabbanāmānaṃ nāmikapadamālāyo vuccante –

Now, the nominal paradigms of the numeral words 'dvi', 'ti', and 'catu', which are pronouns and always occur in the plural, are stated.

Dve, dve, dvīhi, dvībhi, dvinnaṃ, duvinnaṃ, dvīhi, dvībhi, dvinnaṃ, duvinnaṃ, dvīsu. Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ pana “dvinnanna”nti padamālā āgatā. Imāni ahaṃsaddādīni viya itthi liṅgādibhāvavinimuttānipi tīsu liṅgesu yujjante “dve purisā, dve itthiyo, dve cittāni”iccevamādinā. Imānipi liṅgattayasādhāraṇāni rūpāni.

Dve, dve, dvīhi, dvībhi, dvinnaṃ, duvinnaṃ, dvīhi, dvībhi, dvinnaṃ, duvinnaṃ, dvīsu. In the Cūḷanirutti, however, the paradigm form 'dvinnanna' is found. These forms, like 'ahaṃ' and other words, are used in all three genders, being free from feminine gender and other distinctions—'two men, two women, two minds,' and so forth. These forms are also common to all three genders.

“Dve”ti rūpaṃ dvisaddassa, yaṃ samāsamhi taṃ bhave;

Dvitippakatikaṃyeva, nānādesehi sā siyā.

The form 'dve' is of the word 'dvi'. When it is in a compound, it has the base form 'dvi' itself; that base may undergo various substitutions.

Dvibhāvo ceva dvebhāvo, dvirattañca duvassako;

Dohaḷinī dupattañca, taddhitatte dvayaṃ dvayaṃ.

Dvibhāva and also dvebhāva, dviratta and duvassaka; dohaḷinī and dupatta—in the sense of taddhita, there are 'dvayaṃ' and 'dvayaṃ'.

Tayo[M 0.0382], tayo, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīsu. Imāni pulliṅgarūpāni.

Tayo, tayo, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīsu. These are masculine forms.

Tisso, tisso, tīhi, tībhi, tissannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tissannaṃ, tīsu. Imāni itthiliṅgarūpāni. Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ “tissannanna”nti catutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ bahuvacanamāgataṃ, niruttipiṭake pana “tiṇṇanna”nti. Tāni sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane punappunaṃ upaparikkhitvā dissanti ce, gahetabbāni.

Tisso, tisso, tīhi, tībhi, tissannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tissannaṃ, tīsu. These are feminine forms. In the Cūḷanirutti, 'tissannanna' occurs as the plural for the dative and genitive cases, but in the Niruttipiṭaka, 'tiṇṇanna' is found. These should be repeatedly examined in the Tipiṭaka with its commentaries, in the word of the Buddha, and accepted if they are seen.

Tīṇi, tīṇi, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīsu. Imāni napuṃsakaliṅgarūpāni. Katthaci pana pāḷippadese tīṇisaddassa ṇikāralopopi bhavati “dve vāti vā udakaphusitānī”ti. “Tiṇṇannaṃ kho bhikkhave indriyānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā piṇḍolabhāradvājena bhikkhunā aññā byākatā”ti idaṃ “tiṇṇanna”nti padassa atthibhāve nidassanaṃ.

Tīṇi, tīṇi, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīhi, tībhi, tiṇṇaṃ, tiṇṇannaṃ, tīsu. These are neuter forms. In some Pāli passages, the 'ṇi' of 'tīṇi' is also dropped, as in 'dve vā tī vā udakaphusitāni'. 'Tiṇṇannaṃ kho bhikkhave indriyānaṃ bhāvitattā bahulīkatattā piṇḍolabhāradvājena bhikkhunā aññā byākatā' is an example demonstrating the existence of the word 'tiṇṇannaṃ'.

Yāni rūpāni vuttāni, “tisso tīṇi tayo”iti;

Samāsavisaye tāni, titippakatikā siyuṃ.

The forms mentioned—'tisso,' 'tīṇi,' 'tayo'—when in the domain of compounds, would have the base form 'ti'.

Yasmā tissa samāsamhi, saddhiṃ parapadena ve;

“Tivedanaṃ ticitta”nti, “tiloka”nti ca niddise.

Because of this, when in a compound together with a following word, one should indicate 'tivedanaṃ,' 'ticitta,' and 'tiloka'.

Ettha napuṃsakattaṃva, pāsaṃsaṃ pāyavuttito;

Pumattampettha icchanti, “tibhavo khāyate”iti.

Here, only the neuter gender is praiseworthy due to frequent usage; however, the masculine gender is also desired here, because 'tibhavo' is found.

Cattāro, caturo, cattāro, caturo, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūsu. Imāni pulliṅgarūpāni.

Cattāro, caturo, cattāro, caturo, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūsu. These are masculine forms.

Catasso[M 0.0383], catasso, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catassannaṃ, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catassannaṃ, catunnaṃ, catūsu. Imāni itthiliṅgarūpāni. Itthiliṅgaṭṭhāne “catunna”nti padaṃ cūḷaniruttiyaṃ niruttipiṭake pāḷiyaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu ca dassanato vuttaṃ. Tathā hi cūḷaniruttiyaṃ itthiliṅgaṭṭhāne “catunna”nti āgataṃ, niruttipiṭake “catunnaṃ kaññāna”nti āgataṃ. Pāḷiyaṃ pana soṇadantasuttādīsu “samaṇo gotamo catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo”ti āgataṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu ca pana suttantaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “catūhi acchariyabbhutadhammehi samannāgato catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo”ti āgataṃ. Sattilaṅghajātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “ācariyo panassa catunnaṃ sattīnaṃ laṅghanaṃ sippaṃ jānātī”ti āgataṃ.

Catasso, catasso, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catassannaṃ, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catassannaṃ, catunnaṃ, catūsu. These are the feminine forms. In the place of the feminine gender, the word ‘catunnaṃ’ is said to be found in the Cūḷanirutti, the Niruttipiṭaka, the Pāḷi, and the commentaries. For instance, in the Cūḷanirutti, ‘catunnaṃ’ appears in the place of the feminine gender. In the Niruttipiṭaka, ‘catunnaṃ kaññānaṃ’ appears. In the Pāḷi, however, in the Soṇadanta Sutta and others, it appears as ‘samaṇo gotamo catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo’ (the ascetic Gotama is dear and pleasing to the four assemblies). And in the commentaries, in the Suttantaṭṭhakathā, it appears as ‘catūhi acchariyabbhutadhammehi samannāgato catunnaṃ parisānaṃ piyo manāpo’ (endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities, dear and pleasing to the four assemblies). In the Sattilaṅghajātakaṭṭhakathā, it appears as ‘ācariyo panassa catunnaṃ sattīnaṃ laṅghanaṃ sippaṃ jānātī’ (but his teacher knows the skill of leaping over four spears).

Cattāri, cattāri, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūsu. Imāni napuṃsakaliṅgarūpāni.

Cattāri, cattāri, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūhi, catūbhi, catubbhi, catunnaṃ, catūsu. These are the neuter forms.

“Cattāro”ti “catasso”ti, “cattārī”ti ca sadditaṃ;

Rūpaṃ samāsabhāvamhi, catuppakatikaṃ bhave.

The forms called ‘cattāro,’ ‘catasso,’ and ‘cattāri,’ when in a compound state, would have the base ‘catu’.

Nidassanapadānettha, kamato kamakovido;

“Catubbidhaṃ catussālaṃ, catusacca”nti niddise.

Here, one skilled in sequence should point out the illustrative terms in order: ‘catubbidhaṃ,’ ‘catussālaṃ,’ and ‘catusaccaṃ’.

Imāni dveādikāni sabbanāmikāni bahuvacanāniyeva bhavanti, na ekavacanāni. Cūḷaniruttiyaṃ pana tīsu liṅgesu “catassanna”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ anijjhānakkhamaṃ viya dissati.

These pronominal words, beginning with ‘dve’, are only plural, not singular. In the Cūḷanirutti, however, ‘catassannaṃ’ is said to be in the three genders, which appears to be unacceptable.

Idāni tumhaamhasaddānaṃ nāmikapadamālā vuccante, tesu yena katheti, tassālapane tumhavacanāni bhavanti.

Now, the nominal paradigms of the words ‘tumha’ and ‘amha’ are stated. Among them, when one speaks to another, in addressing them the forms of ‘tumha’ are used.

Tvaṃ, tuvaṃ, tumhe. Taṃ, tuvaṃ, tvaṃ, tavaṃ, tumhe. Tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebhi. Tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. Tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebhi. Tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. Tayi, tvayi, tumhesu[M 0.0384]. Tatra “tvaṃ puriso, tvaṃ itthī, tvaṃ citta”ntiādinā yojetabbāni.

Tvaṃ, tuvaṃ, tumhe. Taṃ, tuvaṃ, tvaṃ, tavaṃ, tumhe. Tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebhi. Tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. Tayā, tvayā, tumhehi, tumhebhi. Tuyhaṃ, tava, tumhaṃ, tumhākaṃ. Tayi, tvayi, tumhesu. There, they should be applied with examples such as ‘tvaṃ puriso’ (you are a man), ‘tvaṃ itthī’ (you are a woman), ‘tvaṃ cittaṃ’ (you are the mind).

Attayoge amhavacanāni bhavanti.

When referring to oneself, the forms of ‘amha’ are used.

Ahaṃ, ahakaṃ, mayaṃ, amhe. Maṃ, mamaṃ, amhe. Mayā, amhehi, amhebhi. Mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. Mayā, amhehi, amhebhi. Mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. Mayi, amhesu, asmesu.

Ahaṃ, ahakaṃ, mayaṃ, amhe. Maṃ, mamaṃ, amhe. Mayā, amhehi, amhebhi. Mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. Mayā, amhehi, amhebhi. Mayhaṃ, mama, amhaṃ, amhākaṃ, asmākaṃ. Mayi, amhesu, asmesu.

Ettha pana “kathaṃ amhe karomase”ti pāḷidassanato “tumhe”ti paccattavacanassa viya “amhe”ti paccattavacanassapi atthitā veditabbā, “ahaka”nti rūpantarampi icchitabbaṃ. Tassa atthibhāve “ahakañca cittavasānugā bhāsissa”nti esā pāḷi nidassanaṃ. Ettha hi ahakanti ahaṃ iccevattho. Tatra “ahaṃ puriso, ahaṃ kaññā, ahaṃ citta”ntiādinā yojetabbāni. Imānipi liṅgattayasādhāraṇarūpāni.

Here, however, from the Pāḷi citation ‘kathaṃ amhe karomase’ (How shall we act?), the existence of ‘amhe’ as a first-person pronoun should be known, just like ‘tumhe’ as a second-person pronoun. The variant form ‘ahakaṃ’ should also be accepted. Regarding its existence, this Pāḷi citation is an example: ‘ahakañca cittavasānugā bhāsissaṃ’ (And I, following the sway of the mind, will speak). Here, ‘ahakaṃ’ has the very meaning of ‘ahaṃ’. There, they should be applied with examples such as ‘ahaṃ puriso’ (I am a man), ‘ahaṃ kaññā’ (I am a maiden), ‘ahaṃ cittaṃ’ (I am the mind). These forms are also common to the three genders.

Kaccāyanacūḷaniruttiniruttipiṭakesu pana “tumhākaṃ amhāka”nti ca dutiyābahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Kaccāyane “tumhānaṃ amhāna”nti ca paṭhamādutiyābahuvacanaṃ, “tumhaṃ amha”nti ca catutthīchaṭṭhekavacanaṃ, paṭhamādutiyābahuvacanañca vuttaṃ, cūḷaniruttiniruttipiṭake pana “tumhaṃ amha”nti ca dutiyekavacanaṃ vuttaṃ, “tumhe amhe”ti ca catutthīchaṭṭhībahuvacanaṃ vuttaṃ. Etāni upaparikkhitvā sāṭṭhakathesu suttantesu dissanti ce, gahetabbāni.

In the Kaccāyana, Cūḷanirutti, and Niruttipiṭaka, however, ‘tumhākaṃ’ and ‘amhākaṃ’ are stated as accusative plural. In the Kaccāyana, ‘tumhānaṃ’ and ‘amhānaṃ’ are stated as nominative and accusative plural, and ‘tumhaṃ’ and ‘amhaṃ’ are stated as dative and genitive singular, and also as nominative and accusative plural. In the Cūḷanirutti and Niruttipiṭaka, however, ‘tumhaṃ’ and ‘amhaṃ’ are stated as accusative singular, and ‘tumhe’ and ‘amhe’ are stated as dative and genitive plural. Having examined these, if they are seen in the Suttas with their commentaries, they should be accepted.

Tumhaamhasaddānaṃ pana parapadehi saddhiṃ samāse “maṃdīpā”tiādayo payogā tathāgatādimukhato sambhavanti. “Ete gāmaṇi maṃdīpā maṃleṇā maṃsaraṇā”ti hi tathāgatamukhato, “tayyogo mayyogo”ti niruttaññumukhato, kābyādāse ca “tvaṃmukhaṃ kamaleneva, tulyaṃ nāññena [M 0.0385] kenacī”ti ca “candena tvaṃmukhaṃ tulya”nti ca kavimukhato.

However, in compounds of the words ‘tumha’ and ‘amha’ with subsequent words, usages such as ‘maṃdīpā’ and so forth arise from the mouth of the Tathāgata and others. For indeed, from the mouth of the Tathāgata: ‘Ete gāmaṇi maṃdīpā maṃleṇā maṃsaraṇā’ (These, village headman, are my lamps, my shelters, my refuges). From the mouth of the etymologist: ‘tayyogo mayyogo’ (your connection, my connection). And in the Kāvyādarśa, from the mouth of the poet: ‘tvaṃmukhaṃ kamaleneva, tulyaṃ nāññena kenacī’ (Your face is like a lotus, comparable to nothing else), and ‘candena tvaṃmukhaṃ tulyaṃ’ (Your face is like the moon).

Tattha hi ahaṃ dīpo etesanti maṃdīpā, ahaṃ leṇaṃ etesanti maṃleṇā, evaṃ maṃsaraṇā. Tumhena yogo tayyogo, tumhasaddena yogo iccevattho. Amhena yogo mayyogo, amhasaddena yogo iccevattho. Tava mukhaṃ tvaṃmukhaṃ. Bahuvacanavasenapi nibbacanīyaṃ “tumhākaṃ mukhaṃ tvaṃmukha”nti. Ettha ca pāḷiyaṃ “maṃdīpā”iccādidassanato “tvaṃdīpā”tiādīni kābyādāse ca “tvaṃmukha”nti dassanato tvaṃvaṇṇo, tvaṃsaro, maṃmukhaṃ, maṃvaṇṇo, maṃsaroādīni gahetabbāni. Tattha tvaṃ dīpo etesanti tvaṃdīpā, tumhe vā dīpā etesanti tvaṃdīpā, tava vaṇṇo tvaṃvaṇṇo. Mama mukhaṃ maṃmukhaṃ, amhākaṃ vā mukhaṃ maṃmukhanti nibbacanāni. Esa nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu.

Therein, ‘ahaṃ dīpo etesanti maṃdīpā’ (I am a lamp for them, thus ‘maṃdīpā’); ‘ahaṃ leṇaṃ etesanti maṃleṇā’ (I am a shelter for them, thus ‘maṃleṇā’); similarly ‘maṃsaraṇā’. ‘Tumhena yogo tayyogo’ (connection with you is ‘tayyogo’); this has the very meaning of ‘connection with the word tumha’. ‘Amhena yogo mayyogo’ (connection with us is ‘mayyogo’); this has the very meaning of ‘connection with the word amha’. ‘Tava mukhaṃ tvaṃmukhaṃ’ (your face is ‘tvaṃmukhaṃ’). By way of the plural also, it should be explained as ‘tumhākaṃ mukhaṃ tvaṃmukhaṃ’ (your face is ‘tvaṃmukhaṃ’). And here, because in the Pāḷi, ‘maṃdīpā’ etc. are seen, and in the Kāvyādarśa, ‘tvaṃmukhaṃ’ is seen, therefore ‘tvaṃvaṇṇo’ (your complexion), ‘tvaṃsaro’ (your voice), ‘maṃmukhaṃ’ (my face), ‘maṃvaṇṇo’ (my complexion), ‘maṃsaro’ (my voice), etc., should be accepted. Therein, ‘tvaṃ dīpo etesanti tvaṃdīpā’ (you are a lamp for them, thus ‘tvaṃdīpā’), or ‘tumhe dīpā etesanti tvaṃdīpā’ (you all are lamps for them, thus ‘tvaṃdīpā’); ‘tava vaṇṇo tvaṃvaṇṇo’ (your complexion is ‘tvaṃvaṇṇo’). ‘Mama mukhaṃ maṃmukhaṃ’ (my face is ‘maṃmukhaṃ’), or ‘amhākaṃ mukhaṃ maṃmukhaṃ’ (our face is ‘maṃmukhaṃ’) are the explanations. This is the method in other similar instances as well.

Samāse tumhaamhākaṃ, honti parapadehi ve;

“Tvaṃmukha”nti ca “maṃdīpā, tayyogo mayyogo”ti ca.

In a compound, the forms of ‘tumha’ and ‘amha’ indeed occur with subsequent words; such as ‘tvaṃmukhaṃ,’ and ‘maṃdīpā,’ ‘tayyogo,’ and ‘mayyogo’.

Etthāha “kiṃ ettakameva tumhaamhasaddānaṃ rūpaṃ, udāhu aññampi atthī”ti? Atthi “te me” iccādīni. Yadi evaṃ kasmā padamālā visuṃ na vuttāti? Avacane kāraṇamatthi. Atridaṃ kāraṇaṃ –

Here one asks: ‘Are these the only forms of the words ‘tumha’ and ‘amha’, or are there others as well?’ There are, such as ‘te,’ ‘me,’ and so forth. If so, why were they not stated separately in the paradigm? There is a reason for not stating them. Herein is the reason:

“Te me vo no”ti rūpāni, parāni padato yato;

Tato nāmikapantīsu, na tu vuttāni tāni me.

Since the forms ‘te,’ ‘me,’ ‘vo,’ and ‘no’ are subsequent to a word, therefore they were not stated by me in the rows of nominals.

Ettha ca mayaṃ me vo nosaddānamatthuddhāro vuccate – tesaddassa pana vuttova. Yasmā aṭṭhakathācariyā mayaṃsaddaṭṭhānepi mayāsaddo, mayāsaddaṭṭhānepi ca mayaṃsaddo icceva vadanti, tasmā mayampi tatheva vadāma. Mayaṃsaddo “anuññātapaṭiññātā, tevijjāmayamasmubho”tiādīsu asmadatthe āgato[M 0.0386]. “Mayaṃ nissāya hemāya, jātā mandosisūpagā”ti ettha paññattiyaṃ. “Manomayā pītibhakkhā sayaṃpabhā”tiādīsu nibbattiatthe. Bāhirena paccayena vinā manasāva nibbattāti manomayā. “Yaṃnūnāhaṃ sabbamattikāmayaṃ kuṭikaṃ kareyya”ntiādīsu vikāratthe. “Dānamayaṃ sīlamaya”ntiādīsu padapūraṇamatte. “Pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ uḷāra”nti ettha vikāratthe padapūraṇamatte vā daṭṭhabbo. Yadā hi suvaṇṇameva sovaṇṇanti ayamattho, tadā suvaṇṇassa vikāro sovaṇṇamayanti vikāratthe mayasaddo daṭṭhabbo. Nibbattiatthotipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Yadā pana suvaṇṇena nibbattaṃ sovaṇṇanti ayamattho, tadā sovaṇṇameva sovaṇṇamayanti padapūraṇamatte mayasaddo daṭṭhabbo.

And here the explanation of the meaning of the words ‘-maya’, ‘me’, ‘vo’, and ‘no’ is stated; the meaning of the word ‘te’ has already been stated. Since the commentary teachers say that the word ‘-mayā’ is used in place of the word ‘-maya’, and the word ‘-maya’ in place of the word ‘-mayā’, therefore we also say the same. The word ‘-maya’ appears in the sense of being made of, as in ‘anuññātapaṭiññātā, tevijjāmayamasmubho’ (permitted and acknowledged, we both consist of the three knowledges). In ‘Mayaṃ nissāya hemāya, jātā mandosisūpagā,’ it is in the sense of designation. In ‘Manomayā pītibhakkhā sayaṃpabhā’ and so on, it is in the sense of being produced. ‘Manomayā’ means produced by the mind alone, without an external cause. In ‘Yaṃnūnāhaṃ sabbamattikāmayaṃ kuṭikaṃ kareyya’ and so on, it is in the sense of modification. In ‘Dānamayaṃ sīlamayaṃ’ and so on, it is a mere expletive. In ‘Pīṭhaṃ te sovaṇṇamayaṃ uḷāraṃ,’ it should be seen either in the sense of modification or as a mere expletive. For when the meaning is that ‘sovaṇṇa’ is gold itself, then the word ‘-maya’ in ‘sovaṇṇamayaṃ’ should be seen in the sense of modification, as a modification of gold. It is also possible to say it is in the sense of being produced. But when the meaning is that ‘sovaṇṇaṃ’ is what is produced from gold, then the word ‘-maya’ in ‘sovaṇṇamayaṃ’ should be seen as a mere expletive.

Mesaddo “kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsitu”ntiādīsu karaṇe āgato. Mayāti attho. “Tassa me bhante bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu sampadāne, mayhanti atthoti vadanti. “Pubbeva me bhikkhave sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato”tiādīsu sāmiatthe, mamāti atthoti ca vadanti. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

The word 'me' occurs in the instrumental sense in phrases like 'kicchena me adhigataṃ, halaṃ dāni pakāsitu' (with difficulty it was attained by me; now it is enough to reveal). The meaning is 'by me.' In phrases like 'Tassa me bhante bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū' (Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief), they say it is in the dative sense, meaning 'to me.' In phrases like 'Pubbeva me bhikkhave sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato' (Before my full enlightenment, bhikkhus, while I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta), they also say it is in the possessive sense, meaning 'of me.' Here it is said:

Karaṇe sampadāne ca, sāmiatthe ca āgato;

Mesaddo iti viññeyyo, viññunā nayadassinā.

It occurs in the instrumental, dative, and possessive senses; thus the word 'me' should be understood by the wise one who sees the method.

Ettha [M 0.0387] pana ṭhatvā aṭṭhakathācariyehi kate te mesaddānamatthavivaraṇe vinicchayaṃ brūma tesamadhippāyappakāsanavasena sotūnaṃ saṃsayasamugghāṭanatthaṃ. Tathā hi aṭṭhakathācariyā temesaddānaṃ sampadānatthavasena “tuyhaṃ mayha”nti atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇesuṃ, sāmiatthavasena pana “tava mamā”ti. Evaṃ yvāyaṃ tehi asaṅkarato niyamo dassito, so sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane kuto labbhā. Tathā hi temesaddatthavācakā tuyhaṃ mayhaṃsaddā tava mamasaddā ca sampadānasāmiatthesu aniyamato pavattanti.

Here, taking our stand on the explanation of the meaning of the words 'te' and 'me' given by the commentary teachers, we shall state a decision in order to reveal their intention and dispel the doubts of the listeners. For the commentary teachers explained the meaning of 'te' and 'me' in the dative sense as 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ', and in the possessive sense as 'tava' and 'mama'. Thus, this rule shown by them without confusion, where can it be found in the Buddha's word, the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries? Indeed, the words 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ', and 'tava' and 'mama', which express the meaning of 'te' and 'me', occur without restriction in the dative and possessive senses.

Tatrime payogā – idaṃ tuyhaṃ dadāmi. Tuyhaṃ vikappemi. Tuyhaṃ maṃsena medena, matthakena ca brāhmaṇa, āhutiṃ paggahessāmi. Esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho. Tuyhaṃ pana mātā kahanti. Mayhameva dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, na aññesaṃ, mayhameva sāvakānaṃ dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, na aññesaṃ. Na mayhaṃ bhariyā esā. Assamo sukato mayhaṃ. Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ. Tāta mayhaṃ mātu mukhaṃ aññādisaṃ, tumhākaṃ aññādisaṃ. Mayhaṃ sāmiko idāni marissati. Tava dīyate, tava silāghate, mama silāghate, pabbajjā mama ruccati. Tava putto. Ubho mātāpitā mamāti evaṃ aniyamato pavattanti.

Here are these usages: 'This I give to you.' 'I assign it to you.' 'With your flesh, fat, and head, O brahmin, I shall make an offering.' 'For this is indeed your father, the lion among men.' 'But your mother, where is she?' 'The gift should be given to me alone, not to others; the gift should be given to my disciples alone, not to others.' 'This is not my wife.' 'My hermitage is well-made.' 'Omniscience is dear to me.' 'Dear one, my mother's face is of one kind, yours is of another.' 'My husband will now die.' 'It is given to you,' 'it is praised for you,' 'it is praised for me,' 'the going forth is pleasing to me.' 'He is your son.' 'Both mother and father are mine.' Thus, they occur without restriction.

Cūḷaniruttiyañhi yamakamahātherena catutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ anaññarūpattaṃ vuttaṃ “catutthīchaṭṭhīnaṃ sabbattha anaññaṃ, tatiyāpañcamīnaṃ bahuvacanañcā”ti[M 0.0388]. Yadi evaṃ aṭṭhakathācariyā “namo te purisājañña. Namo te buddha vīratthū’tiādīsu tuyhaṃsaddassa vasena sampadāne, tuyhanti hi attho. ‘Kinte vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariya’ntiādīsu sāmiatthe, tavāti hi attho”tiādīni vadantā “ayuttaṃ saṃvaṇṇanaṃ saṃvaṇṇesu”ntipi, “passitabbaṃ na passiṃsū”tipi āpajjantīti? Yuttaṃyeva te saṃvaṇṇayiṃsu, passitabbañca passiṃsu. Tathā hi te “saddasatthampi ekadesato sāsanānukūlaṃ hotī”ti paresamanukampāya saddasatthato nayaṃ gahetvā sampadānatthavasena te mesaddānaṃ “tuyhaṃ mayha”nti atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇayiṃsu, sāmiatthavasena pana “tava mamā”ti. Saddasatthe hi catutthīchaṭṭhīrūpāni sabbathā visadisāni, sāsane pana sadisāni. Tasmā sāsane sāmaññena pavattāni catutthīchaṭṭhīrūpāni saddasatthe visesena pavattehi catutthīchaṭṭhīrūpehi samānagatikāni katvā paresamanukampāya sampadānatthe tuyhaṃ mayhaṃsaddānaṃ pavattiniyamo, sāmiatthe ca tava mamasaddānaṃ pavattiniyamo dassito. Yasmā pana paresamanukampāya ayaṃ niyamo, tasmā karuṇāyevāyaṃparādho, na aṭṭhakathācariyānaṃ. Tāya eva hi tehi evaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā katāti.

Indeed, in the Cūḷanirutti, the great elder Yamaka stated the non-differentiation of the fourth and sixth cases: 'The fourth and sixth cases are everywhere non-different; and also the plural of the third and fifth cases.' If this is so, then why did the commentary teachers, when explaining phrases like 'namo te purisājañña, namo te buddha vīratthu' (Homage to you, noble man; homage to you, Buddha, may you be victorious), interpret 'te' in the dative sense as meaning 'tuyhaṃ' (to you), and in phrases like 'kinte vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariya' (What is your vow? What is your holy life?), interpret it in the possessive sense as meaning 'tava' (your)? Did they thereby fall into the faults of 'they explained an inappropriate explanation' and 'they did not see what should have been seen'? They indeed explained appropriately, and saw what should be seen. For they, out of compassion for others, taking a principle from the science of grammar, and considering that 'even grammar is in part favorable to the Dispensation,' thus, in the dative sense, they explained the words 'te' and 'me' as meaning 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ', and in the possessive sense, as 'tava' and 'mama'. Indeed, in grammar, the forms of the fourth and sixth cases are entirely distinct; but in the Dispensation, they are similar. Therefore, having made the forms of the fourth and sixth cases that occur generally in the Dispensation have the same course as the forms of the fourth and sixth cases that occur specifically in grammar, out of compassion for others, they showed the rule of usage for the words 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ' in the dative sense, and for 'tava' and 'mama' in the possessive sense. Since this rule was established out of compassion for others, the fault, if any, lies with compassion itself, not with the commentary teachers. For it was indeed through that compassion that they provided such explanations.

Keci panettha evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – nanu ca bho aṭṭhakathācariyehi saddanayaṃ nissāya te mesaddānaṃ sāmiatthe vattamānānaṃ “tava mamā”ti atthavacanena “tuyhaṃ maṃsena medena, na mayhaṃ bhariyā esā”tiādīsu sāmivisayesu vibhattivipallāsanayo dassitoti sakkā vattuṃ, tathā saddanayaññeva nissāya te mesaddānaṃ sampadānatthe vattamānānaṃ [M 0.0389] “tuyhaṃ mayha”nti atthavacanena “bhattaṃ tava na ruccati. Pabbajjā mama ruccatī”tiādīsupi sampadānavisayesu vibhattivipallāsanayo dassitoti sakkā vattunti? Na sakkā, gāthāsu viya cuṇṇiyapadaṭṭhānepi tuyhaṃ mayhaṃ tava mamasaddānaṃ aniyamena dvīsu atthesu pavattanato. Na hi īdise ṭhāne gāthāyaṃ vā cuṇṇiyapadaṭṭhāne vā vibhattivipallāso icchitabbo. “Tassa rajjassahaṃ bhīto. Kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmī”tiādīsuyeva pana ṭhānesu icchitabbo.

But some might say here: 'Venerable sirs, is it not possible to say that the commentary teachers, relying on the grammatical method, by stating the meaning of 'te' and 'me' when they occur in the possessive sense as 'tava' and 'mama', have thereby shown the principle of case inversion in possessive contexts, such as in 'tuyhaṃ maṃsena medena' (with your flesh and fat) and 'na mayhaṃ bhariyā esā' (she is not my wife)? Similarly, relying on the same grammatical method, by stating the meaning of 'te' and 'me' when they occur in the dative sense as 'tuyhaṃ' and 'mayhaṃ', have they not also shown the principle of case inversion in dative contexts, such as in 'bhattaṃ tava na ruccati' (food does not please you) and 'pabbajjā mama ruccati' (the monastic life pleases me)?' No, it is not possible, because the words 'tuyhaṃ', 'mayhaṃ', 'tava', and 'mama' occur without restriction in both senses, both in verses and in prose passages. Indeed, in such instances, whether in verses or in prose passages, case inversion should not be intended. However, it should be intended only in places like 'Tassa rajjassahaṃ bhīto' (I am afraid of his kingdom) and 'Kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ tassa sukhassa bhāyāmī' (Why indeed should I fear his happiness?).

Yadi saddanayaṃ nissāya “tuyhaṃ maṃsena medenā”tiādīsu vibhattivipallāso icchitabbo siyā, “brāhmaṇassa piyaputtadānaṃ adāsi. Brāhmaṇassa pitā adāsī”tiādīsupi saddanayaṃ nissāya “brāhmaṇāyā”tiādinā vibhattivipallāsattho vacanīyo siyā catutthīchaṭṭhīrūpānaṃ satthe visuṃ vacanato. Evañca sati ko dosoti ce? Attheva doso, yasmā dānayoge vā namoyoge vā āyādesasahitāni catutthīchaṭṭhīrūpāni sāṭṭhakathe tepiṭake buddhavacane nupalabbhanti, tasmā “brāhmaṇāyā”tiādinā vibhattivipallāsatthavacane ayaṃ doso yadidaṃ avijjamānaggahaṇaṃ. Yasmā pana īdisesu ṭhānesu vibhattivipallāsakaraṇaṃ sāvajjaṃ, tasmā “tuyhaṃ maṃsena medenā”tiādīsupi vibhattivipallāso na icchitabbo.

If a case irregularity were to be desired based on grammatical rule in phrases like “tuyhaṃ maṃsena medenā” (with your flesh and fat), then in phrases like “brāhmaṇassa piyaputtadānaṃ adāsi” (He gave a gift of his dear son to the brahmin) and “brāhmaṇassa pitā adāsī” (The brahmin’s father gave), a case irregularity meaning “brāhmaṇāya” and so on should also be stated, based on grammatical rule, since the forms of the fourth and sixth cases are distinctly stated in the grammatical treatises. And if this were so, what would be the fault? There is indeed a fault, because in contexts of giving or of homage, the forms of the fourth case accompanied by the substitution ‘āya’ are not found in the Buddha’s words in the Tipiṭaka together with the commentaries. Therefore, in stating a case irregularity with phrases like “brāhmaṇāya,” this fault arises—namely, grasping at what does not exist. Moreover, since making case irregularities in such instances is blameworthy, a case irregularity should not be desired even in phrases like “tuyhaṃ maṃsena medenā.”

Catutthīchaṭṭhīrūpāni hi anaññāni dissanti “purisassa adāsi, purisassa dhanaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ adāsi, brāhmaṇānaṃ santaka”nti. Tathā hi pāvacane sa naṃsaddā sampadānasāmiatthesu sāmaññena [M 0.0390] pavattanti, tappavatti “aggassa dātā medhāvī”tiādīhi payogehi dīpetabbā. “Aggassa dātā medhāvī”ti ettha hi “aggassā”ti ayaṃ saddo yadā kriyāpaṭiggahaṇaṃ paṭicca sampadānatthe pavattati, tadā “aggassa ratanattayassa dātā”ti atthavasena pavattati. Yadā pana kriyaṃ paṭicca kammabhūte sāmiatthe pavattati, tadā “aggassa deyyadhammassa dātā”ti atthavasena pavattati. Evaṃ sabbathāpi vipallāso tumhākaṃ saraṇaṃ na hotīti. Tathā saddanayaṃ nissāya “sampadānavacana”nti tumhehi daḷhaṃ gahitassa mayhaṃsaddassa sāmiatthavasena paṇṇattiyaṃ dassanato vibhattivipallāso tumhākaṃ saraṇaṃ na hoteva. Tathā hi –

For the fourth and sixth forms are indeed seen as not different, as in “purisassa adāsi” (he gave to the man), “purisassa dhanaṃ” (the man’s wealth), “brāhmaṇānaṃ adāsi” (he gave to the brahmins), “brāhmaṇānaṃ santakaṃ” (belonging to the brahmins). Thus, in the canonical texts, those words with ‘-sa’ and ‘-naṃ’ endings function generally in the senses of the dative and genitive cases, and their usage should be explained through examples like “aggassa dātā medhāvī” (the wise one is a giver of the foremost). In the phrase “aggassa dātā medhāvī,” the word “aggassa” functions in the dative sense when it relates to the recipient of an action, conveying the meaning “a giver to the foremost Triple Gem.” But when it relates to the action as the object, it functions in the genitive sense, conveying the meaning “a giver of the foremost gift.” Thus, in every way, case irregularity is not your refuge. Similarly, relying on grammatical rule, because the word ‘mayhaṃ’—which you firmly hold to be a “dative expression”—is seen used in designation in the genitive sense, case irregularity is certainly not your refuge. For indeed—

“Sakuṇo mayhako nāma, girisānudarīcaro;

Pakkaṃ pipphalimāruyha, ‘mayhaṃ mayha’nti kandatī”ti

“A bird named Mayhaka, roaming in mountain caves, having climbed a ripe fig tree, cries ‘Mine! Mine!’”

Ettha mayhakoti ekāya sakuṇajātiyā nāmaṃ. So hi loluppacāritāya “idampi mayhaṃ, idampi mayha”nti kāyati ravatīti mayhakoti vuccati mayhasaddūpapadassa ke re ge saddeti dhātussa vasena.

Here, ‘mayhaka’ is the name of a certain species of bird. For, due to its greedy behavior, it cries out, “This is mine, this is mine,” hence it is called ‘mayhaka,’ by virtue of the root ‘ge’ (or ‘ke,’ ‘re’), meaning ‘to sound,’ preceded by the word ‘mayha.’

Atrāyaṃ padasodhanā – yadi tuyhaṃ mayhaṃsaddā dhuvaṃ sampadānatthe, tava mamasaddā ca sāmiatthe bhaveyyuṃ, evaṃ sante lokavohārakusalena sabbaññunā tassa sakuṇassa “mayhako”ti paṇṇatti na vattabbā siyā anantogadhasampadānatthattā, antogadhasāmyatthattā pana “mamako” icceva paññatti vattabbā siyā. Etthapi “mayhako”ti idaṃ vibhattivipallāsavasena vuttanti ce? Na, paṇṇattivisaye vibhattivipariṇāmassa aṭṭhānattā anavakāsattā.

Here is the word analysis: If the words ‘tuyhaṃ’ and ‘mayhaṃ’ were invariably in the dative sense, and the words ‘tava’ and ‘mama’ invariably in the genitive sense, then, in that case, the Omniscient One, skilled in worldly usage, should not have designated that bird as ‘mayhako,’ because that name would imply an unlimited dative sense. Whereas, due to its nature of limited ownership, the designation ‘mamako’ should have been used. If it is said that ‘mayhako’ is used here due to a change of case, the answer is no, for in the realm of designation, there is no basis or occasion for a change of case.

Apicettha mayhaṃsaddo sarūpato vibhatyantabhāvena tiṭṭhati kasaddena ekapadattūpagamanato, evaṃ santepi “mayhako”ti [M 0.0391] ayaṃ sakuṇavisesavācako saddo paccattavacanabhāve ṭhitoyeva īsakaṃ sāmiatthampi jotayati sujampati rājapurisasaddā viya. Imināpi kāraṇena vibhattivipallāso tumhākaṃ saraṇaṃ na hoti. Iti “mayhako”ti paṇṇattiyaṃ vattamānassa padāvayavabhūtassa mayhasaddassa avipallāsavacanalesena tuyhaṃ tava mamasaddesupi vibhattivipallāso na icchitabboti siddhaṃ. Tasmā aṭṭhakathācariyehi sampadānasāmiatthesu sāmaññena pavattānampi samānānaṃ tuyhaṃ mayhaṃ tava mamasaddānaṃ saddanayaññeva nissāya paresamanukampāya vuttappakāro niyamo dassitoti avagantabbaṃ. Iccevaṃ –

Moreover, here the word ‘mayhaṃ’ stands in its own form as an inflected word, due to its becoming a single word with the suffix ‘ka.’ Even so, this word ‘mayhako,’ denoting a particular kind of bird, while remaining in the singular, also slightly suggests a sense of ownership, just like the words ‘sujampati’ or ‘rājapurisa.’ For this reason too, a change of case is not your refuge. Thus, since the word ‘mayha,’ which is a component of the term occurring in the designation ‘mayhako,’ is spoken without a change of case, it is established that a change of case should not be sought even in the words ‘tuyhaṃ,’ ‘tava,’ and ‘mama.’ Therefore, it should be understood that the commentary teachers, relying solely on grammatical principles, have shown such a restriction out of compassion for others, even though the words ‘tuyhaṃ,’ ‘mayhaṃ,’ ‘tava,’ and ‘mama’ are commonly used in both the dative and genitive senses. Thus:

“Tuyhaṃ mayha”ntime sadde, sampadāne garū vaduṃ;

“Tava mamā”ti sāmimhi, nayamādāya satthato.

“These words ‘tuyhaṃ’ and ‘mayhaṃ,’ the venerable ones said are in the dative; ‘tava’ and ‘mama’ are in the genitive, taking the principle from the scriptures.”

Evaṃ santepi etesaṃ, niyamo natthi pāḷiyaṃ;

Koci tesaṃ viseso ca, diṭṭho amhehi taṃ suṇa.

Even so, there is no fixed rule for these in the Pāli canon; and some distinction among them has been seen by us—listen to that.

Sāmyatthasampadānatthā, sambhavanti yahiṃ duve;

“Tuyhaṃ mayha”ntime saddā, te payogā na dullabhā.

Where both the genitive and dative senses are possible, these words ‘tuyhaṃ’ and ‘mayhaṃ’ are used, and those usages are not rare.

“Tava mamā”time saddā, pāyā sāmimhi vattare;

Sampadāne yahiṃ honti, te payogā panappakā.

These words ‘tava’ and ‘mama’ mostly occur in the genitive sense; where they are in the dative sense, those usages are indeed few.

Tavato mamato tuyhaṃ-mayhaṃsaddāva sāsane;

Pāṭhe nekasahassamhi, sāmiatthe pavattareti.

In the Dispensation, the words ‘tava,’ ‘mama,’ ‘tuyhaṃ,’ and ‘mayhaṃ’ occur in the genitive sense in many thousands of passages.

Sabbāpi imā nītiyo paramasukhumā sududdasā vīrajātinā sādhukaṃ manasi kātabbā.

All these principles are extremely subtle and very hard to discern, and should be carefully borne in mind by those of noble character.

Vo nosaddesu pana vosaddo paccattaupayogakaraṇasampadānasāmivacanapadapūraṇesu dissati. “Kacci vo [M 0.0392] anuruddhā samaggā sammodamānā”tiādīsu hi paccatte dissati. “Gacchatha bhikkhave paṇāmemi vo”tiādīsu upayoge. “Na vo mama santike vatthabba”ntiādīsu karaṇe. “Vanapatthapariyāyaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmī”tiādīsu sampadāne. “Sabbesaṃ vo sāriputtā subhāsita”ntiādīsu sāmivacane. “Ye hi voariyā parisuddhā kāyakammantā”tiādīsu padapūraṇamatte. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

Among the words ‘vo’ and ‘no,’ the word ‘vo’ is seen in the senses of personal reference, application, instrument, dative, genitive, and as a mere expletive. For example, in phrases like “Kacci vo anuruddhā samaggā sammodamānā” (Are you, Anuruddhas, living in harmony and mutual appreciation?), it appears in personal reference. In “Gacchatha bhikkhave paṇāmemi vo” (Go, monks, I dismiss you), it is seen in application. In “Na vo mama santike vatthabba” (You should not stay near me), it appears in the instrumental sense. In “Vanapatthapariyāyaṃ vo bhikkhave desessāmī” (Monks, I will teach you the Discourse on the Forest Life), it is used in the dative sense. In “Sabbesaṃ vo sāriputtā subhāsita” (All of you, Sāriputtas, have spoken well), it appears in the genitive sense. And in “Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhā kāyakammantā” (For those of you who are noble and pure in bodily conduct), it serves merely as an expletive. Herein, it is said:

“Paccatte upayoge ca, karaṇe sampadāniye;

Sāmissa vacane ceva, tatheva padapūraṇe;

Imesu chasu ṭhānesu, vosaddo sampavattati”.

“In personal reference, application, instrument, dative, in the genitive sense, and likewise as an expletive; in these six instances, the word ‘vo’ occurs.”

Nosaddo paccattopayogakaraṇasampadānasāmivacanāvadhāraṇanusaddatthesu paṭisedhe nipātamatte ca vattati. Ayañhi “gāmaṃ no gaccheyyāmā”ti ettha paccatte dissati. “Mā no ajja vikantiṃsu, rañño sūdā mahānase”tiādīsu upayoge. “Na no vivāho nāgehi, katapubbo kudācana”ntiādīsu karaṇe. “Saṃvibhajetha no rajjenā”tiādīsu sampadāne. “Satthā no bhagavā anuppatto”tiādīsu sāmivacane. “Na no samaṃ atthi tathāgatenā”ti ettha avadhāraṇe. “Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ mahārājā”tiādīsu nusaddatthe, pucchāyantipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati. “Subhāsitaññeva bhāseyya, no ca dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇe”tiādīsu paṭisedhe. “Na no sabhāyaṃ na karonti kiñcī”tiādīsu nipātamatte. Etthetaṃ vuccati –

The word ‘no’ is used in the senses of personal reference, application, instrument, dative, genitive, emphasis, in the sense of the particle ‘nu,’ in prohibition, and as a mere particle. For example, in “Gāmaṃ no gaccheyyāmā” (We would go to the village), it appears in personal reference. In “Mā no ajja vikantiṃsu, rañño sūdā mahānase” (Let not the king’s cooks cut us up today in the royal kitchen), it is seen in application. In “Na no vivāho nāgehi, katapubbo kudācana” (No marriage with nāgas was ever performed by us), it appears in the instrumental sense. In “Saṃvibhajetha no rajjenā” (Share the kingdom with us), it is used in the dative. In “Satthā no bhagavā anuppatto” (Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived), it appears in the genitive sense. In “Na no samaṃ atthi tathāgatenā” (There is none equal to the Tathāgata for us), it serves for emphasis. In “Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ mahārājā” (Do you, great king, remember?), it is used in the sense of the particle ‘nu,’ and it can also be said to be used in questions. In “Subhāsitaññeva bhāseyya, no ca dubbhāsitaṃ bhaṇe” (One should speak only well-spoken words, and not speak ill-spoken words), it appears in prohibition. And in “Na no sabhāyaṃ na karonti kiñcī” (Indeed, they do nothing in the assembly), it serves as a mere particle. Herein, it is said:

Paccatte [M 0.0393] cupayoge ca, karaṇe sampadāniye;

Sāmyāvadhāraṇe ceva, nusaddatthe nivāraṇe;

Tathā nipātamattamhi, nosaddo sampavattati.

In personal reference, application, instrument, dative, in the genitive and for emphasis, in the sense of the particle ‘nu,’ in prohibition, and likewise as a mere particle—the word ‘no’ occurs.

Idāni sabbanāmānaṃ yathārahaṃ saṃkhittena missakapadamālā vuccate –

Now, a concise mixed paradigm of all pronouns is stated as appropriate:

Yo so, ye te. Yaṃ taṃ, ye te. Yena tena. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Yā sā, yā tā. Yaṃ taṃ, yā tā. Yāya tāya. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Yaṃ taṃ, yāni tāni. Sesaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Iminā nayena liṅgattayayojanā kātabbā.

Yo so, ye te. Yaṃ taṃ, ye te. Yena tena. The rest should be expanded. Yā sā, yā tā. Yaṃ taṃ, yā tā. Yāya tāya. The rest should be expanded. Yaṃ taṃ, yāni tāni. The rest should be expanded. In this way, the application of the three genders should be made.

“Eso so, ete te. Ayaṃ so, ime te. So ayaṃ te ime”tiādinā yathāpayogaṃ padamālā yojetabbā. Tathā hi “yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako. Ete te bhikkhave ubho ante anupagamma majjhimā paṭipadā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā. Ayaṃ so sārathi etī”ti evamādayo vicittappayogā dissanti. Iti sabbanāmikapadānaṃ missakapadamālā yojetabbā.

“Eso so, ete te. Ayaṃ so, ime te. So ayaṃ, te ime,” and so on—the paradigm should be constructed according to usage. For example, phrases like “Yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako” (That Blessed One, self-existent, without a teacher), “Ete te bhikkhave ubho ante anupagamma majjhimā paṭipadā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā” (These, monks, are the two extremes not to be approached; the Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata), and “Ayaṃ so sārathi eti” (This very charioteer comes)—such varied usages are seen. Thus, the mixed paradigm of pronominal words should be constructed.

Mayā sabbatthasiddhassa, sāsane sabbadassino;

Sabbattha sāsane suṭṭhu, kosallatthāya sotunaṃ.

For the sake of the listeners' skill everywhere in the Dispensation of the All-accomplished, the All-seeing One, this has been well composed by me.

Asabbanāmanāmehi, sabbanāmapadehi ve;

Saha sabbāni vuttāni, sabbanāmāni pantito.

With non-pronominal nouns and with pronominal words, all pronouns have been stated together in sequence.

Etesu katayogānaṃ, sukhumatthavijānanaṃ;

Akicchapaṭivedhena, bhavissati na saṃsayo.

For those who have applied themselves to these, there is no doubt that understanding of subtle meanings will be achieved with effortless penetration.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise in the ways of expression in the nine-limbed Tipiṭaka with its commentaries,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise composed for the sake of skill,

Sabbanāmataṃsadisanāmānaṃ nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo nāma

the section on the nominal paradigms of pronouns and nouns similar to them, named

Dvādasamo paricchedo.

The Twelfth Chapter.

13. Savinicchayasaṅkhyānāmanāmikapadamālā

13. The Nominal Paradigm of Numerical Nouns, with Analysis

Ito [M 0.0394] paraṃ pavakkhāmi, saṅkhyānāmikapantiyo;

Bhūdhātujehi rūpehi, aññehi cupayojituṃ.

Henceforth I shall explain the series of numerical nouns, to be used with forms derived from the root ‘bhū’ and with others.

Yā hi sā heṭṭhā amhehi eka dviti catuiccetesaṃ saṅkhyāsabbanāmānaṃ nāmikapadamālā kathitā, taṃ ṭhapetvā idha asabbanāmānaṃ pañca cha sattādīnaṃ saṅkhyānāmānaṃ nāmikapadamālā bhūdhātumayehi aññehi ca rūpehi yojanatthaṃ vuccate –

Indeed, setting aside that paradigm of the numerical pronouns ‘eka,’ ‘dvi,’ ‘ti,’ and ‘catu,’ which was stated by us previously, here the nominal paradigm of the non-pronominal numerical nouns such as ‘pañca,’ ‘cha,’ ‘satta,’ etc., is stated for the purpose of combining them with forms derived from the root ‘bhū’ and with other forms.

Pañca, pañcahi, pañcabhi, pañcannaṃ, pañcasu. Sattannaṃ vibhattīnaṃ vasena ñeyyaṃ. “Pañca bhūtā, pañca abhibhavitāro, pañca purisā, pañca bhūmiyo, pañca kaññāyo, pañca bhūtāni, pañca cittānī”tiādinā sabbattha yojetabbaṃ. Cha, chahi, chabhi, channaṃ, chasu, chassu itipi. “Chassu loko samuppanno, chassu krubbati santhava”nti hi pāḷi. Satta, sattahi, sattabhi, sattannaṃ, sattasu. Aṭṭha, aṭṭhahi, aṭṭhabhi, aṭṭhannaṃ, aṭṭhasu. Nava, navahi, navabhi, navannaṃ, navasu. Dasa, dasahi, dasabhi, dasannaṃ, dasasu. Evaṃ ekādasa. Dvādasa, bārasa. Terasa, tedasa, teḷasa. Catuddasa, cuddasa. Pañcadasa, pannarasa. Soḷasa. Sattarasa. Aṭṭhārasa, aṭṭhārasahi, aṭṭhārasabhi, aṭṭhārasannaṃ, aṭṭhārasasu. Sabbametaṃ bahuvacanavasena gahetabbaṃ.

Five, by five, by five, of five, in five. It should be understood according to the seven cases. “Five elements, five conquerors, five men, five lands, five maidens, five elements, five minds”—and so on, it should be applied everywhere. Six, by six, by six, of six, in six, and also ‘chassu’. For the Pali text states: “The world arises in six, one makes acquaintance in six.” Seven, by seven, by seven, of seven, in seven. Eight, by eight, by eight, of eight, in eight. Nine, by nine, by nine, of nine, in nine. Ten, by ten, by ten, of ten, in ten. Likewise, eleven. Twelve, twelve. Thirteen, thirteen, thirteen. Fourteen, fourteen. Fifteen, fifteen. Sixteen. Seventeen. Eighteen, by eighteen, by eighteen, of eighteen, in eighteen. All of this should be taken in the plural form.

Ekūnavīsati, ekūnavīsaṃ iccādipi. Ekūnavīsāya, ekūnavīsāyaṃ, ekūnavīsa bhikkhū tiṭṭhanti, ekūnavīsaṃ bhikkhū passati, evaṃ “kaññāyo cittānī”ti ca ādinā yojetabbaṃ. Ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūhi dhammo desito, ekūnavīsāya kaññāhi kataṃ, ekūnavīsāya cittehi kataṃ, ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūnaṃ cīvaraṃ deti, ekūnavīsāya kaññānaṃ dhanaṃ deti, ekūnavīsāya cittānaṃ ruccati, ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūhi apeti[M 0.0395]. Evaṃ kaññāhi cittehi. Ekūnavīsāya bhikkhūnaṃ santakaṃ, evaṃ kaññānaṃ cittānaṃ. Ekūnavīsāyaṃ bhikkhūsu patiṭṭhitaṃ. Evaṃ “kaññāsu cittesū”ti yojetabbaṃ. Ekūnavīsati, ekūnavīsatiṃ, ekūnavīsatiyā, ekūnavīsatiyaṃ.

Nineteen, and also 'ekūnavīsaṃ', etc. The forms are 'ekūnavīsāya', 'ekūnavīsāyaṃ'. 'Nineteen monks stand', 'one sees nineteen monks'; thus it should be combined with 'maidens', 'minds', etc. The Dhamma was taught by nineteen monks; it was done by nineteen maidens; it was done by nineteen minds; one gives robes to nineteen monks; one gives wealth to nineteen maidens; it pleases nineteen minds; one departs from nineteen monks. Likewise with maidens and minds. Belonging to nineteen monks, likewise to maidens and minds. Established in nineteen monks. Thus it should be combined with 'in maidens', 'in minds'. The forms are 'ekūnavīsati', 'ekūnavīsatiṃ', 'ekūnavīsatiyā', 'ekūnavīsatiyaṃ'.

Vīsati, vīsatiṃ, vīsatiyā, vīsatiyaṃ. Vīsa, vīsaṃ, vīsāya, vīsāyaṃ. Tathā ekavīsa dvāvīsa bāvīsa tevīsa catuvīsa iccādīsupi. Tiṃsa, tiṃsaṃ, tiṃsāya, tiṃsāyaṃ. Cattālīsa, cattālīsaṃ, cattālīsāya, cattālīsāyaṃ. Cattārīsa iccādipi. Paññāsa, paññāsaṃ, paññāsāya, paññāsāyaṃ. Paṇṇāsa, paṇṇāsaṃ, paṇṇāsāya, paṇṇāsāyaṃ. Saṭṭhi, saṭṭhiṃ, saṭṭhiyā, saṭṭhiyaṃ. Sattati, sattatiṃ, sattatiyā, sattatiyaṃ. Sattari iccādipi. Asīti, asītiṃ, asītiyā, asītiyaṃ. Navuti. Navutiṃ, navutiyā, navutiyaṃ.

The forms for twenty are: vīsati, vīsatiṃ, vīsatiyā, vīsatiyaṃ; and also vīsa, vīsaṃ, vīsāya, vīsāyaṃ. Likewise for twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-two, twenty-three, twenty-four, and so on. The forms for thirty are: tiṃsa, tiṃsaṃ, tiṃsāya, tiṃsāyaṃ. The forms for forty are: cattālīsa, cattālīsaṃ, cattālīsāya, cattālīsāyaṃ; and also cattārīsa, etc. The forms for fifty are: paññāsa, paññāsaṃ, paññāsāya, paññāsāyaṃ; and also paṇṇāsa, paṇṇāsaṃ, paṇṇāsāya, paṇṇāsāyaṃ. The forms for sixty are: saṭṭhi, saṭṭhiṃ, saṭṭhiyā, saṭṭhiyaṃ. The forms for seventy are: sattati, sattatiṃ, sattatiyā, sattatiyaṃ; and also sattari, etc. The forms for eighty are: asīti, asītiṃ, asītiyā, asītiyaṃ. The forms for ninety are: navuti, navutiṃ, navutiyā, navutiyaṃ.

Itthañca aññathāpi saṅkhyārūpāni gahetabbāni. Ekūnavīsehi, ekūnavīsānaṃ, ekūnavīsesu. “Channavutīna”nti ca ādināpi saṅkhyārūpānaṃ katthaci dassanato keci saddasatthavidū ūnavīsatisaddaṃ sabbadāpi ekavacanantamitthiliṅgameva payuñjanti. Keci “vīsatiādayo ānavuti ekavacanantā itthiliṅgā”ti vadanti. Keci panāhu –

And in this way, and in other ways too, numerical forms should be understood. For example: by nineteen, of nineteen, in nineteen. And because numerical forms are seen in some instances, as with 'channavutīnaṃ' (of ninety-six), etc., some grammarians always use the word 'ūnavīsati' (nineteen) as singular and feminine. Some say: 'Twenty and so on up to ninety are singular and feminine.' Others, however, say—

“Saddā saṅkhyeyyasaṅkhāsu, ekatte vīsatādayo;

Saṅkhatthe dvibahuttamhi, tā tu cānavutitthiyo”ti.

“The words ‘twenty’ and so on, when counting, are in the singular; but when referring to the counted, in the dual and plural, those numbers up to ninety are feminine.”

Ettha dvivacanaṃ chaḍḍetabbaṃ buddhavacane tadabhāvato. Sabbesampi ca tesaṃ yathāvuttavacanaṃ kiñci pāḷippadesaṃ patvā yujjati, kiñci pana patvā na yujjati vīsativīsaṃtiṃsaṃiccādīnañhi saṅkhatthānaṃ saddānaṃ bahuvacanappayogavasenapi pāḷiyaṃ dassanato[M 0.0396], kaccāyane ca yovacanasambhūtarūpavantatādassanato. Tasmā yathāsambhavaṃ yathāpāvacanañca itthiliṅgabhāve tesamekavacanantatā veditabbā atthi natthisaddānaṃ viya.

Here, the dual number should be discarded because of its absence in the Buddha's words. And the aforementioned statement concerning all of them is applicable to some Pali passages, but it is not applicable to others. For indeed, words like 'vīsati', 'vīsaṃ', 'tiṃsaṃ', etc., which denote the things counted, are seen in the Pali text even in the plural, and in Kaccāyana's grammar, the characteristic of having forms that arise from any number is seen. Therefore, according to possibility and according to the texts, their singular nature in the feminine gender should be understood, like the words 'atthi' and 'natthi'.

Atthinatthisaddā hi nipātattā ekattepi bahuttepi pavattanti “puttā matthi dhanammatthi. Natthi attasamaṃ pemaṃ. Natthi samaṇabrāhmaṇā”tiādīsu. Aliṅgattepi panetesaṃ katthaci itthiliṅgabhāvo diṭṭho. Abhidhamme hi dhammasenāpatinā anudhammacakkavattinā vohārakusalena vohārakusalasādhakena “atthiyā nava. Natthiyā navā”ti ekavacanantaṃ itthiliṅgarūpaṃ dassitaṃ, tasmā vīsativīsatimiccādīnampi yathāsambhavaṃ yathāpāvacanañca itthiliṅgabhāve ekavacanantatā veditabbā.

For the words 'atthi' and 'natthi', being particles, occur in both the singular and the plural, as in 'puttā matthi dhanammatthi' (I have sons, I have wealth), 'Natthi attasamaṃ pemaṃ' (There is no love equal to oneself), 'Natthi samaṇabrāhmaṇā' (There are no ascetics or brahmins), etc. However, even though these are genderless, in some instances their feminine gender is seen. For in the Abhidhamma, by the General of the Dhamma, the Turner of the Wheel that follows the Dhamma, skilled in usage and establishing skill in usage, the singular feminine form 'atthiyā nava' (by existence, nine) and 'natthiyā nava' (by non-existence, nine) is shown. Therefore, for words like 'vīsati', 'vīsatiṃ', etc., their singular nature in the feminine gender should be understood according to possibility and according to the texts.

Tattheke “hetuyā adhipatiyā”ti ca idaṃ liṅgavipallāsavasena gahetabbaṃ maññanti. Tammativasena “hetumhi adhipatimhī”ti pulliṅgabhāvo paṭipādetabbo, “hetupaccaye adhipatipaccaye” iccevattho. Atha vā “hetuyā adhipatiyā”ti dvayamidaṃ itthiliṅgarūpapaṭibhāgaṃ pulliṅgarūpanti gahetabbaṃ “hetuyo jantuyo”tiādīnaṃ itthiliṅgarūpapaṭibhāgānaṃ pulliṅgarūpānampi vijjamānattā, “atthiyā natthiyā”ti idaṃ pana liṅgavipallāsavasena vuttanti na gahetabbaṃ atthi natthisaddānaṃ aliṅgabhedattā. Na hi atthi natthisaddā tīsu liṅgesu ekasmimpi antogadhā. Etesu hi atthisaddo ākhyātanipātavasena bhijjati “atthi santi saṃvijjati. Atthikhīrā brāhmaṇī”tiādīsu[M 0.0397], natthisaddo pana nipātoyeva. Iccevaṃ atthi natthisaddānaṃ nipātānañca liṅgavacanavasena kathanaṃ yujjati itthiliṅgādivasena ekattādivasena ca appavattanato. Vuttañca –

There, some think that 'hetuyā' and 'adhipatiyā' should be taken as a case of gender inversion. According to that view, the masculine gender forms 'hetumhi' and 'adhipatimhī' should be established, with the meaning 'in the condition of cause, in the condition of dominance,' which is equivalent to 'hetupaccaye adhipatipaccaye.' Or alternatively, these two, 'hetuyā' and 'adhipatiyā', should be taken as masculine forms that resemble feminine forms, since masculine forms resembling feminine forms, such as 'hetuyo' and 'jantuyo', also exist. However, 'atthiyā' and 'natthiyā' should not be taken as stated by way of gender inversion, because the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' are not differentiated by gender. Indeed, the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' are not included in any of the three genders. For among these, the word 'atthi' is differentiated as a verb and a particle, as in 'atthi, santi, saṃvijjati' and 'atthikhīrā brāhmaṇī', etc., whereas the word 'natthi' is merely a particle. Thus, it is not appropriate to speak of the words 'atthi' and 'natthi', and other particles, in terms of gender and number, because they do not function in terms of feminine gender, etc., or singular number, etc. And it has been said—

“Sadisaṃ tīsu liṅgesu, sabbāsu ca vibhattisu;

Vacanesu ca sabbesu, yaṃ na byeti tadabyaya”nti.

“That which is the same in the three genders, and in all cases, and in all numbers, that which does not change, is an indeclinable.”

Ettha siyā – nanu ca bho “atthi sakkā labbhā iccete paṭhamāyā”ti vacanato atthisaddo paṭhamāya vibhattiyā yutto, evaṃ sante kasmā “sadisaṃ tīsu liṅgesū”tiādi vuttanti? Saccaṃ atthisaddo paṭhamāya vibhattiyā yutto, tathā natthisaddo atthisaddassa vacanalesena gahetabbattā yugaḷapadattā ca. Idaṃ pana “sadisaṃ tīsu liṅgesū”tiādivacanaṃ upasagganipātasaṅkhāte asaṅkhyāsadde sandhāya vuttaṃ, na ekekamasaṅkhyāsaddaṃ sandhāya. Tathā hi “asaṅkhyā”ti ca “abyayā”ti ca laddhavohāresu upasagganipātesu upasaggā sabbepi sabbavibhattivacanakā. Nipātānaṃ pana ekacce paṭhamādīsu yathārahaṃ vibhattiyuttā, ekacce avibhattiyuttā. Tattha ye yadaggena vibhattiyuttā, te tadaggena tabbacanakā. Upasagganipātesu hi paccekaṃ “idaṃ nāma vacana”nti laddhuṃ na sakkā, sabbasaṅgāhakavasena pana “sadisaṃ tīsu liṅgesū”tiādi pubbācariyehi vuttaṃ. Kaccāyanācariyenapi imamevatthaṃ sandhāya “sabbāsamāvusopasagganipātādīhi cā”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi āvusosaddato sabbāpi vibhattiyo labbhanti, atha kho ālapanatthavācakattā ekavacanikaanekavacanikā paṭhamāvibhattiyoyeva labbhanti. Ayamasmākaṃ khanti.

Here it might be said: 'But, sir, since it is stated, “atthi, sakkā, labbhā, etc., are in the first case,” the word “atthi” is connected with the first case. If that is so, why is it said, “similar in the three genders,” etc.?' It is true that the word 'atthi' is connected with the first case, and similarly, the word 'natthi' should be understood by implication from the word 'atthi' and because they are a pair of words. However, this statement, 'similar in the three genders,' etc., is made with reference to indeclinable words designated as prefixes and particles, not with reference to each individual indeclinable word. For indeed, among prefixes and particles, which are known as 'indeclinables' (asaṅkhyā) and 'immutables' (abyayā), all prefixes have all case and number forms. Of the particles, however, some are connected with the first case, etc., as appropriate, while some are not connected with any case. Among these, those that are connected with a case ending in some respect, have that number and case in that respect. Indeed, with regard to prefixes and particles individually, it is not possible to determine, 'this is a form of this number,' but the ancient teachers have stated 'similar in the three genders,' etc., in a comprehensive way. The teacher Kaccāyana also spoke with this very meaning in mind when he said, 'and with all the 'āvuso' (vocative particles), prefixes, and particles.' For not all case endings are obtained from the word 'āvuso,' but because it expresses the meaning of address, only the singular and plural forms of the first case are obtained. This is our understanding.

Keci [M 0.0398] pana sabbehipi nipātehi sabbavibhattilopaṃ vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. “Atthi sakkā labbhā iccete paṭhamāya. Divā bhiyyo namo iccete paṭhamāya ca dutiyāya cā”tiādivacanato, padapūraṇamattānañca avibhattiyuttānaṃ atha khalu vata vatha iccādīnaṃ nipātānaṃ vacanato. Etthāpi siyā “nanu ca bho avibhattiyuttānampi nipātānaṃ sambhavato atthi natthisaddānaṃ avibhattiko niddeso kātabbo, atha kimatthaṃ ‘atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā’ti savibhattiko niddeso kato”ti? Sabbathā vibhattīhi vinā atthassa niddisitumasakkuṇeyyattāti.

However, some say that all particles undergo the elision of all case endings, but that should not be accepted. This is because of statements like, 'Atthi, sakkā, labbhā, etc., are in the first case; Divā, bhiyyo, namo, etc., are in the first and second cases,' and because of the statement concerning particles like 'atha', 'khalu', 'vata', 'vatha', etc., which merely fill out the sentence and are not connected with case endings. Here it might also be said: 'But, sir, since particles not connected with case endings also exist, shouldn't the explanation of the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' be given without case endings? Why then is the explanation given with case endings, as 'atthiyā nava' and 'natthiyā navā'?' The reason is that it would be impossible to indicate the meaning in every way without case endings.

Yadi evaṃ “atthi sakkā labbhā iccete paṭhamāyā”ti vacanato atthi natthisaddā luttāya paṭhamāya vibhattiyā vasena paṭhamāvibhattikāyeva niddisitabbā, evamakatvā kasmā sattamyantavasena “atthiyā natthiyā”ti niddiṭṭhāti? Saccaṃ, atthi natthisaddā paṭhamāvibhattiyuttāyeva niddisitabbā, tathāpi “atthipaccaye nava, natthipaccaye navā”ti etassatthassa paridīpane paṭhamāya okāso natthi, sattamiyāyeva pana atthi, tasmā “atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā”ti vuttaṃ. Iti atthiyānatthiyāsaddānaṃ sattamyantabhāve siddheyeva tatiyācatutthīpañcamīchaṭṭhiyantabhāvopi siddhoyeva hoti. Tasmā “atthibhāvo atthitā”tiādīsupi atthiyā bhāvo atthibhāvo, natthiyā bhāvo natthibhāvo, atthiyā bhāvo atthitābhiādinā samāsataddhitaviggaho avassamicchitabbo. Yadidamamhehi vuttaṃ, taṃ “pāḷiyā virujjhatī”ti na vattabbaṃ pāḷinayānusārena vuttattāti.

If so, then according to the statement, 'atthi, sakkā, labbhā, etc., are in the first case,' the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' should be indicated as being in the first case by means of the elided first case ending. Not having done so, why are they indicated by means of the locative ending, as in 'atthiyā, natthiyā'? It is true, the words 'atthi' and 'natthi' should be indicated as connected with the first case ending. However, in explaining the meaning 'nine in the condition of presence, nine in the condition of absence,' there is no occasion for the first case, but there is for the locative. Therefore, it is said, 'atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā.' Thus, with the words 'atthiyā' and 'natthiyā' being established as ending in the locative, their ending in the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth cases is also established. Therefore, in expressions like 'atthibhāvo, atthitā,' etc., the analysis of the compounds and derivatives—such as 'atthibhāvo is the state of atthi,' 'natthibhāvo is the state of natthi,' 'atthitā is the state of atthi,' and so on—must necessarily be accepted. What has been stated by us should not be said to contradict the Pāli, for it has been stated in accordance with the method of the Pāli.

Evaṃ hotu, kasmā bho “atthiyā, natthiyā”ti itthiliṅganiddeso kato, nanu nipātopasaggā aliṅgabhedāti? Saccaṃ, idaṃ pana ṭhānaṃ atīva sukhumaṃ, tathāpi pubbācariyānubhāvaññeva [M 0.0399] nissāya vinicchayaṃ brūma. Yathā hi vīsatiiccādīnaṃ saṅkhyāsaddānaṃ sarūpato adabbavācakattepi dabbavācakānaṃ latāmatirattiitthī yāguvadhūsaddānaṃ viya itthiliṅgabhāvo saddasatthavidūhi anumato, evaṃ adabbavācakattepi atthi natthisaddānaṃ katthaci itthiliṅgabhāvo saddhammavidūhi anumato. Tenāha āyasmā dhammasenāpati “atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā”ti. Atha vā “atthiyā, natthiyā”ti imāni liṅgabhāvavinimuttāni sattamiyantāni nipātapadānītipi gahetabbāni, na ettha codetabbaṃ, evarūpāni nipātapadāni pubbācariyehi vuttāni na santi, tasmā chaḍḍetabbamidaṃ vacananti.

Let it be so. But why, good sir, was the designation of feminine gender assigned to 'atthiyā, natthiyā'? Are not particles and prefixes without gender distinction? Indeed, this point is extremely subtle. Nevertheless, relying solely on the authority of the ancient teachers, we make this determination. Just as, for example, number words like 'vīsati,' though not denoting substances in form, are treated as feminine in form—similar to words like 'latā,' 'mati,' 'ratti,' 'itthī,' 'yāgu,' 'vadhū,' which denote substances and whose feminine gender is accepted by grammarians—so too, though 'atthi' and 'natthi' do not denote substances, their feminine gender is accepted in certain contexts by experts in the good Dhamma. Therefore, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati said, 'atthiyā nava, natthiyā navā.' Alternatively, 'atthiyā, natthiyā' can be taken as indeclinable particles in the locative case, free from gender specification. No fault should be found here, nor should one object, 'Such indeclinable particles were not mentioned by the ancient teachers; therefore, this statement should be discarded.'

Pāvacanasmiñhi garūhi aniddiṭṭhānipi anekavihitāni nipātapadāni sandissanti, nāpi “hetuyā, adhipatiyā, atthiyā, natthiyā”ti evamādīsu “apasaddā ime”ti virodho uppādetabbo. Na hi acinteyyānubhāvena pāramitāpuññena nipphannena anāvaraṇañāṇena sabbaṃ ñeyyamaṇḍalaṃ hatthatale āmalakaṃ viya paccakkhaṃ katvā passato buddhassa vacane aññesaṃ vācāvippalāpo avassaṃ labbhatīti. Nanu ca bho “hetuyā, adhipatiyā, atthiyā, natthiyā”ti ca idaṃ sāriputtattheravacanaṃ tena nikkhittattā. Tathāgatena hi tāvatiṃsabhapane desitakāle imāni padāni na santi, evaṃ sante kasmā “buddhavacana”nti vadathāti? Buddhavacanaṃyeva nāma. Āyasmato hi sāriputtassa tathāgatena nayo dinno, tenapi pabhinnapaṭisambhidena satthukappena aggasāvakena satthu santikā nayaṃ labhitvā byañjanaṃ suropitaṃ kataṃ. Sabbepi hi paṭisambhidappattā ariyā dunniruttiṃ na vadanti niruttipabhedasmiṃ sukusalattā, tasmā aññesamavisayo esa ariyānaṃ vohāroti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In the teachings of the venerable ones, various kinds of particles, even those unmentioned, are found, nor should one raise an objection, saying, 'These are improper words,' in phrases like 'hetuyā, adhipatiyā, atthiyā, natthiyā.' For indeed, with the inconceivable power of perfected merit and unobstructed knowledge, the Buddha directly perceives the entire sphere of knowable things as clearly as an āmalaka fruit in the palm of his hand—how then could the contradictory speech of others necessarily be found in the Buddha's word? But, good sirs, this phrase 'hetuyā, adhipatiyā, atthiyā, natthiyā' is the word of the Elder Sāriputta, and thus it was established by him. For at the time of the teaching in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, these words were not present in the Tathāgata's discourse. If so, why do you call them 'the Buddha's word'? They are indeed the Buddha's word. For the method was given by the Tathāgata to the Venerable Sāriputta, and he—endowed with the analytical knowledges, the chief disciple who was like the Teacher—having received the method from the Teacher, skillfully arranged the wording. Indeed, all noble ones who have attained the analytical knowledges do not speak incorrectly, being highly skilled in the distinctions of language. Therefore, this usage of the noble ones should be seen as a sphere beyond the comprehension of others.

Idāni [M 0.0400] satādīnaṃ nāmikapadamālā vuccate –

Now, the paradigm of nominal forms beginning with 'sata' is stated:

Sataṃ, satāni, satā. Sataṃ, satāni, sate. Satena, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ. Satā, satasmā, satamhā, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ. Sate, satasmiṃ, satamhi, satesu. Evaṃ sahassaṃ, sahassānīti yojetabbaṃ. Dasasahassaṃ satasahassaṃ dasasatasahassanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panettha payogo “sataṃ bhikkhū, sataṃ itthiyo, sataṃ cittāni. Bhikkhūnaṃ sataṃ, itthīnaṃ sataṃ, cittānaṃ sataṃ. Sahassādīsupi eseva nayo. Itthañca aññathāpi saddarūpāni bhavanti. Koṭi, koṭī, koṭiyo. Rattinayena ñeyyaṃ.

Sataṃ, satāni, satā. Sataṃ, satāni, sate. Satena, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ. Satā, satasmā, satamhā, satehi, satebhi. Satassa, satānaṃ. Sate, satasmiṃ, satamhi, satesu. In this way, 'sahassaṃ, sahassāni' should be construed. The same method applies to 'dasasahassaṃ, satasahassaṃ, dasasatasahassaṃ'. Here is an example of usage: 'sataṃ bhikkhū' (a hundred monks), 'sataṃ itthiyo' (a hundred women), 'sataṃ cittāni' (a hundred minds); 'bhikkhūnaṃ sataṃ' (a hundred of monks), 'itthīnaṃ sataṃ' (a hundred of women), 'cittānaṃ sataṃ' (a hundred of minds). The same method applies to 'sahassa' and so on. And in this way, there are also other word-forms. Koṭi, koṭī, koṭiyo. This should be understood according to the pattern of 'ratti'.

Ekappabhutito yāva, dasakā yā pavattati;

Saṅkhyā tāva sā saṅkhyeyya-ppadhānāti garū vaduṃ.

The venerable ones have said: the number that proceeds from one up to ten has the enumerated as predominant.

Vīsatito yāva satā, yā saṅkhyā tāva sā pana;

Saṅkhyāppadhānā saṅkhyeyya-ppadhānāti ca vaṇṇayuṃ.

But as for the number from twenty up to a hundred, they describe it as being both number-predominant and enumerated-predominant.

Apica –

Furthermore:

Vīsato yāva koṭiyā, saṅkhyā tāva hi sā khalu;

Saṅkhyāppadhānā saṅkhyeyya-ppadhānā cāti niddise.

Indeed, the number from twenty up to a crore should be declared as both number-predominant and enumerated-predominant.

Tathā hi “asīti koṭiyo hitvā, hiraññassāpi pabbaji”nti, “khīṇāsavā vītamalā, samiṃsu satakoṭiyo”ti ca pāḷi dissati.

For thus the Pāḷi is seen: 'Having abandoned eighty crores, he went forth even from gold,' and 'A hundred crores of taintless ones, free from defilements, assembled.'

Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne sabbesaṃ saṅkhyāsaddarūpānaṃ pākaṭīkaraṇena viññūnaṃ sukhumañāṇapaṭilābhatthaṃ sāṭṭhakathaṃ udānapāḷippadesaṃ aññañca pāḷippadesamaṭṭhakathāvacanañca āharitvā dassayissāmi –

In this place, however, for the purpose of making clear all numerical terms and their forms and for the wise to attain subtle knowledge, I will present a passage from the Udāna Pāḷi together with its commentary, and other Pāḷi passages and commentary statements.

“Yesaṃ [M 0.0401] kho visākhe sataṃ piyāni, sataṃ tesaṃ dukkhāni, yesaṃ navuti piyāni, navuti tesaṃ dukkhāni. Yesaṃ asīti…pe… yesaṃ sattati. Yesaṃ saṭṭhi. Yesaṃ paññāsaṃ, yesaṃ cattārīsaṃ, yesaṃ tiṃsaṃ. Yesaṃ kho visākhe vīsaṃ piyāni, vīsati tesaṃ dukkhāni. Yesaṃ dasa. Yesaṃ nava. Yesaṃ aṭṭha. Yesaṃ satta. Yesaṃ cha. Yesaṃ pañca. Yesaṃ cattāri. Yesaṃ tīṇi. Yesaṃ dve. Yesaṃ ekaṃ piyaṃ, tesaṃ ekaṃ dukkha”nti.

Indeed, Visākhā, for those who have a hundred dear things, there are a hundred sorrows. For those who have ninety dear things, there are ninety sorrows. For those who have eighty... seventy... sixty... fifty... forty... thirty... Indeed, Visākhā, for those who have twenty dear things, there are twenty sorrows. For those who have ten... nine... eight... seven... six... five... four... three... two. For those who have one dear thing, there is one sorrow.

Tattha sataṃ piyānīti sataṃ piyāyitabbavatthūni. “Sataṃ piya”ntipi keci paṭhanti. Ettha ca yasmā ekato paṭṭhāya yāva dasa, tāva saṅkhyāsaṅkhyeyyappadhānā, tasmā “yesaṃ dasa piyāni, dasa tesaṃ dukkhānī”tiādinā pāḷi āgatā. Keci pana “yesaṃ dasa piyānaṃ, dasa tesaṃ dukkhāna”ntiādinā paṭhanti, taṃ na sundaraṃ. Yasmā pana vīsatito paṭṭhāya yāva sataṃ, tāva saṅkhyeyyappadhānā saṅkhyāppadhānā ca, tasmā tatthāpi saṅkhyeyyappadhānaṃyeva gahetvā “yesaṃ kho visākhe sataṃ piyāni, sataṃ tesaṃ dukkhānī”tiādinā pāḷi āgatā. Sabbesampi ca yesaṃ ekaṃ piyaṃ, ekaṃ tesaṃ dukkhanti pāṭho, na pana dukkhassāti. Ekasmiñhi padakkame ekarasāva bhagavato desanā hotīti. Tasmā yathāvuttanayāva pāḷi veditabbā. Ayaṃ tāva sāṭṭhakatho udānapāḷippadeso.

Here, 'sataṃ piyāni' means a hundred things that are dear. Some also read it as 'sataṃ piya'. In this connection, since from one up to ten the enumerated is predominant, therefore the Pāḷi passage 'yesaṃ dasa piyāni, dasa tesaṃ dukkhānī' etc., occurs. Some, however, read it as 'yesaṃ dasa piyānaṃ, dasa tesaṃ dukkhānaṃ' etc., but that is not good. Moreover, since from twenty up to a hundred, they are both enumerated-predominant and number-predominant, therefore there too, taking the enumerated as predominant, the Pāḷi passage 'yesaṃ kho visākhe sataṃ piyāni, sataṃ tesaṃ dukkhānī' etc., occurs. And for all, the reading is 'yesaṃ ekaṃ piyaṃ, ekaṃ tesaṃ dukkhaṃ,' but not 'dukkhassa.' For in a single sequence, the Blessed One's teaching is of one flavor. Therefore, the Pāḷi should be understood just according to the method stated. This, then, is a section of the Udāna Pāḷi along with its commentary.

Idāni añño pāḷippadeso aṭṭhakathāpāṭhappadeso ca nīyate –

Now another passage of the Pāḷi text and a passage from the commentary are presented –

“Sataṃ [M 0.0402] hatthī sataṃ assā, sataṃ assatarīrathā;

Sataṃ kaññā sahassāni, āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā;

Ekassa padavītihārassa, kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasi”nti

A hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred mule-drawn chariots; A hundred thousand maidens, adorned with jeweled earrings; Are not worth a sixteenth part of a single footstep.

Pāḷi. Ettha “sataṃ hatthī”tiādīni visesitāni, “sahassānī”ti visesanaṃ, tasmā sataṃsaddaṃ sahassasaddena yojetvā “hatthī”tiādīni pana upapadaṃ katvā attho gahetabbo. Hatthī sataṃ sahassāni. Assā sataṃ sahassāni. Assatarīrathā sataṃ sahassāni. Āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā kaññā sataṃ sahassāni. Idaṃ saṅkhyeyyappadhānavasenatthagahaṇaṃ. Saṅkhyāppadhānavasena pana ayampi attho gahetabbo “hatthīnaṃ satasahassaṃ, assānaṃ satasahassaṃ, assatarīrathānaṃ satasahassaṃ, āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalānaṃ kaññānaṃ satasahassa”nti. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo. “Yojanānaṃ satānucco, himavā pañca pabbato”ti ayamaṭṭhakathāpāṭho. Ettha “pañcā”ti saddaṃ satasaddena saddhiṃ yojetvā “sippikānaṃ sataṃ natthī”ti ettha viya himavā pabbato yojanānaṃ pañca satāni uccoti saṅkhyāppadhānavasena attho gahetabbo. “Pañca satānī”ti ca addhuno accantasaṃyogavasena upayogavacanaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo. Satamiti saddo “sataṃ homi, sahassaṃ homī”tiādīsu ekavacano. “Athetthekasataṃ khatyā, anuyantā yasassino”tiādīsu bahuvacano. Evaṃ sahassādīnampi ekavacanabahuvacanatā labbhati. Tathā hi “bhiyyo naṃ satasahassaṃ, yakkhānaṃ payirupāsatī”ti ettha “satasahassa”nti ekavacanaṃ. “Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavissantī”ti ettha sahassanti bahuvacananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Pāḷi. Here, 'a hundred elephants' and so forth are the specified terms, while 'thousands' is the specifying term. Thus, the word 'hundred' should be combined with the word 'thousand,' and the meaning should be understood by treating 'elephants' and so forth as subordinate words: A hundred thousand elephants. A hundred thousand horses. A hundred thousand chariots drawn by mules. A hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings. This is the way of understanding the meaning with the enumerated as predominant. Alternatively, the meaning can also be understood with the number as predominant: 'a hundred thousand of elephants, a hundred thousand of horses, a hundred thousand of chariots drawn by mules, a hundred thousand of maidens adorned with jeweled earrings.' This method should be applied in other similar instances. The commentary passage states: 'The Himavā mountain, with five peaks, is a hundred yojanas high.' Here, the word 'five' should be combined with the word 'hundred,' and the meaning should be understood with the number as predominant, as in 'the Himavā mountain is five hundred yojanas high,' just as in the phrase 'there are not a hundred artisans.' The words 'pañca satāni' (five hundred) are an accusative of usage in the sense of continuous connection with a measure of distance. This method should be applied in other similar instances. The word 'sataṃ' (hundred) is singular in phrases like 'may I become a hundred, may I become a thousand,' and so forth. In phrases like 'Here, one hundred Khattiyas, glorious attendants,' and so forth, it is plural. Similarly, the singular and plural forms of words like 'thousand' can also be found. For example, in the phrase 'more than a hundred thousand yakkhas attend upon him,' 'satasahassaṃ' (a hundred thousand) is singular. In the phrase 'but his sons will be more than a thousand,' 'sahassanti' is plural—this should be understood.

“Kappe [M 0.0403] ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye;

Amaraṃ nāma nagaraṃ, dassaneyyaṃ manorama”nti

In a hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables, there was a city named Amara, lovely to see and delightful.

Pāḷi. Ettha “kappe ca satasahasse caturo ca asaṅkhiyeti sāmiatthe upayogabahuvacanaṃ, tasmā “mahākappānaṃ satasahassānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhiyānaṃ matthake”ti attho gahetabbo, “matthake”ti cettha vacanaseso. “Kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhiyānaṃ matthake”iccevattho. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

Pāḷi. Here, 'kappe ca satasahasse caturo ca asaṅkhiye' is a plural of usage in the sense of the genitive. Thus, the meaning should be understood as 'at the peak of a hundred thousand great aeons and four incalculables,' where 'at the peak' is the omitted part of the statement. The meaning is 'at the peak of four incalculables exceeding a hundred thousand aeons.' This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Kappe ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye;

Etthantare yaṃ caritaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ bodhipācana”nti

For a hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables, whatever conduct was in that interval, all that was for the ripening of enlightenment.

Pāḷi. Ettha “kappe”ti accantasaṃyogavasena upayogabahuvacanaṃ. “Satasahasse kappe”ti kappasaddasambandhena cāyaṃ pulliṅganiddeso upayoganiddeso ca. Samānādhikaraṇañhi idaṃ kappasaddena. “Caturo ca asaṅkhiye”ti acchantasaṃyogavasena upayogabahuvacanāni. Kassa pana asaṅkhiyeti? Aññassa avuttattā kappassa ca vuttattā pakaraṇato “kappāna”nti ayamattho viññāyateva. Na hi vuttaṃ vajjetvā avuttassa kassaci gahaṇaṃ yuttanti. Casaddo sampiṇḍanattho “mahākappānaṃ caturo asaṅkhyeyye satasahasse ca mahākappe”ti. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

Pāḷi. Here, 'kappe' is a plural of usage in the sense of the accusative of duration. 'Satasahasse kappe' is a masculine designation and a designation of usage in connection with the word 'kappa,' for this is in apposition with the word 'kappa.' 'Caturo ca asaṅkhiye' are plural accusatives of duration. But incalculables of what? Since nothing else is stated, and 'kappa' is stated, from the context the meaning 'of aeons' is clearly understood. Indeed, it is not proper to abandon what is stated and take up something unstated. The word 'ca' has the meaning of combining, yielding the sense: 'four incalculable great aeons and a hundred thousand great aeons.' This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Ghaṭānekasahassāni, kumbhīnañca satā bahū”ti pāḷi. Ettha ghaṭāti ghaṭānaṃ. Sāmiatthe hi idaṃ paccattavacanaṃ. “Ghaṭānaṃ anekasahassāni” iccevattho. Kumbhīnañca satā bahūti anekāni ca kumbhīnaṃ satāni. Ettha nikāralopo daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

'Many thousands of pots, and many hundreds of jars.' Pāḷi. Here, 'ghaṭā' means 'of pots' (ghaṭānaṃ). For this is a singular word in the sense of the genitive. Thus, the meaning is 'many thousands of pots.' 'Kumbhīnañca satā bahū' means 'and many hundreds of jars.' Here, the elision of the letter 'n' should be understood. This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Dasavīsasahassānaṃ[M 0.0404], dhammābhisamayo ahu;

Ekadvinnaṃ abhisamayo, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyo”ti

A realization of the Dhamma occurred for ten or twenty thousand; the realization for ones and twos was countless in number.

Pāḷi. Ettha dasavīsasahassānanti dasasahassānaṃ vīsasahassānañca. Dhammābhisamayoti catusaccappaṭivedho. Ekadvinnanti sīsamattakathanaṃ, tena “ekassa ceva dvinnañca tiṇṇaṃ catunnaṃ…pe… dasanna”ntiādinā nayena asaṅkhyeyyoti attho. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

Pāḷi. Here, 'dasavīsasahassānanti' means 'of ten thousand and of twenty thousand.' 'Dhammābhisamayo' means the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. 'Ekadvinnanti' is merely a summary statement; by this method, the meaning is that 'of one, and of two, of three, of four... up to ten' indicates a countless number. This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Cattāri satasahassāni, chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā;

Dīpaṅkaraṃ lokaviduṃ, parivārenti sabbadā”ti

Four hundred thousand, endowed with the six higher knowledges and great psychic power, always attend upon Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the world.

Pāḷi. Ettha cattāri satasahassānīti idaṃ liṅgabhedavasena “chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā”ti imehi dvīhi padehi samānādhikaraṇaṃ. Īdisesu hi ṭhānesu asaṅkhyeyya vācakopi saddo napuṃsakova hoti, tasmā “cattāri satasahassānī”ti ca “chaḷabhiññā”ti ca “mahiddhikā”ti ca etaṃ padattayaṃ samānādhikaraṇaṃ. Atha vā chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikāti chaḷabhiññānaṃ mahaddhikānanti sāmiatthe paccattavacanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ panatthe “cattāri satasahassānī”ti ayaṃ saṅkhyāvacano bhavati. “Tīṇi satasahassāni, nāriyo samalaṅkatā”tiādīsupi ayaṃ nayo netabbo. “Tā ca satta satā bhariyā, dāsyo satta satāni cā”ti pāḷi. Ettha satāti “satānī”ti napuṃsakavasena gahetabbaṃ, na itthiliṅgavasena. “Satā”ti hi “pañca cittā vipākā”tiādīni viya napuṃsakarūpaṃ. Itthiliṅgabhūtā hi satasaddo natthi, tathā pulliṅgabhūto. Yadi ca dviliṅgo satasaddo siyā[M 0.0405], evañca sati “puriso, kaññā”ti ca okārantapulliṅgaākārantitthirūpehipibhavitabbaṃ. Rūpadvayampi satasaddassa natthi, tena ñāyati “satasaddo ekantanapuṃsako”ti.

Here, 'cattāri satasahassāni' is in apposition with these two terms, 'chaḷabhiññā' and 'mahiddhikā,' by way of a difference in gender. For in such instances, even a word denoting a number is neuter; thus, these three terms—'cattāri satasahassāni,' 'chaḷabhiññā,' and 'mahiddhikā'—are in apposition. Alternatively, 'chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā' should be understood as a singular term in the sense of the genitive, meaning 'of those with the six superknowledges, of those with great power.' In this sense, 'cattāri satasahassāni' becomes a numerical term. This method should be applied in similar instances such as 'three hundred thousand, adorned women,' and so forth. The Pāli is: 'And those seven hundred wives, and seven hundred female slaves.' Here, 'satā' should be taken in the neuter sense as 'satāni,' not in the feminine sense.
