For 'satā' is a neuter form, like 'five resultant consciousnesses,' and so forth. Indeed, there is no feminine form of the word 'sata,' nor a masculine form. If the word 'sata' were of two genders, then, as with 'puriso' (man) and 'kaññā' (maiden), it would have to occur in both masculine forms ending in -o and feminine forms ending in -ā. But neither of these two forms of the word 'sata' exists; thus it is understood that the word 'sata' is exclusively neuter.

Nanu ca bho “tā devatā sattasatā uḷārā”ti ettha satasaddo itthiliṅgo hutvā dissatīti? Na, napuṃsakoyevāti. Nanu ca bho devatāsaddena samānādhikaraṇoti? Saccaṃ samānādhikaraṇo, tathāpi napuṃsakoyeva. Īdisesu hi saṅkhyāvisayesu samānādhikaraṇabhāvo appamāṇo. Tathā hi “pañca paccekabuddhasatāni imasmiṃ isigilismiṃ pabbate ciravāsino ahesu”nti napuṃsakaliṅgena pulliṅgassa samānādhikaraṇatā dissati, tasmā “tā devatā sattasatā uḷārā”ti etthāpi “sattasatānī”ti napuṃsakabhāvoyevāti avagantabbo. “Satta hatthisate datvā”tiādīsupi satasaddo napuṃsakoyeva. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

But, sir, does not the word 'sata' appear as feminine in the phrase 'tā devatā sattasatā uḷārā' (those seven hundred great deities)? No, it is indeed neuter. But, sir, is it not in apposition with the word 'devatā'? True, it is in apposition, yet it is indeed neuter. For in such numerical contexts, apposition is not a standard. For example, in the phrase 'pañca paccekabuddhasatāni imasmiṃ isigilismiṃ pabbate ciravāsino ahesuṃ' (five hundred Paccekabuddhas long dwelt on this Isigili mountain), the apposition of a neuter gender with a masculine gender is seen. Therefore, in the phrase 'tā devatā sattasatā uḷārā,' it should be understood that it is indeed a neuter form, 'sattasatāni.' Similarly, in phrases like 'satta hatthisate datvā' (having given seven hundred elephants), the word 'sata' is also neuter. This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Navutikoṭisahassehi, parivāresi mahāmunī”ti pāḷi. Ettha “navutikoṭisahassehi bhikkhūhī”ti vā “bhikkhūnaṃ navutikoṭisahassehī”ti vā saṅkhyeyyasaṅkhyāpadhānavasena attho gahetabbo. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

The Pāli is: 'The Great Sage was surrounded by ninety thousand koṭis.' Here, the meaning should be understood as 'with ninety thousand koṭi monks' or 'with ninety thousand koṭis of monks,' according to whether the counted object or the number is prominent. This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Satasahassavassāni, āyu tassa mahesino”ti pāḷi. Ettha “satasahassavassānī”ti kālassa accantasaṃyogavasena upayogavacanaṃ. Tathā “dasavassasahassāni, agāra’majjha so vasī”ti pāḷiyampi. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

The Pāli is: 'The lifespan of that great sage was one hundred thousand years.' Here, 'satasahassavassāni' is a usage in the sense of the accusative of duration. Similarly, in the Pāli: 'For ten thousand years, he lived in the household life.' This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Ito [M 0.0406] satasahassamhi, kappe uppajji nāyako”ti pāḷi, “ekanavute ito kappe”ti pāḷi ca. Ettha satasahassamhi kappeti satasahassānaṃ kappānaṃ matthake. Ekanavute kappeti ekanavutiyā kappānaṃ matthaketi bhummavacanassa sāmibhummavacanavasena attho gahetabbo. Tathā hi “bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”ti ettha bhummavacanassa “bhagavato santike”ti sāmibhummavacanavasena attho gahito. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

The Pāli is: 'A hundred thousand aeons ago from here, the leader arose,' and also the Pāli: 'ninety-one aeons ago from here.' Here, 'satasahassamhi kappe' means 'at the head of a hundred thousand aeons.' 'Ekanavute kappe' means 'at the head of ninety-one aeons'—the meaning of the locative case should be understood in the sense of the genitive-locative. For example, in 'bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī' (the holy life is lived in the Blessed One), the meaning of the locative case is taken in the sense of the genitive-locative, as 'in the presence of the Blessed One.' This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Yadi tattha sahassāni, satāni nahutāni ca;

Nevamhākaṃ bhayaṃ koci, vane vāḷesu vijjatī”ti

If there were thousands, hundreds, and myriads, no fear whatsoever from wild beasts exists for us in the forest.

Pāḷi. Ayametassā attho – tattha vane vāḷānaṃ sahassāni ca satāni ca nahutāni ca yadi vijjanti. Atha vā sahassāni satānīti satasahassāni, vāḷānaṃ satasahassāni ca nahutāni ca yadi vijjanti, evaṃ vijjantesupi vāḷesu kocīti kvaci. Kocisaddo hi “ko te balaṃ mahārājā”ti ettha kosaddo viya kvasaddatthe vattati, nimittatthe cāyaṃ niddeso. Tena “koci kvaci kismiñci vāḷe ekassapi vāḷamigassa kāraṇā nevamhākaṃ bhayaṃ vijjatī”ti attho gahetabbo. Atha vā kocīti kiñci appamattakampi. Ettha pana “vāḷesū”ti nimittatthe bhummaṃ. Vāḷānaṃ kāraṇā appamattakampi amhākaṃ bhayaṃ na vijjatīti. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

This is its meaning: In that forest, if there are thousands, hundreds, and myriads of wild animals. Or alternatively, `sahassāni satāni` means `satasahassāni` (hundreds of thousands); if there are hundreds of thousands and myriads of wild animals. Even with such wild animals present, 'koci' means 'somewhere.' For the word 'koci' here functions like the word 'ko' in 'ko te balaṃ mahārājā' (What is your strength, O great king?), in the sense of 'where,' and this designation is in the sense of a cause. Therefore, the meaning to be understood is: 'Nowhere, on account of any wild animal, even a single wild beast, does fear exist for us.' Or alternatively, 'koci' means 'anything,' 'even a little.' Here, however, 'vāḷesu' is a locative in the sense of a cause. The meaning is: 'Because of the wild animals, not even a little fear exists for us.' This method should be applied in other similar instances.

“Sabbaṃ satasahassāni, chattiṃsaparimaṇḍalaṃ;

Dasañceva sahassāni, aḍḍhuḍḍhāni satāni cā”ti

All complete: thirty-six hundred thousands; and ten thousand, and two hundred and fifty.

Aṭṭhakathāpāṭho[M 0.0407]. Ettha yasmā saddato samānavibhattiliṅgavacanānaṃ padānaṃ asamānavibhattiliṅgavacanānaṃ vā atthato pana samānānaṃ dūre ṭhitānampi ekasambandho hoti, itaresaṃ samīpe ṭhitānampi na hoti, tasmā “sabba”ntidaṃ “parimaṇḍala”ntiminā sambandhitabbaṃ. “Chattiṃsā”ti idaṃ pana “satasahassānī”timinā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

The commentary text. Here, because words that are the same in case, gender, and number in form, or different in case, gender, and number but the same in meaning, have a single connection even when placed far apart, while others, even when placed close, do not, therefore, 'sabbaṃ' should be connected with 'parimaṇḍalaṃ'. 'Chattiṃsa', however, should be connected with 'satasahassāni'. This method should be applied in other such instances as well.

“Duve satasahassāni, cattāri nahutāni ca;

Ettakaṃ bahalattena, saṅkhātāyaṃ vasundharā”ti

Two hundred thousand, and four myriads; by so much thickness is this earth reckoned.

Aṭṭhakathāpāṭho. Ettha “duve”ti visesanaṃ, “satasahassānī”ti visesitabbaṃ. Tathā “cattārī”ti visesanaṃ, “nahutānī”ti visesitabbaṃ. Tathā hi “satasahassāni nahutāni cā”ti imāni “duve cattārī”ti imehi visesitabbattā “dvisatasahassaṃ catunahuta”nti atthappakāsanāni bhavanti. Evaṃ santepi “duve”iccādīnaṃ saṅkhyāsaddānaṃ “satasahassānī”tiādīhi saṅkhyāsaddehi samānādhikaraṇatā pubbācariyehi na vuttā. Yasmā pana yathā “duve puthujjanā vuttā. Satasahassaṃ bhikkhū”tiādīsu samānādhikaraṇatā labbhati dabbavācakattā visesitabbapadānaṃ, na tathā “duve satasahassānī”tiādīsu adabbavācakattā visesitabbapadānaṃ, tasmā īdisesu ṭhānesu samānādhikaraṇatā na icchitabbā yuttiyā abhāvato. Yadi evaṃ “kusalā, rūpaṃ, cakkhumā”tiādīnaṃ viya imesamaññamaññasambandharahitā siyāti? Na, visesanavisesitabbabhāvena gahitattā. Yajjevaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvo laddhabboti? Na, niyamābhāvato. Ekantena hi [M 0.0408] guṇaguṇīnaṃyeva visesanavisesitabbānaṃ samānādhikaraṇabhāvo, na itaresaṃ visesanavisesitabbattepi.

The commentary text. Here, 'duve' (two) is the qualifier, and 'satasahassāni' (hundred thousands) is the qualified. Similarly, 'cattāri' (four) is the qualifier, and 'nahutāni' (myriads) is the qualified. Thus, these terms, 'satasahassāni' and 'nahutāni', being qualified by 'duve' and 'cattāri', become expressions of meaning like 'two hundred thousand' and 'four myriads'. Even so, the appositional relation of number words like 'duve' with number words like 'satasahassāni' was not stated by earlier teachers. For, whereas in instances like 'duve puthujjanā vuttā' (two ordinary persons are mentioned) and 'satasahassaṃ bhikkhū' (a hundred thousand monks), apposition is obtained because the qualified terms denote substances, it is not so in instances like 'duve satasahassāni' (two hundred thousands), where the qualified terms do not denote substances. Therefore, in such cases, apposition should not be accepted, due to the lack of logical justification. If so, would they be devoid of mutual connection, like 'kusalā' (wholesome), 'rūpaṃ' (form), and 'cakkhumā' (possessing an eye)? No, because they are taken as having the relationship of qualifier and qualified. Should appositional relation then be obtained? No, due to the absence of a fixed rule. For, strictly, appositional relation exists only between qualities and their possessors when they are qualifier and qualified, not for others, even when they have the nature of qualifier and qualified.

Tattha “ettaka”nti pamāṇavacanaṃ. “Bahalattenā”ti visesane tatiyā. Ubhayena imamatthaṃ dasseti “ayaṃ vasundharā bahalattena yojanānaṃ duve satasahassāni cattāri nahutāni ca ettakaṃ saṅkhātā”ti. “Ettaka”nti padassa ca “duve satasahassāni cattāri nahutāni cā”ti imehi vā “vasundharā”ti iminā vā samānādhikaraṇatā na icchitabbā. Ettakanti hi bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, yaṃ saddasatthe kriyāvisesananti vadanti. Tassa “ettakena pamāṇena”iccevattho. Apica “duve satasahassāni cattāri na hutāni cā”ti imesampi “vasundharā”ti iminā samānādhikaraṇatā na icchitabbā “bhikkhūnaṃ sata”nti ettha satasaddassa viya saṅkhyāvacanamattattā. Tathā hi “ettaka”nti vuttaṃ. “Saṅkhātā”ti pana “aya”nti ca imesaṃ “vasundharā”ti iminā samānādhikaraṇatā labbhati. Sabbopāyaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

Here, 'ettakaṃ' is a term denoting measure. 'Bahalattena' is the instrumental case used as a qualifier. Both indicate this meaning: 'This earth, by thickness, is reckoned as so much—two hundred thousand and four myriads of yojanas.' The word 'ettakaṃ' should not be construed as having the same referent as 'two hundred thousand and four myriads' or as 'earth'. For 'ettakaṃ' is a neuter adverb, which in the science of grammar is called a qualifier of action. Its meaning is 'by this much measure'. Moreover, 'two hundred thousand and four myriads' should not be construed as having the same referent as 'earth', because, like the word 'hundred' in 'bhikkhūnaṃ sataṃ' (a hundred monks), it merely denotes a number. For this reason, 'ettakaṃ' is stated. However, 'saṅkhātā' (reckoned) and 'ayaṃ' (this) can be construed as having the same referent as 'vasundharā' (earth). This method should be applied in all other such instances.

“Dasettha rājiyo setā, dassanīyā manoramā;

Cha piṅgalā pannarasa, haliddā tā catuddasā”ti

“Here ten royal she-elephants are white, beautiful, and delightful; six are reddish-brown, fifteen, and those fourteen are yellow.”

Pāḷi. Ettha cha piṅgalā pannarasāti cha ca pannarasa cāti ekavīsati piṅgalā rājiyoti attho gahetabbo.

Here, 'cha piṅgalā pannarasa' (six reddish-brown, fifteen) means that six and fifteen make twenty-one reddish-brown royal she-elephants; this is the meaning to be understood.

Tathā –

Likewise—

“Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ‘ekanāmā’ti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā”ti

“He had many sons, I have heard, all of a single name; eighty, ten, and one, mighty ones named Indra.”

Pāḷi[M 0.0409]. Ettha pana “ekanavutī”ti vattabbe “asīti dasa eko cā”ti vuttaṃ. Vicitrasaddaracanañhi pāvacanaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo aññesupi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

Here, instead of saying 'ekanavutī' (ninety-one), it is said 'asīti dasa eko ca' (eighty, ten, and one). For the Teaching is indeed varied in its word arrangements. This method should be applied in other such instances.

“Tiṃsapurisanāvutyo, sabbevekekaniccitā;

Yesaṃ samaṃ na passāmi, kevalaṃ mahi’maṃ cara”nti

“Thirty-and-ninety companies of men, all resolute; among whom I see no equal, solely walking this earth.”

Pāḷi. Ettha “purisānaṃ tiṃsasahassāni navuti ca satāni tiṃsa nāvutyo”ti vuccanti. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne tiṃsasaddato sahassasaddassa navutisaddato ca satasaddassa lopaṃ katvā “tiṃsa nāvutyo”ti vuttanti na gahetabbaṃ. Evañhi gahaṇe sati yattha katthacipi edisī saddaracanā kātabbā siyā, katāya ca edisāya saddaracanāya atthāvagamo vinā upadesena suṇantānaṃ na siyā, tasmā nevaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Evaṃ pana gahetabbaṃ – “tiṃsa nāvutyo”ti idaṃ lokasaṅketarūḷhaṃ vacanaṃ, saṅketarūḷhassa pana vacanassattho yasmā gahitapubbasaṅketehi sutvā ñāyate, na upadesato, tasmā brahmadattena raññā vuttakālepi satthārā taṃ kathaṃ āharitvā vuttakālepi sabbe manussā vināpi upadesena vacanatthaṃ jānantīti gahetabbaṃ.

Here, 'thirty thousand and ninety hundred men' are referred to as 'tiṃsa nāvutyo'. However, in this context, it should not be understood that 'tiṃsa nāvutyo' is stated by omitting the word 'thousand' from 'thirty' and the word 'hundred' from 'ninety'. For if it were understood so, such a word arrangement could be made anywhere, and if made, its meaning would not be clear to listeners without instruction; therefore, it should not be understood in this way. Rather, it should be understood thus: 'tiṃsa nāvutyo' is an expression established by worldly convention. Since the meaning of a conventional expression is known by hearing from those who have previously grasped the convention, not from instruction, it should be understood that when King Brahmadatta spoke it, and also when the Teacher related that account, everyone knew the meaning of the expression without instruction.

Tiṃsañceva sahassāni, navuti ca satāni tu;

Tiṃsa nāvutiyo nāma, vuttā umaṅgajātake.

Thirty thousand indeed, and ninety hundreds too, are called by the name 'Tiṃsa nāvutiyo', as stated in the Umaṅga Jātaka.

Yasmā pāvacane santi, nayā ceva acintiyā;

Vohārā ca suguḷhatthā, dayāpannena desitā.

Since in the Teaching there are methods, indeed inconceivable, and expressions with profound meanings, taught by the compassionate one.

Tasmā sāṭṭhakathe dhīro, gambhīre jinabhāsite;

Upadesaṃ sadā gaṇhe, garuṃ sammā upaṭṭhahaṃ.

Therefore, a wise person, in the profound teaching of the Conqueror together with its commentary, should always receive instruction, having rightly attended upon a teacher.

Garūpadesahīno hi, atthasāraṃ na vindati;

Atthasāravihīno so, saddhammā parihāyati.

For one who lacks a teacher's guidance does not find the essence of the meaning; devoid of the essence of the meaning, that person falls away from the true Dhamma.

Garūpadesalābhī [M 0.0410] ca, atthasārasamāyuto;

Saddhammaṃ paripālento, saddhammasmā na hāyati.

But one who gains a teacher's instruction and is endowed with the essence of the meaning, by protecting the true Dhamma, does not fall away from the true Dhamma.

Saddhammatthāya me tasmā, saṅkhyāmālāpi bhāsitā;

Sappayogā yathāyogaṃ, sahevatthavinicchayā.

Therefore, for the sake of the true Dhamma, this garland of numbers has been spoken by me, with its applications as appropriate, together with the determination of its meaning.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise, skilled in the modes of expression in the nine-limbed Teaching with its commentary and the three baskets,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the purpose of skill,

Savinicchayo saṅkhyānāmānaṃ nāmikapadamālāvibhāgo

the Classification of the Garland of Nominal Terms with the Analysis of Numerical Names,

Nāma

named

Terasamo paricchedo.

the Thirteenth Chapter.

14. Atthattikavibhāga

14. The Division of the Triad of Meanings

Bhūdhātu tāya nipphanna-rūpañcāti idaṃ dvayaṃ;

Katvā padhānamamhehi, sabbametaṃ papañcitaṃ.

The root `bhū` and the form derived from it—this pair—having been made the main topic by us, all this has been elaborated.

Bhavatissa vasā dāni, vakkhāmatthattikaṃ varaṃ;

Atthuddhāro tumantañca, tvādiyantaṃ tikaṃ idha.

Now, by the power of Bhavatissa, we shall speak of the excellent triad of meanings: the extraction of meaning, the tum-ending forms, and the tvā-etc.-ending forms—this triad here.

Tasmā tāva bhūdhātuto pavattassa bhūtasaddassa atthuddhāro nīyate –

Therefore, first, the explanation of the meaning of the word 'bhūta,' which is derived from the root `bhū`, is presented—

Khandhasattāmanussesu, vijjamāne ca dhātuyaṃ;

Khīṇāsave rukkhādimhi, bhūtasaddo pavattati.

The word 'bhūta' is used in the sense of aggregates, beings, non-humans, what exists, elements, the taintless ones, and trees and so on.

Uppāde cāpi viññeyyo, bhūtasaddo vibhāvinā;

Vipule sopasaggoyaṃ, hīḷane vidhamepi ca;

Parājaye vediyane, nāme pākaṭatāya ca.

The word 'bhūta' should also be understood by the discerning in the sense of arising. This word, when prefixed, is used in the sense of abundance, contempt, dispelling, defeat, experiencing, designation, and manifestation.

Vuttañhetaṃ – bhūtasaddo pañcakkhandhāmanussadhātuvijjamānakhīṇāsavasattarukkhādīsu dissati. “Bhūtamidanti bhikkhave samanupassathā”tiādīsu hi ayaṃ pañcakkhandhesu dissati. “Yānīdha [M 0.0411] bhūtāni samāgatānī”ti ettha amanusse. “Cattāro kho bhikkhu mahābhūtā hetū”ti ettha dhātūsu. “Bhūtasmiṃ pācittiya”ntiādīsu vijjamāne. “Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto”ti ettha khīṇāsave. “Sabbeva nikkhipissanti, bhūtā loke samussaya”nti ettha satte. “Bhūtagāmapātabyatāyā”ti ettha rukkhādīsūti. Mūlapariyāyasuttaṭṭhakathāya vacanaṃ idaṃ. Ṭīkāyamādisaddena uppādādīni gayhare. Vuttañhetaṃ – “jātaṃ bhūtaṃ saṅkhata”ntiādīsu bhūtasaddo uppāde dissati. Saupasaggo pana “pabhūtamariyo pakaroti puñña”ntiādīsu vipule. “Yebhuyyena bhikkhūnaṃ paribhūtarūpo”tiādīsu hīḷane. “Sambhūto sāṇavāsī”tiādīsu paññattiyaṃ. “Abhibhūto māro vijito saṅgāmo”tiādīsu vidhamane. “Parābhūtarūpokho ayaṃ acelo pāthikaputto”tiādīsu parājaye. “Anubhūtaṃ sukhadukkha”ntiādīsu vediyane. “Vibhūtaṃ paññāyā”tiādīsu pākaṭīkaraṇe dissati, te sabbe “rukkhādīsū”tiādisaddena saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbāti.

It is said: the term 'bhūta' is seen in the sense of the five aggregates, non-human beings, elements, existing things, taintless ones, beings, trees, and so on. For instance, in passages like, 'Monks, do you perceive this as what has come to be?' it refers to the five aggregates. In 'Whatever beings have gathered here,' it refers to non-human beings. In 'Monks, the four great elements are a cause,' it refers to the elements. In 'There is a pācittiya offense regarding what exists,' it refers to existing things. In 'One who has become a devourer of time,' it refers to a taintless one. In 'All beings in the world will indeed lay down their bodies,' it refers to beings. In 'Regarding the destruction of plant-life,' it refers to trees and so on. This is a statement from the commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta. In the sub-commentary, by the word 'ādi' (etc.), arising and so on are included. It is said: in passages like 'born, become, conditioned,' the term 'bhūta' refers to arising. When prefixed, as in 'The noble one makes abundant merit,' it conveys abundance. In 'for the most part being an object of contempt for the monks,' it conveys contempt. In 'Sambhūta of Sāṇavāsī,' it conveys designation. In 'Māra is overcome, the battle won,' it conveys dispelling. In 'This naked ascetic Pāthikaputta is indeed defeated,' it conveys defeat. In 'pleasure and pain have been experienced,' it conveys experiencing. In 'made manifest by wisdom,' it conveys making manifest. All these should be understood as included by the word 'ādi' in 'trees and so on.'

Idāni tumantapadāni vuccante –

Now, the tum-ending forms are explained—

Bhavituṃ, ubbhavituṃ, samubbhavituṃ, pabhavituṃ, parābhavituṃ, atibhavituṃ, sambhavituṃ, vibhavituṃ, bhotuṃ, sambhotuṃ, vibhotuṃ, pātubhavituṃ, pātubbhavituṃ vā, pātubhotuṃ. Imāni akammakāni tumantapadāni.

Bhavituṃ (to be), ubbhavituṃ (to arise), samubbhavituṃ (to originate), pabhavituṃ (to come forth), parābhavituṃ (to be defeated), atibhavituṃ (to overcome), sambhavituṃ (to be born), vibhavituṃ (to disappear), bhotuṃ (to be), sambhotuṃ (to be generated), vibhotuṃ (to disappear), pātubhavituṃ, or pātubbhavituṃ, pātubhotuṃ (to appear). These are intransitive tum-ending forms.

Paribhotuṃ [M 0.0412] paribhavituṃ, abhibhotuṃ abhibhavituṃ, adhibhotuṃ adhibhavituṃ, atibhotuṃ atibhavituṃ, anubhotuṃ anubhavituṃ, samanubhotuṃ samanubhavituṃ, abhisambhotuṃ abhisambhavituṃ. Imāni sakammakāni tumantapadāni, sabbānetāni suddhakattari bhavanti.

Paribhotuṃ, paribhavituṃ (to despise, to use); abhibhotuṃ, abhibhavituṃ (to overcome, to dominate); adhibhotuṃ, adhibhavituṃ (to possess, to rule over); atibhotuṃ, atibhavituṃ (to transcend, to surpass); anubhotuṃ, anubhavituṃ (to experience, to feel); samanubhotuṃ, samanubhavituṃ (to experience fully); abhisambhotuṃ, abhisambhavituṃ (to realize fully). These are transitive, active voice tum-ending forms; all of them are in the active voice.

“Bhāvetuṃ, pabhāvetuṃ, sambhāvetuṃ, vibhāvetuṃ, paribhāvetuṃ”iccevamādīni hetukattari tumantapadāni, sabbānipi hetukattari tumantapadāni sakammakāniyeva bhavanti. Uddesoyaṃ.

“Bhāvetuṃ (to cultivate), pabhāvetuṃ (to increase), sambhāvetuṃ (to esteem), vibhāvetuṃ (to make clear), paribhāvetuṃ (to perfect)”—these and similar forms are causative active tum-ending forms, and all causative active tum-ending forms are indeed transitive. This is the summary.

Tatra samānatthapadesu ekamevādipadaṃ gahetvā niddeso kātabbo – bhavitunti hotuṃ vijjituṃ paññāyituṃ sarūpaṃ labhituṃ. Ettha vuttanayānusārena sesānampi tumantānaṃ niddeso vitthāretabbo, sabbāni tumantapadāni catutthiyatthe vattanti “tvaṃ mama cittamaññāya, nettaṃ yācitumāgato”ti ettha viya. Yācitunti hi yācanatthāyāti attho. Tasmā bhavituntiādīnampi “bhavanatthāyā”ti vā “bhavanattha”nti vā “bhavanāyā”ti vā ādinā attho gahetabbo. Apica “nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato”ti ettha “daṭṭhu”nti padassa “disvā”ti atthadassanato yathārahaṃ tumantāni tvāsaddantapadatthavasenapi gahetabbāni. Etāni ca nipātapadesu saṅgahaṃgacchanti. Vuttañhi niruttipiṭake nipātapadaparicchede “tuṃ iti catutthiyā”ti. Tatrāyamattho “tuṃ iti etadanto nipāto catutthiyā atthe vattatī”ti.

Here, among terms with similar meanings, one should take a single initial term and give the explanation—such as 'bhavituṃ' meaning 'to be,' 'to exist,' 'to appear,' or 'to obtain a form.' Following this method, the explanation of the remaining tum-ending forms should be expanded. All tum-ending forms function in the sense of the fourth case (dative), as in the example: 'You, having understood my mind, came to ask for my eyes.' Here, 'yācituṃ' means 'for the purpose of asking.' Therefore, 'bhavituṃ,' etc., should also be understood as 'for the purpose of becoming,' or 'for becoming,' or 'for the sake of becoming,' etc. Moreover, as in 'seeing renunciation as safe,' where the meaning of the word 'daṭṭhu' is seen as 'having seen,' tum-ending forms should also be understood as appropriate, sometimes with the meaning of tvā-ending forms. These also come under the category of particles. As stated in the Nirutti Piṭaka, in the section on particles: ''tuṃ' [is used] in the sense of the fourth case.' The meaning here is: 'The particle ending in 'tuṃ' functions in the sense of the fourth case.'

Tumantakathā samattā.

The discussion of tum-ending forms is complete.

Idāni [M 0.0413] tvādiyantapadāni vuccante –

Now the tvādi-ending forms are explained:

Bhavitvā, bhavitvāna, bhavituna, bhaviya, bhaviyāna. Ubbhavitvā, ubbhavitvāna, ubbhavituna, ubbhaviya, ubbhaviyāna. Esa nayo “samubbhavitvā, parābhavitvā, sambhavitvā, vibhavitvā, pātubbhavitvā”ti etthāpi. Imāni akammakāni ussukkanatthāni tvādiyantapadāni.

Bhavitvā, bhavitvāna, bhavituna, bhaviya, bhaviyāna. Ubbhavitvā, ubbhavitvāna, ubbhavituna, ubbhaviya, ubbhaviyāna. The same principle applies to 'samubbhavitvā, parābhavitvā, sambhavitvā, vibhavitvā, pātubbhavitvā.' These are indeclinable tvādi-ending forms denoting eagerness or exertion.

Bhutvā, bhutvāna, paribhavitvā, paribhavitvāna, paribhavituna, paribhaviya, paribhaviyāna, paribhuyya. Abhibhavitvā, abhibhavitvāna, abhibhavituna, abhibhaviya, abhibhaviyāna, abhibhuyya. Esa nayo “adhibhavitvā, atibhavitvā, anubhavitvā”ti etthāpi. Idañcettha nidassanaṃ. “Tamavoca rājā anubhaviyāna tampi, eyyāsi khippaṃ ahamapi pūjaṃ kassa”nti. Anubhutvā, anubhutvāna. Adhibhotvā, adhibhotvāna.

Bhutvā, bhutvāna, paribhavitvā, paribhavitvāna, paribhavituna, paribhaviya, paribhaviyāna, paribhuyya. Abhibhavitvā, abhibhavitvāna, abhibhavituna, abhibhaviya, abhibhaviyāna, abhibhuyya. The same principle applies to 'adhibhavitvā, atibhavitvā, anubhavitvā.' Here is an example of this: 'Having experienced that, the king said to him, "You should go quickly, and I too, to whom shall I offer homage?"' Anubhutvā, anubhutvāna. Adhibhotvā, adhibhotvāna.

“Saṭṭhi kappasahassāni, devaloke ramissati;

Aññe deve adhibhotvā, issaraṃ kārayissatī”ti

For sixty thousand eons he will revel in the deva-world; having surpassed the other devas, he will wield sovereignty.

Idamettha pāḷinidassanaṃ, imāni sakammakāni ussukkanatthāni tvādiyantapadāni. Imāni cattāri suddhakattariyeva bhavanti.

This is the canonical example here. These are transitive tvādi-ending forms denoting eagerness or exertion. These four are purely in the active voice.

“Bhāvetvā, bhāvetvāna. Pabhāvetvā, pabhāvetvāna. Sambhāvetvā, sambhāvetvāna. Vibhāvetvā, vibhāvetvāna. Paribhāvetvā, paribhāvetvāna”iccevamādīni sakammakāni ussukkanatthāni tvādiyantapadāni hetukattariyeva bhavanti. Uddesoyaṃ.

'Bhāvetvā, bhāvetvāna'; 'Pabhāvetvā, pabhāvetvāna'; 'Sambhāvetvā, sambhāvetvāna'; 'Vibhāvetvā, vibhāvetvāna'; 'Paribhāvetvā, paribhāvetvāna.' These and similar forms are causative active, transitive tvādi-ending forms denoting eagerness. This is the summary.

Tatra samānatthapadesu ekamevādipadaṃ gahetvā niddeso kātabbo – bhavitvāti hutvā paññāyitvā sarūpaṃ labhitvā. Evaṃ vuttanayānusārena sesānampi tvādiyantapadānaṃ niddeso vitthāretabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso [M 0.0414] bhutvāti sampattiṃ anubhutvāti sakammakavasena attho gahetabbo. Bhutvā anubhutvāti imesañhi samānatthataṃ saddhammavidū icchanti. Atridaṃ vuccati –

Among terms with similar meanings, one should take a single initial term and give the explanation—such as 'bhavitvā' meaning 'having been,' 'having appeared,' or 'having obtained a form.' Following this method, the explanation of the remaining tvādi-ending forms should be expanded. Here, however, there is a distinction: 'bhutvā' should be understood in a transitive sense as 'having experienced prosperity.' For 'bhutvā' and 'anubhutvā,' those well-versed in the good Dhamma consider them to have the same meaning. On this point, it is said:

“Bhutvā bhutvāna”iccete, “anubhutvā”timassa hi;

Atthaṃ sūcenti “hutvā”ti, padassa pana neva te.

'Bhutvā' and 'bhutvāna'—these terms indeed convey the meaning of 'anubhutvā,' but they are not the meaning of the word 'hutvā.'

Keci “bhūtvā”ti dīghattaṃ, tassa icchanti sāsane;

Dīghatā rassatā ceva, dvayampetaṃ padissati.

Some desire the long form 'bhūtvā' for it in the Teaching; both long and short forms are seen.

Saddasatthe ca “bhūtvā”ti, dīghattasañhitaṃ padaṃ;

“Bhavitvā”ti padassatthaṃ, dīpeti na tu sāsane.

And in grammar, the word 'bhūtvā' with the lengthened vowel conveys the meaning of the word 'bhavitvā,' but not so in the Teaching.

“Hutvā”iti padaṃyeva, dīpeti jinasāsane;

“Bhavitvā”ti padassatthaṃ, natthi aññattha taṃ padaṃ.

The word 'hutvā' itself indicates the meaning of the word 'bhavitvā' in the Jina's Teaching; that word is not found elsewhere.

Iccevaṃ savisesantu, vacanaṃ sāradassinā;

Sāsane saddasatthe ca, viññunā pekkhitabbakaṃ.

Thus, this statement with its distinctions, made by the seer of the essential, should be considered by the wise in the Teaching and in grammatical treatises.

Evaṃ ussukkanatthe pavattāni tvādiyantapadānipi niddiṭṭhāni, sabbānetāni avibhattikānīti gahetabbāni. Niruttipiṭake hi nipātaparicchede avibhattikāni katvā tvādiyantapadāni vuttāni. Saddatthavidūnaṃ pana mate paṭhamādivibhattivasena savibhattikāni bhavanti.

Thus, the tvādi-ending forms occurring in the sense of eagerness have also been explained; all of these should be understood as indeclinable. For in the Nirutti Piṭaka, in the section on particles, tvādi-ending forms are stated as indeclinable. However, in the opinion of grammarians, they are declinable by way of the first and other cases.

Imasmiñca pana tvādiyantādhikāre idañcupalakkhitabbaṃ – bhutvā gacchati, bhutvā gato, bhutvā gamissasi, kasitvā vapati. Umaṅgā nikkhamitvāna, vedeho nāvamāruhi. Bhutvāna bhikkhu bhikkhassu iccādī samānakattukānaṃ dhātūnaṃ pubbakāle tvādisaddappayogā. “Bhutvā gacchatī”ti ettha hi “bhutvā”ti idaṃ pubbakālakriyādīpakaṃ padaṃ. “Gacchatī”ti idaṃ pana uttarakālakriyādīpakaṃ, samānakattukāni cetāni padāni ekakattukānaṃ kriyānaṃ vācakattā. Tathā hettha yo gamanakriyāya [M 0.0415] kattā, so eva bhuñjanakriyāya kattubhūto daṭṭhabbo. Ayaṃ nayo aññatrāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

And in this section on tvādi-ending forms, the following should also be noted: 'bhutvā gacchati' (having eaten, he goes), 'bhutvā gato' (having eaten, he went), 'bhutvā gamissasi' (having eaten, you will go), 'kasitvā vapati' (having plowed, he sows). 'Umaṅgā nikkhamitvāna, vedeho nāvamāruhi' (Having exited the tunnel, the king of Videha boarded the ship). 'Bhutvāna bhikkhu bhikkhassu' (Having eaten, monk, you should beg) and so on, show the use of tvādi-forms to indicate the prior action of verbs with the same subject. For example, in 'bhutvā gacchati,' 'bhutvā' is a word that indicates the prior action, while 'gacchati' is a word indicating the subsequent action; these words have the same subject, being indicative of actions with one agent. Just so, here, the agent of the action of going should be regarded as the very agent of the action of eating. This principle should be applied similarly in other such instances.

“Andhakāraṃ nihantvāna, uditoyaṃ divākaro;

Vaṇṇaṃ paññāvabhāsehi, obhāsetvā samuggato”

Having dispelled the darkness, this sun has risen; having risen up, it illuminates its beauty with visible radiances.

Iccādīnipi pana samānakattukānaṃ samānakāle tvādisaddappayogā. Ettha hi “nihantvānā”ti padaṃ samānakālakriyādīpakaṃ padaṃ. “Udito”ti idaṃ pana uttarakālakriyādīpakaṃ padanti na vattabbaṃ samānakālakriyāya idhādhippetattā. Tasmāyeva samānakālakriyādīpakaṃ padanti gahetabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo aññatrāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

And these and similar instances are usages of 'tvā' and so forth when the agents are the same and the time is the same. Here, the word 'nihantvāna' is a word indicating a simultaneous action. It should not be said that 'udito' is a word indicating a subsequent action, because here a simultaneous action is intended. Therefore, it should be understood as a word indicating a simultaneous action. This method should be applied elsewhere in similar instances.

Keci pana “mukhaṃ byādāya sayati, akkhiṃ parivattetvā passatī”ti udāharanti. Apare “nisajja adhīte, ṭhatvā kathetī”ti. Tattha byādānaparivattanuttarakālo byādānūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ passanakriyāya lakkhiyati. “Nisajja adhīte, ṭhatvā kathetī”ti ca samānakālatāyapi ajjhenakathanehi pubbepi nisajjaṭṭhānāni hontīti sakkā pubbuttarakālatā sambhāvetuṃ, tasmā purimāniyeva udāharaṇāni yuttāni. Udayasamakālameva hi tannivattanīyanivattananti.

Some, however, give examples like, 'He lies down with his mouth open' (mukhaṃ byādāya sayati), and 'He looks, turning his eyes' (akkhiṃ parivattetvā passati). Others say, 'He studies sitting' (nisajja adhīte), and 'He speaks standing' (ṭhatvā katheti). There, the time subsequent to opening and turning is marked by the act of seeing, which is characterized by the cessation of opening. And in 'He studies sitting, he speaks standing,' even though the actions can be simultaneous, since sitting and standing can precede the acts of studying and speaking, it is possible to consider a prior or subsequent time. Therefore, the former examples are appropriate. For the ceasing of that which is to be ceased is indeed simultaneous with the arising of its cause.

“Dvāramāvaritvā pavisati”iccādi samānakattukānaṃ aparakāle tvādisaddappayogo. Yasmā panettha pavisanakriyā purimā, āvaraṇakriyā pana pacchimā, tasmā “āvaritvā”ti idaṃ aparakālakriyādīpakaṃ padanti veditabbaṃ. “Pavisatī”ti idaṃ pana pubbakālakriyādīpakaṃ padanti. Ayaṃ nayo [M 0.0416] aññatrāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo. Apare “dha’nti kacca patito daṇḍo”ti udāharaṇanti. Abhighātabhūtasamāyoge pana abhighātajasaddassa samānakālatā ettha labbhatīti idhāpi purimāniyeva udāharaṇāni yuttānīti.

The use of words ending in 'tvā' and so forth for actions with the same agent in a subsequent time is seen in examples like 'Dvāramāvaritvā pavisati' ('Having closed the door, he enters'). Here, the act of entering is prior, while the act of closing is subsequent. Therefore, 'āvaritvā' should be understood as a word indicating a subsequent action, and 'pavisati' as a word indicating a prior action. This method should be applied elsewhere in similar cases. Others give the example 'dha’nti kacca patito daṇḍo' (the stick fell with a 'thud'). However, since the simultaneity of the impact and the sound arising from the impact can be understood here, the former examples are indeed more appropriate.

“Pisācaṃ disvā cassa bhayaṃ hoti. Paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā”iccādi asamāne kattari payogo. Ettha hi pisācaṃ disvā purisassa bhayaṃ hoti, paññāya disvā assa puggalassa āsavā parikkhīṇā. Evaṃ samānakattukatā dhātūnaṃ na labbhati dassanakriyāya purisesu pavattanato, bhavanādikriyāya ca bhayādīsu pavattanatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ nayo aññatrāpi īdisesu ṭhānesu netabbo.

Examples of usage where the agents are not the same include: 'Pisācaṃ disvā cassa bhayaṃ hoti' (having seen a demon, fear arises in him) and 'paññāya cassa disvā āsavā parikkhīṇā' (having seen with wisdom, his defilements are destroyed). Here, having seen a demon, fear arises in a person; having seen with wisdom, the defilements of that individual are destroyed. Thus, the verbal roots do not have the same agent, because the act of seeing operates on persons, while the actions of arising and so forth operate on fear and so forth. This principle should be applied elsewhere in similar instances.

Idampi panettha upalakkhitabbaṃ “appatvā nadiṃ pabbato, atikkamma pabbataṃ nadī”iccādi parāparayogo. “Sīhaṃ disvā bhayaṃ hoti, ghataṃ pivitvā balaṃ jāyate, ‘dha’nti katvā daṇḍo patito”iccādi lakkhaṇahetuādippayogo. “Nhatvā gamanaṃ, bhutvā sayanaṃ. Upādāya rūpa”miccāpi byattayena saddasiddhippayogoti.

Here, this should also be noted: the usage of prior and posterior actions, as in 'appatvā nadiṃ pabbato' (the mountain without reaching the river) and 'atikkamma pabbataṃ nadī' (the river having crossed the mountain). The usage indicating characteristic, cause, and so forth, as in 'Sīhaṃ disvā bhayaṃ hoti' (having seen a lion, fear arises), 'ghataṃ pivitvā balaṃ jāyate' (having drunk ghee, strength arises), and '‘dha’nti katvā daṇḍo patito' (the stick fell, having made a 'thud'). Also, the usage of word formation by means of clarity, as in 'Nhatvā gamanaṃ' (going after bathing), 'bhutvā sayanaṃ' (sleeping after eating), and 'upādāya rūpaṃ' (form dependent on clinging).

Iccevaṃ sabbathāpi samānakattukānaṃ dhātūnaṃ pubbakāle tvādisaddappayogo, samānakattukānaṃ samānakāle tvādisaddappayogo, samānakattukānaṃ aparakāle tvādisaddappayogo, asamānakattukānaṃ tvādisaddappayogo, parāparayogo[M 0.0417], lakkhaṇahetuādippayogo, byattayena saddasiddhippayogoti sattadhā tvādiyantānaṃ padānaṃ payogo veditabbo.

Thus, in all respects, the use of words ending in 'tvā' and so forth should be understood in seven ways: when verbal roots have the same agent, in the prior time; when verbal roots have the same agent, in the same time; when verbal roots have the same agent, in the subsequent time; when verbal roots have different agents; in the usage of prior and subsequent actions; in the usage indicating characteristic, cause, and so forth; and in the usage of word formation by means of clarity.

Yadi evaṃ kasmā kaccāyane “pubbakālekakattukānaṃ tuna tvāna tvā vā”ti pubbakāleyeva ekakattukaggahaṇaṃ katanti? Yetuyyena tvādiyantānaṃ padānaṃ purimakālakriyādīpanato. Kaccāyane hi yebhuyyena pavattiṃ sandhāya “pubbakālekakattukāna”nti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana “iti katvā”tiādīnaṃ padānaṃ hetuatthavasenapi pubbācariyehi attho saṃvaṇṇito, tasmā “bhavitvā”tiādīnaṃ bhūdhātumayānaṃ tvādisaddantānaṃ padānaṃ aññesañca “pacitvā”tiādīnaṃ yathāpayogaṃ “bhavanahetu pacanahetū”tiādinā hetuatthopi gahetabbo. Atridaṃ vuccati –

If so, why did Kaccāyana say, 'For those with a single agent in a prior time, [the suffixes are] tuna, tvāna, tvā,' thus including the single agent only in the prior time? Because words ending in 'tvā' and so forth generally indicate a prior action. Indeed, Kaccāyana spoke of 'those with a single agent in a prior time' mostly with reference to common usage. However, since the meaning of words like 'iti katvā' and so forth has also been explained by earlier teachers as expressing a cause, therefore the causal meaning should also be accepted, according to usage, for words ending in 'tvā' and so forth derived from the root 'bhū,' such as 'bhavitvā,' and for others like 'pacitvā,' as in 'for the purpose of being, for the purpose of cooking,' and so forth. Here is what is said:

Hetutthepi yato honti, saddā ussukkanatthakā;

Tasmā hetuvasenāpi, vadeyyatthaṃ vicakkhaṇo.

Since words also exist in a causal sense, and have a meaning of purpose, therefore a wise person should explain the meaning even by way of cause.

“Iti katvā”ti saddassa, atthasaṃvaṇṇanāsu hi;

“Iti karaṇahetū”ti, attho dhīrehi gayhati.

Indeed, in explanations of the meaning of the word 'iti katvā,' the wise grasp the meaning 'as a cause for doing thus'.

“Gacchāmi dāni nibbānaṃ, yattha gantvā na socati”;

Iti pāṭhepi hetuttho, gayhate pubbaviññubhi.

Even in the reading, 'Now I go to Nibbāna, where, having gone, one does not grieve,' the causal meaning is grasped by the wise of old.

“Yasmiṃ nibbāne gamana-hetū”ti hi kathīyate;

Hetutthevaṃ yathāyoga-maññatrāpi ayaṃ nayo.

Indeed, it is said, 'in which Nibbāna, as a cause for going.' Thus, this method applies elsewhere too, according to suitability, in the causal meaning.

Evaṃ bhūtasaddassa atthuddhāro ca tumantapadañca tvādiyantapadañcāti atthattikaṃ vibhattaṃ.

Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the word 'bhūta,' the words ending in 'tum', and those ending in 'tvā' and so forth—this triad of meanings has been distinguished.

Yo [M 0.0418] imamatthatikaṃ suvibhattaṃ,

Kaṇṇarasāyanamāgamikānaṃ;

Dhārayate sa bhave gatakaṅkhā,

Pāvacanamhi gate sukhumatthe.

Whoever holds this triad of meanings, well-distinguished, which is a delight to the ear for those versed in the scriptures, will be one whose doubts are gone regarding the Teaching, which has attained a subtle meaning.

Iti navaṅge sāṭṭhakathe piṭakattaye byappathagatīsu viññūnaṃ

Thus, for the wise who are skilled in the ways of exposition of the ninefold division, with its commentary, in the three Piṭakas,

Kosallatthāya kate saddanītippakaraṇe

in the Saddanīti treatise, composed for the purpose of skill,

Atthattikavibhāgo nāma

The Division of the Triad of Meanings

Cuddasamo paricchedo.

The Fourteenth Chapter.

Evaṃ nānappakārato bhūdhāturūpāni dassitāni.

Thus, the forms of the root 'bhū' have been shown in various ways.

Padamālā niṭṭhitā.

The Word-List is completed.
